rather than shrinking the bar.

Because the bar and the panel are one column, they collapse together. The same
method hides the bar whenever the rail is collapsed (`Ctrl+B`, or the button
floating on the rail's edge), and the page tab strip then runs to the window's
left edge. It is driven off the panels' own show/hide events, so it follows
both routes into `tab_controller.apply_sidebar_visibility` without either of
them having to know the bar exists. Left behind, the bar was a rail-width band
of chrome hanging above an empty column, squeezed to a natural width its three
labels do not fit inside. Re-expanding the rail brings it back — which is also
the only way back to Analyze and Datasets while collapsed, since the bar is the
app's sole mode switch.

The band's right end carries the dataset action cluster — reload, presentation
mode, full reset of saved state, reveal the dataset folder, and reset the view —
and, outboard of it, the help-drawer button. They are built in `AllWellApp`
alongside their handlers and then moved into the band by
`_mount_review_actions`, which appends them after the page-tabs host; that host
holds the band's only stretch, so both are pushed hard right whatever the tab
strip is showing, and the band's pinned height rises to whatever the taller of
the two needs rather than clipping them. Every one of the five acts on the
loaded dataset or on the plots drawn from it, so `_sync_review_actions` shows
the cluster in Review alone and hides it in Analyze and Datasets, where each
would be a control with nothing behind it. Both mode-change handlers call it, so
the cluster follows the seg and the pane stack alike.

The help button is deliberately not one of them, which is why it is mounted
after the cluster rather than inside it: the manual it opens documents all three
modes, and it keeps the band's rightmost slot in every mode while the cluster in
front of it comes and goes. Anything placed inside the cluster inherits the
Review-only gating, and for this control that would leave Analyze and Datasets
with `Ctrl+/` as their only route to the drawer — a shortcut nothing on screen
advertises once the band's right end is empty.

Opening the drawer aims it at the page the user is on.
`_help_section_for_current_page` branches on the current mode and asks that
mode's pane which of its own pages is showing: Review resolves its leaf tab
through `tab_controller.current_centre_tab`, `DatasetsTab.current_help_page`
returns the rail key of the tool page, and `AnalyzeTab.current_help_section`
answers from focus and scroll position, since the Analyze pane is one tall form
rather than a stack of pages. Its sections are recorded by `_section` in build
order in `_section_widgets`, and the lookup reads two signals in order: the
section containing the focused widget, then — among sections with any part of
themselves on screen — the one whose *header* is nearest the viewport top.

Both halves of that second rule are load-bearing, and the two obvious phrasings
are wrong in mirrored ways. The scrollbar's travel is the form's height minus one
viewport, so at the end of the form every remaining header sits *below* the
viewport top: "the last header above the top" names a section several screens out
of sight. And a section whose body is taller than the viewport still clips the top
of it by a few pixels long after the user has scrolled past everything it says, so
"the first section with any part on screen" names the one they have just left.

Geometry alone cannot name the short sections packed into the form's final
screenful — they are all visible at once, and no scroll position singles one out.
That is what the focus branch is for, and it is the only route to those sections'
help; `tests/test_analyze_help_section.py` asserts focus reaches every entry in
`ANALYZE_SECTION_HELP`, not a subset.

`ui/help_topics.py` holds the maps from a page to the exact manual heading that
documents it — `SECTION_BY_PAGE` for Review leaves, `ANALYZE_SECTION_HELP` for
form sections, `DATASETS_PAGE_HELP` for rail labels, and `MODE_OVERVIEW` for the
fallback each mode uses when its pane cannot say. It is Qt-free so
`tests/test_help_topics.py` can check every entry against the real
`README_WellViewer.md` in the fast lane: every value must be a heading that
exists, every Datasets tool and Analyze section must have a key, and no key may
name a page that no longer exists. `tests/test_guards_bite.py` carries that
guard's bite cases, since `scripts/prove_guard.sh` cannot reach a guard whose
maps live in a module the base ref does not have — the run there dies importing
`help_topics` before it measures anything.

**The manual is also checked as it renders, which is a different question.**
`tests/test_help_topics.py` reads the markdown *source*; the drawer shows what
`QTextDocument.setMarkdown` made of it, and Qt's parser treats a bare
`<word>` as an unclosed HTML tag and discards the rest of the document. So a
heading can exist in the file, satisfy every topic check, and have no anchor in
the thing the user sees. `tests/test_manual_render.py` renders the real manual
and asserts three things about it: every heading survives, every one of the
forty-one help targets has an anchor to scroll to, and the render retains most
of its source. It also forbids the shape itself — an unescaped `<word>` outside
a code span — because the other three can only report that *something*
truncated the render. Write such a placeholder escaped (`\<date\>`) or in
backticks; both render as themselves in the drawer and on GitHub.

The action cluster sits on the band
rather than in the window header a row above because that put a second strip of
chrome across the top of the window carrying controls for a mode the user might
not be in. An earlier pass set `rail_w` to whichever mode's content needed the
most room (Analyze's, at 438) and let the other two panes — neither of which
needs anywhere near that width — inherit it unchanged; the result read as an
oversized sidebar with no content to justify it in Review and Datasets.
`rail_w` is now 329 (438 reduced 25%) with Analyze's own form narrowed to fit
it instead: `analyze/form.py`'s row label column shrank
(`_row()`'s `_ROW_LABEL_W`, 150→108) and word-wraps instead of clipping a
label that doesn't fit on one line, its two widest fixed-width combos
(segmentation method, auto-threshold method) shrank to 165 and rely on Qt's
built-in text eliding plus a tooltip carrying the full label, and the Compute
Options page's inline "(…)" hints moved to their own wrapped line below the
row instead of squeezing in beside a narrow field. `tests/test_analyze_narrow_sidebar_fit.py`
drives every collapsible section open (a real `QTest.mouseClick`, since a
collapsed section contributes nothing to the form's measured width until
expanded) and asserts the form's laid-out minimum width fits inside `rail_w`.

**The page tab bars are in this band too**, to the right of the mode bar and
sharing its bottom edge. They used to sit inside each tab's own body, one row
below, so the top of the window was two stacked strips of chrome; they are the
same kind of control as the mode selector, one level down, and belong beside it.
Each bar is **bottom-aligned** inside its page rather than filling it. A
`QTabBar` sizes its tabs from the font and its padding and lays them from the
top of whatever height it is given, so stretched to the band's height it drew
its selected-tab underline part-way up — eight pixels clear of the band's bottom
edge, while the mode bar's fill ran all the way down to it. Pinning the bar to
its own height and pushing it to the bottom puts the underline on the band's
bottom edge, level with the active mode segment beside it, at any font size or
band height.

`build_page_tabs_host` is the slot — a `QStackedWidget` keyed by top-level page
name, whose page 0 is blank and is what the six pages with no sub-tabs
(Statistics, Spatial, smFISH, Review CSV, Batch Export, Saved Plots) show, and
what **Analyze and Datasets** show: the strip names Review's pages, and left
carrying whatever Review was on it offered Bar Plots / Line Graphs / Heat Map
beside the Analyze form. `show_page_tabs` gates on the current mode for that. The
band keeps its height there rather than collapsing, so switching pages never
shifts the content below it. `register_page_tabs` mounts a bar and
`on_notebook_current_changed` swaps them; because pages build lazily a bar can
register *after* its page is current, so registering also shows it.

Plotting's bar is a standalone `QTabBar` and simply moves; so is Batch Export's
Line / Bar / Scatter (cells) / Scatter (aggregate) selector, which is a page
selector like any other and reaches the band the same way. The other two — Image
Browser's and Home's — are `QTabWidget`s whose own API
(`tabText` / `currentIndex` / `count` / `addTab` / `currentChanged`) is read by
controllers, persistence and eight test modules, so `mirror_tab_widget` hides
each one's own bar and drives it from a `QTabBar` in the band instead.
Converting them to a bar plus a page stack would have broken every one of those
readers to change where a strip of tabs is drawn. Hiding the bar also means the
pane border around the body has no frame left to close, so `mirror_tab_widget`
puts the widget in document mode and `ui/theme.py` clears
`QTabWidget#ImageBrowserSubTabs::pane` / `#HomeSubTabs::pane` —
otherwise that border's top edge starts every nested body a pixel below where an
un-nested page's body starts.

The band is pinned to `tab_bar_height()` and carries no vertical padding of its
own, and holds nothing but the mode bar and the current page's tabs.

**Split View shows both panes' sidebar sections.** `on_tab_change` hides every per-tab sidebar frame and then runs the `on_activate` hook of the tab `current_centre_tab` reports — which, while split, is the *focused* leaf. So the other pane's frame was hidden by the first half and never shown by the second: the unfocused pane's controls stayed invisible until the user clicked that pane, on a panel they were already looking at the tab for. The handler now runs the hook for every visible leaf, the unfocused one(s) first so that anything two hooks both write — the plate's mode, the rep-colour map — settles on the focused pane's terms. Only the hook runs for an unfocused pane: the descriptor-less fallback ends in a full `redraw_app`, which belongs to the tab being switched *to*, and the other pane's redraw is already the scope coalescer's job. The `_heatmap_sidebar_frame` follows the same rule, but `sync_heatmap_well_drag_mode` deliberately does not — drag mode changes what a plate *click* does and the plate is shared, so following an unfocused Heat Map would rewire the clicks of the pane being worked in. **The pickers split the same way, and had to be made to.** Three sidebar sections offer a `WellPlateSelector` — the shared one for `_sidebar_main_frame`, plus Segmentation and Image Table — and they were mutually exclusive only for as long as one section showed at a time. Showing every visible pane's section put two on the rail: stacked and identical-looking while selecting for different pages. So the sections all show and only the focused pane's picker is visible — frames follow visibility, interaction follows focus. Every tab change speaks for every plate, including those whose section is off screen: a plate in the shared slot is not hidden by its section being hidden, so a pass that only addressed the visible sections would leave a hidden section's picker on the rail.

**A focused pane with no section of its own hands the picker to a pane that has one.** The rule above resolves to "the frames the focused hook turned on", which is empty in two different situations: two plot tabs sharing `_sidebar_main_frame`, where the shared frame is the right answer, and a focused pane that contributes no frame at all — which Statistics now does. Falling back to the main frame in the second case picks a frame that is *also* hidden, and the rail ends up with no picker whatsoever: measured with Statistics focused beside Segmentation, the rail carried Segmentation's section, its "Click one well to load its images" caption, and nothing to click. So the fallback is the other visible panes' frames first and the main frame last. On a single sectionless page the main frame is hidden only if its own hook leaves it so; Statistics deliberately shows it outside a split (above), and the fallback is what covers a future tab that does not.

**Every rail picker asks the same question, and that is what makes one slot workable.** The shared plate selects wells to plot, Segmentation's picks the one well to preview, the Image Table's picks the wells to tile. All three answer "which wells am I looking at", so a user who cannot immediately say which page a rail picker belongs to has still not been told a falsehood by it. **Statistics owns no rail section for exactly that reason.** A click on its plate does not select anything — it writes a well into a *named comparison group* — and a slot that shows one plate at a time turns two verbs into a mode with nothing on screen to state it. Put that plate in the slot and Plots split against Statistics shows a rail picker that selects wells to plot while `+ Add` a few pixels below it makes comparison groups those wells can never reach: the group comes out empty, and the only route to the plate that fills one is a click into the Statistics pane — a gesture unrelated to the task, on a panel the user is already looking at. So the comparison-group editor — the plate, the group cards, `+ Add` / `Clear All` and the load-from-Replicates action — is built into the Statistics **page** by `features/stats/tab_view.build_stats_group_editor`, between the control band and the results, with the plate at the `editor` role's caps and a `PLATE_MIN_WIDTH` floor under it — laid out beside the cards it is the first thing a box layout shrinks, and the cards are the half that can afford to give, being text that scrolls. The two sit in a `ResponsiveRow` so that a pane too narrow for both stacks them rather than drawing one over the other, and the whole editor is a `CollapsibleSection`: defining the groups is a phase of the work rather than a constant, and once they exist the strip is a band the user reads past on the way to the results. Its header carries the group count, because a folded section that reports nothing is one you have to unfold to find out whether you need it unfolded. The actions — **+ Add group**, **Clear All**, **↻ Load from Replicates** — sit at the foot of the card list they act on, in a `ButtonRow`: a box layout's minimum width is the sum of its buttons, and three of them made the column too wide to sit beside the map, stacking the row at a pane width where side by side still fitted.

**The armed group is painted, not merely recorded.** `stats_refresh_group_list` sets `state="selected"` on the active group's card, and the rule for `QFrame#StatsGroupCard` in `theme.qss()` is what makes that visible — a left rule in the accent over an elevated fill, rather than a tinted row, because each card already carries its group's rank colour as a dot and a filled background would compete with it for the same meaning. The property was being set with no rule for that object name anywhere, which is a comment rather than a selected state, and the editor's own instruction ("select a group below, then drag wells on the map") depends on it: which row is armed is the difference between a drag landing where the user meant it and landing somewhere else. The results placeholder is refreshed from the same funnel and states only what is still owed — two groups, one more, or just a test — because a panel asking for two groups with both listed above it is the page disagreeing with itself.

**The page below the band scrolls** (`widgets/responsive_row.ResponsiveScroll`). Three things on it have a real minimum height — the map, two rows of group cards, and the results — and on a short pane in Split View their sum exceeds what is there. Something has to give, and the honest answer is that the page is longer than the window rather than that the map is nine pixels of row. Horizontal scrolling is **on demand**. Off was the first choice, reasoning that a page which cannot be dragged sideways is a page whose rows must fit — but the rows flip on the *viewport's* width, which a horizontal bar does not change (it costs height), so nothing about the decision depended on it. What off did cost is the case below the floor: stacked, a row can be no narrower than its widest panel's minimum, and a pane narrower than that has to put the difference somewhere. With the bar off it went behind the page's edge, unreachable and unannounced — measured at an 800×600 window in a split, 54px of the editor simply gone. Degraded output that looks like good output is the one thing §7 will not have, so the shortfall is a scrollbar now: absent at every size where the flip can fit the page, visible when it cannot. There is no matching height floor on the plate — one was written and measured to change no geometry at any of nine window sizes, because the section hugs its content and the page scrolls; `tests/test_stats_group_editor_layout.py` pins both: `test_the_map_keeps_its_floor_rather_than_being_squeezed` is the one that bites when the floor is removed, and `test_a_well_never_shrinks_below_what_it_can_be_dragged_at` states the outcome a reader cares about — a well never smaller than `PLATE_MIN_WIDTH / 12`. The outcome test does not catch the floor's removal on its own, because with groups defined the row stacks and the map then has the whole pane; it is the mechanism test that fails.

**What the rail does while Statistics is on screen.** Statistics contributes no `_sidebar_*` frame at all, so in a split the rail belongs unambiguously to the other pane and painting a group needs no focus change. **Outside a split it shows the shared frame,** because there is then no second claimant: the rail selects wells to plot as it does on every other page, the page's own map paints groups, and no slot is carrying two verbs. `_activate_statistics` gates that on `ctx.runtime.split.active` — doing it in a split is precisely the ambiguity the move exists to remove, and leaving the rail empty in both cases reads as an unfinished screen rather than as a page that owns its own controls. The rule for the slot follows from it: a fourth plate that *selects* belongs there; a fourth verb does not. `tests/test_stats_groups_need_no_focus.py` pins it.

**One picker slot, above the sections.** `review/core/rail_plate.py` owns it. While each section built its plate into its own top, a picker's place on the rail was a function of whose section it was — and the sections are stacked in a fixed order, so choosing a picker was also choosing a set of heights. The unfocused section collapsed by the height of the picker it was no longer showing and carried everything below it up the rail; measured on a 1600×1000 window with two plate-bearing panes side by side, the plot-groups drawer sat at y=789 under one and y=456 under the other. Reserving the missing picker's space instead is the same problem seen from the other side: no movement, and a picker-shaped hole — 303px of empty rail. Neither is fixable while the picker lives inside a section, so all three are mounted through `mount_rail_plate` into one slot that sits above the section frames, and exactly one is visible. The sections below hold only their own controls, their heights no longer depend on which pane has the focus, and nothing on the rail moves when the focus changes. `mount_rail_plate` takes a fallback layout for a build with no shell — a frame assembled directly by a test — which would otherwise show no picker at all. A mounted plate records the section it serves (`section_of`) rather than the slot keeping a roster of which sections have pickers: a roster is a second place to update when a fifth one grows one. `_section_plates` reads that association and still walks the frame as a fallback.

`settle_slot` runs after each pass and is not optional. Hiding a widget only *posts* the layout invalidation that reclaims its space, and the rail is laid out again before that event is delivered — so the slot went on reserving room for the picker it had just hidden. Returning the focus to the pane it started on then produced a *third* layout rather than the first: the slot 336px tall with the picker squeezed to 168 against the 233 it has everywhere else. `tests/test_split_sidebar_shows_both_panes.py` pins the sections; `tests/test_split_sidebar_one_well_picker.py` counts the pickers — the assertion whose absence let the duplicate ship, since a visibility flag is not a picker — and compares the geometry of the whole rail across a focus change and across a round trip, rather than any one widget's.

**Split View borrows the bars.** With two pages side by side there is one band
and two strips to draw, so each pane mounts its own page's bar in a header of
its own and the band shows its blank page — `lend_page_tab_bar` /
`return_page_tab_bar` move the bar out and back, and `show_page_tabs` returns
the blank page while a split is active. See §5.10.

The **collapse toggle** is not in the band. It floats on the left panel's own
right margin, straddling the boundary with the centre pane
(`_build_rail_toggle`, `position_rail_toggle`). It is parented to the **window**
and positioned by hand, which is the whole trick: a toggle inside the rail would
be hidden along with it, so the one control that collapses the rail would be the
one control the collapse takes away. Floating it over the boundary keeps it
reachable in both states — it slides to the window's left edge once the rail is
gone. Straddling rather than sitting inside the rail's content also keeps it
clear of the dataset head and the plate picker.

The same toggle collapses all three modes' panels, so it has to find the one on
screen rather than assume Review's rail: `visible_left_panel` returns the first
visible of the rail and the Analyze / Datasets panes' `_left_sidebar`, and the
edge is **mapped** into window coordinates rather than read off `geometry()` —
the button is an overlay on the window while the panels sit at different depths,
Analyze's and Datasets' inside their own pane's splitter rather than the shell's.

It is **vertically centred on whichever panel is showing**, in all three modes
— a user scanning down the panel's right edge for it finds it at the same
predictable spot regardless of mode or what that panel currently contains,
rather than pinned near the top the way an earlier "level with the rail head"
placement read as stuck. Review's sidebar carries an 8×12 well-picker plate
near the top of its content, and true centring lands on it at common window
heights — turning a click-and-drag well selection into an accidental sidebar
collapse. `position_rail_toggle` detects that specific overlap against
`win._sidebar_plate`'s own bounds and nudges the toggle just below the plate
instead of covering it; Analyze and Datasets have no such widget to dodge, so
there it's a plain panel-height centre. The rail head still carries an `xl`
right inset so its caret has room regardless of exactly where the toggle
lands.

A mode switch re-parks it twice: once immediately, and once through a
`QTimer.singleShot(0, …)`. The first call runs while the pane being shown still
carries the geometry it had before it was laid out into the stack, so it parks
against a width that is about to change; the queued call sees the settled
layout. `position_rail_toggle` also installs the placement filter on whichever
panel is current, so a splitter drag re-parks it too — re-installing an
already-installed filter only moves it to the front, which is why that is safe to
run on every reposition rather than tracked.

Two things follow from it being an overlay. It has no layout to size it, so
`position_rail_toggle` calls `adjustSize()` — left at Qt's default a widget with
no layout keeps 100×30 and paints its chrome around an off-centre glyph. And it
needs its own fill and border in `theme.qss` (`#RailToggle`), unlike every other
`IconButton` in the app, because there is nothing behind it: without them it is
a glyph hanging in mid-air over whichever pane is underneath. `_RailTogglePlacement`
re-parks it on every window resize, and `apply_sidebar_visibility` re-parks it on
every collapse and mode change.

The mode bar is a `ModeBar`, not the `SegmentedControl` the rest of the app uses
for view toggles. Review / Analyze / Datasets are three applications sharing a
window; switching replaces the whole interface, and the control says so at rest
by keeping every segment filled (§7).

Directly beneath it, as the rail's own head, is the **dataset control**:
`app_shell_view._dataset_button`, full rail width, naming the loaded folder and
carrying `Open…` and the datasets opened recently. It replaces both the
`SECTION` caption (the rail's items are self-evidently sections) and the `Open`
button that sat alone at the far end of the topbar — the action and the thing it
acts on are now in one place, and the loaded dataset finally has a durable
on-screen identity rather than living in a hidden label and the OS window title.
The history is under it because this is the control a user reaches for to change
plate: offering only a folder picker there meant the way back to the plate opened
ten minutes ago was to remember where it lived, while Home had known the answer
the whole time. `_fill_dataset_menu` rebuilds the menu on `aboutToShow` rather
than filling it once — every load adds to the history and Home's × takes rows off
it, so a menu built at window construction shows the list as it stood at launch
for the rest of the session, and nothing about that looks broken. It offers
`RECENTS_IN_MENU` rows, fewer than the store holds, because a ten-item list under
a folder button is a file manager with a caret. `refresh_dataset_button` is called from
`load_controller` on every load. Long names elide in the **middle**, because
dataset folders differ in their tail as often as their head
(`plate3_run2_2024-06-11` against `…-12`) and a right-elided name can leave two
datasets indistinguishable; the full path is on the tooltip.

The name shown is not always `dataset.data_dir.name`. The standard
Analyze-pipeline layout loads the sibling `out/` folder as `data_dir` (the
`in/` + `out/` split `load_path` detects), so a naive last-path-component read
would show the literal string "out" for every such dataset — useless for
telling two datasets apart. `refresh_dataset_button` detects that layout
structurally, the same way `load_path` does (`data_dir.name == "out"` and a
sibling `in/` folder exists), and climbs one level to the dataset root's own
name in that case; a folder that happens to be named `out` but has no `in/`
sibling — a genuinely flat, non-split dataset — keeps showing its own name
unchanged. The tooltip still shows the literal `data_dir` path that's actually
loaded (the `.../out` path in the split case), not the climbed display name.

#### Empty states and build failures

`ui_helpers.wrap_with_empty_state` wraps every centre tab whose body needs a
dataset — Home, the plots, Statistics, Spatial, Review CSV, Batch Export and
smFISH — so a tab with nothing to show renders the same placeholder rather than
an empty table, a blank panel, or a bare matplotlib canvas that reads as a
failure. The wrap registers a `QStackedWidget` on `win._plot_empty_stacks`
(page 0 the `EmptyState`, page 1 the body) and the refresh helpers flip all of
them together, which is what keeps the wording and the moment of the swap
identical across tabs.

**A placeholder may carry one action, and the action replaces the hint.**
`EmptyState.setAction(label, on_click)` adds a button *in place of* the hint;
without it there is no button at all, which is what every site but Home wants —
their hint names a control somewhere else, and that sentence is the only
instruction they have. Home is the page the application opens on, so its
placeholder is the first screen and gets an explicit *Open a dataset*. The
hint's job is to say where the way out is; where the way out is the button
itself, a sentence pointing at another corner of the window is a second answer
to the question the button already answers, so the button hides it. The hint's
text is kept, so clearing the action brings the line back.

The suppression lives in the widget rather than at the call site because the
refresher rewrites every placeholder's text, hint and icon on each pass (an
action set once at build time survives it): a site that blanked its own hint at
build time would have it painted back the first time a dataset was closed.

**A placeholder may also carry a column of secondary links, below the action.**
`EmptyState.setEntries(entries)` takes `(label, sublabel, on_click, enabled,
tooltip)` rows and draws each as a borderless `QPushButton`; `clearEntries`
takes them away, and passing an empty sequence does the same. Home is the only
site that sets any — its recent datasets — and the reason they live on the
placeholder rather than on a no-dataset state of Home's own is that the one
moment a recents list matters most is launch with nothing loaded, which is
precisely the moment Home's body is hidden behind this placeholder. Giving Home
its own version would take it out of the shared wording and the shared moment of
the swap, which is the drift `core/empty_state_copy.py` exists to end.

The rows are styled from one definition, `theme.link_row_qss(object_name)`,
because Home's Recent datasets card and this placeholder draw the same list in
the two states of one page. They cannot share an object name (a button on a card
is not part of an empty state, and the name is what a reader greps) and cannot
share a stylesheet host either, since `EmptyState` sets its own so that its
placeholder renders the same wherever it is embedded — so they share the
generator instead. A helper returning QSS for interpolation into another
f-string must emit **single** braces: f-string substitution inserts its value
verbatim and does not process it again, so the doubled braces the helper's own
body appears to call for reach Qt intact, and Qt discards an unparseable sheet
without raising — it writes "Could not parse stylesheet" to stderr and paints
everything unstyled. `tests/test_theme_roles_render.py` holds both halves: no
stylesheet handed to Qt carries `{{`, and the two hosts' rules stay identical.

A row can carry a **×** that takes it off the list, revealed while the pointer is
over the row (`widgets/removable_row`) and styled from one definition,
`theme.row_remove_qss(object_name)`, for the same reason `link_row_qss` exists.
Ten rows each wearing a permanent delete control read as a page about deleting
rather than a page about opening — and the space for it is reserved in both
states, because a control that appears by *widening* the row shifts the label at
the one moment it must not. Hover is counted across the row and every child of
it rather than sampled from `underMouse`: crossing from the row onto the × is a
Leave on one and an Enter on the other, so hiding on any Leave takes the button
away exactly as the user reaches for it.

A row whose folder is not reachable is **drawn, disabled, with the reason on its
tooltip** rather than dropped. Hiding it says the user's history was lost when
what happened is that a drive is unplugged, and the row reappearing by itself
when the drive returns is what makes the list trustworthy. The rows are
`QPushButton`s so they are keyboard-reachable and the disabled state is the
platform's, not a colour this widget chose.
`EmptyState._sync_hint_visibility` carries the one Qt trap involved.

**The wording lives in one module.** `core/empty_state_copy.py` holds
`NO_DATASET_TITLE`, `NO_DATASET_HINT` and the `NO_DATASET_MESSAGE` that joins
them with a newline, and imports nothing. The sentence is said in two media —
this placeholder, and matplotlib text painted onto an empty figure so an
*exported* copy states its own shortfall (`barplot/renderer.py`,
`lineplot/controller.py`) — and the canvas sites cannot reach a Qt widget
module, which is how three spellings of it came to exist and drift apart in
punctuation. `ui_helpers` re-exports the two names for the widget side;
`tests/test_no_dataset_copy.py` fails on a fourth hand-typed copy.

**The placeholder says which "nothing" it is; the axes carry per-plot causes.**
Each wrap site may pass a `reason(ctx) -> EmptyReason | None`, called on every
refresh, where `None` means the tab has something to draw. An `EmptyReason`
carries a title, a hint and optionally a glyph, which are written onto that
stack's own placeholder — one widget, two pages, no third page and no second
placeholder per tab. **`no_dataset` short-circuits ahead of every site reason**:
with no dataset loaded every stack shows the shared "Load a directory." copy,
because asking someone to pick wells on a plate that is not there is a worse
message than the one it would replace.

`selection_controller.has_plottable_selection` is the single predicate behind the
shared `no_selection_reason` — wells picked, or a visible replicate set — and it
is also what the four interactive renderers ask before drawing their own empty
figure: `barplot/renderer`, `lineplot/controller` and `scatter/controller`
twice. They call it rather than spelling `not selected and not active_rsets` out
again, so the placeholder and the figure behind it cannot reach different
verdicts; `tests/test_one_plottable_selection_predicate.py` holds both halves —
that no renderer re-implements the condition, and that each one asks. The
predicate filters selected wells by `well_paths`, because a stale label pushed
through `set_selected_wells` by a saved heat-map layout plots nothing, and
counting it as "plottable" hides the placeholder over an empty figure.
Messages about *other* empty causes — no timepoints, no channel data, no feature
columns, no smFISH/mask pair — stay on the axes, because the placeholder cannot
know about them. `tests/test_no_axes_selection_message.py` enforces the split: no
interactive renderer may paint a message that *asks for a well selection*, and it
reads module constants and the message-drawing helpers as well as direct
`ax.text` calls, because that is how the messages it replaced actually reached
the canvas. Export renderers are exempt per file, since a figure written to disk
carries no placeholder with it and must state its own shortfall (§7).

Two tabs need reasons of their own rather than the shared one. **Heat Map is not
selection-driven**: `redraw_heatmap` fills from `layout.cells` and reads the
selection only to outline cells, so gating it on the selection would hide a
populated saved map the moment the plate was cleared. It gates on an empty
layout — which is the common case rather than a corner, because
`_ensure_sidebar_layout` creates an empty `Sidebar` layout while the sidebar
builds and leaves `active_layout_name` unset, so `active_layout` returns it and
the populated `make_plate_layout` default is never reached. **Spatial gates only
at its three per-frame levels**, where an empty selection otherwise renders the
first key of `well_paths` — one arbitrary well, unannounced. Its Summary level
keeps falling back to every loaded well, which is a defensible default rather
than an arbitrary pick.

Statistics uses the same widget on its own trigger (fewer than two comparison
groups — one group cannot be compared either), so a
user moving between pages reads one treatment rather than two. Batch Export
deliberately does not: the widget wrapped there is the whole panel including
OUTPUT SETTINGS and the Run button, and swapping that for a placeholder would
hide the output configuration exactly while it is being set up.

Two Image Browser sub-tabs are dataset-gated but **not** selection-gated, and for
different reasons. **Image Table** has its own picker plate, so the app-wide
selection does not drive it; its placeholder is generation-gated and lives
outside `_plot_empty_stacks`, so `image_table_refresh_empty_state` swaps its two
strings instead — with a dataset it asks for wells and channels and a Generate,
and without one it says what the rest of Review says, because the picker has no
wells to choose and its own Channels panel already reads "load a dataset to see
channels". **Cell Browser** mirrors the plotting layer's active wells rather than
reading the plate directly and is scoped by its own criteria / timepoint / FOV
filters, so it takes the plain dataset gate; before that it had no empty state at
all, only a blank grid with its explanation in the status bar.

Both build through `image_browser/controller.build_image_browser_subtab`, which is
the Image Browser's **own** lazy funnel and does not pass through
`centre_view._build_pending` — so it repeats the same `refresh_plot_empty_states`
call. That was latent for as long as no sub-tab registered a stack; the moment
Cell Browser got one it reproduced the Spatial / smFISH bug in a new place.

**A reason is only as current as its last refresh, and that is the rule's sharp
edge.** A reason may read any state, but nothing re-evaluates it on its own. The
app-wide triggers cover app-wide state — dataset load, lazy build, selection
change — so a reason reading *feature-local* state must be re-run from that
feature's own funnel, or the placeholder is decided once and then stands over a
page that has something to draw. Heat Map's placeholder says "click Auto-populate
from selection"; doing exactly that filled the layout and left the placeholder up,
because `_persist_and_redraw` is the only thing that knows the layout changed.
Spatial's reason is level-dependent and nothing re-ran it when the level changed.
So `redraw_heatmap`, Spatial's `_sync_empty_state` (called from every
`render_spatial` path), Cell Browser's `apply_filters` and
`stats_refresh_group_list` each end by calling `refresh_empty_state_pages`. When
you add a reason, the question to answer is *what changes the answer, and what
runs then*.

The other way out of that trap is to make the reason read state no build order
can move, and **smFISH is the worked example**. Its reason asks whether the run
had any smFISH channel, and the tab holds an answer to that in
`ctx.runtime.smfish.tokens` — but that list is the tab's own scratch: the builder
sets it to `[]` and `smfish_sync_from_app` fills it in afterwards, with the
lazy-build refresh between the two. Read from there, the reason was computed at
the one moment the list is guaranteed empty, so the first open of the tab told a
dataset full of spot counts that the pipeline had generated none, and any later
refresh cleared it. It reads `ctx.state.dataset.pipeline_info["smfish_tokens"]`
instead — parsed by the loader before any tab is built, so the ordering question
does not arise. `ctx.state.channel.smfish_channels` is the trap next door:
`recalculate_threshold` overwrites it with channels *detected from
`_smfish_count` columns*, so a freshly-processed dataset with smFISH images but
no counts yet would be told it has no smFISH data — which is the tab's primary
use case, since generating those counts is what it is for. The tab's two blank
states are also distinct strings: "the run had no smFISH channel" is a claim
about the analysis, "the sidecar could not be read" is a claim about a file, and
printing the first for both sent users to re-run an analysis that was fine.

**Where the refresh is called from matters as much as the rule.**
`refresh_empty_state_pages` is the cheap half — one reason call and a
`currentIndex()` comparison per stack — and runs from `apply_selection_refresh`,
the sole `selection_changed` subscriber, *before* its per-tab loop: that loop
only touches `_visible_tabs`, and a feature with an `on_selection_changed` hook
never reaches `plot_orchestrator.redraw_app`, so a background page would
otherwise keep whatever state it held when last seen. `refresh_plot_empty_states`
adds the dataset-gated greying of `TabCtrl` / `ControlBand` containers, which is
two recursive `findChildren` walks and answers a question only a dataset load can
change. It is also called from `centre_view._build_pending` after a deferred body
is built: a `lazy_only` tab registers its stack *after* the load-time refresh, so
without that call Spatial and smFISH showed "Load a directory." over a loaded
dataset for the life of the session.

An actual failure says so. A deferred tab builder that raises used to log a
traceback and leave an empty page — indistinguishable from a tab with nothing to
show, with the explanation in a drawer the user has no reason to open.
`centre_view._build_pending` now also puts the tab's name on the status bar,
where every other failure in the app reports itself.

#### The page body: where a page's first row is drawn

Every main page in the app — each Review page, the Analyze pane's output side,
the Datasets pane — has the same body: a `ControlBand` flush against the top of
the page, one row tall, then the page's content directly beneath it.
`widgets/page_body.py`'s `build_page_body(parent, *, content_margins,
horizontal)` lays that out and returns `(band, content host)`. It strips the
page root's own margins and spacing, and there is deliberately no top-margin
parameter: left, right and bottom padding are a page's business (a canvas wants
a gutter, a table does not), but the top is what alignment is made of.

**The band is added whether or not the page has controls to put in it.** Image
Table and the Playground author through a builder shelf and a right-hand dock,
Batch Export selects its mode from the shell band and configures inside its
panels, the Datasets tool pages carry their Run controls down inside each page —
each still reserves the row, so its content starts level with its neighbours'.
That is the same reservation the mode band's page-tabs host makes for pages with
no sub-tab bar (§5.1).

`ControlBand.ROW_H` (28px, `band_height()` == 44 with the band's own padding)
fixes what one row measures. Without it the height came from whichever control
the page happened to hold — Qt sizes a `QPushButton` at 24, a `LabeledComboBox`
at 25, a `QToolButton` at 27 and a `QComboBox` at 28 — so an unwrapped band was
41, 43, 44 or 49px tall and moved the content under it by the same amount. It is
enforced as a real `setMinimumHeight`, not as a floor inside `heightForWidth`: a
parent layout asks the band's `QWidgetItem` for its height, and `QWidgetItem`
delegates to `wid->layout()->heightForWidth()` whenever the widget has a layout,
so an override on the class is never consulted.

A band still *grows*: it wraps to a second row when its controls do not fit the
window's width, and one holding a control taller than a row (the
`SegmentedControl` on Multivariate, Spatial and Scatter) is taller than 44px.
Both move only the content below the band, never its top edge.

`tests/test_page_alignment.py` measures the rule against a real window with
every page and sub-tab built: each page's band starts at the centre stack's top
in all three modes, no page root re-introduces a top inset, no band is shorter
than one row, and a body nested in a `QTabWidget` starts at that widget's own
top. That last one is why `mirror_tab_widget` sets `setDocumentMode(True)` and
`ui/theme.py` clears the pane border for `ImageBrowserSubTabs` and
`HomeSubTabs` — with the bar hidden, `QTabWidget::pane`'s border
closed a frame that is not drawn and started every nested body a pixel low.

#### The band's gating and its ratchet

The band carries the object name `ControlBand`, which is in
`ui_helpers._DATA_GATED_OBJECT_NAMES`, so a tab picks up "grey the controls
until a dataset is loaded" by adopting the band rather than by remembering a
name. `tests/test_control_band_adoption.py` is an AST ratchet over the modules
that have adopted it: one control row per module — a `ControlBand`, a
`build_page_body` or a `plotting_band_slot`, never two of them — no hand-rolled
`FlowLayout` control row beside it, and no plot-card header built only to be
hidden. It also asserts the specific shape of the Plotting page: every one of
its five sub-tabs claims a slot and none constructs a band; and that every
module building a top-level page's tab strip (Plotting, Image Browser, Home,
Batch Export) hands it to the shell band rather than to its own
body. It is a static scan on purpose — a test that builds a tab needs the
`viewer_app` fixture, which `conftest.py` auto-marks `slow`, and
`scripts/test.sh` runs `-m "not slow"`, so such a test would never run in CI.
The geometry itself is checked in the slow lane by `test_page_alignment.py`
above, which builds the window once.

#### The Home page

`features/home/` is the page Review opens on, and it is a notebook. **Overview**
leads it and is everything described below: the report the app opens on. The
tabs after it — **Cell Gating**, **Sample Map**, **Ratios**, **Pipeline
Info** — are where the user *declares* what the wells mean. The two halves are one page because they are one subject: what this plate
is, and what you have said about it. Splitting them across two rail entries is
what put a Notes box on each and needed a mirroring helper to stop one writing
back over the other.

**Three ways of annotating a well, one tab, one plate.** Replicates, Variables
and Well Labels were three sibling sub-tabs that all took a well selection and
all looked alike,
and the distinction that decides which one a user wants is whether it *pools*: a
group and a variable change which bars exist, while a label changes only what a
bar is called. `features/home/collect.DECLARATION_ROLES` is the single roster of
the four ways to say something about a well — those three plus the rail's saved
selections — carrying, per entry, the question it answers, the effect in two or
three words, the sentence the tab states, and where to go when the answer is one
of the others. Three surfaces read it: `features/home/roles_view.build_role_strip`
builds the last two lines, which the Sample Map tab rebuilds above the plate
whenever the layer changes, Overview's *Your work here* column takes the effect, and the manual's comparison table says the same
four things in the user's vocabulary. Written out at each surface the three
copies drifted immediately, which is why the roster is data rather than three
paragraphs. Cell Gating, Ratios and Pipeline Info resolve to `None` through
`role_for_tab` and take no strip: a gate is a threshold and a ratio is a derived
channel, and neither says what a well *is*.

**Overview's nudge asks about the plate; its counts ask about the tabs.**
`your_work` reports one row per declaration, and each row is the number that
tab itself shows — a *Wells labelled* count that included variables would send
a reader to the Well Labels tab to find an editor holding none of them.
`next_step`, the single contextual action below it, is the opposite question:
what does this plate still need? So its two annotation rungs read across the
tabs. *"No sample labels yet"* fires on `wells_named_on_figures`, the count of
loaded wells that a figure calls something other than their token — a typed
label or, through `selections_model.well_display_label_and_source`, the values
the well holds on Variables — and *"No replicate sets yet"* stands down when a
variable is there to pool by. Both used to name the one tab they counted and
call the plate empty: a user who had just filled a dose grid across ninety-six
wells was told there were no sample labels, over figures whose x axis was that
grid, and then told to go and define replicate sets for conditions the plate
already knew. A nudge that is false is worse than no nudge, because the reader
who follows it undoes work they have already done.

**`features/home/sample_map/`** is that tab. `controller.py` holds `LAYERS`
(derived from the roster, so a declaration with no editor is impossible), the
layer switch, and the rule below; `tab_view.py` builds a `SegmentedControl`, a
host the current layer's role strip is rebuilt into, and a `QStackedWidget` whose
three pages are built by the **unchanged** builders in `home/groups`,
`home/variables` and `home/labels`. Nothing about what a layer does moved; what
moved is that one of them is on screen at a time.

Three plates rather than one shared selector painting three things. A single
plate would be the "two plates meaning different things" hazard turned inward —
the same widget answering "which wells are in this group" and "which wells hold
this dose", with two painters racing to say it — and a well label cell takes free
text, which a `WellPlateSelector` cannot show at all (`plate_geometry`'s own
documented exception). Taking turns in one slot is what the user sees; the three
painters stay separate, which is what keeps a dose legend from appearing under a
group list.

**The selection travels between two of the three, and the asymmetry is the
point.** On Variables and Well Labels the plate's selection is *the wells I am
about to act on* — assign a value, add a prefix — so a layer switch carries it
across and publishes it to `ctx.state.selection.selected_wells`. On Replicates it is
not that: the plate shows the **current group's membership**, pushed by
`rep_refresh_map`, and `selectionDragFinished` on it rewrites that group. Carrying
a selection in would hand a group wells nobody put in it — §7's cardinal sin
arriving through a layer switch — so `SHARED_SELECTION_LAYERS` excludes it, and
`tests/test_one_plate_on_the_sample_map.py` asserts both directions. A test that
only checked "the selection is shared" would pass against exactly that bug.

`panel_view._commit_plate_to_current` asks two questions where it used to ask
one: the Home sub-tab must be Sample Map **and** the current layer must be
Replicates. Both halves matter — a layer switch inside a tab nobody is looking at
must not commit either.

**And the tab says what the plots are currently pooling by.**
`core/group_by_controller.grouping_summary` is the one sentence, painted into
both labels named by `GROUPING_READOUTS` — one beside *Group by* on the plotting
band, one under Sample Map's layer switch. The combo names the *setting* and this
names the *consequence*, which are different facts: a user who has painted four
groups and then picks `Group by: Dose` has had those four stop pooling anything,
in the Bar tab, in Statistics and in Batch Export at once, and the only thing
that mentioned it was a shortfall clause about the wells the grouping left out.
The choice is made on the band and the groups are made on Home, so the
consequence has to be legible in both.

It is **derived from the seam**: `plot_replicate_sets` for what will be pooled,
`plot_members.variable_grouping_in_force` for whether the substitution really
happened, and `plot_members.groups_the_variable_replaced` for how many of the
user's own groups it displaced. The last two live beside the seam rather than in
the controller for the reason §7.5 #10 gives — a controller naming the replaced
pooling would hold a second definition of "the user's groups" — and they are
listed by name in `test_group_by_variable`'s exemption roster. They are also
deliberately **two** functions: a variable can be pooling while the user has no
groups at all, so an empty displaced list is not the same fact as "no
substitution happened", and the version that conflated them reported the
fallback sentence over a plate that really was grouped by dose.

Painted into a label rather than the status bar, for the reason `_announce`
already records beside it: the status bar is a single persistent slot and a
redraw with nothing to report writes nothing to it, so a sentence put there
outlives the condition that produced it.

Home owns the page — the control band (carrying **Import**, which merges a
sample-definitions JSON and is hidden on Overview because it names nothing
there), the `QTabWidget`, and the tab-change handler. Each tab body is a
sub-package under `features/home/`, the same arrangement
`features/image_browser/` uses for the three of its four sub-tabs that have
one (Segmentation's body is `review_image/`, shared with the Review CSV jump).

**Home does not name its tabs and does not import their bodies.**
`active_subtabs` is `("Overview", *ctx.features.sub_leaves("Home"))` — the
registry's declaration order, already filtered by the active profile — and each
tab is built by calling its own descriptor's `build(ctx, frame)`. There is no
name ladder and no import of a sibling package. Home used to filter a module
constant through `Profile.includes_subtab`, a bare string check against the
`[subtabs]` allowlist that never consults descriptors, so a manifest could drop
tabs nothing had declared; enumerating from the registry is what makes every
name a `[subtabs]` line can reference a real descriptor.

Two of the four builders do not have the `(ctx, frame)` shape and are adapted in
`features/registry.py`: Cell Gating's takes no frame (it finds its own, because
persistence can build the tab with no frame to hand over), and the Ratios editor
is *returned* rather than mounted. Both adapters are function-local imports
inside the descriptor, which is what keeps the removable sub-packages removable.

Two more per-tab facts are descriptor fields rather than name lists in the Home
package: `subtab_inset` decides whether the tab's frame takes a gutter. It was
a constant keyed by tab name, which is issue #14's shape in miniature — a tab
added to the registry and not to the constant inherits whichever answer the
constant happens to give it, silently.

Two siblings of it are **gone**, both about a rail plate Home no longer has.
`reads_well_selection` decided whether that plate was live while a sub-tab
showed; `owns_plate` decided whether the rail's sample frame was *hidden* rather
than greyed, for a tab drawing a plate of its own — Variables did, coloured by
variable value while the rail's was coloured by group membership, which is the
two-plates-saying-different-things hazard
`groups/panel_view._commit_plate_to_current` guards its commit against. The
Sample Map tab answers that hazard from the other side: one plate on screen,
named by the switch above it, and the rail carries none. With nothing in the
frame there is no state for either field to decide, and a descriptor field with
no reader is a control that does nothing, one level down.

Its sibling `reads_well_selection` is **gone**, not moved. It decided whether the
rail plate stayed live while a Home sub-tab showed, and Home keeps no rail plate:
the one it had composed a group and is a layer of Sample Map now. A descriptor
field with no reader is a control that does nothing, one level down.

`Cell Gating` and `Sample Map` carry `removable=False`. Sample Map's three
layers are built together from one roster, so there is no profile in which two of
them ship without the third; a build that wants none of the three drops the
descriptor whole, which is the granularity that is coherent. `Ratios` and
`Pipeline Info` are removable, with `[[feature]]` blocks in `profiles/full.toml`.

**Overview is built eagerly and the definition tabs are drained, one per
event-loop tick.** Neither extreme works. Home holds the eager first-tab slot,
so building four editors inline would put all of them on the startup path; but
building them on first click would change what exists after a load, and
persistence hydration, the plot tabs' ThreshFracOn quick-edit and the
Playground's context bar all read those widgets without opening a tab. Draining
keeps both properties, and is what the definitions already had when they were a
page of their own that `centre_view` drained. `build_home_subtab` is idempotent
against `ctx.runtime.home.built`, so a click that arrives before the drain
reaches a tab builds it once, not twice.

**Home shows no rail plate, on any tab**, which is what `activate_home`'s
docstring has always said and what the rail's sample frame used to contradict.
That frame carried `_rep_map_plate`, mounted by `centre_view.build_centre`
outside the shared `core/rail_plate.py` slot every other rail picker goes
through, and it was live on Replicates, Cell Gating and Well Labels and greyed on
the rest. Two things were wrong with it. It put a second plate on screen the
moment a tab carried its own — Variables did, `role="editor"`, so that tab
showed two with only the nearer one live. And it did not do what it was
documented to do: measured rather than read, that plate **never wrote**
`ctx.state.selection.selected_wells`. It composed a group and nothing else, so
Cell Gating's CDFs and Add Prefix's fallback — both of which read the app-wide
selection — were running off a selection only Overview's plate could set.

So the plate is a layer of Sample Map, in the page body at `role="editor"`, and
`sync_home_sidebar` keeps `_sidebar_sample_frame` hidden. Sample Map publishes
its Variables and Well Labels layers' selection to `selected_wells`, which gives
those two tabs the picker they were described as having.

The rail plate's disabled state is still worth its paint code — other hosts grey
a plate — and the widget had to acquire one:
`WellPlateSelector` consulted `isEnabled()` nowhere in its paint path, so
`setEnabled(False)` rendered **pixel-identically** — grab the widget enabled,
grab it disabled, compare: zero differing pixels. `paintEvent` now ends by laying
a rail-toned scrim over the finished plate, which takes the same comparison to
roughly seven eighths of the widget. The absolute count is deliberately not
quoted: it scales with whatever size the host gives the plate, so it says more
about the measurement than about the widget. A scrim rather than a disabled variant of each fill, because
every state this widget paints — lit, recessed, dial, ring, marker, path — is
carried by *colour*, so draining the colour is what reads as "not active here",
and one veil does that uniformly where ten paired palettes would drift apart.
`setEnabledWells([])` is not an alternative: an empty socket already means "this
well is not in the dataset", and reusing it would make an inactive tab
indistinguishable from a plate whose wells are missing.
`tests/test_disabled_controls_look_disabled.py` carries the roster this class of
defect is caught by, and the plate is on it.

`ctx.runtime.home.subtabs` is what the plate's commit guard and
`selection_controller.groups_centre_refresh` consult to answer "which tab is
showing" — the refresh tests the *tab*, not the page, because Home is what the
app opens on and a page-level test would be true from startup.

The report itself: it answers what a returning user
asks before anything else — what this plate is, whether the run that produced it
finished, what it was run with, what they have already done to it — and it does
so by **reporting a record rather than measuring**. Establishing per-well
coverage costs a zip central-directory read and a full CSV parse per well, which
a landing page cannot pay on every open, and a cached answer that silently ages
is worse than none. The pipeline records the answer at the end of every run
(§6.2, `pipeline_info.json::run_check`), the Datasets **Validate & Repair** tool
records one for a dataset that has none (§6b), and this page reads whichever is
there. `core/record_sync.resync_run_check` re-reads that one key from the sidecar, so a
scan run while the dataset is open shows up rather than needing a full reload;
nothing else is re-read, because the rest of the sidecar holds user-side blocks
whose in-memory copy may carry edits not yet saved. It is called at both moments
the record can change underneath the page: activating Home, and the shell
returning to the Review pane. The second is not redundant, and it is the one the
page's own next step depends on — "Check it now" leaves for the Datasets pane,
and the user comes back to a Review pane where Home is *still* the current page,
so no tab changed and no activation hook fires. `tab_controller`'s pane handler
therefore re-reads the record itself and repaints Home through the
`home.refresh` service, and only when the record actually changed, so an
ordinary mode toggle costs one small JSON read and no repaint at all.
`tests/test_home_collect.py` pins that literally: it makes `open`, `Path.open`,
`Path.iterdir`, `Path.glob` and `zipfile.ZipFile` raise, then calls every
function on the page.

Everything computable lives in `collect.py`, Qt-free and ctx-first, so the whole
page is exercised in the fast lane against a plain namespace; `controller.py`
paints widgets from what it returns and `tab_view.py` holds the arrangement.

**The Run parameters card names the settings that shaped the numbers, and only
those.** A method's name alone is not a receipt: two plates corrected with
`robust_mesh` at different mesh ratios read identically, and an `empty_well`
correction that never says which wells it measured cannot be reproduced. So
`collect._correction_parameter_rows` renders the radius, the FFT small-structure
cutoff, the mesh ratio and sigma, and the reference wells — but each only when
the chosen method actually consults it. Which those are is
`pipeline.background.BACKGROUND_METHOD_PARAMS` and
`pipeline.flatfield.FLATFIELD_MODE_PARAMS`, kept beside the dispatches that
define them so the receipt cannot drift from the code: listing a mesh ratio
beside `sliding_disk`, which never sees one, asserts an effect that did not
happen, and that is the same class of untruth as omitting the ones that did.
`tests/test_correction_parameter_roster.py` fails if a method is added without
an entry, or if an entry names a parameter `subtract_background` does not take.
The two per-channel-role settings (radius, FFT cutoff) print as one value when
the nuclear and fluorescence roles share it and name both when they differ.
A reference-well correction with **no** well named is painted as a warning
rather than an em-dash: no field was built, so every frame passed through
untouched and the output is bit-for-bit identical to a corrected one — the
silent substitution §7 of `CLAUDE.md` is about, and the reason `severity` is
honoured on a receipt row at all.

**`subtract_background` says when it corrected nothing, for the same reason.**
Four of its paths are the identity transform wearing a correction's name, each
a legitimate response to an input it cannot work with and each previously
indistinguishable — in the output *and* in the log — from a correction that ran.
`fft_bandpass` with a radius of 1 px or less builds an all-ones transfer function
and the round trip returns the frame (a cliff between radius 1 and radius 2);
`robust_mesh` zeroes the whole mesh when not one tile yields a finite level, and
subtracting zero changes nothing; `fov_median` substituted a level of `0.0` for a
frame with no finite pixel, which is a measured zero and an unmeasurable one
written identically; and `empty_well` returns the frame when the channel has no
background field, or when the field it has is a different shape from the frame —
a blank acquired at a different binning or crop from the plate.
`_require_empty_well_models` catches only the case where *no* model was built at
all, so a per-channel gap passed through it. There is nothing else for any of
the four to do, so each warns under the pipeline's own logger naming what did
not happen. A frame whose median really is zero is not one of these and says
nothing.

**A blank can be paired with the wells it corrects, and by default is not.**
Named several blanks, `--background_well H12,G12` pools their frames into one
reference per (channel, timepoint) — the less noisy estimate, and the right one
when the blanks differ only by noise. It is the wrong one when they differ
because of the treatment: a compound that fluoresces puts real signal into its
own block's blank, and pooling spreads that signal over every well on the plate,
producing numbers indistinguishable from corrected ones.
`--background_well_map "H12=A01:D12; G12=E01:H12"` pairs instead, one blank per
block, written as wells, rectangular blocks, or both. `util.well_token`
parses it, and refuses rather than resolves anything ambiguous — a well two
blanks claim, an unreadable token, an empty group — because every rule that
absorbs those ends with a well corrected against a reference the user did not
choose.

`pipeline.empty_well` holds all of it: the sampler, both model builders, the
per-image lookup, and the pairing. `BlankGroups` is the run's plan, and a pooled
run is that class with one group holding every named blank, so pooling is not a
branch threaded through the code but the degenerate case of the same one.
Crucially **the models gain a group dimension and the correction code does
not**: `main` installs the grouped dicts under private keys, and
`shared_kwargs_for_well` swaps in one well's own group as that well is submitted
to the pool, so `process_image_group` and `_correct_image_group` go on receiving
a flat `{channel: {timepoint: field}}` and go on knowing nothing about wells. An
unpaired run is handed the identical object it always was. That is also what
keeps the combined `(raw − B)/(B/mean(B))` correction consistent: its additive
and multiplicative fields must come from the same blank frames, and slicing both
dicts with one key at one place cannot disagree the way two lookups inside two
closures could.

Two consequences the pairing makes load-bearing. `_require_empty_well_models`
is asked **per group**, because the plate-wide question — was *any* model built —
is answered yes by a plate where three of four blocks lost their blank, which is
the silently-uncorrected output that guard exists to refuse. And a well no blank
claims **stops the run**, before an image is read: pooling the unmapped wells
corrects them with other treatments' autofluorescence, and leaving them
uncorrected puts two differently processed populations in one CSV. Both are
invisible in the output, so neither is a default. That refusal and the
ignored-folder one both sit ahead of the model precompute, because each is
decided from the plate's own well list alone and a run that cannot say what
corrects one of its wells should not first spend a model build per blank.

Two things the plan has to get right that read as edge cases and are not.
**A blank is covered by itself.** It is a well the run segments, quantifies and
writes a results file for like any other, and pooling corrected it by a reference
that contained its own frames — so a blank resolving to no group leaves its own
background in its numbers while its CSV looks exactly like a corrected well's,
and `estimate_thresholds_from_outputs` then fits the plate-wide gate over a
mixture of corrected and uncorrected archives. **And pairing is asked per
correction, not per run**, through `BlankGroups.for_mode`: a `basic` flat-field
is estimated from the plate's own images and takes no blank, so it is one field
for the whole plate however the run is paired. Grouping it instead built the
identical field once per blank and then left every well the map does not name
with no flat-field at all — silently, because the coverage refusal is not in
force when neither correction reads a blank.

`--background_well` and the map must also not become two answers to "which wells
are blanks": a blank named beside a map that does not use it is refused, because
`blank_wells_for_run` below takes the union and would stage it as a reference
while the plan called it a sample some blank must claim.

One thing the parser resolves rather than refuses, and it is the exception that
keeps the grammar writable: **a block holds the run's blanks out of itself.**
`G12=E01:H12` is the natural way to pair the bottom half of a plate and its
rectangle contains both blanks, so refusing it made the example printed here and
in the manual a map the parser rejects — caught by a test fixture rather than by
reading it. There is nothing to choose between: a block is a shorthand for a
region, the editor's own splits already write blank-free lists, and a blank is
corrected by the model built from itself in any case. A blank named
*individually* among the wells it corrects stays refused, because that is a
statement about one well and not about a region. The blanks are therefore
canonicalised in a first pass, since one entry's block can contain a later
entry's blank.

"Which wells are blanks?" is `util.well_token.blank_wells_for_run`, and it is one
function because five places ask it and they had already drifted: the remote
runner grew a local whitespace-splitting regex that read `"H12 G12"` as two wells
where the pipeline's own parser reads it as one, and every batch of that run died
on the guard. Two more copies of that regex were still in
`input_resolution_service`'s two incremental-scope readers and are gone;
`_blank_well_tokens` is the seam, and the union it returns is deliberately a
superset — staging a well whole that turns out not to be a blank costs an upload,
while missing one starves a whole block of its correction.

**The map is written on a plate, not in a text box.** `analyze/bg_map.py` holds
the editor — a non-modal window off the Quality Control section, built once and
hidden rather than destroyed. One `WellPlateSelector` in paint mode carries the
whole partition: a colour per blank, a ring on the block being edited, absent
wells disabled so a drag cannot claim a well the folder does not have, and a
live count of the wells no blank claims. That count is
`BlankGroups.uncovered`'s own answer, so what the editor warns about and what
the run refuses are one question asked twice rather than two rules that can
drift. A text field was the cheaper control and the wrong one: the failure the
map exists to prevent is a well quietly landing in the wrong block, and eight
rows of `A01,A02,A03…` read as correct whatever they say.

**The Background well field says which wells are blanks; the editor says only
which wells each of them corrects.** One question, one control, and the field is
the one — it is what the run reads, through `blank_wells_for_run`. The editor's
list is a projection of it, seeded when the window opens and re-synced on the
field's `textChanged` while it is up, and a restored map unions its own blanks
back into the field so the two cannot disagree in that direction either.

**A rectangle is a well list, in the field as well as in the map.** `H01:H12`
names the whole of row H and mixes with ordinary wells, expanded by the same
`_expand_well_range` the map's right-hand side has always used, so `:` means one
thing wherever a set of wells is written. It is expanded inside
`split_background_wells` — the one function every reader of that field goes
through — so the model build, the remote staging planner, the batched hold-out,
both incremental-scope readers, the editor's list, the Review preview and the run
receipt all see the same twelve wells rather than a token one of them might
parse differently. A block whose corners cannot be read falls through as the
token it is and is refused by name, because dropping it would silently remove a
well the user believes is a blank; nothing that parsed before parses differently,
since a token containing `:` was not a well and a run naming one refused to
start.

**The plate names blanks too.** A two-way mode above it — *Choose blank wells* /
*Assign wells to a blank* — because one plate now does two jobs and a click is
ambiguous without one. Choosing writes straight back into the Background well
field, so the plate is another way of typing there rather than a second record —
a second record in this editor is precisely what the rewrite above removed. A
drag latches its direction from the well it starts on, the way the block gesture
does, so sweeping back across your own picks does not undo them. The field is
rewritten as an explicit list, which turns a typed range into its wells the
moment one is clicked — the same reason the map itself is always written out in
full.

**A blank is drawn darker than the block it serves**, and marked. It used to
share its block's fill exactly, so a glyph at 62% of the well was the only thing
separating the reference from the wells it corrects, on a plate whose whole job
is to show that partition. Two channels carry it now and neither is asked to
alone. `darker` and never `lighter`: Qt's lighten drops saturation once value
saturates and walks a state colour to white.

That is a rewrite of the first version, and the reason is worth keeping. The
editor then held a second answer to the same question: an `+ Add blank` button
that named blanks for the editor while the field named them for the run. The
two did not agree in either direction. A blank typed in the field was invisible
in here — the field was read only inside two button handlers, never on open and
never on change — so the list was empty on every cold open, the manual's own
first instruction ("pick a blank in the list") could not be carried out, and
every drag was a silent no-op with no colour, no message and no changed label.
And when the field named nothing, that button took a well off the *end of the
plate* and made it the reference: a sample well held out of the results and used
to correct the other ninety-five, with the editor reporting "Every well is
claimed — this pairing will run" and the form's pre-run gate raising nothing.
There is no add control now, and nothing in the window can invent a blank.

The row **is** the picker — a radio spanning it, in an exclusive group. It
previously held three clickable things: an 18-pixel `●` that was the picker and
said so only in a tooltip, a combo of all 96 wells that looked like the picker
and was actually a rename, and a `✕`. Picking a well from that combo replaced
the user's blank with a sample well and the run then refused with a message
about the input folder, which is not where the problem was. Nothing renames a
blank now; the `✕` clears a blank's block and leaves it a blank, because the
field decides that.

**Every gesture is undoable**, and the transient line names what one took. A
drag takes a well from whoever held it — the right data rule, one well to one
blank, and an invisible interaction: one sweep back across a neighbour's block
moved four wells and the only trace was a count going to zero in a list 70
pixels tall. `Clear pairing` and `Split plate…` push the same stack, which is
why neither asks for confirmation: a dialog guarding an action that can be taken
back spends a click on nothing.

**Two labels, not one.** The coverage line states the number of unclaimed wells
at all times — it is the run's refusal shown early — and anything transient goes
to a second line beneath it. They were one label, so a split that could not fill
the plate overwrote the count with its own message at the moment the count was
largest, and its "name a blank first" refusal outlived the field being filled in.

The map lives on the tab and the widgets are drawn from it, never read back —
the discipline `fold_change_pairing_view` records losing an assignment to
without. Row edits go through a deferred repopulate for the reason that editor
documents too: the control whose signal started the edit is one of the widgets
the repopulate deletes. A rebuilt row is **unparented before** its deferred
delete, because the rebuild runs on every paint tick and `deleteLater` alone
leaves the dead rows children of the host until the event loop turns.

`Split plate…` takes its blanks **only** from the Background well field, and
holds every chosen blank out of every block. Neither is fussiness: the first
version took blanks off the end of the plate when the field named none, so a
row split assigned H12, H11, H10… — wells inside row H's own block — and row H's
blank ended up corrected by itself, producing a map this feature's own parser
refuses. A split with fewer blanks than blocks makes the blocks it can and says
what is left, rather than inventing a reference out of a sample well.

**A blank takes the block it sits in**, and only the blocks nobody sits in are
dealt out in order to the blanks left over. Assigning strictly by list position
put the blank in row H in charge of row A — the opposite of what someone
choosing "one blank per row" is asking for, and invisible until the numbers are
wrong. Each menu entry also states the blocks it makes against the blanks
available, because a split that cannot fill the plate should be visible before
it is chosen rather than as seventy unclaimed wells after it; **even split**
exists for the same reason, cutting the plate into exactly as many blocks as
there are blanks, which is what the common two-blank case actually wants.

The editor offers the plate's real wells through
`input_resolution_service.iter_all_well_tokens`, which is the union
`count_expected_wells` already computed privately, lifted out so both can use
it; `iter_well_tokens` alone reads the grouped layouts only and answers empty
for a plate that is still loose TIFs. It reads the **resolved** input directory
(`_preflight_input`), because on the common `<dataset>/in` layout the path field
names the parent, whose own listing holds no wells at all.

`_background_well_validation_error` moved into that module with the map it now
also validates — `analyze/form.py` was at its line budget, and its own budget
note asks for an extraction with the next section added.

The map is in `settings_digest.KEYED_ON`, so re-pairing a plate declines to reuse
the wells already processed under the old pairing — the reuse decision that would
otherwise hand back numbers built against a different blank and report success.
Its CLI default is `None` rather than `""` for a reason worth keeping: the digest
skips a `None` and includes a `""`, so an empty-string default would have changed
the recorded digest of every plate already on disk and forced a plate-wide
recompute for every user.

`fft_bandpass`'s line says the frame is returned "UNCHANGED", which is true of
that function and not quite of the pipeline: `subtract_background` hands the
result to `_floor_after_subtract`, which zeroes non-finite pixels and clips
negatives. The distinction only matters for a frame that already carries
negatives or NaNs.

**Before a dataset is open, the page is not shown at all.** Home's body is
wrapped in the shared `wrap_with_empty_state` stack like every other Review
page, so the same "Load a directory." placeholder covers it and the same
refresher flips it — a landing page reporting on nothing would otherwise open
the application on a masthead reading "No dataset open" above an empty plate and
a column of em-dashes. The one thing Home adds is an action on the placeholder
itself (`EmptyState.setAction`, optional and unused by the other twelve sites):
elsewhere the hint names a control in the rail, and on the page the app launches
on it is worth being able to press the thing instead. The button stands in the
hint's place rather than beneath it, so Home shows the title and the button and
not also a sentence directing the eye to the rail. It runs `run_home_action(ctx,
"open")`, the same route the next-step row takes, which reaches the window's own
`_browse` rather than opening a second file dialog of its own.

Home's own "is there a dataset" predicate is `collect.has_dataset`, which tests
the **wells** rather than `data_dir`. The two disagree for the whole duration of
a load — `data_dir` is set when one begins — and permanently for a folder that
opened and yielded nothing readable. Since the placeholder covering the page is
gated on the wells, a page gated on anything else could describe a dataset the
placeholder says is not there.

**Opening a dataset always lands on Home**, whatever page the last session
