ended on: the arrival of a *dataset* is the moment a reader most needs to be
told what they just opened, and dropping them onto a plot of a plate they have
not been oriented to is not that. A profile with no Home page falls back to the
saved tab.

That override is opt-in, and only the dataset-load path opts in.
`persistence/view_state.restore` activates the `active_centre_tab` its snapshot
names unless the caller passes `prefer_home=True`, which `load_from_data_dir` —
the one caller that runs on the arrival of a dataset — does. Every other caller
is replaying a view the user asked to see rather than opening a folder, and the
one that exists is Saved Plots' *Restore settings*: it re-applies one figure's
parameters and must leave the user looking at the tab that figure came from.
Sending it to Home instead would apply the whole restored view to a tab nobody
is on, which on screen is indistinguishable from a restore that did nothing.

**A saved plot carries every comparison the Statistics tab had run, not one.**
The comparison store is keyed by `(val_col, target_t, stat)` (§ the Statistics
tab) precisely so that testing a second channel — or a second statistic, or a
second timepoint — adds a comparison rather than replacing the first, and a Bar
plot draws whichever of the stored runs describe the bars in front of it.
`collect._capture_stats_config` therefore walks `stats.runs` and writes one
re-runnable block per stored run into `params["stats"]["runs"]`, each with its
own threshold resolved from its own value column, since the ON cutoff is a
per-channel cut. `stats.pairwise` is a *derived* view of that store meaning "the
last run recorded", so capturing it saved one comparison out of however many the
figure was drawing: a plot of GFP bars saved after a CY5 test had been run came
back from Restore carrying the CY5 config, which matches no bar on it, and
therefore with no brackets at all. The most recent run also sits at the top
level of the block, which is where a record written before the block held
several runs kept its only one — one shape for every reader of a single run's
context, and the read path treats such a record as a one-run list.

`_restore_stats` re-runs each block and rebuilds the store from them, replacing
its contents rather than assigning `pairwise` (which records exactly one run):
the record's runs are what the plot was drawn with, and a comparison left in the
store from earlier in the session is not. A block whose data is no longer there
returns no records, so the restored plot comes back with fewer brackets than it
was saved with — `_report_unreproduced_stats` says so in the status line, because
from the figure alone that is indistinguishable from a plot that never had them.

**Restoring a plot's statistics repaints the group list, not just the state.**
`_restore_stats` re-runs the saved test and writes `stats.groups` /
`stats.pairwise`, and it now calls `stats_refresh_group_list` /
`stats_refresh_map` after doing so. Every *other* route that changes those groups
— add, delete, rename, clear, sync-from-home — funnels through those two, which
are what actually draw the sidebar's group cards and colour its plate; this one
went round them. The result was groups live in every way except the visible one:
the Statistics tab ran its test on them and "Load groups from Home" warned about
overwriting them, while the rail showed an empty list. `_activate_statistics` is
not a backstop, because it re-seeds only when the group list is *empty* — which
the restore has just made false. The refresh sits in its own helper outside the
caller's `except`, so a repaint failure is not reported as "the stats re-run
failed"; they are different problems and the second is the misleading one.

**A restore reproduces a view; it never rewrites a declaration.** A declaration
is what `features/home/collect.DECLARATION_ROLES` says it is — the four ways of
saying what a well *is* — and the restore leaves all four alone. Which wells are
soloed is a view, and `_restore_solo_wells` puts them back. A replicate set is a
declaration: the user built its name, its membership and its plot order by hand
on Home → Sample Map → Replicates, and the restore leaves it exactly where it
is.

The cell-gating block is the documented exception, and it is one because the
roster above already excludes it: a gate is a threshold, not a statement about
what a well is. It also changes the *numbers* the saved figure was drawn from,
so `_restore_thresholds` re-applies it — a restored figure under today's gates
would be a different measurement wearing the saved figure's title, which is the
silent substitution §7 is about. It stays a session change: nothing on that path
writes `pipeline_info.json`, so reloading the dataset brings the user's gates
back. Nothing in a restore writes to disk at all any more, which is the property
worth keeping when the next domain is added to this function. It did not: it deep-copied the record's `selections` over the live ones
and then reached `selection_controller.rebuild_all`, whose tail queues a
sample-definitions autosave because every *other* caller of it has just edited a
definition. Opening a figure saved last week therefore replaced this week's
groups and wrote the replacement into `pipeline_info.json`, with nothing said and
nothing to undo it. The app already treated that as destructive in the one other
place it replays a record — `regenerate_missing_vectors` snapshots the live state
in `_LiveState` and puts it back in a `finally`, and declines the whole repair
when the snapshot fails — and the button had no such guard.

What the button does instead is say so. `_report_group_drift` compares the
record's groups against the live ones through `selections_model.group_drift` and
names, on the status line, the ones this dataset no longer defines and the ones
that now hold different wells, adding that the figure is drawn from the current
groups and the definitions were left alone. Matched by **name** rather than by
id, because `validate_repair` re-mints ids whenever a list is loaded or repaired
and an id-wise comparison would report every group as missing on every restore;
membership is compared as an **ordered** list, because the order is the plot
order. Nothing is said when nothing has drifted, which is the common case.

`restore_saved_plot` still takes `adopt_groups`, off by default and passed by
exactly one caller: `regenerate_missing_vectors`, which has to draw each
record's own figure and is the only caller that can, because of the `_LiveState`
snapshot around it. Even there the groups go on through `_adopt_record_groups`
rather than through `rebuild_all` — replaying a gallery of records used to write
each one's groups to disk in turn, and `_LiveState` restores the session rather
than the file, so the user's groups came back on screen while the last replayed
record's sat in `pipeline_info.json` until some later edit happened to overwrite
them.

Two other ways that restore can look like it did nothing. A tab that renders on
demand rather than on every state change comes back with its controls restored
and its picture untouched — that is the Image Table, which does not regenerate
on a restore (§5.3) and instead marks itself stale so the shelf asks for the
Generate. And a record saved before its tab began storing a per-tab block
restores the cross-cutting state and nothing tab-specific:
`features/saved_plots/controller.py`'s `_report_missing_tab_block` says so in
the status line,
gated on `view_state.owns_tab_block`, which separates "this tab keeps no block"
(true of most tabs, and not worth a warning) from "this record has none of the
block this tab keeps" (worth one — the fix is to re-save the plot, and a user
who is told nothing re-clicks Restore instead).

#### QC Triage (`features/home/triage/`)

The last Home sub-tab is one table of every problem the dataset's own records
report, so a user does not have to read Validate, the Cell Gating panel, the
Segmentation overlay and `errors/` separately to learn what is wrong with a
plate. **It measures nothing.** `collect.triage_rows` reads three records other
parts of the app already wrote: the completeness record (`run_check` — wells
whose CSV is missing, wells staged and never processed, the field groups the
run recorded as failed, the groups found missing, and dataset-wide findings),
every needs-attention well state — a guard holds each state in
`pipeline.completeness.NEEDS_ATTENTION` to a row, via `WELL_STATE_ROWS` — and
the count of wells the check could not read), the traceback files in `errors/`
written since the recorded run began
(`pipeline.completeness.error_files_since`, the listing `errors_since` counts,
so the two cannot disagree about which files belong to the run), and the run's
field-quality verdicts scored by `domain/field_quality_scores`. A source that
cannot speak is a row saying so — no record, a check switched off or stopped, a
plate too partly measured to score — so an empty table means nothing is known to
be wrong and can mean nothing else. The completeness record keeps only the first
few missing groups per well; the rest are one row naming how many were not
listed, rather than a table that silently understates the well. **Every
exclusion has a row**, whether or not its field is still flagged: an exclusion
outlives its finding (a rerun unflags the field, the block goes missing, the
scorer declines) and goes on removing the field's cells, so one with no flagged
row gets a row of its own, with Reopen.

**What a row offers follows from where the problem arose.** A *processing* row
(missing, failed, no CSV, never processed, a traceback) offers **Re-run wells**,
which goes through Home's one Review-side door into Analyze
(`home.controller.open_in_analyze`, also what *Finish this run* uses) with the
selected wells both forced and the only wells run, so nothing else on the plate
is touched; Analyze opens configured and the user presses Run. The hand-off
answers whether it happened, and a build with no Analyze pane is told so rather
than told a rerun is set up. An *acquisition*
row (a field the run measured as unlike the plate) offers **Exclude field…**,
which asks for a reason. Neither offers the other: a missing field has no rows
to exclude, and re-segmenting blurred pictures produces the same blurred
numbers. **Accept** marks a finding seen; **Reopen** undoes Accept and puts an
excluded field back. Every button is enabled only when a selected row supports
it. **Open in Segmentation** calls the `image_browser.show_field` service, the
same jump the Cell Browser's click uses (`review_image/_navigate.py`), placed
beside Segmentation because that sub-tab is the one no profile removes.

**The exclusion is an inclusion layer, not a triage feature.**
`review/data/field_exclusions.py` projects `Excluded_Field_Pass` from
`DatasetState.field_exclusions` (`(well, fov, timepoint)` → reason and time) and
is registered with the other cache projectors unconditionally, so a build that
strips the triage tab still honours exclusions a previous session wrote. It
refuses the wells `Field_Pass` refuses — those whose FOV labels do not identify
their fields — because a per-field key on such a well matches the wrong rows or
none; the triage row says so in its Decision column instead of offering the
button. A well with nothing excluded carries no column. Excluding saves
immediately (`persistence.save`, not the debounce, because a decision to remove
data must not wait on a timer the user can quit through), re-projects every
layer through `qc.recompute_all`, and redraws through `redraw_app`. The
exclusions and the accepted findings are two persistence domains,
`field_exclusions` and `triage_decisions`, both cleared by the *Curation* reset
scope and both recorded in the provenance log (§5.7). A decision is keyed by the
finding's identity (kind, well, field, timepoint, file name) and never by its
sentence, so a count that changes as a rerun recovers groups does not orphan the
decision; decisions for findings no longer reported are kept rather than pruned,
because a finding also disappears when its evidence is briefly unavailable.

Field-level rerun is not offered, by decision. `pipeline.io.merge_records_into_csv`
keeps existing rows and drops new ones with the same key, so re-processing an
already-processed field through the incremental path would leave the old numbers
and report success. Doing it properly means replacing the field's CSV rows,
archive members and field-quality record, carrying that replacement through the
remote upload split and fetch, and invalidating per-cell overrides keyed by the
old nucleus ids — a body of work out of proportion to the case it serves. A
field whose pictures are suspect is excluded instead, and a well that needs
processing again is re-run whole.

#### The headless report (`allwell_report.py`)

`python allwell_report.py --dataset <folder> --output <folder>` draws every
saved plot of a dataset from its current data without showing a window, and
writes `figures/NN_<title>.png` + `.svg`, `report.pdf`, and `manifest.json`.

**It is an entry point, beside `allwell.py`.** It constructs the Review pane,
which only the shell may do — a module inside `review/` may not import
`ReviewApp` (`test_nothing_imports_reviewapp_at_runtime`) — so it is a root
module with its reason in `tests/test_root_holds_only_entry_points.py`, and the
frozen app reaches it through the launcher's `--run-report` dispatch.

**It is the real app, offscreen.** `allwell_report.run_report` constructs `ReviewApp`
under the offscreen platform, loads the dataset, and replays each record through
the `saved_plots.render` service (`features/saved_plots/_render.py`): restore the
record onto its tab, finish the gating pass on this thread, capture the figure
in publication mode — the replay the PowerPoint export's vector repair already
performs. Measured before choosing this route: construction and load of the mini
dataset take about 7 s and 400 MB, no window is shown and no modal is raised.
The alternative — a widget-free context driving collectors and renderers —
would need Batch Export's orchestration lifted out of its panels first and
would be a second definition of how every plot is drawn. The PDF is the
gallery's own builder (`saved_plots.report_pdf`); the report names no
feature and reaches all three through services, so a profile without Saved
Plots gets an exit code and a sentence rather than an `ImportError`.

**A plot that is not drawn is a manifest entry with the reason**, and a plot
drawn from fewer wells than it names carries a `note` saying which; neither is
ever an absence: an Image Table grid (no chart to redraw), a record saved as one panel
of a multi-panel figure (a redraw would draw every panel), a replay that raised.
Copied plots (`copied_from`) are drawn from this dataset's data like any other,
and the entry keeps their origin. Exit codes distinguish complete (0), failed
(1), invalid input (2 — no folder, no wells, or no Saved Plots in this build),
partial (3) and nothing to report (4); the manifest carries the same status as a
word, and is written on every path, including invalid input.

**It does not change the dataset.** The run sits inside
`persistence/_io.writes_suspended` — reached as `ctx.persistence.writes_suspended`,
with `suppressed_writes` and `record_event` beside it on the registry, so the
report imports nothing from the pane except `ReviewApp` — over the dataset
folder and, when `--dataset` is the results folder and the sidecar sits one
level up, that sidecar file too (`allwell_report.suspended_roots`). A suspended
write **raises** `WritesSuspended`, an `OSError`, at `_replace_with_text` and
`atomic_write_text`, and is counted. Raising rather than returning is the
point: a caller told its write landed goes on to do what depends on it — the
legacy-sidecar migration deletes the files it absorbed, the QC migration deletes
`qc_params.json` — and a silently dropped write would have let it delete the
only copy. The two destructive steps that come *before* a write check first
(`_io.is_suspended`): `_doc.write` declines rather than rename an unreadable
`persistence.json` aside, and the v1→v2 sample-definitions backup is refused
before it is copied. Pending debounced saves are flushed inside the suspension,
in a `finally`, so none fires after it lifts. Measured, replays that re-adopt a
plot's groups or move its gating schedule no save at all, so the suspension is
defence in depth that the end-to-end test does not exercise: that test pins the
outcome (the dataset is byte-identical afterwards) and
`tests/test_headless_report.py` pins the suspension, including a legacy sidecar
loaded under it. Each run first removes the figures, PDF and manifest an earlier
run left in `--output` (`clear_previous_output`), so a run that draws fewer
plots cannot leave an old report beside a new manifest. The one write to the
dataset is a `report_generated` line in its provenance log (§5.7).

Batch Export groups are not drawn by the report yet: their orchestration lives
in the panels. Nor does the report apply a recipe first — that would change the
dataset; copy the analysis in the app, then report.

#### Exporting the gallery (`features/saved_plots/_report.py`, `_deck.py`)

The gallery goes out whole, in one of two formats, from a single Export menu on
the page's control band, built by `core.ui_helpers.make_action_menu_button` —
the one path in the app for a click-and-close menu, and the one the theme's
caret rule is written for. That rule styles `QToolButton[hasMenu]`, so a
`QPushButton` carrying a `QMenu` falls through to Qt's own
`QPushButton::menu-indicator`: an unstyled arrow hard against the right edge and
below the text's centre line. The helper puts the caret in the label and hides
the native indicator, which is why every menu in the window reads the same. Both walk the records in **gallery order** —
`controller.gallery_order`, which is `reversed(store.records)` — because the
gallery shows newest first and the ▲/▼ buttons curate that sequence; an export
that walked the records as stored came out in exactly the reverse of the order
the user had arranged, silently, since both are plausible orderings of the same
plots. One function answers it so the two exports cannot drift apart.

**PDF (`_report.py`)** is one page per plot: the captured raster snapshot
embedded large under a header, with the parameter summary as a caption. It draws
through matplotlib's `PdfPages`, so the text around the figure is vector and the
figure itself is the picture the gallery holds.

**PowerPoint (`_deck.py`)** is one *slide* per plot, and the figure on it is not
a picture — it is PowerPoint shapes. A bar arrives as a rectangle whose fill
PowerPoint can change, an axis label as a text box that can be retyped, a marker
as a curve. The whole figure sits in one `grpSp` group, so it moves and scales as
a unit while a double-click still reaches the shapes inside it. That is the point
of the format: restyling a figure for a talk or a thesis stops requiring a
round-trip through All-Well or Illustrator.

Four modules, in the order the data moves through them:

| Module | Does |
| --- | --- |
| `_svg_shapes.py` | Reads a Matplotlib SVG into a flat, ordered list of `PathShape` / `TextShape` / `ImageShape` in absolute user-space points. Applies the transform stack, inherits styles down the tree, expands `<use>` references into real geometry, splits mathtext back into positioned runs, and clips to rectangular `<clipPath>`s. Not a general SVG reader — it handles the subset Matplotlib emits and records anything else in `Drawing.unsupported`. |
| `_drawingml.py` | Turns those shapes into DrawingML. The only module that knows about EMUs (12,700 per point) and hundredths-of-a-point font sizes. `Placement.fit` letterboxes a figure into a target box on the slide. |
| `_pptx.py` | Writes the Open Packaging container — the zip of XML parts, their relationships, one slide master, one blank layout, one theme. No `python-pptx`: the parts a deck of plain slides needs are small and fixed, so the export adds nothing to the runtime stack. |
| `_align.py` | Turns the recorded plotting areas of a whole gallery into the one anchor box every slide places its figure's axes in. Pure arithmetic. |
| `_deck.py` | Lays out the slide (title, source-tab badge, timestamp, parameter column) and decides how each plot reaches it. |

**Vector capture is taken at save time, not at export time.** A gallery record
holds parameters and a PNG, never a figure, so nothing downstream can reconstruct
one — the only moment the figure exists is the moment the user clicks Save.
`widgets/plot_card.py` therefore renders the panel twice in the same
publication-mode capture: the 300 dpi PNG it always did, and an SVG through
`fig_clipboard.render_figure_svg`, which sets `svg.fonttype="none"` so labels stay
`<text>` rather than outlined paths. Both land in `<data_dir>/saved_plots/`, as
`<id>.png` and `<id>.svg`, and `SavedPlot.svg_filename` is empty when there is no
vector twin. The Image Table is the one tab that captures neither, and stores a
per-field frame plan instead — see *An Image Table grid* below.

**A figure is placed by its plotting area, not by its page.** A saved capture is
cropped to its own ink, so the page a bar chart produces grows with its tick
labels, its title and its legend while the axes inside it do not move. Scaling
each of those pages to fill the slide — the obvious rule, and what
`Placement.fit` does — therefore gives two plots authored at the same figure size
axes of different sizes in different places: measured on a 13⅓ × 7½ deck, three
`figsize=(6, 4)` plots differing only in label lengths landed as axes 7.45, 7.10
and 5.73 inches wide at three different origins. Slides like that cannot be laid
beside one another into a composite figure, which is a large part of why anyone
wants editable shapes rather than pictures.

So each capture records where its plotting area sits on its own page —
`fig_clipboard.figure_axes_fraction`, written into the SVG as the
`AXES_RECT_MARKER` comment, the union of every *visible* axes' rectangle as
fractions of the page. Fractions rather than points because the consumer already
knows the page it parsed and a fraction cannot disagree with it. That marker is
only exact if the page is known, which is why `render_figure_svg` resolves
`bbox_inches="tight"` into the explicit `Bbox` it stands for
(`figure_crop_bbox`) before rendering: Matplotlib computes that rectangle inside
`print_figure` and throws it away, and recomputing it afterwards lands a point or
two off — enough to misplace a figure once it is scaled onto a slide. Handed an
explicit `Bbox`, Matplotlib honours it exactly, so the page really is the
rectangle the capture measured against.

`_align.plan_anchor` then turns the whole gallery's markers into **one anchor
box**, and `Placement.anchor` scales each figure so its axes fills that box and
centres it there; everything outside the axes hangs off the box into the space
around it. The box is planned from the deck rather than fixed because the room
decorations need is not knowable in advance — a legend outside the axes wants a
third of the figure's width, and a fixed allowance generous enough for that would
waste the same third on every plot without one. Taking the largest margin any
plot asks for, as a proportion of *that plot's own axes*, gives the biggest box
that still leaves every figure's decorations inside the body of its slide. It is
planned against the **narrowest** figure area any slide will offer, too, since a
plot with no parameter summary is given the full slide width and an anchor sized
to that would push a neighbouring slide's figure under its parameter column. The
planning pass reads only the markers, never the shapes: a regular expression over
the bytes, where parsing a capture into shapes is the expensive half of the whole
export.

What alignment cannot reach is a difference that is real in the figure. With no
layout engine — the default — an axes keeps a fixed position in figure
coordinates, so two plots of one `figsize` have the same plotting area in inches
and land on their slides identically. The Properties sidebar's `layout_tight` /
`layout_constrained` preferences make the axes position depend on the labels
instead, and the same pair then differs by around half an inch: the plotting
areas are genuinely different sizes by the time the capture is taken, and the
anchor can only centre them on one another.

No figure comes out smaller than filling the slide alone would have drawn it: a
gallery of one has its own margins as the maxima and resolves to the same scale
the letterbox chose, differing only in centring the plotting area rather than the
page in whatever slack is left over. A capture with no marker — one filed before
this, or a figure with no axes at all — cannot be aligned, so it is letterboxed
as before and the slide says so under the figure; a figure that *nearly* lines up
is the shortfall a reader cannot see. Where no plot in the deck records one there
is no alignment to fall short of and no slide says anything. A plot placed as a
picture is not aligned either — a PNG carries no axes rectangle — and its slide
already states that it is a picture.

**A plot without a vector capture is placed as a picture, and the slide says so.**
Three things produce that: a record saved before the app captured vector, a
capture that failed to render or to write, and the Image Table — which composes
its gallery snapshot as a raster grid and has no Matplotlib figure to vectorise.
None of them is an error, and all of them are stated rather than glossed. Each
carries its own wording, because they have different fixes: "re-save it" is right
for a record that never had a capture and wrong for one whose capture is corrupt
on disk. `DeckResult` counts `vector` and `raster` separately and
`DeckResult.summary()` names the split in the status line. A deck where some
figures are editable and some are not is otherwise indistinguishable from one
where all of them are — until someone tries to click a bar in front of a room.

**A clip cuts a fill and an outline differently.** A shape that is both filled
and stroked and crosses its clip rectangle needs two geometries: the fill closes
along the clip edge, the outline simply stops there. Closing both — one rule for
the whole shape — draws an edge the figure never had, so a bar running off the
top of its axes acquires a cap exactly at the axis limit and reads as a bar whose
value *is* the limit. That is a wrong number on the slide, produced by the
exporter. `PathShape.stroke_subpaths` carries the second geometry, set only when
a clip actually split the two, and `_custom_geometry` emits both into one
`custGeom` as separate `a:path` entries — one `fill="norm" stroke="0"`, one
`fill="none" stroke="1"` — so the bar stays a single object the user selects and
recolours.

**Mathtext is several runs, not one label.** Matplotlib writes `$\mu$m` as
several `<tspan>`s grouped *by font rather than by reading order*, each carrying
its own list of per-glyph x positions, so an italic span can hold the μ at one
end of the label and an α sixty points along with the upright run between them in
space and after them in the document. `_emit_tspan` splits each span back into
runs at the gaps between glyph positions (`_positioned_runs`, breaking at
`_RUN_BREAK_EMS` times the font size — no glyph in a proportional face is close
to twice its point size wide) and emits each at its own coordinates. µm,
superscripts and Greek are ordinary in microscopy axis labels; concatenating the
element's text gave neither what the figure said nor where it said it.

**Everything the reader could not translate reaches the artifact.**
`Drawing.unsupported` names each construct once — a pattern fill (which is how
Matplotlib writes a **hatch**, and which otherwise resolves to "no paint" and is
indistinguishable from `fill: none`), an elliptical arc, an `<line>` element, a
non-rectangular clip path approximated by its bounding box. A figure that lost
one is drawn, and the slide carries a line under it saying what is missing;
`DeckResult.summary()` repeats the list in the status line, and never behind the
"all editable" branch — a deck can be entirely vector and still have lost a hatch
out of one of its figures. The findings are collected *before* the shape cap
decides anything, so a capped figure's are not discarded.

**Text is sanitised, not merely escaped.** `escape` rewrites `&`, `<` and `>` and
leaves the characters XML 1.0 forbids outright — and a plot title is free text a
user types or pastes, with a paste out of Word carrying `\x0b` for a soft line
break. One of those does not spoil a label: it makes the whole slide part
unparseable, so PowerPoint offers to repair the file while the export reports
success. `_drawingml.xml_text` / `xml_attr` drop them and every user-reachable
string goes through one or the other.

**The export shows a progress bar across both of its phases.** It blocks the
GUI thread from the moment the file dialog closes: it replays old plots onto
their tabs, renders each figure to vector, parses every capture and writes a
zip. `export_deck_pptx` sizes the bar as `redraws + plots + 1` and steps it
through both — `regenerate_missing_vectors` takes an `on_progress(done, title)`
and `build_saved_plots_deck` an `on_progress(done, total, label)`, the latter a
plain callable so `_deck` stays Qt-free and testable without an application.
Every path out of the redraw loop reports, skips included: a bar that only moved
on a successful redraw sits still through a gallery that is all being skipped,
which looks exactly like a hang. The bar is hidden in a `finally`, because one
left running after a failed export is its own false statement.

`_pump` turns the event loop by hand — nothing repaints otherwise — with
`ExcludeUserInputEvents`: the redraw phase moves the app from tab to tab and
rewrites the live selection as it goes, so a click landing mid-export would act
on a view that is about to be replaced and then undone by the restore.

**A plot with no vector capture is redrawn rather than written off.** A record
filed before the app captured vector is a PNG and nothing else, and no amount of
reading it produces shapes — but it carries the parameters that drew it, and the
app can draw them again. `controller.regenerate_missing_vectors` runs before the
deck is built: for each such record it replays the parameters onto the tab
(`restore_saved_plot`, the one caller that passes `adopt_groups=True`), captures
the live figure through
`PlotCard.captureVectorSvg` — the same publication-mode render a save uses — and
keeps the result on the record via `store.attach_vector`. The repair is therefore
a one-off: every later export of that plot is editable without paying for it
again. An existing capture is never overwritten, because the one taken when the
user saved is the better record of what they saw.

The tab-to-card map comes from `wire_save_to_gallery`, which is the one place in
the app where a tab's name and its live card meet; a tab added tomorrow is
covered by wiring itself up rather than by a roster someone has to remember.
A tab with no card — the Image Table, which composes microscopy frames rather
than drawing a chart — is skipped and stays a picture.

**A redraw that would change the figure's scope is declined.** The redraw
renders the whole card, so a record that saved **one panel** of a multi-panel
figure would come back as every panel, under that panel's title and beside that
panel's parameters — a different figure, not a worse one. `SavedPlot.panel_only`
records which a save was, and it is **tri-state**: `None` means the record
predates the field. Defaulting those to "whole figure" was a guess, and it put a
user's three-panel window on a slide in place of the single panel they had
saved.

For an unknown record there is nothing in it that says, so
`_redraw_keeps_the_scope` asks the only question that decides whether a redraw
*can* change the scope: **how many panels the card draws now**. One axis and a
redraw is the same picture as a per-panel save, so it is safe whatever the
record meant; more than one and it is not knowable, and not knowable means not
redrawn. The cost is that an old whole-figure record from a multi-panel tab
stays a picture — the right way to be wrong, since re-saving makes it editable
and nothing is misrepresented meanwhile.

Comparing the stored image's aspect ratio against the live figure's was tried
and is **not** evidence: a plot card takes its size from the widget, so opening
the Properties sidebar alone moves the live figure's aspect by more than 40%,
and the window a deck is exported from is rarely the window its plots were saved
from.

**Those slides say the figure was redrawn**, and `DeckResult.redrawn` counts
them. A redrawn figure is drawn from *today's* data and today's gating, and the
gating recompute is asynchronous, so it can differ from the image the user saved
in a direction nothing else on the slide would reveal. The user's own view is
snapshotted before the loop and restored after it: an export is not a
navigation.

**The vector capture is bounded by rasterizing dense layers, not by refusing.**
`fig_clipboard.MAX_VECTOR_PATHS` is checked against `figure_path_count` — artist
counts, so constant-time in the data — before `render_figure_svg` renders
anything. Past it the figure is **not** refused: `_dense_layers_rasterized` marks
the biggest collections rasterized, biggest first and only as far as it must, so
a scatter of a hundred thousand cells beside a fitted line loses the cloud and
keeps the line, and the axes, ticks, labels, title and legend stay editable
either way. Refusing the whole figure is what shipped first, and it defeated the
format for exactly the per-cell plots that most need restyling.

The threshold is set from how long the resulting deck takes to **open**, which is
the only number that decides it — an earlier version was set from the build time,
which is linear and is not what the user waits for, and produced decks that could
not be opened at all. Opening is superlinear with a hard wall: 10,000 shapes in
8 s, 20,000 in 17 s, 40,000 in 46 s, 100,000 in over two and a half minutes, and
249,000 killed out of memory at 13.9 GB. Passing the threshold costs little,
because the figure is never refused — only its point cloud stops being individual
shapes — so the conservative number is the right one. A test holds
`MAX_VECTOR_PATHS` at or below `MAX_SHAPES_PER_SLIDE`, which is the tie between
two numbers that cannot share a constant: the capture lives in `widgets/` and
must not import a feature. `copy_figure_to_clipboard` is deliberately uncapped —
that caller wants vector for its own sake rather than for a deck.

**`_deck.MAX_SHAPES_PER_SLIDE` is a hard cap, not a quality setting.** A scatter
of a hundred thousand cells is a hundred thousand PowerPoint shapes and a deck
like that does not open — it hangs. Past the cap the figure is placed as a
picture and the slide names the shape count, because "too complex" gives the user
nothing to act on while "180,000 shapes" tells them to plot fewer cells.

#### An Image Table grid: one editable frame per field of view

A grid is not a chart, so none of the above applies to it. There is no vector
figure to capture and nothing to redraw mark by mark: a field of view *is* a
photograph. What a grid does have is structure — a rectangle per field, and a set
of overlays the app draws on each one — and that structure is what makes a slide
editable. So the Image Table stores a **frame plan** where every other tab stores
a vector capture, and the deck places it as one PowerPoint `grpSp` per field:
that field's picture, its identity label as a text box, its "raw" mark as
another, and its scale bar as a filled rectangle. The facet row and column labels
are placed at the *top level* of the slide rather than inside any field's group,
because they name a row or a column — a user dragging one field must not take its
row header with it.

`review/domain/image_frames.py` is the format, and it is in `domain/`
because both features read it and neither may import the other. Geometry is in
**inches from the grid's top-left, y downward** — PowerPoint's frame of reference
rather than matplotlib's, decided once at the boundary so no reader has to guess
which way up a rectangle is. On disk it is a zip: `grid.json` holding the
rectangles and the marks, plus `frames/<n>.png` per field, so a user can open one
without this module. `SavedPlot.frames_filename` names it (`<id>.frames.zip`) and
is empty for every other tab and for a grid saved before plans existed — those
still export as a picture, exactly as they did.

`image_table/_frames.py` builds the plan, inside the same pass that renders the
export figure (`export._build_export_figure(..., frames=collector)`), because the
per-cell disk reads and LUT application are the expensive half and are already
happening there. Two rules hold it to the picture beside it:

* **The frame keeps the field before the chrome is burned in.**
  `image_compose.draw_cell_chrome` writes the identity label and the scale bar
  into the cell's pixels; the collector records the array from *above* that call
  and re-states the same overlays as marks. Recording the drawn cell instead
  would produce a plan that looks identical from the outside and a slide whose
  editable label sits on top of a picture of the old one.
* **Every mark's geometry is shared, not restated.** `bar_rect_px`,
  `bar_ink_rgb`, `bar_thickness_for`, `label_font_px_for` and `label_margin_px`
  are extracted out of `draw_cell_chrome` and used by both surfaces, so the
  deck's rectangle is the same bar at the same length in the same tone. That
  includes both halves of the refusal: `bar_fits` for a bar longer than its
  field, and `chrome_fits` — the array guards `draw_cell_chrome` returns early
  on — for a field that can take no chrome at all, such as a 200×3 crop. Gating
  on the length alone put a rectangle on a slide as a 25 µm scale that the
  picture had refused and the status line had reported as refused. A bar
  shortened or invented states a physical scale nobody measured and looks
  exactly like a correct one. The facet labels come from one
  `renderer.facet_label_specs` descriptor list that the matplotlib figure and
  the frame plan both read, `FacetLabel.band` included — a group strip keeps the
  filled band the figure draws it on.

**A per-axes title goes in the room the figure leaves, not in the strip the cell
reserves.** Turning `show_titles` on grows each cell by `export.TITLE_STRIP_IN`,
but `imshow(aspect="equal")` then centres the axes in the taller slot, so only
about half that strip ends up above the picture. Carving the whole strip out of
the slot first is internally consistent — and put every picture 0.1 in below
where the figure drew it, which is why the test for this measures the plan
against the axes matplotlib actually drew rather than against the slot they
share. A frame's own rectangle is the union of its picture and its marks,
because that rectangle becomes the PowerPoint group's extent and a title outside
it would be drawn but left out of the group's box.

**Everything read back off disk is validated at the boundary.**
`image_frames.from_bytes` refuses a malformed plan with `FramedGridError`
rather than half-reading it, and that now includes a colour that is not six hex
digits and a size that is not a positive number. Both were reaching consumers
that assume well-formed input: `_deck._hex` raises by design, since every colour
it was written for is a theme token, so one bad colour aborted the whole
gallery's deck; and a width that coerced to `0.0` made `_GridFit` scale every
rectangle by five million and put the shapes off the slide with nothing said.
`_try_frames` catches only `FramedGridError`, so the refusal is what makes the
documented fallback — place the picture, keep the rest of the deck — actually
happen.

The marks are measured against the **source** array and the picture is pooled
before it goes into the zip — to the smaller of the caller's own per-cell cap and
`export.FRAME_MAX_PX` (900 px on the longest side, ≈350 dpi over a 2.6 in field).
The gallery route passes the Save-quality preset, so in practice a saved grid's
fields are 280, 480 or 800 px and 900 is the direct-export figure. Measuring the
marks against the pooled copy would pick up its rounding and give the bar a
different length in the deck than in the figure.

A field's picture is stored per field, so a saved grid's `frames.zip` is
materially larger than the single snapshot beside it — roughly the cell count
times a pooled PNG. That is the cost of the fields being separable at all, and
the Save-quality preset is the control over it.

Both routes decline a plan in which **no field carries a picture**
(`FramedGrid.has_pictures`): the flat snapshot is what the user actually saw, so
placing a page of labelled blanks and reporting it as editable trades a picture
of their grid for a picture of nothing. A grid where only *some* fields failed
still goes through as frames — each of those keeps its place and its labels and
carries the figure's own `(no image)` placeholder, and the slide says how many.

`DeckResult.framed` counts these apart from the rest of `vector`, and the status
line says "N image grids as one group per field" rather than folding them into
"all editable" — the labels and the bars are shapes, and the thing at the centre
of each frame is a photograph. The Image Table's own **Save ▾ → Export to
PowerPoint…** writes the same slide directly through
`_deck.build_image_grid_deck`, so the two routes cannot produce different decks.

**`SavedPlotsStore._discard_files` removes every file a record owns.** Delete and
Clear take the snapshot, its vector twin *and* its frame plan; taking only the
PNG would leave the dataset folder accumulating captures for plots the gallery no
longer lists, with nothing left to name them.

#### Recent datasets

The datasets this user opened, newest first, kept in `QSettings` alongside the
window geometry — **not** in any dataset folder. A list *about* many datasets
cannot live inside one of them, and a dataset copied to a colleague must not
carry the author's history of other plates.

`core/recent_datasets.py` is the store and is deliberately Qt-free: every
function takes the settings object as an argument rather than constructing one,
so the whole module runs in the fast lane against a dict stub and no test writes
to the machine it runs on. Entries are `(path, name, opened_at)`, capped at
`MAX_RECENTS` **from the front**, so the dataset just opened can never be the one
dropped. Dedupe is by `Path.resolve()`, not by the string given: a folder chosen
in the file dialog and the same folder typed on the command line are two
spellings of one dataset (on macOS one goes through `/private/var` and the other
through `/var`), and deduping on the raw string would put it in the list twice
with no way to tell the rows apart. `strict=False`, so an entry whose drive is
unmounted still compares equal to itself.

The `QSettings` value is the one input in the app that arrives without a schema —
a user-writable file that survives across versions — so `decode` treats every
failure the same way: absent, not a string, not JSON, not a list, an entry
missing its path, a timestamp that is not a number all mean "there is no history
to offer", and an individually malformed entry is dropped while the rest are
kept. Raising instead would take the window down at startup over a file the user
can simply be given a fresh one of.

**The display name is stored, not re-derived.** `dataset_display_name` asks
whether an `in` sibling exists, which is a second filesystem call per entry on
top of the reachability check the view already makes. Recording it once, at the
moment the dataset actually opened, halves that and says what the folder was
called then. It does not make the paint stat-free — the view still checks each
row — so if a blocking network mount ever becomes real, the fix is to move the
check off the paint rather than to store more.

**The path stored is the resolved one.** `--data_dir ../plate` is a real way to
open a dataset, and a relative path names a different folder from a different
working directory — which a launched `.app` bundle has. Stored raw, that row is
re-resolved on the next launch and either draws disabled under a reason that is
untrue or, if some other `../plate` exists, draws *enabled* under the old
dataset's name and opens a different plate.

**The settings handle comes from `core/app_settings.app_settings()`, a module
function.** Not a method on anything, and that is the whole point: this feature
first shipped completely dead because both call sites read
`ctx.window._qsettings`, which is a method of the `AllWellApp` main window and
not of the `ReviewApp` review widget `ctx.window` actually is, with no
forwarding between them. Nothing was written and nothing was read, while the
full-app test that should have caught it passed — it used
`monkeypatch.setattr(loaded_app, "_qsettings", …, raising=False)`, which
*creates* the attribute the application does not have.
`tests/test_no_invented_app_attributes.py` fails on that shape against any
full-app fixture: if the attribute exists the flag is unnecessary, and if it
does not, the test is measuring something the app cannot do.

**Written on success, and success means wells.** `load_controller.
_remember_if_it_loaded` runs after `load_path` and returns early unless
`well_paths` is non-empty — a folder that opened without raising and yielded
nothing readable is not a dataset the user wants offered back, and offering it
would make the list a record of their mistakes rather than of their work. The
path stored is the one Review was *pointed at*, not the `out` half it may have
descended into, so reopening from the list takes the same branch through
`load_path` the original open took. A settings backend that will not write is
logged and dropped: the dataset is already loaded and on screen by then.

It appears in three places, fed by one function — `core/recent_view.entry_rows`
— so they cannot disagree about which folders are reachable or what a row is
called. On Home's no-dataset placeholder it shows `RECENTS_ON_PLACEHOLDER` rows
— fewer than the store holds, because a launch screen offering ten folders is a
file manager. On Home's Overview it is a card of `RECENTS_ON_CARD` rows, hidden
entirely when there is no history, and with the dataset currently open filtered
out: it is the subject of every other block on that page, and offering to reopen
it is offering to do nothing. That filter is not a string comparison — the list
stores the folder pointed at and `data_dir` is the `out` inside it, which differ
by one level for the standard layout. The third is the rail head's dataset menu,
which passes the same `exclude` for the same reason.

**The display rules are in `core`, not on the Home feature.** Two of the three
surfaces are the shell's own and `core/load_controller` already writes the list,
so `core/recent_view` holds reading it through the shell's settings handle,
deciding what each row says and whether it can be opened, and performing the open
and the forget; Home reads it from there like the other two. With the rules
inside `features/home`, the shell could only have reached them through a feature
service seam or an import the layering forbids. Nothing is cached: the list is at
most `MAX_RECENTS` long, the menu builds its rows when it is about to be shown,
and a cache would need invalidating by a load, by a forget and by the other
surface's forget — three writers for ten rows.

**Forgetting a row.** `recent_datasets.forget` / `record_forget` are the pure
and the stored halves, matched on the resolved path — the same key `remember`
dedupes on, so a row stored under one spelling can be removed by a caller
holding another. `recent_view.forget_recent` writes and then runs the caller's
repaint in one call, because they are one action to the user: a row whose × leaves
it on screen until something else redraws the page is indistinguishable from a
button that did nothing. Home's `recent_rows` supplies a repaint that redraws
**both** of its surfaces, since the card and the placeholder are one list in the
two states of one page. A row can be removable while it is not openable, and that
is deliberate — the row whose folder is gone is the one a user most wants off the
list — so the remove callback is never gated on the row's `enabled` flag. The
rail head's menu asks for no removal at all: a `QMenu` row is a line of text with
nothing to reveal a second control over.

Clicking a row goes through `ctx.window._load_path` with the same 50 ms deferral
the folder picker uses, so a recent open and a browsed open cannot diverge.
Nothing in `collect.py` touches this: the recents come from user settings rather
than from the dataset's own record, which is what that module reads.

#### Home's saved-plot thumbnails

Home's Overview carries a **Saved plots** strip: the newest saved plots as
clickable thumbnails, under the "Your work here" block. Home already counts what
the user has *declared* about a plate; this shows what they have *made* from it.

`home/collect.saved_plots_strip` returns `{"available", "total", "shown"}`.
`available` is False when the build has no Saved Plots feature at all, and the
card is then hidden entirely rather than shown empty — "you have saved no plots"
is a lie in a build where saving one is impossible, and it is not a state the
user can act on. An empty gallery in a build that *has* the feature is a
different fact with an action attached, so it says so and points at how. `shown`
is capped at `SAVED_PLOT_STRIP_LIMIT` and `total` is reported separately: a strip
that showed twelve of ninety and said "12" would make the landing page quietly
disagree with the gallery about how much work is saved.

Each entry carries an image **path**, not bytes. That keeps `collect.py`'s rule
intact — Home reads the record and opens no files — and leaves the one
path-to-pixels conversion in the view, where every other image load in the app
lives.

**Clicking a thumbnail opens that plot, not merely the gallery.**
`home.controller.open_saved_plot` → `saved_plots.controller.focus_saved_plot`,
which selects the Saved Plots page (which is what *builds* it — the feature is
`lazy_only`), repopulates, and calls `tab_view.scroll_to_saved_plot` to bring that
card into view and outline it for a moment (`QFrame#Panel[focusflash="true"]`).
Landing at the top of the list is, from the page, indistinguishable from the link
not working, so `focus_saved_plot` returns False when it could not reach the card
and Home turns that into a status message.

**The scroll is deferred, and aims at the card's top.** The caller has just
switched to this page, so the page has no geometry: the scroll area's range is
still zero and every card sits at y=0, and a scroll issued in that turn of the
event loop is a scroll to the top of a list that has not been laid out. That is
what shipped, and it always landed on the first card while reporting success,
because `QScrollArea.ensureWidgetVisible` returns nothing to say otherwise.
`_settle_scroll` re-aims on every `rangeChanged` the scroll bar emits, which is
what the list growing into its real height looks like from outside: the cards
size themselves from their previews' aspect ratios, so for a while after a
repopulate the position asked for is being clamped into a range that does not
exist yet. A chain of zero-delay timers is not a substitute — it drains faster
than Qt lays the cards out and settles on a stable-looking wrong answer. The
re-aiming stops after `_SCROLL_SETTLE_MS`, so a resize minutes later cannot drag
the user back, and both its timers take the scroll bar as their context object
so neither fires after the page has been torn down. It sets the
scroll bar to the card's own top rather than calling `ensureWidgetVisible`,
because a saved figure is routinely taller than the viewport and "make it
visible" then means scrolling until its *bottom* shows — the user arrives at the
foot of the plot they clicked.

**A gallery card is sized from the file header and decoded when it is
painted.** `tab_view._AspectImage` reads the PNG's declared size with
`QImageReader.size()` — about 0.02 ms, no pixels — and reserves its height from
that aspect ratio, then decodes the image in its first `paintEvent`. Qt does not
paint a widget scrolled out of view, so the paint *is* the visibility signal:
the pixels are read when a card comes into view, once, and never for a card the
user never scrolls to. Decoding at build time instead cost about 18 ms per
saved plot — a 300 dpi capture is routinely 1800×1200 — on every repopulate,
which is opening the tab, saving a plot, deleting one, renaming one, reordering
one; twenty saved plots was some 0.4 s of decoding to show two or three of them.
(`QPixmap(path)` reads from Qt's own file cache when the same path is loaded
twice, so a measurement that decodes one file repeatedly reports the cache and
not the decode.) A file whose header parses and whose pixels do not leaves the
preview labelled `(image unavailable)` rather than blank; a file that cannot be
read at all yields no preview widget, and the card draws the same named
placeholder in its place.

Thumbnails are decoded **at thumbnail size and cached**, through
`QImageReader.setScaledSize` rather than by loading the file and scaling
afterwards (`home/tab_view._thumbnail`). The cache is `QPixmapCache`, keyed on
the file's path, its modification time and the box it was scaled into — so a
plot re-saved under the same name decodes again and nothing else does. Without
it a twelve-plot strip cost ~200 ms of decoding on the UI thread on *every*
`refresh_home` — the page build, a dataset load, every record resync — for
pixels that had not changed; with it, ~10 ms. A saved plot's PNG is a 300 dpi capture,
routinely 1500×960, and Home draws twelve of them at 152 px on every
`refresh_home`, on the UI thread; decoding the full frame first does all that work
and throws it away. The tile itself is a `QPushButton` holding the picture and the
caption as **child labels in a vertical layout** — a button's own `icon` and
`text` are laid out side by side, which on a tile this narrow puts the picture in
the left half and runs the title off the right edge. The labels are transparent to
the mouse, so a click anywhere on the tile still reaches the button.

`populate_saved_plots_grid` rebuilds `ctx.runtime.saved_plots.cards` on every
repaint rather than accumulating it: `clear_layout` has already destroyed the
previous cards' C++ objects, and an index that outlived them would hand out
handles to deleted widgets.

**A rebuild holds the viewport where the user left it.** That same
`clear_layout` leaves the scroll area holding a list of nearly no height for a
few event-loop passes, so Qt clamps the scroll bar into a range that has
momentarily vanished and the value it lands on is what the user is left looking
at — deleting a plot halfway down a gallery of twelve moved the view some 2,400
px away from the card the Delete button was on. `_capture_scroll_anchor` runs
before the clear and records which cards the viewport is on, as (plot id, offset
into that card) pairs; `_restore_scroll_anchor` aims `_settle_scroll` at the
first of them that still exists, so the surviving card comes back the same
distance above the viewport's top edge. The candidates are ordered from the card
at the top of the view *upwards*, because the anchor card is usually the one
being deleted — the Delete button lives on it — and what must then hold still is
whatever is above the gap, with the following card flowing up into it. Anchoring
downwards instead holds the card *below* the deleted one in place, which drags
the whole list up by a card's height: a smaller version of the same jump. Cards
below the viewport come last, for the case where the run above has gone
entirely; at the top of the list their offsets are large and negative, so the
bar clamps to the top, which is where a gallery that just lost its first cards
belongs. Only the most recent aim runs: `_settle_scroll` stamps a generation on
`ctx.runtime.saved_plots.scroll_generation` and an older chain stops when it
sees a newer one, so the restore started by the repopulate inside
`focus_saved_plot` yields to the jump-to-card that follows it rather than the
two fighting over the same scroll bar.

Home reaches all of this through `core.lazy` proxies
(`collect._saved_plots_store`, `controller._focus_saved_plot`) rather than
function-local imports. Saved Plots is removable, and a `lazy(...)` call is not an
`import` statement — it couples nothing at module load and resolves on first use,
which is what keeps both the removability contract and
`test_deferred_imports.py`'s budget intact.

**Every shortfall Home reports offers the same next step: finish the run.**
Failures, partial wells, images without measurements, staged-but-never-processed
— all four route to `run_home_action(ctx, "complete")`, which hands the dataset
to Analyze through the shell's `_open_dataset_in_analyze`, the same entry point
Validate & Repair's *Complete this run in Analyze* uses. That carries four
things a bare folder path does not: the dataset's own recorded sidecar (so the
schema, separator and `csv_prefix` match the run being finished — a mismatched
prefix reads its done-set from files that do not exist and silently reprocesses
the plate), FOV-level incremental mode, the per-well force list, and the subset
the run is limited to. The force list is `collect.wells_needing_force`, the same
rule Validate applies: a well with images and no CSV has nothing missing by the
incremental diff, so it is skipped forever unless named, while a merely partial
well the diff does fix. The subset is `collect.wells_needing_work` — the partial
wells plus the forced ones, mirroring `validate_compute.wells_needing_work` —
sent as `only_wells`, so the completion run touches no well that is already
whole. Sending the reader to a page that shows them the gap a second time is not
a next step.

**A Datasets tool is handed the project folder, not the loaded one.** Review's
`data_dir` is where the CSVs are, which for the pipeline's layout is `out/`;
every Datasets tool wants the folder above it holding both `in/` and `out/`.
`controller.dataset_root` reads `dataset.in_dir`, which the loader sets exactly
when it detected that layout, and falls back to `data_dir` for a flat folder of
CSVs that has no parent to prefer.

**Home's plate takes `role="editor"`, not `"picker"`.** The wells are clickable
— that is what separates it from a dashboard's read-only map — but the built-in
All / Invert / Clear row is not shown. Those act on the plot selection, and
nothing on this page plots, so their effect is invisible from where they sit.

**The masthead carries one action.** Reveal-folder and open-dataset are in the
shell's own action cluster directly above the page, and Analyze and Datasets are
two of the three title-bar mode segments, permanently on screen. Only Reload is
here, because nothing else offers it and this page reports a record another
process can replace underneath it.

**Home is the one page with no rail body.** Every other feature's activation
hook re-shows one of the sidebar's per-page frames, which `on_tab_change` has
just hidden; Home shows none, because its plate is on the page and the rail's
picker would be a second one on screen. That is a supported state rather than an
accident: `RailNav` caps itself at its size hint and the rail column ends in a
stretch-0 spacer, so the surplus height has somewhere to go. Before both, the
nav was the only growable item left in a column stretched to the viewport and
its rows spread from 33px to 81px on every visit to Home.

Three rules the page is built around:

- **A figure it could not obtain renders as an em-dash with its reason, never as
  zero.** `collect.Missing` is a distinct type rather than `None` so a caller
  cannot format it as a number and a test can tell it from a real zero without
  reading prose. Real zeros — the user has defined no replicate sets — read
  "None yet". Conflating *not computed* with *computed as zero* is the bug class
  the completeness record exists to end, and the page reporting it must not
  reintroduce it.
- **Every colour it spends means what it means on the other plate maps.**
  `success` = complete, `warn` = partial, `danger` = an errored well, and
  `accent` = the anomalous one, which here is *images with no measurements* —
  Concatenate paints the identical condition (merged with no measurements CSV on
  one side) in the same token. `text_muted` carries *staged, never processed*,
  the token the Datasets dashboards use for pending and for Validate's "no
  output yet". `accent2` is unused: it means "the other of two normal groups"
  (Merge Plates), which no state here is. The rule is one colour per state and
  no colour that means something else elsewhere; `tests/test_home_plate_colors.py`
  asserts the table, and `tests/test_home_plate_render.py` samples the rendered
  widget, because the two can disagree — a table of legible tokens can still
  arrive as near-black cells if something dims them on the way to the screen.
- **The two states that describe an absence are painted in nothing at all.**
  `unchecked` (no completeness record exists) and `no_output` (the record holds
  the well and it has no evidence at all) both assert nothing, so they get the
  plate's own uncoloured cell and the legend gives them a hollow swatch. They
  cannot be confused, because `plate_cells` can only produce one of them per
  plate: `unchecked` is what a plate with no record is made of, `no_output` can
  only come from a record.
- *Partial* gets a coverage arc as well as a colour — the one state the page
  exists to make visible, and the one that has to survive a small cell and a
  fast skim.
- **The states it paints are renderings, not a second opinion.**
  `pipeline.completeness.health` remains the only classifier; `plate_cells`
  separates a staged-but-never-processed well from a half-finished one on
  `covered_any == 0`, a number already in the record.

It builds on `WellPlateSelector` + `apply_plate_geometry(role="editor")`
directly rather than subclassing `PlateProgress`. That class is a *run
dashboard* — headline, overall bar, ETA, done/failed/cancelled setters — and it
gives its plate the `status` role, which is passive selection *and*
report-only: no corner select-all, no pointing-hand cursor. Home's wells are
clickable, so it takes `editor` instead and borrows only the two lines of
`plate_progress.py`'s own construction that it wants — the lit colouring and
the shared geometry call. Undoing a read-only base's read-only-ness would be
fighting it.

A click **selects** rather than navigates: a click that teleported the reader
off the summary page would make multi-select impossible and an exploratory click
expensive. Navigation lives in the one contextual next-step row, and every
button on the page — masthead and next-step alike — routes through
`controller.run_home_action`, so "open this in Analyze" cannot come to mean two
things depending on which control was pressed.

Home must paint from its **builder**, not from its `on_activate` hook:
`tab_controller.on_tab_change` early-returns until `_line_ax_mean` exists, and
that widget comes from Line Graphs, which is drained after startup. The hook is
for repaints.

#### Batch Export (`features/batch_export/`)

The page takes a set of **export groups** — defined in its own left-hand plate
editor, persisted in `persistence.json`, and deliberately not the Sample
Definition replicate sets — and writes one figure and one CSV per group. Its
modes are a page selector on the shell band, in the order `tab_view._MODES`
declares them: Line, Bar, Scatter (cells), Scatter (aggregate), Response. Each
is a `BatchExportPanel` subclass sharing that base's group editor, output
settings and job runner, and each declares two things about itself — the
`_SOURCE_TAB` whose figure it exports, and a `_mode_key()` that names it in a
file name. Both are read by the extra destinations below, so a subclass that
inherited them silently would file its figures under the line tab's name.

A mode whose figure comes from a **removable** feature names that feature in
`_MODES`, and `_offered_modes` derives the bar from the registry: Response mode
reuses Response Curves' own collector and renderer, and Nanowells mode the
Nanowells page's, so a profile that drops either feature gets no tab for it
rather than one that builds and then raises on Run. The
list is derived rather than written twice, and `_show_batch_mode` falls back to
the default mode for a key this build does not offer — a saved view naming
`response` in such a build lands on Line rather than on nothing.

**One capture point.** Every panel writes its figure through
`base_panel._save_figure`, which resolves the export-style prefs and hands the
figure to the Qt-free `service.save_export_figure`. That single choke point is
what makes the two extra destinations possible, and it is why `_save_figure`
takes `group` and `title` as **required** keyword arguments: a call site that
omitted the group would file a gallery record whose parameters describe whatever
the plotting tab happened to be showing, under this group's name, so Restore
would draw a different figure from the thumbnail beside it — a wrong answer
rather than a missing one.
`tests/test_batch_export_destinations.py` holds every call site to passing both.

**The deck and the gallery** (`_destinations.DestinationSpool`) are two of the
three destinations the **Write to:** row offers, described in full below;
neither is an addition to a folder of image files, and neither depends on one.
Both are offered only where the Saved Plots feature is in the build, since both
are its code:

* **Saved Plots** files one gallery record per exported figure, so a batch run's
  output can be browsed, reordered, renamed and swept into the gallery's own PDF
  report.
* **PowerPoint** writes one `batch_export_<mode>.pptx` beside the figures, a
  slide per group, through the same `saved_plots._deck` writer the gallery's
  Export menu uses — so each figure arrives as editable shapes, and one whose
  vector capture failed is placed as a picture with the slide saying so. One
  deck name per mode, because a user exporting bar and then line figures into
  one folder wants two decks rather than the second overwriting the first.

Neither replaces the per-group files. A run with both ticked writes its PNGs and
CSVs exactly as before, *and* the deck, *and* the records.

**Nothing reaches either destination for a run that did not commit.** The file
writes are staged and committed atomically (`service.commit_staged_export`), so
a run that fails at group K leaves the previous complete export untouched; a
gallery that had filled with K−1 records by then would be the same defect in
different clothes. So the spool stages its captures in a directory of its own
and `_run_batch_jobs` files the gallery records only *after* the commit
succeeds, while the deck is staged **inside** the export's staging directory —
it is an ordinary output file and belongs under the same manifest as the figures
it is built from. What the destinations produced, and what they could not, are
reported separately: `DestinationSpool.summary()` and `.shortfall()`, because a
deck two slides short of the groups it names cannot say so itself.

Four kinds of shortfall are counted rather than inferred, and each is a way this
feature can produce less than it was asked for while looking complete. A
**capture** that could not be rendered (`capture_failures`). A record the
gallery **refused** (`gallery_failures`) — the gallery's writer reports a failed
image write by *returning a status string*, so it neither raises nor appends,
and a count taken from the call returning would have reported ten records filed
over an empty gallery; the count comes from the store growing instead, which is
the fact that matters. A figure filed with **no parameters** (`undescribed`),
because `_capture_group_params` returning `({}, {})` puts a record in the
gallery that is indistinguishable from a restorable one until somebody presses
Restore. And an **earlier run's deck** left in the folder by a run that did not
write one (`stale_deck`): a stale figure is named for its group, so a group this
run did not export shows in the file name, but a deck is named for the mode and
so a stale one carries exactly the name a fresh one would. It is named, never
deleted. The raster-versus-vector split is reported only once a deck exists —
a run that errored discards its staging before the deck is built, and counting
pictures in a deck nobody wrote describes an artifact that is not there.

A capture failure never costs the file the user actually asked for.
`save_export_figure` calls its `on_saved` hook *after* the write and before the
figure is closed — the only window in which a second render of the same styled
figure exists — and a capture that raises is counted into the shortfall rather
than aborting the export.

**A record's parameters describe its group, not the live tab.**
`_capture_group_params` takes the snapshot inside `_app_group_scope` +
`_app_val_col_scope`, so the record's `selections` are the group's own members
and its column is the one the panel exported with. The scope is entered by the
capture rather than relied on from the caller, because the panels differ: the
line mode already renders inside it and the bar mode never enters it at all, so
a capture trusting an ambient scope would be right on one panel and silently
wrong on the next. The snapshot is stamped `params["batch_export"] = {mode,
group}`, which is what lets the gallery summary and
`saved_plots.controller._report_batch_export_origin` say where the record came
from — the parameters reproduce the *group*, while Batch Export's own layout
controls live on the panel and not in view state, so a Restore can draw the same
data in a different arrangement. Those controls are: bars versus beeswarm,
stacked timepoints, the scatter facet mode, and — since the AXES block below —
the per-panel limits and scales and the panel selection itself. A record
captured from a two-panel, y-limited batch figure therefore restores as a
four-panel autoscaled one.

**Which panels a figure draws, and what its axes are fixed to** (`_panels.py`).
A batch figure is not one plot: the line mode stacks four panels and the bar
mode three, each a different quantity. Each mode therefore **declares** its
panels (`_PANELS`), and OUTPUT SETTINGS builds the AXES block from that
declaration rather than from a list written beside it — a shared X min/max and
scale, then per panel a keep-it checkbox, a Y min/max and a Y scale. A mode
whose figure is a single axes declares one panel, so the controls read the same
everywhere instead of appearing only on the stacked modes.

The X row governs only the panels that are actually on that x — `_X_PANELS`,
which is a different question from `_SHARE_X`'s matplotlib linking and has a
different answer on the line mode: its CDF plots intensity where its three
siblings plot time, so an X row filled in hours was clipping the CDF to 0–48
intensity units and giving three correct panels beside a fourth that looked
empty. `None` means every drawn panel, which is what a single-axes mode wants.

`panel_axes` lays the figure out with **only the panels the run kept**, and
gives each excluded panel a real axes on a throwaway figure rather than
``None``: the shared renderers take a full bundle and paint every member of it
— `render_line_series` calls methods on all four of its `LineAxes` — so a
scratch axes keeps them working unchanged while nothing reaches the exported
page. `figure_height` scales the page down with the panels it kept, and the x
sharing re-bases on the first panel that survived, since unticking the top one
would otherwise leave the rest sharing an axis that is not on the figure.

**The limits ride in the preferences; the scale is pinned on the axes.** Every
batch figure passes through `apply_export_style_prefs` on its way to disk, and
that pass re-reads the *application's* export preferences — so a limit stamped
on the axes at render time is one autoscale away from being replaced by the
app's, silently. `AxesSpec.prefs_overlay` therefore hands that pass the run's
own numbers, as a **copy**: `_ensure_export_style_prefs` returns the live
dictionary the Export Style sidebar reads and writes, and merging into it would
leave a batch run's numbers sitting in the sidebar afterwards. A stacked mode
writes `axis_buckets` keyed by the kept panels' positions on the figure; a
single-panel mode writes flat preferences with `axis_target` "All", because its
one logical plot can be several axes — the faceted scatter draws one per group
— and a bucket on the first would leave the rest autoscaled. The scale goes
through `_aw_force_xlog` / `_aw_force_ylog`, the marker that pass checks
*before* the shared `x_log`, which is the same mechanism the Response tab's
dose axis already uses.

Every field is optional and blank means "leave it", falling through to the
app-wide setting; an unreadable one reads as blank rather than as a kept
previous value, the rule the Response fit bounds already follow. **Auto is not
linear**: the scale choice is tri-state, and pinning `False` where the user
chose nothing would take the Response tab's derived logarithmic dose axis
linear. `_axes_block_refuses_the_run` is the single pre-flight every mode's
`_run_batch` opens with, and it refuses three things before the first job, for
one reason: each of them *writes a file* per group that looks like every other
file in the folder. Every panel unticked is a blank page. A `min` at or above
its `max` is a typo under columns headed `min` and `max`, and matplotlib
answers the equal case by expanding the range to an interval of its own. A
`Log` scale bounded at or below zero has no position for that bound, so
matplotlib drops it and autoscales. `_axes_complaints` names every offending
row in one pass — a user who mistyped two rows fixes both before the next run —
and skips the rows of unticked panels, whose numbers describe nothing that is
drawn.

**Which controls a mode offers is a declaration, not a shared form.** Three
class attributes say so, and each exists because the generic control was wrong
somewhere rather than merely redundant. `_X_IS_NUMERIC` is false on the bar
modes, whose x is one position per group member: a numeric bound there is three
bars crushed into the left of every frame, so the row is absent rather than
offered and ignored. `_AXES_SCALE_OFFERED` is false on the scatter modes, whose
own `X log` / `Y log` apply `log10(v + 1)` so cells at zero stay on the figure
— two controls for one axis is worse than either, and the one kept is the one
that is not lossy. `_AXES_FOLLOW_HEADER` is false on Scatter and Response,
whose axes are themselves a choice: the block asking for a range sat above the
rows that pick what the axis *is*, and Scatter carried two rows labelled "X:"
a hundred pixels apart meaning different things. Those two modes call
`_build_output_tail` themselves, after their axis rows. `_X_ROW_LABEL` and
`_Y_ROW_LABEL` name each mode's axes for the same reason: "X:" over a row of
numbers does not say what unit to type.

**"Each export group produces:" is derived from the controls**, in
`_refresh_run_summary`, and connected to every control that changes the answer
(`_wire_run_summary`, which each mode extends through
`_extra_summary_signals`). It was a static string, and by the time the panel
could also write a per-cell CSV, a slide deck, a gallery record and three of
its four panels it was wrong in four ways at once — while being the one block
in the column that says in plain words what pressing Run does. A mode supplies
its own words through `_SUMMARY_FIGURE_LEAD`, `_SUMMARY_FIGURE_NOTE`,
`_SUMMARY_CSV_LINE` and `_summary_footnotes`; the bar and scatter modes
override `_summary_figure_lead` instead, because a toggle on those panels
decides how many figures one group gets.

**Three destinations, none of them privileged.** The **Write to:** row is the
first thing OUTPUT SETTINGS asks, because Folder and Format are consequences of
its answer rather than settings above it. Nothing forces a folder of image
files to be the base a run pays for: `DestinationSpool.capture` renders its own
PNG and SVG from the in-memory figure and never opens the file the folder write
produces, so a deck or a gallery record from a run that wrote no images holds
the same picture. `_wants_image_files` / `_wants_deck` / `_wants_gallery` are
the three answers, `_wants_disk_output` is the pair that need a folder, and
`_sync_destination_widgets` greys what the chosen set does not use — Format
describes the image files alone, the folder is wanted by those and the deck but
not the gallery, and the per-cell CSV is a file in that folder. A run with
nothing ticked is refused by `_run_is_refused`, which is also the one pre-flight
every mode's `_run_batch` opens with.

**The chosen destinations are snapshotted for the life of a run**
(`_destinations`, filled from `_ticked_destinations` at the top of
`_run_batch_jobs` and cleared in its `finally`), for the same reason the spool
and the axes are: the runner pumps `processEvents()` between jobs, so the
Write to: row is live while an export runs. Read per job, unticking **Image
files** halfway gave the first groups their files and the rest none, and then —
because the commit consults the same answer — discarded the ones already
written and reported the run a success. Ticking it halfway was worse: staging
had been placed in a system temp dir on the earlier answer, so the commit
attempted an `os.replace` across filesystems, the one thing `new_staging_dir`
exists to prevent, and the exception escaped into the Run slot with no dialog.
`_set_destination_row_enabled` disables the row for the run's duration so the
panel cannot show a destination that is not the one in use, and re-derives
each control's idle state on the way back rather than remembering it.

The run's headline is built centrally too (`_where_it_went`): each mode used to
interpolate the output folder into its own success and status text before the
run, so a gallery-only run announced `✓ 2 group(s) → out/` and gave the status
bar an absolute path to a directory that does not exist and received nothing.
The modes now pass the group count and the runner appends where the output
actually went.

`_out_path(write_dir, name)` is **the one place a job's output path is built**,
returning `None` for a run that writes no files, and
`save_export_figure` takes that `None` as "style the figure, skip the write,
still call `on_saved`". Nine sites across four modules each held their own
`open()` before this was one function, and converting eight of them would have
been worse than converting none — one folder holding the files of a run that
asked for none.
`tests/test_batch_export_destinations.py::test_every_job_output_path_is_built_by_the_one_function`
is what holds the tenth.

The summary CSVs follow the image files, since they are files in the same
folder: a deck-only or gallery-only run saves pictures and no numbers, which
`_refresh_run_summary` states outright before the run rather than leaving as an
absence afterwards. A gallery-only run also stages **outside** the output
