folder and discards rather than commits — `new_staging_dir` creates `out_dir`
to hold its temp directory, so committing (or even staging there) would leave
the user an empty folder and a manifest describing no files. `DestinationSpool.begin`
takes the directory to stage under for the same reason: on the filesystem the
captures will be copied *to*, which is the output folder for a run that writes
there and the dataset folder — where `saved_plots/` lives — for one that does
not.

**The rows behind a figure** (`_cell_rows.py`). An opt-in checkbox writes the
plot tabs' `Save cell data…` file beside each group's figure — one row per cell
the figure was computed from, with the scope block and the marker columns.
Nothing is re-implemented: the scope comes from the mode's own source tab
(`_CELL_SCOPE` plus `_CELL_SCOPE_FN`, since Scatter's two modes are two
different plots with two different scope builders), the rows from
`export/cell_scope_compute.build_chunk`, and the file is written by
`export/worker.CellExportWriter`, so the batch file's columns, quoting,
blank-versus-zero rule and atomic replace are the tab's. The writer drains a
queue until `DONE`; the batch caller fills and closes the queue first and calls
it inline, which is that contract used without a thread rather than in spite of
one — the GUI path needs a thread because a user is waiting, and a batch job is
already inside a blocking run.

**A tab's scope reads that tab's controls, and a batch run overrides all of
them.** Each `cell_scope` therefore takes explicit-argument overrides —
`val_col` and `timepoints` on Line, Bar and Response; the axis entries, the
resolved columns and the timepoints on Scatter — each defaulting to what the
tab itself says, so the tab's own call is unchanged. Without them the per-cell
file described *the plot on screen*: a bar run over t=24 and t=48 wrote two
files of whatever timepoint the Bar tab happened to be on, each internally
consistent, each named for a timepoint it did not contain. Overriding rather
than rebuilding is what keeps one definition of what each tab's population is —
its markers, its gate layer, its threshold rule.

The write is refused, and said, in three distinguishable cases: no loaded
wells, no readable rows, and a gating recompute still in flight. The last is
the refusal `export/service` already makes for the same reason — the gating
worker rewrites verdict columns in place on the cached frames, and the runner
pumps the event loop between jobs — and without it a run started mid-recompute
gives its early groups one gating state and its later ones another, under one
manifest.

`_write_cell_rows_for` **enters the group scope itself**, for the reason
`_capture_group_params` does: the scope reads the live selections through
`cell_scope_compute.plotted_wells`, and the bar mode never enters that scope at
all, so a writer trusting an ambient one would give every group's file the same
wells under a different group's name. A failure there is recorded as a run
shortfall rather than raised — the figure and the summary CSV are what the run
was primarily asked for — and the notes are counted into the final status line
rather than each overwriting the last.

**Response mode** (`response_panel.py`) renders through Response Curves' own
`collect_response` and `draw_response` rather than a batch twin of them, with
the export group swapped in through `_app_group_scope` — so each figure is the
curve the tab would draw if that group were the only thing selected. Its panel
carries its own Channel and Property (including *Fraction above threshold* and *Events above threshold*), x
variable, series split, x scale, fit model with pinned plateaus, and timepoint
selection; its CSV is the tab's own column shape with `group` in front, carrying
the drawn points, **the members that could not be placed with the reason each
was left out**, and a row per fit including a refused one. A group with no
placeable points writes nothing at all rather than blank axes beside an empty
CSV.

**Nanowells mode** (`nanowell_panel.py`) draws each figure through the
Nanowells page's own composition, `nanowell/controller.draw_view` — the one
function the page's redraw calls for Distribution, Array map, Trajectories and
Position, notes and empty states included — and `resolve_metric` for the
channel and per-nanowell fallbacks. Per export group it writes the chosen view
for each ticked metric (the Array map, which draws one well, once per well) and
one CSV of `distribution_compute.wells_summary`, the per-well summary prepared as
the Distribution view prepares it (per-nanowell metrics at each well's first
timepoint, the fixed cohort when ticked), with the exclusions spelled out by
reason and a row naming each of the group's wells with no nanowell table. A
group's replicate sets stay sets and its solo wells stand alone, as the page
groups a selection (`_figure_groups`); a group with no nanowell table at all is
skipped and says so. An Array map asked for a timepoint a well was not imaged at
is a figure saying exactly that, where the page would fall back to the well's
first timepoint. The tables and the metrics at the chosen baseline are read
once per run — from the page's state when it holds this dataset — and every
control once, before the first job. There is no AXES block (a Nanowells figure
is several panels the page lays out itself), no per-cell CSV and no fold-change
or spread control: a nanowell fold change is against the baseline chosen here.
`_capture_group_params` sets the page's view, metric, axis, baseline, cohort,
well and timepoint to the figure's for the capture and puts them back, so a
gallery record restores to the figure beside it rather than to whatever the page
was showing.

Response mode carries **no fold-change controls** either, and that is a decision
rather than an omission: the other modes normalise through the panel's own
fold-change state, while a response curve normalises inside its collector off
the shared `ctx.state.plot` state every plotting page shares. A panel-local
control there would be offered, moved, and silently ignored by the export it
appears to configure, so `_INCLUDES_FOLD_CHANGE` is False and the panel's info
text says where the setting lives instead.

That difference reaches one more place than the controls.
`_control_selections` carries the replicate set a fold-change control names
*into* the group scope, hidden, so a control belonging to another export group
still resolves — and which controls those are comes from
`_fold_change_control_refs`. The base class answers from its construction-time
snapshot, which is right for a mode whose own Control combo edits it. Response
overrides it to read the **live** shared state, because that is what its
collector reads: from the snapshot, a control the user set on the plotting band
*after* opening the mode would be absent from the scope,
`resolve_control_wells` — which scans exactly that scope — would resolve it to
no wells, and every point would drop out of a figure whose y axis still read
`÷ DMSO`. Where a scope and the collector inside it touch one piece of state,
they have to read the same copy of it.

### 5.3 Centre tab builders: `features/<feature>/tab_view.py`

Each module exposes a single `build_<name>_tab(ctx, parent)` function —
`ctx` is a `ViewerContext`. Each builder references `ctx.state` / `ctx.widgets` /
`ctx.runtime` (and the held collaborators `ctx.notify` / `ctx.figures` /
`ctx.coordinator` / `ctx.persistence` / `ctx.features`, plus the lone window
accessor `ctx.window`) directly — there is no `ctx.app` (the `CTX_APP_BUDGET = 0`
ratchet hard-bans it).
The function:

1. Creates a `make_plot_with_right_dock(parent)` host (returns
   `(plot_area, layout, right_dock)`) — the right-side dock is reserved for
   the Properties / Export Style sidebar.
2. Adds the per-tab controls row (channel, metric combo, timepoint combo, an
   **Export** dropdown, **Properties**). Plotting's row is the shared
   `ControlBand` (§5.2).
3. Mounts a `PlotCard` from `widgets/plot_card.py` (matplotlib figure +
   custom toolbar inside a styled panel).
4. Stashes the figure / canvas on `app` so controllers can reach them
   later (`app._line_fig`, `app._bar_canvas`, …).

Every `PlotCard`-based tab (Bar Plot, Line Graphs, Scatter — cells and
aggregate, Distribution, Heat Map, Spatial, Multivariate) gets its **Save**
dropdown from one builder, `core.ui_helpers.build_plot_save_menu`, rather than
assembling it itself. The builder is the reason the eight menus agree: written
per tab they had drifted to six "Save Figure…" against two "Save figure…" and
seven "Export CSV…" against one "Export Summary CSV…", and — the part that
matters more — a menu written per tab is a menu that can *miss* an entry per
tab. `cells_cb` is therefore a required keyword, so a tab cannot acquire this
menu without offering the cells its plot was computed from; the two data
callbacks and the card key are all a tab supplies, and per-tab variation
(Spatial's own first-entry label and the action handle it enables with the
level, Multivariate's tooltip) is a parameter rather than a fork.
`tests/test_plot_save_menu.py` holds both halves, matching the button label
with and without the caret because `_with_caret` appends one. It also scans
every plot tab's string constants for the retired "Export CSV" label: the
rename swept the menu construction and left two Spatial tooltips telling the
user to click a button that no longer exists, which the menu-shape tests could
not see because a tooltip is an ordinary string rather than an
`add_menu_action` argument. `tests/test_guards_bite.py` carries its bite cases.

The five standard entries: an export-data action specific to the tab, "Save
cell data…" (§ below), "Save figure…"
(`save_active_card_figure`, a Save-As dialog), "Copy figure as SVG"
(`core.plot_card_actions.copy_active_card_as_svg`), and "Save to Saved Plots"
(`core.plot_card_actions.save_card_to_gallery`, which calls the card's
`saveFigureToGallery()` — a public wrapper around the hover-save button's
whole-figure capture, added so a persistent menu action can trigger it without
hover-axis context). **All three take the card's registry name**
(`copy_active_card_as_svg(ctx, "<card_attr>")` and so on), and a tab-local menu
must pass its own: the alternative is resolving "the first visible card" from
the `_CARDS` roster, and in Split View two cards are visible at once, so Bar
Plots' own "Copy SVG" copied the line figure.
`tests/test_export_menu_acts_on_its_own_card.py` holds every tab's three items
to naming the same card. The name is optional only for a global toolbar action
that belongs to no tab, which is what the fallback exists for. A tab's `PlotCard` must
also call `ui_helpers.apply_plot_card_decorators(ctx, card, "<Tab Name>")`
for the hover-based gallery save and Saved Plots registration to exist at
all, and its widget-registry attribute name must be listed in
`core/plot_card_actions.py::_CARDS`, which maps a card name to its default
export filename, backs the global "first visible card" fallback, and is
re-exported as `PLOT_CARD_ATTRS` — the roster the global Screen/Publication
toggle (`allwell.py::_on_present_toggled`) iterates, calling `setPlotTheme` on
each name it finds in the widget registry. The roster is a hardcoded allowlist,
not auto-discovered from the feature registry, so a plot tab absent from it
silently gets no Screen/Publication toggle and no global Copy/Save.

That allowlist has now been short three times — Spatial, Multivariate and
Response Curves — and the third time is what the two rules below are between
them for. A card the toggle never reaches does not merely fail to flip on the
click: `plot_style.tokens_for` resolves the theme by asking
`figure._plot_card.plotTheme()`, so every subsequent redraw faithfully repaints
the stale answer, and the tab looks broken in a way no redraw corrects.
`tests/test_plot_card_roster.py` holds both halves — that the roster is written
**once** (no module restates the names; the shell reads `PLOT_CARD_ATTRS`), and
that it is written **completely**: the expected set is derived by scanning the
source for a `register("_x_card", …)` in a module that constructs a `PlotCard`,
so a new tab that skips the roster fails there instead of shipping. Home's
`_home_recents_card` and `_home_saved_plots_card` are named in that test as the
two registered cards that are deliberately outside it — a gallery thumbnail and
a recent-datasets tile, neither with axes to restyle or a figure to copy.

The card also floats a small button row over whichever axes the cursor is on:
**copy**, always; **save to Saved Plots**, once a tab has wired a save handler
through the decorator above; and **save the whole figure**, on multi-axis
figures only, where it differs from the per-panel save. Copy was
multi-axis-only too, justified in its own docstring by "the whole-canvas Copy
button" — which no longer exists, since the card's header was retired when the
shared ControlBand took over its controls. The only whole-figure copy left is
the `Save ▾` menu's "Copy figure as SVG", so on the five single-axes plot tabs
the rule removed the affordance rather than de-duplicating it, and the hover
row showed a lone save glyph. The button's tooltip and its toast follow the
figure: on one axes it copies the plot, and calling that "this panel" names a
division the reader cannot see.

`PlotCard._panel_bbox` decides what a per-panel capture crops to, for both the
copy and the save path: the axes' tight bbox on a multi-axis figure (with the
siblings hidden, so a neighbour's ink cannot bleed into the crop), and the
whole figure on a single-axes one. The two differ only in what they discard,
and which is worth measuring rather than reasoning about — an axes-tight crop
**does** carry a free `ax.text` drawn below the axes (Response Curves' omission
caption survives it) and does **not** carry anything the figure owns, so
Distribution, which titles its single-axes figure with a `suptitle`, had been
filing untitled plots in the gallery that looked complete.
5. Wires signals to the feature's controller / renderer entry points
   (e.g. matplotlib clicks → `features.scatter.controller.on_scatter_click`,
   button presses → `features.barplot.renderer.redraw_bars`).

Each feature package owns the full vertical slice for its tab — the
tab-builder, the controller, the renderer (where applicable), and any
panel-shaped sub-views the tab embeds. `centre_view` (under `core/`) just
calls the per-feature `build_<name>_tab` from a single registration loop.

#### The feature registry (`core/feature_registry.py` + `features/registry.py`)

Core never imports a feature directly. Every feature is declared once as a
`FeatureDescriptor` in the `FEATURES` list in `features/registry.py` — the
**single sanctioned importer** of `review.features.*` (enforced by
`tests/test_architecture_contracts.py::
test_no_module_scope_imports_of_removable_features`). A descriptor bundles
everything core used to hard-code:

- `build(ctx, frame)` — the tab body (a lazy wrapper over `build_<name>_tab`);
- `group` / `lazy_only` — placement + drain policy the page-stack reads;
- `states` — the `AppState` slices the feature owns (`StateSpec(attr, factory)`),
  attached at construction by `attach_feature_state` so `core/app_state.py`
  imports no feature state class (the import-inversion);
- `on_activate` / `on_selection_changed` / `on_channel_changed` /
  `on_dataset_loaded` — dispatch hooks (the bodies that used to live in
  `tab_controller.on_tab_change`, `selection_controller._refresh_tab_view`,
  `channel_state_controller.recalculate_threshold`'s fan-out, and
  `load_controller`'s per-feature post-load refresh). Core fans each out over
  `registry.with_hook("<name>")` in declaration order, so it names no feature;
- `redraw` — a **lazy factory** returning a plot feature's figure-redraw
  callable, `() -> ((ctx) -> None)`; core plot orchestration
  (`plot_orchestrator.redraw_app`, tab activation, the Properties sidebar)
  triggers a redraw by name via `registry.redraw(ctx, "<tab>")`, which calls
  `d.redraw()(ctx)`, so it names no renderer (Bar Plots / Line Graphs /
  Response Curves / Scatter Plot / Distribution / Heat Map / Spatial /
  Multivariate register it). The factory shape is load-bearing and is checked
  by calling it: a `_lazy_hook` — a `hook(ctx)`, one shape short — sits here
  perfectly happily and makes every dispatch through the registry raise
  `TypeError` before it reaches the figure, which is what Response Curves
  shipped, past a guard that asked only whether the field was set. **The
  Image Table deliberately registers none.** Its render reads images off disk,
  so it happens when the user presses Generate and at no other time — including
  on a Saved Plots restore, where a saved grid can be hundreds of frames and
  paying for them is the user's decision to make. What restore owes the reader
  instead is not implying the pictures match the controls: `apply_image_table`
  marks the table stale (`runtime.image_table.builder_dirty`), which is the flag
  a shelf edit already sets, so the shelf header carries its standing
  "edited — press Generate" cue;
- `fold_change_scope_factory` — the feature's fold-change redraw scope
  (`core/scope_registry` registers these from the descriptors);
- `plot_card_decorator` — a feature that decorates every plot card (Saved Plots'
  "save to gallery" hover button); plot tabs apply *all* registered decorators
  via `ui_helpers.apply_plot_card_decorators`, so no tab imports Saved Plots;
- `view_state_io` — a feature that owns its own `view_state` snapshot/restore
  pair (Image Table and Heat Map); `persistence/view_state.py` fans this out and
  so never names the feature (each `view_state_io.py` is imported only when its
  feature is present). Heat Map's captures the colormap / scale / vmin·vmax /
  toggles / active layout by reusing the layout-sidecar serializer. Image
  Table's `apply_image_table` restores `ctx.state.image_table`'s row/col dims,
  channel options, per-cell values, **and the table's scope** — the
  `active_wells` / `active_timepoints` / `active_fovs` selections that decide
  *what the table is of*, as against how it is laid out. That scope is the half
  that has to be captured deliberately, because an **empty** set does not mean
  empty: `grid_layout._axis_dim_values` reads it as *all*
  (`sel if sel else _well_options(ctx)`). A snapshot that omitted it therefore
  restored a saved three-well, one-timepoint grid as the whole plate across the
  whole time course, with the right channels on it — which reads as a restore
  that did nothing rather than one that lost something. The sets are stored as
  sorted lists (wells in `parse_rc` plate order) because the block is written
  into `persistence.json` and `json.dump` cannot serialize a `set`; an empty
  selection is omitted rather than written out well by well, since the omitted
  and empty forms restore identically. A missing key **leaves the live value
  alone** — the one place in this module that does not overwrite from state,
  because every plot saved before the scope was captured is silent about it and
  clearing the user's plate selection on their behalf would be its own bug.
  Restoring the wells also re-lights the Image Table's sidebar plate, which is a
  separate selection from `selection.selected_wells`; state is written first, so
  `picker_view._on_plate_changed` short-circuits and no second layout rebuild
  fires. It then calls `builder_view.builder_refresh`
  so the drag-and-drop shelf's own widget tree reflects the restored spec right
  away — the shelf caches its built spec (`ctx.runtime.image_table.builder_spec`)
  and only rebuilds when something invalidates it, so a restore that skipped
  this call left the shelf showing whatever it was built with on the tab's first
  construction (typically its "nothing chosen yet" fallback: every channel, the
  last timepoint) even though the underlying state was already correct. It also
  sets `ctx.runtime.image_table.restored_this_load = True`, reset to `False` at
  the top of every `load_controller.load_directory` call — `registry.
  _loaded_image_table`'s post-load reset checks this flag and skips wiping the
  grid back to fresh-tab defaults when a saved one was just restored earlier in
  the same load;
- `per_well_selection` / `single_well_selection` — selection-behaviour flags
  that replaced the hard-coded tab-name sets in `selection_controller`;
- `services` — named callables the feature offers to core, keyed
  `"<area>.<verb>"` (`"labels.grid_refresh"`, `"cell_gating.start_worker"`,
  `"heatmap.build_layout_sidebar"`), each a lazy factory exactly as `redraw` is.
  This is the seam for what a fan-out hook cannot express: a refresh aimed at
  **one** named feature rather than broadcast to all of them, a widget builder,
  and a **query** — a call that returns a value, which an `fn(ctx) -> None` hook
  has nowhere to put. Core calls them as `ctx.features.call(key, …)` (void, and
  the return says whether anything ran) or `ctx.features.query(key, …,
  default=…)`, where the default is what the app believes when the feature that
  would have answered is not in this build. The **support libraries** — QC,
  crop, the export-style panel — own no tab and so carry no descriptor; they
  register into the same lookup through `FeatureRegistry.register_service`, from
  the same `features/registry.py`, so there is one answer to "what can core call
  by name". Two features declaring one key is rejected at registration: a key is
  how core addresses one feature, and two claimants would mean the call reaches
  whichever loaded first.

  A string key fails differently from an import, and silently — a typo, a
  one-sided rename, or a feature that stops declaring a service leaves `call`
  returning `False` and the refresh simply never happening. So
  `tests/test_feature_services_partition.py` relates the two sides in both
  directions: every key called from the tree must be declared, and every
  declared service must be called. The first half catches the typo; the second
  catches the service left behind by a rewritten call site, which would
  otherwise sit there looking like live wiring.

`parent` links a sub-leaf to its composite container (Plotting / Image Browser /
Home); `registry.sub_leaves(parent)` enumerates a container's
sub-tabs from the descriptor list, so a container never hard-codes its leaf names
and dropping a leaf is a one-line/manifest edit.

`ReviewApp.__init__` builds the registry (`app._features`) before `AppState`;
`centre_view`, `tab_controller`, `selection_controller`, `channel_state_controller`,
and `scope_registry` all read it. Every hook callable imports its feature lazily,
so building the registry pulls no heavy deps.

Building it is also what wires the two lower layers that need a feature callback
but may not import one: the **row-cache projectors** (`data/cache_projectors`,
run by `data_loading.load_and_project` — curation, then QC, then crop) and the
support services above. Both live in `build_feature_registry` because it is the
one place allowed to name a feature; `core/` holds no wiring module for either.
**Both are registered lazily**, resolving their target on first call exactly as
the hooks do (`_lazy_projector`), because the alternative breaks the laziness
this section opens with: registering the resolved `apply_qc_to_cache` reaches
the data layer and pandas through it, which took a registry build from 15ms to
6.6s in a process that had not already imported them. The app does not feel that
— `runtime_app` imports `data_loading` at module scope anyway — which is why
`tests/test_registry_build_stays_light.py` measures it in a subprocess that
imports the registry and nothing else.
`core/scope_registry.register_default_scopes` completes the picture from the
other end: it takes the registry the caller hands it (the window's, or one
passed directly) and never builds one, because a caller with no registry to
offer has no feature scopes to register — an empty run is the honest answer, not
a transient registry standing in for the app's.

**`review/core/` and `review/data/` therefore import no feature at
all** — not at module scope, and not function-locally either. That is the
roadmap's terminal condition 3, and `CORE_FEATURE_IMPORT_BUDGET == 0` in
`tests/test_guardrails.py` holds it there. The practical difference is that a
subset build's call sites now no-op *by contract*: before, a site like
`channel_state_controller.refresh_heatmap_aggregation_options` survived the thin
profile only because its widget-presence check happened to return before the
import, which is an accident of layout rather than a decision.

**To remove a feature, comment out its line in `FEATURES`.** Its rail entry,
dispatch, state slice, fold-change scope, and persistence drop out together, with
no other edit and no startup error — the same one-line-removable property §5.10
gives Split View, generalized to **every** Review feature.

Every removable feature also tolerates having its package **deleted** from disk,
not just commented out. Three mechanisms make this hold (and three guards keep it
from regressing):

- **Incidental feature-state access from core** is read through
  `AppState.feature_slice(name)`, which returns `None` when the feature is
  disabled (the slice was never attached) — so e.g. Image Browser's
  `preview` / `review_image` / `image_table` accesses in dataset-load,
  stats-cache-invalidation, and channel-switch no-op cleanly.
- **Genuinely-shared state / utilities don't live on a feature slice.** The
  group-statistics result cache is core (`core/stats_cache_state.py`,
  `AppState.stats_cache`) — it holds the per-well aggregation and CDF memos
  alongside the replicate-set results, which is what makes every existing
  invalidation site clear all three — not the Statistics feature's `StatsState`; the
  dataset-level `get_all_timepoints` lives in `data/data_loading.py`, not
  `scatter`.
- **No module-scope import of a removable feature exists** outside
  `features/registry.py`. Core/`runtime_app`/inter-feature delegates are bound
  through the `core/lazy.py` proxy (resolves on first call) or imported
  function-locally, so importing any module never imports a removable feature.
  Support libs (`export`, `preview`, `crop`, `qc`) are always present.

Guards: `test_no_module_scope_imports_of_removable_features` (repo-wide import
rule), `test_disabling_a_leaf_feature_drops_it_everywhere`, and
`tests/test_feature_removal.py` (full-app boot+load comment-out *and*
`sys.meta_path` deletion tests for Image Browser, Statistics, scatter, barplot).

#### Build profiles — running / building / shipping a feature subset

The one-line-removable property above is the mechanism a **profile** drives at
scale: the full app is the single source of truth, and any thin subset is a
*profile* of it, not a fork. A profile is a small TOML manifest under `profiles/`
naming the top-level features (and an optional per-parent sub-tab allowlist) to
keep; `review/core/profile.py` loads it (stdlib-only — safe to import from
the pipeline side too). It applies at three levels, all sharing the one
`Profile.includes` predicate so they never disagree:

- **Runtime** — `build_feature_registry(profile)` keeps only the admitted
  descriptors, so `ALLWELL_PROFILE=thin python -m allwell` runs the subset off
  the *full* tree with nothing deleted. The active profile is the
  `ALLWELL_PROFILE` env var, or a baked `active_profile.txt` marker in a frozen
  bundle, else the full app. **A reduced profile announces itself**, once per
  process, at WARNING, naming the profile and which of those two chose it. A
  subset build is degraded output — whole features and their state slices are
  absent — and without the line it is indistinguishable from the full app until
  something reaches past the gap and raises `AttributeError: AppState.<slice>
  is unavailable`. A stray `active_profile.txt` left in a working tree by a
  profile build does exactly that, permanently and silently, which is the case
  the message is written for. The full app says nothing, because a warning on
  every launch is the noise that gets real warnings ignored.
- **Binary** — `all_well.spec` reads the same profile: it omits excluded
  features' source from the bundle and **drops their unique heavy deps
  automatically** from the catalog (`profiles/full.toml`'s per-feature `deps`).
  Both matter — adding a dep to PyInstaller `excludes` only prunes the module
  graph, so the spec *also* skips that package's `collect_all` (which is what
  keeps its `.so`/`.dylib` payload out). A StarDist-only `thin` binary thus drops
  `torch`/`torchvision`/`cellpose` (Cellpose) and `sklearn`/`umap`/`pynndescent`
  (Multivariate). The pure decision math is `scripts/profile_build.py`, which
  also owns `bundle_name(version, profile)` — the unit-tested helper that names
  the output `AllWell-{version}` for the full app or `AllWell-{version}-{profile}`
  for a subset (e.g. `AllWell-<version>-thin`), so a full build and a thin build are
  distinguishable by name. `all_well.spec` uses it for the
  COLLECT/BUNDLE output name and the macOS `CFBundleDisplayName`, while keeping
  the internal executable name `AllWell` so `CFBundleExecutable` and the
  re-exec/launcher paths are unaffected.
- **Source** — `scripts/derive_profile.py --apply` physically deletes the
  excluded features' paths/tests for a shippable stripped tree.

Two seams keep this honest beyond the registry: **cross-build data safety** — a
`persistence.json` written by another build round-trips untouched (unknown
sections / `view_state` tabs / `pipeline_info` blocks are preserved, never
rewritten) — and the pipeline's **lazy Cellpose import** (`process_microscopy`
resolves `pipeline/cellpose.py` via a PEP 562 module `__getattr__`), so a
StarDist-only build can omit that file entirely. Guarded by
`tests/test_feature_profile.py` (subset boots + loads), `test_derive_profile.py`
(the strip plan), and `test_profile_build.py` (binary dep-gating).

**The two shipped profiles.** `thin` is the distribution subset: Plotting,
Statistics, Home and the Image Browser narrowed to Segmentation + Image Table.
Statistics is in it because the group comparisons are what most users open the
plots to argue about — a build with the bar chart and without the test behind it
answers half the question. `plotting_only` is Plotting alone, and exists as the
minimal case the profile guardrail boots: it proves the registry filter drops
whole features and the app still starts and loads a dataset off what survives.

**Defining a profile.** A named build *is* a file: `profiles/<name>.toml`. The
`<name>` is the filename (minus `.toml`), and the same `ALLWELL_PROFILE=<name>`
env var selects it for both running and building — there is nothing else to
register. To author one, write the manifest and list the features you want:

```toml
# profiles/myapp.toml  →  select with  ALLWELL_PROFILE=myapp
name = "myapp"                                    # must match the filename

# STRICT ALLOWLIST of top-level tabs: list EVERY tab to keep.
# Anything omitted is dropped from the build.
features = ["Plotting", "Image Browser", "Home"]

# OPTIONAL. Only NARROWS a parent already listed in `features` — keep just
# these sub-tabs of it. Omit a parent here and ALL its sub-tabs are kept.
[subtabs]
"Image Browser" = ["Segmentation", "Image Table"]
```

The two rules that decide what ends up in the build:

- **`features` is a strict allowlist** of top-level tabs — list *every* tab you
  want; anything not listed is removed. (An empty/missing `features` means the
  full app — that is what the absence of a profile gives you.)
- **`[subtabs]` only narrows**, never adds. A parent that appears there keeps
  *only* the sub-tabs you list; a parent you leave out of `[subtabs]` keeps all
  of its sub-tabs. Listing a sub-tab under a parent that isn't in `features` has
  no effect (the whole parent is already gone).

**Valid names** — the source of truth is `review/features/registry.py`
`_features()` (entries with a `group=` are top-level; entries with a `parent=`
are that parent's sub-leaves), so this list can't silently drift from the code:

| Put in `features` (top-level tabs) | Put in `[subtabs]` (parent → sub-leaves) |
| --- | --- |
| `Plotting` | `Plotting` → `Bar Plots`, `Line Graphs`, `Scatter Plot`, `Distribution`, `Heat Map` |
| `Statistics` | |
| `Multivariate` | |
| `Spatial` | |
| `Image Browser` | `Image Browser` → `Image Table`, `Cell Browser`, `Playground` |
| `smFISH` | |
| `Review CSV` | |
| `Home` | `Home` → `Ratios`, `Pipeline Info` |
| `Saved Plots` | |
| `Batch Export` | |

**A sub-package in the catalog is removable from its siblings too.** A nested
`[[feature]]` block — Image Browser's three sub-tabs, Home's two — is a directory
`derive_profile` deletes on its own, so nothing outside it may name it at module
scope, and that includes the package next door.
`test_architecture_contracts.py::test_a_container_feature_does_not_import_its_own_removable_sub_packages`
reads the nested blocks out of the manifest and enforces it, because the
sibling-level guard compares only the first path segment under `features/` and
reads an intra-`image_browser` import as intra-feature.

A function-local import is **not** the repair: a lazy import of a deleted module
fails just as hard, one frame later. Shared code moves down a layer instead.
That is why an address-to-pixels lookup lives in `data/frame_load.py`, the
per-dimension option lists in `data/dataset_dims.py`, and the channel-tint
palette in `widgets/lut_cmaps.py` — each was owned by one Image Browser sub-tab
and reached for by another, so deleting the Image Table took the Cell Browser
with it while the manifest said all three were independent.

**Some sub-leaves cannot be narrowed away.** A descriptor carrying
`removable=False` is admitted by `Profile.includes` whatever a `[subtabs]` line
says, so it never appears in the table above and listing it there does nothing.
Home's `Cell Gating` and `Sample Map` and Image Browser's `Segmentation` are the
three. The flag exists because a container that enumerates its sub-tabs from the
registry hands the profile a lever over *every* leaf, including ones other code
reaches unconditionally: Sample Map's three layers are built together from one
roster and Overview reports the counts of all three, so a profile dropping the
tab would leave a page naming groups, variables and labels with no editor for any
of them. Declaring the tab and then relying on nobody excluding it is not a
contract. `test_feature_profile.py` holds the flag and `profiles/full.toml`
to the same story: a non-removable descriptor must not carry a catalog entry,
since `derive_profile` would delete source the registry insists is present.

**The one non-tab name: `Cellpose`.** It's a pipeline unit, not a Qt tab, so it
lives only in `features` (never `[subtabs]`). List `"Cellpose"` to keep the
Torch-backed segmenter; omit it and a subset *binary* drops
`torch`/`torchvision`/`cellpose` (StarDist stays the default segmenter). This is
why `thin` and `plotting_only`, which don't list it, are StarDist-only.

**End to end.** Write `profiles/myapp.toml` as above, then:

```bash
ALLWELL_PROFILE=myapp python allwell.py            # run the subset off the full tree
ALLWELL_PROFILE=myapp scripts/build_executable.sh  # build a subset binary
```

For a physically stripped source tree (not just a runtime/binary filter), feed
the same profile to `scripts/derive_profile.py --apply`, which deletes the
excluded features' `paths`/`tests` per `profiles/full.toml`.

One Qt builder sits in `core/` rather than under a feature package:
`core/fold_change_controls_view.py` exposes
`install_fold_change_controls(ctx, parent, layout, scope=…)` — the
Control + Baseline dropdown pair installed on both the Bar Plots and
Line Graphs control rows (inside each tab's `Fold change ▾` popover, not
on a visible row). It is in `core/` because both of its consumers
are features, and because it owns the cross-tab widget sync
(`_sync_widgets_to_state`) that mirrors each state change into the
other tab's widget instances, so the shared `state.plot.fc_*` values stay
visually in lockstep across tab switches. Its pure-logic half — the
scope registry and dirty-flag helpers it re-exports — stays in
`domain/fold_change_scopes.py`, which is what lets the unit tests reach
that logic without importing Qt.

### The Cell Gating tab

The most control-dense tab in Review, and the one whose layout carries the most
meaning, because it composes four gating layers that are easy to confuse. It is
laid out as the two questions it answers, in the order the app applies them:

1. **Cell inclusion**, glossed by its hint as *which cells count at all*. The QC
   debris gate leads, labelled *always applied*: it composes with everything
   below and is not one of the alternatives. Then a radio pair for the source of
   the inclusion decision — per-channel intensity floors, or the Scatter Plot's
   rectangular gates.

   `qc/tab_view.build_qc_gate_controls` lays the gate out as a grid with one row
   per *measured quantity* — Area, Solidity, Region area, Circularity — and its
   min / max bounds in aligned columns, rather than the single wrapping strip of
   six independently-labelled fields it was. A quantity that admits only one
   bound (solidity has no upper, region area no lower) renders an em-dash in the
   other column: a bound that does not exist must not look like one left blank.
2. **Fraction-on**, glossed as *which of the included cells count as ON*. The
   same radio pair shape: per-channel cutoffs, or a scatter gate. Then
   Auto-threshold and the button that opens the optimizer.

Each section title is a short noun phrase and the sentence explaining it lives
in the header's hint, one line below. The gloss used to sit in the title itself
("Cell inclusion — which cells count"), where it made the title long enough to
wrap in a header row over a thousand pixels wide. A lead-in line above each
radio pair — *Always applied:*, *Then include cells by (choose one):*, *Count an
included cell as ON by (choose one):* — names the choice and states that the
pair is exclusive; the lead-ins take the `Secondary` object name so the section
reads heading → lead-in → controls rather than as one flat column of body text.

Radio pairs rather than checkboxes because the code has always treated the two
sources as exclusive — ticking the scatter option *replaces* the per-channel
numbers rather than composing with them — and each layer's gate picker sits
inside its own radio's row, since the two pickers are otherwise identical
buttons reading "All gates". Only the scatter radio of each pair is registered
(`_cell_gating_use_scatter_gates_cb` / `_cell_gating_use_scatter_thresh_cb`,
names kept from the checkboxes they replace): exclusivity means one signal
carries the whole state, and the controller keeps reading a single
`isChecked()`. Gates are drawn on a *different* tab, so whether the scatter
option is selectable is refreshed by `_cell_gating_refresh_gate_filter` — which
also shows or hides the "no gates drawn yet" hint — rather than decided once at
build time.

Each section carries **its own** per-channel table, built by
`controller._cell_gating_build_channel_controls` into `_cell_gating_inner`
(the inclusion floors) and `_cell_gating_thresh_inner` (the ON cutoffs), one row
per fluorescence channel and ratio metric. The fraction-on table has two value
columns, because the cutoff that applies follows the selected Property:
`ThreshFracOn` for an intensity, `ThreshCountOn` for an smFISH count. A channel
with no spot-count column renders an em-dash in the count column rather than an
empty cell — it has no count cutoff to set, which is not the same as one left
unfilled. Two tables rather than one with two
columns: the numbers share a shape but not a meaning — one decides membership of
the dataset, the other only how members are counted — so a shared table needs a
heading that names neither decision, which is the original defect (both columns
under the ThreshFracOn header) wearing a politer label. The columns also grey out
independently, since `_cell_gating_apply_scatter_gate_mode` disables whichever
layer a scatter gate has replaced, so a shared table is half-dead whenever either
layer is gate-driven. Neither table is inside a scroll area of its own: the tab
already scrolls as a whole, and a second, height-capped scroll around the primary
input surface scrolls inside the scrolling page.

Under the table sits the readout: the gate summary, then the **inclusion
funnel** — `gating_compute.inclusion_funnel`, each layer applied on top of the
one above it in `df_included_mask`'s own order, so the last figure equals the
Included total. A layer whose column is absent reports `None`, rendered "not
applied", never "−0": a layer that was never applied and one that removed
nothing are different facts (§7 of CLAUDE.md). Manual curation and the intensity
gate share one line because they write the same `Included` column and cannot be
separated from the frame — the label says so rather than implying a split the
data does not support.

The **CDFs** follow immediately, so a threshold edit and the distribution it is
placed against are on one screen. Each **fluorescence-channel** panel carries two
vertical lines, because that panel is where both cutoffs are chosen and they
are constantly mistaken for each other: the FluorGating floor (dashed, `warn`)
and the **ON cutoff** (dotted, `accent`) drawn at its *effective* value — the stored one, or the
channel's default, which is not the readout default for the nuclear channel.
A cutoff of zero draws no line, because zero is "no cut" and a line on the axis
edge claiming to be a threshold is worse than none — which is also why the
nuclear channel, whose ON default *is* zero, shows only its gate line. The
cell-area panel carries the `min_area` line alone and the ratio panels carry
none: neither has an ON cutoff of its own. The effective value comes from
`channel_state_controller.get_thresh_frac_on`, the canonical accessor, so the
line and every statistic that divides by that cutoff read the same number
through the same key resolution. Editing either cutoff
replots the CDFs; a ThreshFracOn edit used to leave its own line where the old
value was, on the panel the user was looking at to choose it. The optimizer — fourteen controls answering an
occasional question — is not on the tab at all: `optimizer_view` builds it into
its own **non-modal** window (non-modal because its answer is judged against the
CDFs behind it), hidden, at tab-build time, so every optimizer widget handle
registers at the same moment as the rest and the refreshers that repopulate
those combos on a data change need no build-state guard.

### 5.4 The left sidebar

`core/sidebar_view.build_sidebar(app, parent)` builds the well picker
(`widgets/well_plate_selector.WellPlateSelector`, sized by the shared
`widgets/plate_geometry.apply_plate_geometry` — see §7) plus the **Select all /
Select none** buttons, the selection-count chip, and the group hint label.
Selection signals route through `review/core/selection_controller.py`
functions (`on_sidebar_plate_selection_changed`, `…_drag_finished`,
`…_well_activated`, `…_row_activated`, `…_col_activated`,
`…_well_dropped`); `ReviewApp._on_sidebar_plate_*` are 1-line proxies
to those functions, kept so the sidebar's `signal.connect(app._on_…)` wires
still resolve.

The same module builds the **Saved selections** drawer. Both halves of the
drawer — capturing a selection and loading one — branch on which mode the
sidebar plate is in, because the two modes keep "the current selection" in
different stores.

**The name on screen is "Saved selections"; the symbols are still
`plot_group`.** The drawer saves a set of lit wells and pools nothing, while
Home's groups are replicate sets and pool everything — every plot, Statistics,
Batch Export and every saved fold-change `ControlRef` keys on them. One word for
both is a collision that costs a paragraph of disambiguation wherever either is
described. Renaming the user-visible strings costs nothing; renaming
`persistence.json::plot_groups` would be a migration with a compatibility window,
and no user reads that key. So `build_plot_groups_drawer`,
`_wells_for_new_plot_group`, `plot_group_visibility_plan` and the `plot_groups`
section keep their spelling, and `tests/test_one_word_per_concept.py` holds the
boundary at the string literals.

What a new group captures depends on which sidebar's Add was pressed, so
`build_plot_groups_drawer` takes a `wells_source` callable and each caller
supplies its own. The default is `_wells_for_new_plot_group`, the plotting
sidebar's plate: in group-visibility mode (replicate sets defined and no
well-editing pane on screen, the same condition
`selection_controller._plate_passive_in_group_mode` resolves) the plate paints
set visibility and clicks toggle a set's `hidden` flag, so what is on screen is
the union of every visible set's wells plus `active_solo_wells` — the same
active set the plots draw from. `selection.selected_wells` is not consulted in
that mode at all: nothing keeps it current there, so it holds whatever a
per-well tab or an earlier saved-selection load last wrote. In per-well mode the
plate *is* a well selector and `selected_wells` is the answer.

The Image Table's sidebar passes `image_table_active_wells` instead, because its
picker is a second, independent selector — it ignores replicate sets and writes
`state.image_table.active_wells`, never `selection.selected_wells`. Threading
the reader in from the caller keeps core out of the business of knowing where a
feature's sidebar keeps its wells; branching inside the builder would have meant
core naming a feature's state.

Loading a group writes the saved wells through `set_selected_wells` — per-well
tabs and the Image Table read them from there — then reconciles replicate
visibility through the pure `plot_group_visibility_plan`, because in replicate
mode the plotting tabs draw one trace per *visible* replicate set and never read
`selection.selected_wells`. Every set the group's wells touch is shown, the rest
hidden, and wells belonging to no set become `active_solo_wells`. This is
visibility only — no replicate set's membership is edited, so a saved selection
never mutates the sample definitions.

Saved selections have two homes on disk: the `plot_groups` section of
`persistence.json` (written on every drawer edit) and a copy inside the
`sample_definitions` block of `pipeline_info.json` (written whenever sample
definitions autosave). The `pipeline_info.json` hydrator runs first on load and
`persistence/plot_groups.load_from_data_dir` runs second; an *absent*
`persistence.json` section leaves the hydrated groups in place rather than
clearing them, so a folder shared or copied without the sidecar keeps its
groups. The corollary matters for anything that clears them: writing only one of
the two copies clears nothing, because the surviving copy re-hydrates on the next
load. The Sample definitions reset scope writes both (§5.7).

Other sidebar bodies live with their feature: the preview picker is
`features/preview/preview_view.py` and the image-table picker is
`features/image_browser/image_table/picker_view.py`. Statistics has no sidebar
body at all — its comparison-group editor is part of the Statistics page (see
the Split View section above for why) — and Home has none either: its
`_sidebar_sample_frame` is registered and stays empty and hidden, because the
plate that used to fill it is a layer of the Sample Map tab. They're stacked
inside the same sidebar QWidget
and shown/hidden by `core/tab_controller.on_tab_change` based on the
active tab.

The collapse toggle (`Ctrl+B` / the button floating on the rail's edge) routes through
`tab_controller.apply_sidebar_visibility`, which drives **whichever** sidebar
belongs to the current mode from one flag: the Review rail (`_sidebar_root`) in
Review mode, and each secondary pane's own `_left_sidebar` (the Analyze form
sidebar via `app._analyze_pane`, the Datasets page rail via `app._datasets_pane`)
in its mode — so the same button collapses the left panel symmetrically in every
mode.

### 5.5 Controllers

Every non-trivial behaviour lives in either its feature's `controller.py` /
`renderer.py` (under `review/features/<feature>/`) or in
`review/core/` for cross-cutting responsibilities. The convention is:

- Functions (`def foo(app, …)`) that take the `ReviewApp` — or, where
  the call site has one, a `ViewerContext` — plus any extra args.
- Read and mutate runtime state through the typed domain-state objects:
  `app._app_state.channel`, `app._app_state.selection`, … (or
  `ctx.state.<domain>`). The state modules (under `review/core/` for
  cross-cutting, `review/features/<feature>/state.py` for feature-local)
  are import-safe — they never reach back into `runtime_app`, so a
  controller can import them directly with no circular dependency (the
  `test_state_package_import_contract` guardrail enforces that boundary).
  Prefer that to reaching for loose attributes.
- Don't import `ReviewApp` itself — that would be circular. The remaining
  un-extracted behaviour is reached via the `app` argument.
- One module per *behaviour domain*: a feature's `controller.py` /
  `renderer.py`, not a per-tab handler module. The behaviour outlives the
  tab name.

Cross-cutting controllers (in `review/core/`):

| Module | Role |
|--------|------|
| `core/load_controller.py` | Open a dataset folder, scan CSVs, populate caches, schedule first redraw. Its bulk pass over the plate's CSVs (`_open_wells`) goes through `ctx.state.repo.open_well(key, path, load_rows=…)` — the same `data_loading.load_and_project` a cache miss reaches — rather than reading and caching each frame itself. **It reads rows while the plate fits the row-cache budget and not after**: once a load has had to evict a well (`RowCache.evictions`), the remaining wells are opened from their per-well summaries (`data/well_summary.py`) without a row read. A plate that fits therefore opens exactly as it always did, every well held; one that does not opens with the wells that fit, a summary of every well, and the rest one `get_rows` away. That is not a tidiness: while it read them itself the eager and lazy paths carried different layers, the loader applying manual curation on top of QC and crop while a reloaded well got only the two registered projectors, so a well the cache dropped came back with the user's per-cell exclusions silently missing. The post-load hydration sequence still runs afterwards and still matters — `persistence.load` for cell overrides, QC parameters and the crop region, each followed by its re-projection over the held frames — because the wells are read before those settings are on disk-loaded, and that ordering is why the projections cannot simply move into the loop. |
| `core/selection_controller.py` | Plate-selection events; commits a selection change into the redraw pipeline. Importing selections is split in two for the reason `features/home/groups/controller.py` splits its dialog: `import_selections_from_json` opens the file picker and reports, and `merge_imported_selections(ctx, payload)` is the loop that adds them — a modal blocks for ever under the offscreen QPA, so every rule in that loop was reachable only through a picker no test can answer, and a guard written one step past it against `sel_add` passes with the whole loop deleted. It returns the count added, or `None` for a payload holding no selections at all: "this file has no selections" and "every selection in it failed to add" are different sentences to show the user, and one integer cannot say both. |
| `core/tab_controller.py` | `on_tab_change` dispatch, tab history, scope flush, and the repaint that follows a restore. That last one is a seam worth naming: `on_tab_change` draws the tab and **then** drains any view-state pending for it — deliberately, because the apply step validates its values against combo items the draw has populated — which leaves the figure drawn from pre-restore defaults, one step behind controls that have already moved. `redraw_after_restore` closes that gap, and it resolves the tab through the feature registry rather than from a list: it was an `if/elif` over three tab names while six tabs own a block, and the three it did not name were simply not repainted. Response Curves was one — its Series button came back naming the split the user had saved, over curves drawn as a single undivided set, and the first thing that reached a redraw was the user toggling a series off and on. Heat Map was another. Distribution still goes through `redraw_app`, the call the rest of the app makes for that scope, and the Image Table is still not repainted (it reads images off disk and renders only on *Generate*; the restore marks it stale instead) — both rows with the reason written down rather than absences, and `tests/test_restore_repaints_the_tab_it_restored.py` states the rule against the registry. |
| `core/channel_state_controller.py` | Channel-state machinery: `recalculate_threshold`, `set_active_channel`, `update_channel_selector`, `refresh_metric_combo_for_channel`. Owns the per-channel `(min, max)` cache that turns repeat channel toggles from an O(total cells) scan into an O(1) lookup. **Ordering contract:** `recalculate_threshold` publishes the freshly-detected `smfish_channels` set *before* it calls `update_channel_selector`, because that call ends in the Property-combo refresh and the combo reads the set to decide whether `smFISH Count` is selectable — publishing it afterwards leaves the item greyed out against count columns that already exist. Every combo asks that question through `domain/metric_registry.channel_supports_smfish`, which case-folds both sides: the global combo passes the normalised token (`gfp`) while the scatter, stats, and batch-export combos pass the displayed label (`GFP`), and a raw membership test disabled the item permanently on the upper-case side. **A dataset with no values resets the range rather than keeping the last one.** When `_recalculate_threshold` finds no values for a column it returns early — the fan-out below it is deliberately reached only afterwards, and `load_controller` calls `_load_gating_from_pipeline_info` separately in the same load — but returning used to leave `threshold_min`/`threshold_max` holding the *previous* plate's numbers, because `begin_load` clears the per-column cache and nothing else. Undefined is not unchanged, so the branch calls `reset_threshold_range(channel_state)` and logs first. That helper reads the defaults off a fresh `ChannelState` rather than restating them as literals, so the declared defaults and the reset cannot drift apart. |
| `core/selection_controller.py::note_group_visibility_changed` | Showing or hiding a replicate set changes which computed results are *drawn*, not what any of them is — ``active_replicate_sets`` filters hidden sets out before anything is computed, and no cache key carries ``hidden``. So a visibility toggle keeps the plate's statistics instead of discarding them, which on twelve groups is 312 cached entries kept per toggle rather than recomputed. It is reached through ``rebuild_all(ctx, invalidate=False)`` rather than beside it: the toggle still needs the Replicates panel, the plate map and the visible redraws that ``rebuild_all`` performs, and an earlier version that notified and then called ``rebuild_all()`` separately had its statistics thrown away by that call's first line — the change bought nothing while its test, which drove the notifier rather than the toggle, stayed green. The refresh has to *know* not to invalidate; being told separately is not the same thing. |
| `core/record_sync.py` | `resync_run_check` — re-read the sidecar's `run_check` block, the one part of a loaded dataset's sidecar Review does not own (the pipeline writes it at the end of a run, the Datasets **Validate & Repair** tool at the end of every scan). It takes that key and nothing else, because the rest of the sidecar holds user-side blocks whose in-memory copy may carry unsaved edits, and it returns whether the record changed so a caller repaints only when something arrived. In `core/` rather than in Home, the page that reports the record: what it re-reads is dataset state, and its second caller is `tab_controller`'s pane handler, which cannot import a feature. A sidecar that has gone unreadable keeps the record already loaded; one that is readable and no longer carries the block drops it, since reporting a stale record as current is the failure this exists to avoid. |
| `core/csv_export.py` | **The one CSV Save-As dialog**, plus the plain writer beside it. `ask_save_csv` roots the picker at the open dataset, parents it to the window and offers one filter; `write_csv_rows` is the open / write / status / `OSError` block that four export paths had each written out with their own wording. In `core/` because it knows nothing about plots, batches or metrics, so a feature wanting to save a table need not import another feature at module scope. **Every CSV export in the app goes through it** — the export service's seven, the Spatial summary and the Multivariate feature matrix — and that is the point rather than a detail: while those kept private copies there were two "all files" filters (`(*)` here, the DOS-era `(*.*)` in the service, which Qt honours literally on some platforms and which then hides every extensionless name behind a label saying it shows everything), two answers to whether the picker starts beside the dataset, and two to whether it suggests a filename. Only the *writers* stay with their callers, because a dict-writer's schema is its field names. `tests/test_one_csv_save_dialog.py` fails on a second CSV `getSaveFileName` anywhere else; it resolves module-level string constants, because its first version read only the literals inside each call and walked past the one site that held its filter in a constant — the site that had actually shipped. |
| `core/plot_orchestrator.py` | Default-scope fan-out (line + distribution + heat map). Per-tab scopes (bar / scatter / scatter-agg) have their own entry points that consume scope-specific state. Distribution and Heat Map are drawn only when their tab is **on screen**, resolved through `fold_change_scopes.visible_scope_names` so the unfocused pane of a Split View still counts as visible. A built-but-hidden figure is added to `PlotState.fc_dirty_scopes` — the set `flush_dirty_scopes` already drains from the tab-change handler — rather than to a second flag of its own; both tabs are registered redraw scopes and both carry `on_activate` hooks that re-enter this fan-out on show, so there are two routes to the repaint and one record of whether it is owed. Guarding on the canvas handle alone asked whether the tab had ever been *built*, and a built tab stays built, so a session that had opened both paid for all three figures on every selection change. The visibility test **fails open**, and takes an empty answer as unknown to do it: ``visible_scope_names`` swallows its own lookup failures and returns an empty set, so "no plot tab is in front" and "I cannot tell" are indistinguishable — reading the empty set as an answer deferred both figures indefinitely for a window whose tab lookup throws, or in a build whose scope registry was never populated, which is failing *closed* under a comment claiming otherwise. Unknown draws everything built: a redundant redraw costs time, a skipped one costs a figure that disagrees with the plate. The conflation's price is that a genuinely non-plot tab redraws both rather than deferring them, which their ``on_activate`` hooks would have done on the way back anyway. Note that ``redraw_scopes_after_load`` matches the default scope **by name**: ``line``, ``distribution`` and ``heatmap`` all register the same ``_redraw_app_scope`` callable, so an identity test on ``scope.redraw`` cleared the dirty marks of the two hidden ones and left them neither drawn nor owed. |
| `core/plot_style.py` | `apply_ax_style` — token-aware axes styling for matplotlib. `apply_export_style_prefs` then stamps the Properties-sidebar prefs (fonts, line/marker, grid, legend) over every artist, which means it can overwrite something a renderer meant as data. It is a coordinator over one pass per preference family, run per axes in an order the families depend on: `_style_axis_typography` (all a colour bar takes), `_style_x_tick_angle`, `_style_lines`, `_style_marker_collections`, `_apply_grid`, `_apply_scales_and_limits` (scale before limits), `_apply_tick_prefs` (after the scale, which resets locators), `_apply_legend_prefs` (after the marks its swatches copy), the typed-limit hold last, and `_apply_layout_engine` once for the figure. `_AxisPrefs` answers what a pref is for one panel (that panel's `axis_buckets` entry, else the global value; limits fall back to the flat pref only on the targeted axis), and `_MarkPrefs` the line and marker prefs, its numbers read only when an artist needs them. `tests/test_export_style_passes.py` holds the two promises the split's mutation pass found unpinned — error-bar caps keep their own marker and size, and a rescaled time axis keeps its labels through a log scale. Three per-artist opt-outs bound it: `_aw_no_style_override` (skip the artist entirely — decorative lines like significance brackets), `_scatter_only_artist` (keep markers-only; don't join the points with a line), `_aw_marker_is_data` (keep the marker *shape*; size and open-vs-filled still apply), and `_aw_marker_face_is_data` (keep the marker's **face** — filled versus hollow — which is a separate claim from the shape and needs a separate flag: the aggregate scatter encodes a well in the shape and is content for the user to make every point hollow, while the Line tab's grey mode encodes a trace in the shape *and* the fill, half its cycle being the same six shapes open), and `_aw_linestyle_is_data` (keep the **dash pattern**, the third cue that mode encodes). Line *width* is deliberately not opt-outable: it carries no identity, so the Properties row governs it on every figure. **Grid off is off.** ``ax.grid(False, alpha=…, linestyle=…)`` does not hide a grid: matplotlib reads line properties beside a false first argument as "style the grid", enables it, and warns. So Properties → Grid → Show grid moved nothing on any plot in the app, in either direction, and the warning went unread. The styling kwargs now go in only when the grid is being drawn; `tests/test_grid_show_turns_the_grid_off.py` compares rendered PNGs rather than gridline attributes, because a gridline's own `get_visible()` is not what `ax.grid(False)` clears and an assertion on it passes against the defect. **The legend prefs reach every legend on the axes, not only `ax.legend_`.** `legends_on` enumerates them off `ax.get_children()`, which holds both the legend `ax.legend()` built and any standalone `Legend` a renderer constructed and handed to `add_artist` — the aggregate scatter draws both of its keys that way, and `ax.get_legend()` returns neither, so the font size, the colour, the family and *Show legend* all walked past them and that tab was the one place where Properties → Legend → Font size did nothing at all. `legend_loc` stays the **primary** legend's alone, because pinning their own corners is exactly what those keys are off `ax.legend_` for: repositioning both drops one on the other. A legend's **title** takes the same size as its entries, so a key headed `Timepoint` no longer keeps its creation-time size while its own rows resize underneath it; an untitled legend's blank title is left alone rather than given a size, which would pad every ordinary legend with an empty 21pt `Text`. The pass ends each axes with `sync_legend_handles`, which copies width, dash, marker shape, size and both marker colours from each trace onto the legend swatch that names it — matplotlib builds a legend from copies taken when it was created, so before this every one of those prefs reached the traces and none reached the key. Copied from the trace rather than re-read from the prefs, and paired by **label** rather than by position: re-deriving would collapse a grey figure's twelve distinguishable swatches onto one look, and index pairing would shift every swatch by one as soon as `_capped_legend` appended its "+N more" entry. The last is what the aggregate scatter sets, because there the shape encodes well identity and the legend is keyed on it — without it every point took the pref's shape while the legend kept advertising one per well. There are per-*axes* opt-outs too: `_categorical_xaxis` / `_categorical_yaxis` keep the log-scale pref off an axis whose ticks are category labels, `_aw_force_xlog` / `_aw_force_ylog` let an axis pin *whether* an axis is logarithmic against the shared pref — not what base it is drawn in, which stays the user's on every figure — and **`_aw_colorbar` takes an axes out of the pass entirely from the tick-rotation step onward**. A colour bar is a legend for its mappable's norm, not a plot axis: `fig.axes` includes it all the same, so without the flag the walk reset a `LogNorm` bar to a linear scale — discarding the log locator and formatter matplotlib installed, leaving the colours log-mapped beside linear labels — and drew gridlines and marker-edge styling over the bar's mesh. Typography and colours are applied before the opt-out, so a flagged bar still tracks the plot theme. Every colour bar the app creates (Heat Map, Spatial, Multivariate) sets it; the Heat Map re-stamps it each redraw because it refills a persistent `cax` through `cla()`. `apply_axis_log_scale` is the one way an axis's log state is set, and it takes the base with it: `log_base_value` reads the Properties field's text (`"10"`, `"2"`, `"3"`, `"e"`, or any number above 1; anything at or below 1 is not a base and falls back to 10 rather than taking the axis down). **Setting an axis to the scale it already has is a no-op there**, because `set_xscale` is not idempotent — re-setting an unchanged scale still rebuilds it and replaces the locator and formatter. The Response tab ticks one tick per concentration the experimenter gave, and the restyle that follows every redraw put matplotlib's decades back in their place; `_aw_force_xlog` could not prevent that, because it decides whether the axis is log while the reset happens inside the call that sets it either way. The base it compares against comes from `axis_log_base`, which reads the axis's own transform (`Axis.get_transform()` is public and a `LogTransform` carries its `base`) rather than a value this module remembers writing — this module is not the only writer, since the Distribution tab sets its scales in its renderer and `ax.hist(log=True)` sets one inside matplotlib, and a remembered base goes stale the moment either runs. An axis whose transform carries no base is treated as not matching and rebuilt. It also installs the **standard subdivisions** — `log_minor_subs` / `apply_log_minor_ticks` — because a log axis without them is a pair of labelled powers with an unmarked gap, and nothing else was putting them there: the only thing that drew minor ticks anywhere was the Properties *Minor ticks* row, which is a preference about tick density on a linear axis and is off by default. Base 10 subdivides at 2…9, any whole base at its whole multiples (base 3 at 2), and base 2 — the one offered base with nothing whole inside it — at its log-space midpoint (`e` is not that case, since 2 lies strictly inside it). They are unlabelled, because nine numbers per decade crowds the axis past legibility, and re-installed on **every** call including the ones whose scale-setting is skipped, since the restyle can have cleared the locator since the scale last changed. `apply_export_style_prefs` therefore decides the two axes separately — `minorticks_on`/`off` act on the whole axes, so a log y beside a linear x was one decision until this split them — and a log axis keeps its subdivisions whatever the *Minor ticks* row says, which goes on governing the linear axes beside it. Once matplotlib thins the majors (every other decade on a six-decade view) it draws no subs at all, which is its rule and the right one: a tick between two *unlabelled* powers says nothing a reader can use. **And only where the majors are the powers.** A subdivision is defined against the power it sits under, not against whatever tick is drawn to its left, so on an axis whose major locator is something else the two do not line up and the count between one pair of labels differs from the count between the next — the Response tab, which ticks one dose per concentration the experimenter gave, had matplotlib's decades put back between its doses after every redraw and read 1, 6, 1, 6 marks between its labels, on a break-and-column axis where an unexplained mark reads as data. `apply_log_minor_ticks` therefore installs nothing on an axis whose major locator is not a `LogLocator`, and takes away the subdivision set a *previous* call left there, since that locator outlives the redraw that pinned the new majors. It removes only its own: a minor locator this module did not install belongs to whoever did. **A typed axis limit is applied after the scale, and is the last word.** Order first: a limit can only be validated against the scale the axis will actually be drawn in, and `ax.clear()` leaves it linear at the top of every redraw. Applied before the log step, a **non-positive** bound is accepted in silence — matplotlib refuses one only when the axis is *already* logarithmic — and survives into an axis where 0 means `-inf`. That is a whole reported defect: a **fraction** axis, whose quantity is bounded 0 to 1 so `0` is the honest floor and the one number a log axis cannot show, drew every trace in the top thousandth of the figure, and re-typing the identical numbers fixed it because *that* path met an axis that was already log and had the bound refused — which is exactly the shape of a bug that reads as the control not working. `limits_a_log_axis_can_take` drops the impossible bound, keeps the possible one, and **says so**, naming the axis and what to do instead; silently substituting a floor would leave the number in the Properties field while the plot is drawn to a different range, with nothing to tell that from the setting having worked. Then the hold: the steps after the limits — the tick locators, the legend, the layout engine — are each a chance to lose them, since matplotlib re-autoscales on a good many. So `_hold_typed_limits` re-asserts them at the end and **logs** the discrepancy rather than quietly correcting it: something autoscaling over a user's limit is a defect with a cause, and a silent re-application would hide it from the next reader exactly as well as it is hidden now. The failure is otherwise invisible by construction — the number is still in the Properties field and still in the store, and the plot is simply drawn somewhere else, which reads as the control not working. A bound the user left blank stays autoscaled, so half a range does not become a whole one. The sidebar's **Interval per timepoint** row states the *interval*, not the stored multiplier: it opens at `time_rescale.displayed_interval` — the plate's measured spacing (`observed_interval` over `dataset.all_timepoints_cache`) put through the factor in force — and a typed number becomes the stored factor through `factor_for_interval`. `PlotState.time_scale` goes on holding the multiplier, so nothing downstream learns a second spelling and an older settings file still means what it said; what changes is that the row stops reading `1` on a plate imaged every four hours, which described the identity map rather than the data. `observed_interval` returns `None` — never a mean or a modal gap — when there is no one spacing: fewer than two timepoints, a non-finite one (measuring across the hole reports a gap the plate does not have), a zero gap, or gaps that disagree. The row then falls back to the multiplier it always was, and the section summary says "uneven" only when gaps actually disagree, since a one-timepoint plate has no gap rather than an irregular one. The row is re-seeded on every panel open (`_resync_time_interval`, beside the segment re-seed) because the number is measured from the plate while the panel is built once per figure and cached for the process. A third per-axes stamp, `_aw_time_rescale`, carries the Properties sidebar's **time-axis label correction** (`PlotState.time_scale` / `.time_offset`, `domain/time_rescale.py`) through the pass: `apply_time_rescale` installs a `FuncFormatter` that prints each tick as `filename hours × factor + offset`, and because the log step above calls `set_xscale` — which resets an axis's locator and formatter — the pass re-installs from the stamp rather than trusting the renderer's one call. The stamp holds the whole `TimeRescale` value rather than the multiplier alone, so the re-install cannot drop the offset here and nowhere else. The correction is **labels only**: tick positions, plotted values, the timepoint menus, the Statistics tab and every export keep the hours the pipeline parsed out of the filenames, so nothing that reads a timepoint can desynchronise. The deliberate cost is that a corrected axis disagrees with those readers, which is why `domain/time_rescale.axis_label` is the only way a time-axis label reaches a figure — it appends the correction, and `tests/test_time_rescale_marker.py` scans the source for any time-axis label that bypasses it. **A figure with no time axis states the correction in its title instead.** `figure_timepoint_label` does that for one timepoint picked from a menu (the Heat Map, the Distribution tab, the batch-export scatter) and `figure_timepoints_label` for several drawn as series (Response Curves). Those two and `metric_labels.timepoint_title` are the only three builders of a figure's timepoint clause, and all three spell it `t = 24 h`: one spelling, because two on one plate's figures is a reader wondering whether they mean different things, and a sibling pair this closely named disagreeing about its one output is the hazard §7.6 #4 describes. `tests/test_response_curves_honour_the_time_correction.py` holds each of them against `timepoint_title` rather than against a literal — a literal is what let one of them pin a spelling the rest of the app did not use — the plural brackets its list the way `metric_labels.timepoint_title` does, and states the marker **once**, since the correction describes the plate rather than each curve. Response Curves is the case that shows why the whole figure has to move together: it names an hour in four places — the title, every legend entry, the `No fit at …` note and the omission caption — so a half-corrected figure disagrees with *itself*, which is worse than one corrected nowhere. `draw_response` therefore resolves the rescale once, above its empty-state return, and threads it to `_curve_label`, `_fit_caption` and `collect.omission_caption`; `renderer._scaled_tp` formats the legend and no-fit sites and `collect._tp` the omission caption — two call sites of one rule rather than one function, because `collect.py` is Qt-free and pure and does not import the renderer. Both fall back to the raw `%g` for a value the rescale cannot format, and both are byte-identical to the `%g` those sites used to write while no correction is set. `figure_timepoints_label` falls back the same way, so the title cannot name fewer timepoints than the legend shows. **The fold-change suffix is part of that title and is corrected with it.** `domain/fold_change.fold_change_suffix_for` builds `fold change vs t=24h` from the baseline timepoint, and the Response title appends it verbatim beside its own corrected clause — so a raw baseline hour put one moment on one title twice, once corrected and once not, which is worse than the raw-throughout title it replaced. The suffix carries no marker of its own: Bar and Line append the same string and state the correction on their axis label, Response in its timepoint clause, and a second copy would read as a second correction. `tests/test_response_curves_honour_the_time_correction.py` holds it, and its source guard fails on any fifth site that formats an hour raw — with an allowlist, per site and with the reason, for the ones that legitimately keep filename hours (the timepoint pickers and the exported CSVs). |
| `core/plot_annotations.py` | The **value-label overlay** — the `mean ± spread` text the Bar and Line renderers draw above each point when Properties → Overlays turns it on (`PlotState.show_value_labels`). Shared rather than per-feature because the two tabs draw the same statistic and must print it identically; it holds no matplotlib import of its own, only calls `annotate` on an axes handed to it. Two rules in the formatting are load-bearing, and both are the repository's computed-as-zero-versus-not-computed rule restated in text. **The ± half is printed only when a spread was computed and an error bar drawn** — a spread that came back `NaN`, or (on the bar panels, which consult `bar_err_settings`) Properties → Statistics on *Show: Mean* or *Error bars: None*, leaves the label as the mean alone, because `± 0` over a bar with no whisker claims the replicates agreed. The line panels have no such control and draw a band whenever there is a spread, so their labels always carry the ±; the invariant that holds on **both** surfaces is the one that matters — a label states the spread its own panel draws and never any other. And **each half is formatted from its own magnitude** unless the user typed a format. Sharing one is what a pair of numbers wants typographically and is wrong arithmetically: the mean's format comes from the mean, a whole-number mean takes `%d`, and `%d` truncates — a two-well set counting 27 and 33 has a mean of exactly 30 and an SD of 4.24, which under a shared format read `30 ± 4`, understating the drawn whisker by 43%. A user-typed format does govern both halves, and even then a spread it would round away keeps its own precision (`1200 ± 0.400`, never `1200 ± 0`); `_rounds_to_zero` scans for a significant digit rather than calling `float`, which raised on exactly the unit-bearing and `%%`-carrying formats most likely to produce the case. `value_label_settings(ctx)` reads the pair off the plot state and answers *off* for `ctx=None`, which is what keeps the batch-export bar path — which renders with no ctx on purpose — from drawing an overlay by accident; that path resolves the pair from its own ctx and passes it explicitly, exactly as it does the colour mode. The module also owns the three headroom multipliers (`LABEL_HEADROOM`, `LABEL_SPAN_HEADROOM`, `LABEL_FRAC_CAP`) the panels apply to their y-limits, because the label's offset is in typographic points and no data-space number expresses it exactly; keeping them here stops the Bar and Line panels reserving different amounts for the same text. A label drawn in the plot's ink is tagged `follows_theme`, and one drawn in a trace's colour is not — the bar labels take the chrome ink and repaint with the rest of it when a capture flips the card to publication, while a line label wears its own series colour, which is data and must never be repainted into the theme's ink. `annotate_value` makes that call from whether the caller handed it a colour at all.
