The overlay is a fact about the **axis** too, not only about the text: the label sits above the error cap, so a panel fitted to the cap alone draws it over the title. `barplot/_axis_fit.fit_bar_panels` takes a `value_labels` flag and widens all three panels (and lifts the Fraction panel's 1.05 ceiling to `LABEL_FRAC_CAP`, which is deliberately `LABEL_HEADROOM` applied to a full fraction — a rounder, smaller cap binds before the headroom does and makes Fraction the one panel starved of the room every other panel gets); `lineplot/controller._finalize_line_axes` widens the mean and N panels' already-autoscaled spans **and the Fraction panel under fold change**, which is exactly when `redraw_line_plots`' clamp does not run and nothing else was giving that panel any room. Miss one of those and the labels are still drawn (`annotation_clip=False`) — visible, but on top of the title. Three details of the fitting are there because the obvious version of each was wrong: `autofit` **adds** the headroom to the span rather than multiplying it into the top (multiplying moves a negative ceiling *down*, so asking for more room gave less of it, and every top is negative under a subtractive fold change); it applies `floor_hi` **before** measuring the pad (that floor can multiply the span several times over, leaving a pad that is a fraction of a fraction); and `pad_below` extends the floor, because a label on a negative bar is drawn *below* it and the top padding that serves every positive bar does nothing for it. A pinned y-limit is the case no widening can serve, since `apply_export_style_to_current` re-applies it afterwards: `_annotations.user_y_ceiling` — the same lookup the significance brackets stack under, which is why it lives beside them now rather than in `renderer.py` — turns a label near that ceiling inward instead. The brackets themselves are lifted clear of the labels by `_points_to_data_y(ax, _LABEL_CLEARANCE_PT)`, since both are anchored at the same `value + spread`. **The Scatter tab answers the same switch two ways**, because it draws two different things under one name. Its Aggregate view plots one `mean ± spread` per well/group and timepoint on *both* axes, so `features/scatter/_annotations.annotate_agg_points` labels every point with both of its coordinates through `annotate_point`: `format_point_label` pairs two `format_value_label` calls and yields nothing at all when either coordinate is unprintable, since a lone number beside a marker on two measured axes does not say which axis it belongs to. Each label wears its own point's colour — the timepoint's place on the viridis gradient — which is data and therefore untagged, exactly as a line label wears its trace's. The per-cell view has no statistic under a point (one point there is one cell), so it draws no labels, the same answer the CDF panel gives; unlike the CDF it *says* so on the figure, in muted type through `note_value_labels_unavailable`, because the CDF sits beside labelled panels while the per-cell scatter is a whole tab on which the switch would otherwise be indistinguishable from a broken one — which is how it was reported. `pad_axes_for_labels` reserves the room, taking the line panels' `LABEL_SPAN_HEADROOM` and applying it in log space on a logarithmic axis, where a linear pad is either invisible at the top or an invalid limit at the floor. Both of Batch Export's aggregate-scatter jobs resolve the pair from their own ctx and hand it over, as the bar and line exports do. `tests/test_scatter_value_labels.py` holds the runtime half and two AST guards: every surface that draws a scatter answers the switch, and no call site invents the pair it draws from. |
| `core/bus_wiring.py`, `core/redraw_coordinator.py` | Wire the `EventBus` signals to the redraw coalescer. |
| `core/frame_scope.py` | "Which wells / FOVs / timepoints does this act on?" — the Qt-free half of the Segmentation tab's two scope controls. A `ScopeSpec` names the three `set \| None` fields on typed state plus the wording and the un-armed meaning; `scope_options` / `current_frame` / `describe_scope` / `refresh_scope_button` and the state writers are shared by both, so the delete's scope and the crop's cannot drift in normalisation or in readout grammar. **Writing a field and re-deriving from it are separate calls** (`write_scope_field(..., apply=False)` then `apply_scope_change`) because their costs differ by orders of magnitude: the write is an attribute set, while the crop's re-derivation re-projects `Crop_Pass` over every cached well, redraws the active plot and re-renders the canvas. A `CheckableDropdown` emits `changed` once per ticked item, so the popover has to be able to do the first eleven times and the second once. The `None`-vs-empty-set distinction is load-bearing on both: `None` is the un-armed field (the spec says whether that means "this frame" or "all frames"), an empty set names no frames at all, and collapsing the two would turn a stray click into either a plate-wide delete or a silently disabled crop. Lives in core because two features consume it — `crop` owns one spec, `preview` builds both popovers — and a shared module that either one owned would be a feature the other had to import to reach its own control. |
| `core/scope_registry.py` | Register each feature's fold-change scope with its redraw callable (`features.barplot.renderer.redraw_bars`, `core.plot_orchestrator.redraw_app`). Called once from `wire_event_bus` during construction so the domain-layer `fold_change_scopes` module stays free of `features/` imports. |
| `core/status_view.py` | The status/log footer, and `_GUILogHandler`, which routes `review` log records into the drawer's `QTextEdit`. It is attached at DEBUG and gated on nothing, so it sees every record the app produces — including the `review.swallowed` breadcrumbs written from inside `except` blocks on worker threads — and `emit` is therefore entered off the GUI thread as a matter of course. It crosses that boundary through a `core.worker_bridge.GuiLogRelay`, never a timer; §10.1 has the mechanism and why the distinction is not cosmetic. Two further rules keep it from outliving its widget badly. **It never logs from its own failure path.** A failed append is caught as `RuntimeError` and handled silently — deliberately *not* `swallowed()`, whose DEBUG record would propagate straight back to the logger this handler is attached to, fail in the same place, and log again; a redraw's `processEvents()` drains that queue forever, which is a hang, not a slow run. **A handler whose widget is gone detaches itself** from every logger holding it, because nothing removes it on teardown — in a process that builds more than one window (the test suite) the dead handlers otherwise stay subscribed and every record fans out to widgets that cannot receive it. The document is capped at `_LOG_MAX_BLOCKS`, so the drawer is a bounded tail rather than an unbounded archive. |
| `core/ui_helpers.py` | Cross-cutting widget helpers (combo population, button factories, theme application). |

**An artist drawn in the plot's ink is tagged to follow the theme.**
`PlotCard.setPlotTheme` repaints the parts of an Axes matplotlib names — the
facecolor, spines, ticks, axis labels, the title, the legend — and a free
`ax.text` / `ax.annotate` / `ax.plot` is not one of those. That matters because
a capture does not redraw: `_publication_capture` flips the card to publication
and suppresses `plotThemeChanged` on purpose, so one Save click does not run two
full recomputes. An annotation coloured from `tokens_for` at draw time therefore
kept the *screen* theme's near-white ink and went onto white paper — the
significance brackets were reported that way, `#E6E9EF` on `#FFFFFF`, roughly
1.1:1.

**The theme pass owns colour, and only colour.** `apply_axes_style` runs on
every `setPlotTheme` — every Screen/Publication switch, and every capture, since
`_publication_capture` flips the theme for the duration of a Save figure, a Copy
panel, a Copy as vector and a gallery capture. It used to end with
`ax.grid(True, color=…, linewidth=0.7, linestyle="-")`, which is three
Properties settings decided by a colour pass: the grid came back on the moment
the theme moved, so **Show grid** looked broken, and every figure exported from
a plot drawn without a grid carried one. It recolours the existing gridline
artists instead, the way `_apply_rcparams` beside it already did —
`ax.grid(color=…)` is not available for that, because matplotlib reads line
properties with no visibility argument as "style the grid, and switch it on".
Whether a grid is drawn, and in what dash and opacity, is
`apply_export_style_prefs`'s to say.

`plot_style.follows_theme(artist, muted=…)` is the tag (`_aw_theme_ink`, defined
in `widgets/plot_card.py` because the repaint that honours it is
`setPlotTheme`'s), and `repaint_theme_ink` applies it over each axes and over the
figure — a footnote written with `fig.text` belongs to no axes. Data colours are
never tagged: repainting one would substitute the theme's ink for a value the
plot is using to mean something, which is why the rule is an opt-in tag rather
than a match on the outgoing colour. It is the mirror of `_aw_no_style_override`
above — that one takes an artist *out* of a styling pass, this one puts it *in*.
`tests/test_theme_ink_artists_are_tagged.py` fails on any free artist coloured
from `tokens_for` without it.

**And on any free artist with no colour at all**, which is the same rule seen
from the other side. An `ax.text` that names no colour takes matplotlib's
black — legible on the publication theme and near-invisible on the screen
theme's `#131A24` — and, having no ink token in it, is not tagged either, so
`repaint_theme_ink` walks straight past it and no later flip corrects it. The
ink guard could not see that shape, because it begins by reading the call's
`color=`; the two halves are asserted separately in the same file. A site
genuinely drawing onto a non-themed figure is exempted by
`module::function` with its reason, and a companion test fails when an
exemption stops describing a real call. Today there is one: the image-table
export's `(no image)` placeholder, drawn inside a cell whose axes the exporter
has just set to white.

Per-feature controllers / renderers (under `review/features/`):

| Feature package | Role |
|-----------------|------|
| `features/lineplot/controller.py` | Line Graphs: redraw the 3-stacked-subplot figure. |
| `features/barplot/{controller,renderer}.py` | Bar Plots: redraw + bar-draw math (split because batch export reuses the math). The three annotation passes over the panels — the per-cluster headers, the `n/a` undefined-spread mark, and the `mean ± spread` value labels — sit in `barplot/_annotations.py`, the same kind of seam as `_axis_fit.py`: nothing there decides what a bar *is*, only what is written over it. The mark and the label are drawn at the same anchor with the same alignment and point size, so the value takes `_LABEL_OFFSET_OVER_MARK_PT` and stacks above the `n/a` rather than on it — at one shared offset they were pixel-identical, and a single well with no replicate set has an undefined spread on every bar, which is the commonest selection there is. The drag-to-reorder handlers sit beside them in `barplot/_drag_reorder.py` — press / motion / release, the Reset Order button, and the event-to-data-x helper — and `runtime_app` and `tab_view.py` import them from there; the arithmetic they run on (`bar_idx_at_x` / `bar_drag_xs` / `bar_guide_x`) is Qt-free and lives in `barplot/collect.py`. **Significance brackets are matched to bars by identity, not by position.** `draw_significance_brackets` takes each pairwise record from `StatsState.pairwise` and resolves both compared groups to a drawn bar: first by name (a Statistics group seeded from a replicate set shares its name), then by well membership. The membership map covers both bar modes — the active replicate sets, keyed by the whole set of wells each pools, *and* the per-well bars, each keyed by the single well its bar token names, since in per-well mode a Statistics group holding one well has no replicate set to match through. A bar key that is also a replicate set's name is left out of the single-well half of the map: there the key stands for whatever the set pools, which need not be the one well of the same name, and bracketing a pooled bar with a comparison computed on a single well would overlay a result on data it was not computed from. A comparison that resolves to no bar (a group spanning several bars, say) is skipped rather than drawn on data it was not computed from. **The context check is a lookup, not a gate.** `draw_significance_brackets` asks `StatsState.runs` for every run whose context fits the bars currently drawn and draws all of them, so switching the plot to another channel shows that channel's own comparison instead of showing none. `_match_pairs_to_bars` owns the half with no matplotlib in it — which compared pair resolves to which bar, and how tall that bar is — which is what keeps the drawing under the complexity ratchet now that the run loop sits above it. **Every way the brackets can go missing states its reason**, through `_no_significance`, and the first three are phrased as what the store holds rather than as what was last run, because the check is a lookup: nothing stored at all, nothing stored on the channel or metric the bars show (the note names the measures it does hold), nothing at the timepoint they are drawn at (it names the timepoints it has), the tested measure's panel absent, bar positions unavailable for the layout, and no comparison matching the bars. A build with the Statistics feature left out reports itself the same way, from the `feature_slice` miss. A seventh is reported by `redraw_bars` rather than by the renderer, because the renderer is never reached: Violin, Beeswarm and Properties → Statistics → "Show: All points" all return from `draw_per_cell_bar_mode` first, and none of them draws a bar for a bracket to sit on. The note names the control that is on (`_per_cell_mode_name`) rather than "per-cell mode", since three separate switches reach it and the sidebar one is the reason it reads as a bug. The gates are all deliberate — the Statistics tab carries its own Channel / Property / Timepoint selectors, independent of the Plotting band's, so the two sides drift apart in ordinary use — but silence made a conditional feature read as an unreliable one, most obviously in Split View where both panes are on screen and either side is a click from changing. The reason goes onto the panel itself in muted type, tagged `_aw_significance_note`, and **not** to the status line. It went to both at first, which was wrong in a way worth recording: `ctx.notify.set_status` writes the *persistent* status bar — the one its own docstring contrasts with the self-dismissing `toast` — so the message outlived the condition. Running a test cleared the panel note on the next redraw while the bar went on insisting no comparison was stored, contradicting the plot above it with no redraw able to correct it, because a successful draw has no reason to write anything. A note that lives on the figure cannot go stale: the redraw that resolves the condition is the same redraw that clears it. It is also the better channel on the merits — attached to the artifact, carried into a copy or an export, and beside the plot rather than at the other end of the window. Only the user switching the toggle off draws nothing and says nothing. An eighth case is not a decline at all and needed a different fix: the brackets were drawn, then hidden. The renderer grew the panel's y-limit to fit them and `apply_export_style_to_current` re-applied the user's own axis limits **last**, clipping the growth back off — and since the brackets carry `clip_on=False` they were drawn outside the panel rather than clipped. Every gate had passed, so no note could describe it. `_user_y_ceiling` now reads the panel's `y_lim_max` up front through the same `figure_prefs` / `axis_scoped_value` lookup `apply_export_style_prefs` uses — axis limits are figure-scoped, so the flat global pref is the wrong place to read — and the brackets are stacked to fit under it. The user's ceiling is never overridden to make room; when it leaves no headroom above the bars, that is reported like any other withheld comparison. The note is an ordinary artist, so the next redraw's `cla()` clears it. The empty-store note deliberately does not claim no test was run: `stats.compute_pairwise` also returns `[]` *after* a run — under two groups with wells, a group with under two replicate values, a misconfigured KS test, scipy missing, or every pair erroring — and in several of those the Statistics tab has already printed the reason, so a note denying the run would contradict the panel beside it. With every decline reporting itself, a report of "toggle on, no note, still no asterisks" now means the brackets were drawn and something downstream removed them, which is a different investigation; the `review_bar_debug` line at the end of the draw prints how many comparisons arrived, how many resolved to bars, and the y band they were placed in, so that case is answered by one instrumented run rather than by reading. `tests/test_bar_significance_says_why.py` holds one case per gate, in both directions. **What a bracket says is a setting, not a constant.** `PlotState.significance_label_mode` picks between the asterisk ladder, the p-value itself and both, from a picker beside the Significance toggle in the bar Display popover — the one surface in the app that draws a bracket, and the place the question only arises once the toggle above it is on, which is why the picker is enable-gated on it the way the Smooth slider is on Violin. The wording is `domain/significance.py`'s; `_significance_label_mode` reads the mode off the plot state through `getattr` so a renderer driven with a hand-built state still draws the stars, and `_bracket_font_pt` drops the text a point size when it carries a number, since there is one label per bracket and a whole expression is more ink than two glyphs. **A numeric label has to fit, and past a certain number of comparisons it does not.** The brackets stack at a fixed `step` and the axis is then set to exactly the span they occupy, so the panel is divided into one row per comparison; measured on the app's own bar figure (6.2 × 11.0 in at 100 dpi, three panels, so the Mean panel is 249 px), six groups give each level 10.6 px against a 7 pt line and nothing collides, while seven give 8.4 px and 17 of the 21 labels print through the one above. `_levels_are_far_enough_apart` compares the per-level pixel height against the text's own point size — the threshold that splits those two cases exactly — and when it fails the run is drawn with stars and `_no_significance` says so. Widening the step cannot fix it: `top` is derived from the step and the closing `set_ylim` rescales the growth straight back out, which is measured rather than assumed. Falling back keeps every bracket and every verdict and drops only the precision that would have been unreadable, and it is reported rather than silent, because a panel showing a different label than the one that was picked is a substitution whether or not the brackets are all there — which is why `_no_significance` covers this case despite not being a decline. `_match_pairs_to_bars` carries a fourth field per matched pair for it — whether the `p` beside it is the BH-adjusted value — because a label printing the number has to name it, and the values alone cannot tell the two apart: `_bh_adjust` adjusts nothing across a single comparison and the record stores the raw p under `p_adj` regardless. `compute_pairwise` stamps `p_adj_applied` so every run this app produces carries the answer — a restored saved plot included, since `_restore_stats_config` re-runs `compute_pairwise` rather than persisting records; a record without the flag is hand-built, and is read from the run's size, since BH runs across at least two comparisons and a run's records are exactly the comparisons that produced a p-value. **The two widgets are re-synced on restore.** `view_state` writes `PlotState` and the figure reads it on the next redraw, but nothing else calls `setChecked` / `setEnabled` on the toggle and its picker, so a restored view drew p-value brackets above a popover whose picker read `Stars (*)` and was greyed out — the picker being enable-gated on a toggle still showing "Off", which made the control the user would reach for the one they could not use. `_sync_significance_controls` pushes both, with the picker's signal blocked so a restore cannot trigger a redraw mid-restore; the tab builder seeds both from the same state, because a tab body builds lazily and is routinely built after a restore has already turned the brackets on. |
| `features/multivariate/collect.py` — `collect_feature_matrix` | **Reads narrowly; holds its matrix.** Each well is read through `data/narrow_rows.narrow_rows` (the features — a ratio's two inputs — the timepoint, and what the verdicts read), so building the matrix neither reads whole frames nor evicts the wells other views hold, and its group / well / timepoint columns are built from per-well arrays rather than per-cell lists. The matrix itself is kept whole — its correlation, PCA, k-means fractions and facet aggregates are each over every cell — while the projections and hierarchical clustering fit on their own stated samples. Measured on 8,835,840 cells at five features: 2,800 MiB peak and 5.3 s, against 3,760 MiB and 11.3 s reading whole frames into lists. `tests/test_multivariate_reads_narrowly.py` holds the narrow matrix to the held-frame one row for row. |
| `features/home/cell_gating/renderer.py` — the CDF panels | **Drawn through their own vertices above a cap.** The CDF inputs are one image per well (the first field's first timepoint, `gating_compute._cell_gating_first_frame_rows`), but in nanowell mode that image is the whole mosaic. `cdf_points` returns the exact empirical CDF, thinned above `CDF_MAX_POINTS` (2,000) to evenly spaced vertices always including the first and last — not a sample of cells: every vertex drawn lies on the full curve and the x range is every cell's. `_note_thinned` says so on the figure. `tests/test_cell_gating_cdf_is_drawn_through_its_points.py`. |
| `features/scatter/{controller,callbacks}.py` | Scatter Plot (cells + aggregate). The per-axis fluor-gate (`fluor_gate_x` / `fluor_gate_y`) comes from the Cell Gating tab's per-channel floors, looked up by the axis's channel — which the scatter holds as the upper-cased dropdown label, so `_cell_gating_resolve_key` matches case-insensitively (a case-sensitive lookup returned the 0.0 "gate off" default and the tab's gate silently did nothing here). In the per-cell (Cells) mode it is bypassed when an axis column ends with `_smfish_count` — the gate is a fluorescence-intensity floor and would strip every integer-count cell on a count axis — while the mixed-axis case (one count, one intensity) still gates the intensity axis. The per-well (Wells, internally `aggregate`) mode gates differently and deliberately: it passes `get_all_fluor_gates` wholesale to the aggregator, which decides cell *inclusion* against every channel's `_mean_intensity`, so the two modes can report different populations when a fluor gate is non-zero. Each Wells axis reads its ON cutoff through `on_cutoff_for_column` keyed on its own per-axis channel, so a count axis is cut against `ThreshCountOn`. A Wells axis's Property offers the intensity flavours plus the two synthetic entries `metric_labels.SYNTHETIC_METRIC_LABEL_TO_KEY` names — *Fraction above threshold* and *Events above threshold* — which `compose_scatter_agg_stat` spells `Fraction On GFP` / `Events On GFP` and `collect.parse_statistic` reads back as the `frac` / `events` aggregation over the channel's mean-intensity column; `_agg_wells` reduces the matching `ReplicateStat` field (`frac` / `n_above`), so an events point is the Bar Events statistic, and a well with no cells above the cutoff plots at 0 rather than dropping out as its undefined above-cutoff mean does. When that collector returns nothing it reports *why* through a `cut_sink`: an axis whose cells were all cut names the channel, the cutoff and the kept/total counts, which is a different message from having no cells at the selected timepoints — conflating the two told users to fix a selection that was never wrong. A third case is recorded apart from both: a replicate whose `n_above` is NaN — a well with unusable FOV labels under Spread: FOV, whose mean and fraction survive but whose per-field count does not — leaves an Events axis empty, and the sink records it as `undefined_count` rather than as a cut, so the message names the FOV labels instead of sending the user to lower a cutoff that removed nothing. The prose an empty aggregate draws — and its status-line mirror — lives in `scatter/_messages.py`, not in `collect.py`: writing to the status bar is a Qt side effect, and `collect.py` is the pure-collection half. `clear_cut_status` runs once at the top of `redraw_scatter_agg_orchestrate`, not on the branch that succeeds in drawing: every other exit — no timepoints available, none ticked, no wells selected, a collector error — replaces the figure while leaving the shared status line telling the user to lower a cutoff for a plot that is no longer on screen. The interactive rectangular gates live in `scatter/gating.py` (a documented naming exception): each box is stamped at draw time with its axis metric columns (`x_col`/`y_col`) and a `name` (auto-assigned `Gate N`, shown on the plot, editable in the Properties sidebar's gate list via `rename_gate`, which captions each row with those two columns via `data/metric_labels.gate_axes_label` so a gate list spanning several metric pairs is readable), so beyond the on-plot "% inside" labels its `compute_gate_inclusion` (matplotlib-free, reuses `_in_gate` + `resolve_value_series`) lets the Cell Gating tab turn the selected gate(s) into the `Gate_Pass` inclusion layer. So an untrusted well contributes one pooled replicate with an undefined count, not a six-times-too-large one — and not *nothing*, which would drop real cells out of the Mean and Fraction panels and make a solo untrusted well's bar vanish as if it had no data. | `features/stats/controller.py` | Statistics tab: groupwise tests, KS CDF. The replicate unit is the **one rule** `domain/stats_compute.replicate_unit` — shared with the bar/line error bars so the test's `n` and the plotted spread never disagree. In **FOV mode** every FOV **across all of a group's wells** is an independent replicate (`n` = total FOVs, pooled across wells); otherwise each well is one replicate. Pooling FOVs across wells is pseudo-replication (smaller p-values than a well-level test) — an explicitly chosen mode. **Nine tests, one roster.** `TESTS` is the single declaration of what the tab offers and what each entry needs — is it rank-based, does it pair, does it want a control or a sample variable — and `tab_view` fills the combo from it rather than from a second hand-written list, because the three facts were previously re-derived from each label's spelling at every site that asked. Beyond the original five (Welch, Student, Wilcoxon rank-sum, Mann-Whitney U, KS) it carries **Dunnett against a control group**, **paired t** and **Wilcoxon signed-rank**, and a **two-way ANOVA**. Two additions are not combo entries at all and run on every ordinary pass: an **effect size** (Hedges' *g* with its small-sample correction, plus a seeded percentile bootstrap interval on the difference of means) under each pairwise line, and an **omnibus** — one-way ANOVA or Kruskal-Wallis, matching the parametric choice — printed above them. The omnibus never *suppresses* the pairwise results: which comparisons a reader may look at is not this app's policy, and saying what it found beside them is. The three pickers the newer tests need are hidden until a test asks for one, which is the opposite call from the Variables tab's disabled unit field and for the stated reason: greying a control out states a rule the user can act on, and a Welch t-test has no control group for them to supply. Dunnett's control comes from the tab's **own** comparison groups rather than the shared fold-change control picker — that picker names a `ControlRef` over replicate sets and plate wells, and a Dunnett control must be one of the k+1 groups actually compared. A run of one of the three alternative tests **stores no all-pairs records and clears none**: it produces none of the pairwise comparisons the brackets read, and an earlier pairwise run under the same key is a true record of a comparison that really happened, which `StatsState.runs` keeps deliberately — that is why `invalidate_stats_run` is a documented no-op. Every stored record names the test that produced it, so no bracket can be attributed to a run that did not make it. |
| `domain/stats_tests.py` | **What a statistical test is**, as pure functions over lists of floats — Qt-free, ctx-free, and so driven entirely by the fast lane rather than by pressing *Run test* and reading a panel. Hedges' *g* and a bootstrap interval, the omnibus pair, Dunnett, the paired pair, and a two-way ANOVA. **Every result says when it could not be computed, and why**: each dataclass carries an `undefined` string that is empty exactly when the numbers beside it are real, with `EffectSize.g_undefined` kept separate for the *partial* case — two constant groups have a real difference and a real zero-width interval and no pooled standard deviation, so collapsing the two would either hide the reason or hide the numbers, and the report prints both; so an interval that did not converge, an ANOVA with an empty cell and a paired test with unmatched replicates each reach the report as a reason rather than as a blank or a plausible zero. **Nothing here is random**, even where the method is: the bootstrap seeds from a constant, because `compute_pairwise` promises a saved plot re-runs to the exact brackets it was saved with and an interval drawn from entropy would break that in the direction of looking like real movement in the data. **Pairing is by key, never by list order** — which replicate of one group corresponds to which of another is a fact about the data, expressed as a sample variable, and a test that zipped two lists would produce a number with a plausible face and no basis. The two-way ANOVA takes **Type II** sums of squares by model comparison on `numpy.linalg.lstsq`: plate data is rarely balanced and a sequential decomposition would give each main effect a different answer depending on entry order. It ships without `statsmodels` — the dry-run resolves cleanly but adds six packages to a bundle already carrying pyarrow — and was checked against it on one balanced and two unbalanced designs, with the reproducible half of that check living in the tests as an independent closed-form derivation. An empty cell refuses the interaction and names the missing combination instead of computing one from a rank-deficient design, and two **confounded** factors — each level of one appearing with exactly one level of the other, so the two are the same partition of the plate under two names — refuse *both main effects*. That second refusal is not cosmetic: least squares still solves such a design, the model comparisons collapse, and the table otherwise reports `F = 0, p = 1` for both factors on data whose levels differ by nine residual standard deviations. |

A block that could not be computed prints its reason **where the number would have gone**: not a blank, not a dash and never a zero, because an omnibus that declined and an omnibus that found nothing are different facts and the panel is the only place either can be said. Every p goes through `domain/significance` like the rest of the app, so a number here and a bracket on the Bar plot beside it cannot be spelled two ways. |
| `features/image_browser/image_table/controller.py` | Image Table grid: render-model assembly + Generate/export orchestration. The "turn cache + state into pixels" work is split into sibling modules it re-exports (so call sites and external importers are unchanged) and which `test_monolith_budgets.py` ratchets: `image_compose.py` (LUT palette + per-channel cmap/LUT resolution, array loading, mask/threshold rendering, the RGB cell composer `cell_display_rgb`, the boundary overlay, and the channel-overlay blender `overlay_cell_rgb`), `grid_layout.py` (axis/cell layout math + the per-dimension well/channel/FOV/timepoint option lists), `build_layout.py` (flat + nested grid assembly + `image_table_apply_spec`), and `facet_view.py` (faceted render placement — axis labels + group spacing). **One facet plan, two surfaces.** `facet_view.plan_facets` computes the placement and the label text from the builder's nesting; `facet_view.render_facet_chrome` turns that plan into the live grid's `QLabel` axis strips, and `renderer.py` replays the *same* plan onto the export figure's `GridSpec`. So Export to File, Copy PNG, Copy SVG and Save to Saved Plots all carry the row/column axis labels, the rotated group strips, the corner label and the inter-group gaps the user sees on screen — the per-cell titles (`show_titles`) are an Export-settings opt-in on top, off by default because the axis labels already identify every cell. `renderer.py` is Qt-free: it duck-types the plan through its argument rather than importing `facet_view`, so the geometry is unit-testable without building a widget, and it restates the label palette in dark-on-light because the figure is saved transparent and lands on a white page where the app's dark chrome colours are unreadable. The export gridspec **pins its own margins and solves `wspace`/`hspace` for an absolute inch pad** (matplotlib spreads one uniform separator between adjacent slots, sized as `wspace × usable/n` before the ratios apply). It deliberately does not use `tight_layout` or `constrained_layout`: both redistribute space to fit each axes' content, which flattens exactly the group gaps the layout exists to express. **Brightness parity.** The Saved Plots snapshot pre-shrinks each cell to a pixel budget with an *area-average* pooler (`export._area_pool_rgb`) — the same averaging Qt's smooth transform applies to the live thumbnail — so the saved image reads at the grid's brightness; peak-preserving pooling dilates sparse fluorescence and makes the snapshot brighter than its source. Symmetrically, the live thumbnail passes an explicit `(0.0, 255.0)` window to `make_overlay_thumb`, because `cell_display_rgb` has already applied the channel's LUT and colormap and re-fitting a finished image to its own min/max distorts any colormap whose ends are not black and white. **The decode cache owns the pixels, and nothing else holds them.** A rendered grid keeps no frames: `ctx.runtime.image_table.cells` and `state.image_table.last_render` record *which* cells drew, never their arrays, and a cell's `QLabel` carries `_raw_shape` (an `(h, w)` tuple, the contract `crop_tool.label_source_shape` reads) instead of the frame itself. The pixel readout fetches its cell's array on demand (`controller._hover_array`, which holds the one cell under the cursor so a drag across it decodes once); the export figure already lazy-loads on a missing array, and that load is a decode-cache hit. This is what makes `_DECODE_CACHE`'s byte budget an actual ceiling rather than a suggestion: when the render model and the widgets each pinned every frame, the budget bounded nothing — emptying the whole cache released no memory — and resident pixels grew as (cells × frame size), which at the 2048×2048 frames microscopy produces is ~16 MB a cell and over a gigabyte for a plate walk. The budget is sized from installed RAM (`image_discovery._default_max_decode_bytes`, ~15% clamped to [512 MiB, 2 GiB]) precisely because it is now the ceiling: a grid larger than the budget re-decodes through LRU eviction, which is slow, instead of exhausting memory, which fails allocations and surfaces as frames that decode for some cells and not others. **Decode caching is two-tier and shared across every export path.** `ctx.state.image_table.image_cache` holds the per-`(well, chan_lower, variant)` ref-dicts (which files exist for a well+channel); `data/image_discovery.py`'s module-global `_DECODE_CACHE` holds the actual decoded pixel arrays, keyed by `(resolved_path, greyscale, mtime_ns)`. `export._build_export_figure` writes into the *same* `image_cache` object `image_table_generate` uses (never a throwaway copy), and calls the identical threaded `controller._prefetch_cell_arrays` warm-up Generate uses before rendering — so a Save to Saved Plots or Export to File run benefits from a prior Generate's decode work and vice versa, and a save without a prior Generate still decodes in parallel rather than one cell at a time on the GUI thread. `_prefetch_cell_arrays` dedupes across calls via `state.image_table.prefetched_cells`, a persistent `set` of `(well, chan_lower, variant, tp, fov)` tuples already submitted to the thread pool — a *per-cell* key, unlike `image_cache`'s per-well+channel ref-dicts, because a grid faceted by timepoint or FOV needs every distinct cell warmed, not just one representative per well+channel. Because `export.py` needs one function out of `controller.py` (which already imports `export` at module scope as its re-export point), that one edge is a function-scoped import inside `_build_export_figure` — the standard cycle-break pattern the codebase uses elsewhere in this feature (§ `test_deferred_imports.py`'s budget). **Save to Saved Plots quality is a tunable preset**, not a fixed constant: `GALLERY_QUALITY_PRESETS` (`export.py`) maps `draft`/`standard`/`high` to a `(cell_max_px, gallery_max_px)` pair — the per-cell pre-shrink budget and the assembled grid's longest-side cap — so a single user choice (the Save menu's quick-pick submenu, or the "Export settings…" dialog) scales both together; scaling only one independently would either cap quality at the other's bound or waste compute. Export to File / Copy PNG / Copy SVG always render full resolution — only the gallery-save path reads this setting. **A Generate pass degrades cell by cell.** `image_table_generate` clears the grid before it draws anything, so an exception escaping mid-pass leaves a wiped or half-drawn table and no account of why. Every pre-pass — the parallel prefetch, the pooled Auto-LUT window, the chrome plan, the facet plan — is wrapped and degrades to a usable default (per-cell auto-fit, no scale bar, a plain unfaceted grid), and each cell's render is wrapped on its own, so one unreadable frame costs that one cell instead of abandoning every cell after it. A cell that produces no pixmap carries a *reason*: `(no image)` when nothing decoded, `(no mask)` when it asks for a mask / ≥threshold view the segmentation output can't supply, `(render failed)` when the render raised (logged with the cell's well / channel / timepoint / FOV). The status line counts the holes — a table that quietly draws fewer cells than it was asked for reads as a finished table. **A binary render never falls back to the intensity image.** `cell_display_rgb` returns `None` when a mask / ≥threshold cell can't resolve its segmentation mask, rather than composing the fluorescence it would otherwise show: that fallback made a threshold view come out half switched, with the cells whose mask resolved turning into silhouettes while the rest kept showing their picture, indistinguishable from cells with no signal above threshold. `_load_mask_array` resolves through the *same* `_match_image_ref` tiers as the image lookup (exact → normalized → numeric-close, plus the ambiguous-FOV refusal), so the mask and the image agree cell for cell instead of the mask resolving a subset of what the image does. **It also drops the cells the analysis does not count**, through `data/inclusion.drop_excluded_labels`: a pipeline mask holds every object that was segmented, including cells deleted by hand on the Segmentation tab and cells a crop excluded, and outlining those states that they are counted while every plot, statistic and export has already dropped them. Every mask this tab draws from arrives through that one call — the boundary overlay, Binary (mask), Binary (threshold), and the mask channel's own LUT pass — so the filter is applied once rather than at each of the four. The exception is the pipeline's pre-rendered **NUC+SEG overlay** channel, whose boundaries are baked into a saved image and cannot be filtered; that channel still shows every segmented cell. The dependency runs one way only: a binary cell draws its segmentation and never reads an intensity value, so when no fluorescence frame resolves it falls back to the mask as the cell's array (which also carries the source shape the crop-drag conversion and the pixel readout need) rather than reporting `(no image)` for a cell it could have drawn — and a cell with no mask either is labelled `(no mask)`, the thing that is actually absent. **An empty scan is remembered for one pass, not for the session.** `image_cache` outlives every Generate (it is dropped on dataset load), so an empty `find_well_images_and_masks` result written into it pins "this well/channel has no images" until the dataset is reloaded — and empty is not always permanent: a drive that stalls, a directory a running pipeline is still writing, a transient `OSError` inside the walk all produce it, and the affected cells then read `(no image)` forever while their neighbours render. `_load_well_channel` caches only non-empty results (including the `__mask__` sentinel dict) and records the empty ones in `state.image_table.scan_misses`, cleared at the top of each Generate / export run — so one pass still scans a genuinely absent well/channel only once, and the next pass gives it another chance. `_prefetch_cell_arrays` marks only the keys that actually decoded, for the same reason. **Headless plain-data render model.** `ctx.runtime.image_table.cells` is a `rows × cols` grid of plain `{"well","chan","tp","fov"}` string dicts — the render contract, no Qt widgets. The renderer (`image_table_generate`), the layout math, the per-cell override popover (`grid_ops.py`), and `persistence/view_state.py` all read/write those strings directly; off-axis held values live on `state.fixed_vals` (read by `grid_layout._fixed_off_axis`) and grid size on `state.rows`/`state.cols`, so there are no held-value combos or grid-size spinners. A **grouped/tiled** ("Wrap cols") layout (`group_size`, 0 = off) folds the columns into vertically-stacked bands of that many columns and repeats the whole rows axis under each band; it persists through `persistence/view_state.py` (`group_size` / `group_row_span`). Both assembly paths band, and through the same helper: `grid_layout.banded_indices` maps a grid cell `(r, c)` onto `(row_idx, col_idx)` in the un-banded axis value lists, and the flat single-dim path and the nested (mixed-radix product) path each resolve their cells through it. Banding the *column product* is what lets a nested layout wrap — with FOV › Channel down the rows and Wells across the columns, wrapping at 3 gives three wells per band and repeats the four FOV/channel rows beneath each — so the only pairing the shelf's Wrap box is disabled for is plate mode, which pins both axes to the plate's own row/column dims and has nothing left to band. A column index past the last value (the ragged final band) blanks that cell's row *and* column dims rather than leaving them unset, so it stays empty instead of falling back to the held off-axis value and drawing an image nobody asked for. A wrapped grid gives up its column headers: `facet_view._disagreeing_columns` finds that a column holding A01 in one band and A04 in the next cannot be described by the single header strip, and omits those labels rather than showing a stale one (the row labels are unaffected and repeat per band). **Builder shelf.** The **sole** authoring surface is `builder_view.py` — a root + nested-channels drag-and-drop tree: each axis gets a root (Well/Timepoint/FOV) with channels nested under it, each channel carrying its own render options (raw/corrected · mask · ≥thr · boundary · colormap/LUT) via a ⚙ menu; a derived **Fixed** panel auto-lists the off-axis roots with value pickers; a **Separate ↔ Overlay** switch (`state.composite`) collapses a root's channel axis to a single entry and additively blends every selected channel into each cell — "blend this root's channels into one cell" (the layout emits the `image_compose.OVERLAY_CHAN` sentinel as the sole channel value via `grid_layout._axis_dim_values`; `image_compose.overlay_cell_rgb` blends it in both the live grid and export, and the flag round-trips through `view_state`); wells come from the sidebar plate. **Every drop carries a position, because the position is the whole point of a list.** Each nested-channel pill is a drop target in its own right (`_ChanPill`), not just a drag source: the half of the pill under the cursor picks a side, drawn as an accent rule on that edge, and `_on_pill_drop` turns it into an insert index that `_move_channel` / `_add_channel` honour through their `at=` argument. The axis zone behind the pills still appends, which is what a drop on its bare background means, and a root token dropped on a pill is deliberately left unaccepted so it propagates out to that zone — the widget that knows how to place a root. Without a positional target the zone was the only place a drop could land, so a channel dragged within its own axis could reach nothing but the bottom of the list, and dragging the bottom one did nothing at all. Chips also claim the mouse press that starts a drag rather than letting `QFrame` ignore it and hand the press to the parent zone, and they carry themselves as the drag pixmap so the gesture reads as moving that chip. The shelf edits a Qt-free `TableSpec` (`state.py`) and calls `build_layout.image_table_apply_spec`, which flattens it onto the existing `row_dims`/`col_dims`/`active_*`/`composite`/`group_size` state (+ a per-channel `channel_opts` block) and drives the layout + a debounced `image_table_generate`. Per-channel display is **position-independent**: the four `image_compose._row_*` helpers resolve options from `channel_opts` keyed by the cell's channel, and the live generate path is unified onto `cell_display_rgb` so the live grid, the channel-overlay blend, and export always agree. **A channel's render mode is part of its axis token, because the token is the grid's identity for that channel.** `ChannelSpec.axis_token` emits `"<CHAN> (raw)"`, `"<CHAN> (mask)"` and `"<CHAN> (binary)"` for those three renders and the bare `"<CHAN>"` for `corrected` — the default, left bare so previously saved views keep their `channel_opts` keys. That is not cosmetic: `spec_to_state_fields` keys `channel_opts` by the token and `grid_layout._axis_dim_values` derives the channel axis from those keys, so a token that ignored the render gave the same channel shown two ways — its image and its cell mask — one key, one row, and the second chip vanished with nothing on screen saying so (`spec_from_state` rebuilds the shelf from the same keys, so it did not come back on restore either). `image_compose` owns the suffix vocabulary: `is_variant_token` / `_is_mask_variant` / `_is_binary_variant` classify a token and `_base_channel` strips it back to the channel whose pixels get loaded, since every variant loads the same frame and differs only in what is done with it. `_channel_options`' default branch filters every variant out, so a plain "Channels × Time" build is not silently multiplied. **A binary cell paints white or one colour per label.** `ChannelSpec.label_colors` (the ⚙ *Colour cells* item, offered only on `mask` / `≥threshold` since no other render has label ids) reaches the pixels through `image_compose._row_label_colors`, and `_export_binary_mask` keeps the label ids rather than flattening to a membership mask — a boolean array has already discarded the one thing that distinguishes a nucleus from its neighbour. The white-or-colour decision itself is `core.frame_render.fill_label_rgb`, shared with the Playground's binary view, so a cell is the same colour in both panes and there is one deterministic palette rather than two. **The LUT panel offers a row only for channels the LUT can change, and names the ones it cannot.** `builder_view._has_display_range` is the single predicate: a binary (`mask` / `≥threshold`) render paints a silhouette and the `NUC+SEG` channel is a pre-rendered RGB overlay, and `image_compose._compose_image_table_rgb` passes both through without consulting the LUT window, colormap, or log flag. Those channels get no editable row — a control whose every edit repaints nothing is worse than no control — and `_lut_inert_channels` lists them under the rows instead. They still draw an image, so without that line a LUT edit on a grid that mixes them reads as "only part of the table updated", with nothing on screen saying which cells the panel governs or why the rest held still. One row per *base* channel, so a channel shown as both its fluorescence and its ≥Thresh binary appears once (the fluorescence instance drives the LUT) and again in the inert list — under the axis token the grid labels it with, so the line names the row the reader can see. **A cell served the raw frame is marked on the cell.** When the correction pass never produced a top-hat image for a cell's `(fov, tp)`, `_load_array` falls back to the raw frame and records the cell in `state.image_table.raw_fallbacks`. That cell draws, but it draws a different measurement: a corrected image is `img - grey_opening(img)` floored at zero, so its background sits near 0, while the raw frame still carries the camera offset and background. One LUT window cannot suit both — a window tuned on the corrected population pushes the raw cells past its ceiling, where the shared clip saturates them and every further LUT edit produces a byte-identical image. `image_compose.mark_uncorrected` burns a short `raw` badge into those cells through the same `draw_cell_chrome` the scale bar and identity label use (in a corner neither has claimed, after the chrome so nothing paints over it), the tooltip spells out the reason, and the export figure carries the badge too. `_compute_auto_luts` skips them when pooling the per-channel Auto window, because one raw cell's offset otherwise stretches the window every genuinely corrected cell of that channel shares and renders them all near-black. The Generate status line still counts them; the badge is what says *which*. Per-cell tweaks come from right-clicking a rendered cell (`grid_ops.image_table_cell_override_menu`, which writes the cell dict). **Plate (96-well) layout.** A **Plate A–H × 1–12** toggle in the shelf header lays each selected well's image out in true plate positions with correct axis labels, using two *virtual* layout dims — `well_row` (A–H) and `well_col` (1–12), enumerated from the plate selection in `grid_layout` (`_well_row_options` / `_well_col_options`). They never get their own render-model cell key: `grid_layout.compose_plate_well` resolves each `(row, col)` back to the real `well` token (blank when that position is absent), and `facet_view._cv` derives them back from the composed well so the A–H / 1–12 headers label every band — unlike the `group_size`/Wrap trick, which loses its column headers entirely once it bands. It rides the existing `_build_nested_layout` path with `wrap=0` (`row_dims=["well_row"]`, `col_dims=["well_col"]`); the channel is held fixed (`TableSpec.plate` flag round-trips through `spec_to_state_fields` / `spec_from_state`), and it's mutually exclusive with Wrap *and* with channel Overlay (plate mode writes `composite=False`). Because both axes belong to the plate there is nowhere for a channel axis to tile, so **plate mode displays exactly one channel** — the first in the shelf, pinned as `fixed_vals["channel"]`. The LUT panel follows: `builder_view._plate_shown_token` is the one channel that gets an editable row, and `_plate_hidden_channels` names the rest on their own hint line. Offering a row for a channel with no cells is the all-or-nothing sibling of the inert-channel case above — the edit lands in `channel_opts`, nothing reads it, and no cell moves. **Every per-cell lookup names the channel the cell is drawn from.** A cell's `chan` is what the axis calls it, and for two kinds of cell that is not a channel the loader ever opens: an `OVERLAY_CHAN` cell blends the whole selected channel set, and a ratio cell's token is a `RatioMetric` display label whose loader reads the metric's numerator and denominator. `image_compose.cell_source_channels(ctx, cell, overlay_chans)` resolves a cell to those real channels — the overlay member list comes from the caller, because only the layout knows it — and `is_raw_fallback` / `mark_uncorrected` ask their per-pass record through it rather than through the cell's own token, which asked for a channel the loader never wrote and answered "corrected" for a cell that is not. True when **any** source channel fell back, because a blend or a ratio carrying one uncorrected input is an uncorrected image. The badge is applied at the boundary: `_render_cell`'s overlay branch calls `mark_uncorrected` after the chrome, `export.py` passes the same `overlay_chans` so the exported figure badges the cells the screen does, and the status line counts the **cells that carry the badge** rather than entries in the loader's record — that record holds one entry per channel loaded, so an overlay of three fallen-back channels contributed three and a ratio cell two, leaving a number larger than the grid sitting beside the badges it claimed to describe. The same rule governs render-mode and LUT resolution: `_row_display_opts` and `_parse_lut` take the cell's channel and fall back to the row's representative channel only when no channel was named, so a cell drawn from a channel that is not its row's representative one still resolves that channel's own raw/corrected setting and that channel's own shared LUT window, rather than the row's. `tests/test_image_table_channel_identity.py::test_every_render_mode_lookup_names_the_channel_it_is_for` is an AST guard over every `_row_display_opts` call in the package. **One render path, no pre-rendered shortcut.** Every non-overlay cell composes through `cell_display_rgb`, takes the chrome, takes `mark_uncorrected`, and thumbnails at a fixed `(0.0, 255.0)` — the shape `export._build_export_figure` already had. An `ndim >= 3` array needs no branch of its own: `_compose_image_table_rgb` passes such an input straight through, NUC+SEG or not, and the branch that skipped composition for it dropped the chrome, the badge and the fixed window from exactly the cells the pipeline pre-rendered. **A truncated inventory is named on every surface that can produce one.** `image_compose.partial_scan_clause` is the single sentence — the wells, the count and the scans' own reasons — said by the Generate line and by all four saved-artifact surfaces: the PNG/PDF/SVG export, both clipboard copies and the gallery save. Those files outlive the status line and are short by however many frames the scan never reached, with nothing in them to say so. One clause rather than a sentence per surface, and for a measured reason: the two hand-written versions it replaces had already drifted the wrong way, the Generate line naming the count and the reasons and the saved-PNG line naming neither, so the artifact that outlives the session carried *less* than the transient line. The clause is neutral about grid-versus-file because that framing belongs to the caller. **`scale_bar_refusal_clause` answers two different failures, because there are two.** `scale_bar_refusals` is per *cell* — a bar that was computed and would not fit — and the code that records it (`apply_cell_chrome`) is guarded on a bar length above zero, so by construction it cannot see a bar that was never computed at all. Four such paths existed and every one of them was silent: no pixel size, a bar length of zero, a `scale_bar_cells` code naming no cell in this grid (reachable from a saved view state carrying a code the combo no longer offers), and an empty grid. A ticked **Show scale bar** then sat over a table with no bar and no explanation on any surface. `resolve_chrome_plan` now records the reason in `state.image_table.scale_bar_plan_note` — same per-pass lifetime as the three sets beside it, cleared by `reset_scan_misses` — and the clause reports it first and alone, since a control that was never going to draw a bar is a different fix from a cell that could not hold one. It travels with `partial_scan_clause` and `tests/test_both_shortfalls_travel_together.py` requires the two to reach exactly the same functions — per function rather than per file, since a module-level check passes while three of four surfaces in that module say nothing, and a line naming one shortfall while silent about the other convinces the reader it is telling them what is wrong. |
| `features/preview/controller.py` | Preview-panel helpers (well-picker sync for the image tabs). The image pixel-value hover tooltip lives in `review_image/controller.py` next to its only caller. |
| `domain/image_identity.py` | **Single source of truth for image filenames, cell identity, and the suffix/role catalog.** Owns three concerns deliberately co-located so they cannot drift: (1) `CellKey` — `(well, fov, timepoint, nucleus_id)` with one canonical normalisation chain; every site that joins CSV-row data to image-derived data builds keys via `CellKey.from_row` / `cell_keys_for_dataframe` (the smFISH writer, `cell_overrides`, `review_image`'s row keys, and `_process_well`'s counts construction all consume it). (2) `parse_image_filename` / `build_image_filename` — exact inverses driven by a `PipelineSchema` loaded once from `pipeline_info.json` via `load_schema(...)`. No parallel regex fallbacks; single-FOV pipelines are modelled by `has_fov=False` rather than a special-case extractor synthesising `"1"` (the empty-FOV-to-`"1"` rule is enforced uniformly by `normalize_fov`). (3) `ROLE_CATALOG` — declarative `RoleSpec` per role (`fluor`/`tophat`/`mask`/`overlay`/`smfish`/`phase`) mapping suffix, output extensions, channel-scoping, and precedence; `classify_filename_role`, `role_output_filename` and `image_resolver`'s legacy-kind wrapper all consume it, and `image_resolver.OUTPUT_SUFFIXES` is derived from it rather than written out a second time. One role suffix is **not** matched in its bare form: `_phase` is also a plausible *channel name*, and a dataset whose last schema slot holds a channel called `phase` writes `A01_1_phase.tif`, which is indistinguishable from a bare phase-role output of well A01 field 1. `RoleSpec.match_bare_suffix` records that, so only the unambiguous channel-scoped spelling (`_phase_<channel>`) is recognised and such a file stays an ordinary raw frame. `classify_filename_role` strips the matched suffix **and its extension, once**: what is left is the field text, and field text carries dots (`1.5h`), so a second pass through `Path(...).stem` would truncate at the last of them — which turned `A1_f1_1.5h_w2_labels.tif` into the stem `A1_f1_1`, losing a slot off the schema split, stranding the frame from its own mask, and colliding with the genuine `1h` key on a first-hit-wins lookup. (As of the §6.2 self-sufficiency fix this catalog is **reader-side only** — the pipeline writer, `process_microscopy.build_processed_output_path`, uses explicit `suffix=` strings rather than importing `review`. If catalog-driven *writing* is revived, move `ROLE_CATALOG` into a Qt-free `*_core` module first so the pipeline can import it without breaking the contract.) The full time-format matrix (`T01`/`24`/`24h`/`1.0`/`day3`/`02d04h30m`/`timepoint_hours` float) collapses to a single canonical form via `normalize_tp`. `frame_token_series` is the frame half of `cell_keys_for_dataframe` without the per-row `CellKey` construction — normalised `(fov, tp)` Series for a frame, for a caller that only has to decide which frame each row belongs to (the crop scope); both resolve their columns through the same `resolve_identity_column`, so they cannot end up reading different columns off one CSV. Stdlib-only at import; pandas is lazy inside `normalize_fov_series`, `frame_token_series` and `cell_keys_for_dataframe` so `process_microscopy.py` can import the module without adding pandas as a pipeline dependency. |
| `features/export/service.py` | The CSV exporters behind every plot tab's Save menu — the plotted summary (`export_*_data`) and the raw per-cell rows (`export_cell_data`). **Neither holds the plate.** `export_cell_data` (and its batch twin `batch_export/_cell_rows.write_cell_rows`) reads every exported well once for its column list — the header and the missing-verdict note need all of them — keeps only that, and reads each well again as its chunk is cut, one well per event-loop tick (batch: through a two-chunk queue its writer drains on a thread), so one well's frame is alive at a time; `tests/test_no_view_holds_the_plate.py` counts them by weak reference. `export_distribution_data` keeps each group's values as floats and formats them as it writes, rather than holding a string per cell for the whole selection. **A scatter's two axes get distinct column names only when they need them.** `_axis_column_names` is the one place that decides: names that differ pass through untouched, so an ordinary export's headers are the statistic's own names; names that would collide — the same statistic on both axes, or one that collides with the other's derived `_error` column — gain an `_x` / `_y` suffix. Without it a row dict keyed by the statistic's name holds one entry for two axes, and the file carries one axis twice under a single header while claiming to hold both. |
| `features/smfish/{controller,worker}.py` | smFISH spot detection + the background worker. Apply Global Threshold rewrites every per-well CSV's `<channel>_smfish_count` column, then in its after-csv callback persists the threshold to `pipeline_info.json::smfish_thresholds` via `persistence/smfish.py`, drops the per-well DataFrame cache + the aggregation stats cache, redraws plots, and refreshes the Review CSV table — without those last three steps, downstream plots and the review table kept showing pre-apply counts. The after-csv callback is routed through `_WorkerBridge.after_csv` (a queued `Signal(object)`) rather than invoked directly from `apply_global_threshold_async`'s daemon thread — the worker thread has no Qt event loop, so the previous `QTimer.singleShot(0, …)`-from-worker scheme silently dropped the refresh on the floor and the user had to close and reopen the app to see the new counts. Progress crosses the same bridge: the worker's `progress_cb(done, total)` fires once per well in the counting pass and again per well in the CSV-write pass, `_WorkerBridge.progress` (a queued `Signal(int, int)`) marshals it onto the GUI thread, and the tab drives the shared status-row `_progress_bar` — the widget a dataset load steps — through `ctx.widgets.get_or_none`, so the bar is simply absent rather than fatal in a build without it. The bar is shown when the run is launched and hidden by the `done` signal, which every terminal path emits: success, cancel, a crash caught by `_run_guarded`, and the empty-channel guard (that guard returning on a status line alone left the tab's `apply_running` flag set, so the button rejected every later click as "already running"). The write loop reports from a `finally`, so a well skipped for an unresolvable or locked CSV still advances the bar instead of parking it short of its maximum. | `features/image_browser/review_image/callbacks.py` | What a finished rubber-band drag in Delete mode does, and the override writer it shares with the single-cell click. `commit_included_overrides` is the one writer that can span wells: it takes `(well, fov, tp, nid)` keys from `override_key`, projects onto each touched well's cached rows, invalidates the stats cache, schedules the debounced save, bumps `override_version` and re-renders **once** for the whole batch, restoring zoom/pan around the refresh; it counts distinct keys rather than writes, so a CSV with two rows for one cell does not overstate the edit. `override_key` runs FOV / timepoint / nucleus through `CellKey` — the constructor `collect.review_row_keys_series` looks overrides back up with — but leaves the **well** exactly as the dataset spells it: well labels are `extract_well_token(stem) or stem`, so a CSV whose stem is not a well position keeps its raw stem, and canonicalising it here would produce a key no reader ever asks for. `apply_box_delete` deletes on the displayed frame by any-pixel overlap against its label mask; when the **Delete scope** control has armed further wells / FOVs / timepoints, `collect.collect_region_delete_targets` resolves the same rectangle across those frames by *centroid*, sharing `crop/region.centroids_inside` with the crop layer. Both halves are counted separately on the status line, and everything the delete could not judge is named in a warning toast rather than folded silently into a smaller total: wells with no `shape_centroid_*` columns, wells whose rows won't load, and armed wells this dataset does not have. The scoped scan runs on the UI thread and costs seconds on a full plate — the row scan plus one override projection per touched well — so `_busy` puts up a wait cursor and a status line for any multi-well scope and logs the elapsed time; moving it to a worker is the open follow-up. |

| `features/image_browser/playground/{controller,renderer,worker}.py` | Segmentation-page **Playground** sub-tab: an interactive testbed for the pipeline's background-flattening / subtraction methods *and* its StarDist segmentation, on a single frame. **Two frame sources**, resolved by `_resolve_frame`: the dataset frame addressed by the sidebar plate's well plus the channel / timepoint / FOV combos, or — winning when set — a **loose image** opened straight from disk with "Open image…" (`state.loose_image_path`, read through the pipeline's own `load_2d_gray`, cached by path so the correction memo's `id()` key still hits). The loose source is what makes the tab usable with **no dataset loaded at all**, which is the state you are in when choosing settings for a plate you have not run yet; it disables the dataset selectors, has no precomputed mask, and refuses the reference-well correction modes (`empty_well` / `basic`, which need a whole well to sample) **by name** in the status line rather than presenting an uncorrected frame as corrected. Loading a dataset ends loose mode (`PlaygroundState.clear_caches`). Applies the chosen flat-field + background method through `process_microscopy.correct_single_frame` — the **same** per-frame orchestration the batch worker's `_correct` uses (extracted so pipeline and Playground share one code path; a parity test pins the equivalence), so no method is reimplemented. The `empty_well` / `basic` reference fields are estimated from a chosen background well on a daemon thread via a queued-signal bridge (smFISH pattern). **Those fields are cached by everything that decides which one gets estimated** — `("ff", well, channel, mode)` and `("bg", well, channel)` in `state.ref_fields` — because `basic` and `empty_well` produce *different* flat-fields from the same frames (`estimate_basic_flatfield` versus `normalize_flatfield(B)`) and the additive background field is only estimated when the background method is `empty_well`. A cache keyed on less than that answers "already built" for a field it never built, and `apply_flatfield` then no-ops **silently** on the `None` it is handed, so the correction appears to do nothing. `_reference_fields_for` is the single resolver both the render path and the Segment button go through, so the frame on screen and the frame handed to StarDist can never be corrected differently; when a needed field is absent it **downgrades that half of the correction to `none`** and names the refusal in the read-out, rather than reporting a mode that did not run. A build that finds no usable frames is recorded in `state.ref_missing` with its reason — held apart from `ref_fields` so "not built yet" (build it) stays distinguishable from "cannot be built" (report it, and never respawn the worker on the next keystroke). `_build_reference_then_render` captures the well and the modes at *request* time and files the result under keys built from those captures, so a dropdown changed while the worker runs cannot relabel what it computed. The correction itself stays synchronous on the GUI thread, so `playground_on_change` memoizes its result (`state.last_correction_key`/`last_corrected_arr`, keyed on the decoded frame's identity — safe because `image_discovery`'s decode cache returns the same array object on a hit — plus every correction parameter) and skips recomputing when nothing that affects the output changed; `build_playground_tab` triggers exactly one render on first open (via `registry._activate_playground`, which always follows the tab's construction in the same dispatch), not its own redundant call plus the activation hook's. **The stage control — labelled "Correct up to" (`state.source`: raw / flatfield / corrected) — heads the Correction section and is a master switch, not a view option** — `raw` returns before any correction runs and `flatfield` forces `bg_method="none"`, so most of that section is dead on those stages. `correction_controls_enabled(stage)` is the pure rule for which controls each stage consults (radius / small-px / mesh are *background* parameters, so they are dead on `flatfield` too) and `_sync_method_rows` greys out the rest; it previously sat in the Display section two groups below the controls it silenced, which made an inactive panel read as a broken one. A muted caption under it states what it governs — "decides which controls below run — Raw runs none" — because "Stage" named a step of the pipeline rather than the effect on the panel, and a control whose meaning lives only in its tooltip has already failed the reader who did not hover. **The controls dock** (`tab_view.build_playground_tab`) is a fixed `Metrics.dock_w` column whose rows live in a vertical-only `QScrollArea` (`PlaygroundDockScroll`, as the left rail does in `app_shell_view`): the panel is taller than a short window leaves it, and a bare layout handed less than its minimum height squeezes every row at once until the text in each is clipped. Its rows are laid out to fit the dock's width with the scrollbar showing — the three-segment stage control sits under its label rather than beside it, and the Threshold curve… button and its Stop take a row of their own below Segment / Focus distribution… — which `tests/test_playground_dock_fits.py` measures under the real stylesheet. **The read-out** (`_status_text`, the "What you're looking at" box) states in words everything this tab can be ambiguous about, because none of it is visible in the picture: the frame; the stage and the correction *actually applied*; the displayed array's range/mean; the mask's provenance (`_mask_source`), label count, what the QC size filter removed, and whether it even fits the frame; and which rule drew what is on screen. `_render` records those facts in `state.display_facts` as it draws them, so the read-out reports what the renderer did rather than re-deriving it — a second derivation is a second chance to describe something that did not happen. The range is load-bearing rather than decorative: the LUT re-derives its window from the displayed array while it reads `auto`, so a correction can move the data while leaving the picture identical (for `fov_median`, a scalar subtraction, *pixel*-identical), and the numbers are how it proves it ran. **Binary mode is the sharpest case**: `build_frame_rgb` picks between three rules — a per-cell mean gate, a per-*pixel* threshold when no usable mask exists, and the whole labelled footprint when there is no per-cell verdict — which mean completely different things and render identically as white-on-black. `_binary_rule` names which one ran, and the read-out says so along with where the threshold came from (this tab, or the channel's app-wide ON value). Binary mode fills each label in **its own colour** by default (`state.binary_label_colors`, the *Colour cells* toggle): cells painted a common white merge into one shape wherever they touch, so a segmentation that failed to split two nuclei looks identical to one that split them correctly — which is the question the tab exists to answer. `frame_render.label_color_lut` is a golden-ratio hue walk indexed by label id, deterministic and RNG-free so a cell keeps its colour between redraws, with saturation and value stepping on their own irrationals so near-colliding hues still separate; consecutive ids land far apart, which is what matters because touching nuclei are usually numbered consecutively. The per-pixel fallback is left white and reported as such — it has no labels to colour, and colouring it would imply a per-cell distinction it never made. A **Cells** row sits directly under the Segmentation controls with the one number those controls are tuned against: `_count_text` formats the *same* `display_facts` the paragraph read-out uses — a formatting, never a second derivation — giving the labels drawn, what the QC filter dropped, and (only under the per-cell rule, the only one that reaches a per-cell verdict) how many clear the threshold. It reads `—` rather than `0` wherever there is no count to give — no mask at all, or live labels that no longer describe this frame — because zero is a measurement and unknown is not. Display goes through `core.frame_render.build_frame_rgb` (re-exported here as `build_playground_rgb`) and a binary/boundary overlay; per-source LUT memory, click-drag pan, frame-local binary threshold (defaults from but never writes back to the app-wide `ThreshFracOn`), and a QC size-cleanup preview are Playground-local. **Live StarDist preview** (the Segmentation section): a *Live StarDist* toggle, the two detection thresholds, and an explicit **Segment** button run `pipeline.stardist.segment_nuclei` on the frame currently displayed, so the preview is the pipeline's own inference rather than a lookalike — including the input scrubbing and near-constant-field refusal that make StarDist's uncatchable ClipperLib abort unreachable, which matters more here because an abort in the GUI process would take the whole application down. The inference itself lives in `services.frame_preview`, which holds the session's single loaded model and keeps the TF import out of a Qt module (this package is imported at GUI start-up). `worker.stardist_labels_for_frame` is the thin seam onto it; `request_stardist_labels` and `request_reference_fields` both marshal their result back through `core.worker_bridge.run_off_thread`, the one-shot queued-signal bridge (`ctx.runtime.playground.seg_bridge` / `.ref_bridge`). Both also **report while they run**, through that bridge's `progress` / `stage` signals, onto the shared status-row bar the smFISH Apply-to-All and the dataset load already drive (`_show_progress` / `_step_progress` / `_hide_progress`, all GUI-thread). The reference build is determinate — one step per frame decoded, which is where its wall-clock goes. Segmentation is **indeterminate**: one frame's inference has no interior milestones to count and the wait is dominated by a one-off model load, so a percentage would be invented; instead `segment_frame` names its two phases (`STAGE_LOADING` / `STAGE_SEGMENTING`) through an `on_stage` callable and the status line says which is running, because reporting the 10-30 s TensorFlow load identically to the seconds-long segmentation leaves a first Segment looking like a hang. The bar is hidden on **every** exit path including failure — one left sweeping under an error message is its own false statement. The GUI-thread correction (`correct_single_frame`) deliberately gets no bar: it is synchronous, so nothing could animate through it. Segmentation runs on the **corrected** frame whatever stage is displayed, because that is what the pipeline segments — `_segmentation_frame` pins the stage to `corrected` and returns a note naming the mismatch, so a nucleus count can never be read as belonging to a picture it did not come from. For the same reason `seg_key` excludes the display stage: switching Raw ↔ Corrected describes the same pixels and must not invalidate labels. `_mask_source` decides the overlay: live labels when they are current, the pipeline's saved mask when live mode is off, and **nothing** when live labels have gone stale — it must not fall back to the pipeline's mask under a status line describing live ones, which is one mask on screen and a different one claimed. **The threshold curve** answers the one question the Probability field cannot: whether the value in it is a sensible one for this plate. `playground_sweep_now` segments the displayed frame at each of `review.domain.threshold_sweep.sweep_grid()` — 19 thresholds from 0.05 to 0.95, not 0 to 1, because at 0 StarDist keeps every candidate polygon the network emitted and at 1 nothing survives, and both ends cost the most — and `sweep_curve_view.show_threshold_curve` plots count against threshold in a non-modal window modelled on the Cell Gating optimizer's, marking where the user currently is. **It recommends nothing, and that is a decision with a measurement behind it**: the plateau rule it replaced (midpoint of the widest run of small `|Δ log count|`) returns either the sweep's zero tail, suggesting detect-nothing, or its low-threshold shoulder, which reproduces the Analyze form's own hardcoded 0.2 to three decimal places — decided by how `log(0)` happens to be guarded, since a monotone curve has no interior plateau maximum and every widest-flat-region rule therefore lands at an extreme. The module docstring carries the table. Four states are refusals rather than plots — a sweep that never ran, a frame that was **not swept at all**, no nuclei at any threshold, and a count that never moves — and each is drawn *as the figure*, because a line along zero reads as a plate whose nuclei sit below the lowest cut when it is far more often a wrong segmentation channel. The not-swept refusal is the near-constant frame, and it is its own sentence rather than nineteen zeros for the reason this whole subsystem exists: the network never ran on it, so "no nuclei were detected at any threshold" describes a measurement that was never taken and is indistinguishable from a genuinely empty well the network really did scan. `sweep_frame` answers `None` for it, refuses **before** loading the model rather than after a 10-30 s TensorFlow import, and `curve_from_counts` takes that refusal in preference to every rule about counts. **The frame is prepared exactly as `segment_nuclei` prepares it**, through the shared `pipeline.stardist.prepare_stardist_input` — percentile normalisation to [0, 1] plus the input scrubbing — and a near-constant field is refused through the same `is_near_constant`, before anything reaches the network.
