Both are load-bearing rather than tidy. `model.predict` takes `normalizer=None` and assumes its input is already normalised, so handed the corrected frame in raw camera counts it returned 6 nuclei falling to 4 across the whole range where the truth was 86 falling to 0, **did not decline**, and drew the flat line this feature's own manual tells the reader means the threshold does not matter. And a sweep is nineteen NMS passes per press, so nineteen times one Segment press's exposure to the uncatchable ClipperLib abort that would take the application down with it. The sweep then costs **one** inference rather than *M*: `frame_preview._resolve_at_thresholds` caches `model.predict`'s `(prob, dist)` pair and resolves instances from it per threshold. Measured on the shipped path against nineteen full `segment_nuclei` calls on the same frame and grid: **8.8×** faster, with identical counts at every threshold — on a frame whose dimensions are multiples of 16, which is the caveat the docstring states: `predict_instances` selects candidates sparsely on the *padded* probability map while `predict` crops first, so where a frame's height or width is not a multiple of the network's `div_by` the two exclude slightly different border bands and can differ by nuclei whose centres sit in the last few pixels. That resolve API is private, so the fast path answers `None` and the caller falls back to one `segment_frame` per threshold; tiling skips it entirely, because the measurement was taken untiled. `should_stop` reaches inside the loop and a stopped sweep returns and plots the counts it had — a partial curve the user asked for is evidence, but it is drawn and described as a fragment: the x-axis spans the range that was **requested** rather than the part that was measured, a hollow marker says where the measurement stopped, and the sentence reads "Stopped after N of M … so far". Rescaled to the eight points a stopped sweep got, the line runs corner to corner and the picture asserts that the count barely moves on this frame — a conclusion a scientist would act on and an artifact of having stopped. The same scoping applies to the never-moves refusal, which names how many thresholds it saw and says the rest was not measured. The sweep's own sentence is written by the read-out rather than beside it: `_describe_sweep` contributes it to every exit from `playground_on_change` through `_set_frame_status`, including the three early returns that never reach `_status_text`, because the controller used to write it with `_set_status` and then trigger the repaint that overwrote it. **What the curve describes is captured at dispatch, not read back at completion** (`_sweep_key`, `_sweep_subject` and the user's own threshold, all taken before the worker starts): nothing disables the tab while a sweep runs, so a subject read in the completion callback names whatever the user clicked on since, the figure is titled with a frame it never saw, and the staleness check compares that title against itself and finds nothing. `_sweep_key` is the address **and** `_seg_key` minus the probability threshold, because the correction, its parameters, the background well and the NMS threshold all change the pixels without changing the frame's name — NMS most sharply, since it moves every count on the curve. When any of it no longer matches, the read-out says so and keeps the counts underneath, because the dialog is still open showing them. Segment and the sweep are mutually exclusive: both reach the session's single model, so each greys the other's button out and each declines by name if reached anyway, and `frame_preview._MODEL_LOCK` serialises the model regardless — on a first load two threads would otherwise both call the pretrained loader, whose cross-process advisory lock is keyed on the holder's pid and therefore cannot recognise itself, so the second waits out its whole 120 s timeout and then loads a second copy of the weights. Button state is the controller's (`_set_sweep_buttons`), on every exit path including failure and no-frame: `playground_on_change` reflects the *frame* and has never looked at a running flag, so leaving it to that fan-out would be a dead Stop button and a second sweep started over the first. The tab is the app's **only** interactive segmenter, and does two jobs: choosing settings before a run (Open image… a representative frame, tune, then type the two values into the Analyze form's matching fields) and diagnosing after one (a processed well, with the pipeline's own saved mask to compare against). The Analyze form is deliberately the only place the run's parameters are *stored*; re-typing two numbers is cheaper than a second, thinner preview that duplicates this one. |
| `features/image_browser/cell_browser/{controller,collect,worker,tab_view,criteria_view}.py` | Cell Browser gallery: a filtered grid of per-cell crops composed off-thread (`worker.CellImageLoader`, reusing the Image Table loaders + zip cache). Sources cells from the active **plate selection** (`collect.cell_browser_source_wells`). **Deferred render:** every control — filters (criteria/timepoint/FOV/sort), channel chips, the per-channel `LUT ▾` popover (LUT min/max + a colour swatch editing `tint_by_channel`), and the **Raw / Corrected** source `SegmentedControl` (`CellBrowserState.use_tophat`, threaded through `load_page` → `compose_cell_rgb` → `_load_array`) — only *stages* state; the single top-bar **Generate** button (`controller.apply_filters`) re-collects and re-composites. There is no separate "Apply filters" button. **Gate-source mode** (the sidebar's *From scatter gate* checkbox, `CellBrowserState.scatter_gate_mode`) swaps the numeric filter for the scatter gate(s): `criteria_view._set_criteria_enabled` disables the criteria rows + *Add criterion* and reveals a muted line stating why. The checkbox is deliberately sticky — nothing resets it on tab switch or dataset load — so that line is the only on-screen account of an editor that is otherwise inertly greyed out. |
| `features/home/groups/controller.py` | Home → Sample Map → **Groups**: replicate-set editing — adding a set from the plate picker, refreshing the tab's plate, and the Quick-Replicates pairing that chunks the current selection into groups of a chosen size along a Rows / Columns walk. The pure part of that (`make_replicate_pairs`) is here; the colour and membership rules it reads are `domain/selections_model.py`, which `core/` uses without importing a feature. **A group is named after what it is, once the plate can say.** The generated name is the tokens of the wells in it — `A01/A02` — which locates a group and describes nothing, so `name_sets_from_variables` re-reads each set through `sample_variables.names_for_well_sets` and takes the composed name where the variables give one: `HeLa · 10 µM`. Where they do not — a plate with no variables, a group whose wells disagree about every one of them — the tokens stay, because they are a true statement about a group nothing else can describe. The composed name rides onto the `Selection` with `name_is_verbatim`, and it has to: a `Dose` of `10` with no unit typed **is** `replicate_display_label`'s auto-generated-name pattern, so without the flag every axis would draw back the well tokens this naming exists to replace. The **New Replicate Set** dialog does the same live — the name box fills in from the wells being picked on its plate, and stops the moment the user types over it, which is why the last offered name is remembered rather than the field re-derived on each change. `build_rep_add_dialog` builds and wires that dialog and `rep_add` is the `exec` over it, split because a closure reachable only from inside a modal is reachable from no test: a modal blocks for ever under the offscreen QPA, so `tests/test_group_names_from_variables.py` builds the real dialog, selects wells on the real plate and reads the real name box. **Editing a group on the plate keeps the members the plate cannot show.** `panel_view._commit_plate_to_current` carries through the group's wells that are not in `dataset.well_paths` instead of rebuilding membership from the plate alone: a plate can only paint the wells this load holds, so a subset load turned every plate edit into a silent deletion of the rest of the group, autosaved as such. The list can then hold a token with no plate position, so the sort key is `_plate_order` rather than a bare `parse_rc` — sorting a `(None, None)` beside real keys raises. |
| `features/export/{service,style}.py` | CSV export (`service.py`) + the Export Style editor's profiles and the Properties-panel roster (`style.py`). The prefs and apply pipeline are `core/plot_style.py`'s, and `copy_figure_to_clipboard` (Copy SVG → native macOS pasteboard via pyobjc, Qt-clipboard fallback) is `widgets/fig_clipboard.py`'s. |

Shared domain helpers (under `review/domain/`):

| Module | Role |
|--------|------|
| `domain/fold_change.py` | Fold-change normalization helpers (vs control well/rep-set, vs each member's first timepoint). Consumed by line / bar plot, batch export, and `features/export/service.py`. |
| `domain/numeric.py` | `is_number` / `is_numeric` — the one answer to "is this a usable measurement?" and "is this a number at all?". Every numeric guard on the plotting and export paths used to be spelled `isinstance(value, (int, float)) and math.isfinite(value)`, which is False for **every** numpy scalar, and the values reaching those guards come out of numpy reductions several call levels away — so the test asked which class had produced a number rather than whether it was one. When such a value does reach one, the failure is silent and always in the same direction: a real spread becomes "no error bar", a real mean becomes a placeholder — `fold_change._finite_spread(numpy.float32(0.25))` returned `0.0`, measured on the helper directly. No live producer was found: every `AggPoint` field is `float()`/`int()`-coerced in `data_loading`, and `_reduce_reps` coerces too, so this is **hardening against a reachable shape rather than a defect anyone has hit** — which is the honest way to hold a rule whose violations are silent. The two predicates are separate because the distinction is load-bearing — a NaN spread means *undefined*, and folding it to `0.0` says the replicates agreed exactly, so a site that lets NaN through on purpose uses `is_numeric` while a site deciding whether a value can be drawn uses `is_number`. Both reject anything sized, because `float(numpy.array([1.0]))` succeeds and an array in a scalar slot is a bug that must not be converted quietly. `tests/test_numeric_guard.py` holds the five modules that judge measured values to using them. |
| `domain/control_ref.py` | `ControlRef` — the frozen `(kind, name)` a fold-change control is addressed by, plus its storage form. The kind travels beside the name because replicate-set names are unrestricted free text, so no single string can distinguish a well from a set that shares its token (§9.5). |
| `domain/fold_change_state.py` | `FoldChangeState` — the request object every collection path is handed. It is read **by name only**: a request read by unpacking silently drops any field added after the unpack was written, and for this object a dropped field means raw values drawn under a fold-change axis. Emulating a tuple would also break the `__eq__`/`__hash__` contract the denominator cache keys on. `coerce_fc_state` accepts a tuple as input, since many tests spell a request inline; nothing hands one back. |
| `domain/fold_change_series_cache.py` | `ControlSeriesCache` — a per-redraw memo of control denominator series, keyed on the reference. The cross-axis stacking blocks resolve a control inside the member loop and each call rebuilds the whole series, so a 24-member plate over 6 timepoints issued 882 builds on the vs-control + vs-t0 path against 75 with the memo. It captures the threshold, value column, spread mode and gates it was built with and has no invalidation, so it is a collector local and must not outlive one redraw. |
| `domain/fold_change_pairing.py` | `ControlDenominators` is what a collector actually calls: `denoms.at(member, tp)` gives that member's control, its outcome, and the mean / fraction / events denominators **separately**. The three are answered per member and per panel rather than hoisted once per timepoint and shared: sharing one denominator across every member makes a single missing control NaN the whole plate, and sharing one *flag* across the three panels leaves a control with a mean but no fraction series drawing a raw value under a fold-change label. `panel_nan_flags` is that per-panel rule, and both the bar collector and `normalize_member_pts` on the line side apply it. It is built by `control_denominators`, which resolves the mapping when per-member mode is on and otherwise settles the single control's own outcome once. Also: `build_per_member_controls` resolves a whole per-sample control mapping in one pass, returning a `PerMemberControls` of `MemberControl` records — each carrying the member's control, the wells it resolved to, and a `ControlOutcome` saying **why**. A single global control either resolves or it does not; per-sample pairing makes partial failure the normal case, and `unmapped` / `control_unresolved` / `control_no_sample` are three different things to tell a user that all produce the same empty `fold_change_mean`. The renderer's annotations, the status line, the CSV's `fold_change_outcome` column and the editor's Status column read the same record rather than re-deriving the decision. Four outcomes are decidable here; `control_no_sample` is a function of *(member, control, timepoint)* and is stamped by the collector. `self` is decided by comparing resolved wells, never names. Also holds `auto_pair` (the chunk-along-the-plot-order bulk assignment) and the summary / shortfall strings. |
| `domain/plot_members.py` | `bar_member_keys` / `line_member_keys` / `plotted_member_keys` — which members a plot draws, in the order it draws them, plus `member_replicate_sets` for the well → owning-set map. One question with one answer, because more than one consumer asks it: `ctx.runtime.barplot.current_keys()` returns replicate-set names whenever any set is active, while `collect_bar_items` emits **well tokens** once the pool-replicates toggle is off, so anything built on the runtime's list disagrees with the plot in that case. It reaches the bar tab's drag order through a runtime attribute lookup rather than an import, which is what keeps `domain/` free of `features/`. `tests/test_plot_members.py` asserts the keys **equal** those the collectors emit; that equality is the guard, not the extraction. |
| `domain/plot_order.py` | `apply_order` — reorder members so the ones named in a saved drag order come first, the rest in natural order. Pure list manipulation with no notion of what a member is. It lives here because the Line tab, the Scatter tab and member enumeration all need it, and while it sat in the Line controller the Scatter collector imported one feature from another to get at it. |
| `domain/significance.py` | How a significance result is written down — the asterisk ladder, the p-value itself, or both. Two surfaces state the same comparison: the Statistics tab prints a text report of every pair, and the Bar plot draws a bracket over the pair of bars. Both go through this module for **both halves** of the statement — `significance_stars` for the verdict and `p_phrase` for the number — so a p of exactly 0.05 cannot read `ns` on the panel and `*` in the text beside it, and `p = 0.0312` on one cannot be `p = 0.03125` on the other. Sharing only the ladder is the half-sweep that leaves one function holding two definitions of the same word. `significance_label(p, mode, adjusted=…)` assembles what one bracket says under `PlotState.significance_label_mode` — `"stars"` (`*`), `"p"` (`p = 0.0312`) or `"both"` (`* (p = 0.0312)`) — and an unrecognised mode reads as `"stars"`, so a view state written by a later build degrades to what every build draws rather than to a blank bracket. Two rules in the formatting are load-bearing. **A p-value is never printed as zero**: an extreme test underflows the double to exactly `0.0`, and `%g` renders that `0`, which claims a probability of zero where the truth is a number smaller than a float can hold — it is written `p < 5e-324`, a bound against the smallest positive double, which is the repository's computed-as-zero-versus-not-computed rule applied to the one quantity where a printed zero is always a lie. The bound is taken for an exact zero and for nothing else: a threshold of `1e-300` was picked on the belief that the automatic format stopped resolving below it, and measured, `%.3g` renders the whole subnormal range (`1e-310` → `1e-310`), so that threshold demoted real p-values to a weaker statement — the same conflation facing the other way, and no better for erring toward caution. And **the number is quoted by name**: the renderer draws the Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted p whenever the run has one, so a label carrying it reads `p_BH`, the same name the Statistics report gives it. `p` and `p_BH` are different claims about the same pair, and with three or more groups the raw p is the one that overstates the result. A p that is not a finite number yields `ns` from the ladder and an empty string from `format_p_value`, so a caller drawing a figure cannot be taken down by one uncomputable comparison and cannot print the word `nan` over a bracket either. |
| `domain/stats_compute.py` | `compute_rep_stats`, `aggregate_well`, `aggregate_group` — the pure-math layer the bar / line / scatter controllers share. **The collectors call `aggregate_well_cached`, not `aggregate_well`.** It memoises a well's aggregate into the same `AppState.stats_cache`, so every existing invalidation clears it too. The wrapper exists rather than a cache inside `aggregate_well` because that function reads exactly four things off `ctx`, and the pure-logic tests build contexts satisfying precisely that surface — memoising in place would widen a domain function's dependencies to buy a cache. Its key is the arguments the computation is a function of, `_gate_cache_sig`, `_ratio_sig_for` and `DatasetState.rows_version`; it returns a **tuple**, because `aggregate_well` returns a fresh list each call and several callers keep it. `_ratio_sig_for` signs the ratio behind the `val_col` *argument* rather than `active_val_col`: the two coincide only because the batch exporter swaps the active column for the duration of an export, and a caller passing a column without that swap would otherwise get a key describing a different ratio than the one it computed with. Every per-well loop here goes through the wrapper, including `compute_rep_n_above_total`'s — it runs once per group per timepoint, so on twelve groups over six timepoints it alone was 576 full-well passes recomputing what the two producers beside it had already aggregated. `cdf_values_cached` memoises the per-cell values behind a CDF curve on the same key minus threshold and `use_sem`, since that panel draws the raw filtered population rather than a statistic of it; the filter is passed in rather than imported so the memo cannot be keyed on one function while the values come from another. Those arrays are the one per-cell thing the statistics cache keeps, so they are bounded (`_make_room_for_cdf`): an array from an older `rows_version` can never be read again and is dropped, and the rest are capped at `CDF_MEMO_SHARE` (a quarter) of the row-cache budget, oldest first. The well is read only on a miss, since with the row cache bounded a read could load an evicted well from disk only to return the remembered array. `_safe_rows`, which feeds the median and mean-of-all, reads through `repo.rows` rather than the cache-only lookup for the same reason. `aggregate_well` / `aggregate_group` resolve an optional delegate through `ctx.runtime.aggregate.well` / `.group`, which is the hook the pure-logic test `MockApp` uses to short-circuit aggregation (its `_aggregate_well` / `_aggregate_group` methods surface through the runtime's back-compat view); the production `ReviewApp` provides no such delegate, so the value is `None` and the DataFrame path is taken at runtime. The result cache is keyed on everything that can move a number, including `_gate_cache_sig` — the scatter-gate state for **both** layers. Thresholding is in there because gate membership defines the on-population; inclusion is in there because "Use scatter gates" replaces the per-channel intensity floors, and the `fluor_gates` already in the key do not move when that checkbox is toggled. Mode-on-with-no-gates still differs from mode-off (the floors are bypassed either way), so the flag itself is part of the signature, not just the gate geometry. It returns `None` when neither layer is active, leaving a plain threshold-mode session's keys byte-identical. |
| `domain/batch_models.py`, `domain/ratio_models.py` | Plain dataclass models. |
| `domain/selections_format.py` — the **root** package | **The on-disk `sample_definitions` block.** Reading it, writing it, repairing an arbitrary list into a well-formed one, migrating a legacy v1 block, and baking a selection's `color` from the rank of its lowest well. It is shared rather than Review's because **two panes write the same block**: Review whenever someone edits a selection, and Datasets on a plate merge — `merge_plates_compute.merge_sample_definitions` runs both plates through `from_block` and writes the result back through `to_block`, because those are the only things in the codebase that know how to read a saved block. Reading the raw `rep_sets` / `groups` keys instead sees nothing at all in a block written by today's app. The pipeline is **not** a third party to this: `pipeline/sidecar.py` lists `sample_definitions` in `USER_SIDE_BLOCKS`, the blocks with no author on the pipeline side, and `process_microscopy.write_pipeline_info` only carries an existing one across so a re-run does not destroy it — nothing under `pipeline/` or `services/` imports this module. The split from Review's half was measured rather than judged: an AST closure from `from_block` and `to_block` names 22 of the original module's 36 definitions and 465 of its 910 lines. Two of them travel back the other way — Review's half imports `well_rank`, the ordering every colour is keyed on, and `_clean_wells`, the token normaliser, rather than keeping a second spelling of either, and `tests/test_selections_format_is_shared.py` fails if a name is ever defined on both sides. `well_colors` reads `domain/well_palette.py` directly; it used to borrow the palette from `review.domain.plate_layout` behind a `try`/`except` whose fallback was a **ten**-colour list, which on a 96-well plate repeats a colour every eleventh well. That fallback was dead on every real path — `merge_plates_compute` runs inside the Datasets pane, where `review/` is importable — so removing it changes no colour. What it buys is that this module now imports with `PySide6`, `ui`, `review` and `core` all absent, which the borrowing version could not, and that a value written to disk no longer has a second definition waiting behind an exception handler. |
| `review/domain/selections_model.py` — **Review's**, spelled in full here because the row above it is a root-package module of nearly the same name | **What a saved selection means once it reaches a figure** — Review's half of the model, the other half being the root `domain/selections_format.py` above. Everywhere else in this table a bare `domain/` prefix means `review/domain/`; these two rows are the one place that shorthand would name two different packages in one sentence. The colours a plate paints with, which selections the replicate machinery treats as sets, the two block-shape questions a Review view asks (`group_drift`, `block_is_mixed`), and **the one place a well's name on a figure is decided**. `well_display_label_and_source(ctx, token)` answers in three rungs and says which one answered: a label typed on Home → Sample Map → **Well Labels**, then the values the well holds on the **Variables** tab composed by `sample_variables.label_for_well` (`HeLa · 10 µM`), then the bare well token. `well_display_label` is the same answer without the provenance, and it is what every tick label, legend entry, image caption and facet heading in the app already called; `figure_names_map(ctx)` is its map form for the callers that name a whole plate at once — every exported CSV's `well_name` column and the Spatial tab's summary axis — so the rows behind a figure and the figure itself cannot call one well two things. The middle rung is why the seam reports a source at all. Two callers have to tell the rungs apart and cannot from the string: `barplot.collect.bar_well_display_label` rewrites a numeric label into the well token, which is right for a hand-typed `3` and wrong for a `Dose` of `10` declared without a unit, and Home's `next_step` asks how much of the plate is named rather than how much of one tab was filled in. Before the variables rung existed a plate annotated entirely on the Variables tab drew `A01 A02 A03` on every axis, and Home told its user there were "no sample labels yet" over figures whose x axis was the annotation they had just spent the morning filling in. A blank typed label falls through rather than blanking the tick. `replicate_display_label` sits on top for the group case, and `groups_relabelled_on_figures` is what tells the user that a group whose name looks auto-generated is drawn as what its wells are called — either rung of them. |

Data-layer helpers (under `review/data/`):

| Module | Role |
|--------|------|
| `data/auto_threshold.py` | Otsu-based per-channel default threshold estimator. Delegates the shared helpers (`parse_tp_hours`, `pick_endpoint_timepoints`, `sample_cell_and_bg`) to the top-level `pipeline.auto_threshold` so the pipeline and the GUI agree exactly. The Cell Gating tab's *two-well* optimizer shares its numeric core the same way, through `pipeline.threshold_optimize` — the candidate grid, the confidence-bounded separation objective, the separability test and the range validation live there, so the Analyze side's control-well pass and the Review side's "Optimize ThreshFracOn" button reduce to one implementation. `gating_compute` re-exports those names and keeps only what depends on the viewer: the fold-change layer (which would otherwise drag `review.domain.fold_change` into `pipeline/`) and the DataFrame/ratio plumbing. |
| `data/zipfile_cache.py` | Process-wide LRU of open `ZipFile` handles, lock-guarded so `read_member_bytes` / `scan_zip_members` share one open file across the thousands of per-member reads the Image Table / heatmap / smFISH-worker paths issue. Invalidated on dataset swap, through `ImageRepository.invalidate` together with the decoded-array LRU; it also re-opens by itself when a path's mtime changes, so a re-run pipeline cannot be read through a handle onto the old archive. Both caches hand out **shared** objects — the same decoded array to every caller that asks for an image, one serialised handle per zip — so neither is named outside the module that owns it, which `tests/test_image_cache_encapsulation.py` pins. That guard locks in a property that already held rather than repairing one that failed. |

### 5.6 The data layer

The Review pane reads two things off disk:

1. **Per-well CSV files** produced by `process_microscopy.py`. One CSV per
   well, one row per (cell × FOV × timepoint).
2. **Per-well image ZIPs** (`<well>_out.zip`) — masks, top-hat-corrected
   fluorescence, overlays, smFISH-processed channels. Used by Image Table,
   Segmentation, smFISH, and the heatmap.

Plus the sidecar:

3. **`pipeline_info.json`** — schema fields, channel tokens, available
   timepoints, saved selections, persisted gating thresholds, etc.

The relevant modules:

| Module | Job |
|--------|-----|
| `data/data_loading.py` | CSV parsing, channel detection, threshold-aware aggregation, per-well array helpers. `df_included_mask` is the single inclusion chokepoint — effective inclusion is `Included==1 AND QC_Pass==1 AND Crop_Pass==1 AND Gate_Pass==1` (the optional `QC_Pass` / `Crop_Pass` / `Gate_Pass` layers default to pass when absent), and every consumer (overlay, plots, stats, aggregation, export) composes it so QC debris-gating, the Segmentation crop, and scatter-gate inclusion apply uniformly. The `Included` layer is set by the Cell Gating tab's `GatingWorker` from the per-channel FluorGating intensity floors; that tab reports the composed result live — `cell_gating.controller.cell_gating_refresh_included_count` walks the held frames through this same chokepoint (saying "counted over N of M wells in memory" when the bounded row cache does not hold the plate) and renders `gating_compute.format_inclusion_counts` into a muted line under the gate controls ("Included for analysis: N / M cells · K failed QC"). It recomputes rather than reading the worker's own tally, for two reasons: the worker counts the gating layer alone, so pairing that number with a QC count gives a line whose figures do not reconcile (most QC failures sit inside the gating layer's kept set); and a dataset whose gates are all at their defaults skips the pass entirely on load, which would leave a worker-fed label blank on the commonest path. It refreshes on pass completion, on failure (flagged as such), while a pass is in flight (marked `updating…`), on Cell Gating tab activation — the catch-all covering crop edits, manual per-cell deletes and that default cold load — and from `ctx.runtime.qc.changed_cb`, a feature-agnostic seam `qc.recompute_qc_all` fires after rewriting `QC_Pass` so neither feature imports the other; the separate `Gate_Pass` layer carries the scatter-gate inclusion (the union of the Scatter Plot's rectangular gates via `scatter.gating.compute_gate_inclusion`) and, when "Use scatter gates" is on, *replaces* the intensity floors (the worker sets `Included=1`, `Gate_Pass=`membership). Keeping it a separate layer lets the **per-cell scatter** default to `df_included_mask(df, include_gate=False)` so it keeps showing the full cloud (and the gates over it) instead of filtering itself by its own gates, while every other view filters via the default. That tab's **Apply gates** toggle does *not* switch this layer on: it filters on the gate geometry instead (`collect_scatter_data(gates=…)`), because this column can describe a different set of boxes than the plot is drawing. `gates` defaults to `None` for batch export, so a batch job can never inherit the live tab's choice — and `batch_export.scatter_panel._warn_if_live_gates_ignored` logs when the tab is filtering and the batch is not. That log line is a stopgap, not the fix §7 asks for: the shortfall belongs *in the artifact* — a note on the figure or a column in the CSV — because a user comparing an exported figure against the tab has no reason to open the log drawer first. What is there today makes the difference discoverable, not visible. The tab's **own** Export CSV button does pass the gates, because it exports the plot it sits beside. And a gate's percentage label counts against the population the gate was drawn over, not against what survived it — which means the collector must keep a well that has *nothing* inside the gate, since its cells still belong in the denominator: `collect_scatter_data` stashes the pre-gate arrays as `x_ungated` / `y_ungated` / `tp_ungated` when it filters, and `compute_gate_stats` denominates by those — reading the drawn arrays made every gate read `100.0%` the moment the toggle went on. Measurement columns are normalised to lower-case at read time so per-channel lookups are case-insensitive. **The per-cell value arrays stay arrays.** `_all_fluor_values_filtered` returns a numpy array, and every consumer keeps it as one: the Line tab's `LineSeries.cdf_vals`, its batch twin `_line_series_runner._cdf_for`, and the CDF panels themselves, which build their cumulative fractions with `np.arange(1, n + 1) / n` rather than a list comprehension. Boxing a value into a Python float costs 32 bytes against 8, and the CDF path did it four times over — a boxed copy of the array, a sorted copy of that, a list of y-values, and one flattened list of every series' values built solely to take a min and a max. A plate of 537,393 cells raised `MemoryError` inside the last of those. Two consequences worth knowing: an ndarray's truthiness raises, so emptiness is tested with `.size` and never `if vals:`; and readers coerce with `np.asarray` rather than assuming, so a caller handing in a plain list still draws. **And the repeating ones are stored as categories.** `_categorize_text_columns` converts a text column whose distinct values are under half its rows — which in practice is all six: profiling a 537,393-row plate, `experiment` and `channel` held one distinct value each and cost 30 MiB apiece, and the most varied, `filename`, held 1,248. The frame goes from 327 MiB to 135 MiB, and that is steady-state memory in the row cache, held for every well of every open dataset. Three properties make it safe and each was established by running the real consumers both ways: the categories are the *observed* values plus `""`, because a wider list would make `groupby` emit a group per unused category and fabricate per-field statistics; **every consumer normalises the column through `domain/text_columns.py`**, because `Series.fillna(value)` validates *value* against the category list whether or not any cell needs filling, so a direct `df["fov"].fillna("1")` raises `TypeError: Cannot setitem on a Categorical with a new category` on any plate whose fields are not numbered from one; and `pd.concat` of columns whose categories differ falls back to `object`, which is the status quo for pooled frames and measures cheaper than before (pooling 26 wells adds 14 MiB from categories against 29 MiB from strings, the category objects being shared rather than rebuilt). **The reader is `pyarrow.csv` wherever it can read the file** (`_read_well_table`, `_arrow_read`), with `pd.read_csv` as the fallback for a file pyarrow rejects (a row with the wrong number of fields) and for an environment without pyarrow; and for a float column holding an infinity — `inf` text, or a literal such as `1e400` that pyarrow reads as inf and pandas as text coercing to NaN, which cannot be told apart after the read; the fallback logs the file it took. pyarrow is given pandas' own boolean spellings (its defaults add `1` / `0`, which read a column of `True` and `1` as booleans), and running out of memory inside it is raised as `MemoryError` so `_read_making_room`'s release-and-retry runs rather than a pandas parse that needs more memory still. A hexadecimal literal (`0x10`) is the one difference left unhandled — 16 under pyarrow, NaN under pandas — and is stated, since the pipeline writes decimal. On a 1,104,480-row, 513 MB well pyarrow parses in 4.1 s against pandas' 64.8 s, at about the same peak. It is held to pandas' frame, not merely to a plausible one: the column names are pandas' own (read from the header and handed over, so `Unnamed: 4` and `v.1` match), the text columns are typed `string`, `""` is the only null, and a column pyarrow would read as a date or time is handed on as text so the coercion makes it NaN as pandas did. `tests/test_typed_csv_parse.py` holds a corpus of messy files equal frame for frame to pandas run with `float_precision="round_trip"`, and asserts pyarrow did each read, since a fallback would pass every equality trivially. The reference is the round-trip parse because pandas' default float parser is not correctly rounded — measured, 28.8% of the benchmark well's floats differ from the exact value, and values below 1e-3 by up to a relative 1e-12 — while pyarrow gives `float(text)` for every cell; the one other difference is an integer above `int64` but within `uint64`, which becomes the nearest float rather than `uint64`. Both are stated in `_read_well_table`'s docstring. **Only the text columns are read as text.** `load_well_csv` takes the string columns from a `nrows=0` header read and names them as text in the main read, leaving the reader to type the rest natively; the `to_numeric` pass afterwards touches only the columns that still came back `object`, which is the case of a numeric column carrying a stray non-numeric cell. Reading the whole file with `dtype=str` instead makes pandas allocate one consolidated object block of every column at once — `(n_columns, n_rows)` — and fill it with a Python string per cell, including for the columns that are numbers and are about to be converted back: on a 537,393-row × 37-column plate that is a 152 MiB pointer array plus roughly 16.6 million short strings, and it is where such a plate failed to load. Measured on a file of that shape, each read in its own process, peak RSS is 1729 MiB for the string read against 867 MiB for the typed one — separate processes because `ru_maxrss` is a high-water mark that never falls, so measuring both in one reports the first strategy's peak as the second's. `tests/test_the_load_path_stays_small.py` holds both memory wins on a synthetic plate: a `tracemalloc` ceiling expressed as a ratio against the CSV's own size on disk, which the typed read clears and the `dtype=str` read does not, and a direct assertion on the dtypes either side of `_CATEGORY_MAX_UNIQUE_SHARE` — the repeating columns come back `category` and a column whose values are all distinct does not, since a category dictionary as large as the column itself is pure overhead. Chunking the string read is not the alternative — the coerced chunks stay alive until the concat, and it measures marginally *worse*. `na_values=[""]` paired with `keep_default_na=False` is what keeps the two byte-identical: a blank becomes `NaN` in every column (and `""` again in the text ones), while a cell holding the literal text `NA` stays that text in a string column and still coerces to `NaN` in a numeric one, so a well genuinely named `NA` survives the read. `aggregate_with_threshold_df` defines the "on" population as `value > threshold`, and *which* threshold reaches it is decided in one place, because there are three scales and one number cannot serve them: shape/morphology has no ON cutoff and passes `-1.0` to keep every cell; an integer count column is cut against the channel's `ThreshCountOn`, which starts below the minimum a tally can take so a cell carrying no spots still counts (zero spots is a measurement, not a gap); a fluorescence column is cut against its `ThreshFracOn`. `domain/metric_registry.cutoff_kind_for_column` is the predicate that classifies the column and `core/channel_state_controller.on_cutoff_for_column` the resolver that turns that answer into a number — every aggregate path (bar, line, scatter-aggregate, heat map, stats, export, batch export) goes through the resolver rather than choosing for itself, and `tests/test_on_cutoff_sweep.py` fails when one reaches past it for a raw accessor. Feeding the wrong kind is not a rounding error: the intensity cutoff sits above the entire range a spot tally can occupy, so it empties the population and the plot draws nothing at all. `resolve_value_series` emits a deduped WARN naming the missing column when both the direct and case-folded lookups miss, surfacing schema-mismatch bugs that would otherwise show up as silently-empty plots. **The string timepoint columns are read only when a drawn row needs them.** `aggregate_with_threshold_df` resolves each row's timepoint from the numeric `timepoint_hours` column and falls back to `_ordinal_timepoints_df` + `timepoint_text` for rows whose numeric value is missing; both widen the categorical `timepoint` column to `object` and strip every row through a per-element call, and on a plate whose numeric column is complete neither result is ever read. Together they were around nine tenths of the function's cost — four million string strips in one pass over a 96-well plate — so the numeric column is read first and the fallback runs only when a row that can *reach the output* is missing from it. The test is on the **included** rows, not on every row: a row the inclusion mask has already dropped cannot reach the output whatever its timepoint resolves to, because `final` masks it out, and testing every row instead would be defeated by a single excluded row carrying an unparseable token — which real plates carry, since `process_microscopy` writes `nan` for any filename whose timepoint token it cannot parse. Aggregating 96 wells of 21,600 rows: 1,091 ms before, 180 ms after. `tests/test_hot_paths_stay_linear.py` counts the calls: a frame whose numeric timepoint column is complete must not reach `_ordinal_timepoints_df` at all. One pre-existing wrinkle is pinned rather than fixed — `_ordinal_timepoints_df` numbers the unparseable labels present *in the frame it is handed*, so two wells of one plate can put the same label on different numeric timepoints while every collector unions them by that number. |
| `data/metric_labels.py` | The Property combo's label / key / suffix tables, derived from `domain/metric_registry`, plus the **title vocabulary every plot shares**. It also names the two Property entries that are not columns — `FRACTION_LABEL` / `FRACTION_METRIC_KEY` and `EVENTS_LABEL` / `EVENTS_METRIC_KEY`, paired in `SYNTHETIC_METRIC_LABEL_TO_KEY` — which the aggregate Scatter axes, Response Curves and their Batch Export panels offer and `channel_state_controller.col_for_scatter_axis` resolves to the channel's mean-intensity column; they stay out of `METRIC_LABEL_TO_KEY` because the band's consumers compose `f"{channel}_{metric}"` and could not read them. `threshold_qualifier`, `fraction_title` and the two `events_*_title` helpers were already here; `spread_label` and `timepoint_title` joined them because they are the same kind of thing and were not. `spread_label` is the SD/SEM word the `±` in a title refers to, and it had been written out at **thirteen** call sites — eight assigning to `band_lbl`, and five that do not (a toggle's text, two button captions, an events-panel title, the Saved Plots summary line), which is exactly why a grep for the variable name found eight and the guard found the rest. `timepoint_title` is the `t = 24 h` / `t = [24, 48] h` clause, which lived as a helper private to the bar renderer while the Distribution title built its own. Neither is logic — they are words — and a figure whose title says SD over a band drawn as SEM is the silent substitution §7 of `CLAUDE.md` is about, so `tests/test_one_spelling_for_the_plot_title_words.py` is what notices a fourteenth copy. |
| `data/image_discovery.py` | Scans zips / loose directories for masks, overlays, tophat images. Classifies by suffix + schema. **An inventory carries its own provenance.** The scanners must not lose a whole archive to one unreadable member, so a mid-scan failure returns the entries gathered so far — right behaviour, wrong shape, because a short dict of real images is byte-for-byte the same object as a complete inventory of a well that genuinely holds that many frames, and Review draws the two identically: fewer timepoints, no gap, nothing to click on. `data/zip_members.ScanResult` is a `dict` subclass carrying `partial` and `reason`, so every existing consumer keeps working unchanged and only the ones that want to say "incomplete" out loud have to ask. Every abort path marks it (an unreadable nested member, an archive that will not open, an exception mid-scan); `merge_partial` carries the flag from each source scan onto the accumulator a well is assembled from, since an inventory built from one complete and one truncated scan is truncated; and `find_well_images_and_masks` returns through `ScanResult.derive` rather than `dict(sorted(...))`, which would silently drop the flag. `scan_folder_members` is the folder-side twin, with the same treatment and the partial-count warning its zip sibling already had. **The per-well filter over loose raw files asks "could this be someone else's?", never "is this mine?".** The latter is unanswerable for a well label the resolver cannot parse, and guarding the whole filter behind a parsed token meant an unparseable label admitted every file in the directory — which, because such files collide on `(fov, tp)` and the merge is first-hit-wins, showed one arbitrary *other* well's frame under that label rather than a visible mix. `_raw_file_names_some_well` asks the three vocabularies in the open (the pipeline schema, the legacy five-field regex, then `image_resolver`'s shared free-text token pattern, imported rather than re-spelled), and `_raw_file_passes_unknown_well` admits only the files that name no well at all: a file naming any well cannot be claimed by a well we cannot name, and a file naming none contradicts nothing, which keeps working the single-well directory this fallback exists for. |
| `data/image_resolver.py` | Filename → kind classifier (`mask` / `overlay` / `fluor_processed` / `smfish` / `phase`), and the frame-precedence resolver over it. The classifier is a **vocabulary wrapper**, not a second implementation: `classify_filename_kind` calls `image_identity.classify_filename_role` and renames the result into the legacy `kind` strings, and `OUTPUT_SUFFIXES` is generated from `ROLE_CATALOG`. Two independently written classifiers over two copies of the suffix table is what the module used to be, and they drifted exactly as far as an unshared table lets them — the copy here had no `phase` entry, so a processed phase image classified as a raw fluorescence frame and was served as one. Also the single home for `normalize_numeric_token`, the FOV/timepoint token normaliser that collapses `1`, `01` and `1.0` to one key — and which treats only `None` as absent, because FOV and timepoint tokens are legitimately `0`. Every site that compares such a token routes through it: `review_image/collect.review_norm_fov` (the review side's public name, kept because the image-table and review-image call sites are written against it), `core/dataset_state._norm_fov` and `data/frame_load.norm_token` are aliases of it. Tokens reach the viewer from filenames, CSV columns and combo text, so a second copy that formats differently silently strands a filter. **The free-text well-token pattern reads a row letter case-insensitively for every row except F.** A lower-case `f` followed by one or two digits is how this codebase spells a *field*: `pipeline/ome_explode` writes `{experiment}_{channel}_{well}_f{fov}_{tp}`, and the well in that same template comes from `canonical_well_label`, which upper-cases. Matching `f1` as the well `F01` therefore made every plate using the standard convention answer "yes, this is well F01" for every well's first field — selecting F01 in Review drew A01's image and F02 drew B02's, each well rendering another well's frame with nothing on screen to say so — and claimed a file naming no well at all (`sample_f3_t0.tif`) for F03. `well_token_matches_text`'s substring fallback, which answers the same question for a name that glues the well to its neighbours (`plateA01run.tif`), carries the same rule: converting one and not the other would leave two definitions of the same word inside one function. The cost is narrow and deliberate — a plate whose filenames spell a row-F well in lower case (`f01_GFP_…`) is no longer found by the free-text scan, those names being genuinely ambiguous, while the two parsers ahead of this one read such a well by *position*, which is not ambiguous at all. Legacy three-digit fields (`F001`) never matched and still do not. |
| `data/frame_load.py` | An address — `(well, channel-token, timepoint, fov)` — resolved to the float32 array it names, or to the int32 segmentation mask beside it, plus the channel-token vocabulary that decoding one needs (`base_channel`, the ` (binary)` / ` (mask)` / ` (raw)` suffixes, `NUC_SEG_TOKEN`). Three separate tabs ask this question — the Image Table composes a grid of them, the Cell Browser crops per-cell thumbnails out of them, the Playground corrects a single one — and each is independently removable, so the answer cannot live in any of them. **Resolving a render variant is addressing, not rendering:** `"GFP (binary)"` loads exactly the pixels `"GFP"` does, and only what the caller then draws with them differs, which is why the suffix vocabulary is here and the rendering it selects is not. **Two shortfalls are reported rather than absorbed**, through sets the caller owns and passes in: `scan_misses` (a well/channel scan that came up empty and might be momentary, so a pass says it once instead of once per cell and the next pass retries it; an empty scan of folders that exist, walked to the end, is kept in the cache instead) and `raw_fallbacks` (a cell that asked for the corrected top-hat image and was served the raw one — common, since a pipeline often corrects only some of a well's frames, and a grid silently mixing the two would look uniformly corrected). There is a third, `partial_scans`: a well/channel whose image inventory came back truncated (`ScanResult.partial`), recorded once per key by `_record_partial_scan` so a grid of ninety cells over one truncated well says so once rather than ninety times. It is the shortfall a caller cannot infer from what it received — the frames are real and the grid is simply short — and it survives a cache hit, because the truncated inventory is what was written into the session-long image cache. They are parameters, not something read off `ctx`, because they belong to the *caller's* render pass; the Image Table binds its own through thin wrappers in `image_compose` (`partial_scan_report` is the public reader, and `reset_scan_misses` clears the set per pass) and holds them on `state.image_table.partial_scans`, cleared on dataset load beside `scan_misses`; a caller with no pass simply gets its pixels. **An unspecified axis refuses rather than guesses:** an empty FOV or an empty timepoint (an empty dropdown) matches every key, so when more than one distinct value on that axis would satisfy the request, `match_image_ref` returns `(None, "ambiguous_fov")` / `(None, "ambiguous_tp")` instead of whichever entry the dict happened to yield first. Both axes, not just FOV — a rule written for one of two symmetric axes leaves the other returning an arbitrary frame under a successful-looking `"normalized"` status. A genuinely single-FOV or single-timepoint dataset still resolves, and the top-hat-to-raw fallback treats an `ambiguous_*` kind as a deliberate refusal rather than a gap to retry. |
| `data/dataset_dims.py` | The four option lists every image grid starts from — which wells are loaded, which channel tokens can be shown (including each channel's binary variant, `NUC+SEG` when a nuclear token is known, and the user's ratio metrics as virtual channels), which timepoints and which FOVs exist. Each has the same two-tier shape: prefer what the run recorded in `pipeline_info.json`, fall back to scanning the loaded CSVs when it recorded nothing (older runs, custom schemas). The fallback is what keeps a thin-sidecar dataset usable and is deliberately second — the sidecar names every value the run produced, the cache only the ones whose rows happen to be loaded. The Image Table fills its axis dropdowns from these and the Playground fills its single-frame selectors from the same lists, so the two cannot disagree about what a dataset contains. |
| `data/inclusion.py` | The inclusion chokepoint's answer, keyed for an image view: `excluded_nids_for_frame` gives the nucleus ids in one frame that `df_included_mask` rejects, and `drop_excluded_labels` zeroes them out of a label image. An image view that draws straight off a segmentation mask shows curated-away cells as segmented, counted cells — the plots disagree with the picture and nothing on screen says which is right — and filtering the labels once fixes every render that reads them. The per-well map is memoised on the row frame's own `attrs`, keyed by `ReviewImageState.override_version` (the counter `invalidate_stats_cache` bumps on every manual delete, crop, QC and gating change) **and by the frame's identity**, so it dies with the frame it describes, cannot outlive an edit, and cannot be inherited by a derived frame — `attrs` propagates through `df.copy()`, where the counter alone would call another frame's map fresh. A build with no Review-Image slice has no counter to key on and simply recomputes. The all-included case — the common one — short-circuits before the per-row frame-token normalisation, which is the expensive part, and `drop_excluded_labels` returns the array untouched, so a dataset with no curation pays nothing at all. The filter's query is built at 64-bit width and narrowed to the ids the frame actually holds rather than cast to the label array's dtype — casting wrapped an id larger than `int32` into a negative one, and a wrapped value colliding with a live label blanks the wrong cell. A non-integer label array is returned untouched and a read-only one is copied. **An already-rendered grid is not repainted** when an inclusion layer changes: `invalidate_stats_cache` fires `ctx.runtime.image_table.inclusion_changed_cb`, which marks the table stale so the header cues a Generate. Re-rendering would be seconds of decoding per edit, and an edit comes in runs of ten; the cue is what keeps a stale grid from quietly disagreeing with every plot. |
| `core/app_settings.py` | `app_settings()` — the one door onto this user's `QSettings`, and the organisation/application pair Qt keys the file on. A module function rather than a method on any object, because reaching the handle used to mean reaching for `_qsettings` on whatever object a caller happened to hold, and the object a feature has is not the one that defines it: `ctx.window` is the `ReviewApp` review widget while `_qsettings` belongs to the `AllWellApp` main window containing it, with no forwarding. A guarded `getattr(ctx.window, "_qsettings", None)` therefore reads `None` in the shipped app and every setting reads as absent — which is exactly how the recent-datasets list came to write nothing and read nothing while its tests passed. Five construction sites across three modules now go through here. There is no object to have the wrong one of. |
| `data/parquet_cache.py` | A columnar cache of each well's **parsed** frame, written beside its CSV as `.aw_parquet/<well>.parquet`. The parse is the load — 3,068 ms of a 3,119 ms read on a 120,000-row well — and nothing about the file changes between reads, so the parse is repeated work. Through the real path on a plate-shaped fixture that read is 51 ms. **Whole frames for the row cache, deliberately.** Parquet is columnar and a subset read is the larger win — six of thirty-seven columns measures 7 ms — but the row cache holds one frame per well and every `get_rows` caller reads whatever column it needs from it, so a partial frame there answers a later caller's column with a `KeyError` at best and a silently-empty plot at worst; and the verdict projectors fail open on a missing input column, so a QC metric left out of a partial frame would read as every cell passing. So `read_well_frame` never passes `read_cached(columns=…)`. The per-well summaries do: they read the four columns an open needs and never enter the row cache. **Every failure mode is a miss, never an error**: no pyarrow, no cache file, a fingerprint that does not match, a file that will not parse, a read-only output volume. Each costs a slower load and nothing else, which is the only acceptable price for a cache; a missing engine is logged once per session rather than once per well. The fingerprint is `"<size>:<mtime_ns>:v<PARSER_VERSION>"`, stored in the Parquet schema metadata beside pandas' own block rather than in place of it — `replace_schema_metadata` replaces the whole mapping. Size and mtime rather than a content hash: the file is tens of megabytes and this runs once per well per load, while the thing guarded against is the pipeline rewriting the CSV, which an incremental run does when it merges new rows into an existing well, and which moves both. **`PARSER_VERSION` is the half no file-stat can see.** What is being reused is not the CSV — it is `load_well_csv`'s *output*, which is a function of the file and of `_STRING_COLS`, `_CATEGORY_MAX_UNIQUE_SHARE`, the per-channel column rename, the FOV normalisation, the `Included` default and the `shape_circularity` back-fill; every one of those has changed at least once. Without it, adding a derived column to the parser means an untouched CSV keeps serving the frame from before the change — the column simply absent, the dropdown offering it never appearing, nothing said. `tests/test_parquet_cache.py::test_a_changed_parser_invalidates_every_cache` pins the constant against a hash of the parser's own source, so editing it without bumping fails; the cache is registered in `tests/test_reuse_is_keyed_completely.py` like the app's other two reuse decisions, with the written reason per key. **The fingerprint is taken before the parse**, by `read_well_frame`, and `write_cache` re-stats and declines when the two disagree: a three-second read with an Analyze run or a remote fetch writing into the same `out/` would otherwise stamp the new file's identity onto the old file's rows, and that cache is then wrong on every read afterwards. Writes go through a staging file in the destination directory and an `os.replace`, so a crash mid-write leaves the previous cache or none, never half a plate. `prune` runs once per dataset load and removes what nothing can reclaim — a `.parquet` or `.summary.json` whose CSV is gone (unreachable, since the entry is only ever addressed by that name) and any abandoned staging file. It is deliberately not an eviction policy: the cache costs about 400 MB beside a 96-well plate's 600 MB of CSVs, and a plate opened once a year is precisely the one whose five-minute parse it exists to save. The directory is a subdirectory *and* dot-prefixed: every scan that enumerates a dataset's per-well CSVs is a non-recursive `out_dir.glob("*.csv")`, which a subdirectory cannot match, and the dot is the second line of defence. pyarrow is a GUI-side dependency only — the pipeline writes these CSVs and never reads them back, so `requirements-remote.txt` does not carry it and a remote run pays no install for it. Note what the pandas metadata block does *not* do: the categorical dtypes survive without it, because Arrow encodes a category as a `DictionaryType` in the schema proper and `to_pandas` reads it back from there. |
| `data_loading.read_well_frame` | **The one door onto a well's rows** — cache hit, or `load_well_csv` and cache the result. Both call sites go through it (`load_and_project`, `smfish.tab_view._smfish_refresh_app_cache`) and `tests/test_parquet_cache.py` fails on any third, in either spelling. One door is not tidiness. The frame cached here is the CSV's own parse, **before** any verdict column is projected onto it, and that is why the write belongs one level above `load_and_project`'s projector loop rather than anywhere the frame has already been through it: `QC_Pass` / `Crop_Pass` / `Gate_Pass` are recomputed every session from parameters the user changes at will, so a cache holding one session's verdicts would serve them to the next under different thresholds, and every count and fraction downstream would be wrong with nothing to notice it by. A second call site that cached an already-projected frame reintroduces exactly that, which is what makes the door count one rather than two. |
| `data/row_cache.py` | **The per-well row cache, bounded.** `RowCache` is the mapping `DatasetState.cache` holds: least-recently-used wells are evicted once the held frames' size (`memory_usage(deep=True)`, taken as a frame enters and again after its projectors add columns) passes a byte budget — a quarter of physical memory by default (read through `os.sysconf`, or `GlobalMemoryStatusEx` on Windows), at least 512 MiB, and set with `ALLWELL_ROW_CACHE_MB`. The most recently used frame is never evicted, so a well larger than the whole budget is still readable, alone. **Eviction is safe because a well comes back identical and cheap**: every frame enters only through `load_and_project`, which runs the full projector roster, and a well in the Parquet cache re-reads in 0.22 s at 1.1M rows against 15.3 s for the CSV parse. That is also why eviction does not bump `rows_version` — the memoized aggregates keyed on it remain true of the reloaded rows. Thread-safe with snapshot iteration, because the gating worker reads rows off the GUI thread and a read now reorders the cache; `pinned(label)` holds a well against eviction while `load_and_project` runs its projectors, which find the frame by label. The one other path that replaced a held frame — the smFISH write-back — re-reads it through `load_and_project` too, so a held well and an evicted one cannot differ. `release()` empties it for a read that ran out of memory and counts that as eviction, which is what stops the dataset loader reading more rows. **What it changes is what iterating it means**: it yields the wells in memory, not the plate. `tests/test_row_cache_readers.py` enumerates every function that reads it directly — in the attribute spelling and in `getattr(…, "cache", …)` — each with the reason the held frames are what it means: the projector walks (re-applied on reload), the clears, the smFISH refresh of a held well, and the three **live previews** (QC's "flagged", the crop's status line, Cell Gating's "Included for analysis"), which recompute on every edit and so count the held frames and append `data_loading.held_wells_note` — "counted over N of M wells in memory" — whenever those are not the plate. A reader that means the plate goes through `get_rows`, `plate_scan` or the summaries instead and needs no entry. The status is a log line, the first time a plate does not fit, naming the wells held, their size, the budget and the evictions so far. |
| `data/well_summary.py` | **What opening a dataset needs from each well, without its rows.** A `WellSummary` per well — row count, column names (parse columns only, the projected verdict columns excluded), numeric timepoints (`timepoint_hours`, else the label parsed, as `DatasetState.rebuild_timepoints` reads them), FOV and timepoint tokens in order of first appearance, and the `fov_integrity` verdict — a few hundred bytes. Stored beside the Parquet cache as `<well>.summary.json`, stamped with the same source fingerprint (which carries `PARSER_VERSION`) plus `SUMMARY_VERSION`, written through a staging file and declined when the CSV changed during the read, exactly as `write_cache` does. On a miss it comes from a Parquet read of `SUMMARY_COLUMNS` or, with no Parquet cache, from the parse that fills it. Those columns are everything the timepoint and FOV lists read **and everything `check_fov_labels` reads** — `filename` for its first signal, `nucleus_id` for its second; a verdict judged on fewer columns answers "trusted" for a well whose labels pool several images, and the summary would store that under the CSV's fingerprint. The verdict is recorded once per well per dataset, from the summary or the first read: re-judging a well on every re-read cost a second a time on a 1.1M-row well. A file that will not parse as a summary, whatever is in it, is a miss. `DatasetState.summaries` holds one for every opened well; `DatasetState.well_summaries()` adds one taken from any held frame that has none (a test that seeds the cache with frames it built), and `rebuild_timepoints`, `rebuild_fovs`, `dataset_dims.cache_column_tokens`, `focus_gate.dataset_has_focus_column` and the Line tab's nuclei count read them — so those lists are the plate's whatever is held. |
| `data/plate_scan.py` | **Plate-wide values computed one well at a time and remembered small.** `per_well(ctx, kind, label, params, compute)` / `every_well(…)` read each well through `get_rows` and memoize `compute`'s result — never the rows — in the statistics cache under a key carrying `rows_version`, borrowing the invalidation `aggregate_well_cached` depends on: every change to what a well's rows say either bumps the version (gating, curation, a replaced frame, a dataset swap) or clears the statistics cache (QC, crop and the other verdict layers). A context with no `rows_version` computes without memoizing. Its users are the readers that mean the plate: the threshold range (`channel_state_controller._value_extent`, each well's min and max rather than every included value of the plate concatenated — 850 MB at 96 wells of 1.1M cells), `get_all_timepoints` (asked on every tab activation and channel switch), the focus panel's plate counts, the Home plate's quality markers (scored from a four-number `well_composite.FocusTally` per well rather than every well's focus column), and the Spatial tab's timepoints. |
| `data/narrow_rows.py` | **A well's rows with only the columns an aggregate and the verdicts need.** `narrow_rows(ctx, label, want)` reads the Parquet cache for *want*, the identity columns (the text columns, every spelling in `domain.image_identity.IDENTITY_COLUMN_NAMES` — the one list `resolve_identity_column`'s callers pass, so a timepoint column spelled `time`, `tp` or `time_h` is carried and the curation keys and crop scope still match — `timepoint_hours`, `Included`) and the union of what every registered projector *declares* its verdict reads under the current settings; runs the same projectors on that frame through `data_loading.run_projectors`, in a scratch context whose row cache holds that frame alone (`_detached`); and returns it **without putting it in the row cache**. On a 1.1M-row well seven of thirty columns read in 0.04 s and hold 36 MiB, against 0.19 s and 210 MiB for the whole frame warm — and seconds once the plate no longer fits the page cache either. `stats_compute.aggregate_well` / `aggregate_group` read through it (`_aggregate_rows` names the value, a ratio's two inputs, the timepoint, `area_px`, each gated channel and the thresholding on-column), so a plate-wide line or bar aggregate neither reads whole frames nor evicts the wells other views hold. **The fail-open hazard is why the columns are declared rather than guessed.** Every verdict passes every cell when its input column is missing (D2 in the large-dataset tracker), so a narrow frame short one input would read as fully included. Each projector registers with `columns=` (`cache_projectors.register_cache_projector`): QC its shape metrics when the gate is active, the crop its centroids when a region is set, the focus cut `qc_edge_focus` when on, gating the gated channels or its gates' axes (a ratio's two inputs), and curation, field quality and field exclusions nothing beyond the identity columns. A projector without a declaration, a declaration that answers `None` (an unknown ratio) or one that raises sends the read back to `get_rows` and the whole frame. A well already held is returned as held, and with no current Parquet cache the read falls back to `get_rows` too. `tests/test_narrow_rows.py` holds the declarations to the verdicts on a real `AppState` and a real Parquet cache: a 32-cell well in which each of the seven layers excludes cells no other layer does (proved layer by layer), and in which ten columns no verdict reads are left out of the narrow read; with every layer on, for intensity gating and for scatter gates on a ratio axis, the narrow frame's verdict columns and inclusion mask equal the full frame's, and `aggregate_well` / `aggregate_group` from it equal the aggregates of the full frame. |
| `data/cache_projectors.py` | Registry of the inclusion-verdict projectors, plus `project_verdict_column` — the one cache walk they all perform (resolve the target wells, skip empty / missing frames, hand the verdict the frame *and its well label*, write the int column, drop the column outright when the verdict raises, and return the labels it had to drop). **A verdict that could not be recomputed leaves no column rather than the previous parameters' answer.** Every consumer guards its read with `if "<col>" in df.columns` and fails open, so an absent verdict is the one state the stack already handles honestly, whereas leaving the stale int column attached kept filtering those wells by thresholds nobody could see any more. The returned failure list is not decoration: `features/qc.recompute_qc_all` and `features/crop.recompute_crop_all` hand it to `core/notifications.report_verdict_failures`, a module-level function beside `NotificationService` so the two callers cannot drift into two sentences for one situation. It writes the wells to the status line, raises the same text as a toast, *and* returns the message, because the status line is a single slot and every crop action writes its own outcome line one or two calls later — those five lines append the returned text so the warning survives the very actions most likely to produce it, while the toast is the surface the next line of the same handler cannot erase. The label is passed because a verdict can be scoped to particular wells (the crop's `FrameScope`) and a cached frame need not carry a well column — this walk is the only place that knows which well each frame belongs to. `features/qc` and `features/crop` register here and share that walk; the registry is what lets `data_loading.load_and_project` apply them without the data layer importing `features/`, and the shared walk lives here for the same reason — neither feature may depend on the other. `data/curation.py` registers here too, and so does intensity gating (`home/cell_gating/gating_compute.apply_gating_to_cache`, first in the list because the gating pass itself writes `Included` and then re-asserts curation on top), so the roster is the *whole* list of what a freshly loaded frame gets. That completeness is the point of the registry rather than a tidiness: a projection applied anywhere else instead is one that a well the row cache dropped and reloaded comes back without — which, with the cache bounded, is any well at any time. Gating was the last writer outside it: `GatingWorker` wrote `Included` / `Gate_Pass` / `Gate_On` once, so a gated well evicted afterwards reloaded ungated. The pass now records the configuration it applies (`CellGatingState.applied_gating`, cleared on a dataset swap) and the projector re-applies that snapshot — not the live settings — to a frame read from disk, so a reloaded well agrees with the wells the pass wrote. The projector does nothing on the label-less walk `recompute_qc_all` makes on each QC edit: the held frames already carry the pass's columns, and re-gating them there would cost a gating pass per keystroke. **Each registration also declares the columns its verdict reads** (`register_cache_projector(fn, columns=...)`, read back through `iter_projector_declarations`), which is what lets `data/narrow_rows.py` read a well narrowly and still apply every layer; `data_loading.run_projectors` is the one guarded loop both `load_and_project` and the narrow read run. |
| `data/curation.py` | **Manual per-cell curation, projected onto the row cache.** The user's include/exclude decisions from the Segmentation tab live in `ctx.runtime.review.included_overrides`, a `(well, fov, tp, nid) -> "0"/"1"` map that is the source of truth; nothing reads that map when it aggregates, because every consumer reads `row["Included"]` through `df_included_mask`. `apply_curation_to_cache` is what carries the decision from the one to the other, and it is a **registered cache projector** beside QC and crop rather than an errand each caller runs. That placement is the whole point of the module: while the projection was owned by the Review Image feature it ran only where that feature was called — the dataset load, a cell toggle, the end of a gating pass — so a well the row cache dropped and rebuilt came back with the exclusions gone from its rows while the override map still listed them, and every plate reset that clears QC parameters (`persistence/reset_scopes`) or recovers from a stale cache (`core/channel_state_controller`) drops that cache without touching the map. Unlike QC and crop it writes `Included` itself rather than its own verdict column, because an override *is* the inclusion decision for that cell; the three layers never collide, since QC and crop own `QC_Pass` / `Crop_Pass` and neither touches `Included`. **It bumps `rows_version` for its direct callers and not for the projector path**, which is the one place the two differ: the dataset loader and the gating pass project onto frames that are already cached and do not invalidate afterwards, so they need the bump, while a frame `load_and_project` built a moment ago can have no memoized aggregate of its own — and bumping there would strand the entries every *other* well already has, since that counter is part of the `aggregate_well` cache key. The registration binds `note_change=False` for exactly that reason; QC and crop reach the same end by never bumping at all. It fetches through `get_rows` rather than reading the cache dict so the un-scoped form can reach wells the cache does not hold, and re-enters `get_rows` harmlessly when the registry calls it as a projector — `load_and_project` stores the frame *before* running the projectors, so the inner call is a hit. Empty map, no-op: it never *un-writes* a 0, which is why clearing curation goes through `reset_scopes.clear_curation` dropping the row cache so the frames reload their original `Included`. |
| `data/image_repository.py` | **The image-access facade — `WellRepository`'s counterpart for pixels**, reached as `ctx.state.images` and attached in `ViewerContext.__post_init__` beside it. Three modules make up the image path and a feature that wanted a picture had to know all three: discovery (`image_discovery.find_well_images_and_masks`, which walks the dataset's layouts and returns the fluorescence / overlay / mask / top-hat inventories), resolution (`frame_load`, which picks the ref a `(well, channel, timepoint, fov)` names), and decode (`image_discovery.open_imgref_as_array`, memoized in a bounded LRU behind the zip-handle cache). `images_for_well(well, channel)` is the discovery step with the four `ctx.state.dataset` fields — `data_dir`, `in_dir`, `fov_tp_extractor`, `pipeline_info` — read here rather than assembled identically at each call site; `array(ref, greyscale=)` is the decode, a **staticmethod** because a resolved `ImgRef` names its file completely and the Playground's worker thread decodes without a context; `invalidate()` drops both image caches together, which is what a dataset swap needs — dropping one and keeping the other leaves the app choosing between a stale picture and a stale archive handle. `tests/test_image_repo_bypass.py` holds the door shut (`IMAGE_REPO_BYPASS_BUDGET == 0`). **Two deliberate absences.** It owns no inventory cache: the three grid features pass their own dict to `frame_load` and their lifetimes genuinely differ — Image Table and Playground keep one for the session, while Cell Browser's worker keeps one *per page* because it reads on a background thread and a dataset swap mid-read must not leave it serving refs into a replaced archive, so folding them into one cache here would quietly give the worker the session lifetime. And it does not wrap `frame_load.load_frame_array` / `load_mask_array`, which are the grid features' own composed API, take that cache explicitly, and are called with `ctx=None` on one path (`image_compose._load_mask_array`, which reads the context only afterwards for the inclusion filter) — putting them behind a context-bound facade would add a hop without removing one. |
| `data/well_repository.py` | The row-access facade over `DatasetState` + `data_loading`, reached as `ctx.state.repo` (attached in `ViewerContext.__post_init__`, on `AppState` rather than as a `ViewerContext` accessor so the frozen service-accessor surface is untouched). Reads are `rows(label)` (lazy, projected), `rows_or_none(label)` (cache-only, no load), `labels()`, `all_timepoints()`, `all_fovs()`, `has_data` and the `dataset` root; the writes are `load_well(label, path=None)` and `open_well(label, path, load_rows=…)`, the second being what the dataset loader's bulk pass calls: with `load_rows` it loads the well as `load_well` does and takes its summary from that frame when none is stored, without it it records the stored summary (or computes one from a column read) and the FOV-label verdict it carries. `rows_or_none` has one caller, the gating projector, which writes onto the frame `load_and_project` has just stored and pinned; Statistics reads through `rows`, because a cache-only read of a well the bounded cache had evicted answered `None` and turned its median and mean-of-all into NaN. It holds the `ViewerContext` rather than the bare `DatasetState` because the load path runs the cache projectors, and those read the wider `ctx.state` (QC params, crop region). |
| `domain/viewer_state.py` | `read_pipeline_info` + the `make_schema_extractor(sep, fov_idx, tp_idx)` factory used everywhere the app needs a `(fov, tp)` from a filename. It returns the channel-token lists both separately *and* inside the curated `pipeline_info` dict (`fluor_tokens`, `smfish_tokens`), so a consumer holding only that dict can answer "which channels did this run have?" without re-reading the file. An unreadable or unparseable sidecar yields an empty dict, which is how a caller tells "no sidecar" apart from "a sidecar naming no such channel". |
| `domain/plate_layout.py` | `PLATE_ROWS`, `PLATE_COLS`, the 96-colour well palette (one colour per plate position — a shorter, submultiple-of-12 palette repeats colours down each column). |
| `domain/line_colors.py` | The Line plot's colour mode — the Bar mode's sibling, and deliberately not the same rule. A bar is named by the tick label under it, so `bar_colors` can collapse every column onto one ink and lose nothing; a trace is not, and ten identical grey curves is an unreadable figure rather than a cleaner one. So `"grey"` here identifies a trace **twice over**: a shade from `theme.Colors.plot_grey_ramp`, a dash from `LINE_STYLES`, and a marker (shape *and* fill) from `LINE_MARKERS`. **All three advance on every trace**, so neighbouring traces differ in both and the pair is unique across the twelve traces `SCREEN_LEGEND_ENTRIES` names individually — which is the number that has to be distinct, since past it the legend has already stopped naming them. A first draft cycled the marker fastest and moved the shade only on a wrap, which names 48 before repeating and drew nine traces in nine identical greys; the extra period bought nothing a reader could see, and only rendering the figure caught it. The counts — 5 shades, 4 dashes, 12 markers — are coprime in pairs so no two cues ever advance in lockstep (two cues that always moved together would be one cue wearing two coats); their LCM is 60, and the marker alone is unique across the first 12. The ramp spans `#585858`…`#A8A8A8` rather than the narrower `#686868`…`#949494` that clears 3:1 on **both** grounds, because that rule caps the range: a fifth shade inside it drops the step from 14 levels to 11 and reads *worse*.
