The measurement that licenses the wider ramp is that the grounds fail at opposite ends — every shade clears 3:1 on at least one, and nothing measures below 2.3:1 anywhere — so the shade is the fast approximate cue while the dash and the marker, which cost nothing in contrast, are the reliable ones. `tests/test_line_color_mode.py` pins all three rules. **The cycles are one function taking the cues it may spend** — `grey_style(index, cues=…)`, with `GREY_CUES` the three channels and `grey_trace_style` the Line panels' answer of all three. What differs between the plots is not how the greys are chosen but how many channels are free to carry identity, and that is a parameter rather than a rule per tab: written as three modules each holding a constant, the shared half was copied and the differing half was frozen, which is how a tab came to give up a cue in a case where nothing was using it. A cue not asked for comes back `None`, which every caller already reads as "leave whatever the panel draws", so an omitted dash cannot overwrite one the figure is spending elsewhere. `trace_style_for_mode` takes the mode string because `render_line_series` has no ctx — it serves the Batch Export line figure as well as the tab — and `trace_style` is the state-object spelling that delegates to it, so two doors cannot answer one question differently. The CDF panel takes the marker too, spaced by `markevery` rather than drawn at every vertex: it is the one panel with no error band and thousands of points, so a shade alone could not identify it and a mark per vertex would bury the curve. **The renderer tags every marked trace `_aw_marker_is_data`, `_aw_marker_face_is_data` and `_aw_linestyle_is_data`**, because `apply_export_style_prefs` runs on every redraw and pins both shape and face from the Properties prefs — without the second flag half the cycle came back filled and six traces stopped being distinguishable while the legend went on advertising twelve. |
| `domain/variable_series.py` | One sample variable turned into a figure's ink and its bands. *Colour by* and *Split by* ask the same question of each drawn member — which value of the variable it holds — so both answers come from one pure rule — `plot_members.variable_values_for(vset, variable_id, wells_by_key)` — over whichever key space the caller provides: `member_variable_values` supplies the plotted scope's, Batch Export supplies its group's. Keyed on what that surface actually draws rather than on a guess from the key's spelling, since `A01` is both a well and a set someone may have named `A01`. **The two ways of having no value stay apart all the way to the ink**: `roll_up` distinguishes a member whose wells disagree from one holding an unfilled well, and each gets its own neutral colour and its own name, because "you filled these inconsistently" is a mistake the user can go and fix and "these were never filled" is a different one. Colours come from `VALUE_PICKS`, a sixteen-entry roster of plate-palette indices taken in the variable's own order — **measured**, not assumed, twice over. An early version spread the picks across all 96 to avoid "adjacent hues", which made three values 30 apart in RGB (`#E56AFB` beside `#DC81EA`, one colour to any reader) against 199 for the palette's first three. Taking the first *n* fixed that for a trichromat and for nobody else: six values measure 116 apart normally and **28** under protanopia, and eight collapse to **10** under deuteranopia. Roughly one man in twelve reads a figure that way, and *Colour by* carries no second channel saying the same thing, so two values sharing an ink is not a degraded reading of the figure but a wrong one with nothing on screen to say so. The roster is chosen by greedily maximising the closest pair across all four views at once — trichromat and the three dichromacies, under the Viénot–Brettel–Mollon simulation in `tests/_cvd.py` — giving 108 / 92 / 93 / 100 at six values, and two or three values that are *better* on every view than the palette's own head. Past sixteen the order runs on through the rest of the palette rather than cycling, because a repeated ink is the failure the picks exist to prevent. **The picks are shared out across the plate, not restarted per variable.** `colors_for(vset, variable_id)` is the one entry point every surface reads — the chips, the value rows, the plate, *Colour by*, Batch Export's inks and every legend — and it offsets a variable's values by however many values the variables before it hold (`color_offset`). Indexed from zero per variable, `Cell line`'s two values and `Dose`'s first two took the same two inks, so one blue meant `HeLa` in the chip row and `0 µM` on the plate a click later; a colour meaning two things on one plate is the same wrong reading the picks were measured to prevent, arrived at from the other side. The offset is cumulative rather than a fixed stride per variable, which is what keeps the measured head of the roster in play for the plate as a whole — two variables of six values is twelve inks, all of them still inside the sixteen — where a stride would push every variable but the first into the unmeasured tail and lose exactly the dichromat separation the picks were chosen for. The cost is stated rather than hidden: adding or removing a value on one variable moves the inks of every variable after it. That is the right way round — a colour that silently means two things is a misreading, while a colour that changes when you edit the plate is something the user watches happen. `test_no_two_values_on_a_plate_share_an_ink` and `test_a_variables_inks_still_start_at_the_measured_picks` hold both halves. `test_the_palette_entries_are_far_enough_apart` and `test_the_value_inks_stay_apart_for_a_dichromat_too` pin both halves, the first added after a mutation swapping the strategies left the original test green — it asserted the colours *differed*, which every strategy satisfies. A redundant encoding on the bars was considered and declined at `annotate_colour_legend`: a reader who cannot separate two inks cannot use a key to them either, and *Split by* already gives the same fact a labelled position. It also owns **`overlay_glyphs`** and **`glyph_key`** — the short mark a second variable wears on the Variables tab's plate, and the sentence naming each. The rule is **all or nothing across the variable**: initials when every value's first character is distinct, ordinal positions otherwise. Mixing the two per value is what it replaces, and on the series it was built for that was worse than either — `0, 0.1, 0.3, 1, 3, 10` came out `0, 02, 03, 1, 3, 10`, where `10` is a real dose and `02` is a code for `0.1` with nothing distinguishing the two kinds of two-character glyph, so a reader taking `03` at face value read a well as three times the dose it holds. An ordinal cannot be mistaken for a value because it is visibly a numbering, and `HeLa` / `U2OS` keep the `H` / `U` that need no key at all. Here rather than in the tab for the reason the rest of this row exists: it is a rule, and a rule in a signal handler is a rule nothing tests. **One spelling for a value on a figure:** `member_bands` names bands through `value_label` (unit included, `10 µM`), so `band_order` and `legend_entries` — which look those names up — list and match in the same spelling; matched on the bare `value.label`, every band of a variable with a unit missed its rank (bands fell back to member order) and its Colour-by legend came out empty. |
| `features/barplot/_decorate.py` | The decoration applied **once over the finished `BarItem` list**, not at each construction site. It takes the caller's own member key space (`wells_by_key`), because there are two: the plotting tabs' `member_wells(ctx, "bar")` and Batch Export's, whose keys are a `BarGroup`'s replicate sets and solo wells — the same override its fold-change resolver already makes through `scope_wells`. The **rule** is shared and only the provider differs, so a batch figure and the tab it mirrors cannot disagree about what colour a value is; matching the batch bars against the tab's keys instead would ink the members whose names happened to coincide and leave the rest. `collect_bar_items` builds items in four branches, and a sweep that edited them is a sweep with a branch left out — a figure where some bars honour the control and some do not is worse than one where none does, because the ones that do make the rest look deliberate. Splitting re-bands and **stably** re-sorts, so each band is contiguous (`cluster_centers` centres a header over the positions it saw, so a band split across the axis draws its header in the gap between its halves) while the user's drag order survives inside each band. The bar tab already uses bands for timepoints and for wells, and in multi-timepoint mode a bar's name is split across the two rows (header = sample and tick = `t=…` under "Group by well"; the reverse under "Group by timepoint"), so the displaced header is **folded into the tick** by `_carry_displaced_band` — keyed on the collector's `group_mode`, which both collectors pass — giving `<sample> t=<timepoint>` in either mode; overwriting the header alone left every bar in a band reading only its timepoint. With *Then by* set, each banded bar also gets `BarItem.subgroup_key` and the stable sort runs on `(band rank, sub-band rank)`; `collect.clustered_x_positions` inserts `SUBGROUP_GAP` (0.5) between sub-bands and widens the band gap by the same amount so it stays the larger, `collect.subcluster_centers` centres sub-band headers per contiguous `(group_key, subgroup_key)` run (the same dose label recurs in every band, so pooling by label as `cluster_centers` does would draw one header between two bands), and `_annotations.annotate_cluster_headers` draws the sub-band row where the band row normally sits with the band row lifted a line above it. **Timepoint groups.** With more than one timepoint selected, `collect.mark_timepoint_runs` stamps each item's `BarItem.run_key` with the collector's own cluster identity (the sample under "Group by well", the timepoint under "Group by timepoint") in both collectors, *before* decoration, so it survives Split by replacing `group_key`. `clustered_x_positions` draws adjacent items sharing `run_key`, band and sub-band `bar_w × (1 + group_spacing)` apart, capped at one slot, so each group reads as one block; with one timepoint `run_key` is empty and the layout is unchanged. `collect.bar_layout` resolves the drawn width (`bar_width_for`: the user's `BarGeometry.width`, or the automatic `min(0.65|0.6, 5/n)`) and the positions together, so the sliver is measured against the real bars. `render_bar_items` takes a `bar_geometry` (resolved from ctx via `bar_geometry_settings` unless given — Batch Export passes it, since it renders with `ctx=None`), and the multi-timepoint footers are laid out from the positions the renderer stashed rather than recomputed. `_annotations.cluster_header_pad` gives the mean-panel title pad for zero, one or two header rows (6 / 18 / 30 pt), and both figures that draw these headers use it: the tab renderer, and Batch Export's `_render_bar_group_figure`, which styles its title through `apply_ax_style` and so also lowers its axes top by the extra pad to keep the title clear of its suptitle. The tab renderer also drops the multi-timepoint well footers whenever the split displaced those clusters (keyed on `split_notice`, which the decorator sets exactly then), since each tick already names its sample. A split that replaces a band also **says so** on the axes, through `BarPlotState.split_notice` and `_annotations.annotate_decorations` — on the figure rather than the persistent status bar, because the redraw that resolves the condition is the one that clears it. |
| `domain/bar_colors.py` | The Bar plot's colour mode, and the single place that turns it into a colour. `bar_color_mode` reads `PlotState.bar_color_mode`, defaulting anything unrecognised to `"plate"` — a state object from an older build that has no such field, or a direct attribute set, degrades to the colours the app has always drawn rather than to an unknown colour string matplotlib raises on. The on-disk path is guarded a layer up as well: `_apply_bar` validates against `BAR_COLOR_MODES` before assigning, so an edited `persistence.json` is dropped rather than stored. `mono_bar_color` returns the mono ink or `None`; `apply_bar_color_mode` maps a whole `colors` list, always returning a new list of the same length so a caller can zip it against the wells it was built beside without branching on the mode. Deliberately excludes the shortfall marks: the dashed placeholder a missing measurement draws and the undefined-spread tick keep their own colours, because a colour mode is a statement about data ink and greying an absent bar to match a present one is the substitution §7 of `CLAUDE.md` exists to prevent. |
=======
| `domain/sample_definitions.py` | Read / write the `sample_definitions` block inside `pipeline_info.json`. |
| `domain/batch_models.py` | `BarGroup` + `ReplicateSet` — plain dataclasses used by every plot tab + batch export. |
| `domain/ratio_models.py` | Channel-ratio definitions (`gfp/mcherry`-style virtual channels). |
| `domain/plot_members.plot_replicate_sets` | **The one answer to "how does this view pool its wells".** Normally the user's visible replicate sets; when `ctx.state.plot.group_by_variable` names a sample variable, one set per value of it instead, pooling the wells that hold it, in the variable's own order. Grouping this way introduces **no third member-key shape** — pooling the wells that share a dose is structurally what a replicate set already is, so every collector's existing grouped branch is reused, which is why `tests/test_plot_members.py`'s equality guard keeps holding. **Saved per-sample `ControlRef`s are still orphaned by a regroup** — the key *shape* is unchanged but the key *values* become value labels, so an entry keyed on a group name misses. That is reported rather than silent: the member renders `UNMAPPED`, the shortfall phrase counts "N with no control", and the stale entry is listed as unused. An earlier version of this row claimed the references survived, which was simply false; the behaviour was right and the sentence was not. It is one seam by necessity: if the Bar tab pooled by dose while Statistics still pooled by the user's groups, the two would describe one plate differently and neither would say so. Every ctx-fed call site goes through it or through its hidden-inclusive twin `plot_replicate_sets_loaded` — bar, line, scatter, heat map, multivariate, distribution, stats, export, batch export, cell browser, review image, cell gating, fold-change pairing, the selection controller, `member_replicate_sets` and `iter_plot_groups`. **Two raw poolers, not one**, and the first sweep converted only the first: `active_replicate_sets` is the visible sets and `replicate_sets_loaded` the same list including hidden ones, a distinction that does not exist for a variable's values. Four `replicate_sets_loaded` sites were left pooling by the user's groups while their neighbours regrouped, and the consequences were exactly what §7.5 #5 predicts for a half-swept change: Batch Export wrote the identical whole-plate figure into every group's file, and the Heat Map averaged the whole plate into each dose cell while labelling them all with the first group's name. `tests/test_group_by_variable.py` now fails on either name, matching on the *call* so an aliased import is caught, and exempting **functions** rather than files — a file-level exemption is what let `member_replicate_sets` keep the old pooling while living beside the substitution that replaced it. A well with no value for the variable joins no set and is not plotted; `wells_without_variable` is what makes that shortfall reportable, and `wells_the_grouping_adds` is its mirror — with no replicate sets defined the plate selection is what drives every plot, and grouping ignores it to pool every *loaded* well holding a value, so one well selected can be four drawn. That helper is the one caller outside the seam allowed to name `active_replicate_sets`, because comparing the two poolings is its whole job; the guard's exemption is by function and carries the reason at both ends. A variable that groups nothing falls back to the user's own sets rather than emptying every plot in the app — the Variables tab is where that is reported, and a blank Bar tab three clicks away is not an explanation. `ctx.state.plot` may be **absent** (the headless export and CSV paths build a context with only the slices they read), which honestly means "no grouping chosen"; a test pins that the real `PlotState` always carries the field, so that tolerance cannot hide a production context that silently stopped honouring it. `member_variable_values` and `split_members_by_variable` answer "what value does this member hold" in whatever key space the plot is in — and a member takes a value only when **every** well in it has the same one, with the rest returned separately so the caller can say how many rather than drop them. |
| `core/group_by_controller.py` | The band's **Group by** combo: what it lists, what changing it does, and the sentence naming what the choice left out. In the scope zone beside Channel and Property because all three change what *every* tab draws rather than how one tab draws it, and **hidden entirely until a variable is defined** — the band's rule is that it only carries controls that do something, and a Group by offering nothing but the status quo is not one. A change emits `plot_options_changed` rather than redrawing one tab, because every tab's picture changed; `RedrawCoordinator` already coalesces that into one pass with the rest deferred. A variable deleted while selected clears the state as well as the combo, or the next redraw reads a variable the control no longer offers. `group_by_shortfall` names what the grouping changed, in three branches rather than one: the wells it **drops**, because a plate that quietly loses eight wells looks exactly like a plate that had eighty-eight; the wells it **adds**, because with no replicate sets defined it pools every loaded well holding a value and ignores the plate selection entirely; and, when the chosen variable matched nothing at all, that the user's own groups are what is on screen — saying "not plotted" there would contradict the figure the sentence is printed on. All three are §7 in the one place a user is most likely to be comparing two plots. Outside any feature package because the control is cross-tab — a Bar-tab-owned version would be a setting one tab could hold while the others did not. **Colour by**, **Split by** and **Then by** sit beside it in a `Decorate ▾` popover (one `DECORATION_CONTROLS` row each, captions from `DECORATION_TITLES`), not in the scope zone. *Then by* (`sub_split_by_variable`) is a second band level inside Split by's, so `_gate_sub_split` keeps it inside one: its combo is disabled while Split by reads "One band", and clearing Split by — or choosing Then by with no Split by — clears it, since a sub-split held with nothing to nest in would be a setting the figure silently ignores. It also refills Then by without the variable Split by holds, and clears a Then by that comes to name it: sub-bands by the band's own variable would only repeat the band row (`_decorate` drops the same pairing when a saved file carries it). None of the three belongs in the scope zone: none changes what a member *is* or moves a single number, and the scope zone says that it does. Five refusals each carry their own sentence: too few distinct values, a flat response, a parameter at the edge of its range, an EC50 outside the values tested, and an optimiser that did not converge — and each names the user's **own** variable, because this is not a dose–response tab: it plots a measurement against any number someone varied, and telling a user who varied temperature that "no dose changed the measurement" describes a plot they did not make. `fit_response` takes the name rather than choosing one, since the fitter has no idea what it is fitting. A refused fit draws no line — `curve_y` returns `None` rather than an array, so no caller can paint a flat line across the floor of the axes — and its legend entry reads `EC50 — (no fit)` with the reason in the caption, which travels with a saved figure. The interval is symmetric about `log_ec50` and therefore asymmetric in the user's units, which is the truth about a dose estimated on a log axis; when there is no interval, the reason is carried from where it was decided rather than guessed at the call site. **Fold change goes through the shared path, not a second implementation.** The collector builds AggPoint-shaped tuples and hands them to `fold_change_pairing.normalize_member_pts`, the same call the Line tab makes — nine zeros a point, against a whole class of divergence: the last time a caller reimplemented "the same" division with one extra `isinstance` check it turned a `numpy.float32` spread into no error bar at all. The loop is inverted for it, a member at a time rather than a timepoint at a time, because `vs t0` divides a member's whole series by its own baseline and a series has to exist before it can be normalised. `vs t0` is **declined and said**, not applied, when fewer than two timepoints are drawn: with one, every point is its own baseline and the figure would be a flat line at 1.0. What the control could not be resolved for is named per (member, timepoint), and a point whose spread came back undefined is counted rather than drawn as a zero-length error bar, which reads as perfect agreement. The suffix reaches the y label, because the state is shared and this axis can become normalised without anything on this page being touched. **Channel and Property are this tab's own**, as the aggregate Scatter tab's are, and for the same reason: only a tab that owns the pair can offer `Fraction above threshold` and `Events above threshold`. Owning them means the band must **not** also carry its globals here: `ui_helpers.OWN_CHANNEL_LEAVES` is the roster of leaves that scope their own pair, and `centre_view` hides the band's Channel, Property and ON-cutoff for any leaf in it. That test used to be the three scatter titles written out inline, so this tab shipped showing two Channel dropdowns and two Property dropdowns of which one pair did nothing — and, worse, an ON-cutoff box editing the cutoff of whatever channel the *band* held rather than the one the curves were measured on. The cutoff is set on Home → Cell Gating, which the Property combo's tooltip says. That label is not a column — the fraction is the share of cells whose *mean intensity* clears the ON cutoff — so a consumer deriving `f"{channel}_{metric}"` from the shared combo would ask for `gfp_fraction_above_threshold` and read nothing, which is why it cannot go in the band that Bar, Line, Distribution and Heat Map all read. The list itself comes from the shared `populate_metric_combo(..., include_fraction=True)` and the entries from `update_channel_selector`'s roster, so the ratio and shape collapses, the smFISH gating and the section headers have one definition; `_response_ch_cb` is in that roster and deliberately **not** in `set_active_channel`'s sync-to-active one, which would drag the tab back onto the shared channel on every switch. Both fall back to the shared choice until the user touches them, so a tab nobody has configured is not a tab showing something else. `compute_rep_stats` and `compute_rep_per_fov_stats` take an optional `val_col` for this — additive, with the resolved column going into the cache key so a tab-local choice cannot collide with the shared one. **The figure repaints on every event that changes it.** The leaf carries `on_activate`, `on_selection_changed` and `on_channel_changed`, and `set_active_metric` names it beside Bar: `redraw_app` reaches only Line, Distribution and Heat Map, so a Property switched while this tab was on screen changed nothing until the user left and came back — `on_activate` was doing the repaint for them. `tests/test_response_redraw_hooks.py` reads both halves off the registry and the fan-out.  The tab's own `Property` combo offers the channel's Properties, `Fraction above threshold` — which `compute_rep_stats` returns beside the mean — or `Events above threshold`, the Bar and Line Events statistic (`compute_rep_n_above_stats`, the mean of each well's count with the cross-well spread, or the per-FOV count `compute_rep_per_fov_stats` returns at positions 4/5 when `Spread: FOV` is on). `collect.y_metric_for_key` maps the Property's key to `Y_MEAN` / `Y_FRACTION` / `Y_EVENTS` for the tab and for Batch Export alike. The shared plotting band's Property combo carries neither — `include_fraction=True`, which adds both synthetic entries (`metric_labels.SYNTHETIC_METRIC_LABEL_TO_KEY`), is passed only by the tabs that own their pair: this one, the aggregate Scatter tab, and their Batch Export panels — and the Bar and Line tabs surface both as *stacked panels* rather than as Properties, so a single-axes tab has no other route to them. The axis label follows the metric rather than the Property, since an axis reading `GFP mean intensity` over a curve of fractions is the one thing a figure must never do. `collect._member_sample` builds the AggPoint tuple handed to `normalize_member_pts` with each quantity in **its own slot** — the mean at 1/2, the real fraction at 3/6, and, for an events curve, the count at 4 with its spread at 9 (the slots the Line tab's Events panel is normalised through; `n_per_fov=False` selects them). `normalize_pts` divides each slot by the control's series *for that quantity*, so a fraction or a count carried in the mean slot would be divided by the control's mean intensity — a ratio of two different quantities under a fold-change label. The control's series come from `fold_change.member_*_series`, which hand this tab's own column to a replicate-set control as well as to a solo-well one (`compute_rep_n_above_stats` takes an optional `val_col` for it, as `compute_rep_stats` does), so an RFP curve is not normalised by a GFP control. **The `Spread: FOV` toggle is read.** The tab built that control with `with_fov=True` and then called `compute_rep_stats` regardless, so a member of one well had one replicate, no spread, and a point drawn with no error bar under a control the user had switched on; `compute_rep_per_fov_stats` is the sibling the toggle asks for, and `ControlSeriesCache`'s `per_fov_spread` is matched to it rather than pinned `False`, which had a per-FOV numerator normalised against a cross-well denominator. The caption names the unit a replicate actually was, because "add another well" and "add another field" are different fixes. **A figure can carry more than one curve per timepoint.** **The curves are split by a list of variables.** The tab's own `Series` control is a checkbox menu, not a combo — the number of variables a figure can be split by is the number the plate has, and a plate varying cell line *and* RNA across a dose series wants both without spending the plate-wide *Group by* on the second one. *Group by* is a further, outermost layer for the case where the whole app should pool that way. So the members split into one curve per (timepoint, and each chosen value): `Cell line` plus `RNA` is four curves per timepoint, legend `HeLa · shGFP`. `ResponseState.series_variable_ids` holds them **in the order they were ticked**, because that is the order the labels read in and the order the legend sorts by; `view_state_io` restores a block written with the older single `series_variable_id` as a one-element list rather than dropping it. `collect_response` takes an ordered tuple of splitting variables rather than one id, and `plot_members.response_split_variables` is the single place that decides what is in it and in what order — *Group by* first, then each ticked series variable, dropping any that is already on the axis and any the outer layer already names, so picking the same one twice does not label a curve `HeLa · HeLa`. `ResponseCurve` still carries one `series_id` / `series_label` and its `key` is still `(timepoint, series_id)`: the two variables' value ids are joined into one key and their labels into one legend entry, so a second layer costs the renderer, the fit dict and the legend no new shape. The join uses a control character, because a value id is the user's own and a printable separator one of them contains would silently merge two curves. Without it a plate of two cell lines each given a dose series was drawn as *one* line through every member sorted by x, doubling back at every dose: a zig-zag that reads as a curve, one legend entry, and with a fit on, one EC50 fitted across both conditions — §7's silent substitution, since a figure of two conditions looked exactly like a figure of one. The fit dict is keyed by `curve.key` rather than by the timepoint for the same reason: two series at one timepoint would otherwise share a `FitResult`, drawing one curve with the other's line and EC50. **Colour carries the series and the dash pattern carries the timepoint**, so a reader can see which curves are the same condition and which are the same moment; one colour per (series, timepoint) pair would give four unrelated colours to two cell lines at two timepoints with nothing relating them. Properties → Colours offers *Series* or *Grey* on this figure, resolved through `domain/response_colors.py`: grey mode moves the series onto a shade and a marker, and takes the dash as a third cue **only while the timepoint is not using it**. Both come from one function — `line_colors.grey_style(index, cues=…)`, asked for `response_grey_cues` — so what is local to this tab is how many channels are free rather than which greys or shapes to use. Reserving the dash unconditionally was a cue given up for nobody: `_timepoint_styles` draws none at all below two timepoints, which is the commoner figure, and every series came out solid told apart by one step of grey and a small marker. `renderer._curve_styles` derives the two halves together rather than passing the answer as an argument, because `for_curve` applies the timepoint's dash last — a series that wrongly claimed one is overwritten and the figure still draws correctly, so no assertion on the drawn lines can see the mistake, which is exactly the shape of wrong answer worth making unreachable. The default is spelled `"series"` rather than `"plate"`, since a curve is a series pooled across however many wells hold that value and has no plate-picker colour to take. The renderer tags the drawn artist `_aw_linestyle_is_data` **unconditionally** for the same reason: `apply_export_style_prefs` runs on every redraw and would otherwise stamp one pref pattern over four timepoints' worth of dashes while the legend went on naming all four. `_aw_marker_is_data` and `_aw_marker_face_is_data` go on in grey mode, where the shape and the fill together say which series a curve is. The off-scale column takes its curve's own colour: the reason it is drawn unjoined is that a line there would assert a slope across the axis break, which says nothing about the ink, and letting it take the next entry of matplotlib's cycle put a stray colour on a figure the user had just asked to be drawn in greys. A series gets one colour across every timepoint it appears at, the legend entry names only what varies, and both layers exclude whichever variable is on `X` — a split on the axis variable is one curve per dose with a single point on each. A member a splitting variable cannot resolve gets its **own** named curve rather than being dropped or folded into a neighbour: the x axis may refuse a member because a point needs a number, but a series is only a grouping, and dropping a fully dosed member over a missing cell-line label would take real data off the figure. Curve order is the product of the variables' own declared value orders, outermost slowest, not the wells or the alphabet; combinations no member landed in are left out rather than drawn as empty curves, and the oddments — a member whose wells disagree, or that a variable never reached — come last. **There is no un-pooled mode**, and the tab says so when `bar_pool_replicates` is off rather than obeying it: a dose is a property of a condition, and the Bar tab a click away *is* drawing one bar per well, so the two disagree with nothing on either to explain it. The scope is registered through the feature descriptor's `fold_change_scope_factory`, so removing the feature drops the scope with it; `plot_members._ALWAYS_POOLED_SCOPES` is what makes a response key resolve to its set's wells whenever a set is active — with none active every scope is well-keyed, and a response key is a well token that resolves to itself — the predicate there tested `scope == "line"` and so answered *wells* for every scope it had not heard of, which for a set named `CTRL` resolves to nothing at all and takes the whole fold-change axis quiet with it. **A figure with nothing on it draws `collect.empty_reason` in place of the axes**, ticks and frame removed so it reads as a message rather than as a draw that failed. Six causes, six sentences, each naming the pane the fix is made on; `ResponseData.placed` exists so that "no group has a dose" and "every group has a dose and none was imaged then" stop arriving as the same zero. **The tab is repainted by the events every other plotting leaf is**, which it was not: it carried no `on_activate` and no `on_selection_changed`, and the generic `redraw_app` fan-out reaches only Line, Distribution and Heat Map — so a body built while the plate was empty stayed empty, and selecting different wells left the curves drawn from the previous selection, which is a plot of the wrong data that looks exactly like a plot of the right one. Fold-change changes are covered by the registered scope; Channel and Property are covered by `on_channel_changed` and by `set_active_metric` naming this leaf. Its `view_state_io` block is the feature's own for the same reason: the fit is the point of the page and nothing about it is recoverable from the plate, so a saved plot without one restored with no curve and no EC50 while looking like a complete restore. The x variable is stored by **id** — a name is renamed and an index moves — and an unpinned plateau is omitted rather than written as `0.0`, which would turn every restored 4PL into a Hill. The restore pushes the state onto the popover's widgets with their signals blocked, because seeding them at build time and never re-reading the slice is how the bar tab's significance picker came to show `Stars (*)` above p-value brackets. **The shortfall does not reach the status line.** `notify.set_status` writes the *persistent* bar and a successful redraw has no reason to write anything, so the sentence outlived its condition — the same defect the bar significance note was moved off it for; the caption and the empty state cannot go stale, because the redraw that resolves the condition is the redraw that clears them. The caption says when the scale was derived rather than asked for, and where to override it, because seeding the preference to record the derived answer would spend the very distinction `figure_pref_is_set` exists for: once set, the axis can never re-derive for a plate with different doses. The Properties switch stays honest about the axis all the same — with no stored answer it seeds from the axis on screen (`ExportStyleSidebar._log_toggle_seed`) rather than from the unset preference, which read *off* over a plainly logarithmic axis and, because `_persist` writes every field on any edit, meant an unrelated control wrote that `False` down and the next redraw obeyed it. **The builder itself is exercised, not only its parts.** The tab raised `TypeError` on every real app construction for the whole of its existence — `build_plot_save_menu`'s `cells_cb` is required and was not passed — while ~130 of its own tests stayed green, because each drove a control through a stub ctx and none called `build_response_tab`. `centre_view` catches a failing builder, logs it and drops the title from the pending map, so the tab rendered as an empty page and the existing "every tab drained" test passed throughout; `test_app_smoke.py::test_no_tab_builder_raised_while_draining` reads that log instead, which costs two seconds and is the only place in the suite the failure can surface. **Which timepoints exist is asked once, of `core/timepoint_sync.plottable_timepoints`.** That is `dataset.all_timepoints_cache` — the canonical list, merged on load from the numeric column, the parsed text column and `pipeline_info` — plus the `0.0` that `data_loading.resolved_timepoints` files a row with no timepoint token at, which is where the aggregator keeps those points and so where a plot has to ask for them. This tab read `data_loading.get_all_timepoints` instead, which sees the raw numeric column alone: on a plate whose filename schema carries no timepoint slot that column is NaN everywhere, so the picker offered nothing, its button read `Timepoints: 0 selected` and the figure was blank while Bar Plots — which had the fallback spelled into its own menu builder — drew the plate. Both tabs read the shared helper now, so the fallback cannot be present in one picker and absent from the other. It also stops a redraw walking every loaded well's rows to recompute something the dataset caches. The picker's button uses the shared `multiselect_button_text`, so it reads `1/3 selected`: a bare count cannot separate "the user unticked the rest" from "there are no others", and those have different fixes. **The stored selection is reconciled with the plate in both directions.** It used to be filtered only downwards — drop what the dataset lacks, keep the rest — so a stored dict could only ever shrink, and a selection saved while the picker could see one timepoint went on offering that one after the tab could see all of them. That is not hypothetical: the release before the timepoint source was unified saved `{"0": True}` for every plate, and a tab reports what it holds rather than what the plate has, so the fix looked like it had not landed. Answers the user gave are kept, including all-off; timepoints they were never asked about are added **off**; and a stored selection naming none of the plate's timepoints is a selection about a different dataset, so it is replaced rather than filtered to nothing. It carries the Bar picker's All / None pair, which write the state with the checkboxes' signals blocked so twelve ticks are one repaint. `cell_scope_compute.py` names the quantity the curve draws in the file's notes — the mean, the fraction or the count, keyed on the Property's metric key, which Batch Export passes from its run snapshot through `_cell_scope_kwargs` — and carries the **ticked** timepoints rather than all of them, unlike Line's: this tab draws only those, and a file listing twelve beside a figure showing one is the mismatch a cell-scope exists to prevent. `tests/test_response_tab.py` drives the real controls — the X combo, the timepoint picker, the Fit popover's combo and its two line edits — rather than asserting they exist, which is §7.6's lesson: the per-sample control editor shipped unopenable past a lane of ~4,950 tests because every test of it entered one step past the closure that was broken. |

### 5.7 Persistence

**A debounced save is written at the two moments its timer will never fire.**
`schedule_save` coalesces a burst of edits behind a 500 ms `QTimer`, which is
right while the app is running and wrong on quit and on a dataset swap.
`PersistenceRegistry.flush_all` writes every pending domain now, and
`AllWellApp.closeEvent` and `load_controller` both call it — a ratio, a
heat-map layout, a curated cell override, a line order, a saved selection, a note, a
sample definition, a QC parameter or a crop edited within half a second of ⌘W
reaches disk, and a swap cannot leave a timer alive to fire *after* the new data
directory is in place and write the previous dataset's state into it.
`_flush` therefore starts by checking that the domain is still pending: a timer
that survives the flush finds nothing to write rather than re-writing what the
flush already wrote, against whatever directory is now open.

A notes editor is the one thing that reaches the queue by a different route.
The editors commit on focus-out, and neither quitting nor swapping datasets
moves focus, so text on screen may never have been queued at all — draining the
queue would then write every domain except the one the user was typing into.
`ui_helpers.commit_focused_notes` folds the visible text into the selection
slice *and* schedules the `notes` save in the same act, which is why the close
path calls it before `flush_all` and why the scheduling lives in the helper
rather than at each call site.

**An unreadable document is not an empty one.** When `persistence.json` exists
but cannot be parsed — corrupt JSON or an OS error — the in-memory doc is empty
*by failure*, and writing it back would erase every section the file still
holds because one byte failed. `DatasetState.persistence_doc_degraded` records
that, and `_doc.write` renames the unreadable file to
`persistence.unreadable-N.json` before starting a fresh one, so the user's work
stays recoverable by hand.

A `schema_version` this build does not understand is a different case and
carries its own flag, `persistence_doc_foreign`. That file is not damaged, just
written by another build, so it is read as empty and left exactly where it is —
renaming it aside would cost a user who alternates builds the other one's state
on every launch, under a filename claiming it was unreadable. Refusing to
*write* is what keeps both safe, and `_doc.write` returns early for the rest of
the session.

Both states are announced, not merely logged: `load_controller._report_persistence_doc_state`
puts one line in the status bar and a toast at the end of the load. Silence
there looks exactly like a plate nobody has configured, and the natural next
move — defining the ratios and groups again — either writes over the one copy
of the work or goes into a file the app has already decided not to touch.


Every "save state into the dataset folder" path lives under
`review/persistence/`. One module per JSON file:

| File on disk | Module | What it holds |
|--------------|--------|---------------|
| `pipeline_info.json::cell_gating` | `cell_gating.py` | Cell-area + per-channel `fluor_gates` + `thresh_frac_on` + `thresh_count_on`, plus the scatter-gate inclusion state (`use_scatter_gates` + `scatter_gates`, each gate carrying its `x_col`/`y_col`) written only when that mode is on. Only values that differ from their default are written, and the ThreshFracOn default is per-channel: `domain/gating_state.default_thresh_frac_on` returns 50.0 for a readout channel and 0.0 for the dataset's nuclear/segmentation channel (`pipeline_info.json::nuclear_token`, held on `ChannelState.seg_channel_token` and reached through `channel_state_controller.seg_channel_token_of`). That channel is what nuclei are *found* with, so an ON/OFF brightness cut on it has no meaning and the readout default only hid nuclei from the Image Table's "≥ ON threshold" view; the pipeline's own auto-threshold pass writes it `0` for the same reason. The block builder has to know which channel it is, or a nuclear cutoff the user deliberately raised to 50 would diff as "at default" and be dropped. `thresh_count_on` is the same shape for the *count* metrics — a separate row because a spot tally and a brightness are different scales — and needs no such channel knowledge: `default_thresh_count_on` answers -1.0 for every channel. A sidecar written without the key is not migrated; the accessor's default applies, which is the value that lets a count plot draw at all. Three call sites build this block — `persistence/cell_gating.py`, the saved-plot capture (`features/saved_plots/collect.py`) and the auto-threshold pass (`data/auto_threshold.py`) — and the latter two reconstruct it from named keys rather than editing in place, so a key neither reads is deleted on write. |
| `pipeline_info.json::smfish_thresholds` | `smfish.py` | Per-channel smFISH spot-detection threshold (`{channel: float}`). Saved only on a successful Apply Global Threshold so the value the spinbox shows matches the spot counts baked into the per-well CSVs. Restored on dataset open and on channel-combo switch. |
| `pipeline_info.json::sample_definitions` | `sample_definitions.py` (top level) | Saved selections + replicate sets / groups + well labels + notes. **Auto-saves** on edit via the registry (`autosave_to_pipeline_info`, a silent variant — no dialogs/toast, no-op without a data dir) in addition to the explicit Save button; well-label cells and the Notes box commit on `editingFinished` / focus-out (not per keystroke), discrete rep-set/group edits via `rebuild_all`. **The block written back carries the labels of wells this load cannot see.** `load_from_pipeline_info` hydrates a label only for a token in `dataset.well_paths`, which is right — a label for a well that is not here has nothing to attach to — but rebuilding the block from that pruned map alone meant opening one plate's `out/` folder, or any other load that sees a subset of the wells, and touching a single label erased every other well's label from the only place it existed. `_labels_to_write(ds, keep_absent=True)` merges the on-disk map back in: a token this dataset **holds** takes the live value including its absence, so clearing a label still deletes it, and a token it does not hold keeps whatever the file says. The file is the stash here — unlike `view_state`'s `absent_wells`, there is no session state to leak across a dataset swap. One caller passes `keep_absent=False`, through `autosave_forgetting_absent_labels`: the "Sample definitions" reset scope, which is the user asking for every label to go and would otherwise read them all back out of the file it is about to overwrite. |
| `persistence.json::crop_region` | `crop_region.py` | The crop rectangle drawn on the Segmentation tab (`DatasetState.crop_region`, source-mask pixel tuple) **and the frames it is scoped to** (`DatasetState.crop_scope_*`, `null` per field meaning every value). Written as `{"region": [...], "scope": {...}}`; a bare four-element list is the older shape and reads as an unscoped crop. The scope is persisted because it is part of what a saved crop *means* — reloading the region without it would widen a two-well crop to the whole plate and move every number downstream, where the drag-delete's scope is deliberately transient by the opposite argument (it arms a gesture, not a stored verdict). A malformed scope resolves to un-armed rather than to a guess: an unreadable scope must widen to the documented default, never narrow to a set nobody chose. Feeds the `Crop_Pass` inclusion layer; an absent / cleared crop removes the section. |
| `persistence.json::ratios` | `ratios.py` | User-defined ratio channels. |
| `persistence.json::heatmap_layouts` | `heatmap_layouts.py` | Saved heatmap layouts + cmap/scale state, plus the selected timepoint. **The timepoint is stored as a value, not as a position in the combo.** The combo is rebuilt from the plate's own `tp_values` every time those change, so the add-timepoints workflow (§9.7) leaves a saved index pointing at a different hour on a tab whose entire output is one timepoint. `_restore_timepoint` matches the saved value against the plate's live timepoints (`math.isclose`, so a JSON round trip cannot miss); a value this plate does not have restores nothing and logs, because falling back to the index would put up an arbitrary timepoint indistinguishable from a restored one. Only a file written before the value was recorded uses the index. **The collector declines to write anything when the Heat Map tab was never built in the session.** `_tab_was_built` tests the same three widgets `apply_persisted_settings` already tests — named once in `_BUILT_MARKERS` so the save side and the restore side cannot disagree about what "built" means — and when they are absent `_collect_settings` hands back `HeatmapState.persisted_settings` unchanged instead of reading eight typed fields nothing has filled in. Without that guard any save at all (another section's autosave rewrites the whole document) replaced a saved `{cmap: magma, scale_mode: Manual, vmin: 10.0, vmax: 900.0, repset_avg: True, log_scale: True}` block with the dataclass defaults. A reset still empties the section: `reset_scopes.restore_slice_defaults` puts `persisted_settings` back to `None` *before* it saves, so the guard returns `{}` there. |
| `persistence.json::line_order` | `line_order.py` | Line plot replicate-set / well draw order. |
| `persistence.json::view_state` | `view_state.py` | Active tab, selected wells, channel/metric, fold-change scopes, per-tab combos, export-style prefs. Saved on dataset switch + app close. **The two "absent" stashes are per-plate and are cleared before the section is read.** `restore` remembers the wells a saved view names that the plate in front of it does not hold, so `snapshot` can union them back and a subset load does not prune them — but those sets describe one particular `persistence.json`, and they are the only piece of view state written by `restore` and read by `snapshot` without either being keyed to a data directory. `restore` reassigns both, and it only runs when the new plate *has* a `view_state` section; when it has none the assignment never happens and the previous plate's wells were unioned into this plate's saved selection. `forget_absent_wells(ctx)` empties them, called at the top of `load_from_data_dir` before the section is read and therefore ahead of every path that returns without reaching `restore` — no saved block, a section that is not a dict, a document that cannot be migrated. |
| `persistence.json::qc_params` | `qc_params.py` | QC debris-gating thresholds edited on the Home → Cell Gating tab (the fundamental always-applied inclusion layer); seeded from `pipeline_info.json` `qc_options` when unset. |
| `cell_overrides.json` | `cell_overrides.py` | Per-cell `Included` overrides set on the Segmentation tab (kept separate — large + write-heavy). |
| `persistence.json::field_exclusions` | `field_exclusions.py` | Fields excluded by hand from QC triage, as a list of `{well, fov, timepoint, reason, at}` records, read into `DatasetState.field_exclusions`. Feeds the `Excluded_Field_Pass` layer (`data/field_exclusions.py`). A record that cannot be read is dropped and logged rather than guessed at, because a half-read exclusion could remove the wrong field. Written sorted, so an unchanged set writes identical bytes. |
| `persistence.json::triage_decisions` | `triage_decisions.py` | QC triage findings the user accepted, keyed by the finding's stable key → `{state, note, at}`. Only `accepted` is stored: an excluded field's state is read from the exclusion itself, so the two cannot disagree. |
| `bar_groups.json` | `bar_groups.py` | User-picked file for Batch Export's `BarGroup` state (no auto-save). |

`persistence.json` is a single consolidated viewer-state document managed by
`_doc.py`. On first load it migrates any legacy `ratios.json`,
`heatmap_layouts.json`, or `line_order.json` sidecars into the unified file
and deletes them. `qc_params` migrates its own legacy `qc_params.json` (which
wraps its data, so it can't use the generic migrator) inside `qc_params.py`.

Persistence modules expose `load_from_data_dir(app)` / `save_to_data_dir(app)`
function pairs. They are registered, by name, with the **`PersistenceRegistry`**
(`review/persistence/registry.py`, built once in `ReviewApp.__init__`
as `app._persistence`); call sites use `app._persistence.{save,load,
schedule_save}(name)`.

**Atomic writes.** Every save goes through
`review/persistence/_io.atomic_write_json` (or `atomic_write_text` for
the smFISH worker's per-well CSV writer): tmp file + fsync + `os.replace`.
A crash, signal, or full-disk mid-write can no longer leave a truncated
sidecar that the next viewer load reads as empty state and silently
clobbers. The tmp filename is uniquified (`<path>.<pid>.<rand>.tmp`) so
concurrent writers / retry-cleanup races can't collide on a single fixed
`<path>.tmp` name. Both `open(tmp, "w")` and the final `os.replace` retry
on `PermissionError` with exponential backoff (5 attempts, 100/200/400/800/1600 ms)
so the Windows AV-scanner / Excel-viewer / OneDrive-sync race doesn't surface
`[WinError 5] Access is denied` mid Apply-Global-Threshold. The smFISH writer
catches per-well `PermissionError` so one locked well's CSV (e.g. user has
it open in Excel) doesn't kill the rest of the run — the locked well is
skipped with a WARN naming the file + likely cause.

**A read-modify-write of `pipeline_info.json` goes through
`_io.update_json_atomic`, not through a bare read followed by
`atomic_write_json`.** That sidecar has several writers — the smFISH
thresholds, the cell-gating block, the sample definitions, and the pipeline
itself, which owns `fluor_tokens`, `schema` and `available_timepoints` and
rewrites the file at the end of a run. Analyze and Review share one window, so
a run can finish while the viewer sits between its own read and its own write,
and each writer preserving only the keys it *read* made a lost update look like
the run's keys reverting on their own: a viewer that suddenly cannot see a
channel or a timepoint the run produced. The helper takes a `mutate(doc)`
callback, compares the file **byte for byte** against the copy the mutation was
built from immediately before the replace, and re-applies the mutation to the
new content when another writer landed in between.

That is optimistic concurrency, deliberately not a lock. A lock would have to be
honoured by every writer of the file in every process, and the pipeline runs in
a separate process — often on a remote host — that takes none this code could
share. What the guard buys is narrowing the window from "however long the caller
takes to build its block", which is arbitrarily long since callers read state,
format values and log, to the microseconds between the final comparison and
`os.replace`. The residual race is documented in the helper's own docstring.
`mutate` must be free of side effects the caller cannot afford to repeat,
because a concurrent write re-runs it; the sample-definitions writer keeps its
pre-v2 backup to one copy per call with a `backed_up` flag for exactly that
reason, and takes the backup *inside* the mutate so the "was the old block v1?"
test is made against the bytes actually being replaced. Four writers route
through it — `persistence/smfish.py`'s `save_threshold` and `clear_thresholds`,
`domain/gating_state.save_gating_to_pipeline_info`,
`domain/sample_definitions.save_to_pipeline_info`, and
`persistence/sample_variables.save_to_data_dir`.

A refusal comes back as `False`, and each writer turns that into something the
user can see rather than a silent no-op: the sample-definitions writer raises
the `OSError` its explicit-Save caller keys off, the variables writer logs a
WARNING saying the block stays in memory only. Where the write has been handed
to the background writer (below) there is no caller left to return `False` to,
so those two checks travel *with* the write — each writer wraps the call and
the checks that read its outcome in one `_write()` callable, which is what keeps
the pre-v2 backup's abort from quietly becoming a no-op — and the report comes
out on the status line and in the log instead of as a return value.

Both `atomic_write_json` and `update_json_atomic` take `durable`, defaulting to
True. `durable=False` skips the `fsync` before the replace: the replace is
atomic either way so no reader ever sees a half-written file, and what is given
up is only the guarantee that the bytes reached the platter before the call
returns. Every debounced autosave passes False: it fires each time the
user stops typing or clicking, and the value is rewritten seconds later anyway,
so paying an fsync per pause on a network share buys a durability guarantee
nothing here needs.

The registry owns the **one** debounced-save path — `schedule_save`
with a shared pending-set — so signal storms (ratio-panel field edits, heatmap
layout drag-and-drop, cell-override toggles, sample-definition edits, crop
drags) coalesce into one disk write per 500 ms burst; this replaced five
identical per-domain `schedule_save`/`_flush` pairs and their
`_<name>_save_pending` flags. Auto-saving domains: `ratios`,
`heatmap_layouts`, `cell_overrides`, `line_order`, `view_state`, `qc_params`,
`notes`, `sample_definitions`, and `crop_region` (`bar_groups.json` is the lone
explicit user-picked file with no autosave).

**The debounced writes do their file I/O on a background thread**
(`persistence/_writer.py`). `update_json_atomic` is a read-modify-verify-write,
which is seven filesystem round trips — `exists`, `read_bytes`, `exists`,
`read_bytes`, the tmp `open` and `write`, `os.replace`, and the tmp `exists` —
plus the `exists` calls `resolve_pipeline_info_path` makes to find the sidecar
in the first place. On a local disk that is a few milliseconds. On the network
share a plate normally lives on it is around a second, and it was being paid on
the GUI thread half a second after every edit: the Home → Variables tab froze
for a second or two each time the user paused while renaming a variable or
ticking a value onto the plate. The tab's own work was never the cost — a full
rebuild is 7.5 ms at 96 wells and 24 ms at 384 — so nothing about the repaint
path would have helped.

`PersistenceRegistry._flush` runs the domain's `save` inside
`_io.background_writes`, a context manager that installs a **thread-local**
sink. Everything that reads application state still runs on the GUI thread: the
save reads `ctx.state`, builds its block, and closes over the finished payload.
Only the file operations are handed over, and only the ones whose call site
passed `deferrable=True` (or which routed themselves through `_io.defer_io`) —
that opt-in is at the call site because deferring changes what the return value
*means*, so only a site that does not inspect its result in the same call may
take it. The sink being thread-local is load-bearing rather than tidy: the
writer thread runs these same functions to do the actual I/O, and finds no sink
there, so a job cannot re-queue itself for ever.

`PersistenceWriter` is one daemon thread consuming one FIFO queue. Serialized on
purpose — two writes to the same sidecar must not interleave, and the optimistic
concurrency above narrows the race against *other processes*, not against a
second thread of this one — and FIFO on purpose, because the last edit the user
made has to be the last one written. `atomic_write_json` serialises its payload
on the calling thread before queueing, which snapshots it: `_doc.write` hands in
the live in-memory persistence cache, and a worker iterating that dict while the
GUI thread edits it would raise `dictionary changed size during iteration`.

`flush_all` drains the queue before returning, which is what makes its name true
at the two moments it is called — quitting, and loading another dataset. Both
need the bytes on disk before the next line runs; a queue left in flight is the
same lost edit `flush_all` exists to prevent, moved one thread across. The drain
is a sentinel job waited on with a timeout, not a poll of `Queue.empty()`, which
goes true while the last job is still running.

Failures are **reported, not returned**. The writer logs each one and emits
`failed(domain, detail)`, which `PersistenceRegistry` puts on the status line
and in a toast. The connection is made explicitly queued because the emit
happens on the writer while the slot writes a widget (PySide6's default
`AutoConnection` resolves the same way here, dispatching a plain receiver's
bound method against the *sender's* thread affinity — the flag states the
requirement rather than repairing it). Silence would be the defect itself: a
user who fills a 96-well grid into a read-only or stale folder would otherwise
learn of it by finding the grid gone next session.

Nothing outside the debounced path is affected. `PersistenceRegistry.save(name)`
— the dataset-swap force-save of `view_state`, the reset scopes, an explicit
Save button — still writes inline and still gets a real answer, as do the smFISH
threshold writer and the gating block, which never go through the debounce at
all. `cell_overrides.json` v2 stamps
each row with the well's
`<well>_out.zip` mtime so a pipeline re-run drops the now-stale overrides
on load instead of re-binding them to unrelated cells.

A stamped row therefore has **three** outcomes on load, not two, and the loader
counts and warns about each. A row whose stamp differs from the well's current
zip is dropped as stale. A row whose stamp matches is verified. A row whose well
has no `<well>_out.zip` in this data directory at all — never written, deleted,
or a `stat` that failed — cannot be checked against anything, which is not the
same as a match: the row is **kept unverified**, because dropping curation
because a zip was moved would be an unrecoverable loss, and a warning names how
many were kept that way. A row carrying no fingerprint is a fourth case and is
warned about regardless of the file's own `version`: a v2 file can hold rows
with an empty `seg_fp` (the well's zip was missing or unreadable when the
override was saved), and gating that warning on `version < 2` meant exactly the
file that could hold both shapes warned about neither. The version is reported
inside the message instead of deciding whether to emit it.

**The provenance log — what was done to a dataset, in order.** Every other
record describes current state: `pipeline_info.json` is rewritten by every run,
`run_report` / `run_check` describe the last run, the run journal is replaced
when the next run opens, and `persistence.json` holds the gates and groups as
they stand. `util/provenance_log.py` keeps the sequence: `provenance.jsonl`, in
the directory holding `pipeline_info.json`, one JSON object per line, each
carrying `schema_version`, a UTC `ts`, the `event`, its `source` (`analyze`,
`review`, `datasets`, `report`), the `app_version` read from `version.py`, and
an event-specific `detail`.

- **Append-only, and never authority.** A line is added with one `O_APPEND`
  write and fsync; nothing rewrites, truncates or repairs the file, and no
  decision anywhere reads it. That is what makes several unlocked writers
  acceptable: the worst a lost or torn line can do is make the history
  incomplete, and the reader says so.
- **A closed roster.** `EVENT_FIELDS` names every event type and the detail keys
  it must carry; `append_event` raises `ValueError` for an unknown type, an
  unknown source or a missing key (a programming error, found by the test that
  drives the emitting path), and answers `False` with a WARNING for any I/O
  failure, because a save, a run or a repair must never fail because its
  history could not be written. A key may be present as `None` — unknown is a
  value; absent is a missing key.
- **The reader counts what it cannot use.** `read_events` returns a
  `ProvenanceRead`: the events this build understands, plus `unreadable` (a torn
  last line after a crash, or an interleaved append from two processes on a
  network volume or Windows — anywhere in the file, not only at the end),
  `foreign` (a `schema_version` newer than this build) and `missing`. `complete`
  is true only when all three are clear, so an incomplete history never reads as
  a complete one, and one bad line never hides the rest.
- **Review records at the write, from what was written.**
  `review/persistence/provenance.py` is called by `_io._replace_with_text` — the
  one function that replaces a dataset JSON file — immediately before and after
  the replace, on whichever thread performs it. `before_write` reads the file as
  it stands; `after_write` parses the text that replaced it and appends one
  `analysis_changed` per analysis block whose digest differs (`block_digest`, a
  short hash; the history says *that* a block changed, the files say what it is
  now). `STORED_AT` maps each `(file, key)` to its `ANALYSIS_SCOPES` domain, and
  `RECORDED_UNDER` names the one domain with no block of its own (`notes`, which
  lives inside `sample_definitions`). Hooking the write rather than the
  registry's flush is what covers the inline writers — the gating block, the
  smFISH thresholds, a reset's `_save` — that never pass the registry; reading
  "before" at the write rather than remembering it from the load is what keeps a
  block the pipeline changed in between from being attributed to Review; and
  recording after the replace is what makes a failed write record nothing. A
  debounced autosave records once, on the background writer, after it lands.
  Recording failures are logged at WARNING and never fail the write.
  `clear_analysis` appends `reset` naming the scopes that completed, after their
  own writes have recorded what they changed. The log's directory comes from
  `resolve_pipeline_info_path`, so a dataset whose sidecar sits one level above
  its data directory (the Analyze layout) keeps one log, beside the sidecar.
  `tests/test_review_provenance.py::test_every_analysis_domain_reaches_the_log`
  holds every `ANALYSIS_SCOPES` domain to a row of `STORED_AT` or
  `RECORDED_UNDER`, so a new analysis domain cannot be silently left out.
- **The other writers.** Analyze runs are recorded by the runner
  (`services/run_provenance.py`, §6.4); Datasets derivations and repairs by
  `datasets/core/provenance.py` and `datasets/validate/apply.py` (§6b).

Measured growth: an `analysis_changed` line is about 240 bytes and a
`run_started` about 870; a heavy year of 20,000 lines is about 5 MB and reads in
0.12 s, so the file is not rotated.

**Copying analysis from another dataset — a recipe.** The title bar's copy
button (`allwell._on_copy_analysis_clicked`) pops a menu
(`review/core/recipe_view.copy_analysis_menu`, shown with `popup`, never `exec`)
with three actions: copy from another dataset folder, copy from a **recipe
file**, and save the open dataset's analysis as a recipe file. Copying
(`prompt_copy_analysis`) brings chosen analysis decisions into the dataset open
in Review. Three modules, split by layer:

- `review/domain/recipe_compute.py` — the roster and the fit, pure.
  `RECIPE_SCOPES` names what can be copied, keyed like `ANALYSIS_SCOPES`
  (`sample_variables`, `sample_definitions`, `gating`, `ratios`,
  `export_groups`) plus `saved_plots`, each with the `(file, key)` blocks it
  owns. `DECLINED` names the two analysis scopes it will not copy and why:
  *curation* (overrides keyed by the source's nucleus ids, a crop by its pixel
  geometry, an exclusion by a field the source run measured — none identifies
  anything on another plate) and *smFISH* (a threshold is the one the target's
  spot counts would have had to be baked with). `tests/test_recipes.py` holds
  every `ANALYSIS_SCOPES` key to exactly one of the two. `check_fit` reports,
  per scope, the wells and channels the source block names that the target
  lacks, whether it would replace a different value the target already holds
  (the pipeline's own auto-threshold, typically), and whether the source has
  anything to copy at all. It finds names by walking each block's strings and
  keys — a canonical well label is a well; a source channel token, alone or as
  the prefix of a `<channel>_…` column name, is a channel — because a reader
  per block shape would be a second definition of six formats. It reports and
  never rewrites: a gate on a channel the target lacks is inert there, and a
  definition naming a missing well attaches to nothing. A recipe file is one
  JSON document (`recipe_document`: `kind` `allwell-recipe`, `schema_version`,
  the source label and channels, and each block the source holds as
  `{file, key, value}`); `blocks_from_document` reads it back into the same
  `DatasetBlocks` a folder gives, so the fit check and the copy cannot tell the
  two sources apart. It refuses, by name, a document of another kind, a newer
  schema, and a block no recipe scope owns — applying one would write somewhere
  no reset, fit check or provenance domain knows about.
- `review/persistence/recipe.py` — the I/O, Qt-free. `read_dataset_blocks`
  reads a folder as a user picks it (`out/` when present) without loading it,
  and **refuses** a file that exists and cannot be read, or a `persistence.json`
  of a schema this build does not know, by name — an unreadable source block is
  "could not be read", never "nothing". `apply_recipe` writes into the open
  dataset: it **flushes every pending debounced save first** (a timer armed
  just before the copy would otherwise land after it and write the old value
  back), then writes `pipeline_info.json` blocks through
  `_io.update_json_atomic` (never creating a sidecar the pipeline did not write)
  and `persistence.json` sections through `_doc.set_section`, after reading the
  document so a foreign one is reported rather than silently declined. A source
  block that is absent is not copied, so it cannot erase the target's own. Each
  scope is isolated; a failure is reported and the rest run. Every block
  written is an `analysis_changed` in the provenance log by the usual route,
  and the copy as a whole is one `recipe_applied` line naming the source, the
  scopes, what failed, and how many plots were added. `write_recipe_file`
  writes a recipe file atomically and refuses a source with an unreadable file
  (it would read back as a dataset with nothing for those scopes);
  `read_recipe_file` reads one.
- `review/core/recipe_view.py` — the menu and the dialog: pick a folder or a
  recipe file, flush, show one
  checkbox per scope with `ScopeFit.describe()` beneath it (a scope with
  nothing to copy, or unreadable, is shown disabled with its reason rather than
  omitted), copy what is ticked, reload through the same
  `allwell._reload_current_dataset` the reset uses, and report on the status
  line — naming anything that failed rather than calling a partial copy a whole
  one.

**Copied saved plots arrive undrawn.** A saved plot is its parameters *and* a
picture of the source plate's data; copying the picture would put another
plate's figure in this gallery under this dataset's name. So a copied record is
added beside the target's own under a fresh id, with no PNG, SVG or frame plan,
and with `SavedPlot.copied_from` naming its source. `SavedPlotsStore.image_path`
answers `None` for a record with no PNG, and every surface that shows a saved
plot — the gallery card, Home's strip, the PDF report, the PowerPoint deck —
shows `saved_plots.state.undrawn_note` in its place, so a copied plot cannot
pass for a missing file or for a figure of this dataset. Restoring it replays
its parameters against this dataset's data, which is the only way it acquires a
picture here. **A restore names the wells it cannot draw.** A record that names
wells this dataset lacks — a copied plot, typically, or one saved before a
well's files were removed — is drawn from the wells that are here, and the rest
used to drop out with nothing said (measured: a record naming `H12` restored
on a plate without it, drew from `A01` alone, and the status line read only
"1 replicate set(s) · 1 well(s)"). `saved_plots.controller.absent_wells` reads
the record's selected wells, soloed wells and replicate sets against the loaded
wells, and `restore_saved_plot` puts the sentence on the status line — with the
group-drift sentence when there is one, since two calls would leave only the
second — and the headless report puts it in that plot's manifest `note`.

**Resetting saved state — the scope model.** `persistence/reset_scopes.py` is
the one map from what a user names to the state that name owns. State is
modelled in two tiers and both title-bar reset buttons are expressed in them:

- **View** — how the data currently looks: selected wells and group visibility,
  fold-change scopes, per-tab controls, plot and figure preferences, draw order,
  the heatmap arrangement, the Multivariate configuration, the Image Table grid.
  Cheap to rebuild and carrying no scientific decision, it resets as a whole:
  `reset_view(ctx)`, behind the mode band's `rotate-ccw` button.
- **Analysis** — the decisions themselves. One `ANALYSIS_SCOPES` entry each for
  sample definitions, gating, curation, ratio metrics, smFISH thresholds and
  Batch Export groups, picked individually from the checklist behind the
  `trash-2` button (`core/reset_scopes_view.py`), then cleared by
  `clear_analysis(ctx, keys)` and followed by a dataset reload.

The dataset's own image and CSV files are a third tier no reset touches.

A scope names every storage **domain** it owns, and its `clear` is responsible
for all of them — the live typed state and every file the value is written to,
whether that is `persistence.json`, `pipeline_info.json`, or a standalone
sidecar. That is the property the design turns on, because the same value is
often stored twice: saved selections live in both `persistence.json::plot_groups` and
the `sample_definitions` block of the sidecar, and clearing one of the two is a
no-op once the loader (which treats an absent section as "nothing to say", so a
folder shared without its sidecar keeps its groups) re-hydrates from the other.
Manual cell curation is in neither file — it has its own `cell_overrides.json`.

`tests/test_reset_scopes.py` asserts the scopes **partition** the domain set
exactly: every name the persistence registry registers, plus the two sidecar
domains (`cell_gating`, `smfish`), is claimed by exactly one scope. A new
persistence domain that belongs to no scope fails the suite. Its companion
`test_the_partition_guard_bites` proves the guard fires on both halves of that —
an unclaimed domain and a claim on a domain that no longer exists.

Two consequences worth stating, because both were bugs before the model existed:

- **Reset one domain at a time, never the file.** There is deliberately no
  "delete `persistence.json`" helper. Deleting the shared document meant one
  wrong argument at one call site could silently spare every section at once,
  and the failure was invisible because the reload afterwards looked like a
  reload of reset state.
- **What resets live must equal what is dropped from disk.** `view_state.reset`
  restores `PlotState` and `ExportPrefsState` generically via
  `domain/state_defaults.restore_defaults` (so a field added to either slice is
  covered without anybody extending a reset), then **re-saves** the section
  instead of deleting it. Screen and disk therefore agree by construction rather
  than by two lists staying in sync. `reset_view` writes every one of the four
  `VIEW_DOMAINS` it names, and the ordering is part of the rule: the draw order
  lives in two places — two `PlotState` fields, which `restore_defaults` empties,
  and its own `line_order` section of `persistence.json` — so `_save(ctx,
  "line_order")` runs immediately *after* `view_state.reset(ctx)` has cleared the
  live order rather than before it. Leaving that section behind made the reset
  look complete and then undo itself, because the next load re-read the file and
  `line_order._reorder_selections_by_line_order` re-applied the old order to
  `selections`, permanently reordering them.

`reset_scopes.py` imports no feature module. It reaches a built feature's
widgets through callbacks the feature stamps on its `ctx.runtime.<feature>`
namespace — `qc.refresh_widgets_cb`, `image_table.reset_cb`, alongside the
existing `qc.changed_cb` — and recomputes derived columns by clearing the row
cache so the registered cache projectors re-derive `QC_Pass` / `Crop_Pass` on the
next fetch. An unstamped callback means the lazily-built feature was never
built, so there are no widgets to refresh. The Segmentation tab's own "Reset
crop + curation" menu action calls the same `clear_curation` the Curation
checkbox does (`crop.controller.reset_crop_and_overrides_now` wraps it with the
crop-mode exit, the Crop-scope button relabel and the redraw only that entry
point needs), so the two cannot drift. `clear_curation` widens the crop scope
back to every frame along with dropping the region: a scope left armed would
silently narrow the *next* crop the user draws to one they had just reset away.
The Segmentation tab's **Edit ▾ → Clear crop** clears both for the same reason,
so the two entry points leave the same state — and because the persisted section
is dropped once there is no region to save, a scope kept in memory there would
not survive a restart, leaving the running app and the file disagreeing.

Each clear writes through `PersistenceRegistry.save` rather than
`schedule_save`: the reload that follows would otherwise race the debounce timer
and read the pre-reset value back.

### 5.8 The Export Style sidebar

Each plot tab pre-allocates a right-side dock via
`make_plot_with_right_dock(parent)`. The dock is hidden by default and a
**Properties** button on the tab's controls row toggles it. When opened, the
dock hosts an `ExportStyleSidebar` (from `features/export/sidebar_view.py`)
backed by a `plot_style.figure_prefs(ctx, fig)` view. `_build_ui` assembles
the panel from one builder per section — `_build_header`, then
`_build_profile_section`, `_build_scatter_sections`, `_build_cell_values_section`,
`_build_colours_section`, `_build_bars_section`, `_build_axes_section`,
`_build_statistics_section`, `_build_legend_section`, `_build_overlays_section`,
`_build_time_section`, `_build_lines_markers_section`, `_build_grid_section`,
`_build_limits_section`, `_build_layout_section`, and `_build_footer` — in the
order the panel shows them. A builder behind a facet (`_supports`, or one of the
`_is_*_fig` checks) adds nothing on a figure that lacks it. The rows go through
`_SectionGrid`, which owns the scrolling column and each section's two-column
grid (a fixed 96 px label column and an expanding control column) and applies
the pref binding when a row names its key. Builders keep on `self` exactly the
controls the rest of the class reads, and nothing else.
`tests/test_properties_control_contract.py` holds every binding,
`tests/test_properties_hides_what_it_cannot_do.py` which sections each figure
gets, and `tests/test_properties_panel_frame.py` the header and footer buttons
(pressed, not looked for) and the grid's geometry. The widget binds to the
prefs view via `_bind_getter_setter`, so changes flow:

```
Properties widget → figure_prefs(ctx, fig)  ── shared style ─→ export_prefs.style_prefs
                        │                   └─ scoped keys ──→ export_prefs.axis_prefs[fig_key]
                        ↓
                  apply_export_style_prefs(fig, prefs)
                        ↓
                  canvas.draw_idle()
```

**What is shared and what is per figure.** Typography, grid, legend and ticks
are deliberately app-wide: one setting gives a whole figure set a consistent
look for a paper. Two families are per figure instead, keyed by
`figure_pref_key` (`line` / `bar` / `scatter_cells` / `scatter_agg` / `heatmap`
/ `distribution` / `spatial` / `multivariate` / `stats` / `response`) — see
`plot_style.FIGURE_SCOPED_PREF_KEYS`:

- `AXIS_SCOPED_PREF_KEYS` — limits, log scaling, and the per-axis bucket
  bookkeeping. A bar chart's y-limit means nothing on the scatter tab, so an
  unset axis key reads the neutral default and never consults the shared dict.
