  That default is the right answer for a widget binding — a checkbox has to
  show something — and the wrong answer for a tab deciding whether to pick a
  scale for itself, because "the user turned this off" and "the user has never
  touched this" arrive as the same `False`. `figure_pref_is_set(ctx, fig, key)`
  answers the second question and nothing else; Response Curves uses it to
  choose a log x axis from the data only where the user has expressed no
  preference, and to leave their answer alone in both directions once they
  have.
- `MARK_SCOPED_PREF_KEYS` — line width/style and marker size/style/edge width.
  The right mark size is a property of what the plot draws: five aggregate
  points want an 8pt marker, a 50,000-cell per-cell cloud wants 2pt, and
  sharing one value meant restyling the Scatter tab's aggregate sub-tab
  restyled its per-cell sub-tab into illegibility. Unlike the axis keys, an
  unset mark key falls back to the shared dict before the default — nothing
  writes those globals now, so that is the value saved before marks became
  per-figure, and it keeps applying until the user gives a figure its own.


**A figure is shown only the sections it can change.** The panel is built once
per figure and offered nearly all of itself to every plot, so on a figure that
draws no lines the five Lines & Markers rows styled artists that were not
there, the three Legend rows styled a legend that did not exist, and the two Log
scale rows acted on axes carrying row and column *positions*. Each moved the
widget, wrote the pref, redrew the figure and changed nothing — the
control-that-does-nothing shape, arriving from the opposite direction to the
roster failures below: not a tab a list forgot, but a section no list ever
limited.

`_STYLE_FACETS_A_FIGURE_LACKS` in `features/export/sidebar_view.py` states the
exceptions, keyed by the `app` attribute naming the figure, and `_supports(facet)`
reads it. **Only exceptions**: a figure with no row supports everything and a
facet absent from a figure's row is supported by it, so forgetting a figure
leaves a dead control rather than taking a working one away — the safe direction
for a table whose entries can only be established by measuring. Each entry
carries its reason, at the site and in the roster, because a bare facet name is
indistinguishable six months later from one added to make a failure go away.
The Heat Map is the figure measured so far, and it lacks `legend`, `marks`,
`plot_overlays`, `bar_show_mode`, `group_labels` and `log_axes`.

Two rules make this hold up. A gated section is **not built**, rather than built
and hidden: an unbuilt section registers no getter and no setter, so `_persist`
does not write its keys and `_resync_pref_fields` does not re-seed them, and a
widget like the Statistics *Show* segment cannot be re-seeded into writing
`bar_show_mode` from a tab that has no bars. And the claims are **re-measured**
rather than trusted — `tests/test_properties_hides_what_it_cannot_do.py` renders
the heat map twice per hidden pref and compares the PNGs, so a pref that starts
mattering fails there instead of staying hidden after becoming useful. The same
file pins what is *kept*, which is what separates a correct gate from one that
emptied the panel.

The **Axis #** picker lists the figure's plot panels and leaves out its colour
bars. `fig.axes` includes a colour bar, and every per-axis pass in
`apply_export_style_prefs` skips a `_aw_colorbar` axes by design, so the Heat
Map offered an "Axis 2" that selected the bar and moved nothing. The numbering
stays positional — axis 1 is the figure's first axes whether or not a colour bar
sits at 2 — because that is what a stored `axis_buckets` key already means.

`features/export/style.py` also owns the **Properties-panel roster**.
`open_export_style_panel` maps a plot key to the figure, canvas and default
export name it opens over, and a tab reaches it by handing that key to
`core/ui_helpers.make_properties_button`. Both halves are string literals at
opposite ends of the app: nothing imports across the seam, there is no shared
symbol a rename would break, and a key the roster lacks writes `Unknown export
panel: <key>` to the status bar and opens nothing. So the two drifted — a tab
shipped with an inert Properties button, past a full fast lane and a real app
construction, because building a button is not pressing it.
**There are two rosters in that file and a tab needs both.**
`open_export_style_panel` maps the key to its figure; `_resolve_export_dock`
maps that figure to the pre-allocated right-side dock `make_plot_with_right_dock`
builds. A tab in the first and not the second does not half-work:
`launch_export_editor` takes its `dock is None` fallback and appends the sidebar
into the plot card's own layout — inside whatever scroll area the tab wraps it
in — so the panel opens somewhere no other tab puts it, and nothing goes red.
Response Curves was added to the first roster alone and shipped exactly that,
under a commit whose own message argues about rosters drifting.

`tests/test_properties_panel_keys.py` closes both seams: it reads every key any
tab passes to `make_properties_button` and fails on one the panel roster does
not carry; it fails on a figure the dock roster does not name, and on a dock
name no tab registers; it selects the roster dict by the shape of its values
rather than by its variable name, so an unrelated dict in the same function
cannot vouch for a missing row; and it refuses a key it cannot read as a
literal rather than skipping it. Adding a plotting leaf means a row in each
roster and a `make_plot_with_right_dock` call in its `tab_view`.

**A roster is how shared chrome finds a tab, and a roster written before the
tab existed does not.** The Properties-panel pair above is one instance of a
class that has now bitten five times, always the same way: the control is
built, it is wired, it writes its state, and something on the other side is
iterating a list that has not heard of the new leaf — so nothing raises,
nothing goes red, and the failure is a control that does nothing. Every one of
these came from the same branch of reports about Response Curves.

* `core/plot_toggles` repainted after a SD/SEM or Spread: FOV change by calling
  `redraw_app` (Line, Distribution, Heat Map) and then naming Bar Plots. Any
  other registered scope was neither drawn nor marked dirty. It now fans out
  through `fold_change_scopes.redraw_scopes_or_defer`, which every other
  cross-tab setting already uses, passing `skip=scope_registry.redraw_app_scope`
  so the three scopes sharing that callable are not drawn twice — which is why
  that function is module-level and compared by identity rather than a closure
  made per registration.
* `persistence/view_state._activate_tab` decided whether a name lives inside
  the Plotting stack by testing it against a five-entry tuple. A leaf missing
  from it was asked of the *outer* notebook, which has no page by that name, so
  Restore applied every saved setting and never navigated — and the session
  snapshot reopened somewhere else. It now reads
  `features.sub_leaves("Plotting")`, the same source `centre_view` builds the
  stack from, keeping the literal only for a context with no registry.
  `tests/test_restore_reaches_every_plotting_leaf.py` drives every registry
  leaf through the router and asserts which notebook was asked for what.
* `centre_view`'s band swapped its global Channel / Property / ON-cutoff out
  for three scatter titles written inline; `ui_helpers.OWN_CHANNEL_LEAVES` is
  the roster now, held against the builders by
  `tests/test_band_globals_follow_the_leaf.py` — a leaf that adds a channel
  combo to its own band slot and is missing from the roster fails there.
* `plot_card_actions._CARDS` lost the Screen/Publication toggle and the global
  Copy / Save for a card missing from it; `tests/test_plot_card_roster.py` now
  derives the expected set by scanning for the registration itself.
* `data_loading.get_all_timepoints` was a *second answer* rather than a roster,
  which is the same failure with the list turned inside out — see the
  `features/response/` row and `core/timepoint_sync.plottable_timepoints`.

The rule they point at: **when shared chrome has to know about a tab, derive
the list from the feature registry, and when it cannot be derived, write the
roster once and guard it against the thing it is a list of.** A guard that
holds a roster against another roster has moved the problem up one level.

An audit for the rest of them, run after those five were closed, found three
more of the same shape. `selection_controller.PLOTTING_TABS` decides which tabs
mirror the replicate-mode active set: the leaf missing from it painted **no
wells at all** in rep-mode, because the plate took the branch written for the
Image Table, and a well click fell to the legacy handler that knows nothing
about solo wells. The redraw block in `rebuild_all` named Bar, then the three
default-scope tabs, then Scatter — so a replicate-group edit made while a
fourth leaf was on screen left it drawn from the previous groups. And
`runtime_app._PLOTTING_TABS` was a five-name roster with **no readers at all**,
which is the same hazard in its most durable form: a list that looks
authoritative, is wrong, and cannot be caught by any behaviour.

All three are gone. The rep-mirror set is derived (`_rep_mirror_tabs`) from the
Plotting leaves plus the per-well tabs that draw the same active set without
being leaves (`_EXTRA_REP_MIRROR_TABS`: Spatial, Multivariate, Nanowells); the per-well
tabs a group edit refreshes are `_GROUP_EDIT_FOLLOWERS` (those three and the Cell
Browser); the
group-edit and Property-change repaints go through one fan-out, and the dead
roster is deleted.

### Adding a Plotting leaf

`plot_orchestrator.redraw_every_scope` is **the** fan-out for "something changed
that every plot draws" — the error band, the replicate unit, the active
Property, a replicate-group edit. It runs `redraw_app` for the three scopes that
share that callable and hands the rest to the coalescer, so a leaf reaches every
one of those events by being a registered scope rather than by being named. Use
it; do not write a fourth list of tab titles.

What a new leaf still has to join, and what each costs when it is missed:

| Seam | Missed → | Guarded by |
|---|---|---|
| `FeatureDescriptor` in `features/registry.py`, with `build`, `redraw`, and — unless `redraw_app` already covers it — `on_activate`, `on_selection_changed`, `on_channel_changed` | the figure draws the previous answer until the tab is left and re-entered | `test_a_plot_leaf_is_wired_everywhere` |
| `fold_change_scope_factory` on that descriptor | every coalescer fan-out skips it, so each caller has to name it | same (Scatter's exemption is written there) |
| `plotting_band_slot(ctx, "<leaf>")` in its `tab_view` | a second control strip stacks above the plot | same |
| `apply_plot_card_decorators(ctx, card, "<leaf>")` | no hover save, no Saved Plots record | same |
| `plot_card_actions._CARDS` | no Screen/Publication toggle, no global Copy/Save, and `Save figure…` raises into a swallow | `test_plot_card_roster` |
| both rosters in `export/style.py` | an inert Properties button, or a panel that opens in the wrong place | `test_properties_panel_keys` |
| `sidebar_view._FIGURE_OWNING_FEATURES`, unless the sidebar already imports the leaf's redraw | every Properties control that needs a real redraw repaints the **Line** tab instead and reports success | `test_properties_panel_redraws` |
| `app_state._FEATURE_STATE_OWNERS` | a disabled feature's slice raises a bare `AttributeError` | `test_feature_slice_names` |
| `ui_helpers.OWN_CHANNEL_LEAVES` — only if the leaf scopes its own Channel/Property | two Channel dropdowns, and an ON-cutoff box editing a channel the tab is not drawing | `test_band_globals_follow_the_leaf` |
| `plot_style.FIGURE_PLOT_KEYS` | the figure's per-figure prefs fall back to a diagnostic key | — |

Everything else — the restore router, the rep-mirror set, the band's slot
switching, the repaint fan-outs — reads the registry and needs no edit at all.
That is the direction to push each of the rows above in as they come up for
other reasons.

**A Properties control reaches the screen one of two ways, and picking the wrong one is silent.** Most controls only restyle: `_on_fields_changed` persists the field and re-runs `apply_export_style_to_current` over the artists already drawn. That cannot re-decide anything the renderer chose while it built them — a colour picked per column, a histogram's `log=` baseline, an axis scale a tab derived from its own data — so those controls call `ExportStyleSidebar._redraw_bound_figure`, which dispatches on **figure identity**. The log toggles and the log-base field are in that second group: the Response tab picks its x scale from the doses and pins the choice with `_aw_force_xlog`, which the restyle obeys, so only that tab's own draw can change it.

The dispatch resolves the figures whose redraw this module imports directly, then `_FIGURE_OWNING_FEATURES` — figure name to *feature* name, reached through `ctx.features.redraw` so the sidebar imports no further feature module and a profiled-out one falls through. Its final `app._redraw()` is a diagnostic, not a fallback: it repaints the **Line** tab, so a figure missing from both halves had its Properties edits applied to a different tab's figure and `_redraw_bound_figure` still returned `True`. Spatial, Multivariate and Response Curves were all missing from a roster written when there were six plot tabs and nine figures this panel opens on, which is why `test_properties_panel_redraws` now holds the one list against the other. `_redraw_active_plot` — the reset-to-defaults path — dispatches on the tab in view instead and shares the same roster of feature names.

`core/plot_style.py` owns the prefs dict + the apply pipeline;
`features/export/style.py` owns the export profiles and opening the editor.
Every redraw path ends with a call to
`core.plot_style.apply_export_style_to_current(ctx, fig, canvas)` so
the sidebar's toggles (grid on/off, axis label size, log-scale, …) survive
a re-render.

**Plotting import paths.** Each plotting name is imported from the module that
defines it, never through a neighbour that happens to import it: the styling
engine (`DEFAULT_EXPORT_STYLE_PREFS`, `apply_export_style_prefs`,
`apply_export_style_to_current`, the axis and log helpers) from
`review.core.plot_style`; the figure render and clipboard pipeline
(`copy_figure_to_clipboard`, `axis_tight_bbox_inches`, `_render_figure`) from
`widgets.fig_clipboard`, which the registry's `export_style.copy_figure` service
also resolves; bar collection, layout and hit-test math (`BarItem`,
`bar_geometry_settings`, `cluster_x_for_group_keys`, `bar_idx_at_x`, …) from
`barplot/collect.py`; the annotation passes from `barplot/_annotations.py`; the
drag handlers from `barplot/_drag_reorder.py`; and `barplot/controller.py` for
what it defines itself (`render_bar_items`, the redraw, the menus).
`core/plot_style.py`, `barplot/{controller,collect}.py` and
`export/{style,sidebar_view}.py` serve only names they own. The one declared
re-export among them is `plot_style.follows_theme`, so a renderer takes its ink
and its "this is ink" marker from one import. A test may still patch a name one
of these modules imports *and calls*, since that patch is the one that reaches
the call. `tests/test_plotting_facades_are_frozen.py` holds all of it, and
`tests/test_lazy_targets_resolve.py` resolves every `lazy(...)` /
`_import_attr(...)` string target, which no import scan can see. The low-level pass that flattens each figure's x-tick labels to
the `x_tick_angle` preference lives in `core/plot_style._style_x_tick_angle`, one pass of `apply_export_style_prefs`;
it is the single chokepoint every plot tab routes through, so it **syncs
horizontal alignment with the applied angle** — `ha="center"` at 0°,
`ha="right"` at any non-zero angle.

**Per-panel axis limits.** The bar figure is a 3-panel stack (Value / Fraction
/ Events), so axis limits are stored and applied **per-panel** — read from each
panel's own prefs bucket (like the font sizes), not as a single flat `y_lim` —
so a limit set on the Fraction or Events panel sticks instead of that panel
auto-scaling.

**Plot colours are state, not a style pref.** The sidebar's *Colours* section
offers the Bar plot two modes — *Plate*, where each column takes the plate-picker
colour of the well or replicate group behind it so the plate doubles as the
legend, and *Grey*, where every column is one neutral ink (`theme.Colors.plot_mono`)
for a figure whose columns are already named on the axis. Like the *Statistics*
segments, the threshold-line overlay and the two time-axis correction steppers,
it does not go through `figure_prefs` / `_bind_getter_setter`: the colour is
chosen per column while the bars and violins are built, so the restyle pass that
walks finished artists cannot reach it. The segment writes
`PlotState.bar_color_mode` and calls `_redraw_bound_figure`, and the mode is
persisted with the rest of the bar view state (`_snapshot_bar` / `_apply_bar`).

The Bar figure also gets a **Bars** section (`_build_bars_section`, gated on
`_is_bar_fig`): a *Width* row — an **Auto** switch beside a stepper, so the
stepper never shows a number that is not the width being drawn — and a *Group
spacing* stepper. They write `PlotState.bar_width` (0.0 = automatic) and
`PlotState.bar_group_spacing` and redraw, for the colour mode's reason: bar
positions and widths are decided while the bars are built. `_resync_bar_geometry`
re-seeds them on every panel open from `_resync_plot_state_segments`, and both
are persisted in the bar view state (`_snapshot_bar`; `_apply_bar` →
`_restore_bar_geometry`, which drops an out-of-range value on its own).

The Line and Response figures carry the same control over their own fields
(`line_color_mode`, `response_color_mode`), and the Response segment's first
value is *Colour* rather than *Plate* — its curves are palette-coloured values
of a sample variable, never plate-coloured wells. Because the three tabs no
longer share a default, the panel records the default beside the field it built
the segment for (`_color_seg_default`) and the re-seed reads it there: one
hardcoded `"plate"` would move the Response segment, signals blocked, to a
value it does not offer, and then swallow the click that would correct it.

The section is figure-gated (`_is_bar_fig` / `_is_line_fig` / `_is_response_fig`,
beside `_is_heatmap_fig` and the scatter predicates) for the same reason the
Density and Cell values sections are gated: the mode changes nothing on a line, scatter or heat-map figure, and a
control that does nothing is the defect §7.6 of `CLAUDE.md` is about, wearing the
opposite face.

**Segments backed by `PlotState` are re-seeded on every panel open.** That family
has a hazard the pref-backed controls do not: the sidebar is built once per
figure and cached for the life of the process — it is only ever *hidden* on a tab
change — so each segment reads its state exactly once, while `view_state`
`_apply_bar` writes the same fields on every dataset load and `restore_defaults`
writes them again on a reset. *Error bars* and *Across* are covered already,
because the plot cards write `use_sem` / `use_fov_replicates` too and the two
were seen drifting, so both carry observers on `ctx.runtime.sem` /
`ctx.runtime.fov`. *Show* and *Bar colours* have no other UI writer and therefore
no observer, so `launch_export_editor` calls `_resync_plot_state_segments`
alongside `_refresh_line_order_lists` on every open. This is not cosmetic:
re-selecting the option a `SegmentedControl` already believes is current emits
nothing, so a segment left showing the previous dataset's mode makes the click
that would correct it a no-op until the user picks the other option first. The
re-seed blocks signals — the widget is catching up with the state, not a user
changing it — and moves the collapsed section's summary label with it.

Both surfaces that draw these panels honour the mode, and they reach it two
different ways. Three of the four draw paths resolve it themselves from their own
`ctx`: `draw_violin`, `draw_beeswarm` and `draw_per_well_n_bars`, each one line.
The fourth, the bar loop in `barplot/controller.render_bar_items`, cannot — the
Batch Export bar panel calls it with `ctx=None` on purpose, because it does not
want that function's other ctx-derived behaviour — so there the mode arrives as
an explicit `bar_color` argument that each caller states.

`tests/test_bar_render_callers_pass_color_mode.py` holds the mechanical half of
that, and both of its rules are about a check that looks like it is working and
is not. A call site must pass `bar_color=` **with a call to the resolver**, not
merely the keyword: `bar_color=None` satisfies a presence check and silently
reverts that surface to plate colours. A per-cell renderer must **bind** the
result (`colors = apply_bar_color_mode(...)`), not merely call it: the function
returns a new list and mutates nothing, so a bare expression statement is dead
code, and ruff does not flag it because a call is not an unused value. Both
shapes were found by dropping them into the tree and watching the whole suite
stay green. `tests/test_bar_color_mode_per_cell.py` is the behavioural half —
it drives the three per-cell renderers against a stubbed row-fetch and asserts
on the colours of the artists they actually produce, so the renderers are not
guarded by syntax alone.

**Every registered figure needs a key.** `figure_pref_key` falls back to
`f"fig:{id(fig)}"` for a figure it does not recognise, and that is a memory
address: stable within a session, different in the next, so prefs stored under it
are written to `persistence.json` and can never match again — the styling
silently does not come back, and the dead entry stays in the file, because
nothing prunes it and `figure_prefs` creates one on *read*. The fallback
therefore warns, `view_state` drops `fig:`-prefixed keys as it writes, and
`tests/test_figure_pref_keys.py` requires every `register("_*_fig", …)` call in
the tree to have a `_FIG_PREF_KEY_MAP` entry, no entry to name a figure nothing
registers, and no two figures to share a key.

### 5.9 Typed state, the event bus, and the DI context

Five pieces let controllers and tabs depend on typed seams instead of the loose
`ReviewApp` namespace: the typed **state** objects, the **event bus**, the
**widget registry**, the per-feature **runtime** namespaces, and the
**`ViewerContext`** that bundles them. The state modules — cross-cutting ones under
`review/core/` and per-feature ones under
`review/features/<feature>/state.py` — are **import-safe**: they
import only stdlib, numpy/pandas, the Qt-free domain models
(`domain/ratio_models`, `domain/selections_model`, `domain/batch_models`,
`data/data_loading`) and — for `core/event_bus.py` only — `PySide6.QtCore`.
None of them imports `runtime_app`, so any controller can import them with
no circular dependency. `tests/test_guardrails.py` enforces that boundary.

**Typed domain-state objects.** One `@dataclass` per behaviour domain, each
owning its own invariants (behaviour lives *in* the type, not just data):

| Object | Owned by | Lives in |
|--------|----------|----------|
| `ChannelState` | active channel / metric / ratio catalogue / threshold range — `set_active_channel` keeps `active_val_col` consistent | `core/channel_state.py` |
| `SelectionState` | plate selection + the saved-selections ("v2") model; composes `domain/selections_format.py`, the shared half | `core/selection_state.py` |
| `DatasetState` | data dir, well paths, the row cache (a `data/row_cache.RowCache`, bounded by a memory budget, so iterating it yields the wells held rather than the plate), `summaries` (a `data/well_summary.WellSummary` per opened well, which the timepoint / FOV lists are rebuilt from), `rows_version` (a monotonic tick over the row cache's *contents*, bumped through `note_rows_changed` by every path that changes what a cached frame holds — a projected verdict column, a gating rewrite, a curation override, a frame replaced after a write-back, and `begin_load`, because two plates can carry the same well tokens and the memos are keyed on the token; it ticks on change and never on a fresh insert, since bumping per well during a cold load would write each entry under a key the next well's load immediately invalidated), canonical timepoint / FOV lists, `pipeline_info`, and the crop: the rectangle (`crop_region`) plus the frames it filters (`crop_scope_wells` / `_fovs` / `_tps`, where `None` means *every* value of that field and an empty set means none). The scope is persisted with the region and cleared on a dataset swap — it names one plate's wells, and carrying it into the next either quietly filters nothing or filters the wrong thing | `core/dataset_state.py` |
| `PlotState` | SEM/SD, per-FOV, legend, draw order, fold-change normalization, the bar **significance-bracket** toggle (`show_significance`, N7), the Bar plot's **Bars** geometry (`bar_width`, 0.0 = automatic, and `bar_group_spacing`, read through `barplot.collect.bar_geometry_settings`), and the shared **focus timepoint** (`focus_timepoint`, N5 — the one cross-tab timepoint the Heat Map / Distribution combos read/write, synced via `core/timepoint_sync.py`), and the **time-axis label correction** (`time_scale`, 1.0 = off, and `time_offset`, 0.0 = off — see `core/plot_style.py` above, and read together through `time_rescale.rescale_for`), and the three plot **colour modes** (`bar_color_mode` and `line_color_mode`, each `"plate"` or `"grey"`, and `response_color_mode`, `"series"` or `"grey"` — resolved through `domain/bar_colors.py`, `domain/line_colors.py` and `domain/response_colors.py`. Three fields rather than one because grey means something different on each tab, and one shared field would have made picking a mode on any of them change all three; the Response default is not spelled `"plate"` because that figure's coloured mode is not a plate colour), and the **value-label overlay** (`show_value_labels`, off by default, and `value_label_format`, empty = a format chosen per value — see `core/plot_annotations.py` above), and what each significance bracket says (`significance_label_mode`, `"stars"` by default — see `domain/significance.py` above). Beside the dataclass, **`error_bar_settings(ctx)` is the one reading of the Properties → Statistics error controls** — `(err_kind, ci_scale, draw_err)` from `bar_err_kind` and `bar_show_mode` — with `spread_kind_label` for what a `±` drawn under it is called. It lives here rather than beside the bars because the panel is app-wide and offers **four** kinds while `use_sem` records two: a surface reading the boolean alone renders `ci95` as a plain SEM and `none` as a SEM too, so it draws a different interval from the bar beside it and labels it wrongly. `barplot/collect.bar_err_settings` is the Bar tab's name for it and holds no logic; the Heat Map's per-cell `±` asks it directly | `core/plot_state.py` |
| `StatsState` | Statistics-tab comparison groups + the structured **pairwise** results (`pairwise`, N7 — fed to the Bar plot's significance brackets). **The store is keyed by run context, not a single list.** `runs` maps `(val_col, target_t, stat)` to that configuration's records, so several comparisons coexist and each figure looks up its own; `pairwise` is a derived view of the most recent run, kept for the saved-plot capture and for callers that want exactly one. Those three fields are what decide whether a stored run describes the bars in front of you — the column they are drawn from, the timepoint they are drawn at, and which panel the statistic belongs on — so two runs differing only in statistic are a Mean comparison and a Fraction comparison of the same bars, and both are drawn. A record carrying a `val_col` but no `target_t` keys with `None` in the timepoint slot rather than becoming contextless: that is how older records behaved before the store existed (checked against the channel, not against the time), and treating them as matching anything drew a CY5 comparison over GFP bars. The timepoint half of the lookup goes through `domain.tp_match.tp_close` like every other timepoint comparison in the app, so a fractional timepoint that a combo rounded on its way through the widget still matches the run that was stored for it. `invalidate_stats_run` is now a documented no-op. With one stored run it had to clear — a comparison that no longer matched the tab's selectors was one nobody could account for, an empty results panel beside a plot still carrying its asterisks. Keyed, a run under GFP/t=24/mean stays a true comparison of GFP at t=24 however the tab's selectors move, and clearing would make the feature impossible: running a *second* comparison requires changing a selector, so a handler that emptied the store on every change would delete the first run on the way to the second. The results *text* still clears, which is `stats_on_test_change`'s job — that panel shows one run, and the run it shows is the one the current configuration produced. `stats_update_tp_menu` is the counterpart rule: it repopulates the Timepoint combo through `set_combo_values`, which blocks signals and keeps the user's selection when the new list still holds it, and falls back to the earliest entry only when it does not. An unconditional reset there ran on every channel switch and every arrival at the tab, silently moving the tested timepoint and leaving the next run's brackets gated out. The fallback deliberately does *not* suppress its change signal: when the previous timepoint is genuinely gone the tested timepoint really has moved, so letting `stats_on_test_change` clear the run is the right outcome. The group-statistics result cache lives in core (`AppState.stats_cache`), not here. | `features/stats/state.py` |
| `ReviewImageState` / `PreviewState` | Review-image view transform + caches; the armed drag-delete scope (`delete_scope_wells` / `_fovs` / `_tps`, where `None` means "the displayed one" and an empty set means "none" — the inverse of `ImageTableState`'s empty-means-all, and never persisted, so a wide scope cannot survive a restart or a dataset swap); preview image maps (`fluor` / `overlay` / `mask`) shared by the Segmentation review-image and Image Table | `features/image_browser/review_image/state.py` |
| `ImageViewState` | Cross-view image display shared by the image viewers. The per-channel display LUT (`lut_by_channel`), so a brightness tuned in Review Image is the default an *auto* Image Table row inherits (per-row edits override). The **Cell Browser** participates too: its `LUT ▾` popover edits the same `lut_by_channel` (blank = auto per crop), and a per-channel **display colour** (`tint_by_channel`, `get_tint`/`set_tint`) overrides the additive composite tint a channel is painted with (`worker.resolve_channel_tint` — override wins, else the fixed per-index palette) | `core/image_view_state.py` |
| `PlaygroundState` | Playground frame selection (dataset well/channel/timepoint/FOV **or** a loose image path) + chosen correction method/params, the reference-well fields keyed by well+channel+mode (`ref_fields`) and the builds that produced nothing (`ref_missing`), the live-StarDist thresholds and last label image with the key it was computed from, per-source LUT memory, frame-local binary threshold, QC size cleanup, and zoom/pan + caches | `features/image_browser/playground/state.py` |

`AppState` (`core/app_state.py`) is a plain aggregate of all of the above —
*not* a mega-dataclass with behaviour. `ReviewApp` builds one as
`self._app_state`. The cross-cutting state objects live in `core/`; each
feature's local state lives next to its controller / renderer in the same
feature package.

**`EventBus` (`core/event_bus.py`).** A `QObject` carrying a small, capped
catalogue of exactly four cross-cutting signals — `channel_changed`,
`selection_changed`, `dataset_loaded` and `plot_options_changed`. Signal
payloads are the relevant *state object*, never `app`. The catalogue and its
contract are documented in the module docstring. The bus is **load-bearing**:
every signal has a real emitter and a real subscriber.
`test_architecture_contracts.py` asserts the roster it may hold, and — the
other direction, which a frozen roster cannot give — that every name on it is
*mentioned* somewhere outside `event_bus.py` and outside the tests. That is a
substring scan, so it catches a signal nobody references at all (which is what
`redraw_requested` was) and cannot tell an emitter from a subscriber; the
emitter/subscriber pairing is held by the wiring documented below, not by the
scan. Subscribers are
constructed and connected by `bus_wiring.py`'s `wire_event_bus`, called once
from `ReviewApp.__init__`:

- `core/redraw_coordinator.py`'s `RedrawCoordinator` subscribes
  `channel_changed` and `plot_options_changed` (forwarded to the scope
  coalescer) and `dataset_loaded` (a full post-load `_redraw`).
- `SelectionRefreshCoordinator` (`core/selection_controller.py`) subscribes
  `selection_changed` and runs `apply_selection_refresh` — sidebar refresh
  plus a per-tab view refresh.

The emit *is* the trigger (no paired direct call alongside it). Two refreshes
deliberately stay off the bus: `_toggle_sem` (the SEM/SD toggle — its redraw
covers Distribution / Heat Map, which the coalescer does not) and the smFISH tab
resync after a dataset load (a tab-specific data resync, not a redraw). The
`tests/test_redraw_fanout.py` and `tests/test_selection_refresh.py` harnesses
pin these invariants.

**`WidgetRegistry` (`core/widget_registry.py`).** A name-keyed store for Qt
widget handles (figures, canvases, axes). `register("_line_fig", fig)`
stashes the handle by name *and* `setattr`s it onto the bound app, so
`app._line_fig` readers resolve via plain attribute lookup — no `__getattr__`
forwarder is needed, and the registry stays the canonical store. Its backing
dict is **shared with `AppRuntime`** (below), so a handle registered as
`_<feature>_<name>` is also reachable through `ctx.runtime.<feature>.<name>`.

**`AppRuntime` (`core/app_runtime.py`).** Per-feature namespaces for *live,
non-persisted* session objects that aren't typed state — worker bridges, decoded
image arrays, popup figures/canvases, transient toggle banks (SEM/FOV), and live
callback handles. `ctx.runtime.<feature>.<name>` reads/writes a plain
`name → object` **attribute-store** dict (keyed `_<feature>_<name>`) and holds
**no reference to the god-object** (A8 T6): the real app injects one store
*shared with `WidgetRegistry`* so the widget and runtime views resolve one
another's entries. These objects are never serialized — `persistence/` must not
import `app_runtime` (`tests/test_app_runtime.py`). (Legacy / pure-logic test
call sites that construct `AppRuntime(app)` get a back-compat `_AppAttrStore`
getattr/setattr view over that app instead of a standalone dict.)

The stamped-callback namespaces are also how two features notify each other
without either importing the other — the producer fires a **generically named**
slot and the consumer registers for it, so both stay one-line removable. The
`qc` namespace is the pattern at its cleanest: `qc.recompute_qc_all` fires
`ctx.runtime.qc.changed_cb` after rewriting `QC_Pass`, naming no listener; the
Cell Gating tab registers there to keep its inclusion readout current. Delete
either feature and the other degrades to a dead assignment or a `None` callback.
(A namespace's prefix is shared with the widget registry, so
`ctx.runtime.qc.gate_widgets` aliases the registered `_qc_gate_widgets` dict —
by design, not a collision.)

**`ViewerContext` (`viewer_context.py`).** A frozen dataclass — the single typed
handle tab builders and controllers receive **instead of** the `ReviewApp`
god-object. It bundles `state` (typed `AppState`), `bus` (`EventBus`), `widgets`
(`WidgetRegistry`), and `runtime` (`AppRuntime`), plus a handful of **held
collaborator objects** that own what used to be god-object methods: `ctx.persistence`
(the persistence registry), `ctx.features` (the feature registry), `ctx.notify`
(status-bar + toast notifications), `ctx.figures` (Save-As dialog + export-style
panel), and `ctx.coordinator` (the master redraw + sidebar-map refresh). **There is
no `app` field** (A8 teardown, T6 — the `ctx.app` reference count was driven 293 → 0
), and after the A5 teardown there is **exactly one** frozen
named accessor left onto the window shell: `ctx.window` (the god-object *qua*
`QMainWindow`, for dialog parenting / `isinstance` guards / `findChildren` walks).
Everything else features once reached as a `ctx.<verb>()` method — `set_status`,
`toast`, `save_figure_dialog`, `open_export_style_panel`, `rebuild_all`,
`refresh_sidebar_map` — is now a method **on one of the held collaborators above**
(e.g. `ctx.notify.set_status(...)`, `ctx.figures.save(...)`,
`ctx.coordinator.rebuild_all()`), so the window is no longer a behaviour dependency,
only a widget. That single remaining accessor is the *entire* intentional surface
between features and the window shell — never a generic `ctx.app` escape hatch and
never a `__getattr__` passthrough. `ReviewApp.__init__` builds `self._ctx` and
passes it to every tab builder and controller; feature code reads
`ctx.state.<domain>.<field>` / `ctx.bus` / `ctx.widgets` / `ctx.runtime`, the held
collaborators, and `ctx.window`, nothing else.

`tests/test_ctx_app_burndown.py` hard-bans any `ctx.app` (`CTX_APP_BUDGET = 0`);
`tests/test_ctx_service_accessors.py` freezes the accessor set (adding one is a
reviewed act); `tests/test_guardrails.py` holds `runtime_app.py` to ratcheting
line-count, `self._*` attribute-count and defensive-`getattr`-probe ceilings (it
can only ratchet down), plus the state-package import boundary above.

### 5.10 Split View (optional, one-line removable)

**What:** show two *different* top-level tabs side-by-side, both updating live
(selection / channel / plot-option / dataset changes refresh **both** panes).
Two instances of the *same* tab are out of scope (feature figures/state are
singletons). Entry is a top-bar **"Split view"** toggle (`columns-2` glyph) + a
right-pane dropdown; the left pane is whatever tab was active.

**Self-contained by design.** All active machinery lives in one module,
`core/split_view.py`, wired by a *single* call — `install_split_view(app)` in
`app_shell_view.build_ui`. **Comment out that one line and the feature is gone**
with no side effects: no toggle button is created, so `app._split_active` is
never set, the provider hooks below stay `None`, and every resolver collapses to
the ordinary single-tab behaviour. (Guard: `test_split_view.py::
test_not_installed_is_single_tab`.)

**How it works:**

- **Reparenting.** `enter_split(app, a, b)` force-builds both deferred bodies,
  then `NamedPageStack.detachPage`es the two top-level pages into
  `app._split_pane` (a hidden `QSplitter` sibling of `_notebook`, created by
  `install_split_view`) and hides the notebook. `exit_split` reverses it,
  restoring the original tab order via `reattachPage`.
- **Each pane carries its own sub-tab strip.** The page tab bars live in the
  shared band above the centre (§6a), which has one slot — and two pages are on
  screen. So `_wrap_pane` borrows each page's bar out of the band
  (`app_shell_view.lend_page_tab_bar`) and mounts it in a header directly above
  the pane it drives, and `_unwrap_pane` hands it back on exit
  (`return_page_tab_bar`). The band shows its blank page for the duration.
  A single shared strip could only ever name one of the two pages: the other
  page's sub-tabs were drawn nowhere, and were unreachable whenever its pane
  could not take focus (Home is cards and labels, none of them focusable), and
  splitting *from* a page with no sub-tabs of its own left both panes without a
  strip. The header keeps the band's `tab_bar_height()` whether or not the page
  has a bar, closed off by the standard hairline, so the two panes' content
  starts at the same y as it does in single-page view. The bar is *moved*, not
  copied — a mirrored `QTabBar` is wired to the `QTabWidget` it drives — so the
  panes hold containers (`ctx.runtime.split.pane_widgets`) wrapping the page
  bodies (`ctx.runtime.split.pane_bodies`), and it is the bodies that go back
  into the notebook on exit. Guard: `tests/test_split_view_pane_tabs.py`.
- **Provider hooks (the decoupling seam).** `tab_controller` exposes three
  module globals — `split_focus_provider`, `split_visible_provider`,
  `split_nav_intercept` — all `None` until `install_split_view` registers them.
  `current_centre_tab` returns the **focused** pane's leaf (so the sidebar +
  per-tab dispatch follow the last-clicked pane); `visible_centre_tabs` /
  `is_tab_visible` return **both** panes' leaves. The live-refresh chokepoints
  already key off these (`fold_change_scopes.visible_scope_names`,
  `selection_controller._visible_tabs`, the barplot/lineplot `_is_tab_visible`
  self-guards), which is why both panes stay live — and why, uninstalled, they
  fan out to exactly one tab. `selection_controller.rebuild_all` likewise guards
  **each** plot redraw (Bar / Line / Distribution / Heat Map / Scatter) behind
  `_is_tab_visible`: a group edit on Home → Sample Map → Replicates no longer
  tears down and redraws 3–5 off-screen figures — plus the from-scratch stats
  recompute that fed them — on every well click; an off-screen plot is re-rendered
  from current state by its `on_activate` hook the moment the user switches to it.
- **Focus + lifecycle.** A `_SplitFocusFilter` (installed on the QApplication on
  enter, removed on exit) makes a click in either pane the focused one. Focus
  drives the sidebar and the per-tab dispatch only — each pane draws its own
  sub-tabs, so neither page's strip depends on which pane is focused. It
  **defers** the actual focus switch with `QTimer.singleShot(0, …)`: `focus_split`
  reparents the panes and re-runs the visible-tab refresh, so doing it inside
  `MouseButtonPress` delivery (e.g. a click that lands while Image Table
  "Generate" is recompositing the focused pane) would mutate the widget tree
  mid-dispatch and crash — running it on the next event-loop turn lets the click
  finish first. Split auto-exits on a mode switch (connected to
  `app.modeChanged`), on rail navigation (`split_nav_intercept` in
  `_on_section_nav_changed`), and at the **start of a dataset load**
  (`load_controller.load_directory`) — the load restores view-state + redraws
  against the single-notebook layout, so leaving split first avoids driving
  detached pages (the reported open-dataset crash).

  It is also a **Review-only feature**: both panes it splits are Review tabs,
  but the top-bar toggle it lives in is shared across all three modes (Review,
  Analyze, Datasets mount into the same `ReviewApp` central-pane stack —
  see §6b). The same `modeChanged` handler that exits an active split also
  hides the toggle button (and its right-pane dropdown, if open) outside
  Review and shows it again on returning — previously it just sat in the
  Analyze/Datasets top bar with nothing for it to act on.

### 5.11 The Spatial feature

The **Spatial** tab (`review/features/spatial/`) is the Review-side
analysis of **per-cell physical positions in the well plane**. It's the
only feature that consumes the pipeline's always-on
`shape_centroid_row` / `shape_centroid_col` columns for anything analytical
(or, on a nanowell dataset, each cell's `well_x_um` / `well_y_um` — see below)
— the Multivariate tab treats those centroids as ordinary shape features
in z-scored feature space, not as physical coordinates. Spatial is a
one-file-per-role package that mirrors Multivariate (see §5.3 recipe): a
`SpatialState` slice, a Qt-free `collect.py` walker, a `controller.py`
that owns state mutation + the compute→render pipeline, a `renderer.py`
that draws the six MVP visualisations, and a `tab_view.py` builder. Its
per-tab controls live in the top-of-canvas rows; the only right-dock
occupant is the shared **Properties (Export-Style) panel** — the
`tab_view` pre-allocates the dock (`make_plot_with_right_dock`, registered
`_spatial_export_dock`) and a Properties button toggles
`ctx.figures.open_style_panel("spatial")`, so the Spatial figure now styles
identically to every other plotting tab (`render_spatial` re-applies the
export-style prefs at the end of each recompute so edits survive it).

**Which frame positions are in** (`spatial/collect.position_columns`). A nanowell
run's cell table states each cell's position in the well frame, `well_x_um` /
`well_y_um`, shared by every tile of the well; those win, and every payload
carries `unit="µm"`. Otherwise the segmentation's centroid in its field's pixels
(`unit="px"`), which places cells correctly only within one field — a nanowell
well's tiles overlap in pixel space, so reading its centroids put cells from
different tiles on top of one another. The renderer labels axes, nearest-neighbour
distances and Ripley's radius with the payload's unit (`renderer.in_unit`). A
nanowell cell table has a `timepoint` label and no `timepoint_hours`, so
`collect._hours`, the tab's timepoint list and the per-cell export
(`spatial/cell_scope_compute.cell_scope`: the same position columns as required
columns, `tp_fallback=True`, and its first-timepoint rule) all go through
`data_loading.resolved_timepoints`, the loader's one label-to-hours resolver.

**Multi-well faceting.** The per-frame levels (Cell / Colony /
Intra-colony) now draw **one panel per selected well** — a faceted grid
capped at 12 panels (with a note when the selection exceeds the cap) —
rather than collapsing the plate selection to a single sorted-first
"active well". `SpatialState` grows a `frames` list (one payload per well)
and a `frames_truncated` overflow count alongside the existing
`last_result` (still the home of the single Summary matrix); `reset_result`
clears them. The **Intra-colony** level now *always* colours the map by
normalised radial position `r/R`, so toggling Colony↔Intra-colony always
re-colours (Cell/Colony keep metric / colony-id colouring).

**Where the math lives.** All numeric algorithms sit in
`review/domain/spatial_compute.py` — Qt-free, matplotlib-free,
numpy + scipy only (`scipy.spatial.cKDTree` / `ConvexHull` /
`scipy.cluster.hierarchy` — no new third-party dep). The compute layer
returns small dataclasses (`RipleyResult`, `ColonyLabels`,
`ColonyStats`, `IntraColonyGeometry`, `RadialProfile`,
`VarianceDecomposition`) which the renderer consumes directly.
**Undefined is `NaN` here too**, on the same rule as `stats_compute`: a
one-cell radial bin has no spread and gets `NaN` like an empty one, and
`ripley_l` on fewer than two cells returns a `NaN` curve inside a `NaN`
envelope rather than the all-zero curve inside a zero-width envelope it used
to — which drew as a frame measured to be *perfectly* random with no
uncertainty at all, the strongest claim the function can make, from one cell.
The renderer follows: an empty boundary-or-interior partition is named on the
axis rather than substituted with `[0.0]` and drawn as a violin sitting on
zero with a mean marker on it. Colony detection's DBSCAN maintains its
frontier set as the cluster grows instead of rebuilding it per core point,
which is what made expansion quadratic in cluster size — on the GUI thread,
with no worker behind it: a synthetic confluent field of 16 000 cells took
3.57 s and now takes 1.06 s, with identical labels. That is held by counting
rather than by timing: `tests/test_hot_paths_stay_linear.py` patches the
module's own `set` name and asserts `_dbscan` builds exactly one frontier set
per call at 200 points and at 400, where the rebuild built one per core point
expanded. This is
the same split as `domain/multivariate_compute.py` and lets the pure-
Python pytest suite exercise every algorithm without a display.

**When it runs.** Everything is Review-side and on demand. Colony
detection is parameter-driven (method / ε / min-samples / boundary
percentile) so it can't be baked into the pipeline CSV — freezing the ε
would defeat the sweep the user is going to want to do. Per-cell
distance metrics are ~milliseconds via `cKDTree` even at ~10⁴
centroids, cheap enough to compute on tab activation. Ripley's L is a
visualisation choice (envelope size, radial grid), also Review-time. A
future pipeline hook for the deterministic-and-cheap
`spatial_nnd` / `spatial_knn_mean_d` / `spatial_local_density_k5`
columns is documented in the plan file but deliberately not shipped —
schema version bump not warranted yet.

**Scales of analysis.** Spatial classifies everything by **scale** —
sub-cellular, cell, colony, intra-colony — and the tab's Level
segmented control switches between three of them (sub-cellular is
served by the existing shape columns via the Metric picker rather than
a dedicated Level):

| Level | What each cell contributes | Vizs available |
|---|---|---|
| Cell | its centroid `(x, y)` in pixel space | Spatial map, NND histogram, Ripley L |
| Colony | membership in an auto-detected colony | Spatial map (colour by colony id), Colony size histogram, Per-colony distribution |
| Intra-colony | `d_centroid` / `d_edge` / `r/R` inside its colony | Spatial map (colour by r/R), Radial profile, Boundary vs Interior |

**Colony detection.** Colonies are computed, not manually annotated
(`spatial_compute.detect_colonies`). Two methods behind a Method
dropdown:

- **DBSCAN** (default). ε defaults to `eps_mult · median(NND)`, so the
  same multiplier gives roughly the same "grain" regardless of the
  well's density. Cells with fewer than `min_samples` neighbours in
  their ε-ball are marked noise (label `-1`, drawn grey on the map).
- **Single-linkage hierarchical**. Cut the dendrogram at ε; equivalent
  to DBSCAN with `min_samples=1`. Simpler mental model, but doesn't
  reject outliers.

Aggregates per colony are stacked in `ColonyStats`: cell count, convex-
hull area, packing density (`size / hull_area`), covariance-ellipse
eccentricity (`√(1 − λ_min / λ_max)` of the centroid covariance) and
orientation, and the mean centroid. `IntraColonyGeometry` adds per-cell
`d_centroid`, `d_edge` (min distance to the hull's edge segments —
positive for interior points), normalized `r/R`, and an `is_boundary`
flag (bottom-N-percentile of `d_edge` within each colony).

**Inter- vs intra-colony variance.** The Per-colony distribution viz
answers "how much of the signal's variability lives between colonies
vs inside each one?" by drawing one violin per colony (sorted by
median) and stamping the ANOVA-style variance decomposition on the
axes:

- `σ²_between = (1/N) Σ_c n_c · (μ_c − μ)²` — variance of colony
  means, weighted by colony size.
- `σ²_within = (1/N) Σ_c Σ_i (x_ci − μ_c)²` — pooled within-colony
  variance.
- `σ²_total = var(x)` — population variance; equals
  `σ²_between + σ²_within` by construction.
- `ICC = σ²_between / σ²_total` — the intraclass correlation
  coefficient. **1** means variability is almost entirely between
  colonies; **0** means colony identity carries no information about
  the signal.

Noise cells (label `-1`) and non-finite metric values are dropped from
the decomposition, so ICC always reports on the analysed population,
not the raw frame.

**How the compute + render pipeline fires.** The controller's single
entry point is `sp_recompute(ctx)`. Every setter (`sp_set_level`,
`sp_set_viz`, `sp_set_metric`, `sp_set_colony_eps_mult`, …) ends by
calling it. The pipeline:

1. Take the well set from `ctx.state.selection.selected_wells` (the
   per-frame levels now facet **every** selected well into `SpatialState.frames`,
   capped at 12; the Summary level still walks the whole selection into one
   matrix).
2. `collect_spatial_frame(ctx, well, …)` reads each well's DataFrame
   through `data_loading.get_rows` — not a cache-only lookup, because the
   row cache is bounded and a well missing from it may simply have been
   evicted — and returns `{points, metric, timepoint, well, n_cells}`. The
   Summary matrix reads its wells one at a time the same way, and the
   timepoint axis comes from every well through `plate_scan`.
3. Cell-level distance metrics (`nearest_neighbour_distance`) always
   compute — they're cheap and the Metric ▾ popover can gate them off.
4. Colony detection + colony stats + intra-colony geometry compute
   only when the current level *or* viz demands it (the
   Per-colony-distribution viz demands colonies even at Cell level).
5. Ripley's L, radial profiles, and the variance decomposition are
   viz-gated — they only run when the corresponding viz is active.
6. `render_spatial(ctx)` reads the cached payload off
   `SpatialState.last_result` and dispatches on `st.viz`. Every viz
   ends with `canvas.draw_idle()`.

The whole recompute stays under a few milliseconds on the ~1–10 k
centroids a single well/timepoint holds, so control changes repaint
live.

**How the tab satisfies the `ctx.app` burn-down ratchet.** The Spatial
package is the first Review feature written with **zero
`ctx.app` references** — every setter / lifecycle hook takes the
`ViewerContext` directly, widget handles resolve via `ctx.widgets`,
state via `ctx.state.feature_slice`, per-well DataFrames via the
dataset-state cache, and Copy/Save through the held collaborators
`ctx.notify.set_status` / `ctx.figures.save`. The registry
adapters in `features/registry.py` translate the legacy
`_activate_spatial(app)` / `_sel_spatial(app)` / `_channel_spatial(app)`
signatures into `sp_on_activate(app._ctx)` calls; that single
translation is the only place the two worlds meet.

**Tooltips are load-bearing.** Every control on the tab carries a hover
tooltip whose text mirrors the interpretation given in the README's
Spatial section — the module-level `_LEVEL_TOOLTIP`,
`_VIZ_TOOLTIPS`, and `_METHOD_TOOLTIPS` dictionaries in
`tab_view.py` are the single source of truth. `viz_cb.setItemData(idx,
tip, Qt.ToolTipRole)` puts a distinct tooltip on each dropdown option
so hovering `Per-colony distribution` explains the ICC without the
user having to open the docs.

**The Summary level and CSV export.** In addition to the per-frame Cell /
Colony / Intra-colony levels, the tab also exposes a **Summary** level
whose only viz — *Summary panel* — walks the *whole* well selection ×
every loaded timepoint and calls
`spatial_compute.summarise_frame(points, metric, colony_params)` on each
frame. Each call returns a `FrameSummary` dataclass of scalars: cell
count, colony count, median NND, median k-NN mean distance, median local
density, mean colony size, median hull area, median packing density, and
the between-vs-within ICC on the picked metric (`NaN` when no metric is
selected). `collect.collect_summary_matrix` stacks those into a
`(n_wells, n_timepoints)` object array; the renderer picks the chosen
`summary_metric_key` field and draws either a wells × timepoints imshow
heatmap or one line-per-well `matplotlib.pyplot.plot` — selectable via
the `summary_display` combo (`SUMMARY_DISPLAY_HEATMAP` /
`SUMMARY_DISPLAY_LINE`). Same colony-detection params as the per-frame
vizs, so the Summary matrix agrees with what the user sees when they
switch back to Cell / Colony / Intra-colony and scrub through
(well, tp) pairs. This is the only viz that consumes more than one
frame's worth of data.

**Summary CSV export** lives in the Save menu alongside Copy / Save figure and
is enabled only when Level = Summary. It calls
`controller.sp_export_summary_csv`, which flattens the matrix via
`collect.summary_matrix_to_csv_rows` — one dict per (well, timepoint)
with every `FrameSummary` field materialised as its own column — and
writes the result via a `QFileDialog.getSaveFileName` dialog. Output
format is *long*, not wide (row = one frame; columns include every
summary at once), so downstream pandas / Excel work isn't restricted
to whichever summary is currently plotted. `metric_col` (the ICC column
used at capture time) is echoed in every row so post-hoc filtering
can distinguish ICCs computed with different signals.

---

## 6. The Analyze side

### 6.1 `analyze/tab.py` / `analyze/form.py` / `analyze/log_pane.py`

The Qt form that builds the input panel (folder pickers, channel tokens,
top-hat radii, segmentation method, smFISH options, worker count) plus a
live-streaming log panel and a Run / Stop button. `AnalyzeTab` itself is a thin
host: it owns the runner, the queue drain (`_poll_log`), the run-state latch and
the signals a job queue binds to, and it mixes in the three modules that hold
everything else.

**The drain runs in bounded slices, and writes its lines in batches.** Both
because it is on the GUI thread and the queue is fed by a subprocess that can
talk faster than any painter. It used to loop until the queue reported empty —
which a remote run's segmentation phase does not do for minutes — and to write
each line through its own insert. The scroll bookkeeping around an insert reads
`verticalScrollBar().maximum()`, and on a `NoWrap` document that forces a full
re-layout, so a line's cost grew with the document under it: 3.4 ms into an
empty log, 19.1 ms at three thousand lines, 57 seconds for the batch. The
window answered nothing throughout, which is how the "Show raw log" checkbox
came to be unclickable exactly when there was most to read. `PipelineRunner`'s
`_LOG_QUEUE_MAXSIZE` had long anticipated the same failure in its own comment —
it caps the queue so "a stalled UI thread" cannot exhaust memory. A slice now
ends on `_POLL_BUDGET_S` or `_POLL_MAX_LINES` and re-arms immediately when work
remains, and `_log_lines` writes a slice's lines in one insert per colour run:
0.03 ms per line, flat. Terminal `done` / `error` lines flush the buffer first,
so a run's summary cannot land above the output it summarises. Each of the three files carries a line budget
(`test_monolith_budgets.py`).

The split follows the pane's three jobs. *Gathering* what a run is launched with
is `analyze.form.AnalyzeTabFormMixin`: anything that reads the form's
widgets lives with the widgets, so `_collect_run_options` and the well-field
validators are there, and the entry-boundary numeric validation is beside them
in `analyze/domain/fields.py` (`_numeric_option_errors` and the field tables it
reads). *Driving* the run is the tab plus `analyze.run_spec` / `analyze.suspend`.

**Every numeric field is collected as raw text, and coerced once, downstream.**
`_collect_run_options` puts the string the user typed into `opts` for every
number the form asks for — radii, FFT sizes, mesh parameters, worker counts, the
QC bounds, the minimum nucleus area, the Cellpose parameters and the two StarDist
detection thresholds — and `services.pipeline_service.build_pipeline_args` turns
them into argv. That ordering is the whole reason `_numeric_option_errors` can
see anything: a field coerced on its way *into* `opts` reaches the validator as a
number, and a validator handed a number cannot tell a typo from a deliberate
blank. `5oo` and an empty box both became `0.0`, and `0.0` for `qc_min_area`
means *no lower bound* — so debris removal removed nothing, the CSV carried every
speck, and `pipeline_info.json` recorded a value the user never chose. The
StarDist thresholds are the same shape one step along: `pipeline.stardist.parse_threshold`
answers `None` — "use the pretrained model's own threshold" — for anything it
cannot read, so `0,2` segmented at ~0.479 and the sidecar recorded the
model-default sentinel. `_numeric_option_errors` covers all of them, each behind
the control that reads it: the QC bounds only while *Remove debris* is on, the
Cellpose parameters only under the general-Cellpose routine, the thresholds only
under a StarDist one, because a value behind a control that is off cannot change
a run and refusing to start over it would be a refusal the user cannot see.
`analyze.domain.fields` restates `parse_threshold`'s rule rather than importing it —
`pipeline.stardist` pulls numpy, scipy and skimage into whatever imports it, and
the Analyze form keeps them out of its graph — and
`tests/test_stardist_threshold_rule_is_one_rule.py` holds the two rules together
over a corpus of typed values so the restatement cannot drift. *Showing what the run said*
is `analyze.log_pane.AnalyzeLogPaneMixin`, described below — the log view, the
raw-log toggle, the run-outcome surfacing and the idle "Last run ·" card. That
last mixin is inherited by `AnalyzeTab` directly rather than through the form
mixin, so the outcome path is not reached through the class named for form
building. Verbose inline helper paragraphs are collapsed behind hover `ⓘ` icons
(`_info_icon` / `_section(info=…)`).

The form's own chrome — `_section` (a collapsible titled section), `_row`,
`_entry`, `_info_icon`, and `reveal_section` — is `analyze.form_chrome.AnalyzeFormChromeMixin`,
inherited by `AnalyzeTabFormMixin`. `reveal_section(title)` unfolds a folded
section on demand: the fold-by-default rule is right for a user filling the form
in and wrong for a control something else just changed on their behalf, which
otherwise leaves no visible trace at all (see `_open_dataset_in_analyze`).

**A failed run says so where the user is looking.** The runner turns a non-zero
exit into an `("error", …)` event, and the log view that event's text lands in
is hidden at build — on its own that makes a pipeline which refused to start
indistinguishable from a run that was never clicked: progress stops, the Run
button returns, nothing states a reason. `_surface_run_failure` is the whole
outcome path, and it is in the log mixin because the pane it has to open is.

`set_failed` — the same dashboard failure state every Datasets tool uses —
takes the message's first sentence, capped, since the headline is a wrapping
label above the plate and a several-hundred-character refusal pushes the plate
off screen; the untruncated text goes to the same call's `tooltip=`, which is
`set_done`'s contract too. `PlateProgress.clear_outcome` drops both the tooltip
and the outcome colour, because neither belongs to the run that follows: a
tooltip nobody clears makes a hover over a *successful* plate report the
previous run's failure, and a colour nobody clears paints the next run's live
progress and its "Complete —" line in danger red. Every Datasets tool was
immune to the second of those by accident — each calls `set_done` on success,
whose green overwrites the red — so it is the base class's job, not the
callers'.

**Stop never waits on the GUI thread.** A remote run's `RemoteRunner.spawn` is
the whole staging, upload and launch, and `_spawn_tracked` runs it holding
`_proc_lock`; `stop` used to take that lock from the Stop button, so a Stop during
the upload froze the window until the upload ended — and, since `spawn` was not
given the stop event it accepts, the upload ran to the end and the pipeline was
launched only to be killed. `spawn` now gets `stop_event=_stop_requested`, which
`stop` sets first; while `_spawning` is true `stop` signals only the grouping
subprocess and returns, and `_spawn_tracked` signals whatever the spawn launched
if a Stop landed meanwhile. The interrupted upload's rsync failure is reported
through `_enqueue_stopped`, not as a failure. The host-side kill
(`RemoteRunner.cancel` — an ssh `kill`, then `scancel`) runs on a daemon thread
(`_signal_run`) rather than in the button's slot.
`tests/test_stop_never_waits_on_a_remote_upload.py`.

A **Stop or Suspend is not a failure**, and neither is a completion. A Stop
sends SIGTERM, which the pipeline answers by winding down (`pipeline.suspend`),
so it ends either by signal or — when the wind-down beats the SIGKILL five
seconds later — with exit 0. Both arrive as an `error` event: the runner reads
an exit of 0 with `_stop_requested` set as a stop (`_enqueue_stopped`), never as
`done`, so no success hook, "Processing Complete" or Review hand-off follows a
Stop, and a remote one keeps its remote output. A Suspend that winds down
cleanly exits 0 and is reported as its own `suspended` event (below); a remote
one keeps the configured cleanup, which fires only after the fetch is verified,
because the resume uploads only the missing groups and never re-attaches —
it reads the previous directory only for wells that were never downloaded,
and a verified fetch leaves none. While one
that dies by signal arrives as an `error` like a Stop. A Stop, Suspend or queue
Pause that lands while the input is still being grouped ends the grouping
subprocess, and the resolver (`AnalyzeInputMixin._input_failure_text`) words
the resulting failure as the stop it was — "Run suspended while the input was
being grouped", with the grouping step's own message kept in brackets — rather
than as "Input error". Either cancel takes the amber `set_cancelled` and neither opens a
pane the user had closed. For the `error` case, which of the three it was is
read from `PipelineRunner.cancel_state_at_failure`, a snapshot taken when the
failure is *queued*, not from the live `was_stopped` / `was_suspended`. The GUI
drains one timer tick later, and a Stop clicked inside that window would
otherwise turn a genuine failure amber and silent.

The raw log is **open by default** and the "Show raw log" toggle is there to put
it away. Several things are said in that pane and nowhere else — why a run
refused to start, the volume that filled, the `errors/` folder a partial run
points at, the scheduler's queue-wait breadcrumbs — and the app used to have to
override its own closed-by-default to show them, which is the tell that the
default was the wrong way round. The seven Datasets tool pages
(`datasets/core/log_panel.py`) still start theirs closed, deliberately: each
reports a short, bounded job whose dashboard is the whole story.

`force_raw_log_open` therefore covers the user who has closed the pane and then
hits a failure: it re-opens it, because the explanation is in there and they
have no reason to know it at the moment they need it. That tick changes a
setting the user chose, so it is recorded rather than kept:
`_set_running_ui_state` calls `restore_raw_log` at the start of the next run,
which puts the toggle back unless `_on_toggle_raw_log` saw the user work it
themselves in the meantime, in which case the choice is theirs and stands. A message that names a collapsible
section unfolds it, for the same reason `reveal_section` exists at all — naming
a remedy the user cannot see is the same dead end as naming none.

**The earliest error is the cause; everything after it is that cause's
fallout.** That is one rule with two enforcement points, and they must not
disagree, because the second is what the first reports. `_run_error` latches the
first `("error", …)` event of a run and `_surface_run_failure` is called only
for that one, so the dashboard headline and the message `runFinished` carries
are the same string. Inside a single event, `pipeline_runner.exit_message`
quotes the earliest `ERROR` line still in the runner's tail ring beside the
exit code, because "Pipeline exited with code 2" names nothing and for a run
refused before any work it is the only thing the user would otherwise be given.

"Earliest" is over the lines that can *be* a cause, which is not every line
`classify_log_line` scores ERROR. Two shapes are error-level and explain
nothing: the pipeline's own end-of-run summary ("N well(s) failed or produced
partial output — exiting non-zero…"), which restates the exit code and is
emitted *after* the per-well error that produced it, and a traceback's
`Traceback (most recent call last):` header, which scores ERROR on the word
"traceback". Both are dropped first. A traceback is then the one shape read
bottom-up — Python prints frames first and the exception last, and the
intervening `raise Foo(…)` source lines carry the exception's own name — so
inside one the *last* candidate is the reason. With nothing left after the
filter, quoting the summary still beats the bare code.

The `finished` branch gates `_refresh_last_run_summary` on the run having
succeeded: the card's only test is that `pipeline_info.json` exists, and the
pipeline writes that *before* any image work, so on a failure it would describe
a plate that was never produced.

The per-method segmentation parameters are their own mixin,
`analyze.seg_params.AnalyzeSegParamsMixin`: the `NamedPageStack` of
per-routine pages (StarDist / watershed / Cellpose / label-free / classical) plus
two rows that sit *below* the stack because more than one routine reads them:
the Cellpose cell diameter (both Cellpose routines) and the StarDist detection
thresholds (both StarDist routines). Each rides the stack's own
`currentChanged` for visibility, so no second hook in
`_refresh_segmentation_hints` is needed. The
hints and per-method validation (`_refresh_segmentation_hints` /
`_segmentation_validation_errors` / `_collapse_seg_param_stack`) live here too,
beside the panel they drive. Every widget still lands on the `AnalyzeTab`
instance under the attribute name it had when this lived in the form, so
`analyze.pinfo` and `_collect_run_options` reach them unchanged.

Restoring a prior run's settings is another mixin,
`analyze.pinfo.AnalyzePipelineInfoMixin` (`_open_pipeline_info` →
`_pinfo_flat` → `_apply_pipeline_info`), inherited by `AnalyzeTabFormMixin` so
those names stay reachable on the form where every caller expects them. Three
paths arrive there: the "Load previous run" action, the OME converter's
channel-role handoff, and Validate & Repair's "Complete this run in Analyze".
`_pinfo_flat` prefers the sidecar's `execution_options` (the full `vars(args)`
snapshot the pipeline records) and falls back to the top-level/`qc_options` keys
for older sidecars; `None`-valued keys are dropped so a sparse sidecar can't
clobber widget defaults with blanks.
It restores settings and never resumes: nothing here reads the run journal or
the suspend record, ticks Incremental or starts a run — resuming is the resume
banner's job (`analyze.suspend`). **A sidecar can describe another machine.** A
remote run's is written by the host from the host's argv and fetched home as
is, so its `input_dir`, `output_dir` and `scratch_dir` name the host's run
directory and its `no_run_check` is the one the remote runner adds to every
launch. `analyze.pinfo.recorded_elsewhere` recognises such a sidecar —
`suspend_file`, which only the remote runner passes, or a recorded `output_dir`
that is not the folder the file sits in — and the restore then takes the input
from the file's own location and leaves the scratch disk and the completeness
check as the form has them. Host `extra_args` baked into the argv cannot be told
apart from the user's own settings and are restored like any other.

The **Incremental — process only missing FOVs** checkbox in Output & Compute
carries `--incremental` into the run: each well's already-recorded
`(fov, timepoint)` pairs are read from the output folder and only the missing
ones are processed, then merged into the existing per-well CSV and
`<WELL>_out.zip`. Without it a well whose out-zip and CSV both exist is skipped
whole however few of its FOV-groups landed, which is why a crashed run cannot be
completed by pressing Run again — the checkbox is the run mode Validate &
Repair's completion handoff ticks on the way in, and the pipeline ignores it
when `--force` is also set. `select_incremental_scope` may still switch a run to
a full `--force` reprocess during input resolution (loose images landing under a
cross-well flat-field/background model), but it never clears a `True` the form
set: with nothing appended it returns before touching the key.

Rendering the run's progress is a third mixin, `analyze.progress.AnalyzeProgressMixin`:
`_apply_progress_event` turns each `ProgressTracker` event into dashboard state
(headline, overall bar, per-well plate colour, per-well FOV and transfer dials),
`_apply_grouping_event` does the same for the grouping phase's own four events
(`zipper_start` / `zipper_well` / `zipper_done` / `stage_total`), and the ETA cluster (`_update_eta` / `_render_eta` / `_stop_eta_timer`) projects a
deadline from the cumulative per-well rate and ticks it down at 1 Hz between
events. It answers to one rule: **what it draws must never overstate what the run
achieved.** A run that finishes with fewer wells than it announced gets a headline
naming the shortfall ("Complete — 28 of 40 well(s) processed; 12 never reported
completion"), a bar left short of full, and a warning line in the log; a well that
announces completion twice is reported rather than folded into the count.

Picking an input folder through the browse dialog also **auto-fills the schema
and channel fields** from what the folder's filenames look like:
`_browse_input` → `analyze.domain.input.AnalyzeInputMixin._autofill_from_input_scan`
briefly samples the names via `util.schema_infer.infer_from_dir`, which reads all
three grouped layouts — loose TIFs, the members of per-well zips, and the files
inside per-well `<WELL>/` folders — looking in both the selected folder and its
`in/`; it guesses the separator, slot layout, channel tokens and their roles (roles
via `util.channel_roles`, the same heuristic the OME converter uses), and applies
the guess through the existing `_apply_pipeline_info` path. It is best-effort and
editable — a folder whose names don't parse leaves the form as the user set it —
and only the interactive picker triggers it, so the converter's "Open in Analyze"
handoff keeps supplying its own channel roles instead of being re-guessed.

**A guess must be visible and must not destroy.** The fields it writes look no
different from hand-entered ones, so a wrong guess would otherwise first surface
in a sidecar after a run. Two surfaces say what happened, and they are told the
same thing: `_report_scan_guess` writes the run dashboard's status line, naming
the channels found, which of them took the segmentation and phase roles, and how
many sampled filenames will *not* match; and the picker itself carries a readout
directly beneath the control, which persists while the dashboard line scrolls
away. Both refusal paths report too — a scan that returned early used to leave
the previous scan's dashboard line standing, which was invisible while the
dashboard was the only surface and became an open contradiction once the picker
had a readout of its own.

A scan that recognised no channel slot contributes no channel keys
at all, and `_apply_pipeline_info` treats an absent `fluor_tokens` key as "leave
the rows alone" — the same rule its scalar setters follow. An empty list reaching
`_set_fluor_rows` reads as "no channels" and collapses the rows to the single
default one, which would wipe a hand-typed list.

**The user can ask again, and the two hosts judge the answer differently.**
`widgets.schema_picker.SchemaPicker` offers a **Detect from filenames** button
and the readout beneath it, both opt-in behind a `detect_label` argument — a
button that is always built is a button a host can forget to connect, and a
schema detector that does nothing when pressed looks exactly like one that found
nothing. The widget knows nothing about folders: it emits `detectRequested` and
displays sentences it is handed.

The Analyze host answers that signal by making the same `_autofill_from_input_scan`
call browsing makes, so the two cannot give different answers about one folder,
and it stays synchronous for the same reason the scan is bounded at
`_SAMPLE_LIMIT` names rather than walking. The Datasets pane's **Zip Loose
Folder** page shares the control and reaches its own verdict through
`datasets.import_loose.import_loose_compute.detection_for_grouping`, which tests
the pair that page's own `_can_run` requires — `util.schema.PIPELINE_REQUIRED_FIELDS`,
`("channel", "well")`. It reads as though it should be looser, since grouping
only ever places a file by its well, and the first version of it was: it accepted
a channel-less guess on the reasoning that grouping needs nothing else. That
turned a working page into a dead one on a single press, because
`SchemaPicker.errors()` rejects such a schema and `_can_run` blocks on it — and
the comment beside that check already said why, six lines from the contradiction:
*"a schema with no 'channel' produces archives Analyze cannot then read, which is
the only reason to build them."* The verdict differs from Analyze's only in what
it says, not in what it accepts.

**The readout has two registers, because its two halves carry different weight.**
`InferredSchema.summary()` is the neutral statement — what was detected, the
separator, and how many of the sampled names matched. `InferredSchema.shortfall()`
is the statement about the user's *data*: which sampled names do not fit the
layout, and why. It claims a **consequence** only for the well position, which is
the only one that has one — grouping places a file by its well token, so a name
whose well is not a well lands in no archive. The pipeline applies no predicate
to the timepoint or FOV slots at all (`_collect_available_schema_values` reads
them positionally, unvalidated; the only per-file test `_is_nuclear_filename`
makes is on the channel slot), so announcing those names as lost would send
someone off to rename files that process fine. The count carries the *sampled*
qualifier for the same reason `summary()` does: the scan reads at most
`_SAMPLE_LIMIT` names by stride, so on any plate larger than that an unqualified
count is wrong by the sampling ratio, in the register styled so it cannot be
skimmed. The picker shows the first
as muted body text and the second as a `QLabel#Notice` panel (§8), so the two
differ in outline rather than only in hue. A name counts as matched when it
splits into the right number of positions **and** every slot the guess claimed
accepts its token — checked with the predicate that claimed the slot, carried out
of `_classify_slots`, never looked up from the field name. The bare-number FOV
pass claims a slot `_is_fov` itself rejects, so a name-keyed check would report
nothing matched on a plate that is entirely well-formed.

**Slots are classified strictest-predicate-first, and ties go leftmost.**
`t<n>` and `f<n>` can only be what they look like; a 96-well label cannot, because
`f01`–`f12` *are* valid well labels (row F). So the timepoint slot is claimed
first, then the FOV slot, and only then the well slot — asking the well predicate
first let the FOV column answer a question it is not entitled to answer, and on
the default `experiment:channel:well:fov:timepoint` layout both columns scored a
perfect 1.0, the tie went to the rightmost, and every image in the plate was
attributed to well `F01`. A slot of bare integers is deliberately **not** claimed as anything: the same
evidence supports a field number, a timepoint index and a site number equally, and
the module's contract is to leave what it cannot identify as `ignore` rather than
pre-fill the Analyze form with a confident wrong guess — the module already
refuses to read a bare integer as a *timepoint* for that reason, and reading one
as an FOV on identical evidence would contradict it.

The sample the guess is built from is **strided, not a leading slice**
(`schema_infer._spread`). Plates are routinely written with one slot varying
slowest — channel-first filenames, or a per-well archive holding all of one
channel's fields before the next — so the first few hundred names of a sorted
listing can hold a single channel token. A slot with one distinct value is not
recognised as the channel slot at all, so a prefix sample reports *no* channels
on exactly the largest plates.
