The optional sections fold by default; **Auto-threshold** is one of them, and it
owns every threshold-related control: a checkbox driving the pipeline's
`--no_auto_threshold` (which previously had no UI), a **Method** combo choosing
between Otsu and the control-well optimizer, and the two well fields that feed
`--pos_control_well` / `--neg_control_well`.

The method is an explicit selection rather than being inferred from whether the
well fields are filled, so switching back to Otsu does not mean clearing the
wells and losing them — the fields hide but keep their text, and
`build_pipeline_args` emits the flags only under the control method, so dormant
text cannot silently override the choice. On the pipeline side there is no
method flag: naming both wells *is* the method, which is also how
`_apply_pipeline_info` infers the combo back from a sidecar.

Under the control method the pair is validated together — both wells, each a
valid 96-well position, distinct, and present in the input folder — by
`_auto_threshold_validation_error`, which blocks the run the same way the
background-well check does. Under Otsu it does not read the fields at all.

Both presence checks go through `input_resolution_service.well_present_in_input`,
which accepts any of the pipeline's input layouts (per-well `<WELL>.zip`,
per-well `<WELL>/` folder, or loose TIFs parsed via the schema's `well` field).
The form validates the *selected* folder, but a folder holding an `in/`
subfolder — the ordinary `<dataset>/in` + `<dataset>/out` layout — feeds the
pipeline from that `in/`, not the parent (see `resolve_input_output`). The
grouped-layout lookup therefore searches both the selected dir and its `in/`, so
a well packaged as `in/<WELL>.zip` / `in/<WELL>/` is not reported missing when it
lives one level down.

**One layout decision, rendered twice.** Analyze asks "what will this folder do?"
under the input field the moment a folder is picked, and again when Run is
pressed. `services.input_resolution_service.plan_input_layout` is that decision,
and it is pure: it reads the filesystem and returns an `InputPlan` naming the
action, the `(input_dir, output_dir)` pair the pipeline will be handed, and the
one-line message the user sees. `AnalyzeTab._refresh_output` displays the plan;
`resolve_input_output` executes it. The GUI holds no layout rules of its own,
which `tests/test_layout_readout_single_source.py` enforces by requiring the
readout label to be written from a value rather than from a hand-composed
sentence.

**One decision is not enough if the numbers in it come from somewhere else.**
The fold-loose message names a count, and that count used to be a glob over TIF
suffixes while the *act* goes through `plan_loose_append`, which rejects a name
whose well token will not parse and a file already present in its target
archive. On a folder holding one new image, one duplicate and one calibration
frame the readout said "Will fold 3 loose TIF(s)" and the run folded one. Given
the form's `filename_schema` / `filename_sep`, `plan_input_layout` asks that same
planner, so preview and run cannot disagree; without them it falls back to the
file count and says nothing it cannot support. `resolve_input_output` passes
them too — it holds both in its own signature, and omitting them made the *run*
recompute a schema-less plan and log the glob count, which reproduced the
original defect on the log line instead of the readout. A folder whose loose files are
*all* duplicates is reported as `grouped` with the reason, rather than as a fold
of nothing.

`tif_files_in` is the other half of that, and it asks `is_run_input_member`
rather than matching a suffix, because a suffix is not a decision about whether
a file is one of the run's images. The glob it was built on matched
`._<name>.tif`, the
AppleDouble fork macOS writes beside every file copied to a non-HFS volume — so
a real plate arrived with exactly twice as many "TIFs" as images — and it read
`.tif`/`.tiff` only, so a PNG plate looked like a folder holding nothing, and it
did not ask `is_file()`, so a dangling symlink counted as an image the zipper
would then skip as unreadable while the deletion pass unlinked it. That count
feeds the readout, the `tifs > 3` threshold selecting `zip_root`,
`count_expected_wells`' fallback, and the `source_tifs` tuples the post-run
deletion closures are built from: a predicate applied to files it is not
entitled to judge, in the place that decides what gets deleted.

The `tifs > 3` threshold moves in both directions as a result, and neither is
hypothetical. A folder of three real images beside their three sidecars used to
count six and clear it and now counts three and does not, so a very small plate
copied to a non-HFS volume reports "No TIF files or in/ folder found" where it
previously ran; a folder of PNGs used to count zero and now counts them all, so
a plate that could not be grouped at all now can. The `> 3` cliff itself
predates both.

**The decision costs one directory listing, not one metadata call per file.**
Picking a folder answers three questions of it — is this a packed OME-TIFF,
what layout is it, and what filename schema do its names follow — and the
obvious spelling of each, a listing plus `Path.is_file()` per entry, is also one
`os.stat` per file. On macOS and Linux that is a single cheap syscall answered
from the kernel's name cache and is invisible. On Windows it is not: CPython
implements `os.stat` there by opening a handle to the file
(`CreateFileW` → `GetFileInformationByHandle` → `CloseHandle`), because
`GetFileAttributesW` does not traverse symlinks the way POSIX `stat` does. On a
mapped network share, a VPN-ed mount or a cloud-sync root every one of those is
a round trip on the wire, and a filter driver may inspect it on the way past. A
plate of 5,800 loose images cost about 17,000 of them, and picking the folder
sat for twenty minutes at under one percent CPU and a trickle of network
traffic — the shape of a freeze in which nothing is computing anything.

`util/dir_scan.py` is the answer, and on every platform it is a strict
improvement rather than a trade: `os.scandir` carries the entry type with the
listing, so `DirEntry.is_file()` answers from data the enumeration already paid
for. Everything that classifies the entries of an input folder goes through it —
`tif_files_in`, `has_well_zip`, `has_well_content`, `iter_well_tokens`, the
zipper's consolidation passes, and `util.schema_infer`'s sampling of the three
grouped layouts. The symlink semantics are `pathlib`'s, deliberately: a link to
a file is a file, and a dangling link is neither, which is the rule `tif_files_in`
depends on. What it gives up is that the answer describes the directory as it
was listed rather than as it is now, so a file deleted in between is still
reported; closing that window means spending the stat the module exists to
avoid, and every call site already copes with a path that has gone by the time
it is opened.

Reducing the per-file cost to nothing leaves the number of *listings* as the
thing worth counting, and there was one per question. `_plan_grouped_root` reads
the folder once and answers four from that listing: the loose-image count
(`input_images_among`), whether any well archives are present
(`_well_zip_among`), whether any well *folders* are (`_has_well_content_in`),
and the fold plan, which takes the listing as `plan_loose_append`'s optional
`loose_files`. Every layout the pane meets — loose images, zip-grouped,
folder-grouped — therefore lists the input folder exactly once. Stating each
rule once is what makes that safe: two listings of one directory can disagree
about a file written between them, and two spellings of one predicate always
eventually do.

`dir_has_entries` is the deliberate exception and keeps its own listing. It asks
whether the folder holds an entry of *any* kind, which includes the ones a
file/folder split drops because they are neither — a dangling symlink, a socket
— so answering it from that split would turn a folder holding only such an entry
from usable-but-unrecognised into empty. It short-circuits on the first entry,
and it is reached only when the folder has no images, no archives and no well
folders in it.

**A well archive is a file.** `has_well_zip`, `has_well_content` and
`_well_in_grouped_root` all say so, through `_well_zip_among`. A directory called
`A01.zip` — what an expander names an archive it has unpacked in place — used to
answer yes to all three, and each had its own consequence: the fold-loose path,
where opening it as an archive fails, the failure reads as "the archive holds
nothing", and every loose image beside it is reported as new; a `GROUPED` verdict
on a folder holding nothing the pipeline can read; and, worst, a pass from the
pre-run guard that exists to refuse a run whose named background well is not in
the input, so the run started and the correction was never built.

**A folder that cannot be listed is its own answer.** `Path.glob` returns an
empty list for a directory it may traverse but not read — a share whose ACL
grants execute and not read, a mount that has gone stale — so such a folder was
reported as `EMPTY_IN`, *"nothing to process"*: a statement about the plate made
from a failure to look at it. `os.scandir` raises instead, and `plan_input_layout`
turns that into an `UNREADABLE` plan naming the folder and the errno. It is not
in `RUNNABLE_ACTIONS`, and `_layout_error` gives the long form. Letting the
`OSError` out would have been no better than the empty list: the readout is
computed from a `textChanged` slot, where an exception leaves the path field
showing the new folder and every label beside it describing the previous one.

The Analyze pane spends that listing once per pick rather than twice.
`AnalyzeTab._browse_input` changes two things the readout depends on — the path,
which `textChanged` reports, and the filename schema
`_autofill_from_input_scan` infers from the folder — so the readout was computed
first against the new path and the *previous* folder's schema, and then again
once the inferred schema was applied. `_suspend_output_refresh` holds the
intermediate one and a single recomputation runs at the end, from the path and
the schema together. Releasing it in a `finally` is load-bearing: a folder whose
names do not parse leaves `_autofill_from_input_scan` early, and without the
release the readout would go on describing the folder picked before it.
`tests/test_input_scan_costs_no_stat_per_file.py` pins all of this by counting —
the same folder holding four times as many images must cost the same number of
metadata calls, and the layout plan must be computed exactly once, with the
schema the scan inferred. Its plate is written in a layout that is deliberately
*not* the form's default, because a fixture in the default layout makes the
second half of that true of a scan which applied nothing; and it proves its own
counter live first, since a test that patched the wrong function would report
zero against zero and pass. `tests/test_dir_scan.py` counts the other end: one
listing and *zero* stats for a folder of files and sub-folders, which is the
assertion an implementation that enumerated once and then stat-ed each entry
would fail.

The scan applies what it infers, under the rule
`services.run_detect.scan_pipeline_info` states once for both of its users —
this button and the run-time detection a queued job can ask for (below): the
schema and separator only from a *confident* guess, the channel roles only when
channels were found. `_autofill_from_input_scan` hands
`_apply_pipeline_info` a **sidecar-shaped** dict — `schema`, `separator`, and
the channel keys `ChannelTokens.as_pipeline_info` produces — because that is
what `_pinfo_flat` reads. Spelled with the flattened argparse names
(`filename_schema`, `filename_sep`) the two schema keys were the only ones in
the dict that function does not know, so they were dropped on the way in: the
channel roles landed, the status line announced them, and the form silently kept
its default schema, which a plate in any other layout then carried into a run
the user was never prompted to correct.

The same rule reaches the remote runner, because the same plate does.
`_detect_local_input_mode` runs at the start of every remote run and *before*
the mode is known, so on a FLAT plate — a folder of loose images — it looks at
the whole plate; `_unconsumed_loose_tifs` and `_stage_mixed_mode` walk it again
straight after, and `stage_local_zips` walks it twice more, once to find the
well folders it will zip and once for the folders the zipper has left behind.
Every one of them takes the entry type from the listing, so the cost of starting
a run stops growing with the number of images in the plate.

The staging pair is the one this branch first missed, and the shape of the miss
is worth keeping: `folders_after_zipper` was spelled identically to the
`_stage_mixed_mode` site three lines above it and was left asking `p.is_dir()`
per entry — which on a copy-mode run, the default, means one stat per loose TIF
still sitting in the input folder. Measured at 45 stats for 40 images and 180
for 160, i.e. the linear growth this whole section exists to remove, inside a
function nothing counted. `tests/test_remote_input_scan_cost.py` now counts
`stage_local_zips` as well as the detector, because a sweep is only as complete
as the sites something measures; it counts the same way the Analyze test does,
and pairs each count with a test that every layout is still *detected* and
still *staged* — a mode detector that answered FLAT unconditionally would
satisfy the count alone.

The actions are the layouts. A folder **named** `in` is the input directly
(output `../out`); a folder that **contains** `in/` feeds the pipeline from that
subfolder (output `<selected>/out`). Either way the same classification runs on
the grouped folder: loose TIFs beside well zips are folded into those zips
(`fold_loose`), loose TIFs on their own are grouped into per-well folders in
place (`group_loose`), per-well zips or per-well folders are used as they stand
(`grouped`), and a folder holding something else entirely is still handed to the
pipeline (`unrecognised`) with the readout saying what was not recognised —
`in/Plate1_A1.zip`, or a timepoint level between `in/` and the wells, is input
this module cannot name wells for but the pipeline is what reads it. More than
three loose TIFs at the *selected* root outrank an `in/` with nothing usable in
it (`zip_root`), because that is a fresh drop beside a folder an interrupted run
left behind, and it still has to reach `well_plate_zipper`. What remains is
unrunnable and says which: an `in/` that exists and is empty (`empty_in`), a
packed OME-TIFF (`packed_ome`, redirected to the Datasets converter), a path
that is not a directory, or nothing usable at all.

Both selections reaching the same verdict is the point of classifying them
together. `count_expected_wells` takes its grouped root from the same plan, so
the dashboard's denominator counts the folder the run will actually read; it
stays best-effort by design, falling back to the loose-TIF count and then to 1,
because a progress denominator cannot be zero — saying there is no input is
`resolve_input_output`'s job, not the dial's.

**And because that plan names the output directory without writing anything,
everything an earlier run left there can be reported before this one starts.**
`analyze.preflight.AnalyzePreflightMixin` is that report — a mixin for the same
reason `analyze.suspend` and `analyze.progress` are, since `analyze/tab.py` sits
against its line budget. `_refresh_output` hands it the `InputPlan`, and it
reports in two tiers split by what each costs. Tier one is the run journal
(§6.5) — one small JSON read — plus the scope line's `iterdir` of the input
directory and, when loose images are sitting in it, a central-directory read of
every well archive they belong to — the duplicate rule needs to know what each
already holds — with a second pass over those archives when a background or
flat-field method is set to `empty_well`: bounded by the plate's top level rather than a walk
of it, which is what lets it run inline once the field settles. It
says what the last run against this folder did, and whether it *finished* — a
journal still open is a run the app was killed during, which nothing else on
disk records. Tier two runs `completeness.scan_run` on a
worker thread and states real coverage, the same predicate the end-of-run check
and Validate use, because a preview computing its own idea of coverage is a
preview that can contradict the run it describes. The input field's
`textChanged` fires per keystroke and each scan opens every archive in the
plate, so the scan is debounced behind a single-shot timer, its result returns
on a queued signal (a worker thread has no event loop, so a `singleShot` armed
there never fires), and a result that lands after the user has typed on is
discarded rather than shown against the wrong folder.

Two rules shape what it is allowed to say. **It offers; it does not apply.** The
settings behind the existing output are restored only when the user presses
*Load these settings*, through the same `_apply_pipeline_info` the manual **Open
pipeline_info.json** path uses — the journal's `RunSpec` when there is one, the
sidecar otherwise, so it works on datasets that predate the journal. The
run-scope knobs (`force`, `force_wells`, `incremental`, `only_wells`) are never
restored: they say what the *last* run was told to do, and silently re-forcing a
plate because the previous run was forced — or narrowing the next run to the
previous run's subset — is the most expensive kind of surprise.
`_apply_pipeline_info` does not restore `only_wells` from any source either
(`analyze/pinfo.py`), and does not clear the field: loading settings leaves the
scope fields as the user had them. **And it
reports; it does not decide.** Every *claim* in the readout comes back verbatim
from whatever owns it — `ScopePlan.preview` for what the run will do about
images added since last time, `completeness`'s own counts for coverage, the
journal's recorded per-well states for what happened last time — and the pane
supplies only the connective prose between them. That is deliberately weaker
than `test_layout_readout_single_source.py`'s rule over the layout line beside
it, which requires the label to *be* a quoted planner value: that suits a
one-sentence readout, not a paragraph drawn from four sources.
`test_analyze_preflight.py::test_the_scope_line_is_the_planners_own_sentence`
guards the piece that could drift, the scope line, by pinning it to the
planner's own words. A coverage comparison that comes back incoherent (more
field groups covered than the input was measured to hold, which means the
filename schema is not parsing both sides the same way) is reported as such
rather than printed as a ratio over 1.

The report is built to the same stacked shape as the resume strip above it
(§6.5), and for a sharper version of the same reason: its buttons are the wider
pair, so *Load these settings* and *Dismiss* beside the text left the report
**74 px** of the sidebar's 319-px viewport to wrap three sentences into — 224 px
of text two words wide. The two strips share a
holder — the form's own layout runs at zero spacing, and two bordered cards
stacked flush read as one box with a line through it — which takes no margins of
its own, so the cards run the full width of the sidebar and their text sits on
the same 12-px left edge as every section body beneath them, and so that a
holder whose children are both hidden, the normal state, contributes no height
at all.

**It says nothing the card above it has already said.** The resume offer and
this report are built from the same journal, so with an unfinished run on the
folder in the form both used to lead with the same fact and both appended the
journal's own `tally()` — the identical sentence, in two bordered cards stacked
one above the other. While the offer is up for *this* folder
(`_resume_card_covers`, keyed on the folder rather than on the card merely
being visible, since with no folder on the form the offer falls back to the
newest unfinished run on any plate) the report drops its own account of the run
and keeps what only it knows: the coverage line and the scope line. The
decision is made at paint time from the offer's live state and the unsuppressed
sentence is what is stored, because the card can come down with the folder
unchanged — a Discard, a Resume — and the report is then the only surface left
that can say what the last run did; `analyze.suspend._note_resume_card` calls
`resume_card_changed` so that repaint happens, and that repaint is skipped
unless the answer has actually flipped, since it runs `_scope_line` and that
reads the input directory. A report left with its sentence suppressed and no
coverage line yet is *hidden* rather than shown as a bordered strip holding two
buttons and no words; it comes up when the scan lands.
`tests/test_the_two_cards_do_not_say_the_same_thing.py` holds both halves.

The report is refreshed on every change to the input field, once at construction,
and again when a run settles (`resync_preflight`, from `_on_run_settled`) —
hidden for the duration of the run in between. Without that last refresh it would
only ever be computed from `textChanged`, which after a run never fires, so the
sidebar would go on describing the run *before* the one that just ended: on a
failure, reporting the previous run as completed. Its coverage line and any
dismissal are dropped at the same moment, since both described the folder as it
stood before this run rewrote it.

That scope sentence is possible because `select_incremental_scope` is now
plan-then-act like the rest of this module: `plan_loose_append` decides which
loose images would be folded in and `plan_incremental_scope` reaches the verdict,
both reading only; `select_incremental_scope` performs the append and asks the
same `_scope_verdict` for its answer. One rule, two callers, so the preview
cannot describe a decision the run does not make.

The Run path:

1. Validate the form.
2. Call `services.pipeline_service.find_pipeline_script()` to locate
   `process_microscopy.py` (or the frozen-bundle launcher).
3. Call `services.pipeline_service.build_pipeline_args(pipeline, input_dir,
   output_dir, opts)` to assemble argv.
4. `services.pipeline_service.spawn_pipeline(args)` returns a
   `subprocess.Popen` running the pipeline in its own process group / session
   so Stop can signal the entire tree.
5. The Analyze tab streams stdout/stderr into its log view (`tail -f`-style).
6. On completion, the dataset folder is offered to the Review tab.

**Collecting a run's configuration is split from starting it**, in
`analyze/run_spec.py`'s `AnalyzeInputMixin`-style mixin `AnalyzeRunMixin`
(mixed into `AnalyzeTab` alongside `AnalyzeInputMixin`/`AnalyzeTabFormMixin`).
`_collect_run_spec()` turns the live form into a `services.run_spec.RunSpec` —
a frozen, JSON-round-trippable dataclass (`opts`, the chosen remote's *name*
rather than its resolved `RemoteHost`, cleanup/dry-run flags, output filter,
selective-channels flag). `start_run(spec)` launches a `RunSpec` on the tab's
own `PipelineRunner`, re-resolving the remote by name through
`services.remote_config.get_remote` at call time (so a `remotes.toml` edited
between collection and launch is honoured, and a deleted remote fails the run
with a clear message via `RunSpecError` rather than silently running locally)
and re-resolving the pipeline script fresh rather than trusting a stored path
(which would break across a relaunch from a different install location).
`start_run` never raises and never shows a dialog — it returns an error
string, so it stays callable with no form on screen; `_run()` itself is a
three-line delegation (`_collect_run_spec()` → `start_run()` → show a dialog
on failure). This split exists so the Job Queue (§6b) can persist a run's
configuration as plain JSON and start it later, independent of whatever the
live form happens to hold at that moment. The queue's own "+ Queue" entry
point on this page is built here too. The whole run-controls row —
Run / Suspend / + Queue / Stop — is `_build_run_row`, called by
`analyze/form.py` in one line, both because that file is at its line
budget (moving the row out lowered it) and because the queue button belongs
beside the queue hooks. Its layout is a `widgets/flow_layout.FlowLayout`, not
a `QHBoxLayout`: the four buttons want 398px and the panel is `rail_w` (329)
wide and *fixed*, so a box layout cannot fit them and simply compresses the
labels. FlowLayout also watches its children for show/hide, which this row
needs — "+ Queue" appears only once `DatasetsTab` injects a sink via
`set_queue_sink` (which is how the run reaches the queue without this module
importing it), and the row has to re-wrap when it does. An unset sink hides
the button, which is what a build without the Datasets pane gets.

`analyze/domain/job_edit.py`'s `AnalyzeJobEditMixin` (mixed into `AnalyzeRunMixin`,
since it is part of the same queue-facing surface) supplies `hydrate_job`:
the **full inverse** of `collect_spec`, used only by the queue's edit flow.
`show_job` is not that inverse and is not meant to be — it sets the input
folder and nothing else, because a preview only has to make the page *look*
like the job while the queue re-derives a real `RunSpec` from the persisted
JSON at dequeue time. Collecting a previewed page back over a stored spec
would replace every option the preview did not write, in a spec the user
believes they edited one field of, so the two paths stay separate.

Most of the restore is `AnalyzePipelineInfoMixin._apply_pipeline_info`, whose
`execution_options` branch already takes argparse-style keys — and a job's
`spec["opts"]` is argparse-style, being what `build_pipeline_args` consumes.
It is not identical, though, and every difference is a silently wrong value
rather than a crash: `raw` here is the sidecar's `input_dir`;
`auto_threshold` is positive here and recorded as its negative
`no_auto_threshold` there; `auto_threshold_method` is explicit in a spec but
*inferred* from whether both control wells are named when restoring a
sidecar, which is wrong for an Otsu run carrying dormant control wells; the
two StarDist thresholds are raw text where blank means "the model's own
default", while `_restore_stardist_thresholds` skips anything it cannot read
as a float and would leave the previous job's number in the field; and
`remote_batch_size` has no sidecar equivalent at all. `RunSpec`'s
`remote_name`, `cleanup_remote` and `dry_run_cleanup` live beside `opts`
rather than inside it and no sidecar restore touches them.
`tests/test_analyze_job_edit.py` is the guard — a `collect` → `hydrate` →
`collect` round trip over a spec whose every value differs from the form's
default (asserted, since a round trip over defaults restores nothing and
passes anyway), plus a key-set comparison that fails as soon as an option is
added to the form with no hydration counterpart. Two of the cases need shapes
the obvious fixture does not produce: a spec whose method and control wells
agree round-trips even when the method is never restored, and blank
thresholds only prove anything when hydrated over a form already holding real
numbers. Note also that `_refresh_remote_controls` *enables* dry-run only while
auto-delete is checked, so "auto-delete off, dry-run on" is not a state the user
can click their way to; hydrating one from a hand-edited `job_queue.json` leaves
the value alone and simply shows the box disabled.

**Run-time detection.** A queued job freezes the form's filename schema,
separator and channel tokens when it is queued, but the input they describe may
not exist until an earlier job in the queue writes it. The Filename Schema
section's **Detect schema & channels at run time** checkbox
(`AnalyzeSchemaSectionMixin._auto_detect_cb`) sets `RunSpec.auto_detect`, which
lives beside `opts` so it can never reach the pipeline's argv; `hydrate_job`
restores it, and sets it false for a job with no such key. Ticking it greys the
schema picker, whose values are about to be replaced, and
`_refresh_schema_preview` stops requiring a valid schema, since refusing one
would lock the input field the option exists to let the user fill. The
Segmentation channel stays live: which channel to segment is a choice, not a
fact the filenames carry, and detection honours it when the input carries it.
The readout under the input field counts loose files by suffix rather than
under the form's schema (`_refresh_output` passes none), the pre-run report's
scope sentence is left out, and its coverage scan resolves the detected layout
on its worker thread before reading the output folder.

`start_run` resolves it, so every entry point — Run, the queue, the resume
banner — answers the same way: after the busy refusal and before
`resume_aware_spec`, it calls `services.run_detect.resolve_detection`, which
replaces exactly the `opts` keys in `run_detect.DETECTED_OPTS` (schema,
separator, segmentation channel, fluorescent channels, phase channel). The
resume banner's `_resume_suspended` and `resume_aware_spec` both change only
`opts` (`dataclasses.replace`), so a resumed detection run detects again rather
than running the frozen layout its suspend record also holds.

`detect_layout` infers the schema from a dense sample of the input's names
(`_INFER_SAMPLE`, 20,000) but reads the **channel list from every name**
(`_ENUMERATE_LIMIT`): the channel list decides what is quantified, so a channel
a sample misses would be dropped from the run without a word. That costs no
more file I/O than the sample — the sampler already opens every archive — and
measured 0.81 s for a 96-well plate of 103,680 zip members. It runs on the GUI
thread, once per run start, like the form's Detect button and the input
planner: `start_run` refuses before it touches any UI state, and moving the
scan into the runner's worker would make that refusal asynchronous. The sampler itself
(`util.schema_infer._spread`) starts each archive's stride one member later
than the last, because the converters write every archive with the channel
varying fastest and a stride that was a multiple of the channel count read the
same channel from every well; the form's Detect button had the same blind spot.

The segmentation channel is chosen by method, because it is a choice rather
than a fact the names carry. Label-free methods segment the phase channel —
the pipeline remaps the segmentation slot onto it — so detection writes that,
and quantifies every channel. Otherwise the converter's roles win, then the
form's own Segmentation channel when the input carries it, then the name
heuristic in `util.channel_roles`; general Cellpose with a cell-body model is
refused when only the heuristic could choose, since the heuristic picks a
nuclear stain. Unlike the button, which applies whatever part of a guess it
gets because a person is looking at the result, an unattended run requires all
of it: a guess that is not confident, a folder with no image names, no channel
for the segmentation role or no fluorescent channel besides it raises
`DetectionError`, and `start_run` returns its message as the run's failure. It
never falls back to the frozen values, which are exactly the ones the job asked
not to use. The resolved options are then held against every option that
*names* a channel (`run_detect.channel_option_errors`), matched the way the
pipeline matches them — smFISH marks and the watershed cytoplasm channel by
exact membership of the fluorescent list, the Cellpose nuclei channel (which
the pipeline silently ignores when absent) case-insensitively — and against
the phase-role conflict. The detected layout's one-line
`DetectedLayout.summary()` is written to the log and the dashboard status when
the run starts, and carried as the finished job's `jobFinished` message, so the
queue row of a job whose layout was never on any form says what it turned out
to be. `start_run` also refuses a run with no input folder at all
(`run_detect.missing_input_error`): a queued job may be added blank so chaining
can fill it, and reaching the start of a run still blank means it never was.
A blank input field is collected as `""` rather than `Path("")`, and
`RunSpec` round-trips it as blank — `Path("")` serialises to `"."`, which reads
as a real folder.

Validation follows the same split. `_validate_run_request(for_queue=…)` lives in
`AnalyzeRunMixin` beside `validate_for_queue`. With detection on, it skips the
schema, fluorescent-channel and channel-comparing segmentation checks
(`_segmentation_validation_errors(channels=False)` still requires a cytoplasm
token for watershed and a positive minimum nucleus area, which detection
cannot supply). On the queue path it also accepts a blank input and an input
that does not exist yet, and so skips every check that reads the input: the
packed-file redirect and the parts of the background-well and control-well
checks that parse the input's filenames (`check_input=False`), which the
pipeline itself refuses at run start. Those two parse with the form's schema,
so with detection on they are deferred on the Run path as well; without it,
the Run button asks all of them of whatever the field names, as before.

**`_refresh_remote_controls` changes what is reachable, never what is set.** It
shows the *Remote options* group only while a remote is selected and enables the
dry-run checkbox only while auto-delete is checked — and it stops there. It used
to force auto-delete back on whenever "Run on:" was `Local` and clear dry-run
whenever dry-run was disabled, both to a widget that was hidden at the time and
neither undone on the way back. A user who ticked *Dry-run cleanup* to see what
auto-delete would remove, flicked to `Local` and back, and pressed Run had the
per-run remote output directory and the cached input deleted for real; the
mirror case re-armed an auto-delete they had deliberately turned off. Nothing is
lost by leaving them alone, because nothing reads either on a local run —
`PipelineRunner` passes both only down the remote branch, and
`RemoteRunner.verify_and_cleanup` returns before touching anything when
`cleanup_mode` is `"none"`.

**"Run on:" keeps the target on screen.** `_reload_remotes_combo` rebuilds the
combo from `remotes.toml` after every Manage-Remotes change — including a
*failed* bootstrap, which emits `remotes_changed` all the same — and re-selects
whatever was selected before, falling back to `Local` for a remote that has just
been deleted (which is what its docstring had always promised). It does **not**
re-apply `services.remote_config.default_remote_index`. That default decides the
pane's opening state, in `_build_run_controls`, and a rebuild is not an opening
state: re-applying it read `None` — the `userData` of the `Local` item — as
"nothing has been chosen yet" rather than as the target on screen, so any change
in the dialog moved a deliberate local run onto the first configured SSH host.
The rebuild runs under `blockSignals(True)`, so nothing was emitted and nothing
was logged; the next Run rsync'd the whole plate to the cluster.

`AnalyzeTab.runFinished(ok: bool, message: str)` is a **positive-latch**
completion signal: `_poll_log`'s `"done"` branch sets a per-run `_run_ok`
latch, `"error"` records the first message seen, and the `"finished"` branch
emits based on that latch — never on "no error was seen", since several of
`PipelineRunner._run_pipeline_thread`'s early-return paths (stopped before
launch, a cancelled zipper spawn) reach `"finished"` having emitted neither
`"done"` nor `"error"`. The emit is the **last statement** of that branch,
because a job-queue-driven slot connected to it may start the next run
synchronously, re-entering `_set_running_ui_state()` — anything after the
emit would clobber that new run's state. `AnalyzeTab.jobFinished(ok, message,
out_dir)` is a second, separate signal for the Job Queue specifically (kept
distinct so `runFinished`'s two-argument shape stays exactly what it always
was), emitted immediately after `runFinished` for the same reason. A user
Stop makes the pipeline subprocess exit non-zero, which surfaces as the same
kind of `"error"` event a genuine failure would — `PipelineRunner.was_stopped`
(readable after completion, cleared only at the *start* of the next run) is
how a caller tells a cancel apart from a real failure; `AnalyzeRunMixin.was_cancelled()`
exposes it under the name the Job Queue's bridge looks for.

**Single packed OME-TIFF input — the Datasets converter.** A plate scan can
arrive as one OME-TIFF holding every timepoint, channel, Z-plane and stage
position. De-interleaving it is a **standalone converter** in the Datasets pane
(`datasets/ome_import/`, §6b), *separate from processing*: it writes an ordinary
dataset folder, which the user then opens in Analyze and runs like any other
input. Keeping the two apart is deliberate — when the explode ran *inside* an
Analyze run the wells only existed mid-run, so pre-run checks that look for a
well (an `empty_well` background, control-well auto-threshold, both via
`well_present_in_input`) failed against the raw `.ome.tif`. Analyze now only ever
processes **folders**; `plan_input_layout` classifies a raw packed file through
`detect_packed_input`, which returns the plan action (`packed_ome` /
`packed_czi`) *and* the message naming the Datasets page that converts it. The
message travels with the detection rather than being chosen by the caller
because which converter to send the user to is decided by the suffix, and
naming the wrong one sends them to a page that will refuse their file. So the
readout under the input field and the run-time refusal
(`analyze.domain.input.AnalyzeInputMixin._packed_input_hint`, which the pre-run
validation reads) redirect the user to the right converter in the same words
instead of trying to run it. `_packed_input_hint` returns a message for a
check it could not *make*, too, rather than `None`: `None` is the answer that
means "this input is fine, start the run", so answering it for a permission error
part-way through the walk turned the guard off silently and let the run go ahead
against an input Analyze cannot process. The handler stays deliberately broad —
it runs inside the Run button's own slot, where an unlisted exception type would
kill the click instead of reporting anything — and names the exception in the
message.

The conversion itself is `pipeline.ome_explode.explode_ome_tiff`. It reads the
OME-XML for dimension order and channel names, **max-projects Z**, maps each
stage position to a 96-well label via `util.plate_grid`, and writes the planes
named
`<experiment>_<channel>_<well>_f<fov>_<timepoint>.tif` **directly into per-well
`<destination>/in/<WELL>.zip` archives** — the exact layout `resolve_input_output`
accepts as ready input, so Analyze uses it with **no** `well_plate_zipper` pass.
Wells are converted **in parallel** across a `ThreadPoolExecutor` (`workers`,
0 = auto), each worker owning a disjoint set of wells and its own read handle and
writing that well's archive alone (via `util.zip_write.atomic_zip`, so no locking
on the zip handles). Writing per-well zips also collapses what a loose-TIF explode
would cost in per-file fsyncs (one per plane — tens of thousands) into two per
well, and a cancelled/failed well leaves **no** partial archive (`atomic_zip`
discards its staging file). A read-vs-write timing line is logged so the dominant
cost is visible; the parallelism grain is per-well, so a degenerate single-well
grid stays serial.

**Timepoint tokens come from `DeltaT`, in whatever unit the file states.**
`_parse_ome_labels` converts each plane's `DeltaT` to hours through two tables,
consulted in order, and renders the result as `<hours>h`. Those tokens become
the filename's timepoint field and the app's chronological key, so a wrong
conversion scales every hours axis in Review by the ratio of the two units while
leaving the ordering intact — the failure mode where nothing looks broken.

`_DELTA_T_HOURS_PER_SYMBOL` comes first and is matched **case-sensitively**,
because OME's `UnitsTime` enumeration contains both `Ms` (megasecond) and `ms`
(millisecond) and only their case tells them apart: a case-insensitive lookup
read a megasecond as a millisecond, off by a factor of 10⁹. It holds the SI
prefixes that carry that hazard — `Ms`, `ks`, `hs`, `das`, `ds`, `cs`, `ms`.
`_DELTA_T_HOURS_PER_UNIT` follows, matched on the lower-cased unit, and spells
out the values an acquisition realistically writes whose meaning does not depend
on case (`s`, `min`, `h`, `d`, `µs` in both its Unicode spellings, `ns`, plus the
long forms). An *absent* `DeltaTUnit` is seconds, which is the schema's own
default; an empty one is read the same way.

**Every route back to a positional token is announced.** A `t0`/`t1` plate whose
writer recorded no `DeltaT` and one whose elapsed times were dropped produce
byte-identical archives, so the run log is the only thing that separates a file
stating no time from one whose time was lost. `_parse_ome_labels` collects every
reason and warns once, naming it — a unit neither table can read; a `TheT`
outside `0..SizeT-1`, which is a writer using one-based indexing and would
otherwise attach each elapsed time to the wrong array slot while still passing
the completeness count; two elapsed times rendering to the same label, where the
second timepoint's images would be written over the first's; and a time the
app's own parser could not read back. The warning fires only when the fallback
actually happens: one channel's planes carrying a bad unit while another's carry
seconds leaves every timepoint resolved, and a log line asserting data loss that
did not occur sends a user to re-export a plate for nothing.

**The rendering, and the decision to use the readings at all, are shared with
the CZI converter.** `timepoints.hours_token` and
`timepoints.elapsed_hour_tokens` are the single definitions (re-exported by
`explode_common`, which is where both exploders still take them from); `ome_explode`
keeps only `_source_reasons`, which builds the two reasons peculiar to OME-XML
(an unreadable `DeltaTUnit`, a `TheT` outside the file's own T axis). Two
definitions of "render an elapsed hour into a filename token" would answer
differently the day one of them changed, and a plate concatenated from an
OME-TIFF export and a CZI export of one acquisition would then hold `4h` and
`4.0h` as separate timepoints.

`_parse_ome_labels` returns the resulting one-sentence verdict alongside the
tokens rather than only logging it, and `OmeLayout.timepoint_note` carries it to
the converter page, which shows it in the verdict line **before** the run. A log
line arrives after the conversion, which is too late to re-export a plate.

`hours_token` does the rendering, in **fixed** notation at six significant
figures. `f"{v:g}"` switches to exponent form below 1e-4, which was rare while
every `DeltaT` was read as seconds and became routine once the sub-second units
were added: a six-frame time-lapse 100 ms apart rendered `2.77778e-05h`, and
`util/timepoint`'s `_UNIT_RE` matches no exponent — so `parse_hours` answered
`None`, `sort_key` sorted those tokens as text, and frames 5 and 6 landed ahead
of frames 2 to 4. A number the app cannot read back is worse than a wrong one,
which at least orders correctly.

**A measured series is snapped onto its own interval.**
`timepoints.regularise_hours` runs before the rendering, for both
converters. An acquisition that ran every four hours does not produce readings
exactly four hours apart — the stage takes as long as it takes — so a real
series reads 0, 4.00139, 8.00278 and would render as `0h`, `4.00139h`,
`8.00278h`: numbers that are true, unhelpful in a filename, and different on
the next plate of the same experiment. The gaps are measured, their median
taken as *the* interval, and each timepoint named at `first + index ×
interval`.

Three constraints on that, each of which a mutation showed a test had to pin:

- **Only where the series really is regular.** A plate imaged at 0, 4, 8 and
  then 24 hours — a final overnight point, an ordinary design — has no single
  interval, and forcing one would state three spacings the acquisition never
  used. Such a series keeps its measured times and carries a note saying so;
  the tokens are still correct and only the tidying was declined.
- **Only at a granularity the series can carry**, which `_rounding_unit`
  chooses per series from a ladder of units. Rounding is a domain predicate
  (§7.1) and it fails in two directions at once. Too fine and nothing is
  cleaned; too coarse and a time-lapse 100 ms apart lands every timepoint on
  `0h`, collides, and goes to positional names — OME-TIFFs carry millisecond
  `DeltaT` values routinely. The unit is capped at the whole minute, at two
  per cent of the interval, and at half of it: half a unit is how far rounding
  can move one reading, so on a fine interval a whole minute is a visible
  fraction of a gap.

  **Rounding each reading does not accumulate**, and a version of this that
  assumed it did caused two opposite defects at once. It divided the usable
  unit by the number of gaps, which made a long *interval* eligible for a
  coarse unit — a 48-hour run rounded to five minutes — while starving a long
  *run* of any unit at all, so the jitter tidying silently stopped past about
  eleven frames on an hourly plate and archives went back to carrying
  `11.0153h` in their filenames. What accumulates is the snap below.
- **And only when the result still matches what was measured.** The per-gap
  regularity test is not sufficient on a long series: drift that stays inside
  tolerance at every single step accumulates over twenty of them. The snapped
  series is therefore checked against the readings themselves before it is
  used, and a snap that moves any timepoint further than the series' **own
  gap jitter** — or one rounding unit, whichever is larger, and never more
  than five minutes — is declined in favour of the measured times. This is the
  load-bearing check, and it is what makes the other two safe rather than
  merely careful.

  The bound comes from the jitter because that is the only quantity that makes
  the rule statable: a snap that moves a timepoint further than the
  acquisition's own spacing already varied is inventing elapsed time rather
  than tidying it away. Two versions derived it from the *interval* instead
  and each was measured doing damage — a plain fraction named an image taken
  at 1104.94 h as `1104h`, inventing 56 minutes, and a fraction capped at five
  minutes still moved a **perfectly regular** 238.75-minute series onto a
  240-minute grid, which is fabrication in its plainest form: the acquisition
  had no jitter, so there was nothing to clean. The floor at one rounding unit
  is what keeps the feature working, because a constant per-round stage
  overhead has zero gap jitter and is exactly what the rounding exists to
  absorb.

  One cost is accepted rather than hidden. Any threshold is a discontinuity,
  so two plates of one experiment whose per-round overheads fall either side
  of it can be named differently and stop matching in `domain/tp_match.py`.
  Raising the budget moves that cliff without removing it, and removes the
  bound; the remedy for a pair of plates that lands on it is Review's
  *Interval per timepoint*.
- **From the series' own first reading, never from zero.** A CZI's stamps are
  already elapsed-from-the-first-plane so its origin is 0 either way, but an
  OME `DeltaT` is elapsed from the *acquisition's* start and a file whose first
  frame sits at 3600 s legitimately begins at `1h`. Re-basing at zero would
  move every timepoint by that offset invisibly, since the spacing it is
  checked against stays right — and would defeat the collision check the offset
  was hiding behind, turning two frames a picosecond apart at 1 h from a
  correct positional fallback into `0h` and `0.000000000028h`.

**All three converters take a timepoint stride.** *Keep every Nth timepoint* is
the same field, the same `explode_common.timepoint_plan`, the same
mapping-signature key and the same `4 of 12 timepoint(s)` readout on each page;
§6.2a states the rules in full. The OME side carries one trap the other two do
not: a
single-image file's frames are one flat sequence and `_frame_index` locates a
plane with `position × n_timepoints + t`, where `n_timepoints` is what the
*file* holds. `explode_ome_tiff` therefore keeps that name bound to the source
count and counts kept timepoints separately — rebinding it reads the wrong frame
for every position after the first, with the member names and the archive sizes
all still right.

**The file already knows most of the layout.** An OME-TIFF's `<Plane>`
elements carry `PositionX`/`PositionY` — where on the stage each image was taken
— and `read_ome_layout` collects them into `OmeLayout.stage_positions` from **both**
sets of metadata an OME-TIFF carries. The OME-XML's own `<Plane>` elements come
first, and where they have no coordinates the *instrument's* metadata is read
instead: Bio-Formats copies the original file's metadata into the OME-XML as
`<OriginalMetadata>` key/value annotations, and `tifffile` parses the vendor's
own tags into blocks of its own (`micromanager_metadata`, `imagej_metadata` and
the rest of `_VENDOR_BLOCKS`). Both are flattened to `{path: leaf}` and scanned
by `_paired_coordinates`, which pairs an X key with the Y that shares its *stem*
— "Position 3 XPos" belongs with "Position 3 YPos" and nothing else — so a stray
coordinate elsewhere in a block cannot pull a pair out of line, and fewer than
two complete pairs yields nothing at all. `OmeLayout.metadata_blocks` and
`metadata_key_sample` are collected on the same pass and decide nothing: they
exist so a file that yields no layout can report what it *does* hold, since
"no stage coordinates found" and "looked in the wrong place" are otherwise the
same sentence and telling them apart needs the file itself. The `<Plane>` collection is **per
`<Image>`**: a multi-image plate scan is one `<Image>` per stage position and
every one of them numbers its planes from `TheT="0"`, so collapsing duplicates
document-wide keeps the first image and discards the rest of the plate.
`datasets/ome_import/stage_layout.py` reads a plate layout back out of them, on
one physical separation: wells sit on a 9 mm pitch while the fields of view
inside a well are hundreds of micrometres apart, so each axis carries two scales
and the larger one is the well step. Both are measured against the axis's
**smallest** gap, never its median: an axis holding one within-well step and one
between-well step has a median equal to the larger, so nothing is ever three
times it and the two scales read as one. And the smallest instance of whichever
scale wins is the step, because a gap spans a whole number of steps and never a
fraction of one — a scan that skips wells leaves gaps of two and three pitches
beside the ordinary ones, and an average of those is a step no well sits on. The
axes share a plate and therefore a pitch, so an axis showing only the within-well
spacing (a single row or column of wells) takes the other's; an axis that shows a
well gap outranks one that does not, and among those that do the *smallest* wins
(`_pitch`) — taking the larger read a plate imaged on rows A and C as one whose
wells are 18 mm apart. `_well_step` divides by the **wells** between two occupied
groups rather than treating them as adjacent, for the same reason: that number is
the conversion from stage units to plate cells, so a doubled one draws the map at
half scale. There is one pitch for the plate, not one per axis, which is what
makes a one-sided skip recoverable: rows sampled A/C/E with every column present
measure 18 mm down and 9 mm across, and the axis showing the single step supplies
the pitch that reads the other's gaps as the multiples they are. **When the file states a unit, the pitch is known rather than inferred.**
`ome_explode._stage_positions` converts stage coordinates to micrometres
whenever every plane names a length unit for both axes (`PositionXUnit`), and
reports `stage_positions_in_um`; mixed or missing units convert nothing, since
OME's own default is "reference frame" — the microscope's frame, which has no
defined size, and treating it as micrometres would put a confident wrong mapping
on every file that omits the attribute. With a unit, `_known_pitch` uses the
nominal `WELL_PITCH_UM` where the measured steps agree with whole multiples of
it, and that is what maps an **arbitrary selection of wells**: a scattered set
(B02, D07, G11) has no adjacent pair anywhere to learn a pitch from, so relative
spacing alone reads it as three neighbouring wells or refuses outright. It also rescues the case the gap split cannot see at all: sixteen fields on a
2.25 mm step tile the 9 mm pitch *exactly*, so every step in the file is the same
and there is no wider gap anywhere to mark a well boundary — a perfectly regular
6×6 plate read as 24×24 wells of one field, far too big for a plate, and the
drawing said so. `_um_axis_groups` places the boundary instead of finding it:
each coordinate's residue modulo the known pitch says where in a well it sits,
and the boundary goes in the widest empty arc of those residues (the wrap-around
one on a tie, which keeps the first well whole). Taken only when the gap split
produced something that cannot be a plate *and* the result can, so a scan the
gaps already read correctly is untouched and another format's pitch still falls
back to the ratios. It also
settles the oldest ambiguity here — `_one_well` reports a montage across a
single well as one well of N fields, where without a unit a montage and a grid
of wells holding one field each are the same pattern at two scales and the grid
reading had to be taken. A spacing that is not a whole number of 9 mm pitches
falls back to the relative reading, so another plate format is no worse off.

That the two axes share one pitch is a real
assumption — an SBS plate is on 9 mm centres both ways — so it is **checked**
rather than relied on: the two axes' per-well steps must agree within
`_AXIS_AGREEMENT_TOL`, and where they do not there is no layout. Taking each axis
at its own word instead would read A/C/E as adjacent, and letting a disagreement
through is worse: a scan whose rows sit 1.5 pitches apart rounds to 2 and
produces *exactly* the layout a genuine skipped row produces, with the same
confidence. One adjacent
pair anywhere on one axis is enough. Where **every** step on every axis skips —
rows A, C and E in a single column — nothing in the file distinguishes that from
three adjacent wells on a coarser plate, since no absolute unit is trusted here;
it reads as adjacent, which the map draws at plate scale and the user's grid
overrides; where neither shows two scales the reading is genuinely
ambiguous between "one well holding a grid of fields" and "a grid of wells
holding one field each", and the latter is taken because it is the ordinary plate
scan. Coordinates are merged within a fraction of the coarsest spacing first, or
a stage's few-micrometre repeatability reads as a position of its own and the
grid explodes. **A single well imaged as a montage still reads as a grid of
wells**, because that ambiguity has no answer in the coordinates alone — telling
them apart needs the absolute scale, which means trusting the file's
`PositionXUnit` — and the common reading is chosen. Degenerate input is refused
outright rather than answered: every plane at one coordinate, fewer than two
distinct positions, or a scale that is not finite and positive all return
`None`, since a confident layout out of those is offered to the user as the
file's own answer. What is **not** always inferred is which physical well the block starts at: stage coordinates are relative to the microscope's origin, which no file
states in plate terms, so `StageLayout.relative_order` is `(row, col)` offsets and
`place()` puts them at the origin the user chose.

**A shape need not be a rectangle.** An L, a diagonal, a plate with a row left
out: ordinary experiments, and the fields per well and the visit order are right
whatever the outline is. `rows`/`cols` are the block's **extent** and `n_wells`
counts the cells actually visited, with `filled` reporting whether they agree —
`suggest_layout` hands anything sparse over as an explicit `well_order`, since a
`rows × cols` sweep visits every cell and cannot describe one that does not.
Group indices count *wells, not groups* (`_group_axis` advances by
`round(gap / pitch)`), so a skipped well leaves a hole: indexing occupied groups
consecutively closed the gap up, and a scan of rows A and C in two columns
collapsed to two wells, `A01` and `B01`. The one refusal left is **uneven fields
per well**, which no single FOVs-per-well setting can express, and the page says
which of the two it is hit. `stage_layout.path_in_cells` converts the same coordinates into **plate
cells** — one unit per well, fractional inside one — anchored so the first
position sits at the centre of the well the user says the scan starts in.
What reaches it is `stage_layout.single_cycle(...)`, the coordinates with
every return to a place already imaged dropped, because a timelapse walks
the same route once per timepoint: drawn in full that is **one map
overdrawn N times**, every dot landing on a dot, every line on a line, and
the numbering running to N times the count of real positions while showing
the geometry of one. Repeats are dropped rather than the list cut at the
first one, because a file ordered timepoints-within-position repeats its
*second* coordinate and truncating would leave it a single dot.
`ome_import_compute.stage_path_cycles` returns `(drawn, in the file)` and the
page's caption states both whenever they differ — a picture showing a twelfth
of the coordinates must say so in the artifact, not only in the code that
decided it.

**Which way the stage ran is the user's answer, not an inference.** A microscope's
axes are not the plate's: how the plate sits in the holder and where the objective
is decide which way X grows, so a scan that swept left to right across the plate
can be written with X *decreasing*. Read straight it comes out mirrored — the
inferred visit order walks the wells backwards, the map draws the run back to
front, and the conversion writes each image into the horizontally opposite well,
with every count correct and nothing on screen broken. Nothing in an OME-TIFF says
which way the plate faced, and the coordinates alone cannot tell a right-to-left
scan from a left-to-right one on a plate loaded the other way round, so the page
carries two checkboxes (left↔right, top↔bottom) rather than guessing.
`stage_layout.mirrored` negates the chosen axes — a reflection, so shape, spacing
and pitch are untouched and only the direction of travel changes — and
`ome_import_compute.oriented` wraps a layout in the reflected coordinates,
returning the layout itself when neither axis flips so the page's identity-keyed
inference cache still sees one object per file. The page applies it **once**, in
`_read_layout`, so the inference, the suggested grid, the frame order, the drawn
map and the wells a run writes cannot disagree; mirroring only the drawing would
be the worse bug of the two, leaving the picture the user checks the layout
against contradicting the layout the conversion uses. Toggling re-offers the
file's answer whenever the form still holds it — `_holds(suggestion)`, which
compares the controls against the last offer, because `_untouched` asks whether
the form is at its *defaults* and a file whose metadata was applied on load has
left it holding the file's answers instead.
`widgets/stage_path_view.py` draws that under the acquisition plate at the
plate's own scale: a dot per imaged position, joined in acquisition order, over
the same 8×12 lattice. It is the one view that can show anything about the
fields *within* a well, since a plate map has one cell for all of them. Its
geometry comes from `WellPlateSelector.cellRect(row, col)` rather than from its
own width, because the plate reserves room for its headers before sizing cells
and two widgets of equal width otherwise disagree about where a well is. The
scale factor is `StageLayout.pitch`, the **centre-to-centre** well step measured
from the group means — not the gap the grouping threshold uses, which runs from
the last field of one well to the first of the next and is short by the width of
a well's own block of fields; at that scale the drawing shrinks by that fraction
per column and lands a whole cell out of place across twelve of them.
**The inference is a function of the file, and the page is not.** Every box on
the converter recomputes the readout as it is typed in, so `suggest_layout` and
`stage_path_for` both take an already-computed `StageLayout` and the page holds
one per source (`_inferred_for`, keyed on the layout object `_read_layout`
already caches per path+mtime). Left to re-derive itself it ran **twice per
keystroke**; the loops behind it are linear now, but a 96-well plate at 16 fields
over 24 timepoints is 36,864 positions and still ~90 ms, which is not something
to spend per character on the UI thread. Two things in that measurement are worth
keeping in mind for anything else that walks these lists: `c not in cells[:i]` is
the obvious way to take first visits and is quadratic (five seconds at that
size) — `tests/test_hot_paths_stay_linear.py` counts the element comparisons a
list scan makes and a set does not, at two input sizes, and checks first that
every distinct cell came back, since a `_first_visits` returning nothing
compares nothing and would otherwise pass — and a timelapse revisits every position once per timepoint, so counting
*visits* per well rather than distinct coordinates reports a plate's fields
multiplied by its timepoints. `ome_import_compute.suggest_layout`
wraps that for the page, which *offers* it. It returns `None` when `place`
refuses the block — one larger than a 96-well plate, which is what a pitch read
as the *field* spacing produces — and the page then says so, naming the block it
read: the path drawing needs no placement and draws regardless, so a silent
`None` leaves an overflowing picture, an untouched form and no account of
either. Whether it arrives as grid fields or
as an explicit order is decided by **comparing** the placed order against the
serpentine those fields would produce, not by asking whether the scan is a
serpentine: a stage reporting Y or X descending sweeps a perfectly good
serpentine whose first well is the block's *bottom*-left, and the grid always
starts top-left, so the rows come out mirrored with every count still correct.
One comparison covers that, a raster, and any other starting corner.

**The grid says whether it snakes.** `util/plate_grid.block_well_labels` is the
one generator of a block's labels — `serpentine_well_labels` is now a wrapper
that passes `serpentine=True` — and its flag decides what happens at the end of
each line: snake back, or fly back to the near edge and raster. Both are ordinary
acquisition patterns, and a raster read as a snake labels every second line
*backwards*, which is a silent well-mapping error with the right well count. It
reaches the pipeline as `ConversionParams.serpentine` and sits in `_MAPPING_FIELDS`,
so a resume refuses to finish a run under a different sweep than started it. The
page carries it as a Snake checkbox beside the Sweep combo, filled from the
inference like the rest; before it existed, the grid could only generate a snake
and a raster had to be clicked well by well.

**Two more settings come out of the same metadata.** `stage_layout.infer_frame_order`
reads the converter's *frame order* — the one thing the file's own
`DimensionOrder` cannot express, since an OME `<Image>` has no position
dimension — from which coordinates repeat and how: every position visited once
is `single`, a sequence running through all of them before repeating is
`pos_in_time`, one repeating each position consecutively is `time_in_pos`, and
anything else is `None` rather than a guess. That also yields the timepoint
count.

**"The same place" is one definition for the module** — `stage_layout.place_keys`,
which snaps each coordinate to the merged axis values `_distinct` / `_nearest`
group wells with, at the `_jitter_tolerance` both the grouping and the revisit
test read from the coarsest gap on either axis. The question is asked in four
places (how many fields a well holds, whether the sequence repeats and how
often, which places the map draws, which cell a coordinate belongs to), and a
stage sent back to a nominal position reports it a fraction of a micrometre
off, so an equality test finds no repeats at all: the same file then reports a
well's fields *multiplied* by its timepoints and `single` for its frame order,
each contradicting the other. Comparison is O(n log n) rather than pairwise —
a plate timelapse holds tens of thousands of positions and this runs on the UI
thread, on every keystroke. `StageLayout.absolute_origin` reads the **starting well** straight out of the
coordinates when they are stated in the plate's own frame — A01 at the origin,
every well centre a whole number of pitches out — believed only when every well
in the block lands on its grid position within `_PLATE_FRAME_TOL` of a pitch and
inside the plate, since a microscope-framed file has an arbitrary zero and the
same arithmetic would be meaningless. Failing that,
`ome_import_compute.wells_from_names` reads it
out of `OmeLayout.position_names` (each `<Image>`'s `<StageLabel>` name, else
its own) — the only thing in an OME-TIFF that locates a position on the *plate*
rather than on the stage. Every name must yield exactly one well token or the
answer is discarded whole: a set where some parse and some do not is a partial
mapping, and filling the rest by inference is how a plate ends up half
labelled. When every position names its well the visit order is taken from the
names outright, and nothing is inferred at all. The page applies the result
**automatically while the form still holds its defaults** and never over a value
the user has entered.

**The grid and the clicked path are alternatives, and only one of them is an
input.** The converter page draws the grid's serpentine onto the plate as a live
*preview*, and the plate the preview lands on is the same one the user clicks
into. So the page reads `well_order` from the plate **only once the widget is
dirty** (`OmeImportPage.raw_fields`), and `PlateOrderEditor` makes the first click
*replace* the preview rather than extend it: a preview is the host's guess, and
carrying its wells into the order the user is defining makes them positions 1..n,
pushing every clicked well one stage position later — each well then receives the
previous position's images, with no count on screen that looks wrong. A path the *file* supplied is not a hand-drawn one, and the page tracks which it
has (`_order_from_file`): editing Origin re-places the file's order at the new
well (`_reposition_file_order`) rather than being ignored, because the starting
well is the one answer an inference can get wrong in a way only the user can
see. A click on the plate makes the order the user's, and only then do the grid
controls go dead. While a genuinely
hand-drawn path is in force the grid, origin and serpentine controls are disabled
with a note saying why, since they describe the other way of producing the same
order and a control that accepts input and discards it is the page's most
confusing state. `ConversionPlan.summary()` names the wells at both ends of the
order and which input produced it for the same reason: the counts are identical
either way.

**The well ordering need not be rectangular.** Each stage position `i` maps to
`well_labels[i // fovs_per_well]`, so the acquisition path is just an ordered list
of wells (one well × FOV per position; FOVs-per-well is entered explicitly and
cross-checked, or derived). By default that list is the **serpentine** sweep of
the imaged `grid_rows × grid_cols` block (`serpentine_well_labels`). But
`explode_ome_tiff` / `plan_conversion` also accept an explicit **`well_order`** —
an ordered list of wells that need not form a rectangle or any particular shape
(`util.plate_grid.normalize_well_order` canonicalises it and rejects an invalid or
duplicated token) — which replaces the serpentine entirely, with the grid fields
acting only as a seed. The converter page builds this order on
`widgets/plate_order_editor.PlateOrderEditor`, which is the app's shared
`WellPlateSelector` driven in its ordered `"path"` selection model: it draws the
numbered visit sequence plus a subtle arrow tracing position→well across the
plate (the visual confirmation), and clicking wells appends / removes-and-
renumbers them to define an arbitrary order (component 2). The page keeps the
plate a live serpentine preview of the grid until the user clicks (the widget's
*dirty* flag), after which the grid no longer overwrites it.

Two source structures are handled (`read_ome_layout` → `OmeLayout.single_image`),
because OME allows only X/Y/Z/C/T inside one `<Image>` — there is no position
dimension:

- **Multi-image** — several `<Image>` elements (one `tifffile` series each), one
  per stage position; each series' `T` axis is that position's timepoints.
- **Single-image packed** — one `<Image>` whose `T` axis packs *every* position
  (and any real timepoints) into a flat frame sequence. A **frame-order** choice
  (`single` / `pos_in_time` / `time_in_pos`) says how that sequence splits:
  `n_positions = wells × FOVs`, `n_timepoints = n_frames / n_positions`. Planes
  are read **one page at a time** (`_packed_plane` ravels the T/C/Z indices
  against the series' leading-axis sizes, honouring the file's `DimensionOrder`)
  because a packed plate array is routinely tens–hundreds of GB — far too large
  to `asarray` whole.

**The source is validated before anything is written.** `read_ome_layout`
audits the file in the same pass that reads its sizes — all metadata, no pixels,
so the cost is one file open however large the plate — and
`OmeLayout.validation_report()` returns the one blocking problem, ordered by how
far upstream the fault is. **Not an OME-TIFF:** a file *named* `.ome.tif` whose
OME-XML cannot be read has almost certainly been truncated in transit; it still
opens as a valid TIFF, `tifffile` invents a plain series from the pages it could
enumerate, and a forty-frame plate converts silently into one well. A plain
`.tif` stack carries no OME-XML either and is a legitimate input, which is why
the check is keyed on the *name* claiming OME rather than on the metadata alone.
**Metadata that does not describe the pages:** `series_kind` is `tifffile`'s own
verdict, and anything but `"ome"` means it declined the OME structure and fell
back to enumerating pages, so each plane's channel and timepoint is a guess.
**Declared sizes that were not realised:** `declared_sizes` holds `SizeT`/`SizeC`/
`SizeZ` as the XML states them; `SizeT` on a single-image file is the one
compared against the series that actually came out, since that is the axis the
converter splits into positions. The other two are collected for a caller that
wants them and are not themselves a refusal.
**Two labels that reduce to one filename token:** every image is published as
`<experiment>_<channel>_<well>_f<fov>_<timepoint>.tif`, and `util.filename_token.safe_token` keeps
alphanumerics only, so `"488 nm"` and `"488nm"` — or `"GFP-1"` and `"GFP_1"`, or
two channels a file simply names alike — become one token and write the same
member name into one archive. `zipfile` keeps both copies of the bytes under one
name and a reader returns only the last, so one channel is unreachable while the
run reports both as written; `atomic_zip`'s verification cannot see it either,
because the duplicate name appears on both sides of `sorted(namelist())`. Two
`DeltaT` values that render alike at `%g`'s six significant figures collide the
same way. `OmeLayout._colliding_tokens` finds the first such clash across the
channel tokens and the timepoint tokens, and `validation_report` refuses the file
by naming the colliding labels in the spelling the acquisition software shows
them. The timepoint half is a backstop: `_parse_ome_labels` drops a whole file
back to positional tokens when its `DeltaT`-derived ones are not unique, which
names every timepoint distinctly and loses only a number the file did not really
state — there is no such fallback for a channel, whose identity *is* its name — which is why `OmeLayout` also carries `raw_channel_names`, the names
before tokenisation, used for nothing else.
`OmeLayout.warnings` keeps what `tifffile` logged while reading — it diagnoses
every one of these in its own words and writes them to a logger nothing was
attached to, which is the file's own account of what is wrong with it.

**An incomplete source is refused before anything is written.** `tifffile` sizes
a series' page list from the dimensions the *metadata* declares and leaves a slot
`None` wherever the file carries no IFD for it — an acquisition stopped early
(the planned `SizeT` stays in the header), or a multi-file OME whose companion
files are not beside the master. Its own `series.asarray()` zero-fills those
slots, which is exactly the substitution §7's design rule forbids: a converted
plate would carry solid-black planes no downstream step could tell from real
ones. Reading pages individually, as the single-image path must, instead puts the
gap in front of `.asarray()` as a bare `None`. So `read_ome_layout` counts
the gaps in the same pass it reads the sizes (`series_page_gaps`, scanned only
for the series kinds that can hold one) and carries them on `OmeLayout` as
`total_planes` / `missing_planes` / `incomplete_positions` /
`first_missing_plane`, plus `missing_files` — the companion filenames the OME-XML
references that are not on disk beside the source, which is what separates the
two causes and therefore the two fixes. A gap has a **third** cause besides those two, and it needs the
opposite remedy: a *broken index map* — `TiffData` entries pointing at IFDs the
file does not have, or carrying a coordinate outside the declared sizes, which
`tifffile` reports and then leaves as a hole — loses nothing at all, because the
pixels are on disk and only the metadata is wrong. Telling that user to re-export
a shorter file would discard data that is present. `unreferenced_pages` is the
tell: physical IFDs no series slot points at, which is zero for a truncated run
and non-zero for a broken map. `OmeLayout.validation_report()` is the
single wording every caller uses: `explode_ome_tiff` raises it as a `ValueError`
before the destination directory is even created, and `plan_conversion` raises it
as an `OmeImportError` *ahead of* its grid arithmetic — no grid makes a gapped
file convertible, so a divisibility error derived from one would be a red
herring. The converter page shows it in the readout and leaves **Convert**
disabled. `_packed_plane` keeps a per-plane guard behind that check, naming the
frame/channel/Z it was asked for rather than raising on `None`.

**An interrupted conversion is finished, not repeated.** Every well is
published atomically (`util.zip_write.atomic_zip`), so a run that stopped
part-way leaves whole, correct archives and no half-written one — the work
already done is on disk and only the rest is missing. `explode_ome_tiff(...,
resume=True)` skips a well whose archive already holds **every member name these
settings call for** (`explode_common.expected_members` /
`well_is_complete`, read from the zip's central directory, so a couple of seeks
each), reports it through the same
progress callbacks as a converted one — otherwise the plate map shows a finished
well as one that never ran, and the run-wide bar never reaches its total — and
names the count in `ExplodeResult.wells_resumed` and the closing log line.

**Resume is off by default, and gated on the settings rather than the
filenames.** Two different mappings — another grid, origin, ordering, FOVs-per-
well, or another source file — produce *identical* member names from different
images, so an archive on disk cannot say which run made it. `apply.convert`
writes `datasets/ome_import/ome_import_compute.IN_PROGRESS_MARKER`
(`.aw_ome_in_progress`) into the destination before the first archive, holding
the source path and the mapping fields, and removes it on success; so the marker
exists exactly while a run is unfinished. `resume_state` compares it against the
current settings and answers *resumable*, *mismatched* or neither, and
`destination_problem` reads that: a folder carrying this tool's marker for the
same settings is not a refusal but a resume, for different settings it is
refused in its own words, and with no marker at all the ordinary
"already holds converted wells" rule applies. The mechanism itself is
`datasets/core/convert_marker.py`, shared with the CZI converter, which passes
its own marker filename and its own list of mapping fields; the constant above
is this tool's. It is the same device the other Datasets tools use
(`core.dataset_paths.make_dataset_api`), for the same reason: a folder holding
*this* tool's interrupted attempt is a resume, while the same folder holding
another tool's leftovers is not.

**`convert` asks that question itself**, rather than trusting the page to have
asked it. There are two ways in and only one of them goes through a field hint:
a queued job reaches `convert` through `start_from_queue`, which populates the
page and launches without ever consulting the destination's inline validation.
A conversion overwrites each `in/<WELL>.zip` it produces and leaves everything
else in the folder alone, so an unchecked run against a folder that already
holds a plate produces one folder holding two of them, with `out/` measurements
beside inputs that are no longer the ones they were computed from. The marker
is checked at the same point and for the same reason: two mappings write
identical filenames from different images, so finishing one run with another
run's settings stitches a single plate out of two acquisitions. The marker is
written through `util.json_write.write_json_atomic`, because a half-written
marker is a *different* mapping to `resume_state` and the wells already on disk
came from this one.

`explode_ome_tiff` also takes a `progress_fn`/`should_abort` pair (raising
`OmeExplodeCancelled`) so the converter's worker can drive a progress bar and
Cancel. Channel roles are *not* set in the converter — it writes the OME channel
**names** as tokens; the user assigns nuclear/fluor/phase in Analyze's normal
Channel Tokens section on the converted folder. `pipeline/ome_explode.py` and
`util/plate_grid.py` are in the remote manifest so it stays a complete mirror of
`pipeline/` + `util/` (`test_remote_manifest.py`).

**What the converters share lives in `pipeline/explode_common.py`.** The three
exploders differ entirely in how they *read* their source and not at all in what
they produce: the same member names, the same atomic per-well archive, the same
rule for deciding whether a well an interrupted run left behind is finished, the
same worker-count policy and strided well split, the same in-memory TIFF encode,
the same elapsed-hour timepoint naming and stride, the same `ExplodeResult` and
the same `ExplodeCancelled`. `OmeExplodeCancelled` and `Nd2ExplodeCancelled`
