Three, not two: the pipeline's control-well and Otsu passes
(`pipeline/threshold_optimize.py`, `pipeline/auto_threshold.py`) and the Cell
Gating tab's own Auto-threshold button, whose sampler is the near-twin
`review/data/auto_threshold.py`. The viewer's copy imports
`round_stored_threshold` rather than restating the rule, because a rounding rule
that holds on the batch path and not on the button is the one a user meets
first.

**The Otsu mode reads its samples out of the output archives, and pairs them by
name.** `estimate_thresholds_from_outputs` walks `<output_dir>/*_out.zip` and
matches each channel's `_tophat` member to the `_labels` member of the same
FOV-group, which means parsing member stems — output names are the input stem
plus a role suffix — against the run's own `--filename_schema`. All of that is
keyed on `(fov, timepoint)`, computed for both member roles by the single
`_SchemaReader.group_key` so a label and its tophat cannot disagree about either
coordinate; `_index_members`, `_sample_one_well` and `_otsu_per_channel` are the
three steps around it.

A channel the run referenced rather than archived — the phase channel under
`--phase_output reference` — has no `_tophat` member to pair, so
`run_auto_threshold_pass` names it (`_referenced_channels` — the phase token,
whatever this run's `--phase_output`, since a copy-mode run over up-to-date wells
leaves archives with no phase `_tophat`) and `estimate_thresholds_from_outputs` opens `<input_dir>/<WELL>.zip`
beside each output archive (`_open_input_archive`) and indexes its raw frames
for those channels only (`_index_input_frames`, which judges members by
basename because an input archive may nest them, skips `__MACOSX/`, dotfiles
and role-suffixed members, and leaves a multi-page frame to be sampled at its
first plane, as the pipeline measures it). The input archive is found by
canonical well label (`_input_archive_for`), because the pipeline accepts
`A1.zip` and writes `A01_out.zip`. An archived `_tophat` still wins, so a well a copy-mode run wrote is
read from its own archive; a well with no input archive says so and contributes
no samples for that channel. The batched-remote re-run carries `--input_dir`
(the local folder) and `--phase_output` into its rebuilt args for the same
reason. Review's Cell Gating button applies the same rule in
`review/data/auto_threshold` (`_with_raw_frames`, over both of its walks, with
the input archive found through `image_discovery.find_plain_well_zips_in_dir`),
so the two estimates agree.

A schema need not name every slot, and an unnamed slot is not a parse failure.
`well:channel:timepoint` (files like `A01_w2Turq_T04.tif`) has no fov token to
find, and two images of the same well/channel/timepoint cannot exist under it —
they would be the same filename — so an unnamed fov collapses to a constant that
merges nothing distinct. A slot the schema *does* name but a given stem does not
fill is the opposite case: that member is malformed, and a constant there would
merge genuinely different fields, so it stays rejected. The timepoint slot takes
the constant whenever it comes out empty either way, because a single-timepoint
dataset writes filenames with fewer tokens than the schema has fields.

The failure this guards against is a silent one: an archive whose members the
schema cannot place looks exactly like a well that held no images, and every
channel then reports `only 0 sample(s)` — a line that reads as "no data" and
names neither the schema nor a filename. A well that yields nothing while holding
role-suffixed members now warns, naming the schema, the separator and an example
stem; one that yields nothing because it holds no `_labels` member at all warns
in its own words, so the two are told apart at the well rather than left to a
per-channel line that describes neither. **Which members `_index_members` is
entitled to judge is part of that**: the extension test goes through
`util.image_exts.is_group_image`, the one answer to "would the pipeline group
this file", rather than a local `tif`/`tiff` list — a run that wrote `.png`
had every member dropped *before* the role and schema checks, so `unplaceable`
stayed empty, the warning above could not fire, and the only thing the user saw
was `only 0 sample(s)` per channel. Directory entries and leading-dot basenames
(`.DS_Store`, AppleDouble sidecars) are skipped ahead of it. The dispatcher separates the two outcomes it used to report as one, as
well: "no new defaults" (every channel already had a stored value) is routine,
while estimating nothing at all for every readout channel is a warning — and it
cannot hide behind the segmentation channel's unconditional zero, which is itself
a successful write and made such a run read as a partial success.

In both non-skip modes the segmentation channel — `--nuclear_token`, already
remapped onto `--phase_token` for the label-free methods by the time the pass
runs, plus `--cytoplasm_token` under seeded watershed — is written **0** and
excluded from the estimate. It defines cell boundaries rather than being
something to gate on, so any estimate for it is noise. Zero is not the same as
absent: absent means the viewer's 50.0 default, whereas 0 classifies every cell
with a positive intensity as ON, which is how the channel is neutralised.
`_apply_thresholds_to_pipeline_info` never overwrites a value already in the
sidecar, so all of this is a default the user can override — including the zero.

The control-well mode reads the per-well CSVs the run has just written, not the
`*_out.zip` images: those CSV values are exactly what the Cell Gating tab plots,
so a pipeline-chosen threshold lands where the user will later see it on the CDF.
`sample_cell_and_bg` is deliberately *not* reused here — it pools cell means with
matched background pixels, which is right for an Otsu split against background
and wrong for a two-well comparison, where background pixels land identically in
both wells and dilute the gap being maximised.

The objective is symmetric, so it cannot tell the two control wells apart; the
pass logs a warning when the positive control ends up with the *lower*
fraction-on, which is the only signal that the two wells were entered the wrong
way round.

Batched remote runs suppress the per-batch pass (partial-plate data would write
misleading defaults) and re-run it once locally over the full downloaded output
— `services/remote_process._run_local_auto_threshold`, which rebuilds an args
object from the pipeline argv and calls the same `run_auto_threshold_pass` so
the two paths cannot drift. That rebuild forces `no_auto_threshold=False` on
purpose: when the pass is wanted it must ignore the batcher's copy of the flag.

Which makes `--no_auto_threshold` ambiguous on that argv — it arrives there for
two unrelated reasons, the operator unchecking the box and the batcher
suppressing the per-batch pass, and once appended the two are indistinguishable.
So the *decision to call* the local pass is what carries the operator's answer:
`_BatchedRemoteProcess._auto_threshold_off_by_user` reads the flag off
`self._pipeline_argv`, the argv as handed in, which `_run_batches` copies rather
than mutates. Reading it any later answers the wrong question.

**A remote fetch must not take the user's blocks with it.** `verify_and_cleanup`
rsyncs the remote `pipeline_info.json` over the local one, and a remote output
dir starts empty — so the fetched file carries none of the cell-gating
thresholds, sample definitions, ratios or notes the Review side wrote locally,
including the ones `_run_local_auto_threshold` produced moments earlier.
`pipeline/sidecar.py` holds the list of those user-owned keys and the
capture/restore pair around the fetch; `process_microscopy.write_pipeline_info`
preserves the same list when a re-run rewrites the sidecar in place, so the two
paths share one definition of whose data it is. `run_report` keeps its own
merge (`pipeline/run_report.py`) because its records merge per well rather than
being restored wholesale, and `field_quality` keeps a matching one
(`merge_fetched_field_quality`) for the same reason and a sharper consequence:
losing coverage records loses history, but losing quality records produces a
**wrong number**, because the acquisition metrics are scored as a robust z
against the plate. A block silently reduced to the wells one remote
incremental run touched gives each of them a z against its own tiny median,
and the shortfall accounting cannot catch it — every one of those wells is
individually complete, so nothing is marked partial and the scorer proceeds.
The capture is read **before** the rsync and merged after, which is the half a
guard in `tests/test_remote_incremental.py` pins.

Inputs / outputs / contract:

```
Input dir (one of; grouped per 96-well position upstream)
├── A01.zip / A02.zip / … H12.zip          ← per-well zip mode (preferred)
└── A01/ / A02/ / … H12/                    ← per-well folder mode
                                              (compressed to <well>.zip during the run)

Output dir
├── <well>_out.zip                          ← masks + tophat + overlays per well
├── <prefix>_<well>.csv                     ← per-well measurement CSV
├── pipeline_info.json                      ← schema / channels / timepoints / cell_gating
└── (transient tmp_<well>/ directories deleted on success)
```

**Per-cell shape features.** `compute_shape_features(labels, selected)` runs one
`skimage.regionprops_table` pass per FOV and merges `shape_<feature>` columns
(area/eccentricity/solidity/perimeter/…, plus the **always-on**
`shape_centroid_row/col` that cell tracking links across timepoints) into each
cell record; the selection comes from `--shape_features` and is recorded in
`pipeline_info.json`. The feature catalog lives in the Qt-free top-level
`pipeline.shape_features` so the pipeline (emit) and the GUI (detect/label) can't
drift. On the Review side `data_loading.detect_shape_features` finds the columns
and the channel dropdown surfaces them as **sectioned virtual channels** (a
"Shape Features" group via `ui_helpers.set_combo_values_sectioned`), with the
metric combo collapsed and all-cells (`threshold=-1`) aggregation — they are
channel-independent, so they bypass the per-channel intensity gate.

**Quality-control stage.** Two optional QC steps run inside `process_image_group`.
**Flat-field correction** (`--flatfield {none,empty_well,gaussian,basic}`, via
`apply_flatfield` with a mean-1 field) runs *before* top-hat: `gaussian`
self-estimates per image, while `basic` (a **pure-numpy BaSiC** — median stack +
smooth, no jax) and `empty_well` use a per-channel field precomputed once in
`main()` by `build_flatfield_models`. **Debris removal** (`--qc_remove_debris` +
min/max area + min-solidity, via `filter_debris`) drops out-of-bounds label
regions, **reusing the same `regionprops` pass** as the shape features. The
settings are recorded as a `qc_options` block in `pipeline_info.json`
(`read_pipeline_info` defaults it to `{}` on legacy sidecars).

**Segmentation routines + parameters.** `--segmentation_method` selects the
segmenter in `process_image_group`'s dispatch; the Analyze "Channel Tokens"
section shows a **per-method parameter panel** (a `NamedPageStack` swapped by
`_refresh_segmentation_hints`) built by
`analyze.seg_params.AnalyzeSegParamsMixin`, so only the chosen routine's
controls appear. All routines segment the **Segmentation channel**
(`--nuclear_token`, which may be any fluorescent or brightfield channel) unless
noted:
- `stardist_nuclei` / `stardist_seeded_watershed_cell` — StarDist (needs a
  fluorescent stain); watershed adds a cytoplasm token + min-nucleus-area.

  **Seeding the watershed is whole-array work.** `nucleus_seed_markers` plants
  one single-pixel marker at each surviving nucleus's rounded centroid, taking
  the areas from `_label_areas` (a `bincount` over the label image, with an
  `np.unique` fallback for a label image whose ids are negative or larger than
  the array, so the fast path cannot be made to allocate by one stray id) and the
  centroids from one `ndi.center_of_mass` over the whole index list. Both used to
  be per-nucleus calls over boolean masks — one and two full passes over the
  frame *each* — which measured 1.43 s and 23.67 s for 1500 nuclei on a 2048²
  frame against 0.08 s and 0.25 s here, roughly 25 s per FOV and 2.7 hours across
  a 96-well plate at 4 FOVs, none of it visible in the per-FOV `seg` line, which
  times only `predict_instances`. `tests/test_hot_paths_stay_linear.py` counts
  the `center_of_mass` calls at 4 nuclei and at 400 and requires one either way,
  which is the property that makes the cost independent of nucleus count. The arithmetic is identical, ties included:
  NumPy's indexed assignment keeps the last write, which is what the loop's
  overwrite did when two centroids landed on one pixel.

  **A FOV that yields no cells says which reason it was.** Three outcomes were
  silent, in the same function whose nuclear half refuses a near-constant input
  with an explicit warning. A constant cytoplasm channel cannot be
  strictly exceeded by any of its own pixels, so the mask is empty
  (`cytoplasm_mask` warns twice over: once for the constant input and once for
  an empty mask however it arose). That case is **tested for** rather than
  caught: `threshold_otsu` was assumed to raise on a constant image and with the
  pinned skimage it returns the constant value instead, so the handler never
  fired while four places described it as the behaviour. An *empty* frame does
  raise, as `IndexError` rather than `ValueError`, and is its own branch. Every nucleus below
  `min_nucleus_area_px` leaves no seed at all. And a seed outside the mask is
  dropped by `watershed(mask=…)` without a word, which is what happens when a
  cytoplasm stain does not cover its nuclei — those are counted and named. Each
  line carries the FOV label the module already tracks for the `seg-input`
  diagnostics.

  **Detection thresholds.** Both methods take `--stardist_prob_thresh` (the
  object-probability cut applied to the network's objectness map before polygon
  NMS: lower detects more nuclei, including dim and marginal ones; higher keeps
  only confident detections) and `--stardist_nms_thresh` (the polygon overlap
  cut: higher lets more overlapping nuclei survive, recovering touching nuclei
  on a confluent field; lower merges more aggressively). Both default to a
  **negative sentinel** meaning *use the threshold the pretrained weights ship
  in their own `thresholds.json`* (≈ 0.479 / 0.3 for `2D_versatile_fluo`) —
  which is also what `predict_instances` does with `None`, so an untuned run
  makes byte-identical calls to one from before the thresholds were exposed
  (`tests/test_stardist_params.py` asserts the empty kwargs). The rows sit under
  the method stack, shown for both StarDist methods; the run log states the
  thresholds in force beside `Segmentation method`, because a nucleus count is
  only interpretable next to them.

  **One spelling of "auto".** `pipeline.stardist.parse_threshold` is the single
  rule: blank, the word `auto`, unparseable, `NaN`, or the CLI's negative
  sentinel all resolve to `None` (model default); anything else must be a
  probability in `[0, 1]` and is **rejected rather than clamped**, since a
  silently clamped threshold segments a plate with a parameter nobody chose.
  `NaN` is in that list because it is neither `< 0` nor `> 1.0` — it fails every
  comparison — so it passed both bounds and reached `predict_instances`, where
  every candidate nucleus compares false against it. The CLI validates
  through it in `main()`, the Analyze form emits blank-or-in-range text through
  `pipeline_service._emit_stardist_threshold_flags`, and the Playground parses
  its own two fields with it.

  **The form's starting value is not the CLI's default.** The Analyze form ships
  `analyze.seg_params.DEFAULT_PROB_THRESH_TEXT` (`"0.2"`) in the Nucleus
  probability field, because the pretrained model's own ~0.479 is conservative
  for these plates — so a run started from an untouched form detects more nuclei
  than the model default would. `--stardist_prob_thresh` keeps its `-1.0`
  sentinel, so "no flag" still means the model's own threshold and a script that
  passes nothing is unaffected; the GUI emits the number explicitly, so a GUI run
  stays fully described by its command line and its sidecar. Clearing the field
  restores the model's. Overlap (NMS) still starts blank, and the Playground's
  matching control starts blank too — an untouched preview there is deliberately
  not what an untouched Analyze run produces, which is why the help text names
  the form's starting value even when read from the Playground.

  **One description, too.** `PROB_THRESH_HELP` / `NMS_THRESH_HELP` live in the
  same module and are the text both panels show — the Analyze form (through
  `analyze.seg_params._threshold_help`, a function-local import so the form
  does not pull scipy/scikit-image into its start-up cost) and the Playground.
  They previously kept private copies and had drifted into describing the same
  two numbers differently depending on which tab you were standing in. Both
  panels attach the text to the **row and its label**, not only the entry box —
  the label is the word being read and the larger target — and put a
  `widgets.info_icon` ⓘ beside it so the explanation is findable at all.

  **Where the parameters live.** `StarDistParams` (frozen dataclass:
  `prob_thresh`, `nms_thresh`, `tile_px`) is installed once per worker by
  `_worker_init` via `set_params`, mirroring `set_model`. The inference itself is
  `pipeline.stardist.segment_nuclei(img, *, model, params)`, which reads **no**
  module state — `_segment_stardist_nuclei` is the worker-global wrapper over it,
  and the Review pane's Playground calls the same function directly, so an
  interactive preview and a batch run cannot diverge.

  **The two steps before the network are their own functions**, because a
  second caller arrived and the copy it would otherwise have made is the
  copy that gets one of them wrong. `prepare_stardist_input(img)` scrubs
  non-finite values and normalises to [0, 1] on the 1st and 99.8th
  percentiles, using `csbdeep.utils.normalize` where csbdeep is importable
  and a NumPy equivalent otherwise (measured against each other on real
  frames: maximum difference 1.19e-07, float32 epsilon). `is_near_constant(img)`
  is the refusal beside it: a field with no spread is the classic trigger for
  StarDist's ClipperLib abort, which is uncatchable and takes the process
  down, so it is declined before the network sees it rather than handled
  after. `segment_nuclei` calls both, and so does the Playground's threshold
  sweep — which reaches `model.predict` directly for its per-threshold
  resolve, and would otherwise be handing raw camera counts to a call that
  takes `normalizer=None`.

  **Tiling.** Large frames blow up StarDist's peak memory, so `pipeline.stardist`
  can tile the prediction: `--stardist_tile_px` (an Analyze-tab spinner with an
  ⓘ bubble, default `0` = **off** = predict the whole frame) sets the **max
  pixels per tile side** as `StarDistParams.tile_px`, and each worker splits any
  frame larger than that into an `n_tiles` grid (a 4K frame → 2×2 ≈ ¼ the peak);
  small frames stay untiled (`n_tiles=None`) so nothing slows needlessly.
  `set_tile_px` sets that one field without disturbing the detection thresholds —
  tiling is a memory knob, not a detection one, and must never move what is
  detected. `n_tiles` is logged per FOV. The tile-size math is pure integer logic
  covered by `tests/test_stardist_tiling.py`.
- `cellpose` — **general** Cellpose, not phase-locked. Exposes model
  (cyto3/cyto2/cyto/nuclei), diameter (the row shared with the label-free
  preset), `flow_threshold`, `cellprob_threshold`,
  and an optional second **nucleus channel** (`channels=[seg, nuc]`). Models are
  cached per type in `_CELLPOSE_MODELS`; `_worker_init` skips the StarDist/TF load.
- `classical_threshold` — Otsu + distance-transform watershed (no model), general.
- `cellpose_labelfree` — the **only** label-free method: a Cellpose `cyto3`
  brightfield preset that segments the channel marked **Phase**. The Phase
  channel is designated by a per-row checkbox (`analyze.tab._phase_token()`,
  mutually exclusive, not also smFISH) → `--phase_token`; `main()` remaps the
  phase token onto the nuclear slot (only for this method) so all per-FOV grouping
  is reused. Phase is a first-class role (`image_identity.Role.PHASE`, suffix
  `_phase`) recorded as `phase_token` in `pipeline_info.json`. Its one exposed
  parameter is the **cell diameter**: `build_pipeline_args` sends
  `--cellpose_diameter` for both Cellpose methods when it is above 0, and
  `analyze.domain.fields._CELLPOSE_FIELD_METHODS` validates it for both, so a
  typo blocks the run instead of being read as 0. What the value does is
  Cellpose's own (`CellposeModel.eval`, 3.1): a diameter *d* resizes every
  image by `diam_mean / d` (30 px for the cyto models) before segmenting, so the
  time per field scales with `(30 / d)²`; at 0 nothing is resized and nothing
  is estimated, because `pipeline.cellpose` builds `CellposeModel`, which has no
  size model (that belongs to the `models.Cellpose` wrapper). Model and
  thresholds stay general Cellpose's alone. `tests/test_labelfree_takes_a_cell_diameter.py` drives the real Analyze
  tab from the combo to the argv.

**Phase-channel correction passthrough.** A channel designated **Phase**
skips *all* background correction (flat-field + subtraction) for every
well/method — brightfield/phase has no fluorescence background to remove, and
running the correction on it only injects artefacts. The token flows to the
workers as a `--phase_token` arg threaded through `shared_kwargs`;
`_correct_image_group` takes a `phase_token` param and short-circuits that
channel. The Phase channel is still *quantified* like any other: it is a member
of `fluor_tokens`, and that membership is what gives Analyze a channel row on
which to carry the Phase checkbox.

**How the archived images are stored.** Two run options decide how much of
`<well>_out.zip` there is, and neither changes a CSV value: quantification
reads the in-memory float arrays, never the files, so the per-well CSV is
byte-identical under every combination
(`tests/test_output_storage.py::test_the_csv_is_identical_either_way`). The
end-of-run auto-threshold defaults are the one number sampled *from* the files,
so under source bit depth they can move by a fraction of a count. Both are
applied by `pipeline/output_images.write_processed_images`, the per-FOV writer
`process_image_group` calls; their names and defaults live in the import-free
`pipeline/output_policy.py` so `pipeline.cli_args` and the Analyze form can name
them without importing the imaging stack.

* `--phase_output reference` (default) / `copy`. Because the passthrough above
  leaves the phase channel's frame untouched, its `_tophat` is the input image
  pixel for pixel. Under `reference` the writer does not archive it — in the
  nuclear slot for label-free (where `main()` has remapped the nuclear token
  onto the phase token) and in the fluor slot otherwise, matched with the same
  case-insensitive comparison the passthrough uses (`is_phase_token`). Every
  reader then finds the frame in `in/<well>.zip`, and every one of them keys on
  the dataset's `phase_token` (`frame_load.phase_channel`), **never** on the
  recorded `phase_output`: that records what the *last* run asked for, and a
  re-run that found its wells up to date, a run over `--only_wells`, and a
  Merge Plates or Concatenate result (which carry dataset 1's sidecar) all
  leave archives it does not describe. Because the phase frame is never
  corrected, reading it from the input wherever no `_tophat` was archived is
  right for every dataset, and an archived one still wins. The readers are
  Review's frame loader, through
  its existing per-cell `tophat` → `fluor_raw` fallback
  (`review/data/frame_load.load_frame_array`), which does **not** record a
  phase cell in `raw_fallbacks` — the raw frame *is* the corrected one, so
  badging it uncorrected would be false on every cell — and the two Otsu
  estimators as described in §6.2 *The Otsu mode reads its samples out of the
  output archives*. The Image Table names the one case this cannot serve: a
  phase cell with no frame reads `(phase input not found — needs in/)`
  (`frame_load.missing_frame_note`), on the live grid and in an exported
  figure, because the frame was never meant to be in `out/` and "(no image)"
  would send the user looking there. A *composite* cell (an overlay blend, a
  Cell Browser multi-channel crop) still drops a member it cannot load without
  marking it, as it always has for any channel. The Datasets tools (Subset, Concatenate, Merge
  Plates) already carry `in/` with `out/`, so a referenced dataset survives
  them.
* `--tophat_dtype source` (default) / `float32`. A corrected frame is computed in
  float32, and a float32 file of camera counts is twice the bytes before
  compression; after it the saving depends on whether the correction left
  fractional values — a flat-field division does on nearly every pixel, a
  background subtraction alone on integer input often does not (measured on a
  synthetic 12-bit frame: about 60% of the zipped `_tophat` saved with a
  Gaussian flat-field, about 18% with `sliding_disk` alone). `storage_array` rounds a `_tophat` back to its input's integer
  type when, and only when, the input was `uint8` or `uint16` (the ceiling
  `load_2d_gray_with_ceiling` reports, now read for every channel by
  `_load_image_group`, not only the nuclear one) and every value is finite,
  non-negative and fits once rounded. Anything else stays float32 for that
  frame, and the run log says why at INFO for a frame that overflowed (DEBUG for
  a float or signed input, which is so on every frame): a float input may be a 0–1 normalised channel
  that rounding would erase, and a flat-field division can lift a corrected
  pixel above the camera's ceiling, where clipping would invent a saturation
  the data does not contain. `_smfish` and `_cytoplasm_tophat` are always
  float32 — a LoG response is small and fractional by construction. A reader of
  a converted file sees at most half a count of rounding; Review's loaders cast
  every frame to float32 on read, so a dataset mixing both storage types (an
  incremental run straddling the change) displays identically.

Both values are recorded in `pipeline_info.json` as `phase_output` /
`tophat_dtype`; a sidecar written before they existed is read as `copy` /
`float32`, which is what that run did (`LEGACY_*` in `output_policy`). Neither is
in the reuse key (`util/settings_digest.NOT_KEYED_ON` says why: the CSVs do not
change, and keying on options the parser always sets would invalidate every
recorded digest at once), and the remote run id leaves both flags out
(`services/remote_run_id._DIGEST_SKIP_VALUE`) so the same change is treated
alike on both sides. `build_pipeline_args` emits each flag only when the form
turns its default off, so a run at the defaults sends the argv it always did.
The consequence of not keying them is that a changed storage option applies
only to wells a run actually processes: an up-to-date well keeps the archive an
earlier run wrote, and an incremental run keeps that run's members, so a plate's
existing wells change storage only on a forced re-run — which is why the
readers above never trust the sidecar's record of it.

**Phase and segmentation are mutually exclusive outside label-free.** Because
the Phase channel skips correction entirely, naming it as the segmentation (or
cytoplasm) input under a fluorescence routine runs that routine over an
uncorrected brightfield frame — a run that completes and writes a
complete-looking set of CSVs measured on the wrong image. Both entry points
refuse the pairing: `analyze.seg_params._phase_collision_errors` in the form,
and a `parser.error` in `process_microscopy.main()` for anything arriving as
argv (the CLI and remote runs). `cellpose_labelfree` is exempt — segmenting the
phase image is its purpose.

Where the roles come from when nobody types them: `util/channel_roles` guesses a
role per channel name for both the OME converter and the Analyze folder scan. A
strong nuclear stain (`DAPI`/`Hoechst`/…) takes the segmentation role, else a
secondary `NIR`/`RFP` channel, else the first channel that does *not* read as
phase/brightfield (`_PHASE_HINT_RE` — `phase`, `brightfield`, `trans`, `dic`,
`bf`). **Where each of those may match is part of the rule.** A channel read as
phase skips both flat-field and background subtraction and is then written under
the usual `_tophat` suffix, so a fluorescence channel misread as phase is
quantified from raw frames with nothing downstream able to tell — which is what
`trans` as a bare substring did to a transfection marker, and `dic` to
`Ca-Indicator`. The three short alternatives (`trans`, `dic`, `bf`) therefore
carry a boundary on both sides, and neither of them `\b`: no *letter* may
precede or follow the hint (so `GFPtrans`, `BFP`, `Ca-Indicator` and `DICOM` are
out), while a digit may sit on either side (so `w1BF`, the ImageXpress spelling,
is in, and so are `BF1`, `DIC2` and `NIR_BF2`, which a scope with two
transmitted-light paths produces). The bound is letters only rather than
alphanumeric because forbidding a trailing digit rejected those numbered phase
channels and prevented no misreading in return — no fluorescent channel is
spelled as one of these three tokens followed by a digit. `phase` and
`brightfield` stay unbounded deliberately: they are the hints that genuinely do
head longer words, and a trailing bound would reject `PhaseContrast` and
`BrightfieldLED`, while at five letters and more neither turns up as an
incidental fragment the way `dic` sits inside `Predicted`. The secondary *nuclear* tier
(`nir|rfp`) is also left unbounded on purpose: `mRFP` / `TagRFP` / `iRFP` are
RFP-family stains, which is exactly what that tier is for, and its mistake only
proposes which channel segmentation runs on — overridden by any strong nuclear
stain, and editable in the form — rather than silently changing a number.
That last exclusion matters because the channel list arrives in
sorted-filename order rather than acquisition order, so a `DIC` channel leads it
routinely; only when every channel reads as phase does one of them take the
segmentation role, since segmentation still needs an input.

The two vocabularies overlap, and where they do **the phase reading wins over the
secondary tier**: `NIR_BF` reads as both a far-red stain and a brightfield frame,
and the cost of the two mistakes is not symmetric. A phase frame given the
segmentation role runs a fluorescence routine over an uncorrected image, and the
guard that refuses exactly that (`phase_role_conflicts`) compares against
`phase_token` — which stays *empty* when the name is claimed as nuclear instead,
so the guard has nothing to compare and reports no conflict. A strong stain still
wins outright; only the weaker tier defers. The hint pattern is bounded on both sides, and by neither
`\b`: channel names are written as separate tokens (`NIR_BF`, `Cy5_BF`), as
prefixed run-ons (`w1BF`, the ImageXpress spelling this repo's own default tokens
use), and as ordinary words that merely start the same way (`GFP_transfected`,
`GFPtrans`). `\b` finds no boundary at an underscore, so `\bbf\b` matched neither
of the first two spellings; a bare `trans` substring matched the last. The rule is
letters only, on both sides: no letter may precede a hint (rejecting `GFPtrans`
and `BFP`) and none may follow (rejecting `DICOM`), while a digit is allowed
either side (accepting `w1BF` and `DIC2`).

**Worker-pool memory + failure accounting.** Two properties of how the
parent process supervises the per-well worker pool:
- **Don't hoard records (~34 GB leak).** `_run_well_worker_pool` used to
  `extend` every per-cell record of the whole run into one parent-side list only
  to `len()` it for the final summary — at scale that pinned gigabytes in the
  orchestrator. It now keeps a running integer `total_nuclei` and lets each
  well's records free as the loop advances, so the parent holds at most one
  well's worth transiently (per-well CSV writing stays worker-side).
  `tests/test_well_worker_pool.py` pins the count.
- **Completeness is part of the output contract.** A well whose FOV-groups partly
  failed still writes its per-well CSV and `<well>_out.zip` from the groups that
  succeeded, and on disk that output is shaped exactly like a clean well's — so
  every well records how much of its input its output actually covers.
  `pipeline/run_report.py` is that record: each worker drops one small JSON file
  (`groups_total` from the well's input group count, `groups_covered` read back
  from the finished CSV's distinct `(fov, timepoint)` pairs — ground truth from
  the artifact, so it stays honest across incremental runs, resumed per-FOV
  checkpoints, and groups a failing disk never let the run attempt). `main`
  folds them into a `run_report` block inside `pipeline_info.json` and logs the
  shortfall; `core/load_controller._report_incomplete_wells` names the affected
  wells in the status line, a toast and the log at dataset load. One file per
  well, written atomically and never appended to, so the worker pool cannot
  interleave two wells into a corrupt record. **`run_report` describes one
  invocation, not the dataset** — it is cleared at the start of every run,
  merged back wholesale, and written only by wells the run actually processed,
  so an incremental run that adds a timepoint leaves a block naming the handful
  of wells that had new data. That is the reason the completeness *record*
  below is a separate thing rather than a reading of this one. Without this,
  per-field statistics
  silently described whatever fields survived and the first visible symptom was
  an absent error bar several layers from the cause. The per-FOV tracebacks in
  `<output_dir>/errors/` remain the detailed evidence.
- **A well stops attempting FOV-groups once its storage has failed repeatedly.**
  `_MAX_CONSECUTIVE_IO_FAILURES` consecutive `OSError`s abort the well's
  remaining groups (they are still reported as missing, which is what they are).
  Storage that is out of room does not recover mid-well, and `_safe_imwrite` has
  already retried each write five times with backoff before raising — so by the
  third group in a row the volume has had fifteen chances. Non-`OSError`
  failures do not trip it: a segmentation bug throwing on every frame is not a
  storage problem, and aborting would hide how widespread it is.
- **Disk capacity is accounted for in one place: `pipeline/capacity.py`.** It is
  Qt-free and stdlib-only (its free-space primitives and the single wording for
  a full volume live one layer down again, in `util/disk_space.py`, because the
  shared retry shield and the `services/` remote client need them without the
  imaging stack). Four jobs:
  - **Sizing the dataset.** `sample_image_bytes` returns one input image's
    *uncompressed* size — stat'ed from a loose TIF, or read from a well
    archive's central directory, which costs one open and extracts nothing. The
    zip path is not an optimisation but the main one: `in/<WELL>.zip` is the
    layout the pipeline segments from, and sizing a run from the archive's
    compressed size on disk under-states everything downstream.
  - **The up-front preflight.** `preflight_scratch_space` sizes the transient
    working set (per-image bytes × channels + ~6 float32 intermediates per
    FOV-group, times the run's own field/timepoint enumeration, times how many
    wells `--workers` stages at once) and the plate's durable output, and
    — the channel count being `fluor_tokens_for_quant`'s own length, since
    that list already leads with the segmentation channel and adding one for it
    would charge every FOV-group a frame that is not there —
    compares them against the *resolved* scratch base and the output directory.
    Below one well's worth of scratch it exits before reading an image, because
    a run that starts there cannot finish; everything else warns, since the
    estimates are deliberately rough. **That exit is the only hard stop in the
    app driven by an estimate, so it states the figure it tested and it can be
    overruled.** It fires on the one-well need and must quote that, not the
    whole-run figure beside it — the two differ by `--workers`, and reporting
    the larger one under the words "not enough for even one well" describes a
    shortfall the test never measured. `--allow_low_disk` (Analyze → Compute
    Options) downgrades it to the warning path, because a hard exit sitting on
    top of an estimate can refuse a run that would have finished. **The estimate
    is rough in both directions**, which is why it is a refusal that can be
    overruled rather than a number to trust: it takes the *largest* member and
    gives no deflate credit, which overshoots, while `_INTERMEDIATES_PER_GROUP`
    is a flat count where several of those images are written *per channel*,
    which undershoots past about four channels. The free figure it is compared
    against is `statvfs`-available, which on APFS excludes purgeable space and
    reads well under what the machine will hand over — a Mac measured at 14.3 GB
    in Finder reported 6.0 GiB here. Any free figure quoted to a user says so,
    because it will not match their file manager and a check whose numbers
    cannot be reconciled reads as broken. The wording of the override
    lives once, in `capacity.ALLOW_LOW_DISK_HELP`, shared by the CLI flag's help
    and the checkbox's tooltip. When scratch and output share a volume —
    the default, `~/.allwell/scratch` beside an output dir on the home volume —
    the two needs are summed against one free figure, because checking either
    alone reports that the run fits when it does not. The resolved base is
    logged on the `Scratch  :` line either way.
  - **The mid-run projection.** `OutputCapacityMonitor`, fed one call per
    completed well by `_run_well_worker_pool`, measures the output actually
    written and projects the wells still to come. It warns once, naming the
    measured per-well size — a real number, carrying the real compression ratio
    and FOV count, unlike anything the preflight can estimate — while there is
    still room to act. The estimate of durable output in `estimate_well_output_bytes`
    takes no credit for deflate for the same reason: an assumed ratio would be
    invented rather than measured, which is why that half of the preflight only
    ever warns.
  - **Saying so when a volume fills anyway.** `util.disk_space.space_message` is
    the only wording for `ENOSPC`, and `util.retry_io.retry_io` rewrites the
    exception through it (preserving errno 28) for every caller that passes the
    target `path`. A bare `OSError: [Errno 28] No space left on device` names no
    volume, and the volume it happened on is routinely not the one the user
    would check.
- **Exhaustion is the common cause of a partial run, and "there is room next to
  my data" does not rule it out.** The scratch base defaults to
  `~/.allwell/scratch` (§6.5) — the *home* volume — while the dataset usually
  lives on an external or network disk. Each FOV-group stages ~6 float32
  intermediates there, so a 6-field × 23-timepoint well is several GB and a
  plate of them is far more; the input archives, meanwhile, are the only
  compressed copy in the run, so a volume with ten times their size free is not
  close to enough. The durable results compound it from the other side: every
  `<well>_out.zip` stays on the output volume for the rest of the plate, so a
  run can start with room and end without it. `pipeline.io._safe_imwrite`
  retries with backoff and triages disk-full versus transient, but once space is
  genuinely gone every remaining group fails the same way: the run continues,
  logging a failure per group, and produces a full complement of
  complete-looking per-well outputs. Point `$ALLWELL_SCRATCH_DIR` (or the
  Analyze tab's *Scratch disk* field) at a roomier volume when the home volume
  is tight.
- **A well's extracted inputs are reclaimed before its zip-up.** Building
  `<well>_out.zip` while the staging directory still holds every intermediate is
  the well's peak footprint, and on a single-volume setup the extracted TIFs are
  competing for the same bytes at exactly that moment. `process_well_zip_task`
  removes `_tmp_extract_<well>` as soon as the groups are processed; the
  `finally` block still removes it (it has to cover the failure paths) and is a
  no-op by then.
- **Per-FOV failure traces.** A failed FOV-group persists its full traceback to
  `<output_dir>/errors/<well>_<fov>_pid<N>.txt` (`_dump_fov_failure_trace`,
  mirroring `_dump_well_failure_trace`), and `classify_log_line` treats
  "failed" as ERROR so it surfaces in the GUI live log. **A line that states its
  own severity is believed before it is sniffed**: an explicit `[info]` /
  `[warn]` / `[error]` tag wins, and so does a `note:` marker, because the
  keyword pass reads whole lines *including paths* and this directory is called
  `errors/`. On a remote run the fetch pulls that directory back so Validate &
  Repair can read it, and a clean run has none to pull — so
  `[remote] note: …/errors/ not pulled` was painted red by the name of the
  folder whose absence it was reporting, while the identical line about
  `pipeline_info.json` came out INFO. The note itself now says what the absence
  means (`_rsync_optional`'s `absent_note`), since "not pulled" alone reads as a
  fault for a source whose absence is the good case. It stops short of declaring
  the run clean: a non-zero rc covers both "nothing was there" and "something
  was, and it could not be fetched", and the fetch cannot tell those apart.
  Whole-well vs
  partial-FOV failures are accounted separately, with a per-well breakdown and
  PARTIAL warnings that point at `--incremental`. Transient short/zero NAS
  writes are shielded by `pipeline.io._safe_imwrite`'s retry-with-backoff, which
  also triages disk-full vs transient rather than always claiming disk-full.

### 6.3 `all_well_launcher.py`

PyInstaller entry point. Two responsibilities:

1. Set the matplotlib backend to `QtAgg` before any `pyplot` import.
2. Re-dispatch to `process_microscopy.main()` when invoked with
   `--run-pipeline` as the first argument. The Analyze tab uses that path
   when running inside a frozen `.app` bundle — there's no Python
   interpreter on `sys.executable`, so re-exec'ing the launcher with the
   sentinel argv routes the same Python process into the pipeline.
   `--run-zipper`, `--run-bootstrap` and `--run-report` are the same trick
   for `well_plate_zipper.main()`, `services/remote_bootstrap.main()` and the
   headless report's `allwell_report.main()` (which from source is
   `python allwell_report.py`; the spec lists it as a hidden import, since the
   launcher reaches it through a function-level import).

A frozen **windowed** (`console=False`) build leaves `sys.stdout` /
`sys.stderr` — and `sys.__stdout__` / `sys.__stderr__` — set to None even
though the parent attached a live pipe to fd 1/2 and is reading it line by
line. `util.frozen_io.ensure_std_streams` wraps the descriptors back up;
`process_microscopy` and `well_plate_zipper` call it from their own `main()`,
and the launcher calls it in the `--run-bootstrap` branch because that entry
point is reached through `importlib` rather than through a `main()` of its
own. The repair covers `sys.stdout` / `sys.stderr` only, so the bootstrap's
log tee wraps that pair rather than the dunder pair, which stays None for the
life of the process (`tests/test_bootstrap_frozen_dispatch.py`).

### 6.4 `services/`

Small dependency-light service modules used by `analyze/tab.py`:

| Module | What |
|--------|------|
| `pipeline_service.py` | `find_pipeline_script` / `build_pipeline_args` / `spawn_pipeline`. `build_pipeline_args` emits each flag only when present and non-zero (including `--stardist_tile_px` (>0 only) and `--phase_token`); it is decomposed into small table-driven emitters to satisfy the complexity ratchet, behaviour unchanged (`tests/test_pipeline_arg_validation.py`). The StarDist detection thresholds get their own emitter (`_emit_stardist_threshold_flags`) rather than the integer one: they are probabilities, and blank / `auto` / out-of-range emits nothing so the run falls back to the pretrained model's own value. |
| `frame_preview.py` | The GUI-side StarDist inference behind the Playground's **Segment** button. Holds the session's single loaded model (`_GUI_STARDIST_MODEL`) and the `find_spec` dependency probe, and calls the pipeline's own `pipeline.stardist.segment_nuclei` — so what the Playground shows cannot disagree with what a run produces. **TF and StarDist are imported inside `segment_frame`, never at module scope**: the Playground's controller imports its worker (and through it this module) at GUI start-up, so a module-scope TF import would add tens of seconds and gigabytes to launching the app for everyone who never presses Segment. Qt-free and `review`-free, which is why it sits here rather than beside the feature that uses it. `segment_frame` takes an optional `on_stage(name)` — a plain callable, so the module stays Qt-free — and reports `STAGE_LOADING` then `STAGE_SEGMENTING`, because only the first call of a session pays the model load and a UI that reports both phases identically leaves that one looking like a hang. |
| `pipeline_runner.py` | Asynchronous subprocess + stdout-streaming wrapper used by Analyze. Hosts `ProgressTracker`, a stateless log-line parser that turns the pipeline's stdout into structured run events — coarse `("stage", name)`, per-well `("well_stage", (well, stage))` (`upload`/`active`/`process`/`threshold`/`download`) — a completion carries a third element, the word the run journal should record for that well, because the plate's `process` is deliberately lossy about whether anything was computed, per-well FOV sub-progress `("well_fov", (well, done, total))`, per-well transfer progress `("well_xfer", (well, "up"|"down", fraction))`, and `("zipper_well", well)` — which drive the live `RunDashboard`. `download` fires only once **both** the output zip and the well's CSV(s) have landed (a server-side threshold or a zip-only fetch must not read as "downloaded"). Well completion is counted by **identity, not by marker**: the three terminal markers (`Well X — done.`, `Well X — up to date`, `SKIP well X — output already exists`) all feed one set of finished wells, so a well announced terminal twice is counted once and reported as `("well_repeat", well)`. That matters in batched remote mode, where the pipeline is launched once per batch: a well announced terminal by one batch and again by the next drove the headline to "N / N wells (100%)" with wells still outstanding. The batches once shared a remote input directory and relied on the Fetcher having emptied it in time, which is where the repeats came from; the driver's whole-directory swap removes that particular source, and the identity-based count stays because it is the honest way to count a marker that can legitimately repeat. The announced total is a floor, never a ceiling — more distinct wells finishing than the banner promised raises it (a fresh `("well_total", n)`) rather than printing a fraction over 100%. |
| `remote_manifest.py` | `_REQUIRED_REMOTE_FILES` — the one list of files a remote run needs on the worker — and `repo_root`, the directory those paths are relative to (the runner syncs from it; the batched process puts it on `sys.path` for the local threshold pass). A data declaration with no behaviour, and it lives apart from `remote_runner` because the two guards over it pulled opposite ways: `tests/test_remote_manifest.py` requires an entry for every new `pipeline/` or `util/` module, while `REMOTE_RUNNER_BUDGET` caps the file it used to sit in — so a required entry could fail the budget, and the budget could only be met by omitting it. Here a new entry costs the runner nothing. Re-exported by `remote_runner`, so `services/remote_bootstrap`, the PyInstaller spec, the manifest tests and the several `util/` and `pipeline/` docstrings that cite it by that path all keep working — with the same re-export caveat as the row below: patching the name on `remote_runner` does not reach a reader that imports it from here. |
| `remote_transport.py` | How bytes and commands reach a remote host: what this rsync build supports (`_rsync_version` and the capability probes over it), how a path is quoted so the remote shell expands `~` rather than making a directory called it (`_remote_quote` / `_remote_join`), the retry funnel every transfer passes through (`_rsync_with_retry`, `_rsync_run_cancellable`), the non-fatal remote `rm` the Fetcher runs after each well lands (`delete_remote_paths`, which takes paths and knows nothing of wells), and the reader that turns rsync's progress chatter back into lines. Knows nothing about a *run* — no run id, no journal, no well. Callers import these names from here, never through `remote_runner`. Each importer holds its own **binding**, so a patch reaches only the callers that look the name up in the patched module: to steer a caller that lives here (the retry funnel's call to `_rsync_run_cancellable`, say), patch `remote_transport`; to steer the `Fetcher`, patch `remote_fetch`. |
| `remote_run_id.py` | Where a remote run lives, and whether an earlier one's work may be reused — two questions sharing a module because they are keyed on the same facts, and every reuse defect here came from one being keyed on less than the other. `_compute_run_id` and `pipeline_argv_digest` decide the address; `_choose_remote_output_dir` decides whether a recorded one may be used instead; `remote_run_dir` / `remote_run_paths` are its single spelling. Pure — no ssh, no filesystem — which is what lets the highest-stakes predicate in the remote path be tested directly rather than through a harness. |
| `remote_commands.py` | The shell a remote run sends, as strings: `_compose_remote_cmd` (the single-launch line — record the pidfile, optionally exec the scheduler launcher, activate conda, wait for the upload, exec the pipeline), `_compose_driver_cmd` and `_batch_driver_snippet` (the batched driver that holds one allocation and runs a pipeline per batch, stopping early when the run's suspend request appears), `_remote_scratch_export`, the batch handshake names (`BATCH_READY`, `BATCH_DONE`, `BATCH_DONE_MARKER`), and `pack_for_login_shell` / `unpack_login_shell_command`. Both launch paths send their command through `pack_for_login_shell` — gzip + base64 into one short line of plain characters that the login shell unpacks and `eval`s, so `$$` and `exec` still act on the login shell and the pidfile and cancel channel are unchanged. The scripts are thousands of characters across seventeen lines with hundreds of quotes, and on a Windows client the one `ssh` argument they travel in is rebuilt by `list2cmdline` and parsed again by Git for Windows' `ssh.exe`; a batched launch past 8,191 characters failed there with `bash: -c: line 17: syntax error: unexpected end of file`. A remote without `base64` or `gzip` fails with exit `UNPACK_FAILED_EXIT` and a line saying so, never with an empty `eval` that would exit 0. Tests read a spawned command through `unpack_login_shell_command`. No ssh and no I/O, so a quoting decision is tested by reading the string and the driver by running it in `bash`. Re-exported by `remote_runner`; imports the transport's quoting and the conda / wait snippets, never the runner. |
| `remote_suspend.py` | Asking a running remote pipeline to suspend: `request_suspend` (touch the run's request file over ssh, bounded by `SUSPEND_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_S`, telling a batched run's local loop first), and `_AnySet`, the Event-shaped view a batch upload watches so either a Stop or a suspend ends it. `RemoteRunner.request_suspend` is a one-line delegate; `remote_runner` binds `request_suspend` for that and nothing else from here. |
| `remote_recover.py` | Before any unforced remote run stages its upload, `recover_finished_outputs` downloads what the previous run of the plate finished on the host and never brought home: it finds that run's directory through the journal's recorded address (`stored_remote_address`, the three re-attach keys) and runs `FetchedOutputVerifier.verify` against it. Matches on the current argv digest, then on `legacy_argv_digests` so plates recorded by an earlier build are found. Returns a `Recovery`; `pulled` makes `PipelineRunner` stage incrementally, `ok=False` means listed wells could not be pulled and the run is ended rather than re-uploading them. Declines for a forced run. |
| `remote_scratch.py` | The leaves of the remote staging work, stdlib + `util` only: where transient bytes go while a transfer is in flight (`_scratch_dir`, `_transit_dir`, `TRANSIT_SUBDIR`), how a stale one is swept (`sweep_stale_scratch`), whether an archive arrived whole (`_zip_is_complete`), and what the user's own input archives hash to (`fingerprint_archives`, `source_fingerprint` — the discriminator the remote re-attach is keyed on). Nine functions whose only tie to `remote_runner` was one constant; every caller, the runner's own `source_fingerprint` read included, imports them from here. |
| `remote_upload.py` | Getting a run's input onto the remote host, once. `DatasetCache` keys each upload by a stat-based fingerprint of the staged archives, so re-running the same input is a metadata round trip rather than a re-upload; streams rsync's output well by well (`_run_rsync_streaming`, `_UploadWellProgress`) so the Upload rail and each well's dial fill as its archive lands; and keeps the remote cache inside the host's budget. Its short ssh control commands are bounded by `SSH_CONTROL_TIMEOUT_S`. Line-budgeted (`REMOTE_UPLOAD_BUDGET`). |
| `remote_jobs.py` | The scheduler jobs a remote run holds, and making sure none outlives it. `close_remote_job` is the teardown backstop every exit the app survives goes through (it reads the job id from `<pidfile>.slurm` and `scancel`s it); `sweep_orphaned_allocation` is what the next run of the same plate does about an exit the app did not survive, and returns its verdict (`swept`, `owned`, `notmine`, `unknown`, `none`) because the batched path acts on it. Both refuse to cancel a job that is not the caller's (`_only_my_job`), and both are no-ops on a host with no `compute_launcher`. `RemoteRunner.close_remote_job` and `_sweep_orphaned_allocation` delegate here. Line-budgeted (`REMOTE_JOBS_BUDGET`). |
| `remote_process.py` | The run as the GUI sees it: `_RemoteProcess` wraps the single ssh that runs the pipeline and `_BatchedRemoteProcess` the driver that holds one allocation and runs the plate batch by batch. Both present the `subprocess.Popen` surface `PipelineRunner` reads and tee every line to the `Fetcher`, so per-well downloads start the moment a well is announced done; `wait` flushes the `Fetcher` and `terminate`/`kill` cancel it, and every exit path ends the run heartbeat (`_UploadHeartbeat`) exactly once. A batch whose driver vanished marks the run failed (1); a stopped one reports 130. `tests/test_remote_process.py` drives the single-launch wrapper against a real child process. Line-budgeted (`REMOTE_PROCESS_BUDGET`). |
| `remote_staging.py` | Turning the user's input into the per-well archives a remote run uploads: `stage_local_zips` detects the layout (one zip per well, well folders, loose TIFs, or a mix left by an interrupted zip-up), zips folders and loose TIFs **into the input directory itself** so the next run finds zips and skips the zip-up (a folder's archived TIFs are removed the moment its own zip is published), and returns a `ZippedInput`. The channel filter and an incremental run's split are both planned from each archive's member list before any image data is read, and only archives that change are written — to a staging directory beside the input, never over the user's archives. `ZippedInput.cleanup` removes every staging directory a run made (the filter's and the split's, joined), a failure part way through removes its own before the error propagates, and a filter that matches no image in any well is refused before anything moves, on both the ZIP and the MIXED path. Line-budgeted (`REMOTE_STAGING_BUDGET`); `tests/test_remote_staging.py` pins the cleanup contract. |
| `remote_fetch.py` | Bringing a remote run's output home, and proving it arrived. `Fetcher` pulls each well's output the moment the pipeline announces it done (overlapping download with later wells' compute), merges an incremental run's partial zip and CSV into the local ones rather than overwriting them, keeps the mid-run `pipeline_info.json` current, and removes a well's remote files only once its local artefact is in place. `FetchedOutputVerifier` runs after the pipeline exits: it pulls the top-level artefacts, merges the fetched sidecar's run-report, field-quality and user blocks with the local ones, writes the client-side completeness record, checks every expected well's CSV and non-empty `<well>_out.zip` are present (and replaced, for a forced well), re-pulls what is missing, and returns a `FetchVerification`. It never deletes the run's remote directory — `RemoteRunner.verify_and_cleanup` does that, on a passing verdict only. Its collaborators (host, run record, the dataset cache whose ssh it borrows, the stop flag) are passed in, never read off the runner. Line-budgeted (`REMOTE_FETCH_BUDGET`). |
| `remote_run_state.py` | `_RemoteRun`, the record one remote run carries from staging through fetch, and the two enums in it the user chooses — `LocalInputMode` and `OutputFilter`. Shared by the runner, the process wrappers and the `Fetcher`, so it lives in none of them and none has to import another to reach it. |
| `remote_batch_staging.py` | What a batched run's retry may reuse of an earlier attempt's staged uploads. `prune_staged` empties a kept `b<i>` / `bg/` of every entry not in the batch about to be uploaded and logs how many of the batch's wells were already there, falling back to `rm -rf` of the directory on any answer but a clean listing. The reuse is safe because the run directory is keyed on the staged archives' fingerprint; the *Batched mode* paragraph in the `remote_runner.py` row says why. |
| `slurm_batch_script.py` | Turning a JupyterHub profile into an `srun` launcher the way the cluster does: `launcher_from_batch_script` renders the spawner's job template (Jinja-style `{{ var }}` / `{% if var %}` or `{var}`, each `req_<name>` as `<name>`) and keeps the `#SBATCH` resource options only — partition, CPUs, memory, time, GPUs, constraint and their kin — because `--output`, `--export`, `--chdir` and `--ntasks` describe JupyterHub's batch job and would break a step the app runs. `directive_flags` sorts one directive's words into flags and stray words. `single_task` folds a task count into the CPU count: a template that asks for cores the batch way (`#SBATCH -n {nprocs}`) gives a batch job that many CPUs, while `-n` on the app's `srun` would start the pipeline that many times, so the step asks for one task with *tasks × cpus-per-task* CPUs — dropping it left the step one CPU and the pipeline one worker. A resource option whose whole value is a variable the profile leaves unset is skipped quietly (the profile asks for no such resource); one with more around the variable is reported. A stray word, or a resource line that needs a value the profile does not set, is reported in `ScriptLauncher.dropped`; nothing is appended to a launcher where `srun` would take it for the program. |
| `JOB_CLOSED_LINE` (in `pipeline_runner.py`) | What `PipelineRunner._note_scheduler_job_closed` prints, on a host with a `compute_launcher` only, once the remote process that held the run's Slurm job has exited — printed locally because the single-run launch `exec`s the pipeline, so nothing inside the job runs after it. `ProgressTracker` turns it, or the batched driver's `releasing the allocation`, into `("slurm_job", ("closed", {}))`, and the node-specs line `pipeline/slurm_node.py` logs into `("slurm_job", ("specs", {…}))`; the Analyze pane's job indicator (`analyze/slurm_job_view.py`) folds those with the existing `sched` events. `tests/test_the_slurm_job_indicator.py`. |
| `remote_srun_retry.py` | The `srun` launch wrapper: prefer powered-on nodes via `sinfo`, retry a node that fails to boot up to three times with it excluded, merge the user's own `--exclude`; and `stray_launcher_words`, which finds a word `srun` would run as the program. The *Scheduled compute* paragraph in the `remote_runner.py` row says why. |
| `remote_wire.py` | The remote client's line vocabulary: `TRANSIENT_PREFIX` / `WELL_XFER_PREFIX` (live-state lines `ProgressTracker` routes to the status line and never logs), the transfer cadences, the exhausted-retry advice, and the `Well X — done.` / mode-banner patterns the `Fetcher` triggers on. Stdlib-only and importing nothing else of the remote client's, so every stage reads it without a cycle. |
| `remote_runner.py` | The remote-execution path: uploads the input zip-set to a worker host, runs the pipeline there, and the `Fetcher` (in `remote_fetch.py`) pulls each well's `<well>_out.zip` + CSVs back. The runner orchestrates; turning the user's input into the archives it uploads is `remote_staging.py`, getting them onto the host once is `remote_upload.py`, the run as a process the GUI reads and stops is `remote_process.py`, bringing output home and proving it arrived is `remote_fetch.py`, the scheduler jobs a run holds — closing one, and sweeping one a crashed run left — are `remote_jobs.py`, the record a run carries is `remote_run_state.py`, and the lines its stages print and parse are `remote_wire.py`. **It pulls `pipeline_info.json` too, as early as the remote has one**, so the plate can be opened in Review while the run is still going: per-well CSVs arrive as each well finishes, and without the sidecar there is nothing to interpret them with — no filename schema, no channel tokens, no `available_timepoints` / `available_fovs`, so the viewer falls back to guessing channels from CSV column names. Nothing on stdout announces that file, so `Fetcher._sidecar_loop` polls for it on its own thread every `SIDECAR_POLL_S` rather than waiting on a marker; the first attempt waits out an interval, because the thread starts in the same breath as the ssh that launches the pipeline and at that instant the remote cannot have written it. The window is hours (`SIDECAR_POLL_MAX_S`) since what it waits out is the scheduler queue, not the pipeline's start-up. Two rules keep it from fighting the other writers of that path. It **never overwrites**: a sidecar already present locally belongs to a previous run of this dataset and carries cell-gating thresholds, sample definitions, ratios, notes and the `run_report`, none of which the remote's copy has. And what it installs is **stamped `provisional`**, because a sidecar written by a job still running describes only the input that job was handed — one batch's split, in batched mode — so its `available_*` are short of the plate and there is no `run_report` at all; `verify_and_cleanup` replaces the file wholesale at the end and the mark goes with it, while a run that never got there leaves the mark in place, which is the honest outcome. The poll is off by default (`poll_sidecar`) so a `Fetcher` built to exercise one method in a test never reaches the network on a timer; both production call sites enable it and `tests/test_remote_midrun_sidecar.py` fails if a third one forgets. All rsync calls funnel through `_rsync_with_retry` (transient exit codes 10/11/12/30/35 retried on the `_RSYNC_RETRY_DELAYS = (2,4,8)`s schedule, slept in ≤0.25s chunks so the Stop button stays responsive; 11 is *error in file I/O*, what a fault on the local end of a transfer looks like). Every write the client itself makes on a user volume — staging copies off the input dir, `Fetcher._materialize`, the `pipeline_info.json` rewrite — goes through `util.retry_io.retry_io` for the same reason (§6.5). `_zip_is_complete` (`zipfile.is_zipfile`) guards the final fetch so a timed-out-but-materialised rsync isn't mistaken for a still-pending one — the bug where the last download "just sat there." **Which conda env the pipeline runs in** is `_conda_env_selector`'s answer, resolved once per runner from the host's `remote_python` and used by both the argv builder and the shell composer so they cannot disagree: left at its default the field is a *placeholder* and the env is resolved by name (`conda run -n allwell`), which is what makes a host with a pre-existing system conda work at all; set by the user to an `<env>/bin/python` it selects that prefix (`conda run -p <env>`). `_conda_env_guard` then verifies the env exists on the remote — inside the scheduler allocation when there is one, since the compute node is where it has to exist — and aborts with a `[remote]`-prefixed message naming the host, conda's base, the envs it can see, and the fix. Without it the run reached `conda run` and died on conda's bare `EnvironmentLocationNotFound`, which in a scrolling log is indistinguishable from an error the pipeline raised. A cache hit execs `true` and skips the check. **"Does the env exist" is conda's own question** — a prefix is an environment iff it holds `conda-meta/history` — and the shell that answers it, `CONDA_ENV_SHELL_HELPERS`, is shared with `services/remote_bootstrap.py` so the runner's check and the bootstrap's create-or-skip decision cannot disagree. See §6.6 for why that mattered. **Scheduled compute (HPC lobby/login nodes):** when the host's `compute_launcher` is set (e.g. an `srun …` line), `_compose_remote_cmd` wraps *only* the pipeline command into a scheduler allocation (`srun … bash -lc '<conda>; exec python …'`) so the work lands on a compute node the cluster schedules while staging/cache/fetch/cleanup stay on the login node against the shared filesystem; the run records `$SLURM_JOB_ID` and `close_remote_job` (`scancel`) guarantees the allocation is torn down on completion / failure / cancel. **An `srun` launcher is wrapped** by `services/remote_srun_retry.wrap_srun_launch`, from `remote_commands._launch`, which both composers end in. On a cluster that powers idle nodes down, Slurm can grant a sleeping node and boot it; `srun` waits only as long as the cluster's `ResumeTimeout`, then prints `Something is wrong with the boot of the nodes`, gives the allocation back and exits (`NODE_FAIL`), and nothing in Slurm retries an `srun` step. The wrapper, a POSIX `sh` loop on the login node, asks `sinfo` before each attempt and passes `--exclude` for every node of the launcher's partition that is not powered on (`AWAKE_STATES`: `idle`, `mix`, `alloc`, `comp`), when at least one is. Before launching with that exclusion it asks Slurm, with `srun --test-only` (which queues nothing), whether the request could run on those nodes at all; when it could not — the awake nodes are the wrong instance type for a `--constraint`, say — it drops the exclusion and prints `no powered-on node matches this request — Slurm will start one`, rather than letting the first real `srun` fail with `Requested node configuration is not available`. A request the test passes but the real launch still finds unsatisfiable (a node's state changed in between) is retried once without the exclusion. On a boot failure the wrapper adds the node `srun` named to the exclusion and launches again, up to `SRUN_BOOT_RETRIES` (3) times, then names every failed node. Each retry prints a `[remote] scheduler: requesting allocation via:` line, which `ProgressTracker` already reads as "waiting", so the progress view returns to its queue clock. The user's own `--exclude` / `-x` is merged in rather than passed twice, because Slurm keeps only the last. The loop cannot `exec` srun, so each attempt records srun's own PID through `sh -c 'echo $$ > pidfile; exec …'`, keeping the `kill -TERM $(cat pidfile)` cancel channel pointed at srun. The launch's output is copied to `<pidfile>.srun-err` with `tee` and only lines beginning `srun:` are searched. It is `tee` and not an `awk` filter because `mawk`, the default `awk` on Debian and Ubuntu login nodes, fills its whole input buffer before handling a line: a filter held the job's first lines back until more output arrived, and a run that had just been allocated a node sat silent (`test_the_job_s_first_line_arrives_before_the_job_ends` measures the delay). **A launcher with a loose word is refused**: `srun` stops reading options at the first word that is not one, so a word such as an instance type left after `--mem=60G` becomes the program, and the job fails with `execve(): <word>: No such file or directory` only once a node starts. `stray_launcher_words` finds a non-option word that follows an option written with `=` or another such word (a word after a bare option may be its value and is left alone); the Remotes dialog refuses to save such a launcher, and `remote_commands._launch` refuses to launch one, since a saved host is never re-checked by the dialog. Any other launcher is exec'd unwrapped as before. `tests/test_srun_boot_retry.py` runs the wrapper under the system `sh` with stand-in `srun` and `sinfo`, and checks that the composed job script reaches `srun` byte for byte as it reaches an unwrapped launcher. Empty `compute_launcher` = direct-on-host execution (the default). **A queue wait is announced, timed, and named**, because it is otherwise indistinguishable from a hang: the upload finishes and the log stops. `_scheduler_handoff_lines` writes the hand-off and is called from **every** launch path — the batched one composed the same launcher but announced nothing, so a batched run fell silent at the exact moment it began waiting. `ProgressTracker` turns those lines, plus the scheduler's own `srun: job N queued and waiting for resources` / `has been allocated resources`, into a `sched` event, and `AnalyzeProgressMixin._on_scheduler` runs a 1-Hz clock reading *Waiting for the scheduler — 4m12s (job 4812345)* with a log breadcrumb every two minutes repeating the elapsed time, the job id and the **request** (an unsatisfiable one — a partition that does not exist, a `--gres` the cluster cannot honour — is the usual cause of an indefinite queue). The job id comes from the scheduler's stderr rather than the `.slurm` sidecar because the sidecar is written from *inside* the allocation and so does not exist while the job is pending; a site whose scheduler words those lines differently still gets the wait announced and timed off the app's own lines, and loses only the id. The wait is what finally retracts the plate-wide `Transferring… N%` label: `set_transfer(None)` otherwise fires only on a *compute* event, which by definition has not happened while the job is queued, which is why the status sat on `Transferring… 100%` for the whole wait. **A remote run does not write to the client's home volume.** Every downloaded `<well>_out.zip` used to be staged through `~/.allwell/scratch` and then materialised into the output directory, so each byte of a plate's results crossed two filesystems and the first of them was one the run had no reason to touch — a full home volume stopped runs whose own input and output volumes had room, which is the `ENOSPC` users hit. `_transit_dir` puts a file in transit beside the volume it is going to (or, for the upload-side archive rewrites, the one it came from): a dot-prefixed `.allwell-transit`, so every dataset scan in the app skips it, removed as soon as the file it held is in place, and swept by `sweep_stale_scratch(also=…)` when a hard quit leaks one. This does not re-create what `pipeline.io.scratch_base_for` warns about — that warning is about the *pipeline's* per-FOV working set, tens of thousands of create/fsync/rename operations from every worker, where this is one file per well written once and moved once, onto a volume that already receives exactly those bytes by copy. What changes is that the move becomes a same-volume rename and the home volume is off the path. A volume that refuses the directory falls back to the scratch base and **says so**, once per volume; falling back silently would be the original failure with the explanation removed. **The pipeline's scratch on the remote is a per-host setting**, `remote_scratch_dir`, exported as `ALLWELL_SCRATCH_DIR` inside both composed commands (single-shot and batch driver) because that is what `pipeline.io.scratch_base_for` reads; `services/pipeline_runner` sets the same variable in the GUI's own environment, which reaches a local subprocess and nothing else. Empty leaves the remote on its `~/.allwell/scratch`, which on a cluster is the home quota — the worst available volume for a working set of several uncompressed images per field. It is the one path in the file deliberately **not** run through `_remote_quote`: the values that matter (`$TMPDIR`, `$SLURM_TMPDIR`, `/scratch/$USER`) need remote-side expansion, so it is emitted in double quotes with a leading `~` rewritten to `$HOME` first, and a value carrying shell syntax is refused rather than composed into a command that would fail on the remote naming nothing. The `remotes.toml` schema is the live contract in `services/remote_config.py`. **The end-of-run completeness check runs client-side, once, after the fetch.** `_build_remote_argv` appends `--no_run_check` to every remote launch and `verify_and_cleanup` calls `run_client_side_completeness_check` instead, immediately after `refresh_pipeline_info_available_from_outputs` (which rewrites the very `available_*` fields a check would otherwise read stale) and before the `ok` gate, since a run that came back short is exactly the one whose record is worth having. Three reasons it cannot run remotely, and they compound: an incremental run's remote output dir holds only the uploaded split, so a record written there inventories the wrong tree; the fetched sidecar overwrites the local one, so the record would be destroyed on arrival; and a batched run is N separate pipeline launches, each of which would describe its own slice as if it were the plate. Running on the client also answers a strictly better question — *did it get here*, rather than *did the remote produce it*. Whatever `run_check` the fetch brought back is **dropped before the local check runs**: the remote's suppression writes the same "turned off" stub a user's own `--no_run_check` would, and that stub surviving would tell a user they had turned the check off when they had not. The two outcomes are therefore an honest record or none at all, and none reads as "not checked", which is what happened. **Empty-well correction reaches every batch from one upload.** The pipeline builds its `empty_well` background and flat-field fields from whatever blank wells are in the directory it is pointed at, at the moment it starts — and batched mode stages one batch at a time, so a blank left in the ordinary slicing corrected the batch it landed in and nothing else. Wells sort alphabetically and blanks are conventionally H12/G12, so in practice it was the last batch, and every earlier one produced numbers with the background left in whole. Nothing marked them: `_empty_well_field` returns `None` for a channel with no model and the frame passes through untouched, so the output is bit-for-bit the raw input and indistinguishable from a corrected well. A blank is a full well of uncompressed frames — the same size as any other — so it cannot be copied into each batch. `_empty_well_blanks` reads the run's own argv for `--background_well` plus an `empty_well` mode, holds those archives out of the batch slicing, and uploads them **once** to `runs/<run_id>/bg/`, outside the staging the driver's `rm -rf in && mv b<i> in` replaces. The pipeline's `--background_dir` names that directory, so every batch builds the same reference; the driver hard-links each blank that still needs processing into the final batch (`ln`, one filesystem, no bytes) so it is run once for its own output — named one by one rather than globbing `bg/`, since on a re-run some blanks are references only and linking those back in would reprocess a well the user's own re-run declined. **The staging filters do not touch a blank at all**: `stage_local_zips` takes the background wells and `_plan_staging` stages them whole, the way a `--force_wells` well bypasses the incremental diff. Without that, an incremental re-run finds every one of the blank's FOVs already processed, drops it, and starves the whole plate of the correction — and a blank with *some* new fields would be thinned to those, so the field would be estimated from a fraction of the reference while the log reported it built. When the only wells left to run are blanks, they are treated as ordinary wells instead: an empty batch would be uploaded to a directory the driver cannot then `mv`. **And a correction that cannot be built stops the run.** `_require_empty_well_models` raises when `empty_well` was requested with named wells and no model came back, naming the wells and the directory searched — an `INFO` line reading `(none found)` was the only previous signal, for a run that had explicitly asked for the correction. **Rewriting a well archive is a cost decision, and it says why.** The upload planner (`_plan_staging`) reads each archive's central directory — member names *and* compressed sizes, one read — and rewrites an archive only when the channel filter (or an incremental run's already-done FOV-groups) drops members worth at least `remote_config.REWRITE_MIN_SAVING` of its bytes. Rewriting costs a full local read and write before a byte is uploaded and buys only a smaller transfer, so shedding two small frames from a multi-gigabyte well is a bad trade — the remote ignores channels it was not asked for anyway, so sending them costs bandwidth and nothing else. Either way the plan line names the count, the fraction and **the reason**: the channel token parsed out of the dropped members' own names (or the bare filename, when the name does not decompose under the run's schema, since a guessed token is worse than none), or the FOV-group count for an incremental drop. Previously the log said only *that* it was rewriting, which left "every channel is selected, so why is it copying my plate?" answerable from no line the run emits.
