An archive from which nothing is dropped is passed through untouched and logs nothing — `keep is None` holds exactly when nothing was dropped, which is the invariant every diagnosis of this path rests on. **What counts as an image is one question with one answer**, `util/image_exts.GROUP_IMAGE_EXTS`, read by both `process_microscopy`'s scanners and this planner: they had drifted to `.tif`/`.tiff` here against `.tif`/`.tiff`/`.png`/`.jpg`/`.jpeg` there, so a `.png` member was invisible to the planner and was silently dropped from any archive rewritten for another reason — input the remote would have processed. **Batched mode** (`remote_batch_size > 0` → `_BatchedRemoteProcess`) uploads and runs the plate in slices so peak remote disk is one batch of input plus about one well of output. **One allocation serves every batch.** Each batch used to compose its own `srun`, so a scheduler-backed host queued once per batch and handed the node back in between — an allocation is the expensive thing to obtain and the cheap thing to keep. `_batch_driver_snippet` builds a loop that stays inside one job: it waits for each batch's `BATCH_READY` file, swaps that batch's staged directory into place, runs the pipeline, writes the exit code into `BATCH_DONE` and prints `BATCH_DONE_MARKER`, which the local reader thread consumes (it never reaches the log — `ProgressTracker` has no reason to see the handshake). **The swap is the barrier.** Batched input now lives in the run directory rather than the shared dataset cache, batch *i* is uploaded to `b<i>` beside it, and the driver does `rm -rf in && mv b<i> in` — atomic within one filesystem, so a batch's pipeline sees exactly its own zips. The old shared directory relied on the Fetcher having deleted the previous batch's input in time and nothing waited for it, which is what `ProgressTracker.well_repeats` counts. **A retry keeps what an earlier attempt staged.** The driver is launched before batch 1 is uploaded, so a node that then fails to boot (`srun: error: Nodes … are still not ready` / `Something is wrong with the boot of the nodes`) leaves batch 1's wells sitting in `b1` untouched. `_start_driver` clears only `in/` — a batch the driver had already swapped in and may have half-processed — and keeps every `b<i>` and `bg/`. That is safe because `run_id` is keyed on the name, size and mtime of every staged archive (`fingerprint_archives`), so a file of a given name in the run directory is a whole or partial copy of the archive this run would send under that name: rsync's quick check skips the whole ones and `--partial` resumes the rest. What a kept directory can still hold is a well that belongs to a different batch now, because the local-completion filter can shift the slicing between attempts; `services/remote_batch_staging.prune_staged` runs `find … ! -name <each kept zip> -exec rm -rf {} + -o -print` immediately before each upload, so the driver's `mv` still hands the pipeline exactly one batch, logs how many of the batch's wells were already there, and falls back to `rm -rf` of the whole directory on any answer other than a clean listing — a re-send costs time, a stray well in a batch costs a duplicate result. `tests/test_a_retry_keeps_the_staged_batches.py` drives attempt, dead driver, attempt against a local directory standing in for the remote, running the remote commands under `bash`. **A failed batch keeps the node**: the loop carries on, the run's own code carries the first failure, and an end-of-run tally names which batches failed. **The stream ending is the only signal that the run is over.** Stop reaches the batched wrapper through `signal_subprocess`, which reads `proc.pid`; with one driver held for the whole run that is always a real pid, so the process group is killed and `terminate()` — the method that sets the stop flag and cancels the Fetcher — never runs. The reader thread therefore treats EOF with batches still unreported as the run being over: it sets the flag and cancels the Fetcher itself, which is what gets the worker out of the rsync it is sitting in (`upload_subset` watches that flag). A walltime expiry or a node failure arrives the same way and is reported differently, since one is the user's doing and the other is not. Two things do end it, both meaning the app is gone rather than slow — a heartbeat that stopped advancing and a batch that never arrived — and each batch is additionally wrapped in `timeout` at the budget the operator's original `--time` set for one batch, so one wedged well cannot burn the whole run's walltime. That `--time` is scaled by the batch count *plus one* (`remote_config.scale_launcher_time`, clamped at `MAX_HELD_ALLOCATION_S`) because it sized a single launch and now has to cover the plate: the node is also held through every upload after the first, since the driver waits for each batch inside the allocation, so budgeting only the compute puts the expiry somewhere in the last batch of any run whose transfers are not free. The extra batch's budget is a guess and the log line says so. A launcher that sets no `--time` is left alone, since inventing a number is worse than inheriting the cluster's. Each batch is still its own pipeline invocation and so emits its own "N well(s) to process" banner for its own slice; `_run_batches` therefore injects one synthetic `Zip mode: <N> wells — batched` line ahead of batch 1, and `ProgressTracker` locks the run's denominator onto the first banner it sees. That `<N>` is the whole **staged** plate, including the wells the batched path skips because their per-well CSV is already complete locally — each skipped well gets its own `SKIP well …` marker on the same stream, so it is counted and painted on the plate map instead of leaving the run reporting 100% against a denominator smaller than the plate the user staged. **The allocation is asked for before the plate is uploaded.** A queue wait and a transfer are independent waits, and spending them end to end adds the whole queue to every run; requested first, they overlap. The job `srun` places starts the moment a node is granted, which may be long before the last byte lands, so the composed command blocks on an `UPLOAD_SENTINEL` file written into the run directory once rsync returns — announcing both edges of that wait, because a granted node waiting on bytes looks exactly like a hung one. `UPLOAD_WAIT_TIMEOUT_S` bounds it, since the node is idle and billed throughout; a failed upload cancels the allocation immediately rather than leaving it to time out. That deadline is for an uploader that is alive but wedged — the case that actually happens is the app being *killed*, and for that the uploader beats `UPLOAD_HEARTBEAT` every `UPLOAD_HEARTBEAT_S` (a daemon thread, not a per-file hook: rsync can spend minutes inside one large archive). A beat that stops advancing frees the node within `UPLOAD_HEARTBEAT_STALE_S` however long the upload legitimately needed. The file is touched over ssh, so the mtime the job compares against its own `date` is the remote clock and no skew between two machines is being measured. **Crash recovery closes the other half.** `close_remote_job` covers every exit the app survives — clean quit, finished run, Stop — because it reads the job id from memory; a SIGKILL, segfault or power cut runs none of it. The id is on the shared filesystem the whole time and `run_id` is deterministic in (input, arguments), so `remote_jobs.sweep_orphaned_allocation` lets the *next* run of the same plate find and cancel exactly the job the crashed one left. That determinism cuts both ways — two sessions on the same plate compute the same `run_id` — so the sweep refuses to touch a job whose heartbeat is fresh or whose sidecar was written moments ago, and returns which of the four verdicts it reached (`swept`, `owned`, `notmine`, `unknown`) rather than only logging it: the batched path is about to clear that same run directory's `in/` and prune its staged batches, and on `owned` it stops the run instead, since both sessions would otherwise stage batches into one directory. **Nothing it cannot measure is treated as dead.** The ages come from `stat -c %Y` *or* BSD's `stat -f %m`, and a host that answers neither gets `unknown` and keeps its job — the earlier code gave the two files opposite defaults for the same failure (epoch 0 for the heartbeat, *now* for the sidecar), so such a host silently never swept anything. The beat itself runs for the **whole** run rather than just the upload, on both paths, because it is what the sweep reads: stopping it when the transfer ended made an hour-long compute look abandoned to the next session on the same plate. **Neither cancel path will touch a job that is not the caller's**: both ask `squeue` who owns the id and stop if the answer is not `id -un`, and both pass `-u` to `scancel` as well, so a job that changed hands between the question and the answer still cannot be cancelled. Slurm would refuse a non-owner anyway — but that is the scheduler's policy rather than this app's promise, and it does not hold for an operator account. The overlap is taken **only** where there is something to queue for: a host with no launcher runs on the login node as soon as ssh connects, and a cache hit runs `true`, so both keep the old upload-first order — starting either early would run the pipeline against an input directory that is still filling. The run directory can be known in advance because `cache_key` is a local computation over the input archives; `spawn` checks the upload landed under that same key, since a divergence means the bytes went somewhere the waiting job will never look.  **`spawn` reads as its phases**: `_prepare_run` addresses the run (cache key, run id, the re-attach decision) and records it in the journal, `_preflight_cache_hit` decides whether the pipeline needs to run at all, `_compose_launch` builds the argv and the remote command and returns whether the allocation overlaps the upload, and `_start_ssh` / `_upload_input` do the two outbound steps. The overlapped launch's ordering and its failure handling — sweep, heartbeat, allocate, upload, sentinel, and handing the node back if either of the last two fails — stay in `spawn` itself, because that ordering is the behaviour `tests/test_remote_allocation_overlap.py` pins and a helper would hide it. What `spawn` leaves behind for the rest of the run (the suspend request armed only when a pipeline was launched, and the `Fetcher` that `cancel` stops) is pinned by `tests/test_remote_spawn_phases.py`. The module carries a line budget (`test_monolith_budgets.py::test_remote_runner_line_budget`), and each owner module beside it has its own, because the complexity ratchet cannot supply one — the functions here are long rather than branchy, so length is the dimension that needs the limit. Every recurring fault in this file has been a half-finished sweep of a fact derived in N places, and a module keeps acquiring those for as long as adding one more costs nothing. **Its supported import surface is its `__all__`** — `RemoteRunner`, `OutputFilter`, `LocalInputMode`, `ZippedInput`, `stage_local_zips`, `input_well_containers`, `repo_root`, `TRANSIENT_PREFIX`, `WELL_XFER_PREFIX` and the packaging contract `_REQUIRED_REMOTE_FILES`. No file reaches any other name through `services.remote_runner` — not by `from … import`, by `rr.X`, by a named `setattr`/`patch.object`, or by a `"services.remote_runner.X"` patch string, including a deeper one such as `"services.remote_runner.subprocess.run"`, which patches the shared `subprocess` module and is written `"subprocess.run"` — and the runner re-exports nothing outside `__all__`. Every caller imports from, and every test patches, the module that owns the name; a test that steers code the runner calls patches the module where that code lives. `tests/test_remote_runner_facade.py` enforces both directions; the scan behind it is `tests/_facade_scan.py`, and `tests/test_guards_bite.py` shows it seeing each access form. |
| `remote_config.py` | Per-host remote definitions loaded from `~/.config/allwell/remotes.toml` (or `$ALLWELL_REMOTES`). Each `[remote.<name>]` entry is an SSH alias + `remote_python` / staging dirs / cache budget, plus the optional **`compute_launcher`** (the `srun …` scheduler line consumed by `remote_runner`) and **`jupyterhub_config_path`** (where to find `jupyterhub_config.py` on the remote). Hosts are picked + edited in `analyze/remote_dialog.py`, which can **Fetch** the cluster's discrete compute options by reading the remote's `jupyterhub_config.py` spawner `profile_list` over SSH (no JupyterHub webpage needed) — picking a profile fills in the whole scheduler command. The snippet that runs on the remote also returns the spawner-wide `batch_script` and `req_*` defaults; `profile_launcher` renders that template with the profile's values (see `slurm_batch_script.py`) and falls back to mapping the `req_*` fields by name only when the config sets no template. `parse_jupyterhub_profiles_json` returns what any profile had to leave out as its detail, which the dialog shows beside the ✓. |
| `input_resolution_service.py` | `plan_input_layout` is the one answer to "what will this folder do?" — pure, returning an `InputPlan` that Analyze's readout displays and `resolve_input_output` executes (§6.1). Around it, the module validates the input folder shape (zip set vs flat) and drives the loose-TIF **grouping (zipper) phase** — `run_zipper` shells out to `pipeline/well_plate_zipper.py`, which discovers every TIF with one `os.walk` and copies (or, with `--move-source-tifs`, moves) each into its per-well subfolder. `group_by_well` filters discovered entries through `os.path.isfile` (which follows symlinks) so a **broken symlink** — a link whose target is on an unmounted/moved volume, still listed by `os.walk` among `files` because it is a non-directory entry — is skipped at discovery with a per-file warning rather than being handed to `folder_well`'s symlink-following `shutil.copy2`, where opening the missing target raised a bare `FileNotFoundError` that crashed the subprocess and failed the whole plate. This matches the rest of the pipeline's discovery, which already treats a broken link as absent (`process_microscopy.organize_loose_tifs_into_well_folders` and `find_image_groups` both gate on `Path.is_file()` / an existence check). `folder_well` places each discovered file into its per-well subfolder **first-write-wins**, the rule the zip writers already apply to a duplicate member name. `copy2`/`move` onto an existing name simply overwrite it, and under `--recursive` two subfolders can hold one basename: the first file's bytes were replaced by the second's, and with `--move-source-tifs` the loser's original was gone as well — one image destroyed with no copy anywhere — while the per-well progress line printed the *source* count, so the pipeline read one image fewer than the log claimed. The loser is left untouched where it is, the collision is named on stderr with both paths (`run_zipper` merges stderr into the Analyze log), and the count printed is what actually landed. `_same_file` makes a file already sitting in its own well folder a no-op that still counts as placed — the state a recursive re-run over `--output-dir == --search-dir` produces, which previously raised `shutil.SameFileError` — and treats a path it cannot compare as a different file, so the caller warns and leaves both alone rather than overwriting on a guess. The app never passes `-r` (`services.input_resolution_service.build_zipper_cmd` has no `--recursive`), so the collision is reachable only from the CLI today; it is still a documented, supported entry point. `well_plate_zipper.main` first calls `util.frozen_io.ensure_std_streams` — in a frozen windowed (`console=False`) build the bootloader leaves this subprocess's `sys.stdout` / `sys.stderr` set to `None` even though the parent piped fd 1 / fd 2, so without the rebind every per-well progress line and every skip warning is a silent no-op and the grouping phase looks frozen; the same shim backs `process_microscopy._ensure_pipeline_io_ready`, so both subprocess entry points share one implementation. |
| `env.py` | `validate_env` — a pure startup check of the `ALLWELL_*` overrides (`ALLWELL_SCRATCH_DIR` / `ALLWELL_REMOTES` / `ALLWELL_SEG_DEBUG`), returning warnings for any that are set but unusable so a mistyped path is not a silent fallback. |
| `ssh_key_setup.py` | Ed25519 keypair generation at `~/.ssh/allwell_<alias>` + the `ssh-copy-id` walkthrough behind the remote-host wizard. |
| `subprocess_kill.py` | Kills a spawned pipeline's whole process group / session (what Stop uses): `os.killpg` on POSIX, `CTRL_BREAK_EVENT` on Windows. **A child it signals must be started in a group of its own**, and `own_process_group_kwargs()` is the one place that spells both halves — `start_new_session` on POSIX, `CREATE_NEW_PROCESS_GROUP` on Windows — for `Popen` to spread. On Windows the Ctrl-Break goes to a console process group, and a child that leads none passes it to every process on the console, the app included, which Windows then ends with `STATUS_CONTROL_C_EXIT`: no traceback and nothing in the boot log. Both remote `ssh` spawns asked only for the POSIX half, so Stop on a remote run closed the app when it had been launched from a terminal. `tests/test_spawned_processes_lead_their_own_group.py` fails on any function that asks for a POSIX session without the Windows group, and pins the two `ssh` spawns to the helper. |
| `subprocess_text.py` | `TEXT_UTF8` — the one spelling of "decode this subprocess's output as UTF-8", splatted into every `subprocess.run` / `Popen` whose text-mode output the app reads. `text=True` on its own decodes with `locale.getpreferredencoding(False)`, which is UTF-8 on macOS and Linux but the ANSI codepage on Windows — so the `✓` / `→` markers, the em-dash in `Well X — done.` and any non-ASCII byte in a path either mojibake or raise `UnicodeDecodeError` out of a reader thread, skipping the `proc.wait()` behind it. `errors="replace"` is the second half: a `?` in a log line beats an exception that makes the GUI report a run as never started while it keeps going. `tests/test_subprocess_text_decoding.py` fails on any text-mode call in the tree that names no codec, including one whose flag sits in a kwargs dict; `services/remote_bootstrap.py` spells the same three arguments out because it stays stdlib-only. |
| *(pipeline)* `settings_record.py` + `util/settings_digest.py` | Which configuration produced each well's output, recorded beside it as `<out>/.aw_settings/<WELL>.json`. `KEYED_ON` is the roster of what invalidates a prior result — the segmenter and every one of its thresholds, the channels quantified, the QC gate, both top-hat radii and FFT bands, the mesh background parameters, the flat-field and blank, the auto-threshold controls and their control wells, and the filename schema — with the reason each entry is in it; `settings_digest` hashes whatever of them a run states. **The keys are `process_microscopy.build_parser()` destinations**, because the one caller digests that parser's namespace: a key spelled any other way contributes nothing, silently, which is how the first version of the roster came to name six options that do not exist and leave fifteen real ones unkeyed. `NOT_KEYED_ON` is its complement, carrying the reason each remaining option is outside the key, so the two partition the parser exactly and a newly added option fails the suite until someone classifies it. Both of the pipeline's reuse predicates consult the record: the plain re-run skip (`well_skip.output_exists_for_well`) and the incremental done-set. Without it, re-running a plate with a different segmenter was answered "up to date" while `write_pipeline_info` rewrote the sidecar to advertise the new configuration, so the plate described a setup that had produced none of the numbers in it. The marker is written by the worker, after both the CSV and the archive are on disk and past every short circuit — a well that logged "up to date (no new FOVs)" computed nothing and must not be credited with this run's settings. A remote run's marker is written on the worker host, so `Fetcher._pull_settings_marker` brings each well's back with its output rather than the client recomputing a second copy of the digest. **A well with no recorded digest is accepted**, so introducing the check forces nobody to reprocess anything; the cost is that a plate written before the record existed keeps the old behaviour until its next forced run. The digest is deliberately blind to the paths, to `--force`/`--incremental` and to anything about the machine, so a plate computed locally and on a worker host produces the same key. Registered in `tests/test_reuse_is_keyed_completely.py`, which drives every key through `well_settings_allow_reuse` itself rather than only through the digest. |
| `run_detect.py` | Run-time detection of an Analyze run's filename schema, separator and channel roles from its input (`resolve_detection`, for a `RunSpec` with `auto_detect`), preferring a chained converter's recorded `upstream_layout`, and the checks that the detected channels fit every option naming a channel (`channel_option_errors`). Detection that cannot decide raises `DetectionError`; it never falls back to the job's frozen values. `scan_pipeline_info` is the confidence rule the form's **Detect from filenames** shares. |
| `run_journal.py` | The record of what a run intended, where it sent the work, and what became of each well — opened before the first well is processed, amended as the run goes, closed with an outcome, so a record still open at the next start-up is a run the app was killed during (§6.5). Stdlib-only. Writes `<output_dir>/.aw_journal/`: `run.json` for the run (its `remote` address, plus the `remote_history` of up to `REMOTE_HISTORY_MAX` addresses earlier runs of the plate used, which `stored_remote_addresses` reads so a later run cannot erase where finished output was) and one `wells/<WELL>.json` per well, `pipeline/run_report.py`'s one-atomic-file-per-unit shape so the orchestrator, the worker pool and the Fetcher thread all record without a lock. **Evidence, never authority** — `pipeline.completeness` stays the answer to "is this well complete" and the artefacts stay the done-set, so a journal that goes missing costs answers rather than making a good dataset look empty. It drives exactly one decision, the remote re-attach above. A well record can name the run it belongs to: `open_run` returns a token, and a writer that hands it back cannot file its progress under a previous run's surviving record — which is what a run whose own `open_run` failed would otherwise do. The local path passes it (`analyze.progress._journal_well`); the remote writers — `_record_remote_in_journal` and the Fetcher's three `record_well` calls — do not, so they are trusted writes and that protection does not extend to them. The consequence is worth stating rather than leaving implied: on a *remote* run whose own `open_run` failed, those four still write into whatever record survives in that directory, which in that exact scenario is the previous run's, still open because the index is holding it for resume. Measured: run 2's remote address and its uploaded wells land inside run 1's record. Re-attach is keyed on the cache key and would therefore decline, so no wrong numbers follow — but run 1's tally and per-well detail are corrupted, and its resume offer describes a run that did not produce them — while a run's *own* completion lines, which are parsed on the GUI thread and therefore arrive after the worker thread closed the record, are still accepted. Asking the cheaper question instead, "is a run open here", refused the tail of every plate: a 24-well run recorded four wells and the pre-run readout said so. `tests/test_a_run_end_to_end_records_every_well.py` drives a real run through a real drain and is the only test on either side of this record that does. `WELL_STATES` is the single roster of what a run can have done to a well, guarded by `tests/test_no_second_journal_vocabulary.py` — which walks dict keys as well as tuples, lists and sets, because a states-to-words table is presentation only for as long as the module holding it also consults the canonical roster; one that does not is holding its only copy, and anything iterating it drops every state it fails to spell. |
| `run_provenance.py` | An Analyze run's two lines in the dataset's provenance log (§5.7). `PipelineRunner._open_journal` calls `begin_run`, which appends `run_started` (mode, input folder, the exact pipeline argv, and the run-scope options `force` / `force_wells` / `incremental` / `only_wells`) and fingerprints the sidecar's current `run_check` block; `_close_journal` calls `finish_run`, which appends `run_finished` with the journal's outcome and this run's `run_check` totals. Emitted by the runner rather than the pipeline because the runner is the one process that sees the start and end of every run — a remote pipeline's own writes would stay on the worker host, since the fetch pulls named files only — and because `process_microscopy.py` is at its line budget. The cost is stated: a pipeline launched from a terminal writes no run events. **The `run_check` is quoted only if it changed during the run.** A run that died before its end-of-run check leaves the previous run's block in the sidecar; its timestamps are second-resolution, so two runs of a small plate can share one, and comparing them let a failed run quote the previous run's healthy totals. Comparing a digest taken at `begin_run` instead has no resolution limit; a run that rewrote a byte-identical block is reported as having none, which errs toward unknown. `argv` is recorded rather than a settings digest because the client's opts are not the pipeline's parsed namespace, so a client-side digest would not match `.aw_settings/`. Pinned by `tests/test_provenance_log.py`, which drives the real runner twice (the history grows while the journal is replaced) and the remote open/fetch/close order. |

These modules deliberately have no Qt imports beyond what the Analyze tab
itself uses — keeping them potentially reusable for a CLI driver.

### 6.5 Scratch, staging, and where each write lands

A run touches two classes of storage, and keeping them apart is what makes it
survive an unreliable output volume.

**Remote staging moves only what it uploads.** A remote run in zip mode with a
channel filter or `--incremental` cannot use the user's archives directly — both
paths rewrite the zip (dropping unused channels / already-done FOV-groups), and
rewriting in place would corrupt the user's dataset. So it stages. The staging is
**plan-then-materialise** (`remote_staging._plan_staging` / `_materialize_staging`):
the plan pass reads each archive's *member list* only — that comes from the zip's
central directory, a small read at the end of the file, so planning a whole plate
costs a handful of seeks even across a network mount — and the materialise pass
then writes only the members that will actually be uploaded, reading nothing
else. This ordering is the point: staging by copying each archive in full and
*then* rewriting it down to the wanted members pulls the entire dataset across
the network before a single byte reaches the remote, which is exactly backwards
when the data lives on a NAS — the normal case. The channel-filter typo guard
runs in the plan pass, so a mistyped channel name names every offending well
before any bytes move.

**"Changed" is decided on the images alone.** `_is_image_member` splits each
archive's member list before the channel filter sees it: anything with a leading
dot or a non-image suffix — `.DS_Store`, directory entries, AppleDouble sidecars
— is not a channel, so the filter has no opinion on it and it can never be the
reason an archive counts as changed. Without that split a single stray file per
zip made every archive on the plate look filtered (a report of 276 of 279 members
kept, on a plate whose zips held only the two requested channels) and rebuilt the
whole dataset into scratch to strip a few hundred bytes a well. The zero-match
guard and the incremental up-to-date check read the images too, so junk can
neither satisfy a typo'd channel filter nor keep a finished well in the upload.
An archive that survives is used exactly as it is, junk and all — the remote
ignores it anyway, since `find_image_groups_in_zip` skips the same members — and
one that is rewritten carries only the images the remote will read.

**Only an archive that actually changes is staged.** A plan that keeps every
member is not written anywhere: its source path goes straight into the upload
list and rsync reads it from the input dir. Copying it into scratch first would
move the same bytes twice — once onto the local scratch volume, once to the
remote — and only the second copy is the one anybody needs.
`_open_staging_if_needed` therefore creates the staging directory only when some
plan has a rewrite in it, and `stage_local_zips` returns `cleanup=None` and the
input dir as its `zip_dir` when none does; `well_zips`, not `zip_dir`, is the
authoritative list of what gets uploaded, and it can name files in both places.
This is not an edge case: the Analyze tab always requests selective channels, so
a run whose channel list happens to cover every image in the plate takes the
filtered path with a filter that drops nothing — and used to copy the whole plate
into the OS temp dir to get there. It also makes the upload cache work as
designed, since `RemoteRunner.cache_key` hashes each archive's `(name, size,
mtime)`: a freshly-written staging copy has a new mtime every run, so an
unchanged plate keyed differently every time and re-uploaded; passing the source
through keeps the key stable and the second run skips the transfer.
**MIXED mode** — some wells zipped, others still folders, the signature of a
run that died mid-compression — stages through the same two passes; it is the
mode most likely to arise on a slow share, so a full copy there was the worst
place to keep one. Its leftover folders are still zipped into the *input* dir
(persisted deliberately, so the next run sees plain ZIP mode and re-zips
nothing), and with no channel filter it uploads from the input dir with no
staging at all. `_filter_channels_in_staging` survives for the FOLDER / FLAT
path, which filters zips it has just written itself.

**An archive that *is* rewritten keys differently every run, and the run journal
is what stops that losing work.** The pass-through above keeps the key stable
only for archives nothing was dropped from; a channel filter that clears
`REWRITE_MIN_SAVING`, and every incremental split, write a fresh copy into
scratch, so the file being hashed was created moments ago and the plate resolves
to a different `runs/<run_id>/out` on each run. Whatever the previous one
computed but had not yet fetched then sits somewhere nothing will look again.
So `spawn` records the address it used into the output directory's journal
(§6.5) and `_reattach_output_dir` consults it on the next run:
`_choose_remote_output_dir` is a module-level function, given the freshly
derived address, the recorded one, whether the run is forced, and whether
`_list_completed_wells_in` found anything still in the recorded directory. The
journal proposes and the remote listing decides — a recorded address is a
statement about where work was *sent*, not that it is still there — and a forced
run never re-attaches, since landing in a directory already full of the previous
run's output is exactly how a forced re-run gets skipped. **Neither does an
incremental run**, and its own output directory is emptied before it launches:
its upload is a split holding only the groups still missing, so a previous
run's outputs in the directory can only mislead it — the remote pipeline runs
without `--incremental` and skips any well whose output exists, and a resumed
run of a resumed run otherwise re-attached to the first resume's directory and
was declared complete over a partial well. For the same reason the pre-flight's
full-cache-hit check (`remote_run_id._pipeline_launch_is_pointless`) never fires
for an incremental run, and otherwise asks whether every *uploaded* well is
present, not whether the directory holds as many out.zips as were uploaded.

**What the previous run finished is downloaded before any run stages.**
Staging decides what to upload from the *local* folder alone — the incremental
split by its done-set, batched mode by its per-well CSV check, a plain
single-shot run not at all — so a well the previous run finished on the host
and never downloaded (the state a Suspend, Stop, dropped connection or closed
laptop leaves once the remote compute is done) looks unprocessed and would be
uploaded whole and recomputed, while its output sits in a directory that an
incremental run never re-attaches to and a batched run never lists. So
`PipelineRunner._recover_remote_outputs` runs before `stage_local_zips` on
**every unforced remote run**, incremental or not, single-shot or batched:
`services/remote_recover.recover_finished_outputs` gathers every directory an
earlier run of this plate and configuration may have left wells in
(`_candidate_dirs`), lists each, and — for each that holds wells this folder
lacks — runs the ordinary `FetchedOutputVerifier.verify` against it. The
candidates come from two places that complement each other. **The journal's
addresses**, the current one and every earlier one `run_journal.record_remote`
kept in `remote_history` (`stored_remote_addresses`), each held to the same three
keys as the re-attach — with, for finding work only, the digests an earlier
build recorded (`remote_run_id.legacy_argv_digests`), so a plate already stuck
on a host is found. The history exists because every run records its own
address before it uploads a byte: a run stopped during its upload used to
overwrite the only record of where the previous run's finished output was, and
the next run looked in the stopped run's empty directory and uploaded the
plate again. **The address the name implies**: a run's directory is
`runs/run-<upload key>-<argv digest>` (`_run_id_body`, the one spelling), and
for a plate that is one zip per well uploaded as it is, the upload key *is*
`source_fingerprint` of the user's own archives — so an earlier whole-plate
run's directory, single-shot or batched, is recomputed with no record at all,
from the same images and settings the journal would have been matched on. That
is what finds a plate whose address was lost before the history existed. A run
whose upload was rewritten (a channel filter dropping at least
`REWRITE_MIN_SAVING` of the bytes) keyed on a fresh copy, and only the journal
can find it. A search that finds nothing says so in one log line naming every
place it looked. Each pull is the verifier's: sidecar merge, `errors/`, the per-well pull (which brings each
well's `.aw_settings` marker too, as the in-stream fetch does), the fetch
report — so there is one fetch implementation, not a second one for this
case. When it pulled anything the run is **staged incrementally** whatever was ticked,
because only the split leaves a locally complete well out of the upload on
every path; when nothing is left, `_nothing_left_to_upload` ends the run with
"Nothing to upload" rather than launching the host on an empty input. An
empty-well blank on its own counts as nothing left once its own output is here
(`_only_measured_blanks`): staging uploads a blank whole on every run, because it
is the input the correction is built from, so with every sample well complete
it was the only thing in the upload and a node was asked for to recompute it. A pull
that cannot bring every listed well home **ends the run with an error** instead
of falling through to the upload: the wells that failed would be re-uploaded
and recomputed, and the incremental run then empties its own output directory,
which can be the very one still holding them. A forced run skips all of it.
`tests/test_a_resumed_remote_run_downloads_before_uploading.py` drives the
app's sequence — run one (single-shot or batched) suspended before its
download, run two through the real `_run_pipeline_remote`, with incremental on
and off — against the fake host, and holds the other direction too: a changed
setting that alters the numbers never matches.

A **full cache hit uploads nothing.** When the pre-flight finds every staged
well's output already in the (re-attached) directory, the pipeline is replaced
by `true` and the upload is skipped with it: nothing will read that input, and
a plate whose staged archives keyed differently from the last run's was
otherwise sent in full for a run that computes nothing.

Only the *output*
directory moves: the input keys on this run's own staged archives, and the
pidfile, sentinel and heartbeat stay under this run's own `run_id`, because
`_sweep_orphaned_allocation` finds a crashed session's job by recomputing that
address and must not be pointed at another run's — and both directories are
created, since a re-attached run's output lives under a *previous* `run_id` and
nothing else would make its own.

`remote_run_dir(host, run_id)` and `remote_run_paths(host, run_id)` are where
that address is spelled, and the only place. It was a format-string literal in
nine places across three classes while the dataset address beside it had one
definition, so every change to "where does a run live" was a sweep with no way
to enumerate its own sites — which is how the `mkdir` came to use the output
path and leave the pidfile's parent uncreated, and how the cleanup after it
derived a third spelling again. `remote_run_paths` returns the run's paths
(output, pidfile, upload sentinel, heartbeat and suspend request) together so they cannot disagree about their parent, and
`tests/test_one_definition_of_the_run_dir.py` fails on a tenth literal,
matched on the static text so the spelling of the run-id expression cannot
dodge it. Cleanup mirrors that split: the borrowed
directory is left in place and named in the log, while the run's own is removed
like any other, because nothing prunes `runs/` (`DatasetCache.gc` covers
`datasets/`) and it holds only the pidfile, sentinel and heartbeat this run
wrote.

Which flags count as "the same configuration" is `pipeline_argv_digest`,
extracted from `_compute_run_id` and recorded in the journal, so the address and
the reuse key cannot come to disagree. It is computed over the local argv **plus
`RemoteRunner._host_argv_extras`** — the flags a remote run appends that nothing
local produces: `--no_save_tophat` for a CSV-only fetch, the host's `extra_args`,
and `--cpu_only`. Each of those changes what the remote computes or writes, so
leaving them out let a plate run against a CPU-only host, or with a segmentation
threshold overridden per host, address the directory another configuration had
already filled, be found complete by the pre-flight check, and have that
configuration's numbers fetched back as its own. One definition feeds both the
launched command and the digest.

It is computed over the *flags*, never the launcher — `sys.executable` and
either the local path to `process_microscopy.py` or the frozen bundle's
`--run-pipeline` sentinel are sliced off first. None of that reaches the
worker, which runs its own interpreter against its own uploaded copy of the
script, so folding it in keyed the reuse decision on facts about the client
that cannot change a byte of the result. The failure was over-keying rather
than under-keying, and it is quieter: an identical plate re-attached or did not
depending on whether the user launched the app bundle or ran from source, where
the checkout lived, and which Python was on PATH — each miss re-uploading the
plate and recomputing it with nothing logged. `test_the_launcher_does_not_reach_the_digest`
compares the three shapes directly, which a pinned digest literal cannot do:
one computed from `sys.executable` is itself machine-specific.

The flags `util.settings_digest.NOT_KEYED_ON` lists as execution or
re-processing knobs are sliced off for the same reason
(`_DIGEST_SKIP_VALUE` / `_DIGEST_SKIP_FLAG`: `--incremental`,
`--incremental_prior_dir`, `--workers`, `--tf_threads`, `--focus_min`,
`--allow_low_disk`, `--no_run_check`, beside `--force`). None changes what the
remote writes, and two of them cost the most: `_build_remote_argv` drops the
incremental pair before the host sees the command, yet hashed they made a
resume — which is always incremental — a differently configured run from the
one it resumed, so the download-before-staging step above could never fire;
and "Load previous run" does not restore `--allow_low_disk`, so ticking it once
hid a plate's finished output from every later run. A settings round trip
through a remote run's `pipeline_info.json` and "Load previous run" otherwise
reproduces the argv exactly — measured, not assumed — so the reloaded form
finds the plate.

Every call that turns a configuration into an address or a reuse key folds
those extras in — `spawn`'s two, and `_BatchedRemoteProcess`'s run id *and* its
journal record. Missing one makes that call's key smaller than its siblings',
and a smaller key matches configurations whose output is not interchangeable:
a batched CSV-only run journalled a digest identical to a plain full run's, so
a later full run re-attached to its directory and fetched back output with no
tophat images. `test_every_keying_call_folds_in_the_host_extras` is the AST
sweep that holds it.

`stored_remote_address` compares three keys, and `tests/test_reuse_is_keyed_completely.py`
carries the written reason for each: the argv digest, `source_fingerprint` (the
user's own input archives, which separates "staging rewrote" from "the images
changed" — the two reasons the upload key churns), and the host alias, because
the recorded address is a path on one machine and two hosts that share a
filesystem will happily resolve each other's.

`cache_key` hashes `int(st_mtime)`, so two staged copies written inside one
wall-clock second key identically. That is why this drift is invisible in a
tight loop and certain in practice, and why the test that pins it stamps the
mtimes rather than racing the clock.

**Suspending a run.** Stop is a kill — SIGTERM to the process group, SIGKILL
five seconds later — and whatever each worker was mid-way through is lost.
Suspend (`PipelineRunner.suspend`) sends the same SIGTERM with the escalation
suppressed (`subprocess_kill.signal_subprocess(..., escalate=False)`, since a
well finishing its FOV-group can easily outlast five seconds), and the pipeline
*catches* it: `pipeline/suspend.py` installs a handler in the orchestrator and in
every pool worker, the per-group loops stop taking on new FOV-groups, wells not
yet started are cancelled, and each well that did any work returns through the
normal end-of-well path so its CSV and `<well>_out.zip` are written. A second
signal is a hard stop — the handler restores the previous disposition before
returning, so a suspend that hangs is still escapable. Nothing the app does
sends that second signal by accident: `PipelineRunner.suspend` ignores a second
local suspend, the Suspend button only notes that the run is already winding
down, closing the window leaves a suspending run to finish rather than Stopping
it, and `watch_parent` does not signal an orphan that is already suspending.
Suspend pressed while the run is still preparing its input — busy, with no
pipeline yet — says there is nothing to suspend yet.

**A local run winds itself down when the app goes away.** The app launches the
pipeline in a session of its own so Stop can signal the whole tree, which also
means a crashed app used to leave it running, writing to a pipe nobody read.
Restarting and resuming the same plate then raced it: the new run's grouping
removed the `in/<well>/` folders the orphan was reading ("No such file or
directory"), and whichever run wrote a well's CSV last won. `spawn_pipeline`
now passes the app's pid as `ALLWELL_PARENT_PID`, and `process_microscopy.main`
arms `pipeline.suspend.watch_parent` on the output directory: a thread that
notices the reparenting and sends SIGTERM to the pipeline's own process group —
the suspend signal, so every well worker winds down and writes what it
finished — and that keeps `<out>/.aw_pipeline.alive` (its pid) fresh while the
run lives. `analyze.run_spec.start_run`, which Run, Resume and the job queue all
go through, refuses to start a plate whose output folder has a live heartbeat
(`live_pipeline_pid`: fresh within `ALIVE_STALE_S` *and* the pid exists), so a
restarted app waits for the orphan rather than racing it. A CLI or remote run
sets no variable and is not watched; neither is Windows, which does not
reparent an orphan.

**A remote run is suspended through a request file, not a signal.** On the host
the process the app can name is the login shell's `conda run` or `srun`, not the
pipeline, so a SIGTERM reaches the pipeline only if those forward it; and the
signal Stop sends locally goes to the ssh session, which ends the session — the
run's output stream, the Fetcher's per-well downloads (`RemoteRunner.cancel`
stops them) and, on a scheduler, the allocation (`scancel`). So
`PipelineRunner.suspend` signals nothing for a launched remote run. On a thread
of its own it calls `RemoteRunner.request_suspend` (a delegate to
`services/remote_suspend.request_suspend`), which touches
`RemoteRunPaths.suspend_request` (`<run_dir>/.aw_suspend_request`) over a fresh
ssh bounded at `SUSPEND_REQUEST_TIMEOUT_S`; the pipeline was launched with
`--suspend_file` naming that path, and `pipeline.suspend.watch_request_file`
publishes it through `ALLWELL_SUSPEND_FILE` so every well worker inherits it.
`is_suspended()` then answers true for the file as well as for the signal, at
every FOV-group boundary it was already asked at, and the run winds down and
exits 0 over a stream that never broke, with the Fetcher still downloading. The
file lives under the run's own directory rather than `out/` so a re-attached run
still owns its request, and both launch paths `rm -f` it first: `run_id` is
deterministic, so a resume lands in the directory the suspend was requested in,
and a leftover request would suspend it before it did anything. The pipeline
only ever reads it. A well the pool had already queued when the request landed
returns before it starts (`process_microscopy._well_not_started_for_suspend`),
and one that began just before it but attempted no group returns after the
group loop (`_suspended_before_any_group`); both write nothing and print no
`— done.` — otherwise the Fetcher would expect a CSV for it and fail the run's
verification.
A well the request reaches part way through writes what it finished and prints
`— done.` like any other — the Fetcher has to bring it home for the resume to add
to — so `_process_groups_in_worker` first logs `Well <W> — SUSPENDED part way: N
of M FOV-group(s) not reached`. The run journal still files that well as
`fetched`: its states record where a well's output got to, not whether the output
is whole, which is the sidecar `run_report`'s `incomplete_wells` and the field
quality block's `partial_wells`.

**Whether the run was suspended is settled from the pipeline's own word.** The
ssh call that makes the request cannot say whether it landed: a timeout can fail
after the `touch` ran. So a failed request clears the suspend flag and restores
the cleanup mode — the run is taken to be carrying on — but the pipeline writes
`pipeline.suspend.LOG_MARKER` on its stream whenever it sees a request, however
it arrived, and `_run_pipeline_remote` watches for it
(`_note_suspend_evidence`). When the pipeline exits, `_settle_remote_suspend`
sets the flag from that line and forces the cleanup mode to `none`, so a request
that landed is reported and treated as a suspend even when the app thought it
had failed. Late threads cannot undo later decisions: each request is numbered
(`_suspend_seq`) and each run too (`_run_generation`, bumped by `start()`), and
only the newest request of the current run may clear anything.

**A run is suspendable only once its pipeline is running.** `spawn` sets
`suspend_request` after the upload is complete and the pipeline launched, so a
Suspend pressed while a remote run is still staging or uploading has no request
to make (`can_request_suspend` is false) and stops the run as before — rather
than waiting out the upload, and a node, for a pipeline that would then do
nothing.

A batched run needs more pieces. The driver (`_batch_driver_snippet`) checks
the request at the top of each batch and inside its wait for the next one, and
exits 0 rather than holding the node for a `ready` file that is not coming.
`_BatchedRemoteProcess.note_suspend_requested` is called *before* the `touch`,
so the reader already knows when the driver's early exit arrives and does not
take it for a lost node (which would cancel the Fetcher mid-way through the
batch that just finished); it also stops the local loop sending further batches
(`_suspend_before`) and interrupts a batch upload already in progress, whose
`stop_event` is `_AnySet(_stop, _suspending)`. For a batched run the suspend is
in effect even when the `touch` fails, because no more batches will be sent: the
batch running on the host simply finishes. When the loop ends that way with the
driver still alive — the job still queued, so it has seen no request file —
`_release_driver` terminates the ssh holding the queue position and cancels the
job, as it does for a failed run, rather than letting the job take a node later
only to give it straight back; a driver that has already exited on its own is
left alone. A suspended batched run skips the
end-of-run auto-threshold pass, which is for a finished plate; the resumed run
that finishes it writes the thresholds.

**A suspended run exits 0, and the runner says so rather than calling it done.**
Leaving through the normal end-of-well path means the pipeline's exit code is the
same as a finished plate's, so `PipelineRunner` asks `_suspend_requested` before
reading an exit of 0 as a completion: a suspended run queues
`("suspended", …)` through `_enqueue_suspended` (one of `_CONTROL_KINDS`, so it
is never dropped on overflow) instead of `("done", …)`, and the success hooks —
the source-image cleanup `resolve_input_output` hands back, and on the remote
path `zipped.on_pipeline_success` — do not run. `AnalyzeTab._poll_log` routes the
event to `AnalyzeSuspendMixin._on_run_suspended`, which writes a `[Suspended]`
line with the well tally and puts the dashboard in its amber state, and leaves
`_run_ok` false. Everything downstream keys on that: `_on_pipeline_complete`
(the hand-off of the output folder to Review) is never called, `_on_run_settled`
keeps the suspend record, and `jobFinished` carries `(False, "", "")`, which is
how the job queue recognises a suspend. Reading the exit code alone had made a
Suspend print "Processing Complete", tell the queue the job had succeeded, and
hand the half-written folder to Review from a `QTimer` callback — where a load
that raised took the application down.

**The done-set is not recorded anywhere — the output directory is it.**
`--incremental` reads the per-well CSVs and out-zips back as the set of
`(fov, timepoint)` groups already processed, so a resumed run recomputes only
what is missing, and a suspended output is indistinguishable from one left by a
run that ended early for any other reason. A group the run never attempted is
deliberately **not** added to the well's `failed` list — it is missing, which the
completeness record already reports as the gap between the input's group count
and the CSV's, and calling it failed would put it in the PARTIAL warning as
though the data were broken rather than unfinished.

What the artefacts cannot say is what the run *intended*, and that is what the
two records beside them are for.

`services/suspend_record.py` persists the `RunSpec` that was running, plus
enough to describe it — the same `to_json` the job queue already uses, so there
is no second serialisation to keep in step with the form. It describes itself
in pieces — `plate()`, `progress()`, `when()` — with `describe()` composing the
one-line form from those three rather than restating them, because the resume
strip sets the plate and the progress into separate labels while the log line
and the discard dialog still want one sentence (§6.5). It lives at
`~/.allwell/suspended_runs.json` rather than in the output folder because at
startup the app does not yet know which output folder to look in, and it holds a
list keyed by output directory so several plates can be suspended at once. The
record is cleared on resume, on discard, and when a run completes normally; a
*stopped* run keeps its record, because a hard Stop also leaves every finished
well's CSV on disk.

`services/run_journal.py` is the other half, and the difference between them is
**when** they are written. Every other record this app keeps about a run —
`run_report`, `run_check`, the remote fetch reconciliation — is written at the
*end*, which is precisely why a run that dies leaves nothing: the app was never
there to write it. The journal is opened before any well is processed, amended
as the run proceeds, and closed with an outcome, so a record still open at the
next start-up **is** a run the process did not survive. It lives in the output
directory as `.aw_journal/run.json` plus one `wells/<WELL>.json` per well —
`pipeline/run_report.py`'s shape, for its reason: one small file per unit,
written atomically and never appended to, so the orchestrator, the worker pool
and the remote Fetcher thread all record without a lock. A small index under
`services.remote_config.default_state_dir` points at the output directories that
have one, since at startup the app does not know where to look.

Two rules define what the journal is allowed to be. It is **evidence, never
authority**: `pipeline.completeness` stays the only answer to "is this well
complete" and the artefacts stay the done-set, so a journal that goes missing —
a read-only output volume, a folder someone edited by hand — costs the user
answers rather than making a good dataset look empty. And it **drives exactly one
decision**, the remote re-attach described in §6.4. Everything else it holds is
reported, not acted on. `WELL_STATES` names what a run did to a well
(`uploaded` / `analysed` / `fetched` / `skipped` / `failed` / `not-fetched`),
deliberately disjoint from `completeness.HEALTH_STATES` so the two vocabularies
cannot be mistaken for each other; `tests/test_no_second_journal_vocabulary.py`
fails on a second literal roster anywhere in the tree.

**What "finished" means depends on where the run happened**, so the tally that
renders those states comes in two groupings and the run's own `mode` picks one.
`analysed` is written from the pipeline's stdout and means the same thing
locally and remotely — *the pipeline announced this well finished* — but locally
the CSV and out-zip are on disk the moment that line prints, while remotely they
are on the host and only `fetched` says they arrived. `TALLY_GROUPS_LOCAL` files
`analysed` under "finished"; `TALLY_GROUPS_REMOTE` gives it a heading of its own,
because a remote run that died before reconciliation otherwise told the user a
well was finished when nothing of it had reached their machine. The roster
liveness test covers both groupings: adding a state to one and not the other is
the same silent omission with a mode attached.

**A well this run did not compute is recorded as one it did not compute.** Three
markers reach `ProgressTracker._count_well_done` — `— done.`, `up to date` (an
incremental well with no new FOVs) and `SKIP … output already exists` (a re-run
without `--force`) — and all three mean the well is complete, which is why they
share a counter and why the plate is told `process` for all three. Only the first
means anything was computed, so the other two carry `skipped` for the journal:
without that, an incremental run that touched 6 of 96 wells recorded 96
`analysed` and the readout said "It recorded 96 finished".

The record's word rides inside the completion event, as a third element beside
the well and the stage, and both halves of that shape are load-bearing. The
stage stays `process` because `RunDashboard.set_well_stage` ignores any stage
outside its own roster — sending it the record's word would have stopped those
wells being marked done, trading a wrong record for a wrong picture. And it is
*one* event rather than two because `PipelineRunner._enqueue` drops anything
outside `_CONTROL_KINDS` when the queue is full, individually: a completion
split across two messages loses "nothing was computed" while keeping "this well
is finished", which is the same wrong record arriving by way of the transport.
Stage-only events — `error`, `upload`, `download` — still carry no third
element and are mapped by `AnalyzeProgressMixin._JOURNAL_STAGES`.

**One surface offers any given unfinished run.** `RunJournal.queued` and
`SuspendedRun.queued` record that the job queue started it, written by
`open_run` and by `_suspend` respectively, and the Analyze pane's banner skips
both. Suspending a queue-driven job closes its journal `suspended`, which is
exactly what `is_unfinished` is for, so the banner offered the plate the moment
`_running` cleared while the queue still held the job — resume from the banner,
let the queue start, and the same plate runs twice concurrently into one output
directory.

**Both** records carry the flag, and that is not belt-and-braces. A suspend
writes both pointers, and `_resumable` ranks the suspend record *ahead* of the
journal offer for the folder on the form — so filtering the journal alone left
the offer standing, unchanged, sourced from the record that was still saying
yes.

**Dismissing an offer is not a claim that the plate finished.** Discard calls
`run_journal.dismiss`, which flags the index entry; it used to call `forget`,
which deletes it. The entry is read by two things with opposite intents (§7.7
#1): the banner, which honours the dismissal, and `resume_aware_spec`, which
reads `unfinished_runs()` to decide whether the next Run must be
`--incremental`. Deleting it therefore disarmed the mid-flight-well recovery as
a side effect of closing a banner — the user who said "I know, I'll just re-run
it" got the permanently-3-of-12 plate the forcing exists to prevent, with
nothing said, while the record on disk still stated the plate was unfinished. A
*new* run of the same directory clears the flag, because `_index_upsert` builds
a fresh entry: the dismissal was about the run that had been offered.

**A forced run is never made incremental.** `resume_aware_spec` returns a
spec with `force` set unchanged: Force means recompute from scratch — the resume
message itself tells the user to tick it for that — and on a remote run an
incremental staging under it uploaded nothing for wells already complete
locally, so Force did nothing on any input with an unfinished run behind it.

**The resume message names the cause it found.** `resume_aware_spec` fires on
every outcome in `UNFINISHED_OUTCOMES` plus a record left open, which is four
different events — a suspend, a stop, a failure, and an app that was killed. One
sentence saying "a suspended run" was true of a quarter of them (§7.7 #4), so
`_input_has_unfinished_work` answers with the phrase rather than a boolean, and
the line names Force as the way to decline.

**Nothing is written on the worker host.** `services/run_journal.py` is not in
`_REQUIRED_REMOTE_FILES`, so the module never reaches the remote and the pipeline
there cannot call it even by accident; the journal is written entirely on the
client, into the local output directory, and `run_client_side_completeness_check`
excludes `.aw_journal/` from a plate's well count so a fetch cannot mistake it for
data. The one state that sounds as though it must cost the remote something,
`analysed`, costs it nothing: it is parsed from the `Well X — done.` marker the
pipeline already prints, on the stdout stream the client is already reading over
the ssh connection it already holds. Nothing polls the host and no extra remote
command is run. On the client a 96-well plate writes about 8 KB across 97 files
and spends roughly a tenth of a second doing it, across a run measured in hours.

Every state has one writer and one trigger, and they sit on three different
threads — which is the reason for the one-file-per-well shape rather than a
single appended log:

| Event | Recorded | Written by | Thread |
|---|---|---|---|
| The run begins, output dir now known | `open_run` | `PipelineRunner._run_pipeline_thread` | worker |
| The remote address is decided | `record_remote` | `RemoteRunner.spawn`, and the batched path | worker |
| A well's archive finished uploading | `uploaded` | `upload_subset`, after that rsync returns | worker |
| The pipeline said a well is done and computed it | `analysed` | `ProgressTracker._count_well_done` → the completion event's third element | GUI |
| The pipeline said a well is done and computed nothing | `skipped` + reason | the same event, third element `skipped` | GUI |
| The pipeline said a well failed | `failed` | the same tracker's error stage, via `AnalyzeProgressMixin._journal_well_stage` | GUI |
| A well's output was pulled back | `fetched` | `Fetcher._fetch_one` | Fetcher |
| A well needed no transfer | `skipped` + reason | `Fetcher._already_local` | Fetcher |
| The end-of-run retry ran | `fetched` / `not-fetched` | `RemoteRunner._retry_missing_wells` | worker |
| The run ends, however it ended | `close_run` + outcome | the worker's `finally` | worker |

`analysed` and `failed` are written from the GUI thread because that is where the
run's stdout is parsed, and they are deliberately hung off the same event the
dashboard paints from, so what the record says and what the user saw cannot
disagree. It is also why the token matters on that path in particular: those
lines are parsed in bounded slices and the tail of a plate lands *after* the
worker thread closed the record.

`analyze.suspend.AnalyzeSuspendMixin` is the seam both records reach the user
through, and `_resumable` decides which run one banner, one Resume and one
Discard are about.

**What qualifies is "did not finish", not "was killed".** `unfinished_runs`
returns an index entry with no `closed_at` — a run the process did not survive —
*and* one closed with any outcome in `UNFINISHED_OUTCOMES` (`error`, `stopped`,
`suspended`). All of them leave every finished well's CSV and out-zip on disk,
which is what `--incremental` reads as its done-set, so what separates them from
`ok` is only that the plate is not done yet. A failure especially: it is the case
where a user most wants to carry on. That roster is named once in `run_journal`
rather than restated by each surface.

It is **wider** than `JobState.RESUMABLE`, and the difference is deliberate. The
queue treats a failed or cancelled job as terminal (`JobState.FAILURE_LIKE`),
because the jobs chained behind it are waiting on output that is never coming and
have to be released rather than left hanging. Nothing is chained behind a resume
banner, so the only question it asks is whether *this* plate has work left worth
picking up — and after a failure it does, in the wells that got through.

**Which one is offered is decided by the folder on the form.** Both records are
ordered newest-first across every plate, so taking the newest outright can
propose a run against a dataset the user is not looking at — and with §6.1's
pre-run report directly beneath describing a different folder, the sidebar
contradicts itself and Resume acts on the plate that is not on screen. So a
record matching the form's own output directory wins, a form naming a folder
neither record describes gets no offer at all (the pre-run report is what speaks
for that folder), and newest-anywhere is the fallback only for an empty form —
the state the app opens in, and the one this banner exists for. "Newest" there
ranks *plates*, each by its newest record, and within a plate the suspend record
still wins: a suspend writes both records and closes the journal after stamping
its own, so ranking records by time alone offered the journal's account of the
very plate the suspend record describes. That is also why
both strips refresh together through `_refresh_folder_banners`, on every change
to the input field and once at construction: a resume offer left over from a
different folder is precisely the contradiction the scoping prevents, and a
banner that is only ever refreshed by a run ending cannot reveal a record written
in a previous session.

Every offer names the **plate**, through `suspend_record.plate_name`. A dataset's
output folder is `<plate>/out`, so naming the folder itself says "out" for
essentially every run and says it identically for two different plates.

Resuming forces `incremental=True` into the spec: that flag is not a preference
here — without it the pipeline skips any well whose CSV exists and reprocesses
nothing, so a half-done plate would come back still half-done with the run
reporting success. The banner's last line is the journal's own per-well tally
(finished / failed / never fetched), reported rather than derived, and it says
nothing about how complete the *output* is — that is `completeness`'s answer and
§6.1's pre-run readout carries it.

**The strip is a stacked card, not a row, and it is not `ContextBanner`.** That
widget (§9) is the app's banner idiom and the right first reach, but it is one
`QHBoxLayout` — glyph, sentence, confirm, cancel — and it fits where it is used
because it is used on a *page*, where a sentence beside two buttons still has
most of the width. This strip lives in the Analyze sidebar, which is
`theme.Metrics.rail_w` and fixed at it, with 319 px of scrolling viewport
inside that. Measured in a real `AnalyzeTab` at the app's default window size,
`Resume` and `Discard` beside the label leave the offer **139 px**, so it
reflows into a 192-px column of twelve lines running down the side of two
buttons floating in the middle of it. Text above its own right-aligned action
row gives the same words **295 px** and four lines.
`tests/test_analyze_banners_are_readable.py` holds that as geometry rather than
as inspection: the label must get at least four fifths of the strip, which fails
for a row layout however it is spelled.

The offer is rendered across four labels rather than as one wrapping paragraph,
because it answers four questions in a fixed order and a single label renders
all four in one weight with nothing to say where any of them ends: a **kicker**
naming the state in two words (`Failed run`, `Suspended run`, `Interrupted run`
for a record the app never closed), an **identity** line carrying the plate and
when the run started, the **prose** saying what happened and what Resume will
do, and the **tally**. `_Resumable` carries those three strings beside the
one-sentence `headline`, which is what the log line and the discard dialog use —
both are prose in a stream of prose and have nowhere to put a layout — and the
headline is composed from the same locals as the parts, so the two renderings
cannot describe the same run differently. `_INCREMENTAL_NOTE` is the single
statement of what Resume does, said by the strip, the headline and the log line
alike; three separately-worded copies of it is how a user comes to read two
different accounts of one behaviour.

`RunRecord.tally` returns a sentence written to be *concatenated* — it opens
with a space and with "It recorded", so it reads on from whatever precedes it.
The pre-run readout still concatenates it, so the shape stays as it is and the
resume strip strips the leading space for its own line; standing alone the
sentence is still correct, because the line above it has just named the run. A
run whose journal recorded nothing has no tally, and that label is hidden rather
than left empty, since an empty `QLabel` still takes its line height and the
column's spacing with it.

`PipelineRunner._run_pipeline_thread` is where the journal opens and closes:
just below where the output directory is created and `_last_output_dir` is set,
and inside the `finally` beside `("finished", None)`. That is the only
chokepoint every mode passes through: local, remote and batched all fork below
it, and the output directory does not exist as a known path any earlier,
because `resolve_dirs` runs inside that thread.

The pipeline's argument list is built one step earlier still, *before* the
directory is created. `build_pipeline_args` is pure string assembly but reads
required keys off `opts` and raises on a missing one, so creating the directory
first left an empty `out/` behind whenever the form could not produce a
launchable command — an output folder, and nothing beside it to say what it
was, for a run that never started. `tests/test_run_leaves_no_empty_output_dir.py`
holds the order. The outcome comes from the runner's own flags rather than the queue it
just wrote to — suspend is asked about before stop, since a suspend sets both and
asking the other way round would record every suspend as a cancel.

The **Datasets Job Queue** can suspend too, and carries the result across a
session. Its Pause button winds the running job down (`suspend_current`, which
probes the runner for a `suspend` hook and falls back to a plain cancel for the
Datasets tools, none of which has an equivalent boundary to stop at); a separate
`Stop job` button is the destructive answer. A wound-down job goes to
`JobState.SUSPENDED` — deliberately not through `mark_finished`, since a suspend
is not an outcome and treating it as a cancel would cascade its successors to
BLOCKED as though its output were never coming.

`SUSPENDED` and `INTERRUPTED` form `JobState.RESUMABLE`: work that stopped
part-way with its results intact on disk. `next_runnable` selects them alongside
`PENDING`, so starting the queue picks such a job up rather than requiring it to
be re-added by hand, and neither is in `TERMINAL` any more — a job with a future
is still worth reordering. `_repair_after_load` turns a `RUNNING` job (the app
went away mid-run) into `INTERRUPTED` and no longer cascade-blocks its
successors: they stay `PENDING` and wait for output that is still coming.

A run the queue started also suspends from the Analyze page, and the queue does
the right thing there: the run ends with `jobFinished(False, "", "")`, and
`JobQueueController._was_suspended` asks the runner's `was_suspended`, so
`_on_job_finished` marks the job `SUSPENDED` and pauses the queue rather than
starting the next one underneath a user who has just asked for their machine
back. What did *not* come
for free is restarting that job from the queue. A queued job's stored spec never
carries `incremental` — it is not a form field — and re-running without it skips
every well whose output zip exists: the wells that never began are recovered, but
the ones that were *in flight* wrote a CSV and an out.zip from the FOV-groups
they had finished, so they read as complete, are skipped, and never get their
missing groups back. The plate returns looking done.
`AnalyzeSuspendMixin.resume_aware_spec`, which every `start_run` routes through,
forces incremental when the input has an unfinished run behind it: a suspend
record naming it, or an unfinished entry in the run journal's index. A journal
is matched on the folder the user picked, which its spec records as `opts.raw`,
as well as on the directory the run was resolved to (`<plate>/in` for a plate
folder or a drop of loose TIFs) — `_journal_names_input` asks both, because the
journal's `input_dir` is the resolved one and the form holds the picked one. A
queue job's restart is covered by the journal, since the queue writes no suspend
record.

**Grouping consumes each well folder as it goes, but deletes only what it
archived.** The FOLDER / FLAT staging path (and the MIXED leftover zip-up) turns
every `<well>/` into `<well>.zip` and drops that folder's images the moment its
own archive is published rather than at the end of the run. `_zip_well_folder`
writes through `util.zip_write.atomic_zip`, which renames a verified archive into
place or leaves nothing at all, so nothing is dropped until a complete archive
sits beside it. Deferring the deletion to the post-success hook meant the input
dir carried both `<well>/` and `<well>.zip` for every well for the whole run: two
full copies of the plate on the user's own volume at peak, on exactly the runs
where the input is largest.

**The folder is not the unit of deletion; the archived files are.** Every one of
these paths packs an *extension-filtered* subset — the folder zippers take
`.tif`/`.tiff` only, and `compress_images_to_zip` adds `.png` — so removing the
folder destroyed everything the filter skipped: OME companion XML, acquisition
logs, mask subdirectories, and on macOS the `.DS_Store` in every folder a user
has opened in Finder, with no copy anywhere.
`util.zip_write.replace_folder_with_archive` is the one answer: it deletes
exactly the files that went into the archive and removes the directory only when
nothing is left in it. A folder still holding something survives carrying just
that remainder, and the caller's log line names what it kept rather than
reporting the folder gone. Four paths route through it —
`remote_staging._zip_well_folder`'s two callers (plus the post-success hook, which
skips any folder the pass preserved),
`pipeline.mixed_input.consolidate_mixed_to_zips`, the Datasets pane's
`_zip_well_folders`, and
`process_microscopy.compress_folder_images_to_zip_and_remove`. The extension
filter stays with each caller: `util/image_exts.py` records why the folder
zipper's set is a different question from what the pipeline will group as input.

**Two questions, two functions, and a guard over the difference.**
`util.image_exts` answers both. `is_group_image` is a pure suffix test and
nothing more — `._Plate_A01.tif` is an AppleDouble sidecar, four hundred bytes
of macOS resource fork, and its suffix is `.tif`, so this returns true for it.
The **done**-side readers use it, because what a resumed run considers already
finished is pinned by
`test_incremental_keys_shared.py::test_zip_reader_keeps_its_own_hidden_file_behaviour`
and must not move when the input rule does. `is_run_input_member` is the
**intent**-side rule: it rejects the sidecars, `__MACOSX/` members, dotfiles and
zip directory entries, and it is what every question about *the user's data*
asks — how many FOV-groups does this plate hold, how much disk will they need,
which timepoints exist, which filenames should schema inference learn from.
Everything on that list has an image suffix and is not an image, and everything
unclassifiable answers wrongly to a domain test applied outside its domain.

The consequences, each measured: a finished two-image well carrying its two
macOS twins reported intent 4 with two permanently missing FOV-groups, because
the twins parse to a *different* `(fov, timepoint)` rather than to nothing; the
disk pre-flight sized a run at 4 KB for a plate of 112 MB frames, since `._`
sorts first and the loose branch returned the first match rather than the
largest its own docstring promised; and schema inference gained a whole extra
field on a 1:1 corpus, so every filename in the plate parsed to the wrong well.
`tests/test_one_definition_of_an_image.py` is the rule that keeps the set from
being spelled a sixth time — it found **twelve** sites against the pre-fix
tree — and exemption is a per-site marker comment carrying its reason, not a
file-level entry: the first version of that guard allowlisted whole files and
reported one offending site out of twelve.
`tests/test_no_unarchived_delete.py` holds the rule, following archive-writing
one call deep within a module so a site that zips through a one-line helper is
still caught.

**A symlink is its own name, never its target's.** A zip member is a name, so
the unit this compares is a name too. `_entry_identity` is
`(os.path.realpath(path.parent), path.name)` — deliberately not
`Path.resolve()`, which follows the final component and so hands back one path
for a symlink and the file it points at. That conflation lost something in both
directions. A link *inside* the folder pointing at an archived file resolved
equal to that file, so it was not counted among the files left behind: the
folder looked empty of un-archived content and was removed, taking a name the
archive holds no member for. And an archived path that is *itself* a symlink out
of the folder resolved to somewhere outside, so it dropped out of the archived
set and was then reported back as `kept` — a caller's "files not archived" log
line naming a file that was archived, with the link never removed. Resolving
only the *parent* keeps a symlinked ancestor directory from splitting two
spellings of one folder apart, while leaving the final component lexical, which
is the level a zip member name lives at and the level at which two hard links to
one inode are correctly two entries. The walk counts every entry that is not a
real directory, symlinks included — a dangling link, and a link to a directory,
are both files left in the folder, and the folder must survive carrying them.

Two folders are still left whole — one holding no images (there is no archive to
replace it with) and one whose well already had a user-written zip (that archive
was not written by this run and nothing here verified it covers the folder).
There is no rollback of the archives written in the pass: unlinking them on a
later well's failure would now delete the only remaining copy of every well that
had already succeeded, and a part-zipped plate is the correct resume state
anyway — the finished wells read as ZIP mode on the next run. A stripped folder
does not change that reading: `_detect_local_input_mode` reports MIXED only for a
well folder with **no** matching zip, and a stripped one always has one.

The remote client resolves its own scratch base — the staging rewrites, transit
output zips, and incremental merge temps — through `remote_scratch._scratch_dir`,
in the same order and to the same default as the pipeline below:
`$ALLWELL_SCRATCH_DIR` → `~/.allwell/scratch` → the OS temp dir (last resort,
when home is unwritable). The two resolvers cannot share a constant, because the
client must not import `pipeline.io` and drag numpy and tifffile into the remote
path, so `tests/test_remote_runner.py` pins them to the same value instead. They
used to disagree, the client defaulting to the OS temp dir: a remote run then
staged gigabytes into `/var/folders/<hash>/T` on macOS, or a tmpfs — RAM — on
Linux, at a path the user had never chosen and could not find.

**Scratch (bulk, transient).** `pipeline.io.scratch_base_for(output_dir)` decides
where per-well working files go: the extracted input TIFs, every intermediate
image, and the per-FOV checkpoints. Resolution order is `$ALLWELL_SCRATCH_DIR`
(set by `--scratch_dir` or the Analyze tab's *Scratch disk* field) →
**`~/.allwell/scratch`** (the default) → `output_dir` (last resort, warned).

The default used to be `output_dir`, and the Analyze field auto-seeded
`<input>/Temp`, so *both* put the whole run's bulk I/O on user-chosen volumes.
That is the bug behind **"many wells fail with `OSError: [Errno 9] Bad file
descriptor` on local runs but never on Slurm"**: each FOV-group writes ~6 images,
each staged tmp → fsync → rename (three filesystem operations apiece), times
every FOV × timepoint × well, times N worker processes — all funnelled through
