one SMB session when the volume is a NAS. macOS's `smbfs` does not re-open
server-side handles across a session reconnect, so every descriptor opened
before the drop returns `EBADF`. Slurm never sees it: inputs are rsynced to the
cluster and the pipeline runs against cluster-local storage. (NFS would give
`ESTALE`, so the errno identifies the protocol.) The scratch base is a dedicated
subdirectory, never `~` itself, because `_sweep_stale_scratch_dirs` *deletes*
what its `_tmp_*` glob finds.

Both modes honour it. Folder mode used to pin its staging to `output_dir` so the
closing commit could be a same-filesystem `rename`; `pipeline.io._commit_staging_dir`
now falls back to a copy on `EXDEV`, so the staging dir is free to live anywhere.
Once the move is complete it drops the well's per-FOV checkpoints (`.fov_*`)
from the committed folder: the CSV was written before the commit, so they are
spent, and left behind they were all `out/<WELL>/` held once its images had
been archived.
`_sweep_stale_scratch_dirs_all` sweeps the scratch base *and* `output_dir` (when
they differ) so staging left by pre-change runs is still reclaimed.

**Results (small, durable).** Only two writes per well must land on `output_dir`:
the per-well CSV and `<well>_out.zip`. Both carry the same retry-with-backoff
shield `_safe_imwrite` has always had, via `pipeline.io.retry_write` — they stage
to `__aw_tmp_` and commit with `os.replace`, so re-running is safe, and a
transient fault costs a retry instead of the whole well.
`_AtomicTextHandle.__exit__` guards its `flush()`/`close()` and aborts the commit
rather than renaming a short file over a good CSV.

**One retry shield, both sides of the app.** The loop itself is
`util.retry_io.retry_io`: run the operation, and on an `OSError` clean up the
staging file, back off and try again, up to five attempts. It lives in `util/`
because both halves of All-Well need it and neither can import the other's —
`pipeline.io` wraps it as `retry_write` (keeping the pipeline's own wording,
which names `--workers` and `--incremental`), and the `services/` remote client
calls it directly, where importing `pipeline.io` would drag numpy/tifffile into
a module that must stay imaging-stack-free. Three behaviours are worth knowing:

- **An error retrying cannot fix fails on the first attempt.** A missing path,
  wrong permissions, a full volume (`_PERMANENT_ERRNOS`) are re-raised straight
  away, so a caller that treats a missing source as an ordinary `OSError` stays
  responsive and the real cause isn't buried under a retry story.
- **`ENOSPC` is the one that gets rewritten on the way out.** Callers pass the
  target `path`, and the failure comes back as `util.disk_space.space_message` —
  the volume that filled, how much is left on it, and that the scratch staging
  may be sharing it — with errno 28 preserved so callers matching on it still
  work. Everything else in `_PERMANENT_ERRNOS` passes through untouched.
- **The exhausted-budget message names the storage.** `volume_hint` maps the
  errno to the protocol behind it — `EBADF` to macOS SMB, `ESTALE` to NFS,
  `EIO`/`ECONNRESET`/`ETIMEDOUT` to a link that dropped — and the caller adds
  its own advice tail. The user gets "this volume is a network mount and it
  dropped" instead of `[Errno 9]`.

**A remote run does the same I/O on the same volumes.** The pipeline executes on
the cluster, but the *client* still reads the whole plate off the user's input
volume and writes every fetched well back onto the output volume, so the same
shield covers each of those crossings:

| Where | What it protects |
|---|---|
| `remote_staging._materialize_staging` | Rewriting each `<WELL>.zip` the upload plan trims, reading it off the input volume into the upload staging dir — possibly a whole plate, back to back, and an unguarded fault here failed the run before a byte was uploaded. An archive that needs no rewrite is uploaded from where it is and never copied. |
| `remote_staging._zip_well_folder` | Packing a leftover well folder read off the input volume. |
| `input_resolution_service` | The mixed-input consolidation and the loose-image append, both of which rewrite archives *on* the input volume. |
| `Fetcher._materialize` | Publishing `<well>_out.zip` into the output dir — the remote run's equivalent of the pipeline's out-zip write. |
| `refresh_pipeline_info_available_from_outputs` | The `pipeline_info.json` rewrite, so one blip can't cost Review its timepoint/FOV lists. |

The per-well CSV pull is rsync's write rather than Python's, so it is covered by
the rsync retry policy instead: `_RSYNC_RETRY_CODES` includes **11** (*error in
file I/O*), which is what a destination-side `EBADF` surfaces as. Permission-class
failures (23, 3) still fail immediately. `Fetcher._rsync_glob` returns
`(listed, pulled)` so the two outcomes are reported apart — "the remote produced
no CSVs" and "the remote has them and the local write failed" used to print the
same line, which sent every diagnosis at the wrong machine.

**Well archives are published, not written in place.** Every per-well archive —
the `in/<WELL>.zip` inputs and the `out/<well>_out.zip` outputs — is built
through `util.zip_write.atomic_zip`, the single writer shared by
`process_microscopy.compress_images_to_zip`, `pipeline.io.merge_images_into_zip`,
`input_resolution_service` (the mixed-input consolidation and the loose-image
append) and `remote_runner` (upload staging and the two upload-filter rewrites).
It stages at `__aw_tmp_<name>.pid<N>`, fsyncs, re-reads the staged file's central
directory to confirm it holds exactly the members that were written, and —
when `verify` is on, which it is whenever `durable` is — decompresses every
member to check its stored CRC, before `os.replace`ing it into position and
fsyncing the parent directory. Three invariants come out of that, the first two
unconditional and the third following `verify`; all of them matter because users
open these archives by hand as often as All-Well opens them:

- *A published archive is readable.* A run killed mid-write — or a share that
  drops — leaves the staging file, never a truncated `<WELL>.zip`.
- *A published archive has members.* A zero-member zip is structurally valid, so
  Python and `unzip` read it as an empty archive, but macOS Archive Utility
  refuses to expand it ("*it is in an unsupported format*") and the pipeline
  reads it as a well whose images vanished. `atomic_zip` raises `ZipWriteError`
  rather than publish one, so callers with nothing to pack must not create the
  file: a well folder with no TIFs is left alone by the consolidation step, and
  a well that produced no output images gets no `<well>_out.zip`.
- *A published archive's members decompress.* The member-list check answers "is
  the index complete?", which is a different question: a truncated tail loses
  entries from the central directory, but bytes corrupted inside a deflate
  stream leave the index untouched, so the archive opens, lists everything, and
  raises `Bad CRC-32` only when something reads a member. The `verify` pass
  closes that gap, and defaults to `durable` for the same reason: an archive
  holding the only copy of data a pipeline just computed is worth the read-back,
  while a Datasets container copy whose source is still on disk beside it is not.
  Measured at 0.55s for a 56 MB, 40-member archive of dense 16-bit image data.

**A JSON file the app will read again is replaced, not overwritten.**
`util.json_write.write_json_atomic` is that rule: a staging file in the
destination's own directory, then `os.replace`. `path.write_text(json.dumps(…))`
truncates the destination the instant it opens, so anything that interrupts the
write leaves a file that is neither the old content nor the new one — and for
`pipeline_info.json` that is the user's gating, sample definitions, ratios and
notes gone at once, which is precisely what the tools rewriting it exist to
preserve. One specialised version stays: `review.persistence._io.atomic_write_json`
wraps both the open and the replace in a retry for Windows `PermissionError`.
The two bookkeeping records — the run journal and the suspended-run pointer —
need a return value rather than an exception, because a run that cannot write its
own bookkeeping must still produce data; that is one line of difference, so it is
`util.json_write.try_write_json_atomic` rather than a copy in each of them. They
had a copy each once and the copies diverged in both available directions: one
caught the `TypeError` a caller-supplied `spec` raises and the other did not, and
one removed its staging file on failure and the other did not. The second gap was
not cosmetic — `suspend_record.save` raising escaped a function whose contract is
a boolean, into `_suspend`'s own handler, which returns *before*
`PipelineRunner.suspend()` is reached, so the Suspend button did nothing at all
and said nothing about it.
`tests/test_dataset_tool_integrity.py` scans every application source file
(`tests/_repo_scan.python_sources`) for the shapes that truncate a destination:
`write_text` / `write_bytes` of a serialised payload, including one bound to a
name first or encoded on the way, and `json.dump` into a handle from a plain
`open`. A scope that renames what it wrote is doing by hand what
`write_json_atomic` does, and clears the rule on that basis rather than by
being named in an allowlist.

The reading side stays tolerant — a `<WELL>.zip` that won't open is skipped by
the samplers and surfaces as a failed well from the worker pool — but nothing
All-Well writes should ever land in that state.

**Remote is pinned, not defaulted.** `remote_runner._build_remote_argv` emits an
explicit `--scratch_dir=<remote_output>` and drops any local `--scratch_dir`, so
Slurm runs keep their pre-change behaviour — a cluster home is typically a
small-quota NFS share, and the remote output dir already lives in the host's
configured staging area.

The run logs its resolved scratch base on the `Scratch  :` line; if that ever
reads back as the output dir on a network mount, that is the failure
configuration.

### 6.5b Per-well CSVs are gzipped, and every reader takes either spelling

A plate's per-well CSVs get very large, so a finished well's
`<prefix>_<well>.csv` is stored as `<prefix>_<well>.csv.gz`. A dataset folder can
hold either spelling, or a mix: wells analysed before compression existed, a run
resumed across the change, an incremental run on top of an old dataset. The one
module that says how the two relate is `util/csv_gz.py`, and the rules are:

- **One logical file, two possible spellings.** `existing_csv` and `glob_csvs`
  return one entry per logical CSV. When both spellings exist the plain file wins:
  the archive is only ever produced from a plain file, so the two coexist only
  when a merge wrote a newer plain file beside an older archive, or when removing
  the plain file after compressing failed (the two are then identical).
- **Names are stripped with `csv_stem`, never `Path.stem`**, which leaves `.csv`
  on a gzipped name. The Review well key, the Parquet cache name and the Datasets
  well maps all use it.
- **Writers are gzip-aware by name.** `open_csv_text(path, "w")` and
  `review.persistence._io.atomic_write_text` write gzip bytes for a `.csv.gz` path;
  writing plain text under that name would leave a file no reader accepts.
  The Datasets tools (Subset, Merge Plates, Concatenate) keep the spelling of their
  source CSV.

**When the pipeline compresses.** Not while a well is being built: the incremental
and resume logic reads a well's rows back (`read_done_fov_keys`,
`merge_records_into_csv`), so the CSV is a plain file until its well is written
for the last time. `pipeline.io.write_well_csv` (a fresh well) and
`merge_well_records` (an incremental merge, which reads the existing file in
either spelling and writes plain) both end by calling `compress_well_csv`, and
`process_microscopy` reaches the per-well CSV only through them
(`tests/test_csv_gz.py` pins that). A compression failure is logged and leaves the
plain CSV: a larger file, not a wrong one.

**Remote runs compress before the transfer.** The remote runs the same
`process_microscopy`, so a well's CSV is already `.csv.gz` on the remote when it
finishes. For a run that was started before compression existed, the remote still
holds plain CSVs; `Fetcher._fetch_one` therefore runs `compress_remote_csvs` (a
small `gzip`-to-`.part`-then-rename script over ssh, in `services/remote_csv.py`) for a well that is not yet in
`run.fetched_wells`, before listing and pulling it. A well already transferred is
never touched again. The listing names both spellings (`*_<well>.csv` and
`*_<well>.csv.gz`), so a host where `gzip` failed still delivers its plain CSV.
After a non-incremental pull `retire_superseded_csvs` removes the other spelling of
every CSV that arrived, because a stale plain `x.csv` from an earlier run would
otherwise shadow the freshly fetched `x.csv.gz`. An incremental fetch merges the
partial into the local CSV (`pipeline.io.merge_fetched_csvs`) and recompresses the
result. The end-of-run retry and the verification step use the same helpers.

### 6.6 The remote conda environment, and one definition of "it exists"

A remote run needs exactly one thing installed on the host: a conda environment
holding the pipeline's dependencies. Two pieces of code care whether it is
there — `remote_runner`'s pre-launch guard, and `services/remote_bootstrap.py`,
which creates it — and they answer with the same shell,
`remote_conda.CONDA_ENV_SHELL_HELPERS` (`aw_env_prefix` / `aw_env_is_valid` /
`aw_env_stale_dir`). That sharing is the point of the module-level constant:
when the two disagreed, the disagreement had no way out.

**Validity is conda's own test.** A prefix is an environment iff it holds
`conda-meta/history`. The bootstrap used to ask a different question — "is the
name in `conda env list`" — and the gap between the two is a real state on a
cluster: a `conda create` that dies part-way (a full home-directory quota is the
usual cause) leaves a directory at the prefix with no `conda-meta/history`.
conda will neither run in that directory nor create over it, so every run failed
with `EnvironmentLocationNotFound: not a conda environment: <prefix>` *and*
every re-bootstrap failed behind it with `prefix already exists`. Nothing the
user could reach from the app repaired it.

Both sides now detect it, and **neither deletes it**. All-Well does not remove
data from a user's cluster account as a side effect of an action they asked for
something else with — the contents of that directory are unreadable to us, and a
wrong guess about which directory is disposable is not recoverable. What the two
sides owe the user is the diagnosis and the exact command:

- The **guard** distinguishes "no environment" from "a directory that is not an
  environment", names the directory, names the likely cause (quota), and prints
  the `rm -rf <prefix>` line to run. A run is not the time to modify the host.
- The **bootstrap** stops before the `conda create` that would fail, with the
  same `ACTION REQUIRED` note. Continuing would only surface conda's `prefix
  already exists`, which states the problem without stating the remedy.

Deletion happens only where the user asked for deletion: `--force`, whose entire
documented purpose is to clear a suspect install. Even there each removal is
echoed before it happens, and a prefix that does not match `*/envs/<name>` is
refused rather than removed, so an unexpected path from conda cannot turn the
flag into an arbitrary `rm -rf`.

**Where the env actually lives.** `conda create -n allwell` lands in the first
writable envs dir, which on a host with a pre-existing system conda (an HPC
module, `/opt/conda`) is `~/.conda/envs/allwell` and not under `~/miniforge3`.
`--force` resolves the prefix through conda before removing it; removing
`~/miniforge3` alone left the env untouched, which made the flag's own promise
("use when the remote env is suspected corrupt") false on exactly the hosts
most likely to need it.

The scripts are built by `env_setup_script()` / `force_clean_script()` rather
than inline in the ssh callers, so `tests/test_bootstrap_env_repair.py` can run
them against a stub conda and a scratch `HOME` — the create-or-stop decision is
the part that strands users when it is wrong, and an ssh call hides it. The stub
refuses `conda create` over an existing prefix the way conda does; without that,
tests of this behaviour pass against the broken script too.

**"The env is complete" means every pipeline package, not TensorFlow.** The
probe reports which of `remote_bootstrap.REQUIRED_IMPORTS` — one import name per
distribution `requirements-remote.txt` installs on Linux — the env cannot find,
via `importlib.util.find_spec`, which locates a module without importing it, so
the probe neither pays for loading Torch and TensorFlow nor risks the two
refusing to share a process. A dotted name (`google.protobuf`) is looked up only
once its top level is found, because `find_spec` imports the parent and raises
when it is absent. `install_pip_deps` skips the `pip install -r` only when
TensorFlow is present and nothing is missing; an env whose python cannot answer
reports `?` and is installed into. The skip used to be TensorFlow alone, so an
env built before Cellpose joined the requirements, or one whose Torch half
failed, reported ready on every re-bootstrap and the run died on the compute node
at `from cellpose import models`. `NOT_PROBED` names the requirement lines the
probe deliberately skips (the macOS-only TensorFlow builds, `tomli` below Python
3.11), each with its reason, and `tests/test_bootstrap_probes_every_requirement.py`
holds the two rosters against the requirements file and runs the probe's own
shell line under bash with a real interpreter. Version drift — a package present
at the wrong pin — is not detected; pip resolves that only when the install
runs for another reason.

---

## 6b. The Datasets side

The Datasets pane (`datasets/tab.py`) is the third top-level mode. Structurally
it mirrors `AnalyzeTab`: a self-contained `QWidget` whose left `_left_sidebar` is
a `RailNav` page navigator (no well picker) over a `NamedPageStack`, with one
page per feature. Features are declared in one local tuple (`_FEATURES`) — a
`_Feature(name, icon, build)` per entry — so adding a Datasets feature is a
one-line change, without pulling in Review's well/selection-scoped
`FeatureRegistry`/`ViewerContext` machinery. The rail's `currentChanged` drives
`NamedPageStack.setCurrentByName`.

Each feature is one `_Feature` entry in `datasets/tab.py::_FEATURES` and a
`datasets/<name>/` package on the standard view/controller/worker + Qt-free
compute/apply split; a completed run hands its output to another pane through
an injected callback (`on_open_in_review` → `AllWellApp._open_dataset_in_review`;
`on_open_in_analyze` → `_open_dataset_in_analyze`). Helpers shared across more
than one feature — dataset-folder resolution, well-container IO, schema-safe
filename rewriting — live in `datasets/core/` rather than being imported
from one feature package into another, so each feature stays independently
deletable:

| Module | What it holds |
|---|---|
| `datasets/core/dataset_paths.py` | `DatasetPaths`, `resolve_dataset`, `read_info`, well enumeration (`in_containers`, `out_csvs`, `out_zips`, `out_folders`, `dataset_wells`), the folder's own answer to how many files claim one well (`well_spelling_collisions`, `describe_well_collisions`), the destination-state predicates (each taking the caller's own in-progress marker filename as a parameter), and the input-side availability scan (`collect_available_schema_values`) that mirrors `process_microscopy._collect_available_timepoints`/`_fovs` without importing the pipeline. That scan is two halves: `collect_input_image_stems(in_dir, known_zip_members=…)` walks the input folder (loose TIFs, one level of well subfolders, well zips' TIF members), taking already-listed member names for any zip the caller has read itself rather than opening it again; `schema_values_from_stems` extracts one field's distinct values out of stems already in hand. `collect_available_schema_values` is the two composed, and remains the entry point for a caller asking about a single field from a cold start (Apply repairs). A caller asking about two fields, or one that has just read every archive for its own reasons (Validate does both), goes through the halves and walks once. `out_folders` is `out_zips`'s folder-mode twin (`out/<WELL>/`, written when `compressed_output=False`) — a dataset is written either zipped or folder-mode, never both, but a caller checking for "done" image evidence regardless of which mode produced it (Validate) should check both maps rather than assuming one. `dataset_wells` unions all four well-enumeration maps, including `out_folders`, matching its own docstring ("every 96-well position present in a dataset's `in` or `out`") — every current caller (Concatenate, Merge Plates, Subset) already refuses folder-mode input before calling it, so this only matters for a future caller that doesn't. `preview_wells(root)` is a best-effort, exception-safe `dataset_wells` a page calls on every keystroke while the user is still typing a path — it returns `[]` for anything that isn't (yet) a real dataset folder instead of raising `DatasetPathsError` the way `resolve_dataset` would, since "not a valid path yet" is the normal, expected state through most of a field edit, not an error to report. `shorten_headline(text, *full_paths)` replaces every occurrence of each of *full_paths* inside *text* with its own basename — a run's success summary is built by formatting a full destination (or source) path into a sentence, right for the log line but unreadable as a dashboard headline; the caller keeps the original *text* for the log and passes it again as the headline's own tooltip, so the full path is never actually lost, only the on-screen headline is shortened. It skips any path that is empty (Import Loose's in-place mode, whose `dest_root` is `""`) — `"".replace` would otherwise insert the basename between every character of *text*. **The four well maps hold one path per canonical well, so they cannot represent two spellings of one position** — `in/A1.zip` beside `in/A01.zip`, the state a plate exported by a scope that does not zero-pad and later topped up by a run that does is left in. Nothing about the surviving map says the other archive exists, and every copy tool reads the map rather than the folder, so the loser's images were absent from the copy while the run reported success with a well count that never mentioned them. Two things answer it, and neither is inside the maps. The survivor is deterministic — a sorted glob, and the spelling that already equals the canonical label wins — rather than whatever the filesystem yielded first. And `well_spelling_collisions(paths)` asks the folder directly, returning `{well: [every path claiming it]}`; `describe_well_collisions` renders the refusal sentence, one line per well naming every file, so the user can see which two spellings to reconcile without going to look. Only genuine same-role duplicates count: two raw-input zips, two raw-input folders, two `<WELL>_out.zip` archives, two `out/<WELL>/` folders, or two measurements CSVs for one well **under the same `--csv_prefix`**. A zip beside a same-well folder is not a collision — `process_microscopy` ignores well folders whenever any zip is present, a settled precedence `in_containers` follows — and two CSVs under *different* prefixes is the mixed-prefix state `out_csvs`' own docstring documents and Validate reports with a cause of its own; refusing either here would reject a layout the pipeline reads correctly. |
| `datasets/core/provenance.py` | `record_derivation(dest, tool=…, sources=…, **detail)` — the `derived_from` line Subset, Merge Plates and Concatenate append to the dataset they wrote (§5.7), naming the source dataset roots plus what the tool's summary states (`wells` kept, the `well_map`, the `offset_hours`). Called after verification and after the destination's `pipeline_info.json` is written, so a derivation that raised part-way records nothing. The importers are deliberately not covered — they write raw input with no sidecar, so no directory holds the dataset's history until its first Analyze run, which the runner records. Validate & Repair appends `repaired` from `datasets/validate/apply.apply_repairs` when it changed something, and nothing for its idempotent no-op. |
| `datasets/core/containers.py` | `copy_container_members` — the one path every Datasets tool moves image bytes through — plus `container_dest` (where a container belongs in a destination directory: `<WELL>.zip` for a zipped well, `<WELL>/` for a folder-mode one, always named for the **well token** rather than for the source file, because a source plate written with unpadded tokens otherwise produced `in/A1.zip` beside an `out/A01_out.zip` from the same run and nothing downstream matched the two up), `read_members` / `write_zip` (collision-safe, first-write-wins), `clear_destination`, `restamp_overrides` / `unstamped_note` (below), and the `timepoint`/`timepoint_hours`/`filename` column-name and cell-overrides constants. **It moves bytes rather than reconstructing them.** No Datasets tool alters image data: Subset filters, Concatenate offsets a name's timepoint field, Merge plates rewrites a name's well token, and in every case the member's compressed payload is identical on both sides — a name lives in a member's headers, not in its data. So the helper publishes one destination archive from one or more source containers, taking a `rename(container, member_name)` callback that returns the destination name or `None` to leave the member out, in three tiers. **Whole-file copy:** a single zip source with every member kept under its own name is copied byte-for-byte and never opened for reading — staged beside the destination and renamed into place, like the other two tiers, so an interrupted copy leaves no partial `<WELL>.zip` behind. That is a wells-only Subset, and it is the case a user would otherwise do by hand in Finder, so it has to cost what Finder costs. **Raw member passthrough:** otherwise each kept member's already-compressed bytes are streamed across by `datasets/core/zip_passthrough.py` — no inflate, no deflate, no CRC recomputation — and a dropped member is never read at all, so a filter that keeps a quarter of an archive costs about a quarter of it. **Fallback:** a folder source, or a member the passthrough declines (a directory entry, an encrypted member), goes through `read_members`/`write_zip`'s ordinary decompress-and-recompress, one member at a time. The tier is chosen from member *lists* only — for a zip that is the central directory, a footer, so planning costs a couple of seeks however large the archive is and however slow the volume holding it — and peak memory is one chunk or one member rather than a whole uncompressed archive per thread. **Tiers 2 and 3 publish through `util/zip_write.atomic_zip`**, the same staged-then-verified-then-renamed writer the pipeline's own archives use (with `durable=False`, and therefore without the CRC read-back, because the source dataset is still on disk beside the destination): a plain `with ZipFile(dest, "w")` writes a central directory for whatever landed before an exception, so a member failing part-way through a well left a structurally valid archive holding fewer images than it was asked for with nothing on it saying so. The tools do write an in-progress marker and clear the destination on the next attempt, but nothing stops a user opening that half-written folder in Review first. **Two consequences of moving bytes rather than rebuilding them are worth knowing.** A whole-file copy reproduces the source exactly, so it keeps directory entries that a re-pack drops — inert either way, since `find_image_groups_in_zip`, `data/zip_members.py`, Validate and `incremental_keys` all filter by basename/extension or on a trailing slash. And a copied member keeps its source's compression method, so a subset or merge of a dataset whose `in/` archives were written `ZIP_STORED` (what `pipeline/ome_explode.py` writes) stays stored rather than being deflated on the way out; the destination can be larger on disk than the old re-packing path produced, which is the cost of not spending CPU to reproduce bytes that already exist. Returns `(written, dropped)`: *written* is what actually landed, so a caller can verify a CSV row's `filename` is really there; *dropped* is only the names lost to a **collision**, which is real data loss, never a member the `rename` callback declined. Nothing is created when nothing is kept — a zero-member zip is structurally valid but macOS Archive Utility refuses to expand it and All-Well reads it as a well whose images have vanished, the same rule `util/zip_write.atomic_zip` enforces for the pipeline's own archives. `read_members` / `write_zip` remain the tier-3 primitives and the shape a caller reaches for when it genuinely needs a member's decoded bytes in hand; both take an optional `progress(done, total)` keyword, called once per member against a total they know up front. `WellFraction` fuses per-pass counts into one dial: copying a well is several passes (the source container, then the QC `<WELL>_out.zip`), so the passes are declared up front as equal-weight *slices*, each pass reports into the slice `slice_progress()` hands it, and a pass with no work closes its slice with `skip()`. `copy_container_members` consumes exactly one slice whichever tier serves it, reporting a whole-file copy or an empty filter as a single closing step. Feeding each pass's own `(done, total)` straight to a dashboard instead would fill the same well's dial from empty once per pass, which reads as the well restarting; leaving a no-work slice unclaimed would strand a finished well short of full. `finish()` closes out whatever remains once the well's non-container work (its CSV) is done. The scale is a fixed 100 steps, deduplicated to whole steps, so a well holding thousands of files emits a bounded number of updates rather than one queued signal and one plate repaint per file. **`restamp_overrides` is the one carry-over rule for `cell_overrides.json`.** Every tool that copies that file has to re-fingerprint it — a repack changes the destination archive's mtime although the segmentation is untouched, and the fingerprint exists to catch a real re-segmentation — so it stamps each entry's `seg_fp` from the destination `<WELL>_out.zip`'s mtime and **returns how many it could not stamp**. A fingerprint that could not be computed is not a fingerprint, so the key is removed rather than left holding the source dataset's value: an entry with no `seg_fp` is the legacy unfingerprinted shape both readers already understand and keep (`review/persistence/cell_overrides.py`, `datasets/validate/apply._prune_stale_overrides`), whereas the source's stamp compared against the destination archive differs, and Validate then pruned the entry — the user's manual cell exclusions vanishing with every step reporting success. The count is returned rather than logged inside the helper so each tool states it in its own cell-override log line through `unstamped_note`: an override carried without a fingerprint survives, but it will no longer be dropped when that well really is re-segmented, and that is a fact about the artifact the run just produced. Subset, Merge Plates and Concatenate all call it, which is what stops the three copies drifting apart again. |
| `datasets/core/zip_passthrough.py` | `copy_member_raw` / `member_is_raw_copyable` / `RawCopyUnsupported` — copying one member's already-compressed bytes from one archive into another. The destination member keeps the source's compression method, CRC and both sizes, so it decompresses to exactly the same data; only its name and its position in the file change. **This depends on four `zipfile` implementation details** — `ZipFile.fp`, `.filelist`, `.NameToInfo`, `.start_dir` (plus the `_didModify` flag) — because the standard library exposes no public API for adding a member whose bytes are already compressed. Two things keep that contained: `member_is_raw_copyable` gates every member first, so a directory entry or an encrypted member is routed to the ordinary path as an expected case rather than an error; and `RawCopyUnsupported` is raised, with the destination truncated back to its exact pre-member state, when an archive's local headers disagree with its central directory. That last case is raised on rather than worked around — the ordinary path would fail on the same member for the same reason, and an archive that quietly holds fewer images than it was asked for is the one outcome this code must never produce. Any ZIP64 record in the source's extra field is stripped before the header is rebuilt (`ZipInfo.FileHeader` appends a freshly-computed one, and the source's describes the member at its old offsets); the data-descriptor flag comes off for the same class of reason, since the copied header carries the CRC and sizes inline where the source kept them in a trailer. **A member that is being renamed also loses Info-ZIP's Unicode Path and Unicode Comment records** (`0x7075` / `0x6375`). Each embeds its own copy of the member's name alongside a CRC of the name it was derived from, so across a rename it is a second, stale name for the same member: a reader that honours it and skips the name-CRC restores the file under its *pre-rename* name, silently undoing the well remap or timepoint offset the copy existed to perform. A member keeping its own name keeps those records, which still describe it correctly. |
| `datasets/core/member_names.py` | `rewrite_member_field` — the schema-safe, field-agnostic zip-member filename rewriter (extension check, field-count check, channel-scoped role suffix preserved) that Concatenate's timepoint shift and Merge plates' well remap both wrap with their own validity predicate — plus `is_os_junk_member`, the shared answer to "is this member operating-system debris rather than data?" (`.DS_Store`, `Thumbs.db`, `desktop.ini`, `__MACOSX/`, AppleDouble `._` sidecars, the Spotlight and Trash directories). It is deliberately a *named set*, not "anything that isn't an image": a `notes.txt` a user put in an archive on purpose is real content, and a caller that refuses to reconcile two conflicting copies of a real file should keep refusing. Concatenate is its only caller — see §6b's Verification note for what carrying that debris through a merge used to do. |
| `datasets/core/tool_controller.py` | `DatasetToolController` — the worker lifecycle every tool controller shares (`jobFinished`, `stop`, `is_busy`, `shutdown`), with the two things that differ between tools as knobs: `_shutdown_label`, and a `_request_worker_stop` hook. The hook exists for one tool. Import Loose's worker spends the run blocked inside the zipper subprocess's stdout read loop and never polls `isInterruptionRequested()`, so Qt's cooperative flag is a no-op there and `request_stop` — which also signals the tracked child — is what actually stops it; a base that hard-coded `requestInterruption()` would have left an orphan process on app close, and `shutdown` swallows the failure it would then hit. `DestinationToolController` adds the run-and-confirm-restart cluster the three copy-into-a-destination tools share (Subset, Merge Plates, Concatenate), with `_destination_has_marker` supplied per tool because a folder holding *this* tool's interrupted attempt is a resume and another tool's leftovers are not. Deliberately **not** on either base: `_on_queue_requested`, `_on_finished` and `_on_succeeded`. Measured across the tool controllers by hashing each one's normalised body, `_on_queue_requested` has a distinct body in every one of them and `_on_finished` five distinct bodies across seven, while `_on_succeeded` diverges further up — Validate's takes `(report, result)` where the others take `(dest_root, summary)`. Pulling them up would trade plain methods for a base full of flags. |
| `datasets/core/dataset_fields.py` | `is_dataset` / `is_free_destination` / `promote_open_button` — the destination-field validators and the success-state button swap the pages share. `is_free_destination` takes its two predicates as arguments for the same marker reason as above. Cross-field rules ("the destination must differ from both sources") stay on the page, since they read fields the helper cannot see. Sharing the *wording* is part of the point: a user moving between Subset and Merge Plates should not be told the same thing two different ways. |
| `datasets/core/equation_row.py` | `build_equation_row` / `EquationRow` — the `dataset 1 + dataset 2 = destination` row, for the two tools that take two datasets and write a third. Merge Plates and Concatenate had built it twice in twenty statements each, differing only in two field labels and the name of the slot the fields report to, down to a byte-identical nested operator-glyph helper and a second copy of that column's width. What stays at the call site is what genuinely differs: the two dataset labels — Concatenate names its inputs "base" and "appended" because the operation is ordered, Merge Plates does not because its is not — and each page's own destination validator, which is bound to that tool's own in-progress marker and must **not** be shared. The builder returns the four widgets rather than assigning them, so each page keeps its own `_ds1_field` / `_ds2_field` / `_dest_field` / `_cross_hint` names, which its validation, its run spec and its reset all read. |
| `datasets/core/concurrency.py` | `pick_workers(workers, n_units)` — the shared worker-thread-count heuristic (0 = auto, capped at 8 and at the CPU count) every tool below uses for its per-well `ThreadPoolExecutor`. It **re-exports** `pipeline.explode_common.pick_workers` rather than defining it: the exploders take it from there, and this module used to hold a second implementation of the same three lines under a comment saying it mirrored the first — which is a heuristic that will be tuned in one place and not the other. |
| `datasets/core/convert_marker.py` | The resume marker the three **packed-file converters** share (Convert OME-TIFF, Convert CZI, Convert ND2) — `mapping_signature`, the marker read/write/clear trio, `converted_wells`, `ResumeState`, `resume_state` and `destination_problem`. It is a different question from `dataset_paths.make_dataset_api`'s, which the copy tools use: theirs is "did I leave leftovers here?", answerable from the presence of a file and cleared by rebuilding. This one is "may I carry on from what is here?", which is a question about **settings** — two different mappings of one source write *identical* filenames, so nothing on disk distinguishes an `A01.zip` made from scene 0 from one made from scene 7, and only a marker recording the mapping can tell a run that may finish another's work from one that must refuse. Each converter passes its own marker filename (a folder carrying *another* converter's leftovers is not a resume either) and its own list of mapping fields; the signature also carries the source's resolved path, size and mtime, so a file replaced at the same name — a re-export, a restore, the next plate saved over the last — is a different source. `workers` is deliberately not a mapping field: it changes how fast the conversion goes and nothing about what it writes, so refusing a resume over it would refuse one that was safe. |

**Every copy tool refuses a dataset that spells one well two ways.** Subset,
Merge Plates and Concatenate each call `well_spelling_collisions` from their own
plan builder — `_refuse_well_collisions`, one per tool so each raises its own
error class, and Merge Plates and Concatenate ask it of both sources — before
anything is written. The check belongs at the plan stage rather than inside the
well maps because the maps are one-path-per-well by construction and cannot
express the problem; and it belongs in all three because the alternative is a
destination that reads as a complete copy while a whole well's images exist
nowhere in it and appear in no count. Validate reports the same condition as an
`error`-severity `well_spelling_collision` finding, so a user who hits the
refusal has somewhere to go and see the rest of the plate.

`datasets/concatenate/concatenate_compute.py` and `apply.py` re-export the
names they lifted from `core`, so their own public API (and every existing
test against it) is unchanged.

All eight tool pages share their status/log furniture through
`datasets/core/log_panel.py::LogPanelMixin`. Each page ends the same way: a
header row naming its output section with a "Show raw log" checkbox, then a
separator and a read-only monospace log the checkbox reveals. The mixin owns
those two ends. The middle — a `ConcatDashboard`, a bare `QProgressBar`, a
`ValidateDashboard` above a findings list — differs per tool and stays on the
page, which is why the extraction stops where it does.

**One implementation of the toggle serves every page, with no overrides.** It
checks `_status`, `_log_sep` and `_log_hdr`; Validate is the only page holding a
log header of its own, and the rest contribute nothing there. Validate also
passes `clear=False`, keeping its Clear in the raw-log header rather than the
Findings one, where it reads as belonging to the findings and wipes a log that
is usually hidden. Per-page differences are parameters: section title, status
`objectName`, placeholder wording, and the toggle tooltip.

Besides that mixin and `equation_row.py`, `datasets/core/` holds only logic
(containers, dataset paths, member names, zip passthrough) — including
`dataset_paths.split_stem_well`,
the pane's single reader of a trailing well token on a longer stem
(`measurements_b10` → `("measurements", "B10")`). That is not
`util.well_token.canonical_well_label`, which judges a whole token; it is
equally deliberately the only place the judgement is made, since the same
regex and zero-padding in three modules is the shape §15 warns about. A shared *view* layer matters here for a
specific reason: without one, a fix to any of this lands on one page,
and the rest keep whatever they had.

Two properties the seam makes enforceable, both swept parametrically over
`datasets.tab._FEATURES` by `tests/test_datasets_log_panel.py` — driven off the
registry rather than a roster written in the test, so the next tool is covered
from the moment it exists. No page may re-define a shared member, and every
page needs a trailing `outer.addStretch(1)` after its last real widget — since
`QScrollArea.setWidgetResizable(True)` grows the content widget to the viewport
and the dashboard is otherwise the only thing willing to absorb the slack,
turning into a dead zone below its own height-capped plate.

**Convert OME-TIFF** (`datasets/ome_import/`) is the standalone OME-TIFF
de-interleaver described in §6.1: `ome_import_compute.plan_conversion` validates
the well-grid / FOVs / frame-order against the file's `OmeLayout` for the live
readout — and, first of all, that the file contains every image plane its
metadata declares (§6.1) — alongside `ome_import_compute.selection_target`, which reads the file's
position/frame budget from the same `OmeLayout` and (when FOVs is pinned) the well
count it implies, so the readout guides how many wells to place before any grid is
entered, not only errors at the end. `apply.convert` calls `explode_ome_tiff` (which writes per-well zips into
`<destination>/in/`, threaded, with progress + cancel), and the shared
`datasets.core.packed_convert.PackedConverterWorker` runs it off the UI thread. **The form is read once, through
`ome_import_compute.RawFields`** — the boxes exactly as typed, with `parse_count`
telling a blank ("auto", a real answer) from a value that is not a whole number.
`RawFields.problems()` returns the user-facing reasons a box can't be read and
`to_params()` the settings it describes; the page shows the former and refuses to
run while there are any, so a typo in FOVs per well or Workers is answered instead
of collapsing into the same silent default as an empty box. The grid boxes are
exempt while the order is hand-drawn, since nothing then reads them. The
destination field carries a validator of its own (`destination_problem`) like
every other tool's: a conversion overwrites the wells it writes and keeps the
rest, so a folder that already holds a plate would end up holding two.
The readout is two labels — neutral context above, and a pass/fail line below it
whose object name switches between `Muted`, `Warn` and `Danger`, because a
refusal and a green ✓ in the same grey differ only by a glyph. **A run locks
every input that would redraw the plate**, not only the plate: the plate is the
progress display, and a grid edit re-seeds its preview, which would swap the
wells being reported on — dials and all — for the ones the grid currently
describes while the conversion carries on against the order it started with.
**A finished conversion says how it went on the page.**
This is the one tool with no dashboard — it reports on the acquisition plate it
already draws (below) — so the verdict has a label of its own under the progress
bar (`set_outcome` / `clear_outcome`), painted by the shared
`widgets.plate_progress.apply_outcome` so a conversion reads the same way here as
on any dashboard headline. It belongs on the page and not only in the raw log,
which `LogPanelMixin` hides by default: a verdict that reaches only a hidden pane
leaves a failed run looking exactly like one that was never started. A terminal
state also lands the progress bar, which a run that ends before it has counted
its planes would otherwise leave in its indeterminate state — a bar still
sweeping is the one thing on the page claiming work is happening. On success
the page's "Open dataset in Analyze" button routes the produced folder to the
Analyze pane (`on_open_in_analyze`) — the output is an Analyze *input*, not a
Review dataset. The page also carries a per-channel **role picker** (one row
per OME channel name, seeded by `ome_import_compute.default_channel_roles`'s
name heuristic — a strong nuclear stain (`DAPI`/`Hoechst`/…) wins the
segmentation role, else a secondary `NIR`/`RFP` channel, else the first channel
that does not read as phase/brightfield); `channel_tokens_from_roles` aggregates
the picks into a minimal `pipeline_info`-shaped dict (`nuclear_token` /
`fluor_tokens` / `phase_token`, with the phase channel remaining a member of
`fluor_tokens` so Analyze has a row to carry its Phase checkbox)
that the open-in-Analyze callback (`AllWellApp._open_dataset_in_analyze`) feeds
to `AnalyzeTab._apply_pipeline_info`, so Analyze's Channel Tokens arrive
pre-filled. The channel names are written into the output filenames regardless
of the roles.

`QLabel#Notice` is the app's "read this, it is not what you wanted" block: the
`warn` tone, a ten-per-cent wash of it, and a two-pixel left rule. It is
**amber, not red**, because red here means a run died — *Failures recorded* on
the plate legend, `failed` in the Wells legend — and spending it on a scan that
merely declined to guess devalues it where it matters. It is a **panel, not a
colour**: measured off the rendered audit, muted body grey and `danger` red sit
at relative luminance 0.241 and 0.233, a three per cent difference, so
desaturated the two read as the same block and hue carried the whole signal.
The wash and the rule change the block's shape, which survives greyscale,
colour vision deficiency and the edge of vision. `QLabel#Error` is the narrower
sibling and stays `danger`: it marks a value that is *invalid*, which the schema
picker's validation labels are and a declined detection is not. Both were
unstyled until the audit was looked at rather than run.

That callback takes a `pipeline_info`-shaped settings dict and an `incremental`
flag, and both of its callers use them: the converter passes the channel roles
it assigned, Validate & Repair passes the dataset's whole recorded sidecar with
`incremental=True`. **It has to be legible on arrival.** Everything it changes
is either a field whose new value is indistinguishable from the old one at a
glance, or — for *Incremental*, the setting that decides whether the run
completes anything at all — a checkbox inside **Compute Options**, which is one
of the sections that fold by default. A correct handoff therefore looked exactly
like landing on an untouched Analyze tab, which is how a working feature gets
reported as doing nothing. So it unfolds that section
(`AnalyzeFormChromeMixin.reveal_section`) and `_announce_analyze_handoff` states
on the run dashboard what was set up, naming the dataset — and, when the sidecar
could not be read, saying in those words that the settings did **not** travel,
since a user who can't tell the two apart presses Run on whatever the form
happened to be holding. It applies the settings **first** and writes the input field
**afterwards** — a full sidecar's `execution_options` carries the `input_dir`
recorded on whatever machine ran the pipeline, and letting that win would point
Analyze at a path that need not exist locally, whereas the folder the caller
names is the one the user just picked. It ends by calling `_refresh_output`, so
the resolved output folder (and with it the incremental run's prior directory)
is on screen before the user presses Run.

The readout and the Convert/"+ Queue" buttons sit above the acquisition plate
rather than below it — every other Datasets tool puts its primary action above
a height-capped plate map, and an uncapped acquisition plate would
push both off the bottom of the fold. It is capped by
`apply_plate_geometry(plate, role="editor")` — the same helper, and therefore
the same cell scale, as every other plate map in the app.

The page also carries that `PlateOrderEditor` (§6.1): the grid fields
seed a live serpentine preview, and the user can click wells to define an
arbitrary `ConversionParams.well_order` (populated from
`PlateOrderEditor.order()`) for a non-rectangular scan, which `plan_conversion`
/ `explode_ome_tiff` use in place of the serpentine.

**That same plate is the run's progress view**, the way Subset's picker is: the
wells on it are exactly the wells being written, so a second plate map would be
a copy of this one. It is locked (`setEnabled(False)`) for the run's duration —
a click would edit the very order being converted — and each well fills as a
dial. `explode_ome_tiff` takes a `well_progress_fn(well, done, total)` beside
its run-wide `progress_fn`, ticking once per plane written with that well's own
share. The denominator is `explode_common.publishing_total` — the well's FOVs ×
timepoints × channels **plus one**, and that last step is reported only after
the well's `atomic_zip` block exits, i.e. once the archive has been closed,
verified and renamed onto `<WELL>.zip`. All three converters (OME-TIFF, CZI,
ND2) do this, because their pages draw a well as finished — green, and a ✓ on
`ConverterDashboard` — from the full step alone; reporting the last plane as
full put the ✓ on a well whose archive still sat under its staging name.
`datasets.ome_import.apply.convert` quantises those ticks through
`core.containers.WellFraction` before they cross the Qt signal boundary, so a
well of thousands of planes emits at most 101 updates rather than one per
plane. `WellFraction` rounds **down**, so only a well that is exactly full
reaches the last step — 999 of 1,000 planes reads 99, never 100. The quantising lives on the `datasets` side
deliberately: what counts as "often enough to be worth a repaint" is a UI
question, and `pipeline/` may not import `datasets/`. The run-wide
`QProgressBar` beneath it is hidden until a conversion starts — an idle bar
reading 0% from page load describes a run nobody asked for.

**Editing the order drops the dials.** A dial says how far through *this* order
a conversion got, so once the order changes it describes wells that are no
longer the ones on screen — `PlateOrderEditor._set_path` and its
`pathChanged` handler both clear the fractions. Without that, the plate mixes a
finished run's fills with a freshly edited path: a well removed from the order
keeps its full accent disc, because a well carrying a fraction is drawn *as*
the dial and never reaches the depressed branch. Subset's picker carries the
same guard (§11).

The page wraps its whole
content in a `QScrollArea`, the same pattern every other Datasets tool page
uses (mirroring `analyze/tab.py`'s own form panel): without it, growing the
status section (the raw log filling with lines, the progress bar becoming
visible) left no room in a fixed-height window for both it and the
`PlateOrderEditor` above, so the plate quietly rendered at a fraction of its
natural size instead of the page scrolling to reach the status section.

Convert OME-TIFF is the sixth and last Datasets tool wired into the Job Queue
(see the Job Queue entry below): `OmeImportController` implements the same
`QueueableController` protocol as the five plate-driven tools —
`collect_spec`/`show_job` round-trip `ConversionParams` (including
`well_order`, serialised through `dataclasses.asdict`) alongside the source and
destination paths, `start_from_queue` calls the same `_launch()` a manual "▶
Convert" press does, and `jobFinished` fires once per run from `_on_finished`.
Its own page carries a "+ Queue" button beside "▶ Convert", matching the other
five tools' run rows.

**Concatenate Datasets** (`datasets/concatenate/`) appends one dataset's
timepoints after another's. Two datasets of the same plate, imaged in separate
sessions, are stitched into one longer timelapse: dataset 2's timepoints are
relabelled to continue after dataset 1's last timepoint by a user-visible time
gap (see *The time gap and raw datasets* below), and the union of both
datasets' wells is written to a fresh destination folder (both originals
untouched).

The package splits along the standard suffix contract, and deliberately keeps
everything that isn't Qt out of the two `QThread`/view modules so the whole merge
is unit-testable without the app (`tests/test_concatenate_compute.py`):

| Module | Role |
|--------|------|
| `raw_compute.py` | Qt-free reading of a *raw* dataset (`in/` present, `out/` missing or empty): `is_raw_dataset`, `raw_paths`, and `raw_info`, which infers the filename schema from the archives' member names (`util/schema_infer`) and returns a sidecar-shaped dict **only when the inference is confident and has a timepoint slot** — a guessed schema would shift the wrong filename field. `check_raw_compatible` compares separator and schema fields (`RAW_COMPAT_KEYS`) where analysed datasets compare the full sidecar. |
| `concatenate_compute.py` | Pure planner. Reads + validates both `pipeline_info.json` (refuses on differing schema/separator/indices/nuclear-token/segmentation-method, and on dataset 1 and dataset 2 being the same folder), detects dataset 1's timepoint label format, computes the hour offset from the gap (`compute_offset(…, gap_hours=)`), enumerates wells, and returns a `MergePlan`. Also owns the gap model (`default_gap`, `choose_gap`, `gap_preview`, `parse_gap_hours`), `scale_warning`, and `open_pair`, which classifies the pair as analysed, raw, or analysed + raw. The page calls `gap_preview` on every keystroke of the gap field, so it reads the pair through `_open_pair_for_preview`, which keeps the last few pairs' readings (a refusal included) keyed on the path as given and resolved, the sidecars, and each input container's size and modification time (an archive written in place, or an image added to a well folder, moves its own time and not the folder's): a raw pair's schema is inferred by opening every archive, which measured about 75 ms on two 60-well plates, and only the typed gap changes between keystrokes. The run never reads through it. Also owns the structural filename-rewrite gate (`rewrite_member_name`) and the in-progress-marker restart check. |
| `apply.py` | Qt-free executor. Given a `MergePlan`, copies dataset 1's per-well inputs/CSVs/QC-zips as-is, re-packs dataset 2's with every timepoint-derived value shifted, stitches shared wells (CSV columns unioned like `pipeline/io.merge_records_into_csv`), carries over `cell_overrides.json`, verifies the result, and writes the merged sidecar. Copying goes through `core.containers.copy_container_members`, so a well that comes from one dataset only is a whole-file copy, and a merged well moves each member's compressed bytes straight from whichever side holds it — dataset 2's under a name whose timepoint field has been shifted, dataset 1's under its own. A timepoint offset changes the name in the member's header and nothing else, so there is nothing to decode on either side. It tracks which member names collided and were dropped rather than silently discarding them; a nonzero drop count marks that well `"warned"` and fails `_verify` outright, since a name that "looks fine" in the merged archive can be the wrong dataset's bytes under it (see Verification below). Progress via a `log` callback, a `progress(well, stage)` callback (`"merging"` → `"merged"`/`"warned"`) that drives the live dashboard, and a `sub_progress(well, done, total)` callback that drives that well's dial *within* the stage (fused across the well's two container passes by `core.containers.WellFraction`). `sub_progress` is the one callback deliberately left outside the callback lock: every call names its own well, so interleaving is harmless, and taking the lock once per member would serialise the parallel copy it reports on. Wells merge in parallel through a `ThreadPoolExecutor` (`pick_workers`) — each owns its own destination files, so `log`/`progress` calls before a well's work starts are the only thing serialised behind a lock; aggregating each future's result into `well_stats`/`dropped_members`/etc. and reporting the terminal `"merged"`/`"warned"` state both happen back on `execute_plan`'s own thread as futures complete, so that bookkeeping needs no lock at all. |
| `worker.py` | Thin `ConcatenateWorker(QThread)`; runs planning + `execute_plan` off the UI thread, marshalling progress/result/errors through queued signals (`logLine`, `wellsPlanned`, `wellStage`, `wellFraction`, `succeeded`, `failed`), and forwards `isInterruptionRequested` as a cancellation check. `wellFraction(well, done, total)` is the per-well sub-progress signal every Datasets tool's worker that copies data carries beside `wellStage` (Validate has none — it inspects rather than copies, so a well has no sub-steps); it is what lets a well render as a progress dial rather than a flat in-progress colour. A controller connects it to its dashboard's `set_well_progress` when that dashboard owns a plate, and straight to its page's own plate otherwise — Subset's dashboard is built `show_plate=False`, so `SubsetController._on_well_fraction` drives the picker plate's `setWellFraction` instead. |
| `view.py` | `ConcatenatePage(QWidget)` — a one-line equation row (dataset 1 + dataset 2 = destination; compact `_FolderField`s showing a basename with the full path on hover, each with its own inline validity hint) above a `ConcatDashboard`, with the raw text log demoted to a collapsible "Show raw log" checkbox (the same furniture as `analyze/log_pane.py`'s log panel, started closed rather than open — see §6.1). Emits `runRequested` / `openInReviewRequested`. Between the equation row and the dashboard sits `ConcatGapField`, a line edit pre-filled from `default_gap` with a label naming the source and a preview of dataset 2's resulting timepoint labels; an unreadable gap blocks Run. |
| `controller.py` | `ConcatenateController` — wires the page to the worker, drives the dashboard's per-well and per-run state at each signal, distinguishes a cancelled run from a failed one, and confirms before resuming into a destination with leftovers from an interrupted attempt. |
| `dashboard.py` | `ConcatDashboard`, built on `widgets/plate_progress.py::PlateProgress` (shared with Analyze's `RunDashboard` — see §7). Two independent state axes: **per well** (`pending`/`merging`/`merged`/`warned` — image data survived on one side with no matching measurements CSV) and **per run**, a phase rail (Validate → Merge → Verify → Finalize) with a terminal Done/Failed/Cancelled outcome painted on the headline. The per-run axis exists because `apply._verify` and the cell-override carry-over run *after* every well already shows green — without it, a verification failure would leave the plate looking like a complete success. Every well's terminal states carry a marker glyph too, not just its colour — `merged` gets `✓`, `warned` gets `!` — so state is legible without relying on distinguishing success-green from accent-blue by colour alone. A well still `merging` carries no glyph: it is drawn as a progress dial, and a glyph would sit in the middle of exactly the area the dial fills. `set_done(summary, *, tooltip=None)` shows a caller-shortened headline (via `core.dataset_paths.shorten_headline`, stripping the destination path down to its basename) while the full original text — the one still written to the log — survives as the headline's own tooltip. |

**The time gap and raw datasets.** Dataset 2's offset is `dataset 1's last
timepoint + gap − dataset 2's first timepoint`, where the gap is the user's
entry (`MergePlan.gap_hours`, `gap_source` of `entered`, `recorded` or
`interval`). The page pre-fills it from the two acquisition records' shared
starts when both exist on comparable clocks (`default_gap`), else dataset 1's
median interval, else leaves it empty and required; `choose_gap` warns, and
goes with the entry, when it differs from the recorded gap by more than
max(2 %, 1 minute). `parse_gap_hours` has its own strict grammar (a bare number of
hours, or `<number><unit>` parts in descending order, a comma as the decimal
point, nothing else) and is deliberately not the timepoint-label parser, whose
trailing-digit fallback read `1,5` as 5 hours and `6h30` as 30. The gap is shown,
stored and used at minute resolution (`format_gap`; the interval default is
rounded to the minute) so the page shows exactly what the merge uses. The worker
parses the text in-thread so
the queue spec carries the text the user typed, and `show_job` restores it.
`record_derivation` stores the gap and its source.

A **raw** dataset has `in/` and no results (`raw_compute.is_raw_dataset`). Two
raw datasets merge to a raw destination: `execute_plan` takes a branch that
writes `in/` only, with no `out/` and no sidecar, and `_verify_raw` checks the
destination archives against the *expected* shifted name and CRC of each
dataset-2 member computed independently of what the copy reported as written
(the copy's own `written` set includes dataset 1's members and is not evidence
about dataset 2). It also returns the dataset-2 images the schema could not shift
(no timepoint field), which `execute_plan` names in the log and counts in the
summary, since they land unchanged and verification cannot call that wrong. Two
datasets that name one well differently (`A01.zip`, `A1.zip`) are refused at
planning (`_refuse_mixed_spelling`), because the merged archive's members would
carry both spellings. A raw merge writes no `derived_from` (there is no sidecar);
with no acquisition records either, the log says the gap is recorded nowhere else.
An analysed dataset 1 followed by a raw dataset 2
(`plan.ds2_raw`) keeps dataset 1's outputs untouched, adds dataset 2's images
to `in/`, writes no "missing CSV" warning for dataset 2, and leaves its
timepoints for an incremental Analyze run. A raw dataset 1 before an analysed
dataset 2 is refused. The tile plan and pixel size may differ between the two
datasets because `in/acquisition.json` is per timepoint: `_merge_acquisition_records`
(via `util/acquisition_record.concatenate_records`) relabels dataset 2's
timepoints, keeps each one's own calibration and positions, validates the
merged record against the merged archives so Analyze's pre-run check accepts
it, and notes when only one dataset had a record (the destination then has
none). Merging several datasets in one run, to avoid one full copy per added
timepoint, is not implemented: every layer here (plan, execute, verify) is
two-way.

**A measurement row's timepoint is carried by three values, not one**, and a
zip member's timepoint lives in its filename — a fourth. The `timepoint` CSV
column is a label string; `timepoint_hours` is the numeric column every
plotting/grouping code path in `review` actually reads
(`dataset_state.rebuild_timepoints`, `data_loading.get_all_timepoints`, …); and
`filename` names the image the row was measured from, which `review`'s
Cell Browser and Scatter tabs use to look up that image. All four are kept in
lock-step for dataset-2 rows and members — a merge that touches only the label
string leaves the numeric column pointing at dataset 2's original,
pre-concatenation hours, so its rows would plot underneath dataset 1's instead
of after them and its images would fail to look up by the stale filename. To
avoid a fifth desync, new labels are never chosen independently of the numeric
value: `render_timepoint` produces the label and `parse_hours` on that same
label produces `timepoint_hours`, so the two can't disagree.

**The timepoint rule.** Timepoints are hour-valued labels read through
`util.timepoint.parse_hours`. Dataset 2's first timepoint is relabelled to
`ds1_last + ds1_interval`, where `ds1_interval` is the median gap between dataset
1's sorted unique timepoints; every other dataset-2 timepoint keeps its relative
spacing (one additive hour offset). `detect_timepoint_format` infers dataset 1's
own label convention (compound `DDdHHhMMm`, `Xh`, `Xd`, `Xmin`, or a bare number)
from its own labels and `render_timepoint` renders every new dataset-2 label in
that same convention — dataset 1's own labels are never rewritten. An
unrecognised convention (an ordinal format like `T01`) falls back to plain `Xh`
with a status-window note. A single-timepoint dataset 1 (no interval) or a
non-time timepoint label is refused with a user-facing message.

**The filename-rewrite gate.** Positionally rewriting a split-on-separator
filename field is unsafe on its own: `parse_hours` reads a plain digit-ending
token as an hour value (`parse_hours("F001") == 1.0`), so a rewrite applied to
the wrong field would silently succeed rather than fail loudly.
`rewrite_member_name` rewrites a zip member's timepoint field only when the name
is structurally conformant to the schema — a recognised image extension,
exactly as many separator-delimited fields as the schema declares once any role
suffix (`_labels`, `_overlay`, `_tophat_<chan>`, `_smfish_<chan>`, …) is
stripped via `domain.image_identity.parse_image_filename` /
`build_image_filename`, and a timepoint field that parses to a finite hour
value. A name that fails any check is copied unchanged rather than guessed at,
and the merge reports how many members that happened to.

**Restart detection.** `execute_plan` isn't incremental — every well is
reconstructed fresh from the two source datasets on each call — so a re-run
into the same destination only needs to know whether it's safe to clear what's
there first. `execute_plan` writes
`concatenate_compute.IN_PROGRESS_MARKER` (`.aw_concat_in_progress`) as its
*first* action and removes it only after `pipeline_info.json` is written and
verified — that marker, not the mere absence of a finished sidecar, is the sole
signal that content under `in`/`out` came from an interrupted attempt.
`destination_is_complete_dataset` (sidecar present) makes `build_merge_plan`
refuse outright — the folder holds a finished dataset, whether from a completed
prior concatenation or an unrelated dataset the user pointed at by mistake.
`destination_has_marker` without a sidecar means the interrupted-attempt case;
`MergePlan.dest_is_restart` carries that verdict to `execute_plan`, which clears
the destination's `in`/`out` folders before rebuilding — but only after the
controller has confirmed with the user, since destination content the marker
*doesn't* explain (e.g. a plate that's been zipped but never analyzed) is
refused rather than assumed to be safe to delete.

**Operating-system debris is left out of dataset 2's side of a merge**
(`_MemberRename`, gated on `core.member_names.is_os_junk_member`). A
`.DS_Store` names no data, so its name is the only thing it has — and both
datasets have the same one as soon as either folder has been opened in
Finder, which is the normal state of any plate someone has looked at. Carried
through, the two copies collided in the merged archive, one was dropped by
first-write-wins, and the verification below read that drop as dataset 2's
data failing to survive: two ordinary plates could not be concatenated at
all, over files neither the pipeline nor Review has ever read. Dataset 1's
copies pass through untouched, as everything of dataset 1's does, and the run
log says how many were skipped rather than dropping them silently. This does
not loosen the check it was blocking — the skip is scoped to
`is_os_junk_member`'s narrow, explicitly-named set, so two datasets that
disagree about a file a user actually put in an archive still collide and
still fail.

**Verification.** Before writing the sidecar, `apply._verify` first checks
whether any zip member collided by name during the merge and was dropped by
`copy_container_members` — a dataset-2 member whose filename fails the structural
rewrite gate (see above) keeps its original, unshifted name, and if that
name coincides with a dataset-1 member (most easily reproduced by pointing
both datasets at the same folder), the merge would otherwise keep only one
side's bytes under a name that still "looks fine" in the archive, with
nothing else able to tell the difference — a dataset-2 row's `filename`
check below only confirms the name *exists* somewhere, not whose bytes are
under it. Any dropped member fails verification immediately, naming the
well and file. A member the rename callback *declined* — dataset 2's OS
debris, above — is not a dropped member and never reaches this check;
"nobody asked for it" and "it was asked for and lost" are different facts,
and conflating them is what made the check fire on `.DS_Store`. It then checks that the merge actually wrote *any*
measurement rows at all — a well's images (`in/<WELL>.zip`, `<WELL>_out.zip`)
existing without a matching `measurements_<WELL>.csv` is individually
legitimate (that well may have segmented zero cells at every timepoint), but
if it's true for *every* well in *both* datasets — most often because
`out_csvs()`'s well-token matching failed to recognise a real CSV's name
rather than because every well is genuinely empty — the old code had nothing
left to check and let the merge report success over a destination with
copied images and zero rows of data. Per well, it further checks that every
row's `timepoint` and `timepoint_hours` agree (via
`domain.tp_match.tp_close`), that dataset-2's shifted hours never
collide with or fall before dataset 1's, that every dataset-2 row's `filename`
is actually present in the merged `in/<WELL>.zip`, and that every distinct hour
across the merged CSVs is listed in the merged `available_timepoints`. Any
image-without-CSV well/dataset pair is also named in the status window as a
note (not necessarily fatal — see above) so it's visible instead of silently
dropped. A verification failure raises before the sidecar is written, so a
broken merge never leaves a destination that looks finished.

On success the page offers to open the merged dataset in Review, routed through
`DatasetsTab._open_in_review → AllWellApp._open_dataset_in_review`, which loads
the destination root into Review and switches to it — the same path
`_on_analyze_pipeline_complete` uses. Every such hand-off goes through
`AllWellApp._load_in_review_later`, which defers the load to a `QTimer` so the
pane switch paints first and catches whatever the load raises: an exception
escaping a Qt callback aborts the process under PySide6, so a dataset that will
not load must cost the load and not the window.

`ConcatenatePage._update_status_preview` reveals `ConcatDashboard` as soon as
both dataset fields are valid, rather than only once "▶ Concatenate" is
pressed — seeded via `core.dataset_paths.preview_wells` on both dataset
roots with a "Ready — N well(s)" headline, so the plate answers "what would
this actually touch" before a run starts rather than sitting invisible with
nothing to show yet. It steps aside once a real run begins
(`ConcatenateController` drives `set_wells`/`set_phase`/well colouring from
that point on) and resets again on the next field edit
(`_on_field_changed`), which also hands the "▶ Concatenate" button's primary
emphasis back from a still-visible post-success "Open in Review" button — see
below. `set_running(True)` locks all three fields
(`PathField.setLocked`, disabling only each field's Browse button, not the
whole field) for the run's duration — previously the one Datasets tool that
locked none of its fields at all, leaving a mid-run pick free to change what a
subsequent Concatenate press would act on. On success,
`show_open_in_review` promotes "Open in Review" to `variant="primary"` and
demotes "▶ Concatenate" to `variant="secondary"` (via `widgets._support.
set_variant`, see §7) — the natural next step is opening the result, not
re-running the same merge. The status section's header/dashboard title read
"Concatenate Output"/"Concatenate Progress" rather than "Merge Output"/"Merge
Progress" so they don't collide with Merge Plates' own identically-purposed
labels; the page heading and the Datasets-pane sidebar entry are both
"Concatenate Datasets", title-cased to match the other five tool headings.

**Validate & Repair Dataset** (`datasets/validate/`) answers a question the
GUI otherwise has no answer for: which `(well, fov, timepoint)` work an
Analyze run actually finished, versus what `pipeline_info.json` — written
*before* any image work, per §6.2 — claims. A crashed or partial run leaves
the sidecar advertising the full plate while `out/` holds a fraction, and a
plain re-run then treats a partially-done well as complete
(`output_exists_for_well` — which now also requires the run's settings digest
to match the one recorded beside the well, but a *partial* well still reads as
complete, because that predicate asks whether the outputs exist and not how
much of the input they cover), so the FOV-level gap is otherwise invisible.

**The rule it applies is not its own.** `pipeline/completeness.py` holds the
single definition of a complete well — the CSV ∪ archive union, the
`intent - done` diff with its single-FOV fallback, and the five health states —
and both this tool and the pipeline's own end-of-run check (§6.2) go through it,
so the two cannot disagree about a well. Validate keeps everything built *on
top* of that answer: run-record evidence, the finding codes, the
per-artefact read budget its tests pin exactly, and repair. The shared functions
open only a well's output container, taking input member names and parsed CSV
rows from whichever caller already has them — which is precisely what lets this
scan delegate without changing how many times it touches the disk.

**Three sources of evidence, because a missing CSV has more than one cause.**
`WellEvidence` merges `pipeline_info.json`'s `run_report` block, the per-failure
tracebacks under `out/errors/`, and the run journal (§6.5), and `_no_csv_finding`
turns them into four different findings rather than one hedged sentence. A well
the run recorded, covered none of, failed nothing in and left no traceback for
*segmented zero cells* — a measurement, so reprocessing produces the same empty
result and it is `info`. Recorded failures or tracebacks are a real gap with the
run's own records naming it. A journal state of `not-fetched` says the output
was produced and never reached this machine, so the remedy is to fetch rather
than to re-segment — forcing a plate to recover a failed download is hours of
compute for nothing, and it is the one cause no artefact can report, since the
evidence for it is the *absence* of a file. And no record at all is reported as
a gap rather than assumed benign, because assuming benign is how a missing CSV
goes unnoticed. A dataset with no journal — every one produced before it
existed, and every one produced by the CLI — simply yields fewer answers; the
scan is unaffected.

**A finished scan is recorded.** `datasets/validate/record.py` writes the scan's
own result into `pipeline_info.json`'s `run_check` block, through the same
`pipeline.completeness.build_block` / `well_record` pair the pipeline's end-of-run
check goes through, so there is one record format rather than a pipeline one and
a Validate one. That closes the loop Review's Home page opens: Home reports a
record rather than scanning, a dataset produced before the end-of-run check
existed has none, and the only action Home offers such a dataset is to open this
tool. Until the scan recorded its answer, following that offer measured the whole
plate and then discarded it, leaving Home saying exactly what it had said before.

The block carries `source`, and the distinction is not cosmetic: a `"run"` record
describes the run that had just finished, a `"validate"` record describes the
folder as it stood when someone looked at it, possibly months later and after
hand-edits. Home's masthead reads *checked <date>* for one and *run finished
<date>* for the other. Two smaller consequences of the same difference — a scan
has no run boundary to filter by, so its `errors` count is every traceback
present in `out/errors/` rather than only those the last run produced, and
`WellReport` carries `intent`/`covered_csv`/`covered_any` alongside `missing`,
because how much is absent does not say how much was asked for and the plate map
draws a fraction from both.

Only a whole scan is recorded. A cancelled one covers an arbitrary prefix of the
plate, and a record built from it would paint every unscanned well as measured
and found absent. A failure to write is reported in the scan log and does not
fail the scan: the findings are the deliverable and are already in hand, and
saying so out loud is what keeps "recorded" and "silently not recorded"
distinguishable — the latter looks, from Home, exactly like a scan that never
ran.

`validate_compute.py::build_report(root)` is a read-only Qt-free scan.
*Intent* — what a well's raw input actually contains — is read through
`pipeline.incremental_keys.fov_keys_from_member_names`, the name-parsing half of
`read_done_fov_keys_from_zip`/`_from_folder`, applied to `in/<WELL>.zip`/
`<WELL>/`'s members instead of the output archive those functions were written
for; nothing about them cares which side of the pipeline a container sits on,
they only parse `(fov, timepoint)` positionally off member names. Validate calls
the name-based half because it has already listed the container (see "one read
per artefact" below); the two path-based readers call it after listing, so all
three agree by construction. *Done* is read the same way `incremental_done_fov_keys` composes it
(CSV rows ∪ out-zip members ∪ output folder — `_well_done` unions all three,
the last via `core.dataset_paths.out_folders`, the `out_zips`-shaped
well→path map for `compressed_output=False` datasets; a folder-mode well
that legitimately segmented zero cells at a timepoint still writes an image
there even with no CSV row for it, the same "done" evidence a zip-mode
