because the field is reserved: `make_selection` collapses it to `None` on every
selection the model builds, so nothing downstream would ever read a remapped
one. Dataset 2's selection and
plot-group names that collide with dataset 1's are suffixed with dataset 2's
folder name rather than silently overwriting a same-named definition. Its
selection ids are dropped and re-minted, because an id is unique only within
the block it came from and dataset 1's must stay stable for `current_id` to
keep pointing at the same selection. Both plates' notes are kept, dataset 2's
under a labelled separator: a note is the one field here whose value is prose a
person wrote, and nothing can reconstruct it.

Every *other* analysis block comes from dataset 1, because none of them can be
combined by rule — `cell_gating`, `ratios`, `qc_options` and
`smfish_thresholds` are decisions made under one plate's imaging conditions.
The plan says which of them dataset 2 also had (`PlateMergePlan.blocks_warning`,
emitted into the run log beside the ragged-timepoint note), since a merged plate
silently carrying half the user's gating is the degraded-output-that-looks-clean
shape this codebase refuses to produce. Cell overrides remap their `well` key
through the well map before the `seg_fp` restamp (from the destination
`<well>_out.zip`, as the last write to that archive) — Concatenate's own
precedent, not reinvented.

**Job Queue** (`datasets/job_queue/`) lines up Analyze and Datasets-tool runs
to work through unattended, built on a Qt-free scheduler
(`services/job_queue.py`) so ordering/gating logic is unit-testable with no
Qt event loop. Four layers:

- **`services/job_queue.py`** — `JobSpec` (one persisted queue entry: `id`,
  `kind`, `label`, a JSON-shaped `spec` for that tool, optional chain
  metadata, `state`, `message`, and whichever of `output_dir`/`dataset_root`/
  `in_dir` it produced), `JobState` (plain string constants — `pending`,
  `running`, `succeeded`, `failed`, `cancelled`, `blocked`, `interrupted`,
  `suspended` — not an `Enum`, so the persisted JSON needs no encode/decode
  step), and `JobQueue`, which only orders and gates jobs; it never runs one
  itself.

  Chaining links a job to a predecessor by **id**, never a list index (an
  index would silently re-point on reorder), a dotted path into its own
  `spec` to set, and which of the predecessor's three possible outputs it
  wants (`chain_kind`). Resolution happens at **dequeue**, via
  `JobQueue.materialise(job_id)`, never at enqueue — Analyze's own output
  location is only knowable after `resolve_input_output` runs. A failed or
  cancelled predecessor cascades every transitive successor still `pending`
  to `blocked` rather than `failed`, so those jobs are distinguishable from
  ones that ran and failed; `set_chain()` rejects a self-chain or a cycle
  before writing the link, and a reorder placing a dependent before its
  predecessor is refused.

  A finished converter job also records a **`layout`** — what it knows about
  the files it wrote (`services.job_kinds.produced_layout`, below) — and
  `materialise` copies it into an Analyze successor's spec as
  `upstream_layout`, beside the path. Only an Analyze successor receives it, and
  only a job that asked for run-time detection reads it; `retry` clears it
  with the other outputs, and a failed job records none.

  The editing half — everything that changes a job after it is queued —
  is `update_spec`, `set_label`, `duplicate`, `retry`, `clear_terminal`,
  `move_to` and `counts`. Two of those carry decisions worth stating.
  `update_spec` deliberately leaves `state` alone: re-arming a finished job
  on edit would strand successors that had already succeeded, whose
  predecessor would no longer read `succeeded`, and that half-state is
  reachable no other way — `retry` is the single explicit backwards move, so
  fixing a failed job and re-running it is two clear steps. `retry` runs
  `_cascade_unblock`, the mirror of `_cascade_block`, returning to `pending`
  only the successors reachable from the retried job; one blocked by a
  different, un-retried failure stays blocked, and since `chain_from` is a
  single id the links form a forest with no second parent to still be
  failing. `duplicate` drops the clone's chain link (a clone inheriting its
  twin's predecessor would wait on output it has no relationship to) and
  takes its new id as a parameter, so the module needs no `uuid` and a test
  can name the copy. `clear_terminal` goes through `remove` per id rather
  than filtering the list, so a survivor chained to a cleared job loses the
  link instead of pointing at a job that no longer exists. `move_to` is the
  drag counterpart of `move`: it shifts the rows it passes rather than
  swapping, because dragging picks a destination, and it validates through
  the same whole-list `_chain_order_valid`. The two are wired to different
  gestures on purpose — the row menu's Move up / Move down go to `move` (a
  neighbour swap), a dragged row to `move_to` via
  `JobQueueController._on_drag_move`, which turns the handle's step count into
  a destination index and *clamps* it, since a drag past either end of the
  list means "put it at the end" rather than "do nothing".

  `JobQueue.from_json` never auto-starts a loaded queue (a relaunch always
  comes up paused — `is_started` is never persisted) and maps a stale
  `running` state to `interrupted`. `interrupted` is in `JobState.RESUMABLE`,
  so the job is picked up again rather than needing re-adding, and its
  successors stay `pending` and wait for it — they are *not* cascaded to
  `blocked`, because the output they are waiting on is still coming.
  `_repair_after_load` also topologically repairs — or, on a genuine cycle,
  drops every chain link in — a hand-edited file whose stored order violates
  its own links, so `next_runnable()` can never deadlock on bad persisted
  data. Its human-readable notes are kept on the instance as
  `JobQueue.repair_notes` and rendered by the page: a repair the user cannot
  see reads as the queue quietly losing their jobs' state.

  Persistence goes through `services.remote_config.default_state_dir()` (a
  tmp-file-then-`os.replace` write of `job_queue.json`), deliberately **not**
  derived from `default_config_path()` — that function honours
  `$ALLWELL_REMOTES`, an override meaning "where my remotes live" rather than
  "where my app state lives", and its Windows branch is conditional on
  whether `remotes.toml` exists, which would silently relocate an
  already-written queue the day a user first creates one. `load_queue`'s
  malformed-file guard wraps `JobQueue.from_json`/`JobSpec.from_json` too,
  not just the `json.loads` call — a well-formed-JSON-but-malformed-*queue*
  file raised `KeyError`/`TypeError`/`AttributeError` uncaught, and
  `load_queue` runs unconditionally and synchronously from
  `QueueBridge.__init__` at `DatasetsTab` construction, so it crashed the
  whole app's startup rather than just the queue page.

- **`services/job_kinds.py`** — the per-kind tables, Qt-free because none of
  it is a view concern and all of it is worth testing without an event loop.
  `KIND_LABEL` (a tool's human name), `CHAIN_TARGET` (the dotted path into a
  job's *own* spec that a predecessor's output fills: `opts.raw` for Analyze,
  `dataset` for Validate, `source` for Subset / OME / Zip-loose, `dataset1`
  for the two-dataset tools), and the sending end of the same link —
  `produced_for(kind, path)` and `CHAIN_KIND`. Together they are why the
  interface can derive a chain from "run after that one" alone; a user should
  not also have to know where each tool receives its input.

  `CONVERTER_KINDS` and `produced_layout(kind, spec)` are the other thing a
  finished job can hand along a chain. The three converters name every image
  themselves, `<experiment>_<channel>_<well>_f<fov>_<tp>` with each token
  passed through `util.filename_token.safe_token`, so the schema and separator
  are stated rather than scanned; the channel roles come from the converter
  page's role rows, which its queued spec carries as `channel_roles`. The
  queue bridge stores the result on the finished job (`QueueBridge._on_job_finished`).
  `services.run_detect.detect_layout` prefers it to a scan for the parts it
  states, still checks its channel names against every name on disk, and
  fails the run naming both lists when they disagree.

  **`CHAIN_KIND` is a constant, `"dataset_root"`, not a per-kind table**, and
  that is the correction it exists to record. Every tool here — Analyze
  included — consumes a *dataset root*, the folder holding the `in/` + `out/`
  pair, and resolves its own way down from there. A per-kind table invites
  handing over the predecessor's most specific output, and Analyze's most
  specific output is its `out/` folder: chained that way, Validate and Subset
  looked for `out/in/`, found no wells, and quietly did nothing.
  `produced_for` therefore records **both** for an Analyze job — `out_dir`
  because it is what Analyze actually built, `dataset_root` because it is what
  a successor needs — deriving the root as the parent, which holds by
  construction since `resolve_input_output` returns `<root>/out` in every one
  of its layout branches. It records nothing at all for an empty path, so a
  `dataset_root` of `""` can never be handed to `materialise` as a real
  answer.

  `describe(kind, spec)` is what a row is actually called. Without it every
  row of a kind reads identically — eight queued subsets all saying "Subset"
  — and picking the right one to reorder, chain or remove is guesswork. It is
  basenames only ("Subset — plateA → plateA_sub"), since a row is an
  identifier and not a path; `describe_detail` carries the full paths for the
  row's second line. Analyze routes through `RunSpec.label()`, which already
  says `(no input)` for a run missing its folder — worth preserving, since a
  row reading plain "Analyze" is indistinguishable from a well-formed job.

- **`datasets/job_queue/controller.py`** — the Qt-touching layer.
  `QueueableController` is the duck-typed protocol every runnable `kind`
  implements: `start_from_queue(spec)`, `show_job(spec)`, `stop()`,
  `is_busy()` (`self._worker is not None and self._worker.isRunning()` for
  every Datasets controller; `self._runner.is_running` for `AnalyzeTab` via
  `AnalyzeRunMixin`), and a `jobFinished(ok, message, output_path)` signal
  that **must** be emitted only once per run, as the true last statement of
  that run's completion handler (mirroring `AnalyzeTab.runFinished`'s
  re-entrancy rule, since a bridge slot may start the next job synchronously
  from inside the emit). Each of the seven Datasets controllers implements this
  directly (a `_launch()` split out of `_on_run()` so `start_from_queue` can
  skip the interactive restart/in-place confirmation a queued, unattended run
  has no one to answer); so does `AnalyzeTab`.

  `QueueBridge` owns the persisted `JobQueue` and a `kind -> QueueableController`
  registry, and is the only thing that actually starts a job: strictly
  serial, tracking the in-flight job as `(job_id, kind)` so a `jobFinished`
  from a controller that isn't the queue's own current job — e.g. the user
  pressed that tool's own Run button by hand while a *different* job was
  running — is dropped rather than misattributed. That tuple can only really
  distinguish by `kind` (`jobFinished` carries no job id), so the guard's
  soundness depends on every `start_from_queue` path eventually emitting
  `jobFinished` exactly once: a launch that silently no-ops on invalid input
  would leave `_current` stuck forever, which is why
  `MergePlatesController._launch`'s remap-failure branch,
  `ValidateController._run`'s "no dataset path" branch and
  `OmeImportController._launch`'s "no source or destination" branch all emit
  `jobFinished` directly rather than returning silently.
  `tests/test_dataset_tool_integrity.py` checks each of the seven launchers
  return by return, against the statement block it sits in rather than the
  function as a whole — one emit elsewhere in the function does not excuse a
  silent return beside it.

  There is one such return the bridge does **not** need an emit for, and it is
  the bridge's own job to make sure of it. Every tool's launcher opens with "if
  a worker is already running, return", which is reachable when the user starts
  that tool by hand while the queue is going — so `_advance` refuses to
  dispatch to a runner whose `is_busy()` is true, and leaves the job pending
  instead. That leaves the queue waiting on something it is not watching, so
  `_on_job_finished` re-enters `_advance` when a completion arrives for a job
  that was *not* the queue's own: the manual run finishing is exactly the event
  the held-back job is waiting for. Without both halves a single by-hand run
  during a queue stopped the queue for the rest of the session.

  On completion the bridge looks up
  `was_cancelled()` on the finishing controller (falling back to the Datasets
  convention that a cancelled worker's failure message starts with
  `"Cancelled"`) to tell a user-requested Stop apart from a genuine failure,
  since cancelling the running job **pauses the queue** — resuming is
  explicit — while a genuine failure just cascade-blocks that job's own
  successors and keeps going.

  Beside `add_job`/`remove_job`/`move_job` the bridge carries the editing
  mutators the page needs — `update_job`, `duplicate_job`, `retry_job`,
  `clear_completed`, `move_job_to`, `set_chain`, `clear_chain` — each
  following the same mutate → `_save()` → `queueChanged.emit()` shape and
  returning a `bool` so the caller can report a refusal. `update_job`
  re-derives the label from the new spec: a label describes its spec, so an
  edited job still named after what it used to run against would be worse
  than one with no name.

  `QueueBridge.show_job` (clicking a queued row to preview it) checks
  `runner.is_busy()` first and no-ops if the target controller already has a
  run in flight — `show_job(spec)` writes page fields **directly**, which
  bypasses `set_running`'s field locks (those only disable widgets against
  user clicks, not this programmatic path) and, for a controller like
  `SubsetController` that paints run progress onto the same picker plate
  `show_job` would repopulate, could visibly corrupt the in-flight run's own
  status display. It returns whether it actually populated, which is what
  lets an edit session refuse rather than open on an untouched page. It also
  hands the runner a deep copy of the job's spec
  (`json.loads(json.dumps(job.spec))`, matching `JobQueue.materialise`'s own
  assumption that a spec is JSON-shaped) rather than the queue's live
  persisted dict.

  **Populating a page and navigating to it are separate, because a running job
  wants one without the other.** `JobQueueController._on_show_requested`
  branches on the clicked job's state. A `running` job is *revealed only* — the
  page is already showing that run's own live progress, which is what the click
  is asking to see, and `show_job` is exactly what must not touch it. Anything
  else is populated and then revealed, since writing fields into a page nobody
  was taken to is the same silence in a quieter form. A job whose kind is busy
  with a *different* run is refused with a notice rather than shown, because the
  fields on that page would describe neither job. Before this split the click
  reached `show_job` alone, whose `False` was dropped: with the row's `Edit…`
  also disabled while running (`row.py`), a running job had no route to its page
  at all and nothing said so. Measured on a real `DatasetsTab`, clicking a
  running row moved the pane not at all and raised no notice.

  Navigation is a hook, `JobQueueController.set_reveal_hook`, supplied by
  `DatasetsTab._reveal_page` — deliberately **not** `_begin_session` with the
  banner suppressed. That one stands a page in for a job being *edited* and runs
  only after the queue has agreed a session may start; this is the plain "take
  me to that tool" half, and keeping them apart is what lets the running case
  navigate without populating. It returns whether it arrived: Analyze is the one
  queueable kind with no rail entry in this pane, so reaching it means changing
  pane, which only the shell can do — `allwell.py` passes
  `on_reveal_analyze=self._reveal_analyze_pane`, and a `DatasetsTab` built
  without a shell (tests, Datasets-only profiles) reports failure so the click
  says why rather than appearing to work.

  `QueueBridge.hydrate_job` is the edit-path counterpart. For the seven
  Datasets tools `show_job` is already a complete inverse of `collect_spec` —
  the two read and write the same handful of keys — so hydration falls back
  to it. Analyze's is deliberately shallow (it sets the input folder and
  nothing else, because the queue re-derives a full `RunSpec` from the
  persisted JSON at dequeue time regardless, so the live form only has to
  *look* right), and collecting a previewed Analyze page back over a stored
  spec would replace every option the preview did not write. `AnalyzeTab`
  therefore supplies `hydrate_job`, which the bridge prefers when present —
  see §6.1.

  `JobQueueController` is the page-level controller (the usual page/worker
  shape, with `QueueBridge` standing in for a `QThread` worker): it owns the
  page, turns clicks into bridge calls, and refreshes the page on
  `queueChanged`.

- **`datasets/job_queue/session.py`** — `QueueSession`, the state of "a tool's
  page is currently standing in for a queued job", as `(kind, job_id or None)`
  where `None` means a new job of that kind. It lives beside the controller
  rather than inside it because its rules are substantial and none of them are
  about wiring a page to a bridge; `JobQueueController` keeps a thin façade
  (`begin_edit`, `begin_new_job`, `session`, `save_session`, `end_session`).

  It holds no widgets and imports no Qt, reaching outside through three
  injected callables — `notify`, `add_job`, and the `on_session` /
  `on_session_end` pair `DatasetsTab` supplies as "show that tool's page with
  this banner" and "take the banner off". That is what lets the whole class be
  exercised in a test with no page at all. `notify` must be dispatched through
  the controller at call time rather than bound at construction: it is the one
  seam a test patches to assert a refusal was reported, and capturing the bound
  method leaves the session calling the original past the patch.

  A session is refused while the job is running or its tool is busy with a run
  of its own, and abandoned with a note if the job starts running or leaves the
  queue while it is open — saving it then would either overwrite a spec already
  handed to a runner or write to a job that no longer exists.

  Three narrower hazards get their own handling, because each one silently
  corrupted the job under edit. **Clicking another queued row** while a
  session is open is refused: preview writes the clicked job's fields straight
  into the same page the session has open, so the next Save collected *that*
  job's settings into this one and turned it into a duplicate — and since
  nothing about the queue changed, the stale-session check never fired.
  **Starting a second session** says the first was closed without saving,
  rather than replacing it silently while its banner vanishes from a page the
  user has left. And `begin_edit` reports a **round-trip loss**: it collects
  the page it has just populated and names anything that was in the spec and
  is now gone. That is deliberately general rather than a per-tool patch —
  Subset builds its timepoint and FOV checkboxes by reading the source
  dataset, so a source that has moved leaves no boxes, `all_timepoints_
  selected()` answers "yes" over an empty list, and a one-timepoint subset
  silently widens to every timepoint on save. A value that merely changed form
  (a well relabelled `A1` → `A01`) is not a loss and is not reported. Every refusal in the class routes through one `_notify`
  seam rather than scattered `Toast` calls, so a test can assert that a
  refusal was reported without standing up a real `Toast` and its fade
  animation and dismiss timer.

- **`datasets/job_queue/view.py` + `row.py`** — `JobQueuePage` and `JobRow`,
  split because the row grew its own menu and drag handling.

  `JobRow` is two lines. The first identifies: drag handle, ordinal, kind
  icon, derived name, an indeterminate progress strip while running (a
  controller only ever reports a free-text status message, never a
  percentage), a `widgets.status_dot.StatusDot` state chip, and a `⋯` menu.
  The second is muted and descriptive — the predecessor's *label* (not its
  ten-hex-character id), `describe_detail`'s paths, and the latest status
  message — elided with `QFontMetrics` against the width the label is
  actually given, from `resizeEvent`, and hidden when empty. The `⋯` menu
  carries *Edit…*, *Duplicate*, *Retry* (terminal states only), *Run after ▸*,
  *Move up*/*Move down* (hidden on terminal rows, where reordering means
  nothing) and *Remove*; it is built by `build_menu()` and `exec()`d only
  from the click handler, so a test can inspect and `trigger()` actions
  without opening a popup that would block under the offscreen QPA. The
  *Run after* submenu is constructed as `QMenu(title, parent)` rather than
  via `addMenu(str)` — the menu that call returns is not kept alive on the
  Python side and can be collected out from under the menu that owns it.

  The ordinal is shown only on `pending` rows: a number on a row that already
  has a terminal outcome doesn't mean "queue position" any more. Rows are
  styled from `theme.qss` keyed on the `#JobRow` object name, **not** an
  inline stylesheet — a bare `border-bottom` set on the row widget has no
  selector, so Qt applies it to every child and each label, tool button and
  progress bar draws its own underline.

  `JobQueuePage` holds its rows in a plain `QVBoxLayout` inside the page's
  `QScrollArea`, not a `QListWidget`. A `QListWidgetItem`'s size hint is set
  once from the row's `sizeHint()`, so a row that later shows or hides its
  second line changes height while the hint does not; and the drag-handle
  reorder is `widgets/saved_selections_list.py`'s, which hosts its own rows
  in a box layout, so matching it is a like-for-like transfer. `set_jobs`
  reuses the existing rows whenever the id sequence is unchanged and calls
  `JobRow.update_from` on each — the page refreshes on every `queueChanged`,
  which during a run includes each status-message tick, and rebuilding every
  row for those threw away scroll position and hover state several times a
  second. Every child of a row is therefore built once and shown/hidden;
  nothing is conditionally constructed.

  The header is `▶ Start queue` (primary, at the left edge, matching every
  other Datasets page's own run button), `■ Stop job`, `+ Add job` — a menu
  of all seven kinds, each opening a new-job session on that tool's page —
  and `Clear completed` at the right. Under it sits a one-line state tally
  (states with no jobs are omitted; "0 failed" is not news) and the load-time
  `repair_notes`. The empty-queue hint is a plain caption, deliberately not
  `widgets.empty_state.EmptyState`: that widget is `Expanding/Expanding`,
  which is exactly the page-height empty container this page was already
  fixed against — one sentence rendered as a bordered box filling the
  viewport. A trailing `outer.addStretch(1)` collects the leftover height.

  Each of the seven Datasets tool pages also keeps its own "+ Queue" button
  beside Run, calling the controller's `collect_spec()` and handing the
  result up through an injected `on_add_to_queue(kind, spec)` callback to
  `DatasetsTab._add_to_queue`.

**`widgets/context_banner.py`** carries a session on screen. `ContextBanner`
is a strip of glyph + sentence + confirm + cancel that says a page is being
used for something other than its own job; without it the borrowed page looks
exactly as it always does and the only way to finish is to guess. It is
host-agnostic — it knows nothing about queues, jobs or datasets, and whoever
shows it decides what confirming means — and it does not block the page
beneath it, which is the point, since the user is editing that page.
`DatasetsTab` inserts it at index 0 of the target page's own layout, which
works uniformly because all seven Datasets pages hold a single `QScrollArea`
there; for Analyze it goes at index 0 of `_form_layout`, where the resume
banner already sits. Its Cancel routes through
`JobQueueController.end_session` rather than tearing the strip down directly:
the controller owns whether a session exists, and dropping only the strip
would leave it believing one was live and willing to save it later.

`datasets/tab.py` wires all of this: each of the seven Datasets controllers is
constructed with `on_add_to_queue=tab._add_to_queue` and stashes itself in
`tab._controllers[kind]`; the `"Job Queue"` `_Feature` entry is built **last**
so `_build_job_queue` can register every already-built controller (plus the
injected `AnalyzeTab`, under kind `"analyze"`) against a single
`JobQueueController`. `allwell.py` injects the already-built `AnalyzeTab` as
`DatasetsTab(analyze_controller=...)` the same way it injects
`on_open_in_review`/`on_open_in_analyze` — so neither `datasets/tab.py` nor
anything under `datasets/job_queue/` ever imports `analyze.tab`. The reverse
direction goes the same way: `_build_job_queue` calls the injected tab's
`set_queue_sink`, which is where Analyze's own "+ Queue" button sends a run,
so `analyze/run_spec.py` never imports the queue either. An unset sink hides
the button, which is what a profile build without the Datasets pane gets.

Each `_Feature` carries the job-queue `kind` its page runs (`None` for the
Job Queue's own page), so a session can find the page for a job without a
second name → kind map to keep in step. `DatasetsTab._begin_session` switches
the rail and inserts the banner; `_end_session` takes it down and returns to
the queue page.

Analyze is the one kind with no rail entry, so its session (both **+ Add job →
Analyze** and a queued Analyze row's **Edit…**) puts the banner on
`AnalyzeTab._form_layout` and leaves the pane through the shell's
`on_reveal_analyze` (`allwell._reveal_analyze_pane`). `_begin_session` returns
whether the page reached the screen; `QueueSession._start` drops the session
and reports it through `notify` when it did not, so a build with no shell to
switch panes refuses the click instead of opening a session behind a banner
nobody can see. The banner's **Add to queue** / **Save changes** and **Cancel**
return through `on_reveal_datasets` (`allwell._reveal_datasets_pane`) to the
Job Queue; `_end_session` itself never changes pane, because a session also
ends when its job starts running and a user on the Analyze pane is then
watching that run. Saving first asks the kind's registered validator —
`QueueSession.register_validator`, which only Analyze supplies, as
`AnalyzeRunMixin.validate_for_queue`, the same `_validate_run_request` gate
its own **+ Queue** uses, with the queue path's deferrals (a blank or
not-yet-written input, and with run-time detection on, the schema and channel
checks) — and a refusal leaves the session open on the form.

---

### 6.6b Why a cell is gone: the Segmentation overlay

Inclusion is the AND of seven verdict layers (`Included`, `QC_Pass`, `Crop_Pass`,
`Gate_Pass`, `Field_Pass`, `Focus_Pass`, `Excluded_Field_Pass`), and the picture that shows a user
their cells is the one place that AND is invisible by construction: an excluded
cell simply has no outline. The **Why removed** toggle
(`renderer.toggle_review_image_exclusion_layers`) outlines each excluded cell in
the ink of the layer that removed it.

Four rules hold it together, and each replaced a way the first version was
quietly wrong.

* **One roster.** `collect.EXCLUSION_LAYERS` names the layers and their order,
  and `review_build_include_map` is *derived* from `review_build_exclusion_reasons`
  rather than recomposing the AND — so the overlay and the inclusion the rest of
  the app honours cannot drift. Order is about the reader rather than about
  precedence: the composition is an AND, so a cell failing three layers is out
  for all three and none of them is "the" cause. Manual comes first because it
  is the one a click undoes.
* **Each answer needs its own colour.** `_layer_inks` maps each label to a design
  token, chosen by measurement: every pairwise CIE76 ΔE is at least 31 and every
  relative luminance at least 0.28, which is what a one-pixel stroke needs on
  this plot surface. Two layers once shared `text_muted` — ΔE of exactly 0, and
  the darkest ink in the set — so the overlay could not distinguish two of the
  answers its own button promises. `accent2` is excluded because the plate's
  colour vocabulary reserves it, and `success` because every cell this marks has
  been removed and green is the app's "good" token.
* **The painter runs outside the draw-mode branch.** It was once inside the
  `else` of the binary split, so Binary mode computed every reason — a row fetch
  and verdict walk per refresh — and discarded them while the button read "Why
  removed: On". Hoisting the call is what makes that unrepeatable, and
  `tests/test_exclusion_layers_overlay.py` pins the structure rather than the
  behaviour of either branch.
* **Three surfaces, and all three exist.** The outline names the first layer,
  the hover readout (`controller._exclusion_phrase`) names every layer, and the
  status line carries a colour key for the layers present in this field —
  including a sentence when the overlay is on and nothing is excluded, because
  an unchanged picture is indistinguishable from a control that does not work.
  The Home plate's rule that no mark may appear without a legend row is borrowed
  here rather than reinvented.

### 6.7 Field quality: what the run measured about its own pictures

Every FOV-group the pipeline processes is measured on six numbers, and the
whole subsystem is built around one distinction: **a metric that could not be
computed is absent, never zero.** `None` travels from the measurement through
the record, the checkpoint, the sidecar and the scorer without ever being
collapsed to a number, because a stored `0.0` where nothing was measured is a
measurement the plate-wide comparison then believes.

**Where each metric can be read, and why it is read there.**
`pipeline/field_quality.py` holds all six.

`focus` is measured **at each nucleus's own outline** (`edge_focus`), and it
measures the **width** of the intensity transition there rather than its
energy. That one choice is the whole design. Defocus is a property of the
optics: it sets how far the intensity takes to travel from inside the object
to outside. Brightness sets the *amplitude* of that transition and not its
width, so a width is independent of gain, pedestal and amplitude by
construction, while every edge-energy statistic confounds the two — a dim cell
and a blurred cell both carry little gradient per pixel.

The signed distance transform gives, for each pixel near the outline, how far
it is from the boundary. Binning intensity by that distance gives the
transition profile directly, and the distance the profile takes to rise from
`EDGE_RISE_LO` to `EDGE_RISE_HI` of the cell's own contrast is the classic
knife-edge width. The score is its reciprocal, so higher stays sharper. There
is no ring, no noise floor and no band geometry to fail — a distance transform
has nothing to mis-size against a nucleus.

**Measured on a shot-noise fixture at a realistic cell size** (20 px across),
against the edge-energy form this replaced:

| varying only | energy | width |
|---|---|---|
| brightness, 80× in amplitude | 1.52× | **1.03×** |
| nucleus size, 14–28 px | 1.09× | **1.01×** |
| read noise, 2 → 30 | 1.02× | 1.01× |
| neighbours, 30 px → contact | 1.14× | **1.02×** |
| chromatin texture, 0 → 0.8 | 1.50× | **1.14×** |
| saturation, clipped to 60 % | 2.87× | **1.45×** |
| gain and pedestal | exact | exact |

So it is comparable between cells, fields, wells and plates, which is the
property the whole layer rests on: a score relative to its own frame cannot
see a frame that is uniformly soft, because every cell in it deviates from its
neighbours by nothing — measured, the relative median is exactly 1.000 at
three very different focus states. **Two residuals qualify that and belong in
any sentence a user reads**: clipping biases it upward, because a flat-topped
nucleus genuinely does have a steeper transition, and chromatin texture
reaches 1.14×. `sat_frac` is recorded per field but does not bound the first
of those — it is capped by the fraction of the frame the nuclei cover, so on a
sparse plate every nucleus can be flat-topped while `sat_frac` stays near a
couple of percent.

**And it is monotone**, which the energy form was not. That form turned back
up past two stops of defocus and recovered 2.24× from its minimum, so a cut
near the soft end excluded the mildly defocused cells and *kept* the
catastrophic ones while reporting a confident count of what it had removed.
Over the same sweep to eight stops this form falls at every step, with every
cell measurable at every stop. An SNR margin was tried first and rejected: it
restored monotonicity by refusing the low-SNR cells, which at one stop of
defocus left 6 % of dim cells measurable against 100 % of bright ones — the
brightness bias again, wearing a refusal.

The value is written per cell as the `qc_edge_focus` column (named in
`pipeline/field_quality_record.py`, which is stdlib-only, so Review's data
layer and the argument parser can have the name without pulling numpy and
scipy in behind it). A field's `focus` is the **median of its own cells'
values** (`field_focus`), so the field-level and cell-level numbers are two
poolings of one measurement rather than two statistics that can disagree. It
is measured on the corrected frame the labels were computed from, so the
outline the estimator reads is the outline that was segmented.

Measuring is on by default and is switched off with `--no_focus_metric`, which
leaves the column **out of the record entirely** rather than filling it: a run
that did not measure focus and a run that measured it and found nothing must
not produce the same CSV. That flag is in the reuse key (`util/settings_digest`)
because it decides whether the column exists; `--focus_min` is deliberately
not, because the run records that number and never acts on it.

Two of the remaining metrics can only be read at particular moments.
`sat_frac` needs the camera's integer ceiling, which `pipeline.io.load_2d_gray`
destroys with its unconditional `float32` cast — "at the dtype maximum" would
then mean "at 3.4e38", identically zero for every field of every plate, for
ever — so `load_2d_gray_with_ceiling` hands that number back alongside an
identical array, and the old function is a wrapper over the new one so the two
cannot drift. `dyn_range` is measured **before correction**, in
`_load_image_group`, because the flat-field division and the background
subtraction both reshape the frame's spread. The remaining three need the
segmentation and are measured after it, in `field_quality.group_record`.

**The scoring is split in two, and the split is the feature.**
`review/domain/field_quality_scores.py` scores the *acquisition* metrics
(`focus`, `sat_frac`, `dyn_range`) as a robust z **within a timepoint, across
the plate**, because those are properties a plate should hold constant by
design. The *biological* ones (`nuc_count`, `nuc_area_median`, `bg_level`) are
scored **within a well, across its own fields**, where the fields are technical
replicates of one biology and disagreement really is a technical fault. Scored
plate-wide they would flag the biology: a cytotoxic compound drops the nucleus
count ten- to twenty-fold, which is `|z| ≫ 5`, so an exclusion built on it
would delete the wells with the largest treatment effect and bias every
dose-response toward null. Timepoints are a grouping axis for the same reason —
pooling t=0 with t=72h makes each mutually anomalous in a time course.

There is deliberately **no combined score**. A max of `|z|` over a varying
number of metrics is not comparable between fields: one scored on three
metrics has a larger maximum than one scored on one, for no reason to do with
the pictures. Zero-inflated metrics take an absolute bound instead of a
relative one, because `sat_frac` is 0 for most fields on a good plate, which
makes the MAD zero and switches the metric off exactly when one saturated
field is the thing worth finding. Where the MAD is zero for any other metric
the answer is `None` and a stated reason — not `0.0`, which would claim every
field sits exactly at the median and could never flag anything.

**The record, and the gap it must not hide.** Each well drops one JSON into a
hidden `.aw_field_quality/` as it finishes, collected into the sidecar's
`field_quality` block at the end of the run and then removed — the same
mechanism `run_report` uses, deliberately kept separate because coverage
accounting and quality measurement answer different questions. A well's record
states `measured_of` as the number of FOV-groups the well **has**, not the
number that produced a measurement, so a well that failed or aborted part way
is visibly partial in the artifact. The per-FOV checkpoint carries a group's
quality in the same file as its records (`_FOV_CHECKPOINT_SCHEMA` 2; a
version-1 checkpoint is refused rather than misread), so a resumed well is
measured as completely as one that ran straight through.

An `--incremental` run — Resume — re-measures only the fields a well is
missing, so its record is **added to** the well's earlier one rather than put
in its place (`field_quality_record.merge_well_records`: fields keyed by
`(fov, timepoint)`, `measured_of` the larger of the two). Locally,
`write_pipeline_info` drops the block when it rewrites the sidecar at the start
of the run, so `main` reads the block first and hands it to
`finalize_field_quality` as `prior_block`, which merges before it writes or
logs anything; the worker is also given the well's full group count
(`measured_of=groups_in_input`), so a resumed well with no earlier record to
add to still reads as partial. Remotely the fetch does the same merge
(`merge_fetched_field_quality(..., incremental=run.incremental)`), where the
host's own count is the split's and the earlier record supplies the well's.
Without either, a well measured on two of three fields read as two of two and
the scorer went ahead. `tests/test_a_resumed_run_keeps_its_field_quality.py`
drives `main` twice through the real well task.

**On the Review side the subsystem reports, and only filters when asked.**
`review/data/field_quality_cache.py` projects the verdicts onto the row cache
as a `Field_Pass` column — the fourth in the same family as `Included`,
`QC_Pass` and `Crop_Pass`, ANDed at the same chokepoint, registered as a cache
projector like the other three. `review/data/focus_gate.py` is the fifth,
`Focus_Pass`, and `review/data/field_exclusions.py` the sixth,
`Excluded_Field_Pass` — a field the user excluded by hand from QC triage, which
refuses the same untrusted wells this layer does. The first two are **not
alternatives**: the field verdict removes a
whole field or none of it, while the per-cell cut removes the soft *part* of a
field — a focus gradient, a coverslip tilt — which is not a whole-field fact
and is not a rectangle either, so it is a column rather than a crop. A field
whose median is fine can still have a soft third. Most of both modules is about
when **not** to write their column, and every refusal has one shape: a filter
applied on evidence it does not have is worse than no filter, because the rows
it drops are chosen by something nobody can account for.

**A verdict layer that can be switched off must be re-projected *and*
removable.** The cache projectors run at load; `qc.controller.recompute_qc_all`
is the pass that runs when a control on the Cell Gating panel moves, and it
re-runs **every registered projector** rather than naming the layers. It
projected `QC_Pass` alone for as long as that panel held one switchable layer,
which was correct then and silently wrong the moment it grew a second: measured
on a plate with one field genuinely flagged, ticking the exclusion wrote no
column at all, the chokepoint had nothing to AND, and the exclusion did not
happen until the dataset was reopened — while the panel reported the flag
correctly the whole time. Going through the registry means a layer added later
is re-projected by having been registered. The mirror image is
`cache_projectors.drop_verdict_column`: a projector whose switch is off
**removes** its column rather than returning early, because returning early
leaves the previous setting's verdict on the frame and unticking the box left
its rows excluded while the panel said they were kept.

* **Both toggles are off by default** (`QCParams.exclude_flagged_fields` and
  `exclude_soft_cells`, on the Cell Gating panel, persisted in the same section
  as the debris gate). Turning either on changes every number in the app, so it
  is chosen after reading what was found rather than discovered afterwards. The
  findings are reported either way.
* **A ticked box stays live** (`tab_view._arm_state`). Both boxes are disabled
  where ticking them would exclude nothing, which is the right rule for an
  *unticked* one — but disabling does not untick, and a box that is checked and
  disabled is armed, persisted as on, and unreachable. Lowering the cut until
  nothing was soft was enough to get there, and raising it later fired the gate
  without the user re-arming anything. Disabling exists to stop someone arming
  a control that would do nothing; a control already armed must stay
  disarmable, and its tooltip says why it currently drops nothing.
* **The counts are over the cells the analysis would otherwise keep**
  (`focus_gate.candidate_rows`), composed from `df_included_mask` minus
  `Focus_Pass` rather than from a second list of layers. Counting every row
  instead made a debris-heavy plate mark every well "needs review — N cells
  carry no focus value", about the shattered fragments `qc_region_area` exists
  to remove and whose outlines `edge_focus` therefore cannot read; and it made
  "currently excluding N cells" count rows the layer *marks* rather than rows
  it *removes*. Subtracting `Focus_Pass` specifically is the other half: the
  full chokepoint would make the panel report nothing to exclude the moment the
  gate was switched on. The count is plate-wide while the plots are
  selection-scoped, and the sentence says "across the plate" rather than
  leaving the reader to assume.
* **The focus cut needs both a switch and a number** (`focus_gate_is_active`).
  A cut with the switch off is a number the user has recorded; the switch on
  with no cut is a request nothing here can honour. `focus_min` is seeded from
  the run's own sidecar — the value depends mostly on the microscope rather
  than on the plate, clipping aside — and is **not** seeded on, because a
  recorded threshold is the user saying "this is my instrument's number", not
  "drop those cells from every plot without telling me".
* **The Playground's curve carries its own qualification.**
  `FocusDistribution.caveats` is drawn on the figure in `warn` ink, above the
  no-recommendation line, and is distinct from `declined`: a caveat does not
  stop the curve being drawn, because the measurement is real and only what
  may be concluded from it is in question. Two are supplied
  (`playground/controller._focus_caveats`). The tab measures whichever channel
  is selected there with that tab's own Correction dropdowns — which is what
  the tab is for — while the `qc_edge_focus` column a cut applies to is always
  the nuclear channel with the run's settings; measured on identical optics,
  geometry and mask, a dim textured reporter reads 1.78× the nuclear median
  with an eightfold p5–p95 spread, so a cut read off the wrong curve can
  exclude the entire nuclear population. And the curve is computed from pixels
  rather than from the CSV, so it draws for a dataset carrying no column at
  all, where the number cannot be applied without re-running the plate. The
  figure's subject also records the correction modes: five of the seven methods
  move the value by ≤2.6 %, but `fft_bandpass` moves it 1.27×, and this window
  has a Save button. A declined curve carries no caveats — a refusal already
  occupies the whole figure and states its reason.
* **The threshold field is bounded by the estimator's own ceiling.**
  `pipeline.field_quality_record.FOCUS_SCORE_CEILING` is 0.8333 — one over
  1.2 px, because the score is the reciprocal of a width measured on a profile
  binned at one pixel, so the width has a floor. Measured rather than derived,
  and identical at radius 6, 10, 16 and 24, since the floor comes from the
  binning rather than from the object. It lives beside `FOCUS_COLUMN` in the
  stdlib-only record module because the Analyze form validates against it and
  must not import numpy and scipy to do so. Refusing an impossible value *is*
  the feedback that form was missing; no "aggressive but legal" band is
  invented, because where that band sits depends on the objective and the pixel
  size, which is the reason the cut is a number about a microscope at all. For
  scale, a sharp plate measures 0.417–0.448.
* **A projector that raises costs one column, never a well.** The registry is
  walked from two places — `data_loading.load_and_project` at load and
  `qc.controller.recompute_qc_all` on a Cell Gating change — and both guard
  each call. The loader's was once unguarded, which was the wrong side of the
  asymmetry: a raise during the recompute loses a verdict column, while a raise
  during the load loses the whole well, because that call is what decides
  whether the frame enters the cache. The four registrations are
  **unconditional** and no profile gates them: each is an inclusion layer, and
  a build that drops a tab must not thereby change which cells count.
* **Analyze remembers the cut between sessions**, alone among that form's
  fields (`qc_section.FOCUS_MIN_SETTING`, through `core.app_settings`). The
  asymmetry is the control's own argument: every other field on the form
  describes the plate being processed, while this one describes the microscope
  and is documented as carrying between plates, so retyping it each run
  contradicts the sentence beside it. A dataset restore runs after the build
  and therefore still wins — what *this* dataset recorded beats what this user
  last typed, which is the same precedence Review's side of the cut takes. A
  cleared box removes the key rather than leaving the old value to reappear.
  And a cut typed with the measurement unticked says it is being discarded:
  the form collects it, the validator skips it (its gate is falsy) and the
  service drops it, so without the notice a typed number vanished with the row
  it sat in.
* **The cut is persisted only when it differs from the run's**
  (`persistence/qc_params.save_to_data_dir`). Every other threshold on the
  panel becomes the user's the moment they touch anything; this one also has
  an authoritative source, and re-recording it is deliberately cheap because
  `focus_min` sits outside the reuse key, so a re-run that changes only the
  cut skips every well and still rewrites the sidecar. Storing it
  unconditionally made that cheap path silently wrong: the section is written
  whenever *any* control on the panel moves, so opening the panel once froze
  the seeded number, and a later re-run recording a different one left Analyze
  and Review showing two numbers for one dataset. Omitting the key means "not
  overridden", and the loader re-seeds. When the user really has chosen their
  own, `focus_gate.recorded_cut_note` names the run's number beside it, which
  is also the only place in Review the recorded value is visible at all.
* **The plate's quality markers are repainted from the cut**
  (`ctx.runtime.home.quality_refresh_cb`, installed by Home's own builder and
  called by `qc.controller.set_qc_params`). `wells_needing_review` is a
  function of `focus_min` and was reachable only through `refresh_home` — page
  activation and load — so changing the cut on Home ▸ Cell Gating and
  switching to Home ▸ Overview left the plate marking wells against the
  previous number, with the tooltips quoting it. The callback runs one way:
  QC calls what Home installed, and neither feature imports the other.
* **A cell with no focus value passes.** Undefined is not soft. Severe defocus
  degrades segmentation, so the column is missing exactly where defocus is
  worst — but so is a nucleus whose boundary profile cannot be read at all,
  and treating the two alike would quietly delete cells on every plate. The count of them is named on the panel, as **kept**, because a
  reader who believed the gate removed everything soft would be wrong about
  exactly those rows.
* **A well whose FOV labels are untrusted is refused, not joined onto.**
  `review/domain/fov_integrity.py` exists because a well whose filenames do not
  match the schema arrives with *every* row labelled field 1, indistinguishable
  from a well that genuinely has one field. A per-field verdict joined onto
  that either spreads one field's verdict across all of them or matches
  nothing, and the second is indistinguishable from a well measured and found
  clean. The refusal is named on screen: a well silently exempt from a filter
  and a well that passed it look identical in a plot.
* **A partly measured plate filters nothing**, and the panel quotes the
  scorer's own refusal rather than paraphrasing it.

**Two surfaces, and the register each uses.** The Cell Gating panel carries the
control and one sentence with four states — no block, a refusal, a finding,
nothing flagged. Only the two where the software could not do what was asked
wear the amber `QLabel#Notice` band; a finding is ordinary text, because a
result is not a failure and dressing them alike collapses the distinction the
states exist for. The Home plate marks a flagged well with a **glyph**, not a
ninth colour: that palette is closed under a written invariant (no state
carries a colour another state carries), `accent2` is reserved and forbidden
for anomaly use, and `threshold` was measured indistinguishable from `warn` by
the plate's own render guard. The glyph is also the right channel on its own
terms — field quality is orthogonal to coverage, and a well can be complete and
out of focus. It carries a legend row of its own whenever the plate shows one,
because that plate's invariant is that no well is left without a row to explain
it, and the same mapping feeds the tooltip so a mark cannot appear without its
reason. That row is separated from the ones above it and counts *wells*: the
column above partitions the plate, its counts sum to the wells, and an overlay
appended flush to it double-counts a well that is already in one of those rows.

**The glyph vocabulary is now two marks and should not become three without a
reason written down.** The Analyze run dashboard paints `✕` on a well that
errored; this plate paints `!` on a well holding a field the run flagged. Both
go through `WellPlateSelector.setWellMarker`, which draws bold at 0.78 of the
well's height in an ink chosen by measuring the fill's relative luminance
(`marker_ink`) rather than by asking whether the well happens to carry a group
colour — that proxy put a dark mark on the `text_muted` fill at a contrast
ratio of 3.88:1, and a 1 px stem picked up subpixel fringing that reads as a
rendering fault.

**The plate's marker is a composite, not the field verdict alone.**
`review/domain/well_composite.py` scores each well over three independent
reasons and `review/data/focus_gate.wells_needing_review` is the adapter that
feeds it the numbers already on disk — no image decode, no output archive
opened. What it feeds is a `FocusTally` per well — total, unmeasurable,
measurable, median, soft count at the cut — read from every well through
`plate_scan` and remembered there, not the wells' focus columns themselves:
those are a million values a well, and holding every well's at once to score
the plate is what the bounded row cache exists to prevent. The case the field verdict alone misses is the one the per-cell column
exists for: a well whose fields all look ordinary while a third of its cells
are soft. Every reason is named in the tooltip, because a composite that shows
only a total is a number nobody can act on.

Each bound is accounted for. A flagged field is the pipeline's own robust
comparison and needs no bound of ours. A well whose **median** focus is below
the cut uses the pooled statistic the measurements support — at a pooling of
thirty cells the in-focus fifth percentile clears the one-pixel-defocus
ninety-fifth outright, where the per-cell distributions at that defocus overlap
heavily. `SOFT_FRACTION` is twice the five per cent a well-placed cut removes
from a perfectly in-focus population by construction, which is the smallest
round number that cannot be the cut's own false-positive rate.
`UNMEASURABLE_FRACTION` is the one bound with no measurement under it and is
much looser, because it states that the *evidence* is missing rather than that
the well is bad, and a plate of genuinely small nuclei carries a standing share
of unreadable outlines.

**Where the threshold comes from, and who applies it.** The number is a
property of the **microscope** — the point-spread function, the pixel size, the
nuclear contrast — so a cut carries between plates taken on one instrument at
one magnification, clipping aside, and it is stated in the Analyze form
(`analyze/qc_section.py`: `Measure per-cell focus`, on by default, and
`Out of focus below`, blank by default). The run **records** it in
`pipeline_info.json` and never acts on it: a threshold is what a user gets
wrong the first time, and a pipeline that dropped the cells would make
revisiting it cost a re-run over the images, while a recorded value seeds
Review's gate where the same cut is one tick to change and one tick to undo.

**Nothing suggests a value for it**, and that is measured rather than cautious.
Otsu's method on the per-cell values — the natural choice, since the population
is multiplicative — returns a cut for a plate with nothing wrong with it and
discards **39.5 %** of its good cells; on a uniformly defocused plate it splits
the bad population against itself and keeps **76 %** of the cells it exists to
catch. Its own separability spans 0.516–0.671 across both degenerate cases and
five useful ones, with the clean plate scoring higher than three genuinely
mixed ones, so there is no statistic to gate a recommendation on. The
Playground draws the distribution instead
(`review/domain/focus_distribution.py`, `playground/focus_curve_view.py`): a
cumulative curve, because a histogram's shape is an artifact of its bin width
while "at this cut, how much of my frame goes" is read off a cumulative curve
directly — with the user's own cut marked, its consequence annotated on the
figure, and the refusal stated on the figure too, since the plot is savable and
a reader who does not know the absence was measured will read it as an
omission. It is the same answer `review/domain/threshold_sweep.py` reached for
StarDist's probability threshold, by a different route, and the two windows are
deliberately built alike.

`pipeline.field_quality.summarize` is the single composition of "what did field
quality find". The end-of-run log prints it and the Analyze tab's pre-flight
strip **quotes** it, so the two cannot describe one folder differently.

## 7. The widget library (`widgets/`)

Every widget under `widgets/` is:

- **Standalone.** It only imports from `ui.theme`, Qt, and the Qt-free top-level
  helpers under `util/` (`util.well_token`, `util.aw_safe`) — plus
  `widgets._support` for tiny RGB helpers and `set_variant`, a runtime
  dynamic-property + repolish helper (see below). It does *not* import
  `review` and knows nothing about `ReviewApp` or any tab. That is why
  a widget's suppressed exceptions go through `util.aw_safe.swallowed`, the same
  helper the pipeline uses, rather than `core.safe`.
- **Token-styled.** Sizes derive from font metrics; colours come from
  `theme.Colors` / QSS object names. No hardcoded device pixels.
- **DPI-aware.** Geometry is computed from `fontMetrics()`, so the widgets
  scale correctly at 1×, 1.5×, 2×.
- **Singly responsible.** One widget per file. The file may contain a
  helper class or two but never another reusable widget.

Notable members worth knowing about by name:

| Widget | What it is |
|--------|-----------|
| `CropTool` (`review/data/crop_tool.py`) | The drag-a-region crop shared by Image Table and Segmentation. `set_status_widget(widget, template=…)` writes the crop state into an existing control's text — the Image Table's Crop button reads `Crop · (full FOV)` — instead of a separate caption beside it; `make_status_label` still returns a standalone label for call sites that want one. |
| `LabeledComboBox` (`widgets/labeled_combo.py`) | A `QComboBox` that paints its own scope label as a fixed prefix inside the closed box ("Channel: RFP", "Timepoint: 4.0h") rather than sitting beside a separate `QLabel`. `currentText()` / `currentIndex()` / every Qt signal still report the plain item value — only `paintEvent` changes, drawing `opt.currentText` set to the prefixed string. `sizeHint()` measures *only what's actually painted* (the current item's text plus the prefix, via `self.style().sizeFromContents(QStyle.CT_ComboBox, opt, content, self)`), not plain `QComboBox`'s default — which measures every item in the list up front (`AdjustToContentsOnFirstShow`) and sizes the closed box to the widest one, so a metric combo showing "N" sat as wide as its longest possible entry ("Property: Fraction Threshold On") the whole time. Callers must not layer `setFixedWidth` / `setMinimumContentsLength` / a QSS `min-width` on top — every one of those re-floors the box wider than its current content needs, which is exactly the waste this widget exists to cut; centre_view.py's Channel/Property combos and `review_csv/tab_view.py`'s Timepoint and FOV combos carried exactly that stale floor from before the box was made self-sizing, until removed. Before a caller populates the combo (or an empty dataset leaves it with no items), `currentText()` is `""` — `_painted_text()` falls back to the bare label ("Timepoint") rather than painting nothing, since a blank sliver reads as broken once the box tracks content width; `paintEvent` calls the same `_painted_text()` rather than duplicating the fallback, so painting and sizing can't drift apart. A repaint recomputes `sizeHint()` and calls `updateGeometry()` when it changed, which is what catches a text change made under `blockSignals(True)` (a common "seed without re-triggering the handler" pattern that suppresses `currentIndexChanged` but not Qt's own repaint scheduling). `ControlBand.add_scope("", combo)` is called with an empty label for one of these — the combo describes itself, so it's added alone rather than paired with a caption. Used for Plotting's page-level Channel and Property combos, every single-select Timepoint combo across Review (Stats, Spatial, Multivariate, Distribution, Heat Map, smFISH, Review CSV, Segmentation preview) — Heat Map's was a `StyledSlider` until unified onto the same combo every sibling tab uses — and every FOV combo (smFISH, Review CSV, Segmentation preview). Not every folded scope control is a `LabeledComboBox`: the checkbox-menu multi-select buttons (Bar Plots' and Scatter Cells/Agg's Timepoints pickers) fold the same way but by a different means, since there's no per-item combo box to paint a prefix on — `core.ui_helpers.multiselect_button_text` builds the readout string and the button's own `setText` carries it. The `ControlBand.add_scope(label, widget)` pairing is still what every other scope control uses — Heat Map's own Aggregation combo included, since there's no per-tab convention for what its prefix would read. |
| `multiselect_button_text` (`core/ui_helpers.py`) | The button-text counterpart to `LabeledComboBox` for a checkbox-menu multi-select control (the "Select Timepoints" pattern Bar Plots and both Scatter sub-tabs use): folds a prefix and a `{token: bool}` selection dict into one string — `"Timepoints: 2/5 selected"`, `"Timepoints: All 5 selected"`, `"Timepoints: 0 selected"` — for the picker button's own text, in place of a separate count `QLabel` beside it. The three call sites (`barplot/controller.py::update_bar_tp_selection_display`, `scatter/controller.py::update_scatter_tp_selection_display` / `update_tp_selection_display`) call it on every selection change; `persistence/view_state.py`'s bar-tab restore path calls it directly too, since it predates and is Qt-free like the rest of `core`. |
| `ControlBand` (`widgets/control_band.py`) | The one control row a Review tab uses, so that switching tabs does not also switch control layouts. Two zones and no third: **scope** on the left (what data is shown — channel, property, timepoint, threshold) and **actions** flush right (how it is shown and what to do with it — `Display ▾`, `Save ▾`, Properties). Which view is being shown is the tab bar's job, not the band's, so nothing is centred. The scope zone is a `FlowLayout` rather than a `QHBoxLayout`: a box layout has no wrap, so at narrow widths Qt compresses the children until a label is drawn over the combo beside it. `add_scope(label, *widgets)` bundles the label and its control through `flow_group` as **one** flow item, so a wrap can never strand a label from what it names, and returns that group so a caller can show or hide the pair. Three details are load-bearing and each cost a render to find: the action zone is `Qt.AlignTop`, or it centres itself against a wrapped scope zone and the buttons drift half a row down; the band's height floors at the action zone's, since `FlowLayout.heightForWidth` returns ~0 for an empty scope zone and the band would collapse behind its own buttons; and the band answers `heightForWidth` from the flow at the width the scope zone will actually get, because a tab built inside a stacked page is first realised at a narrow transient width where `sync_flow_height` pins the fully-wrapped height as the host's minimum — inheriting `QWidget`'s cached hint there left a 45px band 151px tall for good. `ROW_H` (28px; `band_height()` == 44 with the band's own padding) is what one row measures, whatever it holds — set as a real `setMinimumHeight`, because a parent layout asks the band's `QWidgetItem`, which delegates to `wid->layout()->heightForWidth()` and never reaches an override on the class. Its object name is `ControlBand`, which is data-gated (§5.2). A page whose body is a stack of leaf views still gets **one** band: each leaf claims a `ControlBandSlot` through `band.slot(name)`, adds its controls through the slot's mirror of `add_scope` / `add_action`, and `show_slot` shows one leaf's while hiding the rest. A slot is a real widget — a child of the band that is never laid out, so it is never painted — because leaves parent popover contents to what they think is their band. Items claimed by a slot that is not current arrive hidden, since `QLayout.addWidget` shows what it is handed and leaves build lazily. Both `add_scope` and `add_action` pass any `QCheckBox` they are handed through `widgets/checkbox_fit.fit_checkbox_width`, for the same reason `trailing=True` lives on the band rather than in each builder: the rule belongs with the control row, not in a builder's memory. |
| `ButtonRow` (`widgets/button_row.py`) | **A row of buttons that wraps rather than forcing its host wider.** A `QHBoxLayout` of buttons reports the sum of their widths as its minimum, and that minimum propagates: the Statistics comparison-group editor's three actions made the column they sit in about 370px at its narrowest, enough to push the well map out of the row beside it at a pane width where the two still fitted. Wrapping, the row's minimum is its widest single button. It is a widget rather than a `FlowLayout` built at the feature site for a second reason: `ControlBand` owns the one wrapping row of *controls* a page has, `tests/test_control_band_adoption.py` is the guard that stops a tab growing a second one beside it, and a bare `FlowLayout` in an adopted module is indistinguishable from the thing that guard exists to catch. A ButtonRow takes buttons acting on the section around them; anything that selects what a page *shows* is a scope control and belongs in the band. It calls `sync_flow_height` on itself, because a wrapped second line inside a `QStackedWidget` page is otherwise drawn behind whatever sits below it. |
| `ResponsiveScroll` (`widgets/responsive_row.py`) | The vertically-scrolling host a `ResponsiveRow` belongs in when the page it is on can run out of height. Horizontal scrolling is **on demand**, not off: the rows flip on the viewport's width, which a horizontal bar does not change, so the bar costs the decision nothing — and below the floor, where a stacked row cannot be narrower than its widest panel, it is the difference between a shortfall the user can reach and one drawn behind the page's edge. That is also why the scroll area has to push its viewport width into the rows on resize rather than leaving each row to read its own — with horizontal scrolling off, the area sizes its inner widget to at least that widget's minimum, so once a row is too wide the whole page is too wide and every width up the chain repeats the same inflated number; and a row already pinned at its minimum need not receive a resize of its own to react to. `ResponsiveRow` walks up for an enclosing scroll area and reads the viewport itself for the same reason. |
| `ResponsiveRow` (`widgets/responsive_row.py`) | **Panels side by side while the width holds them, a column when it does not.** A `QBoxLayout` handed less width than its children's minimums does not decline to lay them out — it places them in order at the widths they demand and runs the tail off its own right edge — which is how the Statistics comparison-group editor came to show a section title reading "COMP GROU" and a load button cut off mid-word on a 350px pane (an 1100×800 window with the rail open and the pane split). The panels do not overlap and no arrangement of them does; a short box layout clips, so a test asserting they never overlap cannot fail for that reason and the clipping is what has to be measured. The flip point is not a chosen number: it is the panels' own effective minimum widths plus the spacing between them, so the row stacks exactly when one line would start clipping and nobody has to keep a threshold in step with what the panels contain. *Effective* is both halves and neither alone — `minimumSizeHint` is what a widget derives from its own contents and ignores a floor set on it from outside, `minimumWidth` is that floor and is 0 on a widget that never had one, and Qt takes the larger; a first cut reading only the hint missed the map's `setMinimumWidth(PLATE_MIN_WIDTH)` and would have gone on clipping in the place it was written to fix. `add_panel` rather than `addWidget`, because each panel carries the stretch it takes on one line — dropped when stacked, or the panel that grabbed the horizontal slack would grab the vertical and the page below would lose the room the row was meant to leave — and an alignment per orientation, so the map is top-aligned beside the cards and centred above them. Hysteresis on the way back, since the two orientations have different heights and therefore different scrollbar states, and a width sitting on the flip point would oscillate. `features/batch_export/base_panel.py` grew this behaviour first, wired into that panel's class and reading its scroll viewport's width rather than its own; it is not converted here because its version also drives a separator's orientation and its own width caps. |
| `checkbox_fit` (`widgets/checkbox_fit.py`) | **A checkbox wide enough for its own label, under whatever style is painting it.** `QCheckBox.sizeHint()` budgets an indicator, the QSS `spacing` gap and the text; a style that places the label further right than that budget assumed leaves the tail outside the widget, and `FlowLayout` then packs the next control at `x + width + spacing`, so the neighbour butts straight against the cut rather than leaving a gap that would make the clipping legible. Reported on macOS for the Distribution tab's `log x` / `log y` boxes, at every window width — width-independence is what places the defect in the item's own size rather than in pressure from the row. Deliberately not a constant: `theme.Metrics.checkbox_chrome_w` exists for call sites that run before the stylesheet is applied and cannot use `sizeHint()` at all, and the `QCheckBox::indicator` QSS comment records an earlier fixed `margin` added for this and removed for stacking on `spacing` everywhere it was not wanted — the shortfall is per-style and per-context. So it is asked of the style that will paint the widget: `SE_CheckBoxContents` is the rect reserved for the label, and when it is narrower than the text needs, that difference is the floor to add. Measured at the width a layout will actually give the widget (`sizeHint().expandedTo(minimumSize())`), not the bare hint — measuring at the hint reports a shortfall the helper has already closed. Fusion reserves ~6px more than `log x` needs, so it is a no-op there and can only ever add space a style is already clipping away; `tests/test_checkbox_label_fits.py` models the divergence with a checkbox whose `sizeHint` under-reports what its style paints, because CI cannot see this class of bug — exactly as `flow_layout.py` documents for `QMacStyle`'s layout spacing. A `QProxyStyle` overriding `SE_CheckBoxContents` does **not** work for that: once a global stylesheet is installed Qt wraps the widget's style in `QStyleSheetStyle`, which derives checkbox geometry from the stylesheet and never delegates the sub-element back, so the case reproduced when the file ran alone and was silently absorbed in the fast lane. |
| `build_page_body` (`widgets/page_body.py`) | The standard body of a main page: a `ControlBand` flush against the page's top, then the page's content beneath it. `build_page_body(parent, *, content_margins=(left, right, bottom), horizontal=False)` strips the page root's own margins and spacing, adds the band, and returns it together with a content host. There is no top-margin parameter — side and bottom padding are a page's own business, the top is what every page's first row is aligned by. **The band is added whether or not the page has controls for it**: a page with none (Image Table, the Playground, Batch Export, the Datasets tool pages) reserves the row so its content starts level with its neighbours', the same reservation the mode band's page-tabs host makes for a page with no sub-tab bar. `horizontal=True` gives the content host a `QHBoxLayout` for a page whose body is a row rather than a column (the Playground's canvas beside its property dock). No All-Well coupling, so the Review feature packages, `analyze/log_pane.py` and `datasets/tab.py` all build their bodies through it. Measured by `tests/test_page_alignment.py` (§5.2). |
| `owned_action` (`widgets/owned_action.py`) | **A menu or toolbar action released with its owner.** `owner.addAction(text)` creates the `QAction` in C++, and once a Python callable is connected to one of its signals PySide keeps the wrapper for the life of the process, after the menu and the action are both deleted — measured, five menus of one connected action left five wrappers, while the same action built in Python with the menu as parent left none (`addAction(text, callable)` leaves none either). `owned_action(owner, text)` / `(owner, icon, text)` builds it the second way and adds it. Every connected action in the app is built through it; `tests/test_connected_actions_are_owned.py` fails on one built by `addAction`, chained or through a name bound to it, including a name rebound to a second action. |
| `ModeBar` (`widgets/mode_bar.py`) | The app's top-level Review / Analyze / Datasets selector. These are three applications sharing a window, not three tabs of one screen, and the control says so at rest: **every segment is filled at all times** — the active one accent-filled, the inactive ones on `panel_elevated` with full-strength `text_primary` and full-opacity glyphs. Nothing here is muted, because muting is how the rail's section list and the centre tab bar express "not currently selected", and borrowing it demotes a switch between applications to a third tab strip. Segments are flush — no gutters, no radius — so the bar is one band rather than three chips. `addSegment` takes a `widgets.icons` glyph *name*, not a `QIcon`, and repaints it in whichever foreground the segment's state calls for; a fixed `QIcon` draws its Normal pixmap in `text_secondary`, which on the accent fill is a dark glyph on saturated blue. The bar's default height is `tab_bar_height()`, measured off a throwaway polished `QTabBar` so the two bands share a bottom edge through any change to tab padding. That measurement is deliberately uncached — it depends on the application stylesheet and font, and a module-level cache freezes whichever were in force at the first call, which for a widget built during startup is a stylesheet that has not been applied yet. |
| `PlotCard` | The `QFrame` chrome around every matplotlib figure. Provides a custom toolbar (`MplToolbar`), Screen↔Publication mode toggle, and stats chip slot. |
| `WellPlateSelector` | **The app's only painted well grid.** Every 8×12 plate the user sees is this control — Review's rails and the sample-definitions editor, the Datasets tools' pickers and status maps, Convert OME-TIFF's acquisition-path editor, and Batch Export's group map. What differs between them is which *selection model* the host drives it in (`setSelectionModel`): `"set"` (the default, an unordered selection), `"path"` (an ordered acquisition route — a click appends an off-path well or removes an on-path one, the wells carry their visit numbers derived from the list's own order, and an alpha-blended arrow traces the route across the plate), or `"paint"` (the grid owns **nothing** — it reports the press/drag/release gesture as `wellPaintPressed` / `wellPaintDragged` / `paintDragFinished` and the host applies it to whatever it is editing). The corner select-all toggle appears only in `"set"`, since it toggles a selection set the other two models do not have, and a paint gesture ends with `paintDragFinished` rather than `selectionDragFinished` — the latter means "the selection settled", and a paint gesture never changed one. Supports per-well colour overrides, drag-to-select, and drag mime types for the heatmap layout (a drag source arms on press and applies the ordinary click on release, so clicking still selects — see §9.2). **`setSelectionRim(True)`** is for a host that has spent the fill on data of its own. Normally selection is said by the fill — a selected well is lit and an unselected one recessed — but `_paint_lit` takes a colour override as its `base` whether or not the well is in the selection, so on a plate whose colour *is* the data a selected well and an unselected one render identically, and "select these wells, then act on them" has no feedback at all. The rim is drawn **inset**, because outside is taken: `_paint_ring` annotates a well from 7% beyond its edge and a host may need both marks on one well at once. It is `text_primary` rather than the accent for the same reason — the accent is the ring's, and a near-white rim is the one ink no host value can take, so it cannot read as one more category. Turning it on also stops selection *lighting* an uncoloured well: the rank-cycled `traces` palette a lit selection reaches for opens with the same `#6AB2FB` that `variable_series.VALUE_PICKS` opens with, so picking an unannotated well used to paint it the exact colour of a value nobody had given it. Off by default, so every other plate is unchanged — on a plate whose fill is free, lit-versus-recessed already says it and a second mark saying the same thing is noise. `tests/test_plate_selection_rim.py` measures one well rendered twice, selected and not, at one position: its first version compared two neighbouring wells and reported them different against the *unfixed* painter, because each cell rasterises at its own sub-pixel offset and no two wells ever hash alike whatever is drawn in them. The per-well body is `_paint_well`, lifted out of `paintEvent` — that method carries the headers, the grid, the rubber band, the path and the disabled scrim, and a well is the one part of it with a decision tree of its own. Every lightening of a state colour goes through `_lighten` (an RGB blend toward white), never `QColor.lighter`: Qt's version raises the HSV *value* and, once value is at the ceiling, starts dropping *saturation* — it lightens toward white rather than toward a pale version of the hue. Every state colour in the app sits at value 245–253, so `accent2 #B98CF7` came back as literally `#ffffff`; a dial's unfilled share and the sphere gradient's highlight both used it, which is how an uploaded well rendered as a white disc with no hue left to say which stage it was in. `_blend` is the one lerp behind `_lighten` and `_mix_with_rail`. `darker()` needs no equivalent — lowering value never touches saturation. **The sphere gradient is damped on a dial and only on a dial** (`_DIAL_RELIEF`, scaling the stops `_sphere_stops` returns). Blending toward white keeps the hue but *compresses two tones together* — the nearer both are to white, the smaller the gap — so at a plain well's full relief the done and remaining halves of a green well came within 25 luminance of each other under the highlight, against 39 at the centre, and the completed wedge was itself 35 % of the way to white. Reported as "the completed portion is too light and I can't see the difference between complete and incomplete". At 0.43 relief the highlight is 15 % toward white and that worst case is 33. A plain well keeps the full relief because it has no internal boundary for the highlight to compress; only the dial carries a second signal in the same pixels, so only the dial pays. Tone alone still cannot carry green, so the wedge's radii and arc are **stroked** in `base.darker(170)` — skipped at a full dial, where the boundary *is* the rim the well already has. A non-interactive "lit" mode (`setColoredWellsLit`) paints colour-override wells with the raised/lit style instead of the depressed one, plus three decoration layers that stack independently of each other and of the fill: a `setWellMarker` glyph, a `setWellFraction` / `clearWellFractions` progress dial, and a `setWellRing` / `setWellRings` / `clearWellRings` accent ring drawn just *outside* the well body. The dial is used by every live plate map that reports a run, whether that is a dashboard's own status plate (Analyze, Concatenate, Import Loose, Merge Plates) or a page's input plate doubling as the progress display (Subset's picker, Convert OME-TIFF's path editor); Validate has no dial because it inspects rather than copies.
