The ring exists because a host can need a third channel: Batch Export colours a well by which group owns it and rings the wells of the group *currently being edited*, two different questions that would otherwise fight over the same fill. **Every Batch Export mode shares one set of export groups.** Line, Bar, Scatter (cells) and Scatter (aggregate) used to persist under four private slots chosen by `_compute_persist_key`, so groups built in one mode were invisible in the others and anyone exporting the same conditions four ways built them four times; the groups describe the dataset's conditions, not the plot type, so they live in one slot (`base_panel.SHARED_PERSIST_KEY`). A document written before that has its four legacy keys merged in a fixed order and de-duplicated by name, and only when the shared key is absent — otherwise deleting a group would be undone by a legacy slot re-supplying it on the next load. The four panels are cached children of one host toggled by `setVisible`, so `tab_view._show_mode` calls `_reload_persisted_groups()` on the panel it reveals; that is not the auto-resync from the *sample-definition* replicate sets which the same function's comment rules out (that one wiped the user's export groups on every visit). No `EventBus` signal — the catalogue is capped at five by contract and a mode switch is local. Batch Export drives the plate in `"paint"` because an export group's model is replicate sets plus solo wells, not a flat set of clicked wells: `_apply_drag` resolves the well under the cursor to the sample definition that owns it and adds or removes that whole **member**, falling back to a solo well only for a well no sample claims. Membership is compared **by name** — `domain.selections_model.replicate_sets_loaded` builds a fresh `ReplicateSet` on every call and the class defines no `__eq__`, so an identity test never matched an already-present member: dragging across two wells of one sample appended it twice (and the group then exported that condition twice), while dragging a sample back off a group removed nothing. The name is already the identity key everywhere else, being what `_serialize_groups` persists and what hydration matches on. All three decorations, plus the path, are pruned by `setEnabledWells` / `setWellEnabled` — a disabled well paints as an empty socket, and a ring or a dial on a socket describes a well that is not there. Per-well rank colours are now pushed on **every** tab (not just the plotting tabs), so a given well reads as the same colour everywhere in the app. Every host sizes and places its plate through `plate_geometry.apply_plate_geometry` (below) rather than setting its own caps. |
| `plate_geometry` (`widgets/plate_geometry.py`) | The single sizing and placement rule for every `WellPlateSelector` in the app — Review's five rail pickers, the "New Replicate Set" dialog, the saved-selections compose popover, Subset's well picker, Batch Export's group map, Convert OME-TIFF's acquisition-path plate, and each run dashboard's status map. **Every well grid the user can see goes through it**, with two documented exceptions that are not `WellPlateSelector`s at all: Home's *Well Labels* grid (`features/home/labels/tab_view.py`), which is 96 `QLineEdit`s because each cell takes free text, and the window icon's decorative plate in `allwell.py`, which is a painted graphic with no model behind it. `apply_plate_geometry(plate, *, role)` takes a `role` of `"rail"` (action row hidden, host has its own buttons), `"picker"` (action row shown), `"status"` (action row hidden, selection `"passive"`), `"editor"` (action row hidden, interactive, and — unlike `"rail"` — subject to the size caps) or `"canvas"` (an editor whose plate *is* its page's primary surface, taking the larger `PLATE_CANVAS_WIDTH` / `PLATE_CANVAS_HEIGHT` of 470 × 300); the role decides **only** those behavioural things and which of the three ceilings applies. Size, panel treatment and alignment are identical across all of them, which is the point: the same control used to render at three different cell scales depending on the pane. `"editor"` exists for an interactive plate that sits in a page rather than the rail and supplies its own actions — Convert OME-TIFF's acquisition-path plate, whose Generate/Clear buttons sit beneath it; uncapped it grows to the scroll area's full width and pushes the run button below the fold, which is why that page used to restate `330` / `210` as literals of its own. `"canvas"` exists for the opposite case in the same page: the Variables tab's plate is not one control among several but the surface every gesture on the page operates, and it carries four independent marks at once — a value's colour, a ring for an unannotated well, a selection rim, and a second variable's glyph *inside* the well. At the editor ceiling that resolves to roughly 16.5 px of well with a 10 px glyph in it. It is a named third ceiling rather than the rail's exemption, because the exemption is uncapped and reusing it would both inherit an argument written about Review's rail specifically and let this plate grow to whatever width the page has — the failure the width cap exists to prevent. `PLATE_MAX_WIDTH` (330, the rail's own width) caps the card because the selector paints its panel background across its *entire* allocated box while the grid inside sizes cells to `min(width / 12, height / 8)` — past the height cap, extra width stretches the panel into a wide, mostly-empty card with a small grid floating in it. `PLATE_MAX_HEIGHT` (210) is the budget for a plate with its action row hidden; for a `"picker"` the helper *measures* that row from the widget's own layout and adds its height on top, so the grid budget — and therefore the cell size — is the same either way, and no caller re-derives an empirical "+48". `PLATE_ALIGNMENT` is the alignment flag every host passes to `addWidget`, so a container wider than the width cap centres the card instead of stranding it against an edge. **The `"rail"` role is exempt from both caps.** Review's left-rail picker is the app's primary interaction surface rather than a status readout: it scales to whatever width the rail gives it, with no ceiling. Capping it alongside the others shrank its cells from 23.7px to 20.8px — unifying the two by making the one people actually click on smaller, which is the wrong direction. It still takes the shared size *policy*, because the aspect-locked scaling genuinely is the same rule; only the ceiling differs. The module lives under `widgets/` rather than in `review/core/ui_helpers.py` because `widgets/` and `datasets/` both need it and `widgets/` must not import `review` (`test_architecture_contracts.py::test_widgets_do_not_import_the_app`). Every caller names its own role; Review's sidebar plate asks for `"rail"`. One rule the helper cannot enforce for its callers: a plate's container must add no horizontal inset, since the grid paints from the widget's own `width()` and a gutter on one host shrinks that host's plate in both dimensions. |
| `PathField` (`widgets/path_field.py`) | A labelled folder/file picker: caption + read-only path box (basename shown, full path on hover) + icon Browse button, with an optional inline validity hint. Unifies two near-duplicate private widgets the Concatenate and Convert OME-TIFF pages grew independently. The dialog is opened by an injected `pick(current, parent)` callable rather than hardcoded, so the same widget serves a folder dialog (`folder_picker(prompt)`, the common case) or a page-owned file dialog (Convert OME-TIFF's `.ome.tif` source picker) — the picker takes *parent* explicitly because an unparented `QFileDialog` opens as a detached window on macOS instead of an app sheet. `setLocked(locked)` disables only the Browse button, not the whole widget — every Datasets tool page uses it (not `setEnabled(False)`) to lock a field for a run's duration, since the latter dims the *entire* field, including the already-read-only path text, the one piece of context a user watching a long run most wants to check. `show_note(text)` shows a neutral, "Muted"-styled inline note in place of the validator's own red "Danger"-styled hint, until the next `revalidate()` call — used after a successful run, when the validator's own message would otherwise be the exact "already holds a finished dataset" wording a pre-run pick gets, which is technically true but reads as a warning about the very output that run just correctly produced. `show_warning(text)` is its red counterpart, for a rule the validator cannot reach because it spans two fields — a validator sees one path, so "this destination is also the source" can only be decided by the page, and without somewhere to say it the page's Run button goes dark with no reason attached. |
| `StagePathView` (`widgets/stage_path_view.py`) | **Carries its own size hint** (`plate_geometry`'s shared caps) and a `Fixed` vertical policy. A bare `QWidget` has none, so a `QVBoxLayout` gives it nothing and it lays out at 0×0 — every visibility flag true, `setPath` full, and not one pixel drawn; asserting the points it holds cannot see that, only its geometry can. **Navigable, and self-labelling.** The wheel zooms about the cursor (`setZoom`, bounded 1–40×), a drag pans, a double-click fits — zooming about the cursor rather than the widget's centre is what makes a scan of hundreds of positions usable, since the well being looked at stays put instead of sliding away while the view grows around the middle. Fully zoomed out always resets the pan, so "out" is the whole map and never a panned fragment. Positions number themselves when there is **room** — the gap to the nearest neighbour exceeding `_LABEL_ROOM_PX` — rather than under a count: at full extent the marks are pixels apart and labels would overlap each other and the dots they name, while zoomed in the numbers are the reason to have zoomed, so they appear exactly where the eye already went. That spacing test is necessary and not sufficient, so each label is also measured before it is drawn (`QFontMetricsF`) and **skipped where its padded box hits one already drawn**. The gap it clears is between *consecutive* marks and says nothing about a mark from another row landing in the same place, and a four-digit number — which a scan of a few thousand positions reaches — is nearly twice as wide as the gap the test asks for; every label then sat on its neighbours and the result read as white scribble rather than as numbers. Text also gets its own render hint (`TextAntialiasing`), a point-size floor (`_LABEL_MIN_PT`) below which digits stop being distinguishable and a label is not worth drawing, and the panel colour laid under it first — the digits are white and the thing they annotate is the accent route line, which inside a well doubles back through its own labels, so unbacked text is white-on-accent exactly where the numbers matter most. `tests/test_stage_path_view.py` asserts this at the painter, not on the widget's own values: what makes a label legible is where it lands beside the others, and nothing inside the widget knows that. One transform serves the lattice and the path together; drawn at plate scale while the path zoomed, the lattice stopped being the frame the path is read against and became a decoration the path had flown off. **Plate scale only while the path fits a plate.** A run whose well pitch was read too small out of the coordinates spans far more than twelve cells, and at true scale everything past the first few wells falls outside the widget — the user sees a fragment with nothing saying there is more. Then the drawing is scaled to its own bounding box and centred instead, and `isFitted()` says so, because a picture where a square is no longer a well must not be read as one; the page swaps its caption to say the same and to point at the grid, since a pitch that wrong usually means the layout is wrong too. The microscope's actual travel, drawn at a plate's scale and normally directly under it. A plate map answers "which well?"; every field of view inside one well is the same cell there, so the route the stage took through them, and how far off-centre they sit, has nowhere else to appear. Takes points already in cell units (`datasets.ome_import.stage_layout.path_in_cells`) and a reference plate — `setPlate`, anything exposing `cellRect(row, col)` — and does no coordinate maths of its own beyond scaling cells to pixels. It borrows geometry rather than deriving it from its own width because a `WellPlateSelector` reserves room for its row and column headers before sizing cells, so equal widths do not give equal cells. Dots, line widths and the lattice are fractions of a cell, so the drawing scales with the plate instead of pinning sizes that only look right at one width; past `_DOT_BUDGET` positions the per-point dots are dropped and only the route is drawn, since a plate scan's thousands of points merge into a blob that hides the route they were decorating. The first position always keeps a dot, in `success` rather than `accent`: where the scan begins is the one thing on the drawing the user chose rather than read. Carries no All-Well knowledge, so it stays inside the `widgets/` no-app-coupling contract. |
| `PlateOrderEditor` (`widgets/plate_order_editor.py`) | A `WellPlateSelector` driven in its ordered `"path"` selection model, so it is the same painted control as every other plate in the app; this ~90-line subclass adds only what the shared widget has no opinion about. The path model itself — lit wells carrying their 1-based visit number, the alpha-blended arrow tracing the order across the plate, and the click that appends an off-path well or removes an on-path one and renumbers the rest — lives in `well_plate_selector`. A *dirty* flag distinguishes a hand-drawn order from a `set_preview` seed (which is ignored once dirty). Used by the Convert OME-TIFF page to define an arbitrary, possibly non-rectangular `well_order`. |
| `PlateProgress` (`widgets/plate_progress.py`) | The shared chrome behind every live run dashboard: a header (title/status/eta/collapse toggle), a headline label, one overall completion bar, and a 3-column body — a subclass-owned left "rail" slot, the plate map, and a legend. `RunDashboard` (Analyze), `ConcatDashboard`, `SubsetDashboard`, `MergePlatesDashboard`, `ValidateDashboard`, and `ImportLooseDashboard` each subclass it, building their own rail content and well-colour rules into the shared layout so none of them can visually drift apart. **The legend is drawn here, not just hosted here.** Every dashboard's legend is the same picture — a heading over one coloured dot per state, each with its label — so `PlateProgress._build_legend` renders it and the subclass supplies only the heading and the `(colour, label)` rows, through `_legend_items()`. Five subclasses had written those eighteen lines out separately, which is how a legend comes to describe a colour rule the plate beside it stopped using. `_legend_items` still raises `NotImplementedError` by default rather than returning no rows: a subclass that asks for a legend and forgets to say what is in it should fail at construction, not draw an empty column — one that wants no legend passes `show_legend=False` and is never asked. The two dashboards whose rows come from a state token (`ImportLooseDashboard`, `ValidateDashboard`) map them through their own `_state_color`, so the legend and the plate cannot disagree about what a state looks like, and `RunDashboard` builds its list at call time because a remote run gains an Upload row and renames the two after it. The plate map (`self._plate`, a `WellPlateSelector`) takes its size and placement from the shared `widgets/plate_geometry.apply_plate_geometry(plate, role="status")` — the one rule every plate map in the app goes through, so the status map here renders at exactly the cell scale of the Review rail's picker and of the Datasets tools' own pickers. `well_plate_selector._metrics()` derives cell size as `min(available_width / 12, available_height / 8)`, so a height-starved plate renders illegibly small even with hundreds of spare horizontal pixels — every Datasets tool page with a dashboard wraps its whole content in a `QScrollArea` (mirroring `analyze/tab.py`'s own form panel) for that reason: at the app's default launch size (`1640×980`, `allwell.py`), a plain `QVBoxLayout` crushes whatever's at the bottom of a long page instead of letting the user scroll to it. The plate is added with `center.addWidget(self._plate, 0, PLATE_ALIGNMENT)` and no layout stretch, so it sits centred in a centre column that is as wide as the page allows. `PlateProgress` also promotes the selector's per-well dial API onto the dashboard itself — `set_well_fraction(well, fraction)`, `set_well_progress(well, done, total)` and `clear_well_fractions()` — so a controller reports a well's progress without reaching through `self._plate`, which does not exist at all under `show_plate=False`; all three no-op in that case. The `done`/`total` arithmetic lives in the module-level `plate_progress.fraction_or_none`, which returns `None` for a non-positive `total` rather than dividing by it, since "not counted yet" must not render as a definite zero-filled dial — the same picture as a well that has genuinely done nothing. It is module-level because both kinds of dial host need it: `set_well_progress`, and a controller painting its page's *own* plate. **A no-op is the right base-class behaviour but it is not a progress report**, so a controller whose dashboard was built `show_plate=False` must drive the plate it does own instead of calling these and assuming something happened — `SubsetController` routes its worker's `wellFraction` signal to the picker plate's `setWellFraction` for exactly that reason (see the Subset rows in §11). Each host page's own outer layout ends in a trailing `outer.addStretch(1)` after its last real widget (and adds the dashboard itself with no stretch factor) for the same class of reason one level up: `QScrollArea.setWidgetResizable(True)` grows the page's content widget to fill the viewport, and with the raw log hidden by default nothing else in the column was willing to absorb that leftover height — the dashboard was, turning into a growing dead zone below the plate via its own internal `center.addStretch(1)`. The trailing stretch outranks every 0-stretch item above it, so slack collects as blank page background below everything instead. (Validate's page needs neither fix itself — its findings list is always visible with its own stretch factor, so it was already absorbing the slack correctly.) `PlateProgress.__init__` also takes `show_plate: bool = True` — a page whose input already has its own interactive plate map (Subset) passes `False` to skip the centre column entirely rather than leave a redundant second plate map, or worse, an empty-but-still-stretch-1 dead column between the rail and legend; see `SubsetDashboard` above. A second parameter, `show_legend: bool = True`, independently skips the legend column — `SubsetDashboard` passes `show_legend=False` alongside `show_plate=False`, since its counts rail already pairs a coloured dot with a state label per row, and a separate legend column would only repeat those same pairs without the live counts. Skipping either column when the centre plate column is also skipped no longer leaves a wide dead gap between whatever's left: with no widget left carrying a layout stretch factor, a trailing `body.addStretch(1)` collects the leftover width at the row's own right edge instead of Qt distributing it as blank padding around the remaining fixed-width items. The five dashboards on the Datasets-pane tools (`ConcatDashboard`, `ValidateDashboard`, `SubsetDashboard`, `ImportLooseDashboard`, `MergePlatesDashboard`) are each constructed **hidden** (`setVisible(False)`) by their host page, then revealed by that page's own `_update_status_preview` as soon as its inputs are valid enough to answer "what would this actually touch" — seeded with the real wells a run would touch (via `core.dataset_paths.preview_wells`, or the tool's own live preview — Import Loose's `scan_folder`, Subset's own picker selection, Merge Plates' remap-applied union of both sources) and a "Ready — N well(s)" headline, rather than gated on the tool's own run/check method actually starting; each page hides it again on the next input edit that invalidates the preview. This replaced an earlier convention, gating the same reveal on a run actually starting, that read as "something is wrong" — an idle, empty status strip before anything had happened looked like a stuck or broken state rather than "nothing has run yet" (and, for `ConcatDashboard` specifically, an even earlier construction-time-visible default that painted a coloured plate with *zero* wells enabled from the moment the page loaded). `RunDashboard` (Analyze) is the one dashboard that still stays visible from construction — Analyze's own form has no comparable "not yet valid" gate to key a reveal off. Every well-coloured dashboard also marks a well's *terminal* states with a glyph layer (`WellPlateSelector.setWellMarker`), not just its colour: colour alone doesn't distinguish success-green from a warning hue for a user who can't tell the two apart, so each terminal state carries its own glyph (`✓` for success, `!` for a problem, `✕` for an error, and Merge Plates' persistent `"2"` for "this well came from dataset 2"). **A well being worked on carries no glyph anywhere in the app** — it is drawn as a progress dial, and a glyph sits in the middle of exactly the area the dial fills, while the fill and the colour already say the well is working. That is one rule across every plate map, not a per-dashboard choice: the `⚙` a computing/merging/writing/copying well used to wear is gone from Analyze's run dashboard, Concatenate, Import Loose, Merge Plates and Subset alike. Merge Plates' `"2"` is the one glyph that survives on a well mid-dial, because it reports *origin* rather than progress and is the only thing telling the two datasets apart once both sides are coloured dots on a small plate. |
| `RunDashboard` | A thin `PlateProgress` subclass — the live, visual pipeline-run view shown above the Analyze log: a left stage rail (`group → upload → process → threshold → download`, the upload/download rungs only for remote runs) plus a centre plate map that colours each well by the stage it has reached. **Every well that has started is drawn as a dial rather than a solid disc** (`PlateProgress.set_well_fraction` → `WellPlateSelector.setWellFraction`): the well body itself is a two-tone pie of its own state colour — dark for the share completed, light for what is left, filled clockwise from twelve — so the hue still says which stage the well is in while the fill says how far through it is. Before that, a well on its first FOV-group and one on its last looked identical for however long the well took, which on a timelapse plate is most of the run. **The dial tracks whichever stage the well is actually inside**, decided by `_well_fraction`: a transfer in flight wins (bytes of its input zip sent while uploading, bytes of its output zip landed while downloading — a download outranks everything else, since a well being fetched has by definition already computed), then the FOV-group counts `set_well_fov` records from `well_fov` events, then the stages reached. A well sitting uploaded on the remote, waiting its turn, reads as a **full** dial: its archive is there in full, the dial has just spent the whole upload filling with the bytes sent, and what it waits for now is its turn rather than more transfer. Emptying it there — which is what "started but nothing finished" used to mean — reset the well from nearly-full to empty at the exact instant its upload completed, so the transfer appeared to undo itself. A full dial therefore means *uploaded* or *computed* depending on the well's colour, which is the accepted cost of a dial that never runs backwards. A well that is genuinely computing with no group measured yet is the empty dial, and that zero is true. A well with nothing started (grouped at most) and an errored well have no dial at all, since a part-filled ring beside the `✕` would suggest it is still going. Per-well transfer fractions arrive as `well_xfer` events (see `pipeline_runner` in §7) and are held in `_xfer` only while the transfer is live: a fraction of 1.0 *ends* the transfer rather than pinning the dial full, because a well is marked `upload` as rsync starts sending it. `setWellFraction` is opt-in, and only a surface that is *reporting a run* sets it — this dashboard, the four Datasets tool pages that copy per-well data, and nothing else — so Review's rail, the heat-map drag source and the replicate pickers are untouched. A computing well carries **no glyph** — the `⚙` it used to wear sat in the middle of exactly the area the dial now fills, and the fill plus the colour already say it is working; only `✕` for an error survives as a marker. There is no rail of per-well progress bars beneath the plate: the dial carries that information where the eye already is, and the exact counts (`FOV 7/12`, `downloading 42%`) live in the well's hover tooltip. |

The dial covers **transfers as well as compute**: a well filling with the bytes of its own archive while it uploads or downloads, and with FOV-groups while it computes, so the stages that dominate a remote run's wall-clock are the ones the plate describes best. Plate-wide transfer progress is separate and lives on the status line, fed by `remote_xfer` (below). An uploaded-but-not-started well has its own colour on a remote run (`accent2`): it used to share `warn` with a computing well, so a plate mid-run was one block of amber that said nothing about which wells were actually being worked on — and once a computing well gained a dial, the two differed in *shape* while their colour still claimed they were the same state. `accent2` is a neighbour of the `accent` used for "computed, awaiting fetch"; both mean "it is over there", so the pair reads as one family. The legend gains a matching **uploaded** row, on remote runs only.

**The headline is derived from the phase the run is in, never pushed at it.**
`AnalyzeProgressMixin` holds one phase per run — prepare, group, grouped,
upload, queued, launch, process, finalize — and `_phase_headline` renders the
sentence for whichever one is current; `_render_headline` writes it only when it
differs from what the label already says, comparing against
`PlateProgress.headline_text()` rather than against a remembered copy, so the
comparison stays honest when the tab has written a terminal state since. Events
move the run between phases: the grouping events open and close `group`, a
coarse `("stage", name)` event maps through `_STAGE_PHASES`, a `sched` event
means `queued` (or `launch` once the allocation is granted), and any compute
event means `process` — or `finalize`, once every announced well is in, since
the auto-threshold pass, the download drain and the remote cleanup all run after
the last well. `("stage", "download")` deliberately maps to nothing: the fetcher
pulls a finished well's output while later wells are still computing, so
honouring it flips the headline between two phases for the length of a plate.
The phases that count wells read their numerator and denominator from the same
place the rail does (`RunDashboard.stage_progress`), so the two cannot name
different figures for one stage — which matters because the rail lives in the
collapsible body and the headline does not. **A run's terminal state outranks
the phase machine**: `_render_headline` writes nothing once the dashboard
carries an outcome (`PlateProgress.outcome()`, set by the failed/cancelled
setters) or once `_end_run_phase` has latched the end of a successful run — a
remote run keeps talking after it dies, since `verify_and_cleanup` fetches what
it can and logs it, and a phase sentence written over the reason a run failed
would replace the one thing the user needs. The success headline needs the latch
because the tab writes it as plain text rather than through `set_done`: a run
that finished short of the wells it announced says so there, and painting that
green would be the shortfall dressed as a clean plate. Before this, each phase that had
something to say wrote the headline itself and the phases that had nothing to
say wrote nothing, so a remote run's staging step, upload and queue wait all
inherited the grouping phase's last sentence: the reported symptom was a plate
sitting in a SLURM queue under the words "Grouped — pipeline (segmentation +
zipping)…", describing a step that had finished and naming the one thing that
was not happening.

**The status line belongs to whatever phase is current.** `remote_xfer` events carry the plate-wide rsync fraction; `AnalyzeTab` hands them to `RunDashboard.set_transfer(pct)`, and the first compute-phase event (`well_total` / `well_done` / `well_fov`, in `AnalyzeProgressMixin._COMPUTE_PHASE_EVENTS`) hands it `None`. The dashboard holds the fraction as state and formats the label itself. Two different objects drive this dashboard — `analyze.tab` for the runner's own events, `analyze.progress` for the pipeline's — and the label used to be a string one of them pushed and neither retracted, so it sat on the last transfer tick (`Transferring… 92%`) for the whole compute phase, until the end of the run cleared it. Clearing is keyed off the pipeline's own progress rather than off rsync reporting exactly 100%, which it need not do: the final tick before rsync exits can be any value, and in batched mode it is scaled per batch.

**Transfer progress is live state, so it stays out of the log.** A remote
transfer used to write a line every eight seconds (bytes so far, time elapsed)
plus rsync's own percentage stream once a second. A log records what *happened*,
and "still transferring" is a sample of a continuous variable; one line per
sample also evicted the record it was crowding, since the log holds 10 000
blocks and `analyze.tab._log_line`'s scroll-compensation comment already blamed
this stream for making that trimming common. Those lines now carry
`remote_runner.TRANSIENT_PREFIX`; `ProgressTracker.parse` turns them into a
single `("status", …)` event and nothing else, and `AnalyzeTab._poll_log` skips
`_log_line` for them — so they repaint the dashboard's status line beside the
transfer bar and never reach the log. The prefix is applied at the source rather
than sniffed downstream: the per-file `[remote] ↑ <well>.zip` names look similar
and are real events (they drive the Upload rail), so telling them apart by shape
would be fragile. It lives in `remote_runner` with the only code that emits it,
because `pipeline_runner` already imports that module and the reverse is a
cycle. `Fetcher._transfer_heartbeat` runs two cadences out of one loop: the live
sample every `interval`, and a durable breadcrumb every `_BREADCRUMB_INTERVAL_S`
(60s) that *does* go to the log — a status line cannot answer "was it stuck at
3am?" the next morning, and one line a minute is a record rather than a flood.

**A well turns green only when both halves of its output have landed and the
zip is in the output folder** — the `{well}_out.zip` and its per-well CSV(s) are
two separate rsyncs, and `ProgressTracker._mark_fetch_part` fires the `download`
stage on the transition where both are present. The in-stream fetcher holds its
`N CSV file(s)` line back until `Fetcher._materialize` has put the zip in place,
so the second half is never reported while the output still sits in the transit
directory; a materialise that fails logs a `WARN local materialize failed` line
instead, which the tracker does not read, and the well stays "computed, awaiting
fetch" for the end-of-run retry. `_materialize` itself is a rename
(`os.replace`) out of the transit directory beside the output folder, falling
back to a staged copy only on a cross-device (`EXDEV`) rename — copying there
wrote every byte of each well a second time onto the output volume, which on a
network share held the fetcher for minutes after the well had been painted
fetched. Two paths bypass that handshake, and both must announce
themselves or the well stays painted "computed, awaiting fetch" with its data
already on disk: a well the remote skipped as already current
(`[remote] ✓ W: up to date`), and one rescued by the end-of-run backstop. The
backstop reports in the **same two lines** the in-stream fetch uses, tagged
`(end-of-run retry)` — `RemoteRunner._retry_missing_wells` emits both halves for
every well it finishes with, including a half it did not have to re-pull,
because by the time it runs the well has usually registered *neither*: the
in-stream fetcher returns early when the zip pull fails, before it reaches the
CSVs. Reusing the fetch vocabulary rather than inventing a form of its own means
a rescued well reaches green by the same route, with nothing extra for the
tracker to learn. The drain's own chatter (`draining fetcher: N well(s)`,
`fetcher still working… (5/8 wells fetched) — B03: placing the output in …, 2m 10s
so far`) deliberately marks nothing: the heartbeat names the well and the step
the worker is on (`Fetcher._activity`, set at each step of `_fetch_one`) so a
slow post-download step is not reported as "still downloading", but the well id
follows the word `fetcher` rather than the `↓ ` the per-well patterns anchor on.

**Per-well transfer progress** rides the same marker. `WELL_XFER_PREFIX` is
`TRANSIENT_PREFIX` plus `xfer `, so the "never write this to the log" rule
covers it without a second place to remember, and `ProgressTracker.parse`
claims the longer marker first — turning `[remote] ⋯ xfer down C02 0.4180`
into a `("well_xfer", (well, direction, fraction))` event that
`AnalyzeTab._apply_progress_event` routes to `RunDashboard.set_well_transfer`
and thence to the well's dial. A line carrying the marker that does not parse
yields no event at all rather than falling through to the status line, where it
would appear to the user as prose.

The two directions derive their fraction differently, because the two rsyncs
expose different things. **Downloading**, `Fetcher._transfer_heartbeat` already
had the numerator — it sums the growing rsync partial file(s) in the
destination directory — and the denominator comes from
`Fetcher._remote_file_size`, one small `bash -s` over ssh per well that asks the
remote for the size of `<well>_out.zip` (GNU `stat`, BSD `stat`, then `ls -ln`,
so it works on a Linux cluster or a macOS host without knowing which). It is
piped over stdin rather than passed as an argument for the same reason every
other remote script here is: a `~` in the staging path only expands unquoted.
When the size cannot be read the heartbeat still reports bytes-so-far on the
status line and emits **no fraction** — an unknown denominator must not become
an invented percentage. **Uploading**, `--info=progress2` reports bytes for the
whole rsync rather than per file, so a percentage alone says nothing about any
one well; `_UploadWellProgress` pairs it with `--info=name1`, which prints each
filename as its transfer begins. The cumulative total at that moment is the
well's zero point, the local archive's own `st_size` (`_well_zip_sizes`) is its
denominator, and everything until the next filename belongs to it. Files rsync
skips emit no name line and contribute no bytes, so they never open a window at
all — which is correct, since nothing about them is in flight.

The **Upload rail** counts wells off `[remote] ↑ …<well>.zip` lines, which used to come only from rsync's own per-file output. That is a poor thing to depend on: rsync says nothing on a cache hit (it moves nothing), nothing for files an incremental re-send skips, and nothing at all when the local rsync predates `--info=name1` — macOS still ships 2.6.9. In each case the transfer had succeeded and the rail sat at 0/N, reading as a stalled upload. Batched mode was worst, since `upload_subset` had no compensator at all where `ensure_uploaded` at least synthesised lines on a cache hit. `_log_wells_uploaded` now emits one line per archive from both paths' success branch, where the caller knows which archives it asked for and that rsync returned 0; the dashboard de-dupes into sets, so it costs nothing alongside live per-file lines, and a non-zero rc emits nothing rather than drawing a rail ahead of the data. Driven entirely by `pipeline_runner.ProgressTracker` events; tracks each stage as an independent well-set (so a server-side `threshold` can't make `download` read N/N before anything is fetched) and goes blue=computed-on-server vs green=downloaded-locally on remote runs. The raw colour log stays underneath, collapsible. |
| `NamedPageStack` (in `core/centre_view.py`, not `widgets/` — but morally a widget) | A `QStackedWidget` keyed by page name; supports `detachPage`/`reattachPage` (Split View). |
| `RailNav` | The left-rail section navigator. |
| `info_icon` (`widgets/info_icon.py`) | The `ⓘ` hover-for-more marker, styled by the `#InfoHint` QSS rule. A function rather than a class — it returns a configured `QLabel`. Shared by the Analyze form (`AnalyzeFormChromeMixin._info_icon` delegates to it) and the Playground's threshold rows, so the app has one "there is an explanation here" affordance rather than a copy per pane. Sets WhatsThis as well as the tooltip, which is the route that works for someone who cannot hold a hover. |
| `SchemaPicker` (`widgets/schema_picker.py`) | The filename-schema builder: a separator box, one dropdown per filename position, and the colon-delimited schema string the two of them write. The dropdowns and the string are two views of one value and sync both ways, each write blocking the other's signals so they cannot chase each other. Vocabulary and validity come from `util.schema` — the module the pipeline parses schemas with — so the picker offers exactly the fields the pipeline understands, reads a string the way `parse_schema` reads it (empty tokens collapse, rather than the dropdowns showing a layout the run will not use), and reports errors in `validate_schema`'s own wording. `schema()` returns the typed string in preference to the dropdowns, since the string can express more positions than there are dropdowns. `row_factory(parent, label) -> cell` is the layout seam: the Analyze form passes its own `_row` so the picker sits inside that form's label column, and the Datasets pane's Zip Loose Folder page takes the default plain row. Mounted by both, because both ask the user about the same filenames — Zip Loose Folder produces the archives Analyze then reads. **Detection is opt-in**: passing `detect_label` builds a *Detect from filenames* button and the two-register readout beneath it, and a host that will not answer `detectRequested` therefore never shows a button that does nothing. `setDetection(text, note=…, problem=…)` takes sentences the picker neither composes nor understands; the neutral half is muted body text and the note is a `QLabel#Notice` panel, so a result the reader must not skim past differs in outline and not only in hue. |
| `SegmentedControl`, `ChipGroup`, `Stepper`, `StyledSlider`, `ToggleSwitch` | Form controls; each exposes `bindingAdapter()` returning `(getter, setter, change_signal)` for the Export Style sidebar's binding loop. |
| `SavedSelectionsList` | The rich saved-selection list with composition (drag-to-reorder, per-group flat well editing, recolour popovers). A group is one condition — its wells are its implicit replicate set, so there are no replicate sub-partitions / solo strips. An expanded row draws its wells as disabled `ChipGroup` chips, and a row with **no** wells draws a named `(no wells)` placeholder instead — an empty strip and a strip that failed to build otherwise look identical. Nothing wraps the chip build, deliberately: `widgets/chip_group` ships in every profile and every frozen bundle (`all_well.spec` filters by excluded *feature* directory, never by widget), so a catch there could only ever swallow a real fault and render a comma list that reads as a deliberate compact style. Where the row does fall back — a caller's `plate_factory` raising, which leaves the compose popover on a full-grid plate rather than the caller's narrowed one — it logs at WARNING with the exception, because that substitution changes which wells the chooser offers. |
| `LutSelector`, `GradientStrip` | The colour-map picker and its preview strip. |
| `ColorSwatchRow`, `ColorPickerPopover` | The colour picker, in two layers. `ColorSwatchRow` is the constrained one — a row of curated swatches, then the recents, then a conic-gradient **Custom** tile; the Cell Browser's per-channel tint, the Review Image colour and the saved-selection recolour all open it from a button and take its `colorPicked`. The Custom tile lazily builds a `ColorPickerPopover` (an SV square, a hue strip, hex and alpha fields, and its own recents row) and anchors it at the tile. **The two signals mean different things and must not be collapsed.** `colorPicked` is live: it fires on every drag and every field edit, and a caller uses it to preview. `colorCommitted` fires once, when the choice is finished — Return in the hex field, clicking a recent, or dismissing the popover with the colour changed — and it is what writes a recent. A picker that committed on every drag would fill the recents with the colours the cursor crossed on the way. Committing is keyed on a baseline (`_committed`) that `setColor` moves, so opening the popover on a colour is not itself a choice; the corollary is that a handler which commits must not route through `setColor` first, or it resets the baseline and compares the colour against itself. The selection ring is drawn *outside* the swatch, in the margin `sizeHint` reserves for it, so it surrounds the colour rather than eating two pixels of it on each side. |
| `lut_cmaps.lut_cmap` | Qt-free resolver that maps a LUT name to a matplotlib colormap: single-hue names (Reds/Greens/Blues/Purples/Oranges) become a **black→colour** `LinearSegmentedColormap` (so a dark background reads as "off"), Greys stays black→white, everything else is the builtin (`_r`-aware). Routed through `ui_helpers.make_fluor_thumb` / `lut_colormap_to_rgb` and `LutSelector._cmap_stops`, so thumbnails, the Image Table compose/composite/export paths, Playground, and the picker strip all flip together. |
| `ContextBanner` (`widgets/context_banner.py`) | A strip of glyph + sentence + confirm + cancel saying a page is being used for something other than its own job — the Job Queue borrows a tool's page to set up or correct a queued job (§6b). Host-agnostic: it knows nothing about queues or jobs, and whoever shows it decides what confirming means. Deliberately not a dialog and it does not block the page beneath, since the point is that the user is editing that page. It is one `QHBoxLayout`, which is why it suits a *page* and not a rail: the Analyze pane's two folder banners (§6.5) answer the same brief in the 329-px sidebar and stack their text above their own action row instead. `EmptyState` is *not* a substitute for a one-line caption in the same situations — it is `Expanding/Expanding`, so a single sentence in one renders as a page-height bordered box. |
| `removable_row` (`widgets/removable_row.py`) | **A list row whose remove button appears while the pointer is over it.** Built for the recent-datasets list, which two surfaces draw — Home's card and the no-dataset placeholder — and which wants the row itself to be the target with a small × on its right edge. Two decisions carry the widget. The ×'s **space is reserved in both states**: a control that appears by widening the row shifts the label at the instant the pointer arrives, so the button lives inside a fixed-width slot and only the button inside it is hidden. And **hover is counted, not sampled** — moving from the row onto the × is a Leave on one and an Enter on the other, so a handler hiding on any Leave removes the button exactly as the user reaches for it; Enter and Leave are counted across the row and every child, and the count is order-independent because Qt does not promise Enter-before-Leave across a parent/child crossing. `row_entry` and `row_remove_button` are named accessors, because a caller holding "the row at index 2" cannot otherwise tell a wrapped row from the bare widget an unremovable one returns, and a lookup spelled five ways is five places to fix. |
| `Popover`, `Drawer`, `Toast`, `EmptyState` | Generic overlay primitives. `Drawer` slides in from `edge="right"` (default — the Help drawer) or `edge="bottom"` (a full-width panel sized by `height_hint`/`height_fraction` — the Application Log drawer, whose long lines the narrow right panel clipped). |
| `FlowLayout` | A `QLayout` (not a widget) that reflows its children onto multiple lines instead of clipping — the standard Qt Flow Layout adapted to PySide6. Control rows that carry more widgets than fit at a narrow width (the plotting / image-review "TabCtrl" rows) use it so **Split View** halving the pane grows the row taller rather than hiding controls off the right edge. Four rules go with it. (1) A flow row skips hidden widgets when it places items, so *which* widgets are visible is an input to the layout, not merely a blanked slot — `_FlowItemVisibility` watches show/hide on every managed widget and invalidates the layout, without which a row that swaps one option group for another (the Multivariate tab's per-mode row) keeps the positions computed for the previous visible set and paints the newly-shown group on top of them. That watcher resolves the layout from its own `parent()` and keeps **no** per-instance state: its C++ object belongs to the layout, so it outlives the Python instance `__init__` ran on, and PySide builds a fresh wrapper for it once that instance is collected. Anything stashed on `self` is gone by then — a watcher that remembered its layout in an attribute raised `AttributeError` inside the Qt event loop on every subsequent show and hide, and the row stopped reflowing. (2) A label and the control it names must go in as one `flow_group` item, or the row can wrap between them. (3) A host whose row may wrap needs `sync_flow_height`, since a stacked page sizes the row from its one-line minimum and clips the second line otherwise. (4) Spacing is fixed — 14px horizontal, `theme.Spacing.xs` vertical — **not** derived from the platform style, and no call site overrides it. Deriving it asks `pixelMetric(PM_Layout*Spacing)`, which Qt documents as returning -1 on styles that implement the size-class-aware `layoutSpacing()` instead. Measured, the two styles are exact opposites: QMacStyle reports `pixelMetric = -1, layoutSpacing = 14`, Fusion reports `pixelMetric = 6, layoutSpacing = -1`. The layout clamps with `max(0, …)`, so on macOS every row that relied on the derived value packed its controls edge to edge, while CI (on Fusion) saw 6 and looked fine. The 14 is QMacStyle's own button-row spacing, adopted app-wide because it is the one number measured against a real control row — it is deliberately off the `theme.Spacing` scale. Passing `-1` still derives, but now asks both APIs and falls back to the defaults rather than to nothing. |
| `MplToolbar` | The slim toolbar shown under every matplotlib figure (home / pan / zoom / save + coords readout). |
| `WrapCheckBox` | A checkbox whose label word-wraps, for the Analyze form's long-labelled options. A plain `QCheckBox` reports its full text width as its minimum, which pins the whole scroll-area sidebar that wide; this composites a text-less indicator with a wrapped `QLabel`. Because the label wraps, the composite's height depends on its width — and a `QWidget` inherits neither its child's `heightForWidth` nor a size policy advertising one, so it implements both. Without them a parent column sizes the row from a single line and a label that wraps to two spills over whatever sits below it. The indicator↔label gap is the app-wide checkbox `spacing` token (`theme.Spacing.sm`), not a hand-picked constant — the composite draws its own label, so a smaller gap read tighter to the box than every native checkbox beside it, and with no Fusion pin the app renders under the platform style (native QMacStyle on macOS, Fusion only on CI), where that shortfall put the first word on top of the indicator. Same lesson as `FlowLayout`'s spacing rule: a control gap comes from the token scale, never from an off-scale constant or the platform style. |
| `BrandTile`, `IconButton`, `StatusDot`, `KbdHint`, `SelectionChip` | Misc small bits. |

If you find yourself building something that isn't All-Well-specific, write
it as a new `widgets/<x>.py` module. Each widget gets a `__main__` block
that opens a small demo window so you can iterate visually with
`python widgets/foo.py`.

---

## 8. Theming

`ui/theme.py` is the whole theme surface. It holds the Python-side design
tokens — `Colors`, `Typography`, `Spacing`, `Radii`, `Metrics` (control padding,
themeable for density) — plus the `qss()` builder that produces the full
application stylesheet, and the **theme registry** (`THEMES` / `apply_theme` /
`select_theme_from_env`, see "Selecting a theme" below). The `widgets/` package
and most of the app shell read `theme.Colors.*`; the `blue` palette is the class
values written in the module, and is the baseline every theme is applied onto and
restored to — the app itself starts on `grey`.

There is no stylesheet driver, no theme-manager class and no per-theme `.qss`
file: `theme.qss()` is the one stylesheet builder, and it lives beside the tokens
it reads.

At the bottom of the module, in a block marked as such, sit the last two named
colours with no `Colors` home of their own — `CLR_DANGER` and
`CLR_SUCCESS_DARK`, read through `ui.theme.get_color(name)` by batch-export's
progress label. `CLR_DANGER` tracks `Colors.danger`; `CLR_SUCCESS_DARK` is its
own value, because its hex does not match `Colors.success` closely enough for the
swap to be safe. That is the only reason the pair still exists — everything else
the accessor used to carry (surfaces, borders, text, accent, warn, the well
palette, the Publication-mode plot palette) has migrated to `Colors` / `CPub` /
`WELL_COLORS_TUPLE` directly. Give those two an exact `Colors` home and the whole
block goes. New colours never go there.

**Every interactive class the app disables needs a `:disabled` rule, and the
base rule's `color` is why.** A stylesheet colour declared with no disabled
variant is applied in *every* state — it overrides the palette's disabled
group, so `setEnabled(False)` takes effect functionally (the popup will not
open, the click does nothing) with no change on screen at all. `QComboBox` was
the one input class missing the rule, so the Spatial tab's Timepoint picker,
greyed at Summary level by `tp_cb.setEnabled(not is_summary)`, rendered
pixel-identical to a live one; the same omission silenced the Metric picker
beside it and every other disabled combo in the app. It also reached the custom
painter: `LabeledComboBox.paintEvent` takes its pen from
`palette().color(foregroundRole())`, which the stylesheet had forced to the
enabled colour. A widget may answer this itself instead — `StyledSlider.paintEvent`
branches on `isEnabled()` — but then it owes the same visible difference.
`tests/test_disabled_controls_look_disabled.py` asserts it on **rendered
pixels** rather than on the QSS text or on `isEnabled()`: `isEnabled()` was
already `False` throughout and proved nothing, and a text check would pass the
day the rule is spelled differently. `QTextEdit` / `QPlainTextEdit` share the
`QLineEdit` base rule but not its `:disabled` variant; nothing disables either
today (every `…_edit` the app greys is a `QLineEdit`), so that gap is recorded
rather than filled with a rule describing nothing.

**A disabled control should also say what would re-enable it.** Greying tells
the user the control is inert; it does not distinguish "wrong mode for this"
from "broken". The Spatial band does this with a swapped tooltip on both of its
gated pickers — the Metric picker names the vizzes that ignore it, and the
Timepoint picker states that Summary walks every timepoint because they are the
columns of the matrix it draws.

**An object name is not a style.** A widget given `setObjectName(…)` and no
matching rule in `qss()` paints exactly like a bare `QWidget`: no fill, no
edge, no separation from what surrounds it. The Analyze pane's two folder
banners (§6.1, §6.5) each carried an object name for months with no rule behind
either, so an offer to resume yesterday's run read as the first paragraph of the
Analyze form. Both are styled here now — `#ResumeBanner` bordered in `accent`
because it carries an action the user can take right now, `#PreflightBanner` in
`border` because it states what is already true, a shared `panel` fill so they
read as one family of report — and both call sites set `Qt.WA_StyledBackground`,
without which a plain `QWidget` subclass ignores its own background rule
entirely. `tests/test_analyze_banners_are_readable.py` holds both halves.

Their fill is `panel` rather than `ContextBanner`'s `accent_dim`, and the reason
is a measurement rather than a preference. `ContextBanner` carries one sentence
at `text_primary`, which reads 9.07:1 on `accent_dim`. These two carry a ramp of
four — kicker, identity, prose, tally — and on `accent_dim` the quietest tier
measures 2.04:1 in the `blue` theme and 3.16:1 in `grey`, so the tier whose
whole job is to be unobtrusive becomes the tier that cannot be read at all. On
`panel` the same tiers measure 14.38 / 6.79 / 3.23 (blue) and 12.65 / 7.93 /
4.48 (grey). The tally itself takes `text_secondary` rather than `text_muted`
and is ranked below the prose by size instead: it is the one line in the strip
carrying numbers the user is meant to read, which is a different job from a hint
restating a control's own label.

**`accent` and `accent2` mean two different things, and every caller has to
pick the right one.** `Colors.accent` is used across several Datasets
dashboards to flag an anomalous well — one whose state doesn't fit the normal
run (Concatenate's "merged with no matching measurements CSV on one side",
Subset's "no rows matched the filter"). `Colors.accent2` is a second, distinct
hue for the unrelated case of "this belongs to the other of two normal
groups" — currently only Merge Plates' dataset-2 wells — and must never be
reused to mean an anomaly, or a well merely belonging to the other source
would read as suspect on the same plate map. Both are `theme.Colors` tokens
like any other; there's nothing structurally different about `accent2`, only
this convention about what each is allowed to mean.

### Selecting a theme

A **theme** is a bundle of token overrides applied onto the token classes
(`Colors` / `Metrics` / `Radii`) *before the UI is built*. Because `qss()` reads
those classes at call time and every `widgets/*` builder reads `theme.Colors.*`
at construction, applying a theme up-front re-skins the whole app with **no
per-widget rewiring**.

- `theme.THEMES` maps a name → sparse override bundle. Built-ins:
  `grey` (**the default the app starts on** — a colour-only variant: neutral
  charcoal-grey chrome, restrained azure accent, near-black plot canvas, its
  look designed against real Nikon NIS-Elements AR screenshots) and `blue`
  (the **baseline**: an empty bundle, because the class values *are* its
  palette). The version pill reads the `Colors.brand` / `Colors.brand_fg`
  tokens and is transparent with white text in both. Both share the flat, tight
  control feel: the `Radii`/`Metrics` defaults (small radii + crisp
  `control_border` + compact padding) are app-wide, so the `grey` bundle
  overrides only `Colors`.

  **`blue` earns its entry by being the way back.** `apply_theme` restores every
  themeable attribute to the value captured off the class at import and then
  applies the named bundle, so applying `blue` *is* the reset. A registry
  without it cannot return to the palette the classes hold. Both keys are
  therefore spelled as string literals rather than as `DEFAULT_THEME`: written
  `{DEFAULT_THEME: {}, "grey": _GREY}`, pointing that constant at `grey` writes
  the same key twice in one dict literal, the second wins silently, and the
  registry loses `blue` altogether. `tests/test_theme_registry.py` holds both
  halves of that.
- `theme.apply_theme(name)` resets every themeable attribute to its captured
  default, applies the bundle, and fires post-apply hooks
  (`register_theme_hook`). `select_theme_from_env()` reads the **`ALLWELL_THEME`**
  env var (falling back to `DEFAULT_THEME` — `grey` — on unset/unknown).
  `allwell.main()`
  calls it once, before building `AllWellApp`; `--theme <name>` overrides the env
  var. `tests/visual/render_views.py` honours it too, so
  `ALLWELL_THEME=grey … render_views.py` audits any theme.
- **Build-time default (soft).** `ALLWELL_THEME=<name> scripts/build_executable.sh`
  bakes `allwell_theme.txt` at the frozen bundle root (mirroring the profile
  marker); `all_well_launcher._apply_baked_theme` reads it and `setdefault`s the
  env var, so the shipped exe starts on that theme while a runtime `ALLWELL_THEME`
  / `--theme` still overrides. The `.spec` validates the name against
  `theme.available_themes()` and skips baking an unknown one (the build then
  starts on `DEFAULT_THEME` like any other).
- **Startup-only, by design.** There is no in-app live switch — a runtime swap
  would need every cached inline QSS rebuilt on `QEvent.StyleChange` (see the
  per-instance-QSS note below), which hit a ~20 s repaint cascade. Selection is
  a dev-facing env var / flag.
- `WELL_COLORS_TUPLE` (categorical data identity) and `CPub` (white-bg
  publication export) are deliberately **theme-independent**.
- `ui/theme.py` registers `refresh_legacy_palette` as a theme hook, so its
  `get_color()` palette (`CLR_DANGER`/`CLR_SUCCESS_DARK` only, batch-export's
  progress label) re-derives from the freshly-applied `Colors`.

When you add a colour or size: add it to `theme.Colors` / `theme.CPub` (for a
publication-mode plot colour) / `theme.Spacing` / `theme.Metrics` / etc. To
let a theme override it, add the attribute to the relevant bundle in
`THEMES`. **Do not** hardcode hex / px values inline, and never add an entry to
the legacy-accessor block at the bottom of `ui/theme.py` — those two tokens are
a remnant (see above), not a place to route new colours.

### Section headers

`core/ui_helpers.build_section_header(parent, title, *, hint=..., buttons=...)`
builds the labelled block that heads a divided section — the Cell Gating and
Statistics tabs are its main users. It stacks two rows: the title (styled by the
single `QLabel[role="section"]` theme rule) with any action buttons at its right
edge, and, beneath it, an optional muted hint sentence spanning the block's full
width.

The hint goes below the title rather than beside it because a `QHBoxLayout`
cannot give both the width each wants. It hands the non-stretchy item exactly
its preferred width and dumps the remainder on the stretchy one, so one of the
two ends up in a narrow column while the other keeps hundreds of pixels of empty
space beside it.

The title's own sizing is the subtle half, and both directions of it are pinned
by `tests/test_section_header_layout.py`:

* The title is **word-wrapped**, so its *minimum* width is its longest single
  word. Without that, a long title reports its full one-line width as the
  header's minimum, which forces a narrow rail wider than its peers and clips
  the action buttons sitting beside it.
* Word-wrapping also changes what a `QLabel` reports as its *preferred* width:
  no longer the one-line width, but the roughly square block Qt lays the string
  into. `SectionTitleLabel` overrides `sizeHint()` to report the single-line
  width while inheriting the longest-word `minimumSizeHint()`, so a title takes
  one line for as long as the row can hold one and wraps only when it genuinely
  cannot.

### Dividers

Every hairline in the app — the rule under the topbar, the rules between
Analyze's form sections, the vertical rules inside the run dashboard — is a
`QFrame` carrying one of four opt-in names, all matched by a single rule in
`theme.qss()`: `#Separator` (what `build_hline_separator` /
`build_vline_separator` apply), `#HRule` / `#VRule` (the equivalent hand-rolled
spellings — `widgets/plate_progress.py`'s vertical rules, the Batch Export
divider that picks its orientation at run time, and
`datasets/core/log_panel.hrule`), and the
`hline`/`vline` dynamic properties. They all paint `Colors.border_subtle` with
`border: none`, and `#HRule` / `#VRule` are pinned to one pixel in the QSS so a
caller need not also call `setFixedHeight(1)`. `widgets/mpl_toolbar.py` carries
a fifth, `#MplToolbarSep`, because that widget styles itself with a
per-instance stylesheet rather than reading the application QSS — it restates
the same fill and `border: none` there.

The `border: none` is the load-bearing part. A `QFrame` whose shape is
`HLine`/`VLine` otherwise paints Qt's default etched line, which is derived
from the widget palette rather than the theme. Measured against the default
theme:

```
    HLine + #Separator, pinned to 1 px   1 px tall, ink #1b2331 (border_subtle)
    HLine + #HRule                       1 px tall, ink #1b2331
    HLine, unnamed, pinned to 1 px       1 px tall, ink #e6e9ef
    HLine, unnamed, unpinned             3 px tall: #e6e9ef between two rows of background
```

So the ink is the wrong colour in every unnamed case — a pale `#e6e9ef` line
where the theme wants `border_subtle` — and a frame nobody pinned also reserves
three pixels of height for it. Several of the sites this rule displaced already
called `setFixedHeight(1)`, so for those only the colour was wrong.

**Build one with `ui_helpers.build_hline_separator(parent)` or
`build_vline_separator(parent)`** rather than by hand; both name the frame,
set its shape, and pin it to `theme.Metrics.hairline`. `build_hline_separator`
takes a `thickness` keyword for the one divider that is deliberately heavier
(the Image Table's shelf rule, at 2 px). `datasets/core/log_panel.hrule` is
the Datasets-side twin, one helper for the tool pages that build the same
log header. `tests/test_divider_naming.py` fails on any
`setFrameShape(QFrame.HLine|VLine)` whose frame is never given a sanctioned
name.

One divider chooses its orientation at run time: Batch Export's output panel
folds from side-by-side to stacked as the viewport narrows, and its rule turns
with it. It therefore cannot take a fixed name — `#HRule` pins `max-height`
and `#VRule` pins `max-width`, so either name applied to the other orientation
draws a hairline stretched along the wrong axis. `base_panel._apply_split_sep_orientation`
sets the shape and the name together and repolishes, because Qt's stylesheet
cache only re-evaluates a selector on an explicit `unpolish`/`polish` pair —
the same reason `widgets/_support.set_variant` exists for dynamic properties.

The sidebar│centre divider is the `QSplitter` handle, styled by
`QSplitter::handle` (also `border_subtle`, 6 px). Leave the width to the
stylesheet — a `setHandleWidth` call on an individual splitter makes that one
divider a different weight from the rest.

The publication-export plot surface uses `theme.CPub` and feeds the
target figure's axes (`figure.facecolor`, `axes.facecolor`, etc.) when
a `PlotCard` flips into Publication mode. Styling is per-figure (not a global
`matplotlib.rcParams.update`), so toggling one PlotCard doesn't change the
rcParams seen by later figures.

**Widgets with per-instance QSS.** Many widgets in `widgets/` set their
own stylesheet at construction (`self.setStyleSheet(self._build_qss())`
or `self.setStyleSheet(self._qss())`) — that's load-bearing for
per-widget object-name scoping, but it freezes the colour tokens at
construction time. This is why theme selection is **startup-only**: the theme
is applied before these widgets build, so they read the themed `theme.Colors.*`
at construction. A *runtime* switch would additionally need every such widget to
rebuild its inline QSS when Qt fires `QEvent.StyleChange`.

`widgets/_support.install_qss_refresh(widget, qss_factory)` is the opt-in helper
for that future: it installs a single event filter that catches `StyleChange`
and calls `widget.setStyleSheet(qss_factory())` (idempotent). It is currently
**defined but unused** — PlotCard deliberately reverted it (`plot_card.py`) after
the event filter's own `setStyleSheet` re-fired `StyleChange` recursively and
caused a ~20 s load stall. Any future live-switch work must adopt it (with the
equality guard) across the ~20 widgets that freeze inline QSS.

`widgets/_support.set_variant(widget, variant)` is the smaller, everyday
sibling of the same repolish problem: it changes a `QPushButton`'s
`variant` dynamic property at runtime and forces `style().unpolish()` +
`style().polish()`, so a `QPushButton[variant=...]` QSS selector picks up the
new value immediately. `setProperty("variant", ...)` alone does nothing
visible — Qt's stylesheet cache only re-evaluates property selectors on an
explicit repolish. It generalises the precedent
`review.core.plot_toggles.refresh_fov_btn_state` set (a checked-state
button variant flipping live the same way) so call sites don't each
reimplement the unpolish/polish pair by hand; every Datasets tool page uses it
to swap its Run/Open buttons between `primary`/`secondary` once a run
succeeds (§6b).

---

## 9. Key data flows

### 9.1 Opening a dataset

**Per-dataset state is reset by the slice that owns it.** `PlotState`,
`ExportPrefsState` and `ImageViewState` each expose `reset_for_new_dataset`, and
`load_controller` calls all three. The rule dividing what is cleared from what
is kept is *which data* versus *how I like to look at it*: a fold-change
control names a well, a baseline names a timepoint, a line order names wells, a
LUT is a pair of intensities, an `axis_prefs` *limit* is in the units of the
plate that was open — all of those describe a plate that is no longer open.
The band's variable controls — Group by and the three `Decorate ▾` combos
(Colour by, Split by, Then by) — are cleared with them, the decorations through
`group_by_controller.DECORATION_CONTROLS` so another cannot be added to the
popover and missed here. They name *this* plate's variables by id, and an id is
unique only within the set that minted it — so a *Group by* left set does not
offer a variable that no longer exists, it silently regroups every plot by
whatever the next plate's is, under a band still reading the old name.

SEM-vs-SD, log axes, mark styling and the publication style are preferences and
follow the user, which is why the reset drops only `AXIS_LIMIT_PREF_KEYS` rather
than clearing `axis_prefs` wholesale — for a plate that has never been opened,
at least; one with a saved `export_axis_prefs` block gets its own entries back
in full when `view_state.restore` runs a moment later.

A limit is stored twice, and only one of the two copies is the one drawn.
`apply_export_style_prefs` reads `axis_buckets[str(index)]` first — that is what
gives each subplot of the bar stack its own x/y limits — and falls back to the
flat key on the figure's entry only when the bucket has nothing. The Properties
sidebar writes both on every edit. So "forget the limits the user typed" has to
clear both, and every caller that means it goes through
`plot_style.drop_axis_limits`: the dataset switch, and the fold-change change
that moves bar values onto a different scale. Clearing the flat keys alone left
the drawn limit exactly where it was.

The Properties sidebar's **Auto scale** button is the third caller, and it holds
the buckets without the entry around them — `self._axis_buckets` lives on the
panel for its lifetime and is written back on the next persist — so it shares
the key list through `drop_bucket_limits`, which `drop_axis_limits` is built on.
Clearing is only two thirds of the button, though. `apply_export_style_prefs`
only ever *sets* a limit; nothing in the pass can re-enable autoscale, so an
axis keeps the last bounds it was handed until its own renderer builds it again.
So `_autoscale_axes` blanks the four fields, clears every panel's bucket, and
then redraws the bound figure — the same three steps, and for the same reason,
as the Reset button beside it. A redraw that did not run is reported to the
user: the redraw is the button's only visible effect, so a silent failure is
indistinguishable from a button wired to nothing. The log toggles and the base
are deliberately untouched — an axis drawn in log stays in log and merely picks
its own bounds again.

**The store is replaced, not edited, so nothing may hold a piece of it.**
`view_state.restore` rebuilds `axis_prefs` as `{str(k): dict(v)}` and
`reset_for_new_dataset` rebuilds it without the entries that emptied, so every
dict inside it is a different object after a dataset load. `figure_prefs`
therefore returns a `_FigurePrefs` that resolves both the global style dict and
the figure's own entry **per access**, from a key fixed at construction; it
never captures the dicts. The Properties sidebar is what makes that load-bearing
— it is built once per figure and cached for the life of the process, so a view
that captured its entry went on writing every axis limit, log toggle, log base
and per-axis tick size into a dict nothing read, and reported success: the
fields kept the values and the figure never moved. Only the controls that write
`PlotState` (the colour mode, the Show and Error-bars segments) went on working,
which is what a whole Properties panel looks like once it has come loose from
its figure.

The panel's fields need the same catch-up its `PlotState` segments already get.
`_resync_pref_fields`, called from `launch_export_editor` beside
`_resync_plot_state_segments`, re-seeds every figure-scoped field from the store
when the panel is reopened. Without it the fields keep the previous plate's
answers, and since `_persist` writes *every* field on any edit, changing the
title size would put the limits a dataset switch had just dropped back onto the
new plate — the defect the drop exists to prevent, arriving through the panel
instead. The two shared log toggles go back through `_log_toggle_seed`, so a
figure with no stored answer still reads its answer off the axis.

`view_state.restore` cannot stand in for the reset: it early-returns when the
new plate has no saved block, which is exactly the case where the previous
plate's settings carry over. A fold-change control naming a group of plate A's
wells resolves to nothing on plate B, so every bar draws NaN under an axis still
labelled as a fold change — silently.

The same rule reaches into the hydrators, because none of them clears on a
missing section: `persistence/ratios.py`, `heatmap_layouts.py` and
`multivariate.py` each apply an *empty* value when their section is absent
rather than returning. Ratio metrics stay live as virtual channels in every
plot, a heat-map layout names wells and a metric, and the Multivariate
configuration names columns — so inheriting any of them means describing plate
A's work under plate B's name. `reset_scopes.restore_slice_defaults` is the
shared way a feature slice is put back the way a fresh dataset finds it.


```
User clicks Open  or  Ctrl+O  or  --data_dir argv
        │
        ▼
ReviewApp._load_path(path)        ← runtime_app.py
        │
        ▼
load_controller.load_path(app, path)  ← review/core/load_controller.py
        ├── detect in/out layout
        ├── app._read_pipeline_info(out_dir)  ← schema, fluor tokens, smFISH tokens
        ├── app._fov_tp_extractor ← make_schema_extractor(sep, fov_idx, tp_idx)
        └── load_directory(app, dir)
              ├── exit Split View if active (§5.10) — restore the single
              │   notebook before view-state restore + redraw touch it
              ├── glob *.csv, validate header, load each into pandas
              ├── reset prior-dataset state BEFORE hydration (see below)
              ├── populate app._well_paths, app._cache
              ├── _build_tok_to_label, _rebuild_all_timepoints_cache, …
              ├── hydrate persisted state (sample_definitions, ratios,
              │   heatmap_layouts, cell_overrides, line_order, cell_gating)
              ├── _refresh_sidebar_map           ← view side
              ├── _recalculate_threshold        ← invokes _update_channel_selector
              └── app._redraw()                  ← plot_orchestrator.redraw
```

**What the dataset is called is one rule, in one place.**
`domain/dataset_name.dataset_display_name` answers it, and every place that
shows a dataset's name goes through it: the shell's dataset button, Home's
masthead title, and the cover page of both gallery exports. The rule is not
"the folder's name", which is why it needs a home at all — Review loads
`<dataset_root>/out` for the standard pipeline layout, so `data_dir.name` is the
literal `out` on every such dataset, identical for all of them. The climb to the
root is conditioned on a sibling `in` directory, detected structurally the same
way `load_path` decides the layout when opening the folder, so a genuinely flat
dataset whose own top-level folder happens to be called `out` keeps its own
name. Three sites derived this independently and only the dataset button
climbed; `tests/test_dataset_name_is_derived_once.py` holds the rest at one.

**Cross-dataset state reset on swap.** The per-dataset persistence
loaders **early-return** (or merge additively) when the new dataset's
`pipeline_info` / sidecar block is absent, so on a dataset swap any in-memory
field left in place would survive and silently apply to the new data. The load
path therefore clears this state to its empty defaults **before** hydration, at
the existing load-path chokepoints — the new dataset's own sidecar (if any)
repopulates afterwards:

- `DatasetState.begin_load` clears `well_labels`.
- `_reset_sample_definitions_state` (`core/load_controller.py`) clears
  `selections` / `current_selection_id` / `notes_text` (+ the Notes editor
  widget) / `active_solo_wells`.
- `_reset_gating_state` clears the scatter-gate config **and** the gate values
  (`fluor_gates` / `thresh_frac_on` / `thresh_count_on`); `recalculate_threshold`
  later in the load rebuilds the Cell-Gating rows before re-applying any
  persisted values.
- Ratio metrics reset at their hydration point (their channel-combo cascade must
  run against the loaded dataset); stale Review-Image / Preview / Playground
  image caches drop via the `on_dataset_loaded` hooks.

### 9.2 Selecting wells

```
User clicks/drags on the plate widget
        │
        ▼
WellPlateSelector.selectionChanged       ← widget signal
        │
        ▼
ReviewApp._on_sidebar_plate_selection_changed(ids)
        ├── updates app._selected_wells
        └── app._refresh_sidebar_map()   ← updates colours; no plot redraw yet

User releases mouse / clicks "Select all" / "Select none"
        │
        ▼
selectionDragFinished → ReviewApp._on_sidebar_plate_drag_finished
                                or
              click handler → app._on_plate_sel_change()
        │
        ▼
selection_controller.on_plate_sel_change(ctx)
        ├── commits the plate change (SelectionState diffs prev_sel → last_sel)
        └── emits bus.selection_changed
              └── SelectionRefreshCoordinator → apply_selection_refresh(ctx)
                    ├── app._refresh_sidebar_map()
                    └── _refresh_tab_view(ctx, tab) for each visible leaf
                          ├── the feature's registry `on_selection_changed` hook:
              │     Bar Plots      → redraw_bars(app)
              │     Scatter Plot   → scatter_redraw_active(app)
              │     Review CSV     → app._refresh_review_csv()
              │     smFISH         → smfish_sync_from_app(app)
              │     Sample Defs    → cell_gating CDF refresh (no plot redraw)
              │     anything else  → app._redraw()
```

The per-tab dispatch keys off `_current_centre_tab()`, so in **Split View**
(§5.10) it runs once per *visible* leaf — `apply_selection_refresh` loops
`selection_controller._visible_tabs(app)` (→ `visible_centre_tabs`), de-duping
the shared `app._redraw`; channel/plot-option redraws fan out the same way via
`fold_change_scopes.visible_scope_names`. Off split both resolve to the single
active tab, so the flow above is unchanged.

That **two-step "selection-changed (paint) → drag-finished (commit)"** split
is important. Drag-paint events fire many times per second; they should not
trigger a redraw on every cell. Click handlers (`Select all`, `Select none`,
row/column header) must explicitly call `_on_plate_sel_change()` to commit.

**Group (replicate-set) mode vs per-well mode.** When the dataset has
selections (replicate sets / groups) defined, `_refresh_sidebar_map_now` puts
the plate in `"passive"` mode on most tabs: per-well plate clicks are ignored
and the plate paints group membership; clicks instead toggle a group's `hidden`
flag (plotting tabs) or its visibility. The exceptions are
`selection_controller._PER_WELL_TAB_NAMES` = **Home, Review CSV,
Cell Browser** — these stay in `"select"` mode and honour `selected_wells` even with
groups defined (the Cell Browser sources its gallery from `selected_wells`, so
single replicate wells must be pickable there). Because the plate is passive in
group mode, the plate's **corner all/none toggle** (only shown in `"select"`
mode) would vanish; it now also shows in passive mode and emits `cornerToggled`,
which `on_sidebar_plate_corner_toggled` routes to `select_all` / `select_none`
(toggle every group visible/hidden). Corollary on the plot side: in group mode
`selected_wells` is **stale** (clicks don't write it), so `ordered_bar_keys`
(and the FOV-pooled collector) must NOT fall back to `selected_wells` when no
group is visible — groups defined but all hidden ⇒ no bars (otherwise "Deselect
all" resurrected every well).

**Drag-source mode (Heat Map).** While the Heat Map tab is active,
`tab_controller.sync_heatmap_well_drag_mode` sets `WELL_MIME` as the plate's
drag mime so a well can be dragged into the heat-map layout grid. The plate
stays a working well picker under that mode: `_PlateGrid.mousePressEvent` only
*arms* the drag (recording `_drag_press_pos` / `_drag_press_cell`) and defers
the selection action, and `mouseReleaseEvent` replays it through `_press_well`
whenever the pointer never travelled far enough for `mouseMoveEvent` to hand off
to a `QDrag`. So a click selects, deselects, or activates exactly as it does on
every other tab; only press-and-drag paint/rubber-band selection is taken over,
because that is the same gesture as dragging a well out. Row/column headers and
the corner all/none toggle are resolved before the drag-source branch and behave
identically either way.

### 9.3 Switching channels

```
Plotting band QComboBox.currentIndexChanged
        │
        ▼
ReviewApp._on_plot_channel_selected(source=band combo)
        └── _set_active_channel(channel)
              ├── update app._active_channel + app._active_val_col
              ├── sync every per-renderer combo
              │     (each tab keeps a hidden _chan_cb_<x> for back-compat)
              ├── app._recalculate_threshold()
              └── bus.channel_changed.emit(channel_state)
                    ↳ RedrawCoordinator → redraw_scopes_or_defer(app):
                       runs the visible scope's redraw callable
                       (line: redraw_app, bar: redraw_bars) and
