                       marks the rest dirty for redraw on tab switch

ReviewApp._update_channel_selector() (called from _recalculate_threshold)
        ├── populates every channel combo from app._fluor_channels + ratios
        ├── picks a sensible default if the current channel disappeared
        └── snaps the global combo's currentIndex to the active label
            (this last step is what prevents the "drop-down doesn't match
            the plot on first draw" bug)
```

### 9.4 Redrawing a plot

Two rules the fan-out does not enforce for you, and both have been broken by a
feature that looked complete without them. **A renderer ends with
`core.plot_style.apply_export_style_to_current`** — the Properties sidebar's
axis limits, log scales, fonts and mark styling are re-applied by that pass and
by nothing else, so a renderer that skips it silently discards every one of them
on its next recompute. And **a feature that renders from its own cached result
must register a `redraw` hook in `features/registry.py`**: Spatial and
Multivariate are not reached by `redraw_app`'s fan-out, so without the hook the
Properties sidebar's Reset-to-defaults repaints some other tab's figure while
the one on screen keeps the settings the user just cleared.


```
app._redraw()              ← runtime_app.py
   └── plot_orchestrator.redraw(app, …)
         ├── lineplot_redraw(app, …)              ← always
         ├── if Distribution built AND visible: redraw_distribution(app)
         ├── if Heat Map built AND visible:     redraw_heatmap(app)
         │     (built-but-hidden → added to PlotState.fc_dirty_scopes)
         └── for each open ExportStyleSidebar: refresh order list

Each per-tab redraw ends with:
   apply_export_style_to_current(app, fig, canvas)
       ↳ figure_export_editor.apply_export_style_prefs(fig, prefs)
       ↳ canvas.draw_idle()

Bar Plots, Scatter Plot, and Scatter Aggregate redraws are *not* invoked
from `plot_orchestrator.redraw` — they have their own entry points
(`features.barplot.renderer.redraw_bars`, `scatter_redraw_active`)
called from the selection path directly and from the channel-change
path via the fold-change scope registry (see §5.9 "Scope registry").
```

### 9.5 Applying fold-change normalization

Two independent axes, both optional, both stacking. State lives on the
`ReviewApp` so the Bar Plots and Line Graphs tabs share it; the
batch-export panels keep their own panel-local mirror so a batch job
isn't tied to whatever the plot tab has set.

**A vs-t0 baseline is judged against the operation that will use it.** Dividing
by zero is undefined, so a *ratio* baseline must be non-zero — but *subtracting*
zero is perfectly well defined, and zero at t0 is the expected reading for the
fields this matters to: a fraction-on or an event count at the start of an
induction experiment is normally 0. Requiring a non-zero baseline for both
operations meant the requested timepoint was skipped and a later one silently
substituted, so one figure normalised its mean panel against t=0 and its
fraction and events panels against t=24, under a single axis label.
`_baseline_usable(value, op=…)` is the shared predicate, and *shared* is the
load-bearing word. There are six baseline finders in `fold_change.py` — the line
path's `_field_baseline`, the bar path's four `baseline_*_from_points*` variants,
and `member_baseline_value`, which the per-cell overlay uses and whose docstring
promises it agrees with the bar's. All six go through the predicate, and the
operation is threaded in from the collector at every live call site. Converting a
subset is worse than converting none: the first pass took the line path only, so
the symptom survived intact on the bar tab, and the pass after it left
`member_baseline_value` resolving a different timepoint from the bar it is drawn
over — in exactly the case its own docstring says the two agree. (Two of the four
`baseline_*_from_points*` variants have no production caller today; they take the
parameter so a future one cannot reintroduce the split.) The ratio-mode fall-through remains (it is arithmetic, not
a choice) but now says so in the log.

**Two conventions for "undefined" were live at once.** `scale_bar_value`'s
docstring states that an undefined input spread stays undefined through
normalization, and the bar path kept it; the line path's `_scale_pt` folded it to
`0.0`, handing the scaled point an error bar that looks measured. All of them now propagate `NaN` — `_scale_pt` for the mean field and
`_scale_field` / `_subtract_field` for the fraction and events fields, which is
where the second convention was still live after the first pass. Relatedly,
**normalization rescales a field that exists and never creates one**: naming the
events spread's index unconditionally made the tuple-padding helper invent the
slot on a plain per-well point — a 9-tuple, because one well has no replicates to
vary across — and fill it with a propagated error, so a single well came back
carrying an events error band and the panel drew a ribbon around it. Relatedly, what counts as a *number* is now a duck-typed
conversion (`_as_finite`) rather than `isinstance(x, (int, float))`, which is
False for `numpy.float32` — the isinstance spelling silently answered "not a
number" in the most numerically sensitive module in the app, producing a NaN mean
and a vanished error bar rather than an exception.

The math has one important invariant: the **numerator** (each bar's /
curve's value) and the **denominator** (control mean and t0 baseline)
use the **same statistic**. For a rep-set member that's
"mean-of-per-well-means" (`_compute_rep_stats`), or per-FOV pool when
Aggregate-FOVs is on (`_compute_rep_per_fov_stats`); for a single-well
member it's `_aggregate_well`. Mixing statistics gave biased ratios in
the original implementation. The helpers in `fold_change.py` enforce
this — see `member_mean_series` for the dispatch.

The Events (N-above) panel is the same rule applied to a count: a replicate
set's value is the **mean of its per-well counts** with the cross-well spread,
matching the Mean and Fraction panels beside it, on both plotting tabs and both
batch paths. `compute_rep_n_above_stats` is that statistic. A cross-well
**total** is a different number and is reporting-only — it is what the CSV's
integer `events_total` column has always carried, it comes from
`compute_rep_n_above_total`, and `tests/test_events_total_isolation.py` keeps it
out of anything that draws. The two are easy to substitute for one another by
name, and substituting them is what made a set divided by itself land on 1/n
rather than 1.0.

The bar and line CSVs therefore report both: `events_total` (the integer
count) alongside `events_per_replicate_mean`, `events_per_replicate_<band>` and
`replicate_unit`. The unit column is not decoration — nothing else in
the row records whether Aggregate-FOVs was on, which would leave the mean and
its spread ambiguous.

Which AggPoint fields those three read is decided by the Aggregate-FOVs toggle,
and it is the same decision `_paint_series` makes when it draws the Events
panel: with the toggle **on** the value and spread are the per-FOV mean and its
spread (indices 7 / 8) and the unit is `fov`, for a lone well as much as for a
replicate set — a well's fields are its replicates; with it **off** they are the
per-well count and its cross-well spread (indices 4 / 9), and the unit is `well`
for a replicate set and empty for a single well, which has nothing to average
over. `line_metric_row` read indices 4 / 9 unconditionally, so every FOV-mode
row of the line CSV reported `0.000000` events with a `0.000000` spread — index
4 is a placeholder on the collectors' FOV branch — beside a panel drawing the
real mean.

Both CSVs also carry `fraction_<band>`, the spread the Fraction panel bands its
curve with (AggPoint index 6). The line CSV had no such column at all while the
bar CSV had carried one all along, so one figure exported from the two tabs
disagreed about whether the number exists. An undefined spread is an **empty**
cell in every one of these columns, never `0.000000`: a lone well with
Aggregate-FOVs off has one sample of the fraction and nothing to vary across,
and a zero would read as replicates that agreed exactly.

That blank-for-undefined rule is `export/service.spread_cell`, and it is one
function because the writers that had their own answer got it wrong: the
scatter aggregate formatted its errors with a bare f-string on the tab and in
both of its Batch Export jobs, so a group of one replicate — a single selected
well, the commonest case there — wrote the literal `nan`. A spreadsheet reads
that cell as text, so the column stops being numeric for every row below it.
`tests/test_a_spread_reaches_a_csv_as_a_number_or_a_blank.py` is the guard: a
dict entry whose key names a spread column may not be an unconditional
`JoinedStr`, since a bare f-string has no branch in which to say "not computed".

`cells_total` on a replicate-set row is the cells its wells hold at that
timepoint, summed by the collectors from the per-well aggregation they already
walk to build the timepoint list. It was a placeholder zero there, and the
exporter's refusal to print a placeholder then left the column empty on every
row of a replicate-set file. It is a cell count and not the denominator of
`fraction_above_threshold`, which on a set is the mean of its wells' fractions.

The same rule governs the fold-change pair. `fold_change_<band>` is written
only where `fold_change_mean` is: `fold_change.blank_point` blanks a mean whose
control did not resolve and leaves the spread at `0.0`, so guarding the two
independently put a measured-looking zero beside an empty mean on exactly the
rows whose `fold_change_outcome` says the division never happened. The bar
writer's `fc_has` is the **mean's** flag (`BarItem.has_mean`) and says nothing
about the spread beside it — `scale_bar_value` returns a finite value with a
NaN spread whenever the denominator's own spread was undefined — so gating the
spread on it wrote the literal `nan` into a row whose raw `err_<band>` cell was
correctly blank.

A row that measured nothing states nothing, either. A member with no point at
the timepoint still reaches the writer as a `BarItem`, carrying the collector's
placeholder `n_above=0.0` with `has_mean=False`; `_replicate_unit_for` keys on
`has_mean` before the value, because `is_number` says yes to that placeholder
and a unit claimed there brought a `0.000000` replicate spread with it onto an
otherwise-empty row.

`events_total` is an integer count and stays one. `LinePoint.as_aggpoint`
floats index 4 so a replicate set's drawn mean survives, and writing that value
through unchanged turned a plain well's `3` into `3.0` and a NaN one into
`nan`; the row formats an integral value as an integer, a fold-changed ratio
with six decimals, and an undefined one as blank. On the bar side the same
column's float form is chosen by `replicate_unit == "fov"` — the row's own
statement that this cell is a per-FOV mean — rather than by the sign of the
whisker beside it, which sent a mean back through `int()` whenever the fields
agreed exactly. That `> 0` test was the last of the mode flags standing in for
a value test: the bar CSV's second Events spread column carried it too, and blanked a spread of zero
that `events_per_replicate_<band>` two columns along was writing.

Beside the interval, every file that carries one names **what it is over**:
`replicate_unit` on the bar and line CSVs, `spread_unit` on the Heat
Map, scatter-aggregate and Response ones. `export/service.spread_unit_for` asks
`stats_compute.replicate_unit` rather than re-spelling the FOV rule, so an
exported column cannot disagree with the statistic the plot drew; the Response
collector asks the same function rather than keeping the hard-coded
`"FOV"` / `"replicate"` pair it had, which put four vocabularies under one
column name across three files. The word a *sentence* wants is rendered from
that one value at the caption, not stored beside it. A `spread_unit` cell is
written only where there is an interval to have a denominator — a Heat Map of
cell counts measures no spread anywhere, and a column of `well` beside an empty
error column asserts a statistic nobody took. Which interval a spread is stays in its own column name — `fraction_sem`,
`gfp_mean_intensity_sd`, the Heat Map's `<value column>_ci95`, the scatter
file's `x_sem` — so no export carries a column whose only job is to say what
another column's name already could. `spread_band_token` builds that suffix:
the figure's `95% CI` loses its space and percent sign, and its leading digits
move behind the letters, because a name segment opening with a digit reads as a
number rather than a word. `_replicate_unit_for` — the
bar CSV's version of the same question — keys on the Aggregate-FOVs toggle for
the same reason the line row does: with the toggle on, `collect_bar_items` puts
the per-FOV mean in `n_above` for a lone well too, and keying the unit on
`n_above_total` alone left that row stating a per-FOV mean under an empty unit
with its spread blanked.

Stacking when both axes are active is **ΔΔCt-style**:
```
   Y(t) = (X(t) / C(t)) / (X(0) / C(0))
```
because `vs t0` is applied to the post-control values. This is not the
same as `(X(t)/X(0)) / (C(t)/C(0))` in general. Documented on
`normalize_pts`.

Error propagation: each fold-change denominator (control mean, t0
baseline) is divided through with its own spread, and the resulting
relative error combines in quadrature:

```
   (σ_Y / Y)² = (σ_X / X)² + (σ_C / C)² + (σ_B / B)²
```

`scale_bar_value` and `normalize_pts` accept the denominator spreads
via `control_spread` / `t0_spread` / `control_stats`. Callers that
don't have a meaningful denominator uncertainty can omit them; that
recovers the legacy "treat denominator as exact" `spread / factor`
behaviour and is the backwards-compatible default.

```
                            state.plot.fc_vs_control_on ─┐
User → Control combo  ─→    state.plot.fc_control       ─┼─→ fold_change.fold_change_state(ctx)
                            state.plot.fc_vs_t0_on      ─┘        → FoldChangeState
User → Baseline combo ─→ (sets fc_vs_t0_on)

core/fold_change_controls_view.set_fold_change_state(ctx, *, …, initiating_scope)
        │   mirrors the shape of channel_state_controller.set_active_channel:
        │   updates state → _sync_widgets_to_state →
        │     redraw_scopes_or_defer(app) (scope coalescer: visible scope's
        │     callable runs now, the rest are marked dirty)
        ▼
Line tab — lineplot_controller.redraw_line_plots(…) →
            collect_line_series(ctx, …) → list[LineSeries]
   1. Single source of truth, mirrors the bar plot's
      ``collect_bar_items``. Each member becomes a ``LineSeries``
      with a list of ``LinePoint``s (full AggPoint shape so the
      renderer and CSV writers consume the same record).
   2. ``fold_change_pairing.control_denominators(…)`` builds one
      ``ControlDenominators`` for the pass; ``denoms.series_for(member)``
      then answers with that member's control, its outcome, and the
      mean / fraction / events denominator series **separately**.
      Each series is mean-of-per-well-means for rep-set controls
      (per-FOV pool when Aggregate-FOVs is on), single-well agg for
      well controls. Spreads thread through normalize_pts via
      quadrature for proper error propagation.
   3. ``fold_change_pairing.normalize_member_pts(…)`` wraps
      ``normalize_pts`` per member, applying the per-panel rule from
      ``panel_nan_flags``: a panel whose denominator series is empty is
      blanked rather than drawn raw, and the other two are still
      normalized. Drag-order from ``_line_order_rsets`` /
      ``_line_order_wells`` is applied before the per-trace work.
   4. The renderer is the shared ``lineplot.controller.render_line_series``
      (over a ``LineAxes`` bundle): the on-tab redraw and the batch export
      figure BOTH call it, so the four-panel layout (mean / fraction /
      N(above) / CDF) can never drift between them. The batch line CSV /
      figure collect via
      ``features.batch_export._line_series_runner.collect_line_series_for_group``
      — a thin orchestrator for a mixed ``BarGroup`` that reuses the tab's OWN
      statistic per member: rep-set members via ``compute_rep_stats`` /
      ``compute_rep_per_fov_stats`` (mean-of-per-well-means, per-FOV), solo
      wells via ``aggregate_well`` (within-well) so a solo stays byte-for-byte
      identical to its on-tab per-well export. The old pool-of-cells batch
      numerator (a documented divergence here) is gone. The bar batch path is
      the same shape: ``barplot.collect.collect_bar_items_for_group`` pools
      multi-well members via ``compute_rep_stats`` and keeps solos on
      ``aggregate_well``.
   5. After redraw, ctx.notify.set_status(…) surfaces a one-line warning
      built by ``fold_change_pairing.shortfall_from_items`` from each
      trace's own outcome, coalesced by reason. The collector's
      timepoint miss set is passed alongside it, so a control that
      resolved but has no sample at some timepoints still names them;
      it cannot describe a trace whose control was never assigned,
      which is why the outcomes drive the sentence.

Bar tab — barplot_controller.collect_bar_items(ctx, target_t,
                                                miss_sink=fc_misses)
          → list[BarItem]  (single source of truth)
   1. ``denoms.at(member, target_t)`` → that bar's control, its outcome,
      and the mean / fraction / events denominators as separate
      ``(value, spread)`` pairs (or None). Each uses the same stat as
      the bar's numerator (mean-of-per-well-means for rep-set, per-FOV
      pool when Aggregate-FOVs is on).
   2. For each bar's (mean, spread): scale_bar_value(…), with the
      user's per-axis operator and, when both axes are on, ``_stack_axes``
      composing one onto the other's denominator. The batch collector
      ``collect_bar_items_for_group`` reads the same operator, order and
      stacking, so its figure and the tab's cannot diverge.
   3. t0 baseline = member_first_tp_value(ctx, member_label, …) for
      rep-sets (same stat) or first_tp_value(pts) for per-well bars.
   4. If vs-control was requested but a panel's denominator came back
      None, that panel is forced to NaN (no silent fall-back to raw
      values) — per panel, via ``panel_nan_flags``, because a control
      can have a mean and no fraction series. When the control resolved
      but has no sample at ``target_t``, that tp is recorded in
      miss_sink. The status warning is built by
      ``fold_change_pairing.shortfall_from_items`` from the items' own
      outcomes and surfaced by barplot_renderer.draw_grouped_bar_mode.
      The cross-axis stacking that runs when the baseline axis is also
      on is guarded on the same condition, in both the grouped and
      per-well branches — it divides by the control, so reaching it with
      an unresolved one raised a TypeError rather than drawing a
      placeholder.

   The collector is staged so each step above has one home.
   ``_bar_request`` reads everything the redraw needs off the context
   once, into a frozen ``_BarRequest``. ``_BarCollector`` owns what is
   valid for exactly one redraw — the control-series cache, the memoised
   member baselines and the pairing — and builds one bar at a time:
   ``_rset_panels`` / ``_well_panels`` collect the raw Value, Fraction and
   Events panels (a frozen ``_Panels``), ``_Denominators`` carries the
   control and baseline denominators while ``_rset_baselines`` /
   ``_well_baselines`` resolve and stack them, and ``_fold_panels`` is the
   single place a bar is folded or marked undefined, for grouped and
   per-well bars alike. ``_in_emission_order`` lays the bars out tp-major
   or well-major. The Events panel's own NaN flag cannot fire by itself
   today: ``member_n_series`` never omits a timepoint the mean series
   has, so a missing Events denominator always comes with a missing mean.
   ``tests/test_bar_collect_stages.py`` holds the two outputs the split's
   mutation pass found unpinned: an unpooled well taking its set's
   colour, and a well's Events panel stacking both fold-change axes.

Bar tab violin / beeswarm — barplot.renderer.draw_per_cell_bar_mode →
fold_change.build_cell_scaling(…) → {well: factor}, where each cell
value is divided by factor before plotting. factor = control_mean ×
t0_mean (per-well). NaN factor → that well's column rendered as a
placeholder. Title gains the suffix when scaling is active.

Both renderers append a "(fold change vs <ctrl>, vs t0)" suffix to all
three panels' titles / ylabels via fold_change.fold_change_suffix. The
one exception is the Events panel in the per-cell display modes:
``draw_per_well_n_bars`` is not fold-changed, and it writes that panel's
plain title itself so the suffix its caller applied cannot survive over
raw counts.

Float-tolerance: _match_control_mean uses relative tolerance
abs(a-b) < 1e-3 · max(1, |a|, |b|) — the bar tp combo formats with
:.4g so a fractional tp like 2/3 ≈ 0.6667 parses back ~3e-5 off the
original float, which the prior absolute 1e-6 tolerance missed.

CSV output (additive in both line and bar paths):
   On-tab:
     export_service.export_plot_data        (line)
     export_service.export_bar_plot_data    (bar)
   Batch:
     features/batch_export/base_panel._run_group     (line)
     features/batch_export/bar_panel._run_batch      (bar)

   The mean_<ch>_<metric> / err_<band>_<ch>_<metric> columns always
   carry the RAW values. When fold-change is active, five columns are
   appended:
       fold_change_mean             — normalized mean
       fold_change_<sd|sem>         — normalized spread
       fold_change_mode             — "control" | "t0" | "control+t0"
       fold_change_control          — the control THIS row was divided by
       fold_change_outcome          — why the row is what it is

   Both CSVs are implemented via two calls to their tab's own
   collector — collect_bar_items / collect_bar_items_for_group for
   the bar, collect_line_series / collect_line_series_for_group for
   the line: one with FC_STATE_OFF for the raw columns and one with
   the active state for the fold-change columns.

   The scatter-aggregate CSVs (on-tab and both batch jobs) carry
   the same two error columns (each named for the axis it belongs
   to, with the interval as its suffix) plus spread_unit, and
   their figures share the tab's whisker rule
   (scatter/controller.whiskers_or_none): capsize draws a cap at
   every point even where the bar has zero length, so a group with
   no computable spread came out of Batch Export wearing a cross
   the tab does not draw.

   A row is therefore one DRAWN member at one timepoint, on both
   tabs and on both paths. export_plot_data used to re-aggregate
   each selected well itself with a bare aggregate_well, which
   returned a plain 9-tuple: Aggregate-FOVs was ignored, the
   fraction spread was never computed, and the Events replicate
   columns could not be anything but empty on any plate, because a
   per-well point is not an aggregation of anything. In
   replicate-set mode its identifying columns are
   replicate_set / wells / well_names / n_wells; in per-well mode
   they stay well / well_name. The aggregation helpers are cached so the second call
   is cheap. Pre-refactor the bar CSV used to overwrite the raw mean
   column with the normalized value when fold-change was active —
   that was inconsistent with the line CSV's additive schema and
   has been corrected.

Cross-tab widget sync:
   Each tab installs its own QComboBox instances via
   core/fold_change_controls_view.install_fold_change_controls(scope=…).
   The combo handlers funnel every state mutation through
   set_fold_change_state, which calls _sync_widgets_to_state to
   mirror the new state into the other tab's widget set (with
   signals blocked). The smart-repopulation check skips the
   clear-and-readd cycle when the combo's popup is currently
   visible, so user interaction is never yanked out of focus.

   Scope registry. Each tab that owns a fold-change combo set
   declares itself via a FoldChangeScope (name, ctrl combo attr,
   baseline combo attr, redraw callable, tab names). The dataclass
   plus dispatch primitives (register_fold_change_scope,
   redraw_scopes_or_defer, flush_dirty_scopes) live in the
   pure-logic ``review.domain.fold_change_scopes`` module
   so the helpers can be unit-tested without Qt — and so the
   domain layer stays free of imports from ``features/``.

   Registration of the two default scopes (bar, line) lives in
   ``review.core.scope_registry.register_default_scopes``,
   which imports the actual redraw callables
   (``features.barplot.renderer.redraw_bars``,
   ``core.plot_orchestrator.redraw_app``) and binds them to the
   scopes. It is called once from ``core/bus_wiring.wire_event_bus``
   during construction. Adding a third scope (e.g. distribution /
   scatter) is a single register_fold_change_scope call inside that
   function — ``_sync_widgets_to_state`` and ``set_fold_change_state``
   iterate the registry rather than hard-coding scope names. The
   ``redraw`` field is a callable (not a string method name), so a renamed
   or missing target surfaces directly instead of silently no-op'ing at
   dispatch time.

   Redraw deferral. State mutations route through
   ``redraw_scopes_or_defer(app)``: the currently-visible scope's
   ``redraw`` callable runs immediately, every other scope is
   marked dirty. ``tab_controller.on_notebook_current_changed``
   calls ``flush_dirty_scopes(app)``, which redraws any dirty
   scope whose tab just became visible.
   ``channel_state_controller.set_active_channel`` and
   ``set_fold_change_state`` both route through the bus, whose
   ``RedrawCoordinator`` calls this same chokepoint — so every
   redraw-triggering action shares one consistent visibility-aware
   policy. The dirty set lives on ``PlotState.fc_dirty_scopes``
   (``app._app_state.plot.fc_dirty_scopes``).

**A control is a reference, not a name.** `PlotState.fc_control` holds a
`domain/control_ref.ControlRef` — a frozen `(kind, name)` where `kind` is
`"well"`, `"set"`, or `"legacy"` — and `None` means no control. The kind is
carried beside the name rather than encoded into it because replicate-set names
are unrestricted free text: `domain/selections_format.py`'s `_unique_name` strips whitespace
and ensures uniqueness, and reserves no character. A set may therefore be named
`A01 (well)`, or share a token with a loaded well, and no spelling of a single
string can tell the two apart. The combo still shows `A01 (well)` when a well's
token collides with a set name, but that suffix is display chrome: the combo
carries the reference as item data, matches its selection on it, and nothing
parses the text back.

`domain/fold_change.resolve_control` is the single place a control becomes
wells, returning `("set"|"well"|"", name)`. Every path that needs a denominator
goes through it — `resolve_control_wells`, `_label_to_replicate_set` and
`_member_series` are its callers rather than three implementations of the same
decision. A reference that states its kind is believed, so a hidden set can
never capture a well of the same name. Only a `"legacy"` reference — a bare
string, or a document written before the kind was recorded — falls through to
`classify_control_label`, which applies the precedence such a value was saved
under: suffixed-well first, then set name, then bare well token, with a set
whose wells are all unloaded falling through rather than claiming the label.

Persistence writes the object under `control` and keeps the plain token in the
older `control_label` key, so a rolled-back build finds a value it understands.
A legacy string is upgraded to a concrete kind at two moments — when a
fold-change combo populates (`fold_change_controls_view._upgrade_saved_control`,
and the pairing table's rows through `concrete_control`) and when a replicate
set is renamed (`selection_controller._upgrade_fc_controls`, which resolves
before the name it referred to changes) — and the upgraded value is what the
next save writes, retiring the ambiguity once per document. A reference that
resolves to nothing is kept exactly as it was rather than dropped, so reloading
the missing group restores the pairing. `ControlRef.display_name`
is the plain token and is what reaches an axis title, the `fold_change_control`
CSV cell and the saved-plot summary; the suffix never appears in a figure or an
export. The sample-definitions UI does not prevent the name collision at input
time, and does not need to.

**One control, or one control per member.** `PlotState.fc_control_mode` selects
between them — `"single"`, where `fc_control` divides everything, and
`"per_member"`, where `fc_control_map` gives each plotted member its own
reference. The mapping is keyed on the plot's own bar/trace keys, which
`domain/plot_members.py` enumerates: replicate-set names when sets are pooled,
well tokens otherwise. `plot_members.member_wells` gives each key the wells it
is drawn from, which is what lets "is this member its own control?" be answered
by comparing resolved wells rather than names — the only comparison that
survives a well and a set sharing a token. `fc_control_render` says what a member that is itself
somebody's control draws as — `"self"` (normalized against itself, a flat 1.0
for ratio or 0.0 for subtract) or `"hidden"`. There is deliberately no "raw"
value, because a raw control beside ratio bars puts two units on one axis.

The mode is a field rather than an absence. Emptying the control to signal
per-member mode would not fail visibly: the bar collector's force-NaN guard
ANDs with the control, so an empty one makes it falsy, and `_apply_axis`
returns its input unchanged when the denominator is `None` — the plot would
draw **raw** values under a fold-change axis label.

Entries whose member is not currently plotted are retained, not dropped: the
save writes the map unfiltered, `sel_delete` leaves a deleted group's pairings
alone, and the editor collects them under an unused section. A user who hides a
group, or switches pooling off and back on, gets their pairing back instead of
an emptied table. A **rename** is the one thing that rewrites them, and it has
to rewrite all three places a group is named — the map's keys, the map's
values, and `fc_control` — which is what `PlotState.rename_member` does, hooked
into `core/selection_controller.sel_rename`. Rewriting only the keys leaves the
map pointing at a control that no longer exists while the group sits on the
plate under its new name. Because a legacy reference means "whatever this name
resolves to right now", `sel_rename` resolves every reference to a concrete
kind through `fold_change.concrete_control` *before* the group changes name —
afterwards there is no way left to ask.

`BarItem` carries `fc_control` and `fc_outcome`: which control **that bar** was
divided by, and why it is what it is. Under a single global control every bar
carries the same pair; under per-sample controls they differ, and the x-tick's
second line, the CSV's `fold_change_control` and `fold_change_outcome` columns
and the figure's annotations read them rather than each re-deriving the
decision from a value that came out empty.

Three shapes in the bar collector exist because the same thing was written six
times: `_stack_axes` composes the two fold-change axes onto one another's
denominator (mean, fraction and events, in each of the grouped and per-well
branches — and three of the six carried a `None` guard the others lacked, which
is how a control missing at the drawn timepoint could crash a `t0_first`
redraw); `_panel_nan_flags` decides which panels lost their denominator; and
`_fc_scale` applies one axis' `scale_bar_value`.

The Line tab and the batch line runner share `normalize_member_pts`, which
resolves a member's own control series and either normalizes its points or —
when the control did not resolve — blanks them with `fold_change.blank_point`.
Blanking rather than skipping is the point: an empty control series makes
`normalize_pts` skip the control axis without complaint, so the figure carried
raw values under a fold-change axis label, and on the batch path in an export
nobody watched being drawn. A blanked point keeps its timepoint and its cell
counts, because dropping it would leave a gap the renderer bridges with a
straight line between the neighbours, which reads as data.

`fold_change.build_cell_scaling` takes a `control_by_member` map for the same
reason. It is the violin/beeswarm overlay's own resolver; left on one control
the bars would normalize per member while the distribution drawn on top of them
divided by something else — two denominators on one axis, looking like one
measurement.

**Saying which control, everywhere it matters.** The axis title branches on how
many *distinct* controls are actually in use, counted by resolved wells:
`control_axis_phrase` names one exactly as the single-control title does (which
matters, because `Set all to DMSO` is mathematically identical to
single-control mode), names both when there are two, and collapses to
`vs own control` at three. A mapping where nothing resolved reads
`vs own control (none resolved)` rather than claiming a normalization that did
not happen. `fold_change_suffix_for(ctx, scope)` needs the scope because the
member list differs per tab; a caller that names none gets the single-control
reading rather than a guess.

The CSV columns are per row: `fold_change_control` carries **that row's**
control, and `fold_change_outcome` carries its `ControlOutcome`. Without the
outcome column a reader with an empty `fold_change_mean` cannot tell a
normalization that failed from one that was never asked for, and the three
failures are three different things. Both writers — `export/service.py` for the
on-tab CSV and `batch_export/base_panel.py` for the batch one — carry the same
shape, because a plate exported one way and a tab exported the other have to be
comparable.

The bar tab's status line is derived from the collected items' outcomes rather
than from the set of timepoints where a control was missing. Under one global
control that set was the whole story; per-sample controls make partial failure
ordinary, and "control missing at t=24" says nothing about which control, how
many bars it cost, or a bar whose control was never assigned at all.
`saved_plots/collect._fc_summary` reads the persisted block with no `ctx`, so
it counts the entries the document carries and names them when there are few —
it must not claim a resolution count it has no way to compute, since the
document may have been saved against a dataset this session never loaded.

**The editor.** `core/fold_change_pairing_view.py` is a non-modal `QDialog`,
built lazily and hidden rather than destroyed, following
`cell_gating/optimizer_view.build_optimizer_window` — the answer is judged
against the plot behind it, so the window stays open while the user looks. A
`Qt.Popup` dismisses on the first click outside it, and a modal dialog cannot
be reached from a test at all (`tests/conftest.py::_no_modal_dialogs`). Four
columns: **Sample**, **Control**, **Status**, **Resolves to**. The last is the
one that answers the question — the other three describe intent, and intent is
what was already wrong. `pairing_rows` builds them as plain dicts so the
table's content is testable without a window, which matters because the failure
this editor exists to prevent is a table describing a plot that does not exist;
`tests/test_fold_change_pairing_view.py` asserts its members equal the keys
`collect_bar_items` emits.

Stale assignments are retained and labelled `… (missing)`, never reset: a user
who unloads a plate and reloads it gets their pairing back. Assignments whose
member is not currently plotted collect under an unused line rather than
disappearing. Edits live-apply and the footer carries `Close` alone, because a
Cancel that cannot un-draw the plot behind it is a lie.

The Control dropdown reaches it. `Per-sample control…` sits directly under `—`,
above a separator, so the member list below stays exactly as it was; once
active it reads `Per-sample control (22/24)` — resolved out of plotted, not
entries out of entries. `currentIndexChanged` does not fire when the user
re-selects the item already showing, so the combo cannot be the only way back
in: a summary label below it carries an `Edit…` link, hidden unless per-sample
mode is on, alongside the `Controls: normalize to self / hide from plot`
toggle. There is deliberately no "show raw" option — a raw control beside ratio
bars puts two units on one axis.

`Auto-pair` chunks the plotted members N at a time and pairs each chunk to its
first or last, which is Home → Sample Map → Groups' Quick Replicates one level up and reuses
vocabulary the user already has. A plate-geometry rule (row, column, quadrant)
is deliberately absent: it is undefined the moment the members are replicate
sets, which is a domain predicate applied outside its domain. Name-pattern
matching is absent too, because every near-miss looks like a working feature.

A Batch Export panel keeps its own copy of the fold-change request, seeded from
the tab at construction and never written back, so a batch job is not tied to
whatever the live figure has set. The per-sample mapping is seeded the same way
and for the same reason, and the mapping is inherited rather than editable in
the panel — a panel opened while the tab shows a per-sample figure should export
that figure. What the combo has to do, then, is **say so**: while the inherited
mode is in force it offers and selects a `Per-sample (from the plot tab)` entry,
carrying a plain sentinel rather than a `ControlRef` so the handler can tell "the
user re-picked the inherited mode" from "the user named one control". Without
that entry the combo fell through to `—`, which means *no control* everywhere
else in the app, on a run that was about to normalize every member against one.
Re-selecting the entry is not a pick and leaves the panel exactly as it was
seeded. A member of an export group that the inherited mapping does not name
comes out blank and says so, rather than falling back to one control — the
panel's groups are its own, so its member keys need not match the tab's, and a
quiet fallback would export a figure that disagrees with the one on screen.
Picking a single control switches the panel out of per-sample mode, because
naming one control is a request for one control; the inherited entry is then
removed in place with `removeItem` rather than by repopulating the combo, since
this runs inside that combo's own `currentIndexChanged` and clearing a combo
from its own handler is re-entrant.

`_app_group_scope` is what a batch group's collection runs inside, and it does
not add the group to the app's selections — it **replaces** them with one entry
per member. `resolve_control` finds a `kind="set"` reference by scanning exactly
that list, so a control naming a replicate set in another batch group would not
be there — and one batch group per condition with the control as its own group
is the normal layout, which would blank every curve in the group. The scope
therefore carries any replicate set the panel's control names in **hidden**:
hiding a
group takes it off the plot and does not stop it being usable as a control, so
`active_replicate_sets` skips the carried entry and `resolve_control` finds it.
A control naming nothing loaded is left absent rather than stood in for by an
empty group, because that is what lets the outcome vocabulary report it.

The bar path does not enter that scope at all — it enters only
`_app_val_col_scope`, and `collect_bar_items_for_group` computes a replicate
set's statistics from the `ReplicateSet` object rather than by name. Which is
why its fold-change baselines come from each member's own points rather than
through `member_first_tp_*_resolved`, and why that asymmetry is deliberate
rather than an oversight. `_app_val_col_scope` restores the app's previous
`active_val_col` **unconditionally**, matching its sibling `_app_group_scope`:
guarding the restore on "the saved value was not `None`" read *the app had no
column selected* as *there is nothing to put back*, which is the opposite — it
is precisely then that the batch's own column stayed behind on shared app state
after the export, so the next tab plot drew whatever the last exported group
happened to pick.

**A batch run reads its controls once, before the first job.**
`_run_batch_jobs` pumps `QApplication.processEvents()` once per job so the
progress bar can paint, which leaves every combo on the panel live for the whole
export and lands a mid-run edit exactly between two jobs. Reading half the
request up front and half inside each job is the worst of the two: the line and
bar panels used to snapshot the channel and re-read the value column and the
metric, so a user who changed the property mid-run exported channel `gfp` against
column `mcherry_total_intensity` — one job, one manifest, two halves of a request
that never coexisted. `_ch_selected`, `_val_col_selected` and `_metric_selected`
are hoisted together in `base_panel._run_group` and `bar_panel._run_batch`,
and the threshold lookup reuses `_val_col_selected` rather than taking a live
read of its own. Scatter carries the same rule in a dataclass: `ScatterAxes` is
built once by `_snapshot_scatter_axes` before the job loop and threaded through
all four `_run_scatter_*_job` signatures, because each of them resolved both axes
live — and one of them resolved them a second time further down, for the figure,
after writing its CSV from the first read, putting a figure and its own CSV on
different columns inside a single job. `ScatterAxes.mode` is carried for the same
one-value-per-run reason rather than as a fix: it is assigned in `__init__` and
never reassigned, so unlike the combos it cannot drift, and holding it on the
snapshot means the stem, the status line and the branch that picks a job read one
value rather than three live lookups.
`tests/test_batch_export_run_snapshot.py` holds the decidable half as AST guards
— no per-job closure reads a live combo, and the snapshot is taken before the
loop.

### 9.6 Running the pipeline

```
Analyze tab Run button
        │
        ▼
services.pipeline_service.find_pipeline_script()
services.pipeline_service.build_pipeline_args(…)
services.pipeline_service.spawn_pipeline(args) → subprocess.Popen
        │
        ▼ stdout stream → ProgressTracker.parse() → RunDashboard events
                         → Analyze tab log view (collapsible, underneath)
process_microscopy.main()
        ├── per-well loop (ProcessPoolExecutor)
        │     ├── extract zip (or compress input folder) → tmp dir
        │     ├── segment + quantify
        │     ├── write per-well CSV + image outputs
        │     └── compress to <well>_out.zip
        ├── write pipeline_info.json
        ├── estimate_thresholds_from_outputs(output_dir, …)
        │     └── _apply_thresholds_to_pipeline_info(output_dir, thresholds, log)
        │           ↳ pipeline_info.json["cell_gating"]["thresh_frac_on"]
        └── pipeline.completeness.record_run_check(…)
              ↳ pipeline_info.json["run_check"]
        │
        ▼
Process exits. Analyze tab offers the dataset to Review.
```

**The end-of-run completeness check.** `pipeline/completeness.py` holds one
definition of "is this well complete", shared by this check and the Datasets
**Validate & Repair** tool (§6b) — `datasets/validate/validate_compute.py`
delegates its union, its `intent - done` diff and its five health states here,
so a well cannot read complete on one surface and partial on another. What is
*not* shared is the scan: Validate parallelises across wells and layers
findings, evidence and repair on top, while `scan_run` walks a directory the run
has just written. The shared predicate takes data the caller already holds and
opens exactly one thing between its functions — the well's output container —
which is what lets Validate delegate without changing its per-well read count,
a number `tests/test_validate_compute.py` pins exactly. The fifth state is `csv_only` — measurements whole, output archive gone — added because `health` accepted `has_out_zip` and never read it, so a well whose archive had been deleted answered `complete` on the strength of its CSV alone. `pipeline/input_layout.py` holds the three questions about which layout a plate's input is in, including the refusal that stops a run whose loose images were moved into a folder no zip-mode run will read; `pipeline/cli_args.py` holds `build_parser`. Both left `process_microscopy` under its line budget and are in the remote manifest. `pipeline/mixed_input.py` holds `consolidate_mixed_to_zips`, which zips each bare well folder in an `in/` that already has well archives: a folder-mode run archives each well it finishes, so a suspended or interrupted one leaves exactly that, and `main` runs it before reading the layout so that `--incremental` from the command line — the pipeline's own resume advice — works as it does from the Analyze pane, whose resolver calls the same function (`services.input_resolution_service` re-exports it under its old private name). With it in front, the refusal above is reached only if a folder is left unarchived for another reason.

The check runs after the auto-threshold pass and before the exit-code decision,
and records a `run_check` block per well: how many `(fov, timepoint)` groups the
input held, how many the measurements CSV covers, how many the CSV and the
output archive cover between them, which are missing, and the resulting health
state. **It takes no part in the exit code** — a plate that came up short is
recorded and warned about, but whether the *run* failed stays `failed_wells`'
question, which the remote layer depends on.

Three properties are load-bearing:

- **It reads artefacts, never `run_report`.** Its well list is the input map the
  run resolved (passed in, not re-derived — the run has already walked the input
  directory and logged what it skipped) unioned with whatever the output holds.
  A record built on `run_report` would describe an incremental run's 96-well
  plate as the three wells that happened to have new timepoints.
- **Two covered counts.** `covered_any` (CSV ∪ archive) is what an incremental
  re-run treats as done, so it is the honest denominator for "what would
  re-running recover"; `covered_csv` is what every plot actually reads. A well
  whose archive is whole and whose CSV is empty has full coverage by the first
  and none by the second, and one figure alone hides that.
- **`run_check` is deliberately not a `USER_SIDE_BLOCKS` key.** It describes one
  run's output, so carrying it across a sidecar rewrite would leave a run that
  died early holding the previous run's description. Losing a record is visible;
  inheriting a stale one is not.

Its presence is also the only honest end-of-run signal in the sidecar —
`pipeline_info.json` itself is written before any image work, so the file
existing says nothing about whether the run got anywhere. `analyze.log_pane`'s
last-run card reads the block for exactly that reason. Note that a **suspended**
run still reaches the check and writes a record: suspend exits through the
normal end-of-well path, so the block carries a `suspended` flag and the
shortfall is reported as a stop rather than shouted at as a fault.

`--no_run_check` turns it off, spelled negative-sense like `--no_auto_threshold`
because the GUI checkbox is the positive. Turning it off still writes a stub
recording that it was turned off: "the check was off" and "this dataset predates
the check" need different things from a reader, so there are three
distinguishable states on disk, not two. A fourth is a record whose `source` is
`validate` — the dataset was never checked by its run but has been scanned
since (§6b).

---

### 9.7 Adding new timepoints / FOVs to an existing dataset (incremental)

The common workflow "analyze the first half of a movie, then the rest" (or
"add a few more FOVs"): drop the **new** image files into the already-grouped
input and re-run. Only the genuinely-new FOV-groups are processed; their
results are **merged** into the existing per-well CSV and `<well>_out.zip` —
nothing already done is re-segmented. Per-FOV quantification is independent
(no cross-FOV/cross-timepoint state), so this is exact, not an approximation.

**What counts as "new":** a FOV-group is one `(fov, timepoint)` — i.e. the
nuclear file plus its fluor channels for that field+time. "New" = a
`(fov, timepoint)` not already present in the well's existing CSV.

**The completeness record still covers the whole plate.** A well with nothing
new returns before writing a run-report entry, so `run_report` after an
incremental run names only the wells that had new data. The end-of-run check
(§6.2) does not read that block: it enumerates from the input map the run
resolved, unioned with what the output holds, and re-reads the artefacts. So a
run that touched three wells of ninety-six still leaves a `run_check` describing
ninety-six.

**Local, step by step:**

1. **Drop the files.** Put the new TIFs alongside the existing per-well zips in
   `in/` (e.g. the second half's timepoints, or a new well's images). Run.
2. **Append** — `input_resolution_service.append_loose_images_to_zips` folds
   each loose TIF into its matching `<WELL>.zip` (creating `<WELL>.zip` for a
   brand-new well), then deletes the loose source. Duplicate member names keep
   the existing member (the loose copy is skipped, not overwritten).
3. **Scope decision** — `select_incremental_scope` sets `opts["incremental"]`
   when anything was appended, *unless* adding the new data would invalidate a
   model for already-processed work, in which case it falls back to a full
   `--force` reprocess:
   - a `basic` flat-field/background is sampled across **all** images, so adding
     any data changes it for every well → always force;
   - an `empty_well` model is per-(channel, timepoint). Adding a blank for a
     **new** timepoint leaves every existing timepoint's correction (and its
     already-processed FOVs) unchanged → stays incremental. But adding a blank
     at a timepoint the background well **already had a blank for** changes that
     timepoint's field, so the already-processed wells at it would be stale →
     force. The decision is self-contained in the input: it compares the
     appended blanks' timepoints against the background well's existing zip
     timepoints (`_loose_timepoints_for_wells` / `_zip_timepoints`).
4. **Args** — `build_pipeline_args` emits `--incremental` and
   `--incremental_prior_dir <output_dir>` (where the prior per-well CSVs live).
5. **Diff + process** — for each well, `process_well_zip_task` builds the
   done-set (`pipeline.io.incremental_done_fov_keys`): the `(fov, timepoint)`
   pairs from the prior per-well CSV, **unioned** with those recovered from the
   processed-output artefacts — `<well>_out.zip` members and the uncompressed
   output folder, whose names keep the input stem. The output fallback matters
   when a well has its `<well>_out.zip` but no sibling CSV (a remote-only
   materialise, or a CSV that was moved/lost): without it the done-set would be
   empty and every already-processed FOV would be needlessly re-segmented. It
   processes only the groups whose `(fov, timepoint)` isn't in the done-set, and:
   - a well with **no** new groups → logs `Well X — up to date (no new FOVs).`
     and returns (no rewrite);
   - a well with new groups → segments just those, then **merges**:
     `merge_records_into_csv` appends the new rows (dedup by
     `(well, fov, timepoint, nucleus_id)`) and `merge_images_into_zip` adds the
     new images to `<well>_out.zip`;
   - a brand-new well (no prior CSV) → processes in full.
6. **Globals refreshed** — `write_pipeline_info` rewrites `pipeline_info.json`
   with the refreshed `available_timepoints` / `available_fovs` scan while
   preserving curation (`cell_gating`, `sample_definitions`, `ratios`,
   `notes`); the auto-threshold pass re-runs but never overwrites an existing
   `cell_gating.thresh_frac_on` (so established thresholds are stable), and
   carries `cell_gating.thresh_count_on` through untouched — it rebuilds the
   block from named keys, so a cutoff it did not read would be dropped on write.
7. **Review** — stats/plots are recomputed live from the per-well CSVs on
   reload, so the new timepoints/FOVs appear with no extra step.

**Remote** keeps the client smart and the remote a dumb compute engine, so only
genuinely-new bytes cross the wire (see §6.4 / `services/remote_runner.py`):
`stage_local_zips` **splits** before upload — for each touched well it keeps
only the new-FOV members (`_filter_new_fovs_in_staging`, done-set from the local
CSV **unioned** with the local `<well>_out.zip`) and drops wells whose local
output already covers every input FOV (emitting `[remote] ✓ X: up to date
(local)`); the remote argv has `--incremental` stripped (it just processes what
it received); and on fetch the partial outputs are **merged** into the local
full CSV / `<well>_out.zip` with the same `pipeline.io` helpers.

**Dashboard:** up-to-date, merged, and new wells each reach a correct terminal
state — `ProgressTracker` maps the `up to date` / `merging N new FOV(s)` /
`SKIP well … output already exists` markers to per-well done/processed events
(§6.4 covers the separator-tolerant parsing that keeps this working when a
remote UTF-8 stream is decoded on a cp1252 Windows client).
