## 10. Cross-cutting concerns

### 10.1 Logging

- Every module uses
  `logging.getLogger("review")` (the viewer) or
  `logging.getLogger("review.auto_threshold")` (per-domain children).
- `allwell._attach_log_ring_buffer` captures every record into a ring
  buffer that the application log drawer (`⌘L`) reads from. It is attached to
  `"review"` (which does not propagate) and to the root logger, so every
  `allwell.*` and `__name__` logger reaches it too. It also turns on
  `logging.captureWarnings`, so Python `warnings.warn` calls arrive on
  `py.warnings` instead of only on stderr.
- **The application log holds every pane's warnings and errors.** Two of the
  app's logs are not fed by `logging` at all: the Analyze run log is the
  pipeline subprocess's stdout written straight into a widget
  (`analyze/log_pane.py::_log_lines`), and each Datasets tool page's raw log is
  its worker's `logLine` signal (`datasets/core/log_panel.py::append_log`).
  Both of those single entry points call `core.log_mirror.mirror_line`, which
  forwards a line to `allwell.analyze` / `allwell.datasets.<tool>` only when it
  is a WARNING or an ERROR — Analyze passes the tag it already coloured the line
  by, so the two surfaces cannot disagree; a Datasets line is an ERROR when it
  opens with the tools' `✗` failure mark and is otherwise judged by
  `services.pipeline_runner.classify_log_line`. The pipeline's own
  `asctime  LEVEL` prefix is stripped, since the app log stamps its own.
  The mirror loggers sit outside `"review"` on purpose: that logger also feeds
  Review's bottom status log, which is Review's own diary. Nothing in the app
  log is fed back into either pane, so the mirror cannot loop. Ordinary INFO
  lines stay in their pane only — a run says tens of thousands of them.
- **What no pane reports reaches it too.** `startup.boot_diag.install_excepthook`
  writes an uncaught exception to `allwell.uncaught` as well as the boot log,
  and installs a `threading.excepthook` that does the same for an exception
  that kills a background thread (which `sys.excepthook` never sees).
  `install_qt_cross_thread_trace`'s Qt message handler forwards Qt warnings,
  criticals and fatals to `allwell.qt`, behind a thread-local re-entrancy guard
  because the log handler's own queued signal can raise a Qt warning at
  teardown. `tests/test_errors_reach_the_app_log.py` drives each route.
- **A `logging.Handler` runs on whichever thread logged the record**, and in
  this app that includes every background thread there is: the remote runner's
  batch loop and its fetcher, the smFISH and cell-browser loaders, the gating
  `QThread`s, and every `swallowed()` breadcrumb any of them writes. So a
  handler that writes to a widget has to marshal, and `QTimer.singleShot(0, …)`
  is not a way to marshal even though it reads like one — the timer is created
  on the *calling* thread, so the callback never fires there (the line is lost)
  and destroying the abandoned `QObject` as the thread ends raises
  `QObject::killTimer: Timers cannot be stopped from another thread`. Both of
  the app's GUI log handlers go through `core.worker_bridge.GuiLogRelay`, a
  `QObject` built on the GUI thread whose queued signal may be emitted from
  anywhere. `tests/test_log_handler_marshalling.py` forbids the timer shape
  statically; `tests/test_log_handler_thread_safety.py` shows a worker-thread
  line arriving at both widgets.

### 10.2 Debug flags

`review/core/debug_flags.py` exposes module-level booleans, all of them
listed in that module's `FLAG_NAMES`: two master switches (`REVIEW_TAB_DEBUG`,
`ANALYZE_TAB_DEBUG`) and eight per-domain ones (`REVIEW_BAR_DEBUG`,
`REVIEW_SCATTER_DEBUG`, `REVIEW_IMAGE_DEBUG`, `REVIEW_IMAGE_LOAD_DEBUG`,
`REVIEW_IMAGE_CHANNEL_SWITCH_DEBUG`, `MOVIE_MONTAGE_DEBUG`,
`MOVIE_MONTAGE_LOAD_DEBUG`, `CELL_GATING_DEBUG`). `allwell.main()` copies the
top-of-file constants in `allwell.py` onto every name in `FLAG_NAMES`, so
toggling any of them is a one-line edit in one place. Each flag gates
`logger.debug` calls inside its domain, and all of them are off by default —
`tests/test_debug_flags_default_off.py` asserts that, and that the roster and
the wiring cover the same set.

### 10.3 Build / packaging

- **Source run:** `python allwell.py [--data_dir …]`.
- **macOS .app:** `_Docs/_Installation/build_all_well.sh` (mamba env +
  PyInstaller), spec at `_Docs/_Installation/all_well.spec`.
- **Windows .exe:** `scripts\build_executable.ps1 [-Clean]` — the PowerShell
  twin of `scripts/build_executable.sh`, driving the same spec. It invokes
  `python -m PyInstaller` rather than the `pyinstaller.exe` shim (not reliably
  on PATH from a fresh Miniforge Prompt) and reads the same `ALLWELL_PROFILE` /
  `ALLWELL_THEME` environment switches. Output is
  `dist\AllWell-<version>\AllWell.exe`; the spec's `BUNDLE` step is a macOS-only
  no-op, so no `.app` is produced. Both scripts resolve the bundle folder they
  report through `bundle_name()` (§5.3) instead of a hardcoded path, and
  `tests/test_profile_build.py` fails on any instruction that names an output
  folder under `dist/` with no version in it — no build has produced one since
  the name became versioned, and a reader following such an instruction cannot
  tell an empty directory from a build that failed.

  The documented invocation is
  `powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -File scripts\build_executable.ps1 -Clean`,
  and both halves of that prefix earn their place. The environment-setup steps
  put the user in the Miniforge Prompt, which is `cmd.exe` and cannot run a
  `.ps1` at all; and a stock Windows install refuses to run an unsigned local
  script, so PowerShell without the switch answers "running scripts is disabled
  on this system". `-ExecutionPolicy Bypass` is scoped to that one process.

  `build_executable.sh` is the Git Bash entry point on Windows as well as the
  macOS / Linux one, so it resolves its interpreter (`python3`, then `python`)
  rather than assuming `python3`: a Windows conda environment ships
  `python.exe` with no `python3.exe`, and the bundle-name lookup that used the
  bare name came back empty there — reporting failure after a build that had
  succeeded.
- **Feature-subset binary:** `ALLWELL_PROFILE=<name> scripts/build_executable.sh`
  builds a binary containing only that profile's features, with excluded
  features' source and unique heavy deps dropped from the bundle and the profile
  baked as `active_profile.txt` (§5.3 *Build profiles*). Unset = the full app.
- **Pipeline-only run:** `python process_microscopy.py --input_dir … --output_dir …`.
  No GUI deps required.

### 10.4 Running the tests — the full-app OOM caveat (read before `pytest tests/`)

The pytest suite has two very different kinds of test, and running them the
wrong way will **hang the run and OOM-kill the container**. Know which lane
you're in before you type the command.

- **Pure-logic / unit tests** (Qt-free: `pipeline/*`, `domain/*`,
  `spatial_compute`, `multivariate_compute`, layout math, …). Fast, cheap,
  safe to run in bulk. This is the CI "fast lane" — run it with
  **`scripts/test.sh`** (~7,260 tests of ~7,710 collected, ~3.5 min on a quiet
  container). CI invokes that same script, so a local run and the CI run cannot
  drift in flags or config; hand-rolling `pytest tests/ -m "not slow"` skips the
  `--timeout=90` CI applies. Re-count rather than trusting the figure when it
  matters: `python -m pytest tests -m "not slow" -q --collect-only | tail -1`
  prints the split in a few seconds.
- **Full-app tests** (anything using the `viewer_app` / `loaded_app` /
  `loaded_app_shape` / `image_table_app` fixtures — ~70 files). Each one
  constructs a **real `ReviewApp`** under the offscreen QPA. `conftest.py`'s
  `pytest_collection_modifyitems` auto-marks these `slow`, precisely so the fast
  lane skips them.
- **One-feature tests on a minimal shell** (`shell_ctx`, `tests/_minimal_shell.py`).
  A test whose subject is one feature needs that feature's `ViewerContext`, not
  `ReviewApp`. `minimal_shell` builds the context the way `ReviewApp.__init__`
  does — the feature registry, `AppState` with every feature's slice, one
  attribute store shared by the widget registry and the runtime namespaces, an
  `EventBus` — around a bare `QMainWindow` standing in as `ctx.window`;
  `load_dataset` loads a folder through the calls `load_controller` makes (the
  sidecar reader, the repository's per-well load, the timepoint and FOV caches,
  the channel recalculation) without the shell's dialogs, persistence restores
  and repaints. Nothing is stubbed. Measured on the mini dataset with the
  Playground built: 299 QObjects and 17 top-level widgets against the full app's
  4,304 and 158, and no `slow` mark, so these run in the fast lane.
  `tests/test_playground.py` is the first file on it: 21 Playground tests moved
  from `loaded_app`, each shown to fail under the same product mutation on both
  fixtures. A feature can only be mounted this way if it reaches the app through
  `ctx` rather than through `ctx.window` — the Playground read its own state as
  `ctx.window._app_state` until it was moved onto `ctx.state`, which is the
  shape to look for before migrating another feature's tests.

**Coverage is opt-in, and it is not a gate.** `ALLWELL_COVERAGE=1` in front of
either lane's script measures it; `scripts/coverage.sh` combines both lanes'
data and reports, `--zero` lists the modules no test reaches, `--diff` names the
lines the current branch adds that no test executes. Two properties are
deliberate. It is **off by default**, because measured on this container the
fast lane takes **11 min 06 s under coverage against ~3.5 min without** — three
times the cost of the check that gates every push, against a CI job capped at 15
minutes. And it is **never a percentage threshold**: over ~500 source files a
percentage is a number to game, while the question worth asking is which
application modules no test reaches at all. `.github/workflows/coverage.yml`
runs it on demand and monthly on `main` rather than per pull request, and says in
its own header what turning the per-PR trigger on would cost.

**Both lanes must be in the measurement before it is read.** The fast lane alone
reports every full-app-only module as dead — eleven modules, some 1,860
statements, most of them `widgets/` the slow lane exercises — and acting on that
list would delete live code. `coverage combine` merges the two, and two settings are what make that merge
mean anything — both measured after the plausible-sounding version of each
turned out to be false.

Parallel mode alone does **not** stop the slow lane's many short processes
overwriting one another, which this paragraph asserted for a while. pytest-cov
combines at the *end of each session*: it consumes that session's
`.coverage.<host>.<pid>.<rand>` files and writes `.coverage`, a name the next
batch's combine does not pick up and then overwrites. Two sequential runs
measured a module at 86 covered lines and then 68 — the second run's own
figure, not the union. Across the ~54 batches the lane runs, that leaves the
last batch's data wearing the whole lane's name, and it feeds the zero-coverage
inventory, so the error surfaces as "no test reaches this module" about modules
a test reaches. `scripts/test_slow.sh` gives each batch its own
`COVERAGE_FILE`, and the combined union measures 94 lines where the two runs
alone measured 86 and 68.

`relative_files = true` is the other. Coverage stores absolute paths by
default, which is invisible until two machines' data are combined — and the
slow lane is hours of work, so it is the obvious thing to dispatch to CI. A
runner's checkout at a different path yields a data file whose every entry is a
*different file* from the local one; the combine succeeds, reports roughly
twice as many modules as the repo has, and the inventory is wrong in the
direction that invents dead code.

**Getting both lanes into one measurement takes two dispatches.**
`.github/workflows/slow-lane.yml` takes a `coverage` dispatch input — opt-in, so
an ordinary "is the lane green" run is not slowed by a measurement it does not
want — and uploads one data file per shard.
`.github/workflows/coverage-inventory.yml` is the second half: give it that
run's id and it runs the fast lane under coverage on its own runner, pulls the
six shard artifacts across with `actions/download-artifact`, combines the lot,
and prints the inventory into the job log and the run summary. It refuses to
print anything if no shard data arrived, because the fast lane alone names
full-app-only modules unreached and that is the one error worth refusing to
make.

It takes the run id two ways, and the second one exists because not every
caller can use the first. A dispatch takes it as an input, which is what a
person clicking *Run workflow* wants; an assistant session cannot, because its
GitHub token carries `actions: read` and not `actions: write`, so the dispatch
API answers 403 and the measurement would sit waiting for someone to click. The
id can therefore also be written into `.github/coverage-inventory-run-id`, and a
push touching that one path starts the workflow — a trigger anything able to
push the branch can pull. The path filter is what keeps ordinary commits from
starting it, and the resolver validates the value is a bare number rather than
interpolating whatever the file holds into an artifact lookup.

Two workflows rather than one job appended to the slow lane, for two reasons.
The slow lane is six shards of up to 75 minutes, so an inventory obtainable only
by re-running all of it would cost hours for a list that can be rebuilt from
artifacts already paid for. And the finding has to *travel*: artifact downloads
redirect to Azure blob storage, which an egress policy can refuse while leaving
the GitHub API reachable, so a result readable only by someone able to fetch a
blob is a result some readers cannot get at. The job log is readable through the
API, so the log is where the answer goes; the combined data file is uploaded as
well, for anyone who can fetch it.

**Before pushing, `scripts/preflight.sh`** runs ruff, the fast lane, and a
working-tree check in one pass (`--quick` skips the fast lane). The tree check is
the non-obvious one: it fails on *untracked* files, because a hand-run job's
scratch output is what `git add -A` sweeps into a commit — that is how a sweep's
JUnit reports once reached `main`.

**No test may reach a modal dialog.** An `autouse` fixture in `conftest.py`
replaces every `QMessageBox` / `QInputDialog` / `QFileDialog` / `QColorDialog` /
`QFontDialog` opener and `QDialog.exec` with one that raises. Offscreen, a modal
dialog waits for a click that never comes, inside Qt's C++ event loop where
pytest's signal-based `--timeout` cannot reach it — so the run can only die at
the batch wall-clock ceiling, before pytest writes its JUnit report, taking a
whole batch down and skipping the rest of the hanging file. A test that means to
exercise a dialog path patches that specific call itself; its `monkeypatch` is
applied later and wins.

**Why the full-app tests are dangerous in bulk.** Constructing the app builds
about 1,260 QObjects under the window, and about 3,850 once the mini dataset is
loaded and the centre tabs drain, wired together with signal→bound-method
connections (`signal.connect(app._method)`), closures that capture `app`, and
child widgets that keep an `_app` back-reference (coordinators, `LabelGrid`,
`RatioMetricsPanel`, the `WidgetRegistry` / `ViewerContext` / `PersistenceRegistry`).
**A closed window is freed in a plain process.** `tests/perf/bench_app_retention.py`
constructs, closes and collects the app repeatedly; with the mini dataset loaded
no `ReviewApp` survives, no widget or app-class object is left behind, and RSS
grows by about 4–5 MB per construction (allocator and C-level caches; nothing
Python-attributable). Three roots used to hold every closed window, about 31 MB
each, and each is now pinned by `tests/test_a_closed_review_app_is_freed.py`:
a Qt subclass declared inside a builder with methods closing over `ctx` (the Home
notes box — `tests/test_qt_subclasses_live_at_module_scope.py` rules the shape
out everywhere), four hidden per-tab channel combos built with no parent and so
never deleted, and the deferred-tab drain re-arming a static
`QTimer.singleShot(0, callable)` that closed over the window (its timer is now a
child of the window, so a window closed mid-drain takes the drain with it).
Two of those shapes — a widget nothing parents but a signal connection over
`ctx` keeps alive, and a static timer closure over the context — are also
caught in the fast lane, for a feature built into the minimal shell:
`tests/test_a_closed_shell_is_freed.py` builds the Playground there, closes the
shell, and requires the window collected and no top-level widget left. Each
shape, injected into the Playground's builder, fails it; a bare parentless
widget does not, correctly, because nothing holds it once the context goes.
What a closed window left after that was measured and named rather than
estimated (`tests/perf/bench_app_retention.py`, five constructions per run, two
runs each): seven `QAction` wrappers per window, all from the dataset menu's
connected `addAction(text)` entries (see `widgets/owned_action.py`), and — with
no dataset loaded — the log drawer's `_GUILogHandler` with its relay and the
dead `QTextEdit`'s wrapper, which detached only when a later record arrived and
now also detaches on the widget's `destroyed` signal
(`tests/test_gui_log_handler_detaches.py`). With both fixed, every count is
zero per closed window — widgets, top-level widgets, PySide wrappers, objects of
the app's own classes — loaded and empty, in both runs; RSS still moves by a
few megabytes per construction and by a different amount each run (1.8 to
4.9 MB loaded), so it is reported, not budgeted.
`test_a_closed_window_leaves_no_wrapper_and_no_app_object_behind` holds the
zeros, compared by type so a regression names what leaked. **Under pytest the full-app fixtures still accumulate**, because `qtbot` holds
every app it is handed for the life of the test, and deleting the app's widgets
from a teardown fixture segfaults the interpreter *after* the tests themselves
have passed — which is why `conftest.py`'s widget reaper (below) exempts anything
marked `slow`.
pytest runs every test in **one process**, and the container has **no swap**, so
a big slow run:
- **hangs** — the ever-growing live-widget count makes each later test's Qt work
  progressively slower, until the suite crawls; and/or
- **gets OOM-killed** — RSS climbs unbounded until the orchestrator kills the
  container (which looks like a mid-run "restart").

Under pytest this is a property of the full-app fixtures rather than of any one
test — do not try to "fix" it by adding `gc.collect()` to a fixture (it doesn't
help while `qtbot` still holds the app).

**Rules for running tests here:**

1. **Bulk runs use the fast lane only:** `scripts/test.sh`. Never run a bare
   `pytest tests/` (or `-m slow` across everything) in this environment — that's
   the command that kills the container.
2. **Run full-app tests in small, fresh processes.** Invoke them a *file or two at
   a time* — `scripts/test.sh tests/test_app_smoke.py -m ""`,
   `scripts/test.sh tests/test_multivariate_tab.py -m ""` — so the OS reclaims the leaked memory
   when each short-lived process exits. Budget roughly ≤ ~15–20 full-app tests per
   process.
3. **Prefer the pure-logic layer.** New behaviour should be testable without the
   full app wherever possible (the `collect.py` / `_compute.py` / renderer-snapshot
   split exists partly for this). A Qt-free unit test never pays the per-app cost.
   Where a test needs Qt but its subject is one feature, build that feature's
   tab against `shell_ctx` (the minimal shell above) rather than `loaded_app`.
4. **Long runs will be interrupted.** A single `pytest` invocation that takes many
   minutes is at risk of a container recycle. Keep each invocation short; if you
   need broad coverage, script several small invocations rather than one large one.
5. **To run the whole slow lane, use `scripts/test_slow.sh`.** It applies rules 1,
   2 and 4 for you: it discovers the lane from pytest's own `slow` marker (the
   fixture closure in `conftest.py` is the only thing that knows the real
   membership), runs it as many short pytest processes a couple of files each,
   and aggregates the per-batch JUnit reports. A batch that dies before writing
   its report fails the run — that is the OOM / C-level-hang signal, and it must
   never read as success. `--shard I/N` deals the files out round-robin for a CI
   matrix; `--batch 1` is the safest setting on a constrained machine.

   Two ceilings guard a batch, and they do different jobs. `--timeout=300`
   (signal-based) catches a hung *test*. `SLOW_BATCH_TIMEOUT` (default 1800s) is
   the wall-clock backstop for a C-level hang inside Qt, which ignores signals.
   Keep the second one generous: app construction dominates this lane — the
   heaviest pair, `test_multivariate_tab` + `test_playground` (29 tests), takes
   ~12 minutes with the machine to itself and passes — and a batch cut off here
   writes no report, so too tight a ceiling reports green tests as a failure.

6. **Install the application stylesheet once per module, never per test.**
   `QApplication.setStyleSheet` re-polishes every live widget in the process, so
   a function-scoped fixture that installs `theme.qss()` multiplies that cost by
   the file's case count. Files that need the real sheet
   (`test_theme_roles_render.py`, `test_control_band_widget.py`,
   `test_disabled_controls_look_disabled.py`, `test_analyze_narrow_sidebar_fit.py`,
   `test_analyze_help_section.py`) install it from a `scope="module"` fixture and
   pay for it once. Applying the sheet to a single host widget instead
   (`test_control_row_spacing.py`) is cheaper again, and is the right shape
   whenever the assertion does not need it applied app-wide. `--durations=N` is
   how a violation shows up: the cost lands in `setup`, not in the test body.

7. **A fast-lane test does not keep the widgets it builds.** An autouse fixture,
   `conftest.py::_reap_widgets_the_test_created`, deletes the top-level widgets
   a test leaves behind, and it is the single largest thing standing between
   this lane and the state described in rule 1. Nothing in Qt reclaims a
   parentless `QWidget`: the application owns it, so it stays registered, stays
   matched against every rule of the stylesheet, and stays alive for the rest of
   the process. Measured across the forty `tests/test_a*.py` files alone, before
   the fixture existed: **93,446 live widgets, 2,425 of them top-level**, and
   one `QApplication.setStyleSheet` over that population took **70 seconds**.
   Reaping brings the same call back to 0.2 s.

   Only what the *test* built is reaped. The snapshot is taken when the fixture
   is set up, and pytest instantiates higher-scoped fixtures first, so a
   module-, class- or session-scoped widget is already in the snapshot and is
   never a candidate — the naive version deleted an `AnalyzeTab` shared by seven
   tests out from under the second one. Deletion is immediate
   (`shiboken6.delete`) rather than deferred: `deleteLater` posts an event only
   an event loop delivers, and this lane runs almost entirely without one.
   Anything marked `slow` is exempt, for the reason rule 1 gives.

8. **A guard parses the tree through `tests/_repo_scan.py`, never for itself.**
   `parse_source(path)` returns a per-process cached tree, and
   `parsed_sources()` pairs every application source with its own. Parsing the
   tree is 2.8 s — 479 files, 767k nodes — and roughly sixty guards in the lane
   want all of it; each parsing its own copy was about 150 s of the run. The
   cache is keyed on the source *text*, not the path or its stat, so a file
   rewritten in place (which is what `test_guards_bite.py` does between cases)
   is re-parsed rather than answered stale. **The trees are shared: read them,
   never mutate one.** `ast.parse` on a string a test builds is untouched by
   this and stays. `test_the_fast_lane_stays_fast.py` holds the rule.

9. **No test spawns `ssh`, `rsync`, `scp` or `sftp`.** The autouse
   `_no_real_network_tools` fixture hooks `subprocess.Popen.__init__` and raises
   on those four; a bare `rsync --version` (how `resolve_rsync_binary` finds a
   usable binary) is exempt, and every other binary is untouched. Sixteen
   fast-lane tests reached them, all at host aliases that exist nowhere, because
   the remote layer's seams nest: a test patching `Fetcher._rsync` still let
   `_pull_settings_marker`, `_list_remote_glob` and `_retry_missing_wells`
   through to the real thing. Four cost 14.0 s apiece — `_rsync_with_retry`
   reads the failure as a flaky network and makes three attempts 2 + 4 + 8 s
   apart. The `offline_transport` fixture answers those primitives as an
   unreachable host; `tests/test_remote_runner.py` and
   `tests/test_remote_transit_volume.py` take it module-wide with
   `pytestmark = pytest.mark.usefixtures("offline_transport")`. The error names
   the seam to patch. Note that `_retry_missing_wells` lists a well's CSVs with
   its own inline `subprocess.run(ssh … bash -s)` rather than through
   `DatasetCache._ssh_script` — a fourth spelling of "list files on the remote",
   and the one a test is most likely to miss.

10. **No autouse fixture makes a numbered temp directory.** `tmp_path` and
   `tmp_path_factory.mktemp` choose each new directory's number by listing every
   entry already in the session's base temp directory, so a call costs time in
   proportion to the directories the session has made so far. Called once per
   test from an autouse fixture, that makes the lane's total setup quadratic in
   its test count: two `mktemp` calls measured 0.2 ms at the first test, 16 ms
   at the 3,000th and 30 ms at the 6,000th. Three autouse fixtures did it — the
   settings, scan-cache and run-journal isolation — and across ~10,300 tests
   setup came to 316 s against 259 s of test bodies, which put the CI job past
   its 15-minute cap on every branch. They now take a per-test directory from
   `tempfile.mkdtemp` under one session-scoped root
   (`conftest._autouse_scratch_root`, via `conftest._scratch_dir`), whose cost
   does not grow; setup fell to 22 s and the lane from 10 min 27 s to 5 min 13 s
   on the same machine. A test that asks for `tmp_path` itself still pays the
   listing, which is fine at the scale a test's own request happens.
   `test_the_fast_lane_stays_fast.py` holds the rule.

11. **The lane runs in parallel, a file per worker.** `scripts/test.sh` adds
   `-n auto --dist loadfile` when pytest-xdist is installed (it is pinned in
   `tests/requirements-dev.txt`): one worker process per CPU, and every test of
   a file on the same worker, so a module-scoped fixture is still built once and
   tests that rely on running in order within their file still do.
   `ALLWELL_TEST_WORKERS=0` runs serially — the setting for a `--durations`
   profile, which a parallel run splits across workers — and any other number
   sets the worker count. Parallel workers share the machine, so a test may not
   share a path with another test: the pipeline's scratch directory defaults to
   `~/.allwell/scratch` and names a well's extraction directory for the well
   alone, so two tests processing `A01` at once deleted each other's images.
   `conftest._pipeline_scratch_goes_to_a_scratch_directory` gives every test its
   own `ALLWELL_SCRATCH_DIR` (a test measuring the default resolution unsets
   it), and `_session_pipeline_scratch` gives the worker one before any module-
   or session-scoped fixture runs — those are set up before a test's own
   fixtures, and a module fixture that ran a whole nanowell plate otherwise
   extracted into the shared default. The same collision is what two lanes run side by side used to hit. CI
   gates on the JUnit report, which the controller writes from every worker's
   results.

   A worker that crashes takes its file down with it ("node down: Not properly
   terminated"), and the controller can then hang at 99 % waiting on it, so a
   crash a serial run survives by luck is a stopped lane here. The one seen was
   the widget reaper (rule 7) deleting the Analyze pane while the pre-run
   coverage scan's daemon thread (`aw-preflight-scan`) was emitting its answer
   to it; the faulthandler stack in the boot log showed both threads. So the
   reaper first joins every thread the test started, for up to
   `_THREAD_JOIN_SECONDS` (2 s) each, skipping Qt's own threads, which
   `threading` sees as unjoinable dummies. A long-lived worker such as the
   persistence writer never ends, and the sixteen tests that leave one pay the
   full wait — about 8 s of the lane's wall time.

**The slow lane runs on demand, not on PRs and not on a schedule** —
`.github/workflows/slow-lane.yml`, six sharded runners, dispatched by hand from
the Actions tab; `scripts/test_slow.sh` runs the same lane locally. It is not a
PR gate because it takes minutes rather than seconds and its per-test memory
profile is fragile under parallel load. It exists because the ~270 tests it
covers previously had *no* automated coverage anywhere, so a test could sit red
indefinitely with nothing to report it — several did, each one a `ctx`-taking
function called with the raw app from the day that function migrated.

It used to also fire on a 04:00 UTC cron, which is where "run it by hand" came
from being advice rather than the only route. Six shards of up to 75 minutes ran
every day whether anything had changed or not, so the schedule was dropped. That
trade buys back the daily cost and gives up the daily signal: nothing now
notices a full-app test going red except a person choosing to look. Run it
deliberately — before merging anything that reshapes a feature package, and after
any change to the app's construction or teardown.

That particular defect also has a *static* counterpart in the fast lane
(`tests/test_frozen_ctx_guardrail.py`), which scans the test suite's own call
sites: on a real `ReviewApp`, `ctx.window` resolves to Qt's `QWidget.window`
**method** instead of raising, so the failure surfaces frames later — or not at
all, when the callee wraps its body in a `try`, leaving a green test that
asserted nothing. Catching it statically means it no longer depends on the
slow lane being run at all.

**What the environment gives you that CI does not (and vice versa).** The two
lanes are not the same machine, and the differences decide which failures you
can reproduce:

| | CI | A dev machine |
|---|---|---|
| Deps | `tests/requirements-dev.txt`, pinned to the app's stack (numpy 1.24, pandas 2.2, PySide6 6.7.3) | `requirements.txt` — same pins, plus the ML stack |
| ML stack | absent — `importorskip("stardist")` / `("tensorflow")` tests **skip** | present, so those tests actually run |
| OS / Python | ubuntu-latest, 3.11, case-sensitive FS | typically macOS arm64, 3.10.14, case-**in**sensitive FS |
| Timeout | `--timeout=90` per test | same, via `scripts/test.sh` |
| State | fresh clone — no `~/.allwell/scratch`, no datasets, no `__pycache__` | whatever you have lying around |

So a green CI run has *not* exercised StarDist or TensorFlow, and a green local
run has not proven your filenames are case-correct for Linux. The dep pins were
lower bounds until recently, which had CI resolving numpy 2.x / pandas 3.x
against an app that ships numpy 1.24 / pandas 2.2 — the single largest source of
"passes locally, fails in CI". Keep them pinned.

The pytest configuration lives in **`pyproject.toml`** (`[tool.pytest.ini_options]`),
not `tests/pytest.ini`. That matters: an ini under `tests/` is found by
`pytest tests/` (rootdir becomes `tests/`) but *not* by a bare `python -m pytest`
from the repo root (rootdir stays at the root), so markers, `filterwarnings`, and
`testpaths` silently applied in one lane and not the other. A root config is
discovered from either.

### 10.5 End-to-end segmentation tests (`tests/test_segmentation_e2e.py`)

One test per segmentation method the Analyze dropdown offers — `stardist_nuclei`,
`stardist_seeded_watershed_cell`, `cellpose`, `cellpose_labelfree`,
`classical_threshold` — each run through the **real Analyze tab**: a synthetic
plate of schema-named TIFFs is written to a tmp dir, the form is filled the way
an operator would fill it, `_run()` is called, and the Qt event loop is pumped
until the `process_microscopy.py` subprocess the tab spawned exits. Nothing is
mocked, so one test covers the grouping (zipper) phase, the subprocess launch,
the log/progress plumbing, segmentation, quantification, per-well CSV assembly
and output zipping. The assertions are on the artefacts that land in
`raw/out/` (per-well CSV rows, `pipeline_info.json`, `_labels.tif` inside
`<well>_out.zip`) plus the tab's completion contract (the "Processing Complete"
banner and the `on_pipeline_complete` callback).

Complementary to, not a replacement for, `test_segmentation_methods.py` /
`test_labelfree_phase.py` (form state + CLI arg mapping, no run) and
`test_pipeline_e2e.py` (`process_image_group` / `process_well_folder_task`
directly, no GUI).

Test images come from `tests/fixtures/synthetic_pipeline.write_synthetic_channels`,
the multi-channel generalisation of `write_synthetic_fov`: every channel draws the
same nuclei centres, with the kind (`nuclear` / `fluor` / `cytoplasm` / `phase`)
picking disk radius and intensities, so cytoplasm and phase channels are
registered with the nuclei the way a real acquisition is.

Skips and cost. The module is marked `slow` (each test loads a segmentation
model), so the fast lane never picks it up; run it on its own:
`scripts/test.sh tests/test_segmentation_e2e.py -m ""`. The StarDist tests need
TensorFlow + StarDist and the Cellpose tests need Torch + Cellpose *and* the
model weights already cached under `~/.cellpose/models` (or
`CELLPOSE_LOCAL_MODELS_PATH`) — Cellpose downloads them from cellpose.org on
first use, which an offline or egress-restricted machine cannot do. Where any of
that is missing the affected tests skip and `classical_threshold`, which needs
nothing beyond scipy/skimage, still runs. Availability is probed with
`importlib.util.find_spec`, never an import: TensorFlow and Torch cannot always
share a process, and the pipeline keeps each run in its own subprocess precisely
to avoid that.

### 10.6 Environment bootstrap for remote sessions

`.claude/hooks/session-start.sh`, registered as a `SessionStart` hook in
`.claude/settings.json`, provisions a Claude Code on the web container so the
linter and the fast lane can run there. It installs the Qt system libraries
(`libegl1`, `libgl1`, `libxkbcommon0`, `libdbus-1-3`) and
`tests/requirements-dev.txt`, mirroring `.github/workflows/ci.yml`'s setup steps
so a remote session and CI resolve the same pinned versions from the same file.
Both steps are guarded by a presence check, so a cached container re-runs the
hook in well under a second.

**The test stack lives in a virtualenv built from a pinned-compatible
interpreter**, `$HOME/.allwell-test-venv` (overridable with
`ALLWELL_TEST_VENV`), made with `python3.11` — what CI runs — or `python3.12`,
the newest `PySide6==6.7.3` publishes wheels for. The hook never installs into
bare `python3`: that is whatever the image's default happens to be, and when it
became 3.13 pip could resolve no PySide6, the hook exited 1, and the session
started with no test stack at all, because a failing `SessionStart` hook does
not stop the session. The hook then appends `VIRTUAL_ENV` and a `PATH` with the
venv's `bin/` first to `$CLAUDE_ENV_FILE`, which is how a `SessionStart` hook
sets environment for every later command — so `scripts/test.sh`'s plain
`python` and a bare `ruff` both resolve to the venv. With neither interpreter
installed it exits 1 with a one-line message naming the `python3` it found,
rather than pip's list of every PySide6 version it could not use.

Without it a fresh remote container has no test stack at all, and every test
collection dies at `import PySide6` with `libEGL.so.1: cannot open shared object
file` — Qt needs GL/EGL even under the offscreen QPA platform.

Every workflow that installs those libraries — `ci.yml`, `slow-lane.yml`,
`coverage.yml`, `coverage-inventory.yml` — lets `apt-get update` report errors
without failing the step, and gates on the `apt-get install` beneath it instead.
`update` exits non-zero when *any* configured repository's index fails to fetch,
including the third-party ones the runner image ships and this project does not
use, so a stale google-chrome index on `dl.google.com` failed a whole CI run
before a line of Python was executed. The install is the honest gate: a library
that genuinely cannot be fetched still fails it, by name.

The hook exits immediately when `CLAUDE_CODE_REMOTE` is not `true`: a developer
machine has its own environment (`requirements.txt`) and the hook must
never touch it. It also deliberately does **not** install the ML stack —
TensorFlow + StarDist and Torch + Cellpose are several GB and only the `slow`
segmentation tests need them, which is the same line `tests/requirements-dev.txt`
draws. A remote session that needs to run §10.5's StarDist or Cellpose tests
installs that stack by hand.

---

### 10.7 The fake worker host (`tests/_fake_remote.py`)

A remote run is a long sequence of ssh commands whose whole purpose is to
change a filesystem the test cannot see, so a mock that records argv proves
only that a string was built. `FakeRemote` answers instead: it points a real
`bash` at a temporary directory as `HOME` and runs the script the runner
composed, so `mkdir -p`, `test -d`, `touch`, `rm -rf` and the rest have effects
the test asserts against with `exists()` and `tree()`.
`tests/test_a_remote_run_end_to_end.py` drives a real `spawn` and
`verify_and_cleanup` through it.

Three rules keep it from being kinder than production, each of them a bug the
harness reported as a clean run before it was fixed.

**`check=True` raises.** `_ssh_run` passes `check` straight to
`subprocess.run`, so a failing remote command aborts the run; a fake that
swallowed it turned a silent-continue-with-no-directories-created into a
passing test.

**A transfer that moves nothing exits 23**, as real rsync does. Returning 0
made every failure branch downstream unreachable — `Fetcher`'s per-well "could
not pull", `_rsync_optional`'s "note: X not pulled", and all of
`_retry_missing_wells` — so a regression that transferred no bytes read as
success. rsync itself is *modelled* here rather than run, since it is not
installed; the four modelling rules that the runner depends on (a file
destination stays a file, `-R` reproduces the source path, a glob expands, a
missing source fails) are pinned by a test of their own, because untested
modelling is how a harness reports correct code as broken.

**A host it cannot contain is refused.** Containment is one mechanism —
`HOME` points at the fake root, so `~/x` and `$HOME/x` land inside it — and
`_bash` hands the script to the shell verbatim, rewriting nothing. An absolute
`remote_staging_dir` such as `/scratch/$USER`, the normal configuration on a
cluster whose home is a small-quota NFS mount, would therefore run its
`mkdir -p` and its `rm -rf` against the machine running the suite while every
assertion read the empty fake root and passed. `install` refuses such a host
and names the field.

**A test that spawns a run must stop it**, via the `stop_fetchers` fixture in
`tests/conftest.py`. A spawned run owns a `Fetcher` with two daemon threads —
the pull-queue drain and the sidecar poller — and both call rsync on a timer
that nothing reaps when the test ends. Sixteen of them leaked out of one file,
and one of the pollers fired inside `test_remote_midrun_sidecar`'s half-second
window minutes later, appending a pull to *that* test's call list and failing
an assertion about a poller it had no connection to. It presented as a test
failing in CI for no reason it named, on a run whose ordering happened to
differ from a local one. An autouse guard beside the fixture stops any that are
left and fails the test that left them; it judges on whether the fetcher was
*asked* to stop, not on whether its threads have finished — a thread cancelled
a microsecond earlier is still alive, and judging on liveness failed every test
that had cleaned up correctly.

The `Popen` seam matches the same ssh prefixes `_run` does and delegates
everything else to the real `Popen`, captured at import. Both patches land on
the *shared* `subprocess` module — `subprocess.run` looks `Popen` up in its own
globals — so an unmatched patch would answer the fake's own shell calls with
the test's mock, and a seam that matched nothing would record an unrelated
binary as a pipeline launch.

---


## 11. How-to guides

### 11.1 Add a new plotting tab

1. Create `review/features/<name>/tab_view.py` with a
   `build_<name>_tab(ctx, parent)` function. Model it on
1. Create `review/features/<name>/` with `__init__.py`, `controller.py`
   (and, if you're rendering matplotlib, `renderer.py`), and `tab_view.py`.
   The `tab_view.build_<name>_tab(ctx, parent)` minimum:
   - `make_plot_with_right_dock(parent)` for the export dock.
   - A controls row with `btn_secondary("Properties", …,
     icon="sliders-horizontal")` as the rightmost widget.
   - A `PlotCard` that hosts your figure(s).
   - Register the figure / canvas / dock / card in the widget registry:
     `ctx.widgets.register("_<name>_fig", fig)`, etc. (`register` also
     setattrs the widget onto the app, so legacy `app._<name>_fig` reads
     resolve via plain attribute lookup). Do **not** assign new loose
     `app._*` attributes.
2. In `controller.py`, write a `redraw` pure function. Read state from the
   typed objects (`ctx.state.plot`, `ctx.state.dataset`, …); import
   `review.core.<...>_state` / `review.features.<name>.state`
   freely — they are import-safe. Don't import `ReviewApp`.
3. Wire the controller's `redraw` into the redraw pipeline. Either:
   - Add a branch to `core/plot_orchestrator.redraw` (if it should redraw on
     every selection change); or
   - Add an `app._redraw_<name>()` shim on `ReviewApp` and call it from
     the relevant tab-change / selection-change paths in
     `core/selection_controller`.
4. Register the tab in `core/centre_view.py`'s `groups` list (it sits
   under "Analysis" / "Images" / "Data" sections) and create a
   `_build_<name>()` closure that calls your `build_<name>_tab`.
5. Add an icon to `_SECTION_ICONS` in `runtime_app.py` if you want it to
   appear in the rail nav.
6. End your redraw with
   `core.plot_style.apply_export_style_to_current(ctx, fig, canvas)` so the
   Properties sidebar's toggles apply.

### 11.2 Add a sidebar widget for a specific tab

1. Add `<name>_view.py` (or extend an existing `*_view.py`) in the owning
   feature package — `review/features/<feature>/` — with a
   `build_<name>(app, parent)` function. Pure cross-cutting sidebar bodies
   (e.g. the main plate picker) live in `review/core/sidebar_view.py`.
2. In `runtime_app._build_ui`, allocate a `QWidget` for it and hide it by
   default:
   ```python
   self._sidebar_<name>_frame = QWidget()
   QVBoxLayout(self._sidebar_<name>_frame).setContentsMargins(0, 0, 0, 0)
   sidebar_layout.addWidget(self._sidebar_<name>_frame, 1)
   self._sidebar_<name>_frame.hide()
   ```
3. In `core/tab_controller.on_tab_change`, show your frame on the relevant
   tab and hide every other sibling frame.
4. Build the frame body lazily — usually called from the tab's
   `_build_<tab>()` closure in `core/centre_view.py`.

### 11.3 Persist some state to disk

1. Create `review/persistence/<name>.py` with a `load_from_data_dir(app)`
   and `save_to_data_dir(app)` pair.
2. The file lives at `<data_dir>/<name>.json` (or as a key under
   `pipeline_info.json` if it's pipeline-coupled).
3. Add `app._<name>_load_from_data_dir = <name>.load_from_data_dir`-style
   bindings in `ReviewApp.__init__` if you want the shim style, or
   call the module functions directly.
4. Hydrate at load time (`load_controller.load_directory` already calls
   each persistence module's loader at the end). Persist on user-driven
   edits, never on every signal — debounce with a `QTimer.singleShot(0, …)`
   if many small edits arrive together.

### 11.4 Add a new channel-ratio metric or aggregation

1. The ratio model is in `domain/ratio_models.py` (`RatioMetric` dataclass)
   and the persistence layer in `persistence/ratios.py`.
2. Aggregations are configured in `data/data_loading.aggregate_with_threshold_df`
   and `_aggregate_arrays`. Add the new metric as a column or in the
   AggPoint tuple, then teach `bar_metric_row` / `line_metric_row` in
   `features/export/service.py` how to format it for CSV export.

### 11.5 Hook a new keyboard shortcut

Add a `QShortcut(QKeySequence("Ctrl+X"), self, activated=self._handler)`
line in `AllWellApp._install_shortcuts` (`allwell.py`). The help drawer's
shortcut list is in `_toggle_help_drawer` in the same file — keep it
in sync.

### 11.6 Give a new page its help

Adding a Review tab, a Datasets tool, or an Analyze form section means adding
two things: a section in `_Docs/Markdowns/README_WellViewer.md`, and an entry in
the matching map in `ui/help_topics.py` whose value is that heading's exact text.
Without both, the drawer opens on the mode overview for that page and nothing
says so.

For a **Datasets tool or an Analyze form section**, `tests/test_help_topics.py`
fails until they are there: it reads the Datasets roster out of `datasets/tab.py`
and the section titles out of `analyze/form.py`, so neither can be added
without the guard noticing.

For a **Review tab** nothing enforces it. Review leaves are resolved at run time
through `tab_controller.current_centre_tab` and `SECTION_BY_PAGE` deliberately
keeps loose aliases for renamed and prefixed ones, so there is no roster to check
a key against. A new Review tab without a `SECTION_BY_PAGE` entry silently opens
the drawer on the Review overview, and the fast lane stays green. Add the entry
by hand.

## 12. Debugging recipes

### 12.1 "Where is this widget defined?"

The Review pane is built bottom-up; every widget is stored on
`ReviewApp` as `_<noun>`. Grep first for the attribute name:

```bash
grep -rn '_line_fig\b' review/ widgets/
```

That returns both the producer (a `tabs/*_tab_view.py`) and every consumer.
For widgets in the rail nav, search `centre_view.py`. For controls in the
title bar, search `allwell.py`.

### 12.2 "The plot is showing the wrong data"

In order of probability:

1. **Stale `_active_channel`.** Check `_update_channel_selector` ran with
   the current dataset's channel list and that the Plotting band combo's
   current text matches `_active_channel.upper()`.
2. **A controller didn't get the redraw entry-point call.** Check the
   feature's `on_selection_changed` hook in `features/registry.py`, which
   `selection_controller._refresh_tab_view` dispatches to.
3. **The selection was painted but not committed.** Make sure the path that
   changed `_selected_wells` also called `app._on_plate_sel_change()` (the
   Select all / Select none buttons used to skip this).

### 12.3 "The pipeline ran but Review can't see the channels"

`process_microscopy.py` writes `pipeline_info.json` with `fluor_tokens`,
`schema`, `separator`, and `available_timepoints`. The viewer reads those
in `domain/viewer_state.read_pipeline_info`. If the file is missing, the viewer
falls back to detecting channels from a sample CSV's column names
(`data/data_loading.detect_fluor_channels`). Check both:

```bash
cat <data>/pipeline_info.json | python -m json.tool | grep -A1 fluor_tokens
head -1 <data>/<one>_measurements.csv
```

### 12.4 "Auto-threshold reports 'timepoint unknown'"

`review/data/zip_members.classify_member` parses `(fov, tp)` from each
image filename. (`features/preview/controller` re-exports the name for
backward compatibility, and that shim is where this section used to point —
reading it will not show you the parsing.) It prefers the schema-derived fields from
`pipeline_info.json` (`pipeline_fields_extractor`) and only falls back to
the legacy 5-field regex when those are absent. If you see "unknown", the
pipeline_info schema is either missing or doesn't include `fov` / `tp`
fields. Make sure `--filename_schema` was correct at pipeline-run time.

### 12.5 "Tab body doesn't appear when I click the rail"

Centre pages build lazily. The first time you click a page, its builder
runs from `centre_view._on_tab_change`. If the builder raises an exception,
the log captures it — open the help drawer's log tab or run
`python allwell.py` from a terminal and watch stderr. The most common
failure is a missing widget attribute on `ReviewApp` because two
builders touch a shared attribute in the wrong order. Use the
`_centre_lazy_only_titles` set in `centre_view.py` to control which
builders never run from the background drain.

### 12.6 "The figure's Properties panel doesn't stick"

Every figure-styling toggle writes into the shared prefs dict
(`core/export_prefs_state.py`, reached as `app._export_style_prefs`; the panel
itself is `features/export/sidebar_view.py`). Every controller ends its redraw
with `core.plot_style.apply_export_style_to_current(ctx, fig, canvas)`.
If a new redraw entry point you added is "losing" the user's toggles, it's
missing that call at the end.

### 12.7 "PyInstaller .app launches but freezes / can't find a module"

Three places to check:

1. The spec file `_Docs/_Installation/all_well.spec` has explicit
   `hiddenimports` for every non-trivial dependency (numpy internals,
   skimage submodules, stardist, csbdeep, …). Add yours there.
2. The launcher `all_well_launcher.py` sets `matplotlib.use("QtAgg")`
   before `pyplot` import — if matplotlib isn't picking up Qt, this is
   why.
3. The build script `_Docs/_Installation/build_all_well.sh` enumerates
   every required file. Missing inputs fail loudly.

### 12.8 "The app died with no Python traceback (segfault / access violation)"

`startup.boot_diag` is imported before PySide6 and arms `faulthandler` onto a per-launch
**boot log** in `startup.boot_diag.user_state_dir()` — `%LOCALAPPDATA%\allwell` on
Windows, `~/.cache/allwell` elsewhere, the system temp directory if neither is
writable, and also where a frozen build's matplotlib font cache goes — so a
hard native crash dumps a
C/Python stack there even from a windowed build with no console, and a *hang*
leaves its last-reached milestone as the log's final line. `install_excepthook`
writes any uncaught Python exception to the same file.

**A log that recorded a crash is kept.** The boot log is truncated per launch so
it describes the current attempt, which is what makes it useful after a hang.
That erased the evidence in the one case it mattered most: the thing a user does
after a crash is relaunch, and the relaunch deleted the traceback the crash
dialog had just told them to read. `_rotate_if_it_recorded_a_crash` therefore
moves a log carrying a crash marker (`FATAL uncaught exception`, or one of
`faulthandler`'s) aside to `allwell-boot.log.1` … `.CRASH_LOG_KEEP` first;
`crash_log_paths()` lists the survivors, newest first. Logs from launches that
ended quietly are still overwritten, so a dozen ordinary restarts cannot push
the one crash out of the ring. The crash dialog also carries the traceback in
its "Show Details" section, so the usual case needs no file at all — and it no
longer says "failed to start", which was untrue for every crash that happened
after start-up.

**A cross-thread Qt warning names its culprit.** "Timers cannot be stopped from
another thread" and its siblings are Qt *warnings*; the native crash that often
follows dumps the stack of the thread it happened on, which says nothing about
the code that reached across. `install_qt_cross_thread_trace`, installed by
`allwell.main` once the `QApplication` exists, is a Qt message handler that —
for the first `_CROSS_THREAD_DUMPS` such warnings — writes the message, the
thread that raised it and every thread's Python stack to the boot log, then
passes the message on as Qt would. The stacks are formatted by hand from
`sys._current_frames()`, not by `faulthandler`, whose header lines are the crash
markers above: a warning in that format would have the next launch keep and
report a crash that never happened. `tests/test_a_cross_thread_qt_warning_is_traced.py`
stops a GUI-thread `QTimer` from a named worker thread and reads the log.

Run from a terminal to capture the same output live. These usually come from touching a Qt widget tree mid-event-dispatch or after
its C++ object is deleted — e.g. the Split View focus filter (§5.10) defers its
pane switch with `QTimer.singleShot(0, …)` precisely to avoid reparenting during
`MouseButtonPress` delivery.

## 13. The `Markdowns/` library

The `Markdowns/` folder is intentionally small — it holds live reference docs,
not historical plans / status write-ups (those live in git history). What
remains:

| File | What it's for |
|------|---------------|
| `ARCHITECTURE.md` | This document — the developer-oriented architectural overview. |
| `README_WellViewer.md` | User-facing README — install, run, troubleshoot. |
| `GOD_OBJECT_REPOSITORY_ROADMAP.md` | Living plan for the god-object teardown + repository introduction; tracks the ratchet numbers as they come down. |

The on-disk shape of `pipeline_info.json::sample_definitions` (the saved
selections schema) is described in the `domain/selections_format.py`
module docstring; that module is the live source of truth for the
contract.

`_Docs/design/` holds the **non-Markdown** design artifacts — the
HTML mockups (`grey_theme_mockup.html`, `image_table_builder_mockup.html`) — for
visual reference only. Rendered screenshots live under
`_Docs/visual_audit/screenshots/`, produced by `tests/visual/render_views.py` —
a generated directory, git-ignored, so a re-run does not show up as two dozen
modified binaries.

That script builds the real `AllWellApp` off-screen against the `mini_dataset`
fixture and walks every rail entry, inner sub-tab, mode and dialog. Two things
it has to get right, because both have silently cost it coverage: it drives
controllers with the frozen `ViewerContext` (`rev._ctx`), never the window —
passing the window resolves `ctx.window` to `QWidget.window`, a bound method, and
the first controller attribute access raises; and a tab whose alternate views are
a `SegmentedControl` rather than an inner `QTabWidget` needs its own capture pass,
since the generic `_capture_inner` walker cannot see them. Multivariate is the
case in point — its four analysis modes swap different option groups into the
control row, so only a per-mode pass exercises the one that makes the row wrap.

`render_views.py` never opens the Properties dock, so a refactor of the panel
gets its own capture: `tests/visual/render_properties_panel.py <out_dir>` builds
the real `ExportStyleSidebar` for each figure kind whose panel differs, against
the Properties tests' stub app, and writes each panel as opened and fully
expanded plus one JSON fingerprint (widget tree, grid positions, instance
attributes, bound keys, sections, registered observers). Both outputs are
deterministic on one machine — the grabs wait out the toggle-switch animation,
which otherwise leaves a few hundred pixels different between two runs of the
same code — so running it on both trees and comparing with `cmp` and a pixel
diff shows exactly what changed. It takes an output directory rather than
writing into the repository.

## 14. Glossary

| Term | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| **Pane** | One of the three top-level pages: Review, Analyze, or Datasets. |
| **Tab** | A centre-stack page inside the Review pane (Plotting, Statistics, …). |
| **Sub-tab** | A leaf page inside a parent tab (e.g. Plotting → Line Graphs). |
| **Sidebar** | The left rail in the Review pane. Hosts the rail nav + the well picker + per-tab control panels. |
| **Ctxbar** | The horizontal contextual control row above each plot card. Hosts channel / metric / timepoint combos + action buttons. |
| **PlotCard** | The framed container around each matplotlib figure. Provides the screen↔publication toggle, the custom toolbar, and the stats chip slot. |
| **Properties sidebar / Export Style sidebar** | The right-side dock that slides out when the user clicks the Properties button on a plot card. Backed by `app._export_style_prefs`. |
| **Selection** | A named, persisted subset of wells. Lives in `ctx.state.selection.selections` (schema v2). Surfaced in the UI as a **group** on Home → Sample Map → Replicates. |
| **Group** | *Which wells are replicates of one condition?* A `Selection` as the user meets it on Home → Sample Map → Replicates: a named well set with a colour, a hidden flag and a place in the plot order. **It pools.** Every plot, Statistics and Batch Export draw one member per visible group, and a saved fold-change `ControlRef` is keyed on its name. |
| **Replicate set** | The `ReplicateSet` a group becomes when a plot asks what to pool. On Home → Sample Map → Groups a group **is** exactly one replicate set — its `wells` are its replicate members (or a single well); there is no `replicates` sub-partition (the field is reserved/`None`). "Quick Replicates" auto-builds groups of a chosen size N (spinbox) along rows/columns, naming each one from the sample variables its wells hold (`HeLa · 10 µM`) and falling back to the well tokens where the variables cannot say. `domain/plot_members.plot_replicate_sets` is the one place the sets a plot pools into are decided, and a sample variable chosen as *Group by* substitutes for the user's groups there. (The separate batch-export `BarGroup` — from a user-picked `bar_groups.json` — can still hold multiple member sets + solo wells; that is a distinct feature.) |
| **Sample variable** | *What did you change across the plate?* A named annotation axis with a type, an optional unit and an **ordered** list of values, assigned per well (`domain/sample_variables`, `pipeline_info.json::variables`). **It pools, inks, bands and names** — *Group by*, *Colour by*, *Split by*, the Response x axis, the two-factor tests, and, through `sample_variables.label_for_well`, what a well is called on a figure when no well label was typed for it. A variable is not a group: two cell lines at six doses is twelve conditions and nobody has to paint twelve group names. |
| **Well label** | *What should this well be called on a figure?* Free text per well (`sample_definitions.well_labels`), edited on Home → Sample Map → Well Labels. **Display only** — it pools nothing. It is the **first** of the two rungs `selections_model.well_display_label_and_source` answers with, and so substitutes for the well token in legends, tick labels, image captions and exported names, and, through `selections_model.replicate_display_label`, for a group's own name when that name looks auto-generated — except where the group carries `name_is_verbatim`, which is how a group named after a sample variable keeps a dose of `10` on the axis instead of the wells that received it. |
| **Saved selection** | A named set of lit wells in the rail drawer under the plate map, reloadable in one click (`persistence.json::plot_groups`, mirrored into the `sample_definitions` block). **It pools nothing** — loading one lights wells and toggles group visibility, and never edits a group's membership. The symbols and the on-disk key still say `plot_group`; that is a spelling, not a second concept. |
| **`pipeline_info.json`** | The sidecar file written by `process_microscopy.py` next to the per-well CSVs. Holds schema, channel tokens, available timepoints, persisted selections, gating thresholds. |
| **Well token** | Two-letter / two-digit well identifier (`A01` … `H12`). Always uppercase, always zero-padded. |
| **fov, tp** | Field-of-view and timepoint extracted from a filename via the schema-aware extractor in `viewer_state.make_schema_extractor`. |
| **Split View** | Optional mode (§5.10) showing two different Review tabs side-by-side, both live. All machinery is in `core/split_view.py`, wired by one `install_split_view(app)` call (comment it out → feature gone). |
| **Provider hook** | A module-level callable on `tab_controller` (`split_focus_provider` / `split_visible_provider` / `split_nav_intercept`), `None` by default, that an optional feature registers to extend a core resolver without the core importing the feature. The seam that keeps Split View one-line removable. |
